Dark Souls is an excellent game with challenging, yet rewarding gameplay, and excellent level and enemy design. The combat is tight and responsive, and while the game will not hesitate to punish the player for mistimed dodges or incorrectly aimed attacks, it also is quite rewarding and fair. The world is large and intricate, but not so large that it's difficult to make your way around.
However, Dark Souls is not like many modern games, which give you nice objective markers or a huge, flashing arrow to help you find your way. You will have to explore on your own.
In terms of story, Dark Souls is somewhat unique in that you will only be exposed to as much story as you want to be. You can go through the entire game understanding little other than that everything wishes to kill you, or you can dig and begin to uncover the intricate lore of the land. The game also to this day has active cooperative and player-vs-player online play, allowing you to play with or against other players.
It is important to note, however, that the port for Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition is not the best. There are several mods aiming to remedy this, including Durante's DSFix, enabling the game to render in full HD and enabling texture replacement, eur0pa's Dark Souls PvP Watchdog, which helps combat cheating and displays some useful statistics for online play, and Wulf2k's Dark Souls Connectivity Mod, which augments the slow and inconsistent Steam matchmaking for the game with DSCM-Net, which also allows for manual connections to your friends, and shows some details about other players in your online pool. Furthermore, the keyboard and mouse controls for the game aren't the best, so it is highly recommended that you play with a controller.
Other than these pitfalls, Dark Souls is an excellent game and I recommend it to anyone looking for a challenge.

First up it is the only survival game I have played so far. I am not for trying out games and wasting time, so I read and watched a couple of previews ahead before making my decision to buy miscreated. And so far its by far the best 19.90€ I have spent in a long time....
I have played more than 500 hours.... I have never played any other game to such an extend. most games get boring after 20 hours, and only a handful keep me interested for more than 50 hours.
This game has most of the aspects you look for in a survival game (hunting, setting up camp or buidling a base, getting vehicles ready, surviving the pitch dark night...) and as the info from the Developers goes more survival aspects will be implemented (nuclear storms, blizzards.....).
Of course it is in Early Access (like most survival games) and there are many bugs, but once you find those bugs, report them, the developers are on it and try to send hotfixes and patches asap. This can not be said for other early access games I have played.
So let's come to an end.
PROS:
- going more and more in the direction of survival rather than FPS
- The Love to the detail (spray paintings with stories/jokes, world design, crafting options....) is unmatched in MY opinion
- great, outstanding graphics
- great sound
- great community and developers that are actively bringing the game forward
CONS:
- Bugs due to early access
- very demanding on pc (especially if you use an AMD card like me)
I hope this review helps anyone that is looking for a survival game

Edit:
The review was kinda blunt so I'll clear it up a little. I did not mean to call it a clone of those two games, I just meant that I played them a lot so I know how this works etc. So for people who play games like those two you would probably be good at this game. Since a dev responded, I'll add some pros about the game.
Pros:
- Ai is not too bad
- Lots of different guns you can find and pick up
Cons:
- Enemies get repetitive
- Bosses are a simple concept (atleast the first two), all you have to do to win is run around in circles to win
- Not much map variety
- If your good at the bullet hell games you'le be good at this most likely. (Needs a difficulty revamp)
Edit number 2:
The devs took up to my suggestion about making the game harder, and well. they did, but it might actually be TOO hard. Whats the point of having 10 hp when you die in 3 hits? I know I said make it harder, but I didn't neccecarily mean buff up the enemies. I know a game, where a free update came out MONTHS after the game got completed, all it did was make enemies harder, and you had to get achievements for beating it again. People REALLY didn't like what they did, they buffed up some enemies, they essentially turned them into sponges and they were too hard to dodge. (Binding of Isaac if you havn't caught on yet). Now, I'm not saying make the game like the other ones, infact maybe you shouldn't. There are too many similar games with similar concepts.
Well, long story short, you die too fast now. HOWEVER you could, instead of changing it the way back to where it was originally, you could add some twists to the game, that would make you require more skill and still be hard if you didn't have the required skill.
For example, in Enter the Gungeon you had a dodge roll which lets you get away from bullets to not get hit, but its only for a fraction of a second, and you could still roll into bullets. DON'T COPY THIS IDEA!!! Instead make your own. In the Binding of Isaac you get item rooms which buff you up as you go, and you need to be able to get hit to even win that game. Looking back this review in Enter the Gungeon you can get upgrades as well, just less, because you already have the etremely op dodge roll.
If the devs manage to top this off I think I would be satisfied, and I would give this game a good thumbs up. I personally believe they can as they are working very hard from the "Massive" amount of updates that are coming out. (I'm not sorry for that pun).
One last thing, I notice some screens and buttons were less buggy, which is great. It says the devs are doing fine. Just remember that one thing comes above the concept of the game, the gameplay, etc, and it is the playability. If it's buggy how will we play the game? Just make sure you work out any gamebreaking bugs if you come across them, but I'm sure you already do that lol.

I found this game to have a lot of interesting ideas, but it didn't take full advantage of its potential. Dr. Mario with combat elements sounds good on paper, especially since Arkanoid did a similar thing to the Breakout formula, but there are several issues with Dungeon of Elements. For example, while there are many normal enemy types, they only differ in terms of appearance and potential loot; they never move, they never interact with the alchemy pills nor the board, and they all die in a single hit. Boss fights likewise tend to simply devolve into tedium as their abilities are usually defensive in nature, such as teleportation, invincibility shields, and/or some form of regeneration; the few bosses which actually pose a threat by creating and moving units are all fairly early in the game.
Obstacles on the screen are another element of this game which sounds good on paper, but in execution they are sometimes hard to see and at other times (sometimes deliberately) they hide enemies; this isn't so much a challenge as it is a struggle with the aesthetics. Pits which pills can fall into are another interesting idea, but they are rarely anything but beneficial and this leads to one of the bigger overarching issues at play here; the player is given a ridiculously huge advantage from many of the unique aspects of this game. Weapons have fairly length cooldown times, but can devastate a substantial number of enemies in a single hit, even the earliest boots in the game slow down pill drop speeds substantially and shields temporarily slow it down even more (though I never once needed to use my shield until the very final set of stages when playing on Normal and Hard is only unlocked upon completion of the entire game), and crafted consumables range anywhere from large explosions to a pill which will outright kill every single non-boss enemy on the screen.
There's plenty of content here for anyone who *really* likes the Dr. Mario formula and there are many interesting mechanics present, but Dungeon of Elements fails to take full advantage of its systems and ultimately comes across as being a case of quantity over quality and simply ends up feeling repetitive.

I understand the learning curve for this game (and most other fighting games) is ASTRONOMICALLY high. I understand I haven't played this game very much. I just don't...feel the game, though. I love Street Fighter but this one didn't click with me. I'll list my pros and cons below.
PROS:
+ Amazing roster (Edit: ?)
+ Controller variety
+ Ultra Combos are very stunning
+ The re-inclusion of EX moves is great
+ Four bars of meter is awesome
+ Focus attacks are a nice inclusion
Ehs:
= Art Style is very okay
= Stun combos are boring
= Some input lag occasionally online (guess I have to expect that though)
= Awkward game speed (Somewhere between Super Turbo and Third Strike)
= Many inputs to learn, some are very obnoxious to pull off (*cough cough* 720 *cough cough*) (EDIT: See extra cons)
= Ultra combos sometimes do the same amount of damage as eachother, and some have very similar hitboxes
CONS:
- Voice acting...it's not awful but...I don't know... (EDIT: Nope it's awful. Elena and Makoto are probably the worst...too bad they're some of the best characters.)
- Yun is still top tier
- Three joke characters? Really, Capcom? Dan was cool but Rufus and El Fuerte were really unnecessary.
- The roster is very breadth-like. It's very preferential when it comes to breadth over depth but Super Turbo and Third Strike had small, deep casts, and Smash 4's roster is pretty deep for its size (bar the clones...Dark Pit :steamfacepalm:, while Melee's roster and Top 8 are very deep (just like ST + 3S)
- This is pretty subjective but no Alex and Urien? :(
- The music didn't really click with me (EDIT: See extra cons)
- Training Stage...God, I'm so sick of it. Could we at least have some different, still backgrounds instead of the generic white with red-x in the middle?
- Dashes cover much less distance than in 3S
Overall I don't recommend this not because it's bad, but because it's not as good as SFII and SFIII in my eyes.
EDIT: I have honestly even more problems with this game, so many that I actually permanently removed it from my account:
- Dashes are slow (in general)
- Cammy + Robot + New Super = Decapre
- I have listened to more of the music and...God, they botched everything, especially Beats in My Head
- I know this game is a rehash of a pretty old game, but come on...it looks pretty bad. This isn't that big of a complaint though.
- 720 motion is practically impossible in this game (coming from a low-skilled person)
- So you have all the Street Fighter II characters but not even half of the new ones from Street Fighter III? *sigh*...
- Character intros are long and boring. Special intros in SFIII were quick and sweet.
- I don't have a problem with Hugo, but why did they pick him instead of Alex? Furthermore, why did they waste a spot with Decapre instead of adding Alex?
- Some sound effects are seriously distracting, e.g. Dhalsim's dash
- Models look clunky and feel clunky. This might be more personal.
Overall, I strongly dislike this game now. There is such a drastic quality difference between SFII and SFIII versus SFIV I can't honestly believe it's from the same company.
SFIII >= SFII >>> SFIV

State of Decay is a game with a lot of depth to characters and an interesting take on surviving an apocalypse for the "Long-Term". In my eyes it is a game where the goals were about building a strong, large community to rebuild civilization. Most zombie games I have played focused on escaping a threat or surviving relatively short terms of time without safety. State of Decay answers some of the questions of what might happen
.
The tutorial gets you through a typical zombie panic scenario so it can focus on the main aspects of the game. The game really places focus on settling down in a base and holding your ground which is somewhat conflicting with the large map. You will quickly find strength in numbers by teaming up with a community of survivors. The character you play as cannot protect themselves alone and you'll need to take shifts with other characters so that they can heal or sleep. With the community caring for each other you are able to thrive in the apocalypse by maintaining a good base. A good base is maintained and upgraded with obvious essentials like food, fuel, ammo, medicine, and building materials. You can get these essentials by scavenging or trading. By making a strong and safe community you'll gain attention from competing communities and even the military. The military has more power and resources than anyone so gaining their attention and trust allows you to escape and ends the game's story.
I felt like this game had an unclear focus for player objectives. State of Decay places a lot of focus on both exploring a huge map and settling down in a single, small base. I will say that the map for this game is absolutely huge and I was initially very impressed with how much content it had. However, exploration is encouraged but it doesn't really provide any unique incentive to do so.
You could complete the entire game by staying in one base. The benefits from moving to a different base are not very noticeable and the places you can set a base at are very limited (I think 6 or so places). Getting the largest base possible is important to have more people and facilities but the benefits for having a large base is too small. Having a different base might let you have 13 people instead of 10 but having more than 8 people is probably more than enough to easily survive. Some bases allow more facilities but it doesn't really matter as long as you have a few basic ones. Packing up your base and moving is pretty much only dependant on finding a base that can hold as much people as possible and what scenery you like to look at.
There are no areas that offer unique resources. Living in one area is pretty much just as resourceful as living anywhere else. There is no reason to go somewhere far to get something valuable making less of a reason to explore the huge map.
Materials for scavenging are seemingly infinite. I thrived way too easily, I had too much food and medication than I could ever need just by staying around my base. You might scavenge the area around you dry but I never reached that point. Additionally resources are randomly generated so that might be impossible.
At the same time the game places focus on being story driven and infinite playability. Perhaps the only part of the game that actually encourages you to explore unvisited locations is the story. However the story is extremely short and will only show you a tiny percentage of the entire map. The story will easily skip large chunks of the map which shows how useless it was to actually make the map as large as it is. The impact of the story with the rest of the game world is minimal because it struggles with trying to be infinite with filler content.
The events of the story don't matter to the world. The game uses cutscenes sometimes but doesn't give them any cinematic impact. The supposed ending of the game felt as important as tying my shoe. The lack of music made story events all the less unique from the rest of the game. It was very clear that none of the story mattered after the intro which is insanely deceiving when the first moments of the game are very heavy on letting the story drive the player. After that first tutorial "chapter" it quickly feels like nothing matters.
The infinite playability is advertised because of the endless respawning of 10 kinds of very simple missions. It actually felt like the game placed less emphasis on the story as an excuse to say the story doesn't matter and you are meant to endlessly play the game. State of Decay says it's dynamic by randomly generating things like events, missions, resources, and characters which would be interesting if the randomizations had more variables. The random things in this game are basic templates. You will quickly find a character who has the same voice actor as someone standing right next to you. Most characters will literally say the exact same script as someone else. Every random mission plays out the same way. A rescue mission is always a "rescue" mission and nothing unique ever changes with a mission besides the location and people involved. These missions don't even really get harder as you progress through the game. In the end, the "Dynamic" events become annoying, unoriginal filler content way too fast.
I mean you can pay extra to get the DLC which adds a gradual increase in difficulty and more variety but these seem like things that should have been in the game anyways. DLC shouldn't charge to fix a game's flaws or even worse, intentionally reduce a game's core aspects for a quick buck.

State of Decay relies on you controlling multiple characters, swapping out the opportunity for the player to form a one-on-one bond with a character for an omniscient sim-lite perspective wherein the player finds outposts, scavenges food, builds storage and sleeping places, and so on.
You don't play as a survivor, you play as a survivor community.
This has its advantages and disadvantages. The main advantage is that in turning the actual zombie fighting into just a small part of what you're expected to do, it's easy to look past how repetitive, dull, and ugly this activity is. State of Decay was made on a small budget and the developers had the foresight to implement creative workarounds to make this less of a turn off.
The most obvious disadvantage right from the start is that this lack of player empathy makes the game difficult to invest in emotionally. If your starting character gets killed off, you're stuck with a bunch of strangers and it's hugely alienating. If they don't, it's jarring having to switch and watch them walk around the base on their own. This wouldn't be a problem if you really did get full control of the survivor community, but you're only allowed to influence a few sim-like things about it. There's no managing which characters do what and when. You can't send some off to scavenge and some to build. You notice things change around the place but you're only ever given the third-person perspective. You're perpetually on the outside and this is weirdly depressing.
In aiming to bring both third person action and sim elements to the player, it only just hits both targets. I appreciate what the developers were trying to do, particularly on a low budget (this really is a wonderful era for gaming where too much money spoils the thing), but without being either emotionally or intellectually invested in the game it's a difficult one to play for more than a few hours all up.
It goes without saying that a multiplayer dimension would really have helped the game out- making tough decisions about where resource goes would have been further complicated by another human intelligence, and as Left 4 Dead proved, shooting scary things with friends is always good, frustrating, emotionally exhausting fun.
Do you like sandbox games, zombie games or surival games? If you answered yes to at least two of those, buy this game.

Dark Souls is an excellent game with challenging, yet rewarding gameplay, and excellent level and enemy design. The combat is tight and responsive, and while the game will not hesitate to punish the player for mistimed dodges or incorrectly aimed attacks, it also is quite rewarding and fair. The world is large and intricate, but not so large that it's difficult to make your way around.
However, Dark Souls is not like many modern games, which give you nice objective markers or a huge, flashing arrow to help you find your way. You will have to explore on your own.
In terms of story, Dark Souls is somewhat unique in that you will only be exposed to as much story as you want to be. You can go through the entire game understanding little other than that everything wishes to kill you, or you can dig and begin to uncover the intricate lore of the land. The game also to this day has active cooperative and player-vs-player online play, allowing you to play with or against other players.
It is important to note, however, that the port for Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition is not the best. There are several mods aiming to remedy this, including Durante's DSFix, enabling the game to render in full HD and enabling texture replacement, eur0pa's Dark Souls PvP Watchdog, which helps combat cheating and displays some useful statistics for online play, and Wulf2k's Dark Souls Connectivity Mod, which augments the slow and inconsistent Steam matchmaking for the game with DSCM-Net, which also allows for manual connections to your friends, and shows some details about other players in your online pool. Furthermore, the keyboard and mouse controls for the game aren't the best, so it is highly recommended that you play with a controller.
Other than these pitfalls, Dark Souls is an excellent game and I recommend it to anyone looking for a challenge.

This is my first and only experience with the Ace Combat series.  Many reviewers here who are fans of the series often argue that the changes made to the gameplay have deprived the game of any sense of challenge and thus made the experience extremely boring.  I'm inclined to agree with that statement.  The real perpetrator in regard to dumbing down the gameplay is the new "Dogfight mode."  Whenever you get close enough to an enemy fighter, you can trigger a mode where the camera zooms in on your opponent and the game glues your jet to his rear.  At this point, the game practically plays itself for you.  In Dogfight mode, staying behind your opponent requires pretty much no skill at all.  Your fighter is basically placed on a set of rails in DF mode, and there's really no sense of accomplishment when you do take down your foe, because, as said before, there's practically no skill involved.   This might not be so bad, if the campaign did not force you to make use of this mode at certain points.
On that subject, the campaign itself is equally bland.  Most of the time you will be  in your fighter engaging in the rather dull air-to-air combat, broken periodically by the chance to fly an attack helicopter or control the targeting computer of an AC gunship or some other gimic.  To the game's credit, I enjoyed some of these set pieces.  Manning the door gun of a helicopter was good fun, and I thoroughly enjoyed the AC gunship section of the game.  Basically, any part of the game that wasn't marred by the flawed movement and dogfighting was pretty enjoyable.  Unfortunately, air-to-air dogfighting comprises the vast majority of the game.  Periodically, you will be required to line up your aircraft to do strafing runs against ground targets, but the joy that could have been had with that is also ruined due to the mandatory use of a "ground attack mode" that places your jet on a set of rails, again depriving every last iota of challenge or fun.  The one enjoyable aspect that applies to all parts of the campaign is that periodically when you destroy an enemy, the camera will zoom in on your kill, showing off the ensuing fire, explosions and wreckage in all its destructive glory.  These bits were always pretty impressive to watch.  The story is pretty uninspired; something to do with a civil war in Russia and some ultranationalist group.  It's completely forgetable.
On a final note, if you are interested in giving this game a shot, I strongly recommend that you use a controller, as this game does not suit itself well to a mouse.  While AC: AH offers some terrific visuals, the game is held back by some terrible gameplay mechanics, and at the end of the day, a polished turd is still just a turd.

BARELY / WEAKLY RECOMMEND - 51% (Game feels UNFINISHED, Read Below)
In the past, I have played a few great Aldorlea games, so I bought this game on steam on the day it was release. I have played about 40 hours and decide to write a review. This is a relatively weak Aldorlea game, and is actually at the borderline of recommend / not recommend. If I can give percentages in steam, I will give it 51%, but I put recommend in this game.
Let me explain some of the good and bad things about this game in detail.
The GOOD aspects:
1. As with many of the Aldorlea games, the gameworld is beautifully designed and the dev paid lots of attention to minor details to make the game asthetically pleasing. The towns and dungeons are all exquisitely crafted.
2. I like the portraits too.They are well done, and make the game interesting to see new portraits instead of custom ones.
3. I like the different character classes, which make the game interesting. Initially I thought that the fat minster is useless, but it was only much later that I found out how useful he is. He can cast some mass spells to inflict slow and idiot to all monsters and bosses that CANNOT be resisted. Wow, that is useful.
The POOR aspect.
1. The storyline is weak and almost non existent. At the start, you pick 4 out of 8 team members, and then have to go through 9 disjointed dungeons fighting lots and lots of monster to rescue a princess. After a while, it get routine and boring, with just too many uninspired fights. You do not get the pleasure of meeting and recuiting more party members as the story advance (oops, what story?)
2. They have a quest button that is greyed out throughout the ENTIRE game, and I was initially wondering why. Well, there are NO sidequests of any kind in this game. There is no main quest, but implicitly it is just : Finish Dungeon 1, Finish Dungeon 2, Finish Dungeon 3, Finish Dungeon 4, Finish Dungeon 5, Finish Dungeon 6, Finish Dungeon 7, Finish Dungeon 8, Finish Dungeon 9, Finish Final Dungeon to free princess. End.
3. The game is ridiculously unbalanced. There are 9 different mode in terms of difficulty, with the easiest mode being the Story Mode, which is suppose to be a no-brainer. I wanted to do a quick run and tried the no-brainer story mode. Here is what I experienced:
Most of the fights are indeed no brainer, and you can kill all the enemies with 1 shot. However, at later dungeons, some enemy casters can also 1-shot my team, and wipe me out. That is so ridiculous. I am not talking about a speed run. I am a completionist that love grinding, and grind my team until they are at level 50+. I equiped them with all the best armor and weapons in the game, and even have 2 LEGENDARY weapons (one for becoming arena champions for finishing all the fights, and another for killing some very high level boss). My team have ridiculously large amount of HP and my tank, for example has 700+ HP due to excessive grinding. Now when I entered one of the later dungeon called Secular Tumulous, some monsters there can just 1-shot my tank and wipe out my entire team that is armed to the teeth with all the best gears in the game. I am not talking about the final game boss. I am talking about just being wipe out my some random monsters while I am playing in Story Mode!!! That is really really bad game balance, and a big shame on an Aldorlea game. I wonder how much testing has been done.
4. The game itself feels UNFINISHED. The fact that they left a greyed out QUEST button during the entire game makes me feel that they wanted to add something but did not have time. It feels like a rushed release of an Aldorlea game, which seldom happen in the past. Indeed the quality of Aldorlea games have been dropping.
I am not sure I will finish this game or not, but I am taking break from this game for now.
Like I say, I will give this game a score of 51%, but will still put recommend, although it is a weak recommend.

The gameplay is wonderful. It's simple, classic Doctor Mario. Enjoyable RPG elements allow you to craft and find new items that provide play affects like dispatching enemies stuck in corners, or slowing the fall rate of your pills. Terrain details provide a nice twist that brings the play-area to life.
The sound design is abominable. The music is genuinely obnoxious and distractingly bad, while the sound effects are wispy swooshes that don't connect with the action, at all.
Menu animations are pointlessly long, reminding me of Puzzle Chronicles, where half the game is spent waiting for the game to start. There should have been an option to skip these animations.
It's rare that sound design works against a game. I can't remember ever responding so negatively to the way a game sounds, but it's distracting at its best, and flat-out aggravating at its worst. If you turn down the sound effects, turn the music off, and think about what you're doing with your life during the animations, it's a wonderful game. If you try to listen to it? You'll probably go mad.

I'd guess the multitude of negative reviews this game has are connected mostly to the controls. For PC they are abysmal, no doubt. Even after remapping to WASD for movement, the camera shifts and turns so much and at the weirdest points, that you lose reference constantly. You waste a lot of time bumping into things or taking steps to avoid doing so, even when you were moving correctly before the camera turned.
That's not so bad, isn't it? After all, this is an adventure game, you can take your time, adjust your position and do what you intended to do in the first place. Right? Well... not so much. For an adventure game there is a huge amount of timed scenes, stealth-based situations and failure points that result in the characters death. When you die, the scene replays often from a much previous point, sometimes forcing you to watch a whole cutscene all over again. The frustration keeps piling up timed event after timed event. I had often found that the savegame I'd just made before attempting a timed scene just "didn't take" and I was forced to replay a difficult part from a previous point I'd done already.
I didn't mind much the many crates pushing puzzles, or the climbing onto rocks, scaffoldings, etc. (Tomb Raider style), but yeah, it does present a significant amount of those too. They are okay, unless you're again pressed for time and struggling with the controls.
I found myself enduring most of the game, only to reach a part with dialogs, which (it must be said) are great. I love the characters, the voice acting and the writing itself, but unfortunately that's not enough. A game should be enjoyed, not endured, so, sadly, after more than half a playthrough, I uninstalled the game and will be watching a video walkthrough somewhere to know the rest of the story. Such a shame...

What can I say about this game that will do it justice? Short answer. Buy. This. Game.
Luftrausers is a 2D, bullet hell, combo based dogfighting game which sees you playing as what is essentially a Nazi fighter pilot in not-so-WW2. You customise your "Rauser" with tonns of different parts that have their powers and weaknesses, like an engine that lets you fly underwater, but will receive more damage if you fly too high, or a body that explodes like a nuclear bomb when you die, allowing you to do a last ditch Kamikaze into one of the many enemies wanting to ruin your day. You can customise your weapon system, your body, and your engine. Depending on which parts you pick will affect the soundtrack in drastic ways.
Overall, this game is an absolute gem. Any PC can run it, it has a load of replayability, an amazing soundtrack, slick retro visuals and at a fiver, its a bargain. Pick it up and get Rausing.

Trick & Treat Review - Raymond KT
Summary: A young witch named Charlotte and her maid Amelia went trick or treating on the Halloween Eve, and somehow they decided to visit a cursed mansion.
Before Amelia could figure out anything, she was on her own in this huge, ominous house. Dance with the ghosts, play with the dolls, and hopefully, she can uncover the dark past of the house and see Miss Charlotte again.
You'll play as Amelia the Pumpkin Maid. It's about exploring and solving puzzles in a spooky atmosphere. There will be some horror elements, romance, many deaths (bad ends) and a happy ending of true love.
We play most of the story as Amelia as we go from room to room solving basic puzzles, item puzzles and possibly dying. I can't say that death comes harshly at any point because all the puzzles are relatively easy. What killed me most often was just checking objects which I knew better than to check (like standing on the gallows) but I'd just saved a moment prior and figured meh, why not. The only puzzle with any real difficulty (assigning the dolls) has no game over element. Not that death is a bad thing here. There are several Dead Ends to collect, featuring a short scene, a death title, and a basic CG.
Trick and Treat also has a robust amount of replay value. With multiple endings, unlockables in the bonus room, a cute extra costume for Amelia, some additional dialogue and a slot machine-esque minigame you're not likely to stop after just one go. If I were to wish for anything it'd be a new room and puzzle or two when going for True End on a clear save (I saw a room that I could never get into so maybe I just missed it). I also wish you could see a textless version of the bonus art since it looked fantastic. Even better than what's in the rest of the game. Of course going through the game a second time you blast right through it with no hang-ups.

TL;DR: The game is amazing from a design/story point of view, negatively impacted from bad controls and challenging but not as hard as people say after rage quiting the first boss or two.
Lots of reviews out there either absolutely love or hate the Souls series and I would say the differentiating factor is breaking through the wall of really getting into the game. The game is all about feelings of accomplishment while being challenging enough to make the accomplishment seem meaningful. The challenges are also far more fair than most people expect because most enemies follow the same rules you are constrained with during combat.
The ever present "get good" advice does apply but the game is all about perservering to the point it is an intended story element in the game. The game is definitely impacted by rather clunky controls and sometimes bad collision detection but you shouldn't be playing this game because of the elegent fighting system. This game is probably one of my favorites because of all the careful design decisions that went into what seems like almost every aspect of the game.
I would recommend this game to any "serious" gamer who enjoys a challenge. However, if you don't care about game design, lore or story then I would have a harder time recommending the game because all that is left is the feelings of accomplishment. I have played through this game more times than any other game for a reason and still seem to find new things about it I didn't know the previous time through. If you're having trouble getting into it, look up lore explanation videos to get you to be more invested in the world and understand why I'd call it a work of art.

I have to run this game off my laptop in order for it to recognize the controller. I won't recommend this game on pc. DSfix doesn't fix the controller issues. You essentially have to unplug and disable all usb devices for it to recognize a controller. If you're going to play this game, that's all you will be doing with your computer. This game has incredible level design. I can see why it's considered a classic, so it is worth trying on another system, or if you absolutely know it will work on your pc with a controller. There are however issues that are swept under the rug by the community that when brought up cause a cult like attack on forums. The two biggest issues in this game when it works on pc are the camera and the hit boxes. Both are incredibly finicky and difficult to predict or understand. This leads to bosses cornering and stun locking you, enemies attacking through walls when your weapons can't, massive bosses in tight spaces causing the camera to spin if you lock on. This accounts for a lot of my frustration. When those things work this game is incredibly satisfying. It's like a fantasy tactical shooter. You have to check corners and memorize layouts, use shortcuts to get the jump on enemies. It's so close to being an incredible fantasy rpg, but these issues crop up a lot and really dampen the experience. The real shame is that the community jumps on anyone who criticizes these issues and so they remain prevalent in the future games too. When the combat is difficult but fair, the combat system is some of the best the fantasy rpg genre has to offer, but too often technical issues crop up and lead to unavoidable deaths. Git Gud does nothing to fix these issues or grow and improve the franchise.
I'm an avid player of the monster hunter series and the witcher as well. Those two games have the best melee combat design in fantasy rpgs. They require commitment to your swings and strategic positioning. I thought dark souls was heading in that direction but after fighting the silver knights and giant guardians in anor londo I found what makes the combat system so difficult. The rules for combat change from enemy to enemy and move to move. Sword silver knights swing leaving themselves open to attack, but the giants and spearmen passively block with their shield. It's a complete guess as to whether enemies are open to attack or not. Also enemies will spam attacks. Couple that with a broken camera, changing rules, uneven hitboxes and loads of clipping problems and you get a difficult game, yes. Strategic and fair, absolutely not. There is no strategy to this game. Good positioning still gets you hit by the tail end of the spear while it thrusts away from you. Either you perfect the parry and backstab and deal with every enemy that way, or take a gamble on enemy moves and the rules that will apply to the one they are winding up for. Enemy size doesn't matter, they can turn on a dime and skate around 180 degrees mid attack to hit you. Made it around their back successfully, too bad, you still take damage. Enemies can block and attack at the same time as well as queue up new attacks immediately after finishing old ones. The player has their inputs queued up as well so you can press attack, but if the boss hits you first you will get hit again and again only to stand up 10 seconds later and swing, depleting your stamina bar allowing you to be stun locked again. In monster hunter the combat is like a dance. You read the enemy wind up and then respond. It has slow animations, but the rules remain the same for every monster and every player. In the witcher you aggro enemies into moves and then dodge and attack or parry, predicting their next move. The combat system in this game is close but there are so many minor oversights that break the combat flow. The rules are so inconsistent and the risk reward system allows for losing hours of progress when you weren't taking very big risks. That is why this game is frustrating and I don't think it needs that to be as challenging or rewarding as it claims to be. Add to this a huge drop in level design quality towards the later game and it just becomes a boring slog. I'm at the point where I don't feel like I'm learning anything when I die, I'm just backtracking and farming the same enemies over and over again until one of these problems crops up, then I get to do it all over again. I guess I've lost the motivation to play this anymore. The reward of progression and satisfaction of overcoming increasingly difficult enemies is gone. It's just a slog now, and every death feels like a waste of my time. It's really rewarding discovering the map and shortcuts but aside from that I can't find a reason to recommend this game. I like it because I've played for forty hours, but it's not the greatest game of the past decade, and the pc version is certainly not worth $20 for all the work you have to put in just to get the game to function.

The idea is an interesting one to marry an open world RPG system with zombies.  However the problem sets in very quickly with this game...repetition.  You will find yourself playing the same side missions over and over and over.  Do you have a choice to not do these?  Absolutely.  Will you suffer because of it?  Absolutely.  Imagine having three missions across the map and each one is a member of your community needing help in some way or another.  If you don't help them they end up upset with you.  If they are upset with you it brings down the morale of the entire community.  This is just one domino after another.  So you may be driving across the map and have a radio call come in to ask you to deal with something and someone.  In order to keep your harmonious community running you feel completely forced to drop everything and deal with it.  The "RPG" element of this game is fleshed out by having a set of skills level up to level 7.  These level up so quickly that you lose the RPG element very rapidly.  There is almost no character development so you will not find an RPG element there.  All in all it is a decent idea, but unless you want to do the same side missions all night long, I suggest moving along.

To say at the very least, this is a extremely fun game. It has a lot of great ideas and it executes most of them well. The graphics also look very nice and the world is diverse and constantly spawning missions to keep you busy (which can be tedious but most aren't very long). Ammo and fuel are the most scarce and the combat can be tricky. And, while none of the characters are anything more than a blank slate that constantly acts like a snooty jerk, when they die, they're gone for good, so you want to keep them alive because you never know when you will need to utilize your whole tema for something.
However, the game has a lot of glaring issues, the first being the AI. Your team is consisted of idiots who do nothing but find ways to make your life harder. They'll go on scavange runs, then proceed to run into the wall until a horde runs up to them and tear them apart. They'll get stuck on anything if they get anywhere near it and standstill, confused as to how they could possibly walk around this intimidating corner of a house that they have already cleared. Yes, most the time the AI is servicable, but when it matters most expect them to get someone killed eventually.
Then theres the other major issue with the game: the story. Moreso the progression of said story. The first time I played this game, everything when smoothly with no hitches, about 14 hours into the game, however, I was on my way to return a quest back to an NPC and they were killed by a zombie horde. While I appreciate the realism of the game, this particular NPC was covered on all sides by several people and decided, "WELL HEY! That fat zombie over there looks lonely, I'm going to go hug him." Then she died. Because the AI decided that was the best choice for her.
However, yesterday, I decided to give this game a second chance. Here's the results. I was playing the game in parallel with my friend, the did the same quests at the same time with me a little ahead of him. After completing the same quest however, his story line continued, while mine halted to a complete stop. And while this would be ok. I did every other mission I could possibly do and when it came to the famous Ray Santos mission, I could not complete it because the map gave me no indication of where to go. So when I went to look up the mission online and saw where I was supposed to drive to, nothing happened. Being stuck in a complete dead end without the ability to at least expand to a larger home on my second playthrough has lead me to believe that, while this game does a lot right, State of Decay is broken in all the wrong places.
Oh yeah, and imagine a zombie horde attacking your home base, except that they're all stuck in the floor and can't be killed by melee weapons. Get ready to waste your ammo.

Long Live The Queen was a surprise for me. I didn't expect to enjoy it but in the end, I had a lot of genuine fun playing.
The main mechanics in the game use moods to learn different school subjects. You pick two classes each week to take, each class raises your skill in the subject your picked. The events which you run into throughout the game (you get one event each week) are all virtually the same, but the outcome of each event depends on how you react and what classes you have been taking.
There are no fancy visual effects of musical scores apart from the over played British national anthem, the character designs are very pretty, even if they are a little cringey at times for a young girl to be wearing those outfits (anime eh). There is plenty of replayability in Long Live The Queen, I have done a number of different scenarios and runs and I have put almost seven hours into it, each time ending differently.
I would totally recommend this game to anyone, even if you aren't a fan of anime (like me); the price is £6, 99 which for a game like this, is worth it. If you get it on sale, you have yourself a bargain.

For those that like a story, they have included one of those as well, with progressively unlocked chapters as you beat each segment.
So, if you're in the mood for playing a classic puzzle game, with RPG elements, crafting, monsters, a great soundtrack and 3d model art, go ahead and give Dungeon of Elements a try.

I'll be up front. If you're not into games like Dr. Mario, this game is probably not for you, as that's primarily what the gameplay is in Dungeon of Elements. The gameplay is primarily based around you throwing capsules into a room and trying to match 4 of one color, Puyo Puyo style, to remove all of the enemies in said room. If the smoke from the capsules starts pouring out the door, you're forced to retreat and have to start again. Outside of combat, you can take some of the loot you've found and mix it into a cauldron to produce improved equipment for your character as well as emergency use items that can help bail you out of a tough spot, or you can sell it for money.
The difficulty for this game scales relatively well, and the three different difficulty levels affect the starting drop speed for the capsules, boss health, and boss attack speed. Higher levels also start to increase the starting drop speed every now and then, and various obstacles placed within the levels impede your capsule movements, sometimes in downright evil places. But you can also use whatever weapon you have on you to kill off enemies in a small area or bring up your shield to temporarily slow the drop speed greatly (however that works) to help you.
Overall, I'd say this is a game worth at least trying out.

To note, the first game I ever beat on one quarter and one life in the arcade was Contra.  I have enjoyed the Contra series until it moved to Playstation 1 and they started to go off the deep end by confusing collossal and impressive with cartoon comical.  Now, the arcade contra series had a particular nuance in the gun firing control which was interesting and frustrating at the same time.  The NES one- is the one that I believe truly put Contra on the map of every young person who owned the nintendo at that time.  Coop became a 'thing.'  Large bosses became a 'thing.'  Punishing one hit deaths and getting rick rolled by a game became a 'thing.'
Fast forward to this game:
This game has too many human looking eyeballs :P However, overlooking this, it is perfect and I mean perfect in the feel and control of the game to match and duplicate the Nintendo Contra.  Not the later series ones, but the solid NES control and feel.
The game has some of the BEST and imaginative boss fights in a side scrolling shooter I have ever played.  It is worth it to play through the game JUST to get to these fights.  Also be very glad the guns are all auto-fire- especially for the later stages and last bosses.  Unlike many of the Contra games, especially the arcade Super Contra, losing your power ups does not mean you cannot survive the game.  The default gun is great and has a solid ROF.
This game has coop and netplay.  What can I say here, this is excellent.
I will say that some elements of some of the levels are a bit bland and could use some enhancements.  However, you WILL overlook this as you go on further in the game.  Personally, level 3 was the least impressive to me and I WISH it had a lot more environmental terrors in it and that the mid boss played a bit differently.  This is minor though and borders on nitpicking haha
To sum up:
- excellent control, truly an inspired sequel to the first NES Contra titles (Contra and Super C), with some additions to control that make it pro player on every level (ability to fire at angles in a locked standing position for example).
Get this game, support the developers- I would love a sequel :D

This is a fun but somewhat tedious third-person adventure game. Sadly, the fans of the Broken Sword series would have preferred it being a point-and-click adventure.
I got this game as part of the Broken Sword Trilogy package (Broken Sword 1, 2 and 3) and I've been putting up playing this because of the negative reviews and the fact that it looked completely different from the first two games. But I didn't want to go in Broken Sword 5 without at least trying all of the previous games.
It turns out that playing Broken Sword 3 - the Sleeping Dragon can be a good time as long as you know what you are getting into: a third-person adventure game with fixed camera angles from the year 2003 that was obviously made with a controller in mind. You could play this game with a keyboard as well (there's no mouse support) but I strongly recommend grabbing a controller with at least one analogue stick and 8 buttons. The Xbox 360 controller works fine after selecting it in the movement settings and assigning its buttons to the different actions.
I've played the game for 10 hours without any technical issues on a PC running Windows 10 but to be able to play for another hour and thus finish it I had to set the Windows XP SP3 compatibility mode for the executable because in my last playing session the game wouldn't remember the resolution I set. Having to fiddle with compatibility options is acceptable for a game this old.
However having the fixed-camera angles obscure your view while you are trying to figure out one of the environmental puzzles can not be considered acceptable no matter the time of release: the game includes several box-pushing puzzles, which in the later chapters develop into sure sources of frustration because you can't freely look around to see what should go where.
The visuals are okay and you can just look at the screenshots and decide whether you can live with them before purchasing the game. The story is serviceable the VO is good. If you liked the first two games and you can live with the aforementioned problems, you should give this game at least a try.

I'd call myself a fan of the series, but I've only played this one once before (way back when it came out). Now I've tried to play it a second time, I'm remembering the reason it took me this long.
The switch from 2D to 3D was, to put it bluntly, an uninspired decision probably based on trends at the time of release, that adds nothing of importance to the game, and takes a lot away. The visual style set up in the first two games isn't recreated very well here, and half of the series' charm disappeared as a result. The archaic 3D obviously hasn't aged well, and means that every area looks bland, is devoid of detail, and feels empty to explore, which is definitely not a problem with the detailed 2D style of the last two games. The simple point-and-click controls have been replaced by awkward tank controls with fixed cameras, Resident Evil style. All of this just feels... pointless. The series didn't need this. There's no value in this. What were they thinking?
The puzzles in this game are mostly very simplistic compared to the last two, it feels like they really dumbed it down, and there are so. many. crate puzzles. Crate puzzles involve either monotonously pushing crates around, or restacking them into the right positions. You have to do it in almost every single area you visit. It's like they needed to find one thing that wasn't possible in 2D, and then use it over and over again to justify making the game 3D, regardless of how boring that thing is. There are also many more moments where it's possible to die in this game, which you avoid by doing a single-button-press quicktime event that you need almost precognitive reflexes to get right on the first try; and, you guessed it, it's not fun.
On this playthrough, I got half way through the game when I realized I wasn't enjoying myself at all. I won't be finishing it, and I won't be playing this one again. Skip it.

'Massive' is a randomly generated, shoot 'em up, roguelike indie title. In it's current state, it is appealing for short-bursts of play. The gameplay consists of running through randomized levels and blowing away all the enemies, in order to proceed to the next.
It's a very punishing game, in that health, ammo and weapon pickup placement are (presumably) determined as the level is initially generated. This can present a problem during gameplay, as getting bad luck on item placement can very much screw you over mid battle, when you are so reliant upon ammo and health.
Speaking of ammo, if you happen to run out and can't find any ammo or weapons nearby, you are S.O.L, as there is no form of attack should you be so unlucky. This may be intentional by design, but can lead to a very frustrating experience as you get deeper and deeper into your playthrough of the game. If you die, that's it. Game over.
The pixel artwork is fairly well done, and easy on the eyes. The audio could use some more variation, as constant blaring of your weapons firing and various effects going off around you at all times can be a bit distracting.
As far as controls go, I played using a gamepad. They were responsive enough but somewhat confusing. It is a twin-stick shooter, and by default the attack button was set to the right bumper, with dash being set to the trigger. This caused some discomfort while playing, as for the most part you're constantly firing your weapon and having to use both analogs constantly and keeping a finger on the bumper was an awkward position.
The gameplay experience was satisfying, however. And it should be remembered that this game is in early access, and with more polish, depth, and variation to the enemies, objects and environments within it, this could end up being a very fun game to play -- especially with friends.
Note: this game key was provided by the creator for review.

I will start by saying I do not recommend this game if you bore easily, or don't understand that not all games deserve to be played for 5 hours straight.  This game is for those who appreciate exploration, crafting, and survival style games.
**Pros**
Fairly large world
Aggressive sharks and snakes
Building system
Beautiful atmosphere
**Cons**
Slow update progress.  Devs focus on looks rather than functions and new content.
The new Rotating inventory is annoying.  I prefer the old system.  This isnt a console game.
The crafting is limited.  So is loot.  In reality, You would find an abundance of plastic bottles, string, scraps of random materials you could utilize in crafting.  It wouldn't be on every island, but polution is abundant and any documentary on island life shows you how much trash washes up on shore.
Wildlife seems boring.  They have worked on that by adding bats, snakes, boars, etc.  But the Sharks are extremely aggressive, take a while to master killing, and are just an annoyance once you've been playing for a while.
I also think more needs to be done with the rafting system.  A storage box on a raft would make loads more sense to me.  If i'm taking the time to travel to another island, I'm not going to go and bring back only what I can carry.  I would fix my raft up to hold more items to make it worth the trip.  This is something Flame in the Flood understood with their raft system.
**With all of that out of the way, I have owned this game for quite some time.  I realize 40 hours seems low, but for this type of game, with the amount of content, I believe it to be average.  I love this game in short bursts.  I enjoy exploring the islands, killing sharks, and building a shelter.   I think the atmosphere is incredibly beautiful.  The sea forts are a unique change to the typical islands you see.  I do like the ideas the devs post about, but i wish updates felt more worth the wait.  The game has been out for a very long time in early access with very minimal changes, and very little content added.  Some of the content does not feel rewarding.  If i dive deep down to an unexplored wreckage, I would like to find more than 1 piece of cloth, or 1 roll of duct tape.  I realize not every site will be a gold mine, but scrap metal for building, broken storage containers that I can use in my shelter, plastic bottles, rope.  etc, things that don't corrode as quickly under water and would make sense to find would make it more worthwhile to explore and risk shark attacks.  The rafts need improving.  I have all this access to building large shelters, building a larger raft, but the bigger raft serves no purpose other than protecting me from tipping over when a shark is below.  It should serve a better purpose, haul more loot, provide shelter if a storm hits, etc.  These are all things I'm still holding out hope for, which is why i give it a thumbs up.  I do love the potential of this game, and the atmosphere.  I just hope the devs progress more, and maybe a little quicker.

This game does three things I really like in games:
1) A controlled physics sandbox
2) Item synergy and emergent gameplay
3) Multiple layers of depth
Luftrausers is an extension of the flash game Luftrauser, which I played a ton. The first thing you'll notice is the striking visual style; not only is the sepia tone unique but also the way it blends shading and very low resolution rendering to create something that looks like pixels but has the feel and versatility of polygons. There are a ton of bullets on screen at once, defeated enemies blow up into bits, which then make splashes on the water, which by the way shows reflections. It's gorgeous.
I guess the major gameplay mechanic is the jet system, which actually incentivizes not being held down constantly as without it you can turn on a dime. When you combine that with a gravity mechanic you get a really interesting physics sandbox of sorts. The other major mechanic is how you fire and heal; it again incentivizes not holding down a button constantly because you only auto-heal when you're not firing. Altogether these form a bullet hell unlike you've ever played before, with different strategies used for enemies below, above, and amongst you.
What really sells it though is the upgrade system, you get different parts that you can mix and match and are very tangible, with a lot of weight given to their respective properties. This is where it's really emergent, as you can try new possibilities to test how the physics or other elements will respond. Yeah there are bad combos, but that only makes the great ones that much more special. There are even specific challenges curated for each and every part; it feels like a lot of thought went into each one.
Also great is there's a lot of layers to the experience: at the beginning you'll play just to get a hang of manuvering about, and then you'll start trying to take out various enemies, like ships. All the while you'll be ranking up, which you can max out even if you're bad at the game. But then you're going to start unlocking ship parts, and testing each of those out. And then you're going to try to take out a
. And then there are missions to complete, and if you're old-fashioned you can always go for high score. There's a lot of content for such a single faceted game. My one complaint with the game does lie here, however, as I feel the difficulty spike
is a bit much and actually caused me to stop playing a game I would otherwise love to 100%, as there was just too little reward in the last half and probably too much in the first.

I can recommend this game for the obvious reasons but I won't. Everything I was looking for in a zombie-survival game is done right by SoD. The rest however is so screwed up that I'm not able to enjoy this at all..
The complete lack of a tutorial or any usefull explanation whatsoever: you walk out of the base to get some building supplies but there is someome who needs to get recued and also all the food is gone. There is no explanation about the mechanics so there is no way for me to figure out what to do first or last.
How much food do I need? How fast will it run out? What should I do first? Why should I make an outpost? What do I get when I build walls? What penalties are there to dying? What is an infestation and what makes it appear? Why should I bar windows? What are the random outposts with strangers? How does the influence system work.. etc. etc. etc..
This also has to do with the user interface. Which is simply horrible. The interface isn't explained well (an interface that needs an explanation is kind of a problem on it's own). The controls in-game but also in the UI are horrible. It's like playing twister on your keyboard, combine this with a horde of zombies running behind you.. simply frustrating.. Also the gameplay does not feel solid, I never had the idea to be in control of my character. All my input felt more like "suggestions" to my character rather than being in direct control, which turns close-zombie-combat into interpretative dance on acid rather than slick survival horror.
Instead of feeling like battling a never ending stream of zombies I felt more like battling an ever bigger stream of bugs, annoyances, gameplay weirdness and the control scheme.

State of Decay...well I'm coming from a background of more action oriented zombie shooters like the current Resident Evil series and Dead Rising. This game was...different. But in a good way :) I'll try an easy to read run-down of what I thought here...
The Good:
-RPG, RTS, some FPS, and Open World all in one Zombie Survival!
-Really beautiful environmental graphics...once you're used to the style
-Good attempts at realism, felt like I was playing a long episode of the Walking Dead
-Great use of tension: death is permanent and night feels dangerous!
The Bad:
-Not the most intuitive game, fairly steep learning curve, especially for the RPG type elements
-Control scheme doesn't always make sense (but I haven't tried a game controller yet)
-Story is sort of hard to follow, doesn't seem to be a point except "survive/get better weapons/home bases/vehicles" and no clear endgame goals
-A few glitches/bugs that probably should have been worked out/beta tested
The Ugly:
-No real save system...well, not one that an be managed in any way. It auto saves and looks like you can manually save when hitting the Escape (Esc) key. But it's all one game and there are no saved states or games to go back to.
-Sometimes the game goes too far with the realism. For instance, one of my more useful characters just disappeared with no  trace or explanation...I guess that's realistic

-Game sort of has a punishment system for not playing it...? I let the game sit for a few days, launched it back up, and all the parked cars around my base at the time auto exploded. This happened twice. It took time and effort to gather those vehicles and in one instance, gone. Again I
Overall I would recommend giving it a try. State of Decay does pretty well at mixing all the genres up for a unique and fun survival experience. I haven't played in like a month so I'm afraid of what I'll find when I log back in though...I guess that's part of the game's tension and horror elements :)

With multiple different endings, fans of the Princess Maker series and interactive stories will definitely love this game.

I don't play visual novels, but I found myself attracted to the element of fighting off arrows, vengeful duelists, enraged family members, and chocolate for whatever reason. And it was on sale when I purchased it too. So why not.
I also wasn't expecting much fun when I launched this for the first time, so it was surprisingly entertaining. I could not put down my controller until Elodie was crowned queen (after dying, like, 20 times, of course). It's very reminiscent of those "Choose/Pick Your Own Adventure" books, in which all your decisions count (albeit not always significantly).
This game has a variety of paths or endings, giving it a relatively decent replay value.  Loading or saving at certain points is important if you prefer restarting at a familiar situation. You know the drill.
Overall, I really recommend this game to those who want their decisions to actually matter in a game. Also to the bored, like me, who stay up at 1 AM wondering if there's anything new but relatively casual to play.
As for me, I'll be seeing how many more endings I can reach.

All broken Sword games are a treat, and this one is as memorable and enjoyable as the others. Some people whine about keyboard controls and 3D graphics, but it's just whines. As usual, everything is very well thought through, and after a short learning curve you forget about the interface and immerse yourself in the adventure, which is probably the most cinematic of all, and goes completely over the top in the end. Lots of humour, memorable characters, beautiful locations. Highly recommended to any adventure fan.

As an adult, this game is a thoroughly enjoyable 90 minutes or so, more if you decide to replay for the different endings and that final achievement.  I think what really shines, though, is that it fills a niche that's very difficult to fit into--horror game for younger gamers that doesn't feel childish or pandering.  There are a few jumpscares and a generally spooky atmosphere, but, as it describes, in a lighthearted way.  I was easily scared as a kid, and this hearkens back to the days of testing the waters of horror, thrilling but "safe" and fun.  It realls gets the true meaning of Halloween: EVERYONE should be able to have fun.
tl;dr perfect for a slow October evening, even better if you're playing with a tad you love.  And with the price tag, you literally can't go wrong.

Man oh man! Let's talk about wasted potential shall we? Right off the bat I want to say that this game has the most interesting and gripping story. But that's the only thing I can praise this game for, if only they'd kept to the formula…
Now, if you've watched the Godfather trilogy you know there is a noticeable progression line in terms of quality, the Broken Sword trilogy (excluding 4 & 5, obviously) follows the exact same progression, as in, the 1st is really good, the 2nd is an overall improvement over the 1st, and the 3rd is just a disappointment.
Most of it's decisions are just backwards and poorly thought out, which is a shame, because the story is great, it could've been a wonderful movie.
>SPOILERS FOR PREVIOUS GAMES AND 3rd'S INTRO<
Broken Sword 3 starts with Geor ge Stobbart travelling to the Congo to meet a client, he's a patent lawyer now, and has broken up with Nicole for good, but during the flight, the plane crashes terribly because of a sudden storm, luckily for Stobbart, he crashed really close to the place he was supposed to land, but when he got there, he saw his client being questioned and threatened by a mysterious man and his goons, ultimately being murdered by them… After deeper investigation, he heard the scientist's last words, which warned that there might be a deeper conspiracy involving the end of the world and the name of a man, Susarro.
Meanwhile, in Paris, Nicole was supposed to meet a hacker and coder that could've unveiled a conspiracy involving a armageddon and possibly the end of the world (it appears destiny really wants Nicole and George to stay together) but when she got to the man's house, she found him murdered, and after an encounter with the assassin and some deeper investigation, Nicole found out that she could've been framed to seem like she was the killer, soon after she got arrested.
The story is really mysterious and interesting, it also goes much deeper into the lore and what happened to the Neo-Templars, and the ‘magic’ of the world they wanted to control.
The story is great and truly worthwhile, but for all I care, it could've been the Sopranos, but the gameplay still is what's at fault with this game, and part of the reason why I wouldn't recommend it as a game.
If you hadn't noticed, the series goes from a 2D point-and-click adventure to a 3D adventure, and with that brings the reason the gameplay is terrible, you see, most of the puzzles are now reduced to box sliding and climbing. The old intelligent and imaginative puzzles from previous games are reduced to just that, sliding damned boxes and climbing on them. But that's for the better, with such a backwards interface and controls, I wouldn't want to ever open my inventory, the new ‘wheel’ system works against itself, especially when you have to cycle through hundreds of items.
The puzzles are also terribly easy and simple, you can't really do much challenging stuff with just boxes and climbing, you know?
But wait, there's more! The camera and the movement are horrible, tank controls are better, you're never sure if the up arrow will move you up or some other randomized location, and when the camera changes, the controls also change, making you figure out where the arrows will make you go all over again.
Want more? Alright, the dialogue system will make you want to suicide, you can't skip dialogue. That's right, you have to hear what all the characters have to say without skipping, also your character's remarks will get boring really fast, since you know, you can't skip them, so if you missclick on an item you've already inspected, you'll have to hear it all over again. Most of the game will be spent on hearing dialogue.
Moving on, the graphics are okay, they aren't ugly in any way, especially for 2003, but the animations and voice acting will be awkward at times, even cringy, but you can through it just fine, but now, there is something that is bugging me to no end… WHY THE BLOODY ♥♥♥♥ ARE NICOLE'S EYES AND HAIR BLUE??? She's always had dark hair and brown eyes, I mean, I love dyed hair, but I'm confused because of the sudden design decision, she's got daddy issues now or something? (She does, but that's not the point)
The music is OK, but nothing really worth mentioning, it feels kind of recycled from previous games though.
Overall, the game is great in the story and graphical departments, but I found the gameplay unbearable, I do recommend watching this game somewhere, but playing through it is hard, you've really got to love the series to enjoy this one entirely.

This game mixes part zombie horror/survival with some city building and people management.  The game starts with you taking control of a couple guys coming back from a remote fishing trip to find out that the area they are in is now in the middle of a zombie outbreak.  You meet up with other survivors and try to get enough supplies and weapons to survive long enough to..... well I'm not sure to what end cause I'm pretty sure I screwed up somehow and wasn't sure what happened but I got to the end game screen.
I recommend this game because it was fun to play.  I've played it on both Console and PC and both times the game was enjoyable.  That being said there was some design decisions that made sense for the game I guess, but just didn't sit well with me.  Slight SPOILERS ahead I guess.
The game is constantly forcing you to do things, there is never seems to be a break.  There is always someone in trouble getting supplies, or someone missing or someone who wants to take out a zombie infestation.  While you are doing those misssions there are also story missions that are happening and this game doesn't care what else you are doing, if you don't show up for that story mission someone is gonna die and that part of the storyline is gone.  The problem with all these side/main quests happening ALL the time is it doesn't just let you explore the game.  The map is a pretty decent size with some neat areas to find and explore.  The problem is that you don't want to be on the northwest corner of the map when a story mission suddenly pops up on the southeast corner.  Maybe I just failed at seeing the options to tell the people in my little fortification to just sit there and don't leave but it was annoying to have these quests pop up all the time.  Made the game probably a little more of a realistic zombie game but from a guy who likes exploring, the way these  side quests worked just didn't work for me.
I did really enjoy the way the inventory worked in this game, it was really well done.  You can get different sizes of backpack, though you'll pretty well get the biggest size pretty quickly and that is usually enough to get the job done.  You also get the trunk of the vehilce that you're driving (if you use a vehicle to get around).  In addition you can carry one bag of supplies (again the trunk of the vehicle can store multiple bags).  Anything that you find can be stored into the community inventory which gives you influence points (instead of using money), so you can trade things you find for other things in the community inventory(either things that were there originally or things that other survivors have made).  Finishing various side quests or main quests will also give you points to get additional items out of the inventory.  If you get the big bag and use the vehicles trunks/box efficiently you'll have enough points for pretty well anything you'll ever need.
The Zombies were pretty standard zombies, they moved at about the same pace as your characters but could be out run with sprinting, however you can only sprint for a limited amount of time.  There are also several different types of zombies in addition to the average ones ranging from super large/strong to super fast/aggresive and more.  But none of them felt over powering or cheesy in some way.  The fit the game really well.  As well they reacted decently to your actions for the most part.  Driving, sprinting or shooting would all draw in zombies from surrounding areas, pretty standard zombie logic.
You can play as a variety of characters from your base and level each one of them up.  Each character is not exactly unique, they have some individual traits but are pretty interchangable.  The amount of playable characters is decent as each of your characters may become tired/hungry/sick if they've done a lot of exploring or fighting and adds a bit of realisim to the game.  You can either choose to use items to recharge them or switch out characters to let them rest.  Only problem again with this is relating back to the questing point.  One of the characters you use might decide to go off questing while you are playing as another character and then they won't recharge as well.
The one thing I found lacking is that the story is pretty forgetable.  There are some choices in there that will affect your game and the story but for the most part it's pretty standard zombie game.  Survive for a while and then get the heck out of there.
Controls are decent enough, Camera can be a little stupid at times but for the most part never really bothered me.
