Having finished this game, I felt it's time for a proper review, As usual skip to bottom for Pros, cons and small summary
So the story, story is really simple, but often too cheesey and doesn't go into a lot of detail. it disappears from the game at the start after moving and then appears in small, tiny bits and then does a disappearing act constantly till the very end in which only tells how the virus spread, what it originated from and the militaries cover up, not into detail too much which is something good for usual zombie games, but for it comes off as waaaaaaaay to generic and simple.
The gameplay is once again simplistic but fits quite well actually, you have Melee weapons and ranged weapons, plays out like a slower version of Dead Rising but without the huge overuse of odd weapons and tools, it's not ridiculous but has the 3rd person view with slow zombies to either hit or shoot with guns, There's no crafting of weapons, so looting is needed and you will definitely need to often manage your invetory becuase you will fill up really quickly as the largest bag I believe is 10 or 12 slots and how much you can carry with weight is small but that just means you need to either drop everything or head back home.
But that comes to the hardest part of the game, getting around, it's either so slow or just a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ there is no fast travel so have fun driving all the way to the other side of the map to do a fetch mission, tis a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but adds to the realism of it, looting is something different as well since once you clear out a location, it's cleared out for good, don't think about going back for the stuff, infestations are hard because they are huge amounts, stealth is needed to avoid but don't need to, just be careful of your noise, because noise will attract zombies, make enough and they'll come in hordes.
Setting is a pretty generic open world zombie game, not much different from the last really. Same as many George A Romero zombie movies, zombie outbreak happens in rural town, military contains it, military mistake. It's fairly disappointing as to what it could've been and the characters, well the characters just aren't good. They are all really bland and the voice acting is weak
Sound design is pretty decent although definitely not a good soundtrack at all, It's not terrible but it's not great.
Graphics are rather decent but I think it could be better, but coming from a indie xbox title, it's good enough for this game.
Pros
+ Realism make this game playable
+ Gameplay is good enough to playthrough does its job
+ George A Romero inspired for sure
+ Special Infected and certain things make the game harder
+ The loudness design works well because if you alert zombies, or worse off hordes, you will have trouble
+ Does feel like a survival
+ Once characters die, they dead for good
Cons
- Very simplistic story
- Simplistic setting
- Characters are blank robots
- The world is dull
- Missions are repetitve
- World is huge and gets incredibly repetitive to travel around
- Gets repetitive
Overall it's a 7.4/10, it's decent enough to be fun, realism makes it interesting and the overall design mkaes it better, I'd suggest getting this at a low price if you want to waste some time and enjoy some Zombie R&R

Pros:
-Truly a sandbox, beyond some super easy tutorial quests, your really don't have to follow the quest line built into the game if you don't want to.
-The quest line built into the game is a bit rough, but encourages exploration and adds a nice distraction if you get tired of building or fighting. (WARNING: Do not get this game if your mostly into questing, this is not the game for you, it's a game for sandboxers first and foremost.)
-Ancient Vaults allow for 'challenging' end game combat opponents for when planet based creatures become too easy to deal with.
-Pretty fleshed out and engaging crafting system, the cooking/farming system is particularly elaborate.
-Fun artwork, and mildly ammusing NPC chatter. (BOX!)
-Space stations and a variety of world types allow for a variety backgrounds for whatever building project you may want to engage in.
-Newly added Mech system makes the sapce side of the game more exicting, adding more combat/exploration/looting to an alreay fun game.
-Active Developers who release updates quickly after announcing them, and patch roll out bugs almost as fast as they crop up.
Cons:
-The game can suffer from SP lag a bit more than I'd like. I'm not on a monster computer, but it handles BL2 and similar much more resource intense games pretty easily, with little or no SP or even MP Lag. For a 2D sidescroller the SP latency is frankly annoying and feels inexcusable. That being said a quick game restart(which usually goes quick) will clear it up for hours(most of the time.
-Bosses primarily funciton as Damage sponges with predictable attacks.
Summary:
-If you like sandbox builders with some extra cherries on top you'll like starbound.

In essence, this is Assassin’s Creed.
And I don’t like Assassins’ Creed.
But if you’re a fan of Assassin’s Creed – give yourself (and this game) a Thumbs Up!
Is Shadow of Mordor an RPG?
Definitely No.
There are no dialogue trees, no character selection, and all side “quests” or more properly – missions, degrade into assassinating an urk, or whatever.
Is it Open World?
Not really.  While the scale of the map is extensive, there is no element of exploring (think Fallout 3 / New Vegas), and all the locations you discover are by no means locales (like villages with interesting NPC’s) but rather places where the aforementioned target for your assassination is awaiting his doom by your hand.
Is there Character Development?  (Potential spoilers)
Eh . . .  There are skill points you spend to “develop” your character, but all the progress concentrates on combat skills and weapons (obviously, since we already established that this is not an RPG, and skill point cannot be sunk into trade skill, or speech, ect).  I see this more in the same venue as weapon upgrading, not character “development.”
Having said all of this, here’s where I see Computer Gaming.
When I want a story – I read a book.  When I seek atmosphere – I listen to music.  When I require a mental challenge – I play board games with friends.  A Computer Game is unique in that it is able to unite all of those things together.  A good computer game can, at least.
Middle Earth – Shadow of Mordor is not that game.
While having decent mechanics and a good story it simply does not have a good gameplay.  You get the gist of what the entire playthrough will be like in the first 15 minutes or so – run, kill, run, kill, upgrade, run, kill more of the same – no rest for you, because you’re dead or something.  Ahm, ok.  I don’t find such a gameplay fun, which unfortunately I have to bear through to uncover the story.
Speaking of which.
The Story is not only the plot but also the telling.  Shadow of Mordor’s pace is sheer madness – there is no pause, no place to take a break, the urks are constantly spawning, the bosses continually appearing if you’re killed, and so on.  So, of course it is different for everybody, but I want my Tolkien story told by a gray-bearded Socrates looking grandpa, who is peacefully puffing on his cavendish cherry-wood pipe, while turning the burning coals in the fire and sipping his chamomile tea, NOT by a speed-junky, who yells out an extremely abridged “Hobbit” in 3 seconds while flying past me on a motorcycle.  That’s Shadow of Mordor’s story-telling.
So in short, i feel like the game is punishing me for wanting to uncover the plot of the story.  I simply can't move through the main plot at my own speed - i need to do that by grinding through irrelevant, monotonous, repeatative assassination missions.  And that is just not my idea of fun.  Sounds more like work and a waste of time - unfortunately, to get through the story i am forced to those tedious things.
When porting, please, start implementing FOV sliders for PC Gamers.  Yes, we PC Gamers get it – Consoles are the future, and console owners are your target group.  But here’s the thing – we, PC Gamers, still pay you money.  Why not make us happy, and throw in a freebie in the form of the NORMAL, expanded FOV.

Notable features:
I'm still very bad at fighting games. That doesn't really matter with Guilty Gear Xrd Sign, though, because this game is deceptive. Steam, user reviews, and promotional material may lead you to believe that you are putting down money for a fighting game, not an unreasonable assumption at first. As you pick up the game, in fact, the deception continues. You will swear you are playing a fighting game. It's interactive, fast-paced, sidescrolling. There are quarter circles. Potemkin is there. Don't be fooled, however. What you are really paying for is around 12 episodes of an anime set in the Guilty Gear universe. And it is awesome.
OK, I'm being facetious as usual, but the above paragraph is quite accurate. Arcade mode begins the story, and then there are a solid
of cutscene. They split it into its own menu option. Not being a Guilty Gear veteran, said "story mode" didn't make a ton of sense to me overall, but I had a blast nevertheless. The characters are decently developed and play off of each other quite well. There's plenty of over-the-top action and I watched the whole thing in one sitting, eager for more. As for the gameplay, it's pretty much standard for fighting games. There are five distinct attack buttons, you hit the opponent until they fall down twice, some moves flow into each other, you know the drill. Despite my ineptitude, I can tell that this game is solid. The controls are very responsive, and the sound design is top-notch. I would recommend this game to anyone who's even remotely interested, because even if the gameplay turns out to not be your thing the story mode is substantial enough to justify the purchase on its own. And that is not a claim I make lightly.

The plot, – which was supposed to be the strong point here, – is monotonous, scarce and extremely boring; totally unworthy of the huge amount of time it makes you waste.
In the end, you start to suspect after the fist half-hour of gameplay that the only interesting thing about this piece is its nice visual art. You keep going on because the dialogues give you this vibe of something big going to happen next, but it never comes.
Hence, when the game at last finished as plainly and blandly as it was from the beginning, I felt a relief.
Although I would not recommend it, i does have really creative gameplay aspects and i can see why others may like it.

Broken Sword 3 comes from an era when all adventure games felt the need to go 3D with mandatory action sequences and suffers for it, sadly. There are points at which the puzzles are are a little weak, or the conversations a little stilted... But this remains a Broken Sword game. This should be nobody's first Broken Sword game, but if you have passed through the first two games, this is a reasonable next step. However, do be wary of the three million and seven crate-pushing puzzles that this game includes. They will get tedious after the very first.

Too many block pushing puzzles fail to provide any real challenge, off-putting controls make you wish you invested in a proper gamepad, but characters you know and love make you want to see it thorugh the end. Overall, very basic adventure game. 3-D wasn't a way to go.

Overall, this game is a lot of fun vanilla, and can be even more fun and challenging with mods.

My friend and I had about an hour before we were going to the movies so we decided to look on the steam marketplace and what we found was Thinking with Time Machine, a mod for Portal 2. The gameplay mechanic is pretty simple. you (chel) have just escaped from Apature Lab OR DID YOU. Very early onto the game you find your trusty portal gun but with an added twist, a new device that allows you to make one copy of yourself and move as you did within the past (preset keys R and F). While this mechanic is very intresting and makes for some intresting puzzles the game still has it's flaws, the main one being yourself. It is very intresting and very confusing to see yourself move arround within the confines of Apature, but your past self is semi-limited. While I was trying to complete a very complex puzzle, my past self was not able to lift the edgless saftey cube to the area that I wanted too and as a result got me very very VERY mad. Overall I would reccomend this mod to anyone who has a computer to run it. With the intresting game mechanics, fun portal style, and intresting easter eggs this mod makes for one hell of a good time.

One of the appealing aspects of visual novels, for some people, is "mastering" the mechanics: Learning the flags, checks, etc... and using that mastery to obtain an outcome you desire. It's the same sort of engagement you might get from a puzzle game. I think that this game focuses on emphasizing that aspect of enjoyment. The reward for being able to reach new branches of the story is getting to see what happens, and the writing and art is certainly good enough (for me) to make that worthwhile.
When you first play this game a few times, it's just interesting to see what happens based on the choices you make. Eventually, though, you may find yourself more interested in trying to get to the end, and that's where the gameplay changes.
When I first saw this game, I thought that the events that happened to your character each day were just random, so you wouldn't be able to plan your classes very strategically. Well, I was wrong. As far as I can tell, each "week" of the game always has the same event, but what actually happens may change entirely based on what has happened on previous days. So, there's enough stability to give you the ability to strategize.
At this level of play, the game involves a lot of saving and loading as you explore different choices and different classes. The game seems designed with this in mind: saving and loading is really quick. At any point you can right click to bring up the save/load screen. I never found myself getting frustrated by going back and reloading a save. The game makes it easy to remember what you did in each save by including the week you were on and letting you name the save. It also lets you quickly skip through dialogue you've already seen.
If you like visual novels you'll probably really enjoy this game.

why

For starters, the game has a very good atmosphere. Somewhat of a Stalker'ish feel. The game itself plays like a turn based game with battles occuring like the random Final Fantasy random battle style. You walk around the game world and sometimes get caught up in these battles. They aren't random but you never see them coming so moving around a new area is always a bit tense!
As said before, the battles are turn based. You get the first turn to move your men around and use their weapons. The fighting is alot like Chess in a sense. For example, you pistol can only fire in four directions while the assault rifle can also fire diagonally. This kinda feels unrealistic of course, but it adds to the strategic element. Hitting the enemy in the flank or rear also adds more damage, again making the game a bit more tactical.
The graphics are pretty good. The characters are pretty low polygon but the hand drawn enviromnents are great. You may have some problems getting the game to run due to codec problems but I've managed to solve them quite easily. I'm sure GoG-team will issue a better fix for all the other people someday.
Now for the bad; the game is very very hard. Ammo is extremely scarce and you will need to resort to melee weapons in order to conserve it. While this adds some intensity and challenge it also makes it possible to completely screw yourself over early in the game if you use up all your rifle rounds or waste that precious "missile" on a useless enemy.
The "random" fights can be quite annoying as well since you never know you are walking into a mutant death trap and haven't found more quality weapons in order to win that fight. The beginning area for example is quite open, you go into different directions from your starting position. But sometimes you really need to have visited point A first because there you can find weapons you need if you ever want to have a chance against the enemy at point B.
In conclusion : A fun game but the difficulty may scare some people away (and this is coming from someone who loves hard games!). You may need to replay the beginning a few parts to really get the hang of it. Still a recommeded though! And for six bucks, you don't have anything to lose, right?

Pros:
-Truly a sandbox, beyond some super easy tutorial quests, your really don't have to follow the quest line built into the game if you don't want to.
-The quest line built into the game is a bit rough, but encourages exploration and adds a nice distraction if you get tired of building or fighting. (WARNING: Do not get this game if your mostly into questing, this is not the game for you, it's a game for sandboxers first and foremost.)
-Ancient Vaults allow for 'challenging' end game combat opponents for when planet based creatures become too easy to deal with.
-Pretty fleshed out and engaging crafting system, the cooking/farming system is particularly elaborate.
-Fun artwork, and mildly ammusing NPC chatter. (BOX!)
-Space stations and a variety of world types allow for a variety backgrounds for whatever building project you may want to engage in.
-Newly added Mech system makes the sapce side of the game more exicting, adding more combat/exploration/looting to an alreay fun game.
-Active Developers who release updates quickly after announcing them, and patch roll out bugs almost as fast as they crop up.
Cons:
-The game can suffer from SP lag a bit more than I'd like. I'm not on a monster computer, but it handles BL2 and similar much more resource intense games pretty easily, with little or no SP or even MP Lag. For a 2D sidescroller the SP latency is frankly annoying and feels inexcusable. That being said a quick game restart(which usually goes quick) will clear it up for hours(most of the time.
-Bosses primarily funciton as Damage sponges with predictable attacks.
Summary:
-If you like sandbox builders with some extra cherries on top you'll like starbound.

One has to approach the Ace Combat series with the proper expectations.  If you are expecting a deeply-accurate simulation in the tradition of DCS or even Falcon 4.0, you will be sorely disappointed.  This game is essentially a distillation of Sega's Afterburner -- planes with literally a hundred or more missiles, infinite cannon ammo and explosions galore.  This game is perfect for those who want to fly fighter jets, but don't want to have to memorize a 1000-page tome on how to properly start the plane's engines.  The cheesy but serviceable story serves to move the combat from one setting to the next and you won't mind as you shoot down enemy planes from the vintage MiG-21 to futuristic concept designs straight off the blueprints.  Never has aerial warfare looked so beautiful.

If you are thinking about playing this game, but are worried about some people saying it's unfair and an empty experience, here's what I say to you: It's an amazing game, but at no point does it ever "pay off". You have to enjoy getting better and let yourself appreciate the subtle side plots and design decisions. To beat Dark Souls you don't need to practice, or have overwhelming determination, you simply need to accept the fact that death has a strange connotation. It's not "the end", or "the beginning" in any sense. Death is to be strictly avoided, but don't be dissapointed when it happens, because it will happen. Just keep in the back of your head that, while death is still a setback, the world of Dark Souls will not reset as you respawn like other games. When you die to a boss, keep your eyes out on the way back to the fog gate for new oppertunities that you may have missed or that were not there before.

Night in the Woods is one of the most eye-opening games I've ever played. Before this game I had very little idea of the problems that a lot of important people in my life go through, but after playing through this almost 5 times, getting every achievement, and even delving into occasional fan theories and the like, I feel like I now understand what it can be like for them. NITW struck a huge chord for me, and I simply won't be forgetting this game in a long time.
The art is beautiful yet simple, the dialogue is meaningful, hilarious, and heartbreaking all at the same time, and the characters are extremely relatable and cute for certain people. Let's not forget that the game was nominated for the Games for Impact award, and were it not for Hellblade: Senua Sacrifice, it probably would have won it. The game portrays many themes that the player will latch on to. It paints a picture for a part of the world that not many people know about and how that part's inhabitants live in it, deal with it, or get away from it. And it shows what it's like to go through life's trials. It also paints a big picture for a topic that I don't want to mention here, but play the game and it will become clear.
With so many playthroughs, however, I do have some small criticisms. At times things feel like they slow to a crawl, and while these moments are forced, not everything has to be found. A lot of "side quests" or extra dialogue is completely up to the player, but in my opinion it all contributes slightly to the story or the setting. Also, while it fits with the overall themes of the game, the second half of the game almost feels like it switched writers. It changes tonality from life with its ups and downs to a semi-horror story. Again, it recovers pretty well in regards to the overlying themes of the game and story, but it might not be for everybody.
I give Night in the Woods a strong 9/10. I highly recommend this game to any late teenagers, young adults, or even some older adults in order for all of them to get a glimpse of how life can be with natural AND economic problems.

I'm a huge tower defense fan. There are a lot of ways to make a game like this, and in some ways, this is one of the strongest versions of TD I've ever played. It has a lot of ways to experiment, it has weapon and enemy interactions which aren't just raw math and a matter of course--so you have an opportunity to think outside the box and really explore interesting ways to solve the puzzle of beating various waves and difficulties.
But there are two TD mechanisms that really bug me and make me lose interest. They're both related to the idea of building the walls that push the enemies around the map. In a game where you get to build walls, the route you design for the enemy to take is a big part of the game and the puzzle.
First, you don't get the piece that lets you make a wall until you've played for several levels. I encountered a bug where my progress wasn't being saved, and as a result, I had to play the same several levels over and over again to get access to this piece. Also, the wall pieces initially cost a ludicrous amount. When you upgrade them, they cost less, though, only with a mod, do they cost an amount that makes designing paths through the level at all interesting. Otherwise they just seem to take away money better spent on damage dealing traps--in which case, why bother?
Second, the wall pieces do not consistently work. While I'm a fan of physics adding an unpredictable element to a game, when you can't be guaranteed that your walls will even work at all in some circumstances, I get really frustrated. Again--if walls don't work consistently, why have that element at all? Just make me place aggressive defenses, then. Or use the model (That they've incorporated) of putting down friendly units which move around and tie up the enemies.
They have everything in the kitchen sink here, and I think they leaned too heavily on RPG mechanics, both in terms of holding back all the cool stuff you could play the game with, and in terms of being dogmatically rock-paper-scissors about how all the traps work to the extent that there is a monster 'counter' to walls (and I'm not talking about flying--I'm talking about running units who can climb over barriers and do so inconsistently, as well as normal units that just glitch over the barriers--there's also exploding units which destroy your built traps, which as a mechanism would be interesting, but, again, they can cross barriers which means you can't deal with them by building deep--you have to hope you shoot them in time, or a ranged trap--which you don't initially get, thanks to the RPG style gating--gets them).
I'd like it if you had access to all traps, and the monsters didn't arbitrarily run over walls, but had to destroy their way through them consistently, unless they were fliers.

Well, the premise seemed interesting enough and I usually like these sort of text-choice games. But I simply don´t find this one amusing and although I don´t find it horrible, I wouldn´t recommend it.
The story, as I already said, is interesting. The boosting costumes are nice and so is the anime feel.There are many choices to chose from that will impact the storyline and results, and many (too many) skills to improve. It has some supposedly humorous perspectives on events, but I confess I fail to see them even as amusing. After a couple of goes, I mainly skipped the text.
My main issue here is that I can´t seem to get the logic involved in this game. The level of skills you need in order to pass some tests seems many times ridiculous, especially as the tests themselves often depend on silly combination of skills themselves (which I guess was the only way the developers had to actually have some of the skills ever used at all) . As others have pointed out, you probably will have to start making notes in order to progress, and, frankly, that´s not worth it to me. If you use common logic to try and build what would be a good queen, you will end up dead. Many players seem to find dying is a big part of the fun here, that´s not my case.
I wanted something more similar to real role playing games, but the skill system here is lacking -ironically, because it trie sto be so complex-: It also depends partly on your activities options, some of which only are a choice between bad and worse, as you can´t actually imporve what you´d like).
If you focus in a couple of skills in order to be strong there and pass the tests, you will find yourself failing all else and dying too. And there´s a very random mixture of what a real queen would need to excel in in order to suceed and what the developers think their queen needs in order to suceed: For example, it seems you stand better chances of surviving longer if you don´t attend any public events and concentrate on Lumen, Military and Divination. Even at times when their lives where threated, a monarch´s first duty were public appearances! And you can die from chocolate poisoning even if your poison knowledge is over 70!
All in all, it was an ok go to kill time. Some people seem to enjoy the supposedy funny deaths and outcomes, and the challange of finding the right combination to actually survive. I didn´t, and I didn´t find the texts and options good enough as to keep re-reading them over and over. I know saving often is an option, but in these sort of games I find it rather pointless as it kills the whole idea of following a progression. As I have no special interest in getting all the achievements, the whole idea of simply redoing specific choices instead of starting from scratch seems futile. I want to live an adventure more in the original Role playing games (what would your master say if after one bad choice you simply went back on your decision!) .
As I said, the game is not terrible and it is clear many people like it, and I can understand why they do. There´s a cup of tea for everyone, I guess. This one isn´t really mine.

This game is truly amazing. "Long Live the Queen" allows for much more player interaction than your common Visual Novel. The first time I played this game I was amazed at the possible paths to follow....
as well as the large varieties of deaths... Which will happen if you don't play your cards right.
After about Six hours, I finnaly finished the game and the ending finishes off the story quite nicely, giving diferent post-coronation consequences. Note, the game doesn't exactly take 6 hours to beat. For you to successfuly finish this game on a blind playthrough, you must have luck, or many replays.
After finishing the game, I decided to take a look at my achievements, and some written playthroughs. Watching both of those blew my mind. I didn't notice it much at first, but this game has much more paths to follow, actions to do, consequences that will happen, and ways to die, than i thought. Especially since, depending on your playthrough, you barely get hints about some other things that could have happened if you had done something else.
The only downside to this game could be sometimes how annoying it is to repeatedly die because of a stupid mistake. But then again, it show just how high the stakes are in this game. Even after being outrageously annoyed, i still kept at it and did not give up.
Overall, a very pleasent and enjoyable game, with a great story telling and progression, as well as a game filled with options to various different paths, actions and endings.
Rating as a Visual Novel - 10/10
Rating as a Game - 8/10

Personally the selling point for me other than the base building and the 50/ 50 Roleplay vs KOS RDM community was the boats... yes the boats idk why but i have never had so much fun feeling like i was actually surviving out in the ocean on a boat. I have had instances where i had a suppressed M40 out by the big wind turbines in the ocean on my boat and sniping poor unaware base builders and it just felt right.
the last few things before i wrap this amazing review up because  have over 2k hours in the game and could talk about it forever (pros and cons) i have to get in acouple more topics. The updates... yes the updates in Dayz you get an update about every 6 to 8 months and it feels like a whole new game (most of the time). for miscreated the updates are every MONTH and sometimes less (it pretty much depends on how frisky the devs feel at the time of the month in my opinion). plus the updates are huge for a months worth of work, we get new cars/ guns/ map areas/ gear/ houses ect every month and its fantastic .
now for the bugs and downsides... so the bugs are not very common but when you get a bug (YOU GET A BUG!) like its huge weather it just makes you laugh or makes you spawn in the ocean outside of the map border and you lose all of your gear (sounds bad but isnt as bad as say it would be in dayz) my biggest concern which im not dissapointed about just impatient is the map is 100% released yet. i have gotten frustrated with the devs sometimes when they add a completely new house to the game but wont add anything to the progression of any of the northern towns that havnt been released. but obviously they will release them it just takes time. when it comes to hackers and exploits at this stage of the game are zero to none. duping got removed right after i started playing the game and hackers were gotten rid of long before that.
all in all i give this game a early access score of 7/10 you should most definatley buy it, they have 50% off sales all the time. actually at the time of me righting this review its only 10 bucks and i garuntee you, you will not be at all dissapointed!

So far starters I'd like to clarify that I've been playing Ace Combat since Unsung War on PS2, I'm not as experienced as the extreme veterans but I've clocked hundreds of hours into each Ace Combat game that has released since. With that being said, I don't think Assault Horizon strays too far away from its old style with this one. There's this new mechanic called dogfight mode which is a step away from the traditional "Lead your Target" tactic for dogfights. Instead of using your skill to out manuever planes, you can use a snap lock on feature that automatically locks you onto the enemey's tail.
I'm imagining this is where the game gets its hate. I honeslty don't have a problem wth it because it gives a very interesting cinematic approach to dog fights. In this mode the plane sollows completely behind the enemy while the target tries to escape. This can be a number of things in a number of places depending on where you're fighting and I find that interesting.If you ever feel like you're sick of it, just stick to firing rockets-never fails!
Like I said, a step away from intense dogfights but still a solid flight combat game. Another really interesting feat is that you fly multiple typs of airfract, helicopters, AC-130s, etc. This is a step in a new direction of "Ace Combat" glory. Is it enough to stack up to a game that you want to come back to?
Well I like it.

A bad review? Yeah, I don't like the idea of putting in a bad review, but please don't let me stop you from trying a rather decent mod regardless of what I say.
When you first start out, you're offered the ending of Portal 2, and immediately you're thrown back into the middle of testing. I loved this little beginning, but the second I was given controls of the character, I feel as if I was playing with legos. It didn't have the same fluid motions or style which you may be customed to. It felt... Off. Trying to push that aside, there are a few sections of the game that will require you to literally scour over every little detail a bit further than if you were playing Portal, or Portal two. Spoiler, once you get into the lobby where Atlas and P-body was, spam E over at the servers to your immediate right, and then activate 'everything' on the one computer in the corner of the room, with the massive blank screen. Good luck hitting the proper buttons, by the way.
Beyond that, I found the lack of portals disturbing, and I understand they had to cut some of the hardware mechanics out and keep it simple. There was one room, I think right in the middle, 4-5 where you could place one portal on one wall, and directly across the room after turning 180, another. Once that second portal opened up, the game began to chug like a tar-filled piston on a train. There's even a few portal spots that do not require you to use portals at all, despite being desiginated portal walls. Not to mention, one is using an electro emancipator field, so you can't even use it if you wanted to. Why? This is literally the only ceiling portal you can use and the devs decided to close it off? Perhaps I didn't play far enough or work around to see if others were on the ceiling as well, but this seriously bugged me.
Next to that, there's little to no humerous story telling in the entire game. Nor any little tutorials to let me see what keys I had to press to activate the time machine. And before you ask, yes, there were some little cute tutorial videos like in Portal 2,  but the keys to use the time machine seemed to blur out, or the text on the Key was glowing far too much to even recgonize the key binding that was used for the time machine. I had to go into the menu to find the key bindings for the time machine.
Oh. Here's a fun little thing. You want to turn down your settings because your computer can't handle Portal 2 heat? Well make sure you only do this once, other wise you'll be prompted with annoying little text boxes that come up every time you leave the menu to try and fiddle with advanced graphics settings. I'm glad that it tells you what it does, and it's impact depending if you turn it up, down, off, or on. But really? Every time I try to change it? That's just a little nit pick thing, but it's still annoying as hell. After beating the game, and fixing GLaDOs (Spoiler!) I'm greeted to the end credits, and a crash. I tried to redo the game several times, go right for the credits, and every time, I crashed the game. I didn't bother beyond that.
Not saying this game mod is horrible, but if you expect the charm, controls, and portals that you fell in love with in the previous two games, it's not here. But please, let yourself decide and give the game a try.

This game is more like a digital interactive diary than a distinct goal oriented narrative.
In this day an age a digital "game" doesn't have to be all about a streamlined story flow, but it does bring to question as to lack of distinctive goal makes this game somewhat hard to concentrate on to. Slow pacing does not help either.
Stylistic art direction is altogether beautiful and seems to match well with the given enviornment.
Pros
-Beautiful art direction
-Immersive atmosphere makes you feel like being the character.
-Interactive game mechanics is a nice nifty touch
-Open world (just enough freedom, so that it doesn't feel too open)
-Interesting narrative and story
Cons
-Undistinctive goal makes this game hard to keep playing long periods as it's easy to lose interest (It's hard to identify the pitch of the game early on. EX: reuniting with family? Hipster trying to understand herself? Crime investigation?)
It's a narrative, not fine art.
-Slow pacing, (Seeing the protagonist going through her daily rituals, wake up sleep hang around, is interesting but at the same time unnessasary, as to ask why are we seeing this? Are these sequence of daily grind important?)
-Game enviornment mechanics, art direction, Hard time Identifying what the character can stand on or walk on, (Take LIMBO, the game for example, What character can stand or walk is easily indentified through saturation of darkness)
-Little change of scenery and enviornment. The whole game revolves around a small town, we do have small moments of new scenery but the most time the player is spending is in a small town with little room to go around. It becomes tedious and repetitive.

This was a free to play flash game. A very good one infact, a game based around the ability of stalling. If you are questioning if its worth it, type up luftrauser in a search engine, find the flash version. If you like that or any kind of arcade bullet hell games, or, Hell, if you even like planes, Pick this up, its cheap and is extremely replayable.

If you are thinking about playing this game, but are worried about some people saying it's unfair and an empty experience, here's what I say to you: It's an amazing game, but at no point does it ever "pay off". You have to enjoy getting better and let yourself appreciate the subtle side plots and design decisions. To beat Dark Souls you don't need to practice, or have overwhelming determination, you simply need to accept the fact that death has a strange connotation. It's not "the end", or "the beginning" in any sense. Death is to be strictly avoided, but don't be dissapointed when it happens, because it will happen. Just keep in the back of your head that, while death is still a setback, the world of Dark Souls will not reset as you respawn like other games. When you die to a boss, keep your eyes out on the way back to the fog gate for new oppertunities that you may have missed or that were not there before.

I've played my fair share of Zombie survival games, and for me this is the best so far. Unfortunately it's not coop or MP.
The gist off the fundamentals are....
In 3rd person view you progress though an open world on foot and vehicle searching for supplies and weapons.
In the meantime you are reinforcing a compound whilst recruiting survivors to live,work and fight as a community.
Management is paramount to stay alive as a fighter, and keep stocks up for survivors to live in a safely guarded area.
You train and swap as different characters as the characters can become sick and fatigued.
You can also take NPC characters along with you to fight and look for supplies.
Keep in mind you're chars can die for good. This really hurts when you have spent a lot of time leveling a survivor only to lose it due to stupidity or poor decisions. This can and will happen - usually unexpectedly. This is what makes the game so compelling.
This is a port and it runs fine for me on a standard rig. Graphics and sound are fine.
State of Decay relies on gameplay and its cram packed with fear and adrenalin which can be overwhelming and stressful at times - sometimes even unrelenting.
If you want to lead a bunch of survivors in an open world zombie filled adventure, then this is for you. I decided on controller over KB/M and recommend it.
Grab it and good luck!

As a long time vetren of the Ace Combat Series, I was beyond excited to see a new Ace Combat game. That being said, let me be the first to say, please, do not waste your money. This game has neither the charm, nor the engaging storyline of the parent series. In fact, after reading the reviews before I purchased the game, I decided to investigate for myself, and I was sorely wrong. To all of those on the fence about purchasing the game, please take my advice and skip past it.
1. Camera angles are horrible because the "kill cam" cannot be turned off and has caused numerous mission failures for me.
2. The dogfight mode is so intertwined into the game that it is almost impossible to take down the higher level enemies without using this terrible system.
3. Continuing on the dogfight system, it removes all skill from the game the parent series held.
4. Missions are so badly written and timers so badly set up, unless you do the mission absolutely perfectly, you WILL lose
5. Enemies are so overpowered that you cannot even line up shots without several warnings and missiles flying right up your tailpipe, so you end up failing the mission because you spend half of it evading the idiots behind you.
6. The friendly AI is beyond useless and they never do anything to help cover you. In fact, they should be removed completely.
I understand this list may seem excessive, however, I have hundreds of hours in the AC series and this steaming lump of crap needs to be scraped off steam and dumped in a trash bag somewhere.
I was desperate for a new AC game and was so excited when I saw this game. I wish I could get a refund because it is that bad. To all of you reading the reviews, please move on and save your money. I beg of you, dont waste your precious time because you will be just like me afterward, bitter and upset that your wallet is lighter because you bought a porrly designed game.

As this game was just recently released, I'll try to keep my opinion optimistic, as this is an Early Access game and in its current state, is fairly barebones.
Yes, I would recommend this game. I picked it up on sale because it looked interesting, and for the price of $4, why the hell not? I believe that your money will go towards what appears to be a dedicated developer (released patches for bugs soon after launch, and stated to already be working on co-op, expected to be testable in a week or two).
I'll start with the good first:
-fairly solid mechanics
-simple, enjoyable shoot-em-up playstyle, inspiration from games such as Doom/Quake/Serious Sam
-beautiful graphics with the Unreal engine
-bullet physics! you must actually lead your shots! (except with the sniper, which fires a career-ending beam of death)
-shotgun surprisingly satisfying, was nice to watch that purple bolt spread find its home in a ribcage as the skeleton crumpled to the ground
-decent and varied selection of enemies for so early in development
-great character and weapon models, your 3D artist is doing great work!
-smooth animations,  the skeletons' running and attack motions being the most noticable to me
-boss battles! i've only survived through two- one being a necromancer type which summons skeletons and family-ruining orbs of doom, should you not shoot them out of the sky- and the second being a 10 foot tall kite-the-knight, which surprised me when he pegged me with an impromptu shield frisbee. the boss battles occur every 5 rounds in survival and provide a nice mix to the action
-yet to run into any game-breaking bugs, no monsters getting stuck outside the map, etc. the game has flowed smoothly throughout my playtime
And then the bad (some of these may seem like nitpicks or hopeful suggestions, but I put them all here for the developers to see and hopefully incorporate into their game):
-the UI is terrible, hopefully this is just a placeholder, as it looks like a 12 year old created it with Java Swing components
-optimization is rather poor, you'll need a pretty serious rig to run this with 60fps on ultra. my laptop with integrated graphics netted about 20fps on low, with dips to 1fps whenever a lot was going on (guessing the particle effects and such are system heavy) and as such, I waited to review until I could try the game out on my desktop which is a little under the recommended specs. the game ran at about 45-55 fps most of the time, with dips to slightly over 30 fps in busy moments.
-the spellcasting is kinda wonky and ultimately, I found myself not using it at all, besides the occasional fireball into a group of skeletons or a blink to get me out of a jam. the UI for it is also fairly buggy, taking effort to get the cursor unstuck after entering the spell menu.
-the controls feel a little floaty to me, though I got used to them after a few minutes. I still scarcely found myself using dashing (double tapping a movement key). I did it accidentally more than anything.
-the ragdolls could use some work- although they're nice for enemy deaths and are flawless in that respect, they seem to lose most of their structure when on the ground. the second boss' ragdoll was spinning his sword around like a ninja with something to prove.
-currently, the melee enemies are Kite Simulator 2016. although they can catch you offgaurd (if you forgot to check your radar) they can get a few hits in, but ultimately I survived with backpedalling, regardless of how many melee enemies were chasing me. perhaps, some kind of special movement would make the combat more interesting, such as the enemies being able to roll/dash towards you or to dodge your fire (e.g. the imps in DOOM), or having AI that doesn't simply chase you around the map and eventually fall into a konga line. however, i had no real problems with the AI other than that, they seemed to perform well and had great pathfinding and accuracy. the bullet speeds means you don't have to worry about the AI's dead accuracy as long as you keep moving.
-I was surprised at the decent selection of spells, but the game could use more weapons as there are currently only three. perhaps, the pistol that some skeletons carry (since there's already a model in game) or even a melee weapon for sticky situations.
-only three maps currently, four if you count the textureless, arena-style map that is used for challenges. all of which seem to be open, giving long or medium ranged sight lines at almost every point. a more close quarters map might make for some more varying gameplay.
-hit detection seems kind of off when trying to shoot a melee enemy that has you in a corner (unless i'm just firing through his ribcage? :D)
There is a plethora of suggestions I could give, and although they may not exactly belong in a review, I'll put them here in case others may agree with me:
-excited for the co-op, which will possibly playable in a couple of weeks
-forseeable competative multiplayer?
-character/weapon customisation?
-more maps
-more weapons
-more enemy types
-perhaps some sort of campaign?
-workshop support? (user levels, campaigns, weapons, etc.)
Overall, I give this game a 7.5/10, on account of the game being so early in development and as such having a meager amount of content (1-3 hours at most), yet the solid mechanics and gameplay showing potential for a great game. Your $5 will be well-spent; even if you don't enjoy the game, you'll be supporting an up and coming dev team.

As for my touch on the how others who don't like this game, here's the thing, I don't disagree. You think Mae is infurating to play as? I thought so to. But I didn't take that idea and run with it. I didn't stop playing the game. And I most certainly didn't throw all of the other qualities of what makes this game unique out the window. But here's why I love this game, here's why I kept going. One scene you are presented with two dilouge options.
"I don't even know." and "where to even start?" In the way this is presented it forms a sentence, this was also later into the game, but it pulls this trick all the time. sometimes the only context clues are in the dialouge options they are just extra information, and in rare cases they aren't. This may upset people becuase it seems that both options do not matter, "the dialouge just asks a question? Do I get any more choices?" For me, it ended up being the best reson why I love this game, it seems like and endless fight with the dialouge only to have it make you submit. Sometimes you have no choice but to give in, and let the dialouge progess with very little feeling of choice. But also, sometimes it feels like there's a lot of weight behind two dialouge options, and sometimes it took me a few minutes to decide one. But I always thought, after I got over it, what a better way to keep the player on their toes but to make the dialouge not just a set of options to say, but  to surprise the player with what they can do. Keep in mind that my review is only "Recommended" because there's more pros than cons to the game.  However, those cons are infinitely infuriating.
1.  Camera.  I hate this camera with a passion.  It fights me so often.  I have died at least a dozen times solely due to the camera struggles.
2.  This game claims to be difficult and I'm on my first run and I have yet to fight anything difficult.  Well, Sif was a pain at first but his moveset is so limited that it was a quick lesson.
3.  Movement.  Just everything about the characters movement capabilities are total garbage.  I play a VERY light weight character and I still get caught by things that I should've dodged. An enemy I've fought two dozen times hits through a dodge I've successfully pulled off many, many times in the past.
4.  NPC pathing.  Some of the worst out there, folks.  These NPC's are dumb as bricks and will be speaking with actual bricks a lot of the time.  I've seen so many NPC pathing bugs that it's a wonder this company wasn't sued into the dirt for such a broken product.  NPC's will shoot endlessly at walls, walk right off cliffs and (my personal favorite) will slam into solid objects at full speed and never try to stop.  That's just the tip of the iceburg, so to speak.  From Software should truly be ashamed of the terrible work they did there.  Absolutely amateur.
5.  Hit boxes on some bosses is downright frustrating.  I was standing at the center of Sif's belly only to miss every shot.  five swings at the beasts core and nadda.  Thanks.
I'm sure I'm missing a couple of things (such as forced online play) and I don't hate the game but, my God is it a mess.  All in all the aforementioned frustrations don't take too much away from the core game.  They're just annoying and can cause issues once in a while depending on your play style.
Side note:  Speaking of playstyle...  I can't imagine why anyone plays Sorcerer.  That class is far too overpowered.  It ultimately ruins the game.  Most bosses fall like a joke in just under a minute in most cases.

Pretty good game IMO. Pros/Cons listed below.
PROS
+ Fairly realistic environmental/combat/gameplay wise (Stamina bar, Day/Night rotations, you can actually die)
+ Pretty engaging - you'll actually want to help your community survive (getting resources, which get consumed on a dailt basis) unless you're a cold hearted psychopath that wants to see everyone die (you can)
+ Friendly A.I. actually does sh** (doesn't just stand around and they're not invincible either)
CONS
- Once you use a character too much he/she gets kinda OP
- Kinda unrealistic at times (your cars have unlimited fuel, zombies sometimes spawn inside your "safe zone")
- It continues to simulate/consume your resources even when you've closed the game (this is for "realistic" purposes, I understand, but not all of us can spare time to play everyday)
- Buggy at times (crashes for no reason, zombies get stuck in walls/trash cans)
- Your friendly A.I. gets "trapped" and requires "saving" too often
Overall it's pretty good and could keep you playing for at least 20+ hours. Very good deal if on sale. 8.5/10.

As a veteran flower picker it is my opinion that the developers really missed the mark here.  Ive spent countless hours traveling the woodlands of Skyrim picking flowers for my Woodelf alchemist.  Ive wandered the expanses of Hyrule looking for mushrooms and peppers to cook skewers and spicy foods.  Ive searched the islands of Far Cry 3 for yellow flowers, red, white, even plunged into shark infested waters to grab those nifty blue flowers.  I trudged up and down the lands of Dragons Dogma looking for herbs and flowers to make me stronger.  Ive engaged in flower picking across multiple platforms and many generations of video games and I can tell you honestly that with Shadow of Mordor I was not impressed.  I mean sure its got a great story arc, incredible voice acting, exciting combat.  If your into that sort of mini-game stuff then fine, this might be the game for you.  But I bought into the much-hyped flower picking main game and I feel pretty let down.  Here's to hoping Shadow of War has a much improved flower picking mechanic.

When Guilty Gear XX Reloaded came out it was the best fighting game of its time.  Now, ArcSys returns to the franchise that helped establish it in the fighting game arena.  It's hard to judge this title on its own merits; if it were in a vacuum this undoubtably be an easy reccomendation as a great fighting game.
However, Guilty Gear XX was so different at the time mostly due to it's wide variety of character types in its roster (many of which had mechanics that were unseen in other fighting games).  While the characters we're given are very unique it's hard to not think about the miriad of memorable roster cuts from the last instalment of the series.  Also, the spiritual successor of Guilty Gear, BlazBlue, has come and shown us that some of the more eccentric quirks of that made many Guilty Gear characters stand out can be distilled into more focused characters that keep their flavor while being much more intuitive.
So, Guilty Gear Xrd is a little hard to wholeheartedly recommend.  It's a fantastic nostalgia trip for those who remember the older games and a solid fighter for sure.  The innovative take on animating a cel-shaded 2.5d fighter is also almost worth the price of admission alone.  However, I don't think ArcSys' latest is its greatest as BlazBlue really did take what Guilty Gear started and push the envelope into fighting game rocket science.  Even if we avoid comparisons to BlazBlue it's hard to tell if this is even a more complete game than the last Guilty Gear that came out over a decade ago.
So this is a very tenative recommendation.  It's a good fighting game and Guilty Gear deserved a re-visit.  However, this installment isn't enough to make me feel this is the definitive Guilty Gear over the last installment and ArcSys has already gone on to do better things.

Very interesting chess variant that works surprisingly well. The AI is extremely weak so I wouldn't advise getting it for anything more than casual single player. In fact the computer player only exists to help you learn all the new rules and the game is focussed mainly towards multiplayer.
You can choose from several armies each with its own set of new and interesting rules that actually add a great surprise dimension to the classic army (which is also included). Even when using the classical chess set-up there are two main variations on the basic rule set. You win if your king crosses the central horizontal (half way) line without being in check and there is a bidding system (called a duel) when capturing pieces. The graphics are adequate and functional and there is classical background music that seems fitting. Due to the extra complexity involved in coming to understand the innovations I would not recommend this to people who are not already familiar with the usual game but chess enthusiasts should be delighted by how well the changes work.

There are no Game adjustments possible (see also critics of several Game Tests). Problem is that there is some classical Music Playing very loud and you cant adjust the Volume. So if you play a Multiplayer Match you cant hear your Oponent conected to Skype.

The bots are good only to learn how a class is played. Other than that, they make the most basic of mistakes and are pathetic opponents.
Online play is limited; good luck finding people to play against.
Your best option is to arrange to play the game with friends in whatever way suits your fancy (local, online, play-by-mail). If you do that (ideally, getting this on a good sale), Chess 2 offers a remarkable new life to what had become a rather mathematical game. Chess 2 is creative, improvisational, interesting, exciting, and new. It isn't your grandfather's Chess. Consider it a turn-based tactics game like Fire Emblem or Tactics Ogre, except without the leveling or other superfluous elements. It is distilled strategy themed after the Game of Kings.

is a game that is difficult for me to give a simple Yes/No vote for.  It is well made and (mostly) achieves what I think its creators set out to do.  A lot of effort has clearly been put into the world building and branching narrative.  Unfortunately, all of this didn't pay off for me and I was left somewhat underwhelmed and unsatisfied.
The gameplay mostly consists of disparate minigames linked by exploration/platforming sections and conversation trees.  The most developed minigames are the in-game game and dungeon crawler
, and the rhythm game sections when main character Mae plays Bass.  Neither of these is bad, but neither are they spectacular; if that's what you're looking for, better examples exist.
Still, I don't have a problem with games where the gameplay was not the focus.  It does place extra emphasis on the narrative, however, and this has problems.  The story meanders for a while before the plot really gets going, and the
in the later sections don't seem to fit well with the overall tone.  I also found the conclusion rushed and unsatisfying, at least as far as the fate of the main antagonists is concerned.
The real problem, however, lies at the game's heart: main character Mae.  She was my biggest obstacle to finishing the game, and that really shouldn't be the case.  The problem is that she is frequently rude towards friends and family, oblivious to other people's feelings, and generally self-centred.  Later character development and the reveal that she has
helped partially redeem her, but it came too late to save the game as a whole.
The game does do a number of things quite well.  In particular, the setting and mood (mostly) capture the feel of economic depression and disaffection in a way I have seen in few other works in any medium.  The main characters are all well-developed, and there is a lot to find just exploring the setting and talking to everyone.  I clearly liked it enough to finish.  But looking back, I probably wouldn't have gotten this knowing what I know now.

TL;DR: Night in the Woods is a great game (so I recommend it) - but some aspects of it are far from perfect.
First of all: The key part of Mae's personality is the fact she's extremely immature. Almost irritatingly so. At 20 years old, Mae behaves like someone much, much younger. It's a part of the plot, of course. Mae's some kind of anti-hero, someone with so much to learn. [TBH, one of the main reasons I kept playing was her cringy attitude - it was very endearing sometimes.] By the end of the game, Mae *kinda* justifies her behavior, but there's no evidence she's going to change or she's even willing to change. It's meant to be some kind of social critique (millenials are lost and lack any kind of perspective and so on, etc) but her story seems... Lacking something, somehow.
Also, the plot develops at a strange pace. After nine, ten hours of gameplay, the game lacked any evidence the "mistery of Possum Springs" would be solved. Jumping from one roof to the next was fun, very fun, and I loved every side-story, but it's so frustrating seeing everything uncovered and "solved" in a short period of time. I don't know if I'm way too fond of Oxenfree or something, but the apex of the story comes suddenly and it's over way too soon. I even read a few guides expecting a "true ending" and found nothing.
At last, it's a great game, don't get me wrong. Cool soundtrack (okay, Mae's band is some kind of "generic indie rock" thing or whatever - even though she listens to doom rock and Witchdagger seems to be the coolest band ever), the art is flawless and the city is so pretty it's hard not to get obsessed with learning its secrets. I love the characters (Bea and Lori are my favorites) and I care about them all. Played it all in a very short period of time 'cause I was almost unable to stop.
It's not perfect, it's way too overhyped, but it's a great game overall. If you like cute things and naïve humor, Night in the Woods is the game for you.

If I had to describe this game in a sentence it would be this: Night in the Woods is a game with some good beats, but ultimately felt like an over-indulgent slog, I cannot bring myself to reccomend.
This game is a story-focused walking simulator that takes place in a small town that has a tightly knit community. You play as an awkward anthropomorphic cat named Mae that rekindles her old friendships upon returning home after dropping out of college and the shenanigans that ensue.

So much time is wasted on characters or lengthy sections of the game that I would say the majority of this game is filler. Moving around the town isn't fun, it's slow and it makes up waaaaaay too much of the game. The cop aunt Molly and the Janitor are useless characters. Molly makes around 4-7 appearances throughout the game and each time she says the exact. same. thing. and there is no payoff whatsoever for it. The Janitor is discussed as having a deeper meaning for all of his appearances, but that brings me to my second gripe about Night in the Woods:
This game cannot stop over-indulging itself. There is funny meta humor, and there is excessive, existential exposition that make up hours of this game. This game does not earn easter eggs, this game does not earn the right to have a chapter called "The End" that lasts 2 hours where nothing meaningful happens. I sat in front of my screen smashing the A button as nothing of consequence happened and no character grew for what felt like eternity.
The plot is cliche and inconsequential. If I gave someone this game to walk around in the town on day one and the last day, if they didn't stop to get exposition spouted at them on how they should feel, there is no difference other than it is snowing. This game does not impact the town, the focus of the game, it does not impact the characters, who literally say in the final moments of the game that they aren't sure what they learned, it just isnt good.
I cannot reccomend this game.
[1/5]

At first glance this game is about small towns, friends, and ghosts. And yes there is quite a bit of all three of those things. But what this game really is at its core is change. It's about life and people changing around you, its about people leaving as you watch and some people leaving while you aren't even looking. It's about yourself changing, and not always into a better version.
There's a very large chunk of it that wonders if you can really change anything at all, if life is just horrible and you happen to be there at the same time with no way to make it better. But it also makes the case that even though life can be horrible and cruel and uncaring, its the small things that make it better. In any given day, you have so many choices to talk to and interact with various background characters and while those small interactions don't seem like much, at the end of the game you can see the effects.
I didn't know what I was getting into when I played this game but it's what I needed.

Night in the Woods is very, very, slow.
TLDR:  Night in the Woods is really just a needy Milennial simulator. A "game" about being confused and not knowing what to do.
Pros...
-Great artstyle. I looked up how to take screenshots just so I could take some from this game.
-Decent soundtrack. Its not the best OST of 2017, but its fitting and not bad to listen to.
-Fantastic Characters. They interact in real ways and are never just filler. Its like real humans made this game, as it should be
-It brings up some good points. Some. You'll see the yucky ones in like two seconds, but there are some problems with this world we live in now, and its nice when video games acknowledge them.
-Demontower is pretty damn awesome.
-Its pretty funny.
-The script for this game is good. Great story ideas.
Cons...
-The issues it touches on... I just dont like them. It mentions anxiety, Religion, and just general bad stuff. I wouldnt ever want all games to be sunshine and rainbows, but I had trouble relating to most of the characters in the game. They all cared too much. I choose to live life with general apathy because it keeps my worries and stress down. Anxiety is certainly something I've experienced, but its not a recurring problem for me. I understand it sucks a ton to be afflicted with it, but I cant relate. Ive got religion figured out- I believe that any god out there either never existed or is dead. If you think differently, thats fine, but it helps me to see things that way.
-There are a lot of not sentient animals in the game, and it never bothers to explain that. Like Mae owns a bird, why isnt that a crime or considered slavery? I feel like the developers couldve taken only like 4 minutes to crap out some explaination and i'd be satisfied.
-Mae. Moves. So. Slowly. Holy ♥♥♥♥ people complained that Frisk moved way too slow in UNDERTALE, but in this game you see the same sights over and over and over and Mae moves at the speed of a snail with muscular dystrophy. The dream segments were especially tiresome.
-Acheivement hunting would be so ungodly awful for this game because you have to start over everytime. Ugh.
- The worst part? The game is only engaging at the end. The rest of the story up until that point is just waking up, talking to one of three friends, hanging out with them, talking, then going to sleep and only doing the same basic thing for like an ingame fortnight. Its absurd. I wont put spoilers here, but the end (Chapter 4) is the only one that really piqued my interest, before that its just confusion, boredom, and the rare minor spook.
*THE SPOILER BIT*
The only other thing that made me want to keep playing was to figure what happened to Mae in high school and college that we are just as inquisitve about. The devs decided that it would be best to just♥♥♥♥♥♥it out at the end all at once with reasoning that just doesnt excite me. Like seriously, its just because she got depressed after finding out she cant interact with her video games? Im not here to♥♥♥♥♥♥on video games or gamers, I mean im always happiest when I get to be somebody I'm not, but I know that the majority of us are aware that we dont get the opportunity to quest through ruins or solve a kidnapping or become a piece of bread and movie around (although i dont imagine that anybody got emotionally attached to "I Am Bread"). Trust me, I'd want to leave this world and go be in Zelda or Hollow Knight or Skyrim, or maybe even Night in the Woods, but most of us know its not going to happen. The characters dont seem to mind at all that they killed a dozen people at the end. Bea calls it a moral gray area, which would give them reason to be more than "Whatever" about it. Besides, there is no proof that the, uh, cult... was wrong. Perhaps that Hole was going to save Possum Springs, even if it meant the death of 39 people. It annoyed me a lot.
* END SPOILERS*
Night in the Woods has a fantastic presentation. The music and artstyle was enough to keep me interested until the end. If you suffer from the very real problems of anxiety and not having a sense of direction, I've no doubt this game could speak to you and maybe help a bit. There just isnt enough game here to really be satisfied. Its not like one of those "experience" games along the lines of Abzu or Journey, but there is a good story with good characters hidden behind 5 hours of gameplay that arent exciting in the slightest. Gameplay here takes a backseat, but games can do that and still be good (i.e. Owlboy). I can at least understand why people like this game, but just like UNDERTALE and Doki Doki Literature, the potential the developers put in this game to make a unbelievably terrible fanbase is quite present. Night in the Woods kept me until the finish because of its characters and presentation, but in the end im just glad a friend gave this to me so I wouldnt have to waste $20.

Let me just start off by saying that I play console and PC, meaning I've actually had this game on console long before I had it on PC, and that I've also played it vigorously on console, so when you see I have under 20 hours of this on my profile, I've only recently got it on PC, but I've got at least a good 50 -7ish hours on console. Anyways here we go.
State of Decay is a true survival-horror zombie game done right. Resources really are limited, once you've cleared out a house and taken all the supplies from it, it stays empty. There are quite a few vehicles to find out in the game world which are also limited. Sure, you could spend the next hour or two running over hordes (I'll be using the horde example a lot since they're one of your greatest threats in the game) in a truck, but once that thing explodes, you can't fix it. This means that you can't exactly go on a good killing rampage (which is kinda good since that's not the point of the game anyways).
You really do have to manage your resources, including ammunition, medicine, building supplies, fuel, and food. As I stated earlier, things won't respawn, so you have to choose when moving down a horde with a shotgun is a good time or not, givin that you won't be the only survivor needing those shells. You mmust also manage all those resources when your upgrading your base as well. Say you're running low on building supplies and only have enough for one upgrade/new building... do you want to upgrade the infimiry to help prevent your people from getting the Black Plague and other illnesses, or do you want to make a workshop which not only lets your repair weapons and vehicles, but will later allow you to create suppressors for your weapons and other things as well? You'll have to make many choices with these things in mind as you go through the game.
Gameplay is also quite good as well. To put it bluntly, you survive. Sounds exciting, da? Nyet? Fine, here comes your essay you entitled little fuc-
Gameplay is pretty fun. As I'll talk about later int the game, you're no super-hero, you're just a person. A person however, with stats and perks. These stats and perks will benefit that character of course. You have stats such as Cardio, Wits, Shooting, and a few other stats I can't recall currently. With cardio, your stamina increases, allowing you dodge more attacks, sprint longer, perform more actions like jumping and climbing longer without getting tired, and most importantly, you can fight with your melee weapons and attacks longer in combat. Stamina is especially useful in combat since it's tied to so many things. If your still fighting a horde with low stamina, your attacks and reflexes  become slower and weaker, making you much more vulnerable. Wits allows you to search areas faster. This is very important when you're out scavenging, that way you can grab what you can and get out faster. And shooting is exactly what it sounds like. But not only will you become more accurate, you'll also reload guns faster too.
Now for the perks. "Perks" aren't things like "RAMIREZ, KILL 7 ZOMBIES FOR AN AC-130!", they're small little positives or negatives. Positives like the "sharpshooter" perk, which allows your shooting skills to level up faster or "swift-hands" that let's your melee level up faster are small little things that'll have that character slightly in some what. Negavies would be things like "bum knee" makes you lose stamina while sneaking or "a-pack-a-day" which has your cardio level up slower.
Melee combat is what you want ALL of your characters to excel at. Melee is the attack you'll be using most often in this game to help conserve ammo, and not attract the attention of every zombie in a 70 meter radius like a gun would. Basically, you take your melee weapon, and you go crack/slice some heads open. You can also do a normal attack like a kick and push to stun zombies and give you some room. There are also "executions" you can do to a zombie by standing over one on the ground and using the execute key to smash their head open with your weapon, knee, or even your boots. Using this same key while sneaking up behind a zombie in stealth mode will allow you to do a sneak attack, instantly and quietly killing them.
Stealth is also a large part of the game. At times, running out in the open isn't always the best idea. So I hope your character doesn't have the "bum knee" penalty, because you're likely to spend a lot of time crouching around. Not only will you have to stay out of sight, but you also have to be careful about the noise you make too.  Things like crashing through a window will bring you a lot of new "friends"
This game also features permanent death as well, meaning you can't play the super-hero that "dies", then respawns at your base. If you take a character out and get ambushed and die, that character stays dead. Thanks to this, you also have to choose your battles more wisely and fallback more on stealth than other zombie games.
One word. IMMURSION(probably spelled wrong). You truely do feel like you're out in the country surviving in the apocslypse. Zombies everywhere, town feels like your "down souf", weapons feel like they belong there, and the lighting truley does help too. The soundtrack also helps too. The appropriate music always seems to play for whatever you're doing. Nice, comfy music plays when your at the base during daytime upgrading things or just hanging around, a nice ambience plays while you're out exploring, grim, "darker" music plays when your in the middle of battle against overwhelming odds. And did I mention the lighting? When the crack of dawn comes forth and you can finally see things clearly without a flashlight, you truely do learn to love daylight. And then there's night. It's dark. I mean dark dark. Not just any kind of dark, I mean, DARK. You don't want to confront groups of zombies in the dark either, since you can barely even see with your flashlight. This makes raiding houses at night seem much cooler, but you'll barely be able to see anything, even with your light on (almost like real life).
Now for some cons.
1. Zombies enjoy clipping through things such as fences and sometimes the floor of buildings your currently in. While this isn't that bad most of the time, it can become a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when fighting special infected like ferals who are very quick and lethal.
2. Your AI survivors can be quite lazy, resulting in you having to go out and do most of the work. The other characters do leave to go scavenging as well once in a while, but usually they end up getting into trouble and you have to go save them.
3. Your AI survivors are too emotional. Morale is a big part of the game, should it get too low, people start leaving and mutinies can arise. While this might add to the whole "realistic immursion" or however it's spelt/said, these kinds of things happen a little to often for my liking. A character will start becoming depressed and start bringing everyone down, you gotta go back to base, take em out for a quick jog somewhere, kill a few zombies, and return home after a brief warning/talking too. While that doesn't sound bad, it becomes annoying quick when only an hour or two after cheering them up, someone at home is mad and making everyone else mad. Then you go through the jog n kill routine again. While not really a game-killing thing, I just found it annoying after a while when there are more important tasks to attend to.
4. Vehcles control like your driving on a road of cheap gravy. It's mainly just turning in some of the vehicles I have a problem with.
And that's pretty much it for State of Decay.
I'd honestly give it a 8/10.

I can't believe I didn't write a review for this game earlier!
LLtQ is a visual novel about an underage girl whose mother dies and will soon become the queen when she comes of legal age. The problem with this however is that their are many people who stand to gain from her demise and taking over her kingdom so she not only needs to blossom into a woman extremely quickly, she must also remain alive while doing so whch is harder than it sounds with so, so many ways to die just waiting for you.
The game is a joy to play in large parts due to its simple but great writing. Your character is believable because you dictate how she should behave and the choices have weight to them. If the game just stuck to this formula it would still be a fun game but supernatural elements come into play and while you can choose to be a magical princess you have to keep in mind that time spent learning your magical powers is time taken away from ruling your kingdom and trying to juggle everything perfectly is impossible (the game is purposely designed that way) so you are usually choosing between the lesser evil but do you even care? I mean with everyone out to kill you, aren't you just doing what needs to be done to survive?
Your villagers may not see it that way, so be careful! Nor may the very people you thought you could trust and is that dad with another woman so quickly after mom died?!
The game can become quite dark and even depressing at times but that is just part of the charm because it is your actions that are causing the other people to react and while it is tempting to appease others you also have to survive as well and lets not forget that your mother just died too, so maybe you don't want to deal with all these pressures right now.
If I make the game sound difficult it really isn't. You will die but since it is a novel and not an actual living game (IE Civ5) you can eventually die your way to success after you know what to expect. This doesn't mean however that the game loses replay value as it has multiple endings that reflect the actions you took so if you are a completionist, you will find many hours of replay value to be had here.
I heartily recommend this game!
