TL;DR:  3 out of 5 Lumen Crystals
This is a unique, complex, and enjoyable game with likeable characters and an interesting story and subplots.  You play a young princess whose mother has just died and must survive until your coronation.  Many possible deaths follow.  However, it suffers from a lack of beginning skills (which is unrealistic in this setting), lack of skill building on weekends, and Elodie's lack of common sense.  These 3 flaws lost it 2 crystals.
Long Version
This game is a lot of fun.  There are many intricate plot twists, the characters are believable (for what it is), and the complexity is almost staggering.  There are also a number of possible deaths, and many secrets to discover.  You will probably need a guide to win the game the first time, unless you are very skilled, or very lucky.  I died about 5 times without help, got tired of it, and looked up strategies.  After my initial finished playthrough, a few things occurred to me. These are the major flaws of the game.
Firstly, Elodie begins the game with zero points in any skills.  Bear in mind, this girl is 14-14!-and has been attending  a noble school for, presumably, at least 8 years.  At the very least, she should have basic knowledge of History, Economics, Athletics, and Expression (The Arts).  Since it is a school for the children of noble families, she should logically also have some knowledge of Conversation-Court Manners and Flattery, at the least.  The only possible explanation is that her teachers have let her slack off due to her position-which is unlikely, since she is the sole heir.
Secondly, the game does not add any skill points from weekend activities.  True, this is her time to relax and balance her moods, but please explain to me why sitting at Court with her father-the King-doesn't gain her any points in Royal Demeanor?  She must have been doing this since childhood; there's no way she learned NOTHING from it.  She's been groomed for queenship since birth, after all... Nor do you gain Athletic skill from playing sports, or Animal Handling skill from hunting.  Hmm....that's a flawed system.
Finally, Elodie appears to have NO common sense whatsoever.  None.  This is evidenced by several plot points during the game.
The process of increasing skills is, at least, fun and challenging, as you have to decide what kind of queen Elodie will become.  There are a lot of comedic moments, some sad ones, and a LOT of deaths.  Some of them, you will feel you deserved.  Most of them, appropriately, come as a total shock and leave you wondering just what happened and why.  The choices you make DO matter, even if you don't understand how or why at the time.  In spite of its flaws, I recommend you play it for yourself-once, twice, 15 times.  It's worth it.

I got this game in a bundle with a bunch of other visual novels. I didn't actually know anything about it, but I looked through the achievements and I thought, "oh cool, I can die this many ways? better play it."
In two days I was so absorbed I had already played more than 12 hours straight. When you start playing, it seems a lot harder than it is. You start by upgrading skills that you don't really know what they do. For example, you can upgrade your Animal Handling skill to know stuff about dogs. Each of your skills can significantly affect the future you have in your game.
The goal is to keep the protagonist, Elodie, alive for 40 weeks. It's a lot harder than it sounds.
However, if you are used to very skill based games and enjoy strategy, this might be a game you enjoy. There are enough endings and deaths that it becomes a challenge to try and get them all. Like with any visual novel, the endings and flavor text are what create replay value. However, this game includes new flavor text and makes you do skill checks to an extent that every playthrough is still very interesting and there isn't a lot of overlap.
If you're looking for a game to get really in-depth with and are interested in the challenge of building skills and trying to stay alive, this might be the game for you. It reminded me a little of how System Shock 2 starts-- there are a lot of skills that might sound appealing, but might also be incredibly useless if that isn't the track you end up on.
If you're more of a sit-back-and-relax or romance VN fan, this game really isn't for you. There are romance options, but it's not a romance game. It's also very player intensive and oriented. You are making choices constantly and ALL of them change your gameplay. If you enjoy the usual "read the text and make the occasional decision" type of visual novel, you might want to pass on this.
Overall, one of the best VNs I've played in years and I still haven't even found all the perks, texts, and endings. It's a lot of fun.

As it stands right now Miscreated is a ton of fun. It's definitely worth the money There is a lot of content in the game right now and I have spent about 250 hours in the game and still enjoy it.
Lately The devs have been slowing down on the development of the game. In turn, the playerbase has shrunk. If you're looking for full 50 player servers you will find some at almost any time of the day but the numbers are inconsistent.
The main reason I can see that the playerbase is shrinking is because of the developers. They are not listening to the community. A lot of content creators and owners of large communities based around Miscreated have been pleading for the devs to give us a roadmap of what to expect with each update because for the last few months we've been getting hyped up over the next patch and then severely disappointed because instead of adding a new area they'll give us a few bug improvements and some low-level content like some new gear or a new gun.
My main concern is that Miscreated is not going to be pushed out of Early Access. This gives the devs a license to say "well it's early access..." as an excuse for not working on their game. This is what other survival games all have in common, some of the biggest being Ark, DayZ and H1Z1 (Now called "Just Survive"). I would personally be fine if they released a rough outline of what to expect with each update or atleast let us know what they will be working on each month. Something to tell me that my $20 isn't going to waste to order them a pizza for all of their no work. Entrada needs to realize that being an early access developer does not mean they can just leave the community in the dark. They may own the IP, but the community as a whole owns the game. When you put a game in early access it is mean to gain feedback from the community. Entrada has been ignoring ANY and all constructive criticism on their Discord server, even going as far as saying things like "Well when you make your game..." to it's customers.
I really want this game to thrive but I don't think Entrada has what it takes to be a successful early access developer. Their constant ignoring anything that isn't praise makes me worry for the future of this game.
So, do I reccomend this game?
As a game? Hell yeah. It's fun as hell. I definitely got more than my money's worth out of it.
As something to invest your time in? I don't really know. It relies on multiplayer and the developers ignoring the community makes me think this game wont make it out of early access. I might hold off until the reviews go back to positive unless you have some cash to burn. Entrada is being way distant from the community to be allowed to develop in early access.
I'm gonna set this to a do not recommend. If they start listening to us again I'll update my review.

A really cool modern combat flight simulator. It's one of, if not the, most accessible flight sim games I've ever played. Many flight sims are far too heavy, but this game gets it all right in my opinion. You get to control all kinds of fighter planes, helicopters and bombers in combat scenarios. There's also an AC 130 which can be controlled very similiar to how it's done in Call of Duty. The graphics are really detailed but always so smooth. Can't fault the game, it's excellent. I'm astonished at some of the terrible reviews it's got. It's a must play if you want a really accessible and fun combat flying game.

Good, but the game could have been better. Heli and AC-130 missions are a huge pain because objectives are usually timed, enemies have no reticules, and guns have limited zoom (AC-130). Also the AI engages dogfighting near constantly. This leads to a lot of instances where you're trying to chase a mission critical target while the AI is constantly engaging in dogfight mode and lobbing endless missiles.
I also don't know how "realistic" I'd call the story. Outside of the fact the main characters are as bland as Elmer's glue, the magic mcguffin weapon is a nuke in all but name. The story reminds me heavily of CoD:MW's story. If you've played any of the MW games then you'll be able to predict where the story is going. Hell, I called the first plot twist during the first cutscene. In fact the whole game reminds me of a CoD game. Heavily scripted in an attempt to shove you into the best pov to see the explosions. It even has bloody screen so real, and regenerating health.
AC:AH removes the previous AC system of buying planes and instead gives you a whole choice of planes........that the game decides is appropriate for the mission. The problems with that is it removes the feeling of accomplishment from buying your favorite plane, and the game rarely tells you what mission you're preparing for, and what enemies you'll be facing. So be prepared for missions you go into blind, and end up taking the wrong missiles/bombs.
Lastly the missions can be very frustrating, and take vast amounts of luck instead of skill. The mission over Moscow is a prime example of this. In the last section you have to shoot down a plane carrying the magic mcguffin. Problem with this is the game throws in 4 escorts and a boss that all home in on you the moment you enter the same continent. So you have to chase a bomber on a very small timer while 5 guys try to shove perfect accuracy missiles up your nose. I failed that mission so many times because despite any maneuvers I pulled I would have 6 missiles slam into me. I finally beat it because the AI bugged out. The fighters didn't chase me, and the bomber didn't launch it's never ending chaff supply, so missles actually managed to hit it. This is just 1 example out of a dozen. The next best one was the ICBM that could evade advanced A2A missiles, and had to be shot down in mere seconds.
If you just want to flight around and blow things up then this is your game. If your expecting Ace Combat then you'll be disappointed. It's fun, but it isn't an Ace Combat game. It's a shame we'll probably never see a true Ace Combat game on PC. I'd love a reason to break out my old flight stick. maybe add some modding tools for skins, and maps.

Pretty sure every review that isn't oggling Ram has said most of what needs to be said.
Online is smooth and functional. Good luck finding Ranked matches, however. Most play will be in the Player Lobbies. Fortunately, as of the first month, there's usually a good number of lobbies and players with a range in skill, so it's easy to have fun getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked and watching others follow your example. If you've got friends to play with, or want to engage in a great fighter online, then this a pretty gold example in a world where Netherealm servers are still a thing.
The tutorial and challenge modes are some of the best in the genre, easing in new players and vets alike to the system mechanics and basic fundementals before you ever have to tackle a real match. You can spend hours in training without even realizing it. The combat is streamlined compared to past entries, but for the better in most cases (YRCs never needed to be as stupid tight to pull off for how integral they are to Guilty Gear's combat).
Single player is a mixed bag outside of learning. Story is eh, but like the gameplay, does a good job of explaining everything to newcomers to the series, wraps up quickly enough and offers plenty to those willing to sink their teeth into it. Arcade is your simple 8 AI fights wrapping up with a rival and final boss. M.O.M mode is an incredible grind with RPG elements attached to the fighter experience, and that's really all that's left.
These modes might be more enjoyable if the AI were any bit competant but unfortunately they're pushovers. Even on the hardest difficulty setting they rarely play like any decent player, lacking any pressure or severe combos to punish players, and they give no indication as to how the respective character is meant to be played. This is crucial, because now a player not only needs to play against real players to test how valid their practice is, but to also learn matchups outside of the tiny bit the challenge modes cover. The AI is very bland by comparison to the great example SFV has set in place (Even if that is a much simpler game).
Also, as is usual of Aksys, this version of the game will soon be outdated in a few months thanks to their God awful PC Release schedules, and the same will be said of Blazblue CPE once that releases 2 years after the first iteration came to consoles.
If you own a PS3/4, wait for Revelator. If you only game on PC, this is the most accessible, up to date Guilty Gear available. If you've ever wanted to pick up on the series, start here and support more fighting games for PC.

The success that 2014's Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor garnered is undeniable; the title went on to win four Game of the Year awards and over 50 others. Despite some of the controversies that arose, it's the most successful Lord of the Rings based game to this day, and it still has its own large fanbase flocking around it. Developed by Monolith Productions and published by WB Games, the biggest selling point that this title had at the time of release was its unique Nemesis system, which garnered a lot of attention due to its ingenuity.
Players are put into the role of Talion, a captain of Gondor who is stationed in a garrison at the Black Gate of Mordor. Soon after the game begins, the garrison is attacked by Sauron's Orc forces who are led by the Hammer, Tower, and Black Hand of Sauron. Talion attempts to repel the attack, but he finds himself, his wife, and his son mercilessly captured. It doesn't take long for the Black Hand to slit the throats of Talion's wife and child right in front of his eyes, and then lay a curse upon Talion himself as his throat is also slit. The curse causes him to be "banished from death", and in turn he is destined to wander Middle-Earth for the rest of eternity, on a plane between life and death. However, he soon runs into the spirit of an ancient Elf, who turns out to be the legendary Celebrimbor. The two join forces in an effort overthrow the warchiefs of Mordor, regain Celebrimbor's memories, and avenge the deaths of Talion's family.
The biggest selling point that Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor houses is its unique Nemesis system. At the time of original release, nothing else like it had been created, and nothing like it has come since. Essentially, while gamers duke it out against Orcs in Middle-Earth, they can run in to various Orc warchiefs, captains, and other special foes who each have their place within the roster of Sauron. Defeating one of these enemies weakens Sauron's army, but their place will be taken as time goes on; creating a never-ending cycle of Orcs to slaughter. If players are killed by a special Orc, or run away from one in battle, they will remember the player and call them out, along with their previous actions, on the next encounter. It's a deeply detailed system that deserves praise and recognition for its innovation; it should also be noted that it took me over 20 hours of play time to see any Orc twice.
The remainder of the game, however, is extremely overhyped, lackluster, somewhat frustrating, and at times boring. Whether you're a casual lover of Lord of the Rings, or an Elvish-speaking super-fan, the story is as mediocre and basic as it can get; guy sees his family killed, guy goes to avenge his family, guy has startling revelation, good guy wins, the end. As a character, Talion is underwhelming in all aspects, and his fleshing-out is very shallow. This leaves Celebrimbor to pick up the slack, which he does very well since he's a protagonist that's already deeply involved in the lore from Lord of the Rings. There are also huge chunks of the plot missing, more often than not when a cutscene occurs it feels as though something has been missed or played out of order. Random, second-rate characters appear out of nowhere, or so it would seem; unless one has ventured to gather, and listen to, all of the nearby artifact collectibles.
WB Games and Monolith did a wonderful job of taking the older, unpolished, and somewhat broken fighting mechanics from their Batman titles and implementing it into Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor, along with the parkour running and climing from Assassin's Creed II. Effectively, all of the controls in the game feel like a meshing of these two franchises, which can only leave them to be described as clunky at best, and annoyingly cumbersome at worst. Combos are dropped on the regular despite having pressed the appropriate counter-attack buttons, Talion climbs when he's not supposed to and doesn't climb when he needs to, and the amount of button mashing that's present will surely heighten anyone's thumb stamina. It's obvious that when it comes to mechanics, all of the developer's resources went in to the aforementioned Nemesis system.
Comparatively speaking, the size of Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor's world was on par for 2014, though it's significantly smaller in terms of todays titles; especially after the release of The Witcher 3. The game is split up into two maps, each of which have their own missions and collectibles. When it comes down to missions, there are a total of 20 for the main story, 24 for rescuing slaves, and 10 each for upgrading Talion's bow, dagger, and sword. The ones that offer the most diversity, of course, are the missions that revolve around the main story. Other than that, rescuing slaves and upgrading the weapons become exhaustingly repetitive; sneak in here, cut that guy down, repeat 3-7x, or use your bow/sword/dagger to kill X number of Orcs in X way in X amount of time without being seen/triggering an alarm.
Even traversing the maps becomes burdensome over time, and completely aggravating on occasion due to the constant and massive amount of Orcs that are present in nearly every corner. I remember at one point I was fending off some 20-30 Orcs just as I was trying to get from Point A to Point B to pick up an artifact item, and among the horde were 7... yes, SEVEN, special Orcs; needless to say I got slaughtered. Battles can rage from 30-60 minutes easily, especially if one Orc slips away to call for backup, without there being any reason for them to; just due to the sheer density of AI opponents. Forget about taking down warchiefs and the gazillions of enemies that rear their ugly, green heads at that point. The fact that the combat mechanics aren't even good makes this aspect a hundred times more infurating than it needed to be.
Overall, Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor provides a very underwhelming, repetitious, and shallow gaming experience. The title was purposfully overhyped by YouTube content creators who were given free copies of the game on a promise that they would talk positively about it; not to mention the mainstream media over-sensationalization of it. Therefore, there are people that will defend this game to their dying breath. Sure, it's not the worst game ever created, but it's far from the best, and the main selling point (the Nemesis system) is buried within awful combat mechanics and terrible parkour controls. There are a decent amount of upgrades, abilities, and weapon runes to unlock and find, but even this semi-RPG aspect does not help the title to deviate away from its hollow feel. Players that enjoy open world games with an endless supply of battles will probably enjoy themselves the most here, while all others are recommended to look elsewhere for entertainment.

Well, the film wasn't entirely what I'd hoped for (maybe in a sequel someday, it'll get the Mulan-like war tale it deserves!), but me being into Scottish culture (plus the Scots got the best accents in the world bar none), I loved all the Scottish elements and loved Merida as a strong, independent female, so overall, really liked the film to pick this game up on Xmas sale!
The game takes some liberties from the film for gameplay purpose, so we get to explore a lil' more of (a stylized) Scottish/Gaelic nature, outside the films (like the Causeways I guess reminisce Fingal's Cave).
Gameplay:
Knowing that this game was made for kids... I jumped into playing this game on the most difficult "Brave" setting (enemies have way more health and you die in 2-3 hits), so my review is in this context. Even then, it is pretty easy... particularly since you may find one of your arrow attacks extremely overpowered for practically all enemy types (despite them having elemental weaknesses to certain elemental arrows).  On this difficulty, some of the bosses do prove a genuinely difficult challenge though, as you die in 2 hits, and fight a giant creature on a crowded stage. You might die a lot in Dark Souls kinda way then. (I wanna add, to avoid any disappointment like I felt - no, you won't really get to fight Mor'du =( )
Level designs are linear, but are never really boring either... they're just the right length, I'd say.
You do have to suspend your disbelief a bit in some of Merida's skills... they gave her a double jump (*groan* at this trope, but it's useful given the wonky camera angles) and ninja/parkour wall jumps. And as skilled an archer as she is, she doesn't nock her arrows, just fires them quickly like a gun (holding the fire button, charges your arrows for elemental multi-shots).
I like that you can upgrade your skills though, it has a slight, light-RPG feel to it... you won't get everything by the end of the game either. There is a Co-Op feature where a second player can play as a wisp. I didn't play with a friend, but experimented with it via keyboard a bit, and it reminds me a little bit of Tails in the classic Sonic games (game stays fixed on Merida; Wisp doesn't die, and can teleport back to Merida if lost).
There are small sequences you play as Merida's bear mum, where you just rampage and slaughter as many enemies as possible. It's not that fun, and controls are clunky too, but they're fortunately super short and easy. There are also short puzzles where you play as Merida's triplet brothers on each level. They are also super easy (designed for kids, after all). Fortunately, you can skip them when you revisit a stage too.
Controls:
Definitely recommended to play with a controller - controls are fairly solid! An enemy-lock on feature could've been nice, maybe, but you are quite busy running and dodging a variety of enemies. Could've been nice for bosses though. One of the control features I REALLY like that is kinda unique, is that you can fire at any direction you point via Right Analog Stick.
Camera isn't bad... but there are times when it could be much better, especially when platform jumping (you'll need to use your shadow for context on where to properly land; there is no falling to your death, you simply quickly "teleport" back up with a little loss of health... so not a big deal), or hunting for secrets beyond the scope of the camera angles. It's also sorta problematic in boss fights when you move Merida "up" the stage, and your boss stays to the foreground, you can lose sight of your target entirely and could easily be killed for not seeing an incoming attack. That said, the fixed cameras otherwise do offer some nice cinematic feeling to the landscapes.
Art Direction (Graphics/Sound):
Scenery is pretty, very lush and green (even if not super detailed) and loosely represent Scottish/Gaelic landscapes (though linear designs means none of the open Highlands). Character models, however, are not so great. Merida looks a bit unfinished, with these unintentional tired, baggy eyes. Bears look like plastic toys (not furry). I enjoy some of the cinematic hand-drawings (though they are limitly animated).
No real complaints on sound design, I enjoy the cinematic orchestral Celtic music, which are soaring and adventurous. Kelly Macdonald reprises her role, which is wonderful (because I love her and her voice!).
Overall:
It's a fun, fairly solid kid's adventure/platformer game, even despite some shortcomings, and I recommend it too if you liked the movie... if you're an avid gamer, play it on "Brave" difficulty. Again, not hard, but the bosses pose a genuine challenge.

When you were in the older facilities in the original game, you can hear cave johnson say that the test may include trace ammounts of time travel. I'm not sure weather the person who came up with this spin-off had that in mind or what but if you ask me, it's not needed.
At the very begining, it replays the ending scene from portal 2 where you're let out of the facility and GLaDOS gives you an  older-looking companion cube. Then it skips to a scene where you see a crow fly into some screens that create the illusion of  the outside world.
When the whole gameplay had started the screens that layed on the floor were extremely bright and put a large strain on my eyes. When you get into the first actual test chamber the instrictions that are on the screen were not detailed at all. It had illistrated that all you needed to do was press the "F" key in order to use the "Time Machine" but in fact, you need to press "R" first and then press "F". And during that tedious experiance, i had not used the portal gun once at all. The main concept is about time travel. After that, I played the next test chamber and got bored with the concept then just deleted it entirly.

(Before we start, I’d like to mention that this is a free mod, but it does require Portal 2 first)
Hello close friends and strangers of the internet, I'm back to review possibly my favourite thing in the world at the moment. This is a fan made mod created by a steam user named “Strideman” (My favourite person in the universe) and published by “SignHead Studios” (My favourite publishing company.) Seriously though, I wasn't even an hour into this game before i decided to review it.
The storyline is quite basic. GLAdos was overpowered by Atlas and Peabody (The robots featured in Portal 2’s cooperative mode) and forced Chell to reside in Aperture. However, apon reciving a message recorded by GLAdos telling her to find a time travel device to go back and warn GLAdos so they would both survive. but instead of just adding more maps, they implemented a time travel mechanic!
The time travel mechanic is mind-boggling, making the simplest puzzles take a long time to comprehend and interpret. Firstly, you must record certain movements using the time travel device. When your recording is finished, you can activate the recording, and you can interact with this recording. For example, if the recording held picked up and held a cube, you could take the cube from it. This allows for unique puzzle design.
I’m so glad that this thing exists. Portal needed more mechanics, and I just wasn’t satisfied with the additions of gels, light bridges and anti grav tunnels, (Because, ya know.
). This is just what the game needed. I’m willing to look passed the graphics and the bugs because the execution is so incredible, and it’s a fan-made mod that’s free! It just fills a hole inside me that I didn’t realise I had.
The only problem I had with this game was that it was too short. I finished it within 108 minutes (No, that’s not a challenge because I wasn’t speed-running it and I spent 20 minutes on the level with the stairs. I just did not get the concept to that ♥♥♥♥ing level!) I enjoyed every minute I played it (All 108 of them.) It’s understandable considering it’s a free, fan-made mod with (presumably) a limited budget.
What I’m trying to say is, if you have Portal 2, YOU NEED TO GET THIS RIGHT AWAY (AND I MEAN NOW!!!) and if you haven’t got Portal 2 yet, what’s wrong with you, why haven’t you gotten it yet. GO, FLY MY CHILDREN FLY!!!
Okay, that’s all from me. Be sure to leave a like and a comment, regardless of what it says. I’ve gotta get back to ‘dem puzzles, ‘do, so I’ll see you all next time.
Oh wait, I totally forgot. 10/10, would recommend.
Thanks for reading.

The mid-line invasion rule makes the games shorter and more intense and often result in heated battles around the chess boards mid-line. The game feels very balanced, there are no best or worst army.
If you don't like chess or think you are bad at it I would still encourage you to try this game, I think it feels different enough that you might enjoy it even if you don't like normal chess. Also, if you are bad at chess you will feel right at home here, we are all starting from scratch and are trying to figure out how to play this game ;) However, I think you get better at normal chess by playing this game so this might be something for someone who want to get better at normal chess as well.
If nothing else I would recommend this game so you can learn the rules and play it with a physical chess against your friends because it is a really fun chess variation when you get the hang of the new rules. I was quite skeptical in the beginning, especially about the bidding and the new armies but it actually works and fits really nice together. So do yourself a favor and try this strategy game, the worst thing that can happen is that you don't like it :)

This review contains spoilers
'Night in the Woods,' or, Bitter Disaffected Millennial Simulator 2017.
This is a game about Mae, a cat-person who drops out of college in mysterious circumstances, instead going back home to Possum Springs, an ailing town where nobody is happy. It's a game about mental illness and rust belt malaise, except instead of all that it turns out there's just a Lovecraftian cosmic horror jacking everything up.
Some of the characters, like badboy Gregg and Mae's entirely-too-patient parents, are charming. Others, like Mae, are borderline infuriating at times. Still others are dull ciphers who offer little. Sadly, even the best characters can be irritating. I have a hard time understanding why all these early 20s people are still ambling about smashing cars with bats and misspelling everything they write. They're written like preteens rather than college-aged youths.
If you personally identify with the main character's anxiety over her lack of direction in life, I could see the story appealing to you. Even still, the character's backstory is exposition dumped at the end in a very unsatisfying way. And the overarching murder plot is, as alluded to above, resolved very suddenly and in a manner not at all consistent with the rest of the game.
The gameplay is functionally minimal, aside from a couple of decent mini games. The presentation, on the other hand, is phenomenal. The game might be worth its price on the strength of its art alone, which is fortunate since it had very little else to offer.

I've played every iteration and patch of this game, minus the original arcade release (and even the beta Ultra release while in Japan), and would say this is my favorite iteration thus far. The balance is as good as it has ever been, while supporting many different playstyles. This version is a love letter to fans of SF4. Tons of content (arcade mode, trials, robust training mode) for those who shy away from playing online or with a friend, or even competitively.
Having said that, some fighting game fans have a hard time enjoying this one. I would be willing to be this is in regard to mid to high level competitive play. Casual fans of fighting games will find a lot to enjoy. The other issue, as of writing this, is that the online scene has all but faded away. Ranked matches will be your only way of finding competition unless you already know a group of active online players. The player base has moved on to SF5, I suspect.
Regardless of what the online scene looks like, this is one of the most solid entries in the series.  Super Turbo and 3rd Strike players would hate me for saying this, but I honestly think Ultra belongs on the same pedestal.

This is the game that pretty much single-handedly restarted the current renewed interest in fighting games, and it's easy to see why. It's a really smooth and challenging reboot of the series, and every update to the core game has added so much more new content. This final version has *44* characters, which is insanely awesome (if a little overwhelming). It feels like every character has been given so much love and attention, and a lot of care and thought has gone into balance and playability. If you want to get back into Street Fighter after having been away for a few years; if you want to learn more about the whole fighting game world so you can participate in the community; or if you just want to play a really solid and well-balanced fighter, this game is a great budget alternative to Street Fighter V.
I would point out, though, that the game is *tough* to master and has a pretty steep learning curve. It's slow-paced and it takes a while to get into the proper rhythm. The art style is also rather ugly. The 2D portraits on the character select screen/VS screen are really great and stylish, but the 3D models are chunky and kind of hideous. It's hard to look at this game after growing up with Capcom's 2D masterpieces like Street Fighter III and the Alpha series. The new characters are also visually boring and they don't have the same stylistic "oomph" that makes the original cast so memorable (though I admit that Juri and C. Viper have grown on me). On the other hand, while the graphics may not be beautiful, the game can run on even low-power, toaster-class systems, which seems like a fair trade-off.

Stranded deep was released in 2015. It has been three (technically two) years now, and I have decided to give it a new review. My verdict is that this game is a solid negative.
The game itself is fun for the first two hours of gameplay, then just gets really stale. You just travel from island to island searching for more plant fibers that are so rare and precious on small islands, and almost everything requires them.
I first played this game in 2015, and I must say it was rather fun. I racked up around 20 hours (steam is buggy with the hour count) before I finally got bored and stopped playing. Back then, I just loved the feel of the game. You crafted stuff by combining things in the physical world, rather than most games where you just collect then click a button and there ya go. I find it really added to the immersion and fun to the game. Back then, there were only around 4 or 8 inventory slots, so you had to use actual physical space to store things and travel around with them. (stocking up your life raft with coconuts, ah the fond memories) But nowadays they got completely rid of that mechanic, what made it feel unique in its own way. Now you just collects things to push a button, or carry around stuff in your 15-slot backpack. I really liked how you needed to choose what to take with you on a voyage, but now that that mechanic is gone, planning itself is also completely gone, which really sucks. I also remember the dangers of heading out into the ocean, fighting off fearsome sharks and other poisonous little monsters. But now it seems that those dangers of the water and been completely removed. I played a full 4 hours of gameplay and had not seen one shark. Sharks used to be such a cool and fun thing to deal with, but now for some reason I have not seen one and it really ♥♥♥♥ing sucks. It seems that the devs keep on removing what made this game feel unique and adding stuff in that just make it blend in with the rest of these types of survival games, and it really sucks.
Not only that, but since 2015 nearly nothing has been added to the game. I explored around the archipelago for many hours searching for new content, and all I really found was some new menu's, tools, building options and some other minor stuff like a speargun. The only interesting content I really found that was added since I had last played was bigger rocky islands with some pigs that give like two or so meat, and raft building that really only speeds up how fast you can travel from place to place, plus it is extremely expensive just for one foundation. Like 8 lashings for one foundation which is an insane amount. That is literally like an entire small islands worth of lashings. It seems like the devs just want to remove important stuff, then add not-so-important stuff to the game. And it really sucks, cause this game has a lot of potential if the devs just take it to greener pastures.
TL;DR:
Devs remove things that are essential to the game, add in ♥♥♥♥♥♥ things to replace those things then wait another two months to do it again. Development had almost went backwards in time since the release of the game. Game still gets super boring in almost two hours of playtime even though this is a game that has been around for almost two years now. The game also revolves around a new resource of plant fibres which is required for almost everything now and is not very renewable. They removed a lot of the planning of survival and all that and replaced it with some cheap inventory slots too. Just avoid unless development picks up.
Positives:
- Good graphics and glorious framerates (sometimes)
- Guaranteed fun for around two hours (then gets stale real fast)
- Some fun aspects (most removed)
Negative
- Devs seem to be taking the game back in time when it has no past
- Most fun and fundamental aspects of the game have been removed or made into some way that makes it♥♥♥♥♥♥
- Most of the features that made the game unique like having to plan out trips or crafting stuff on the ground with your own hands etc. etc. have been removed.
- Development is going on two years now and all it has done like I said is just go back in time or remove good aspects of the game. The only real content that has been added is a new type of island with 1 new type of animal on it, some new tools, some new building stuff and raft building. Keep in mind that the development has been going on for two years now and this is the meat of what it has to show.
- Gets stale easily in two hours, but still two hours of guaranteed fun
- New really ♥♥♥♥ing annoying sounds
- Even if you wait two years to buy the game it will probably still be close to the same as it always was.
- Game is now a annoying grindfest for materials because of the way plant fibres were implemented.
TOTAL RATING: 4-3/10 It's still a semi-fun game however it really gets boring really fast. Development is also slow as a snail covered in traditional canadian molasses. Maybe in 6+ years it will be worth a shot? But by then I doubt anyone will actually be playing this game. Untill then, save your money for something else.

I am not sorry i got this, but I only recommend it to those with an intelectual interest in chess variants.
It is a decent attempt to break the hold chess theory has on the game for the last 100 years. Chess960 (or Fischer Random Chess) did this to a lesser extent, breaking only the hold of opening theory. This one goes a bit further, adding new sets of pieces, new rules of movement for each set or piece, new mechanics for capture and adding the new victory condition of the king crossing the middle line. From the prespective of a chess fan, this is mind expanding, and liberating. It remains to be seen if there will be opening books for the different chess sets and so on. So, IF you are interested, buy it and study the proposal. Think of the experience as an interactive book on chess variants.
Be warned, however. The AI is very poor. You will probably be able to beat the game very soon on single player. And it doesn't contain or allow for a normal chess engine, so you can't play normal chess with this software (or any other of the many other chess variants out there, for that matter). This software is good IF you become interested in exploring this variant, and even then you will have to go multiplayer.

If I had to describe this game in one word, it would be beautiful. Not exclusively the aethetics themselves (though they are lovely), it's the story presented here as well the message. Now I won't go into specifics so that the person reading this (if anyone actually does) can experience it themselves. However what I will talk about is how this game actively presents a sympathetic and relatable narrative. The characters despite the simplicity in their design (and well being animals) feel like they have real emotions rather than static feelings like many other games do. Every character has a wonderful arch throughout the story and they feel genuine. The game also touches heavily upon emotional turmoil faced by many growing up into the modern society such as the fears of adult life in an uncaring world. However overall the message is what drives this home for me. The way in which it is woven into the story, often relying on callbacks to earlier events in the plot and earlier events in the characters' lives which stay mostly shrouded up until the end. It presents powerful ideas about the reasonings behind why we choose to live life each day, and why we don't just stop and breakdown. (Again trying to be vague here but it's really hard) Look if you have suffered through my ramblings enough, hopefully there is one thing you can gather from it, play this game, those in their teens and young adult life will be able to easily relate to it and for those of older age, it provides a sympathetic look into the thought processes of those younger than you or maybe even your own children who are going through that age right now. Life during that age is tough and those seeking insight into rather it than lambasting someone for the decisions they make at the teeanage and young adult ages, then this is a good look into it. (however you should still probably have a good discussion about the stresses and fears said person is going through, hell a game can't give you all the answers) So overall I highly reccomend this game, and hope you play it. If this review has made you think about playing this game, then I am glad to be of service.

State of Decay was a very fun game to play but like every other game, it has its pros and contras.
Let me first state the good things about this game:
- Open World and basically no senseless restriction of where you can't go
- A lot of playable characters available
- A lot of weapons (from the frying fan to the UZI)
- A lot of upgrades and possibilities to change/fortify the moveable base/fort (outposts, med, cook, and so on...)
- Realistic day and nightshift changing the situation and action of the game
- Available cars to use (from small to sports car)
- Unique places to visit (Forests, small town, camps and even ranches with a broad area)
- Different Zombie types (so called Freaks)
- Soundtrack fits the atmosphere giving it a nice touch
- Beautiful atmosphere and graphics
- Very nice combat gameplay (and the option to be stealthy and kill enemies from behind)
- Items all over the map and every house open for entry
Bad things would be:
- Not enough unique missions (over the time you tend to get to do things over and over again)
- Voice acting is ok BUT the speeches from optional missions of nearly EVERY character repeat and are absolutely the same with few exceptions (recommend playing with own music in the background)
- The game is far too easy, little to no challenge is provided (except if you are without supplies)
- Travelling long distances to fulfill missions which are far away from the base (recommended: use of a car)
- Story is too unspectacular (easy to guess)
- (Open) Ending is dissapointing
Final Verdict:
All in all the game still works fine and you have alot of freedom in the gameplay but there is the high risk of getting bored too fast because of lack of intensive story and mission content.

This game is just like Magical Diary - except it's much more chaotic, unforgiving, unbalanced and - ultimately - not fun,
In both games you're building up skills that should then help you to deal with different events the game tosses at you. Main difference - in MD you could make a character with almost any set of skills, and it would usually work fine, except for losing some plot opportunities. Like, choosing different schools of magic would alter your experience, but whatever your choice had been, you'd always get something useful. There's balance between having freedom to do what you want and having to prepare for the challenges ahead.
On the contrary, in Long Live The Queen if you didn't upgrade a certain enigmatic skill like "Dogs" or "Meditation" at a certain point - it's a guaranteed game over.  And since you've got no bloody idea what skill will the game check next, your only option is to make a dozen saves and constantly switch between them. And with the mood mechanic, that makes it even harder to switch from one skill tree to another when needed, most of the time you'll have to go way back in order to make things right in time. This kind of tedious trial and error is forced onto you, making the experience extremely frustrating.
Overall, it's been a huge disappointment. Although just like in other Hanako Games titles, there's a nice branching story with lots of possible outcomes to any situation. But since the game punishes you so hard for making mistakes, you can't even enjoy the nonlinearity - most choices will lead to your death one way or another, so all you can think about is how to make the exact right decision and survive another week. And while i like challenging games, it's definitely not something i'd want from a visual novel.

Ultra Street FIghter IV has great graphics and overall aesthetics.
But its nothing more than a competitive fighter. There's little meat on the bones of this game and if you want anything else out of it, aside from multiplayer, you're going to find better options elsewhere.
The main problem with fighting games, nowadays, is that the developers focus everything into balancing the characters and designing the game around its multiplayer component. I understand that these games have a huge draw from competitive gamers but there is a lot lost in appealing to this demographic.
I'm not recommending a purchase for this game because it just isn't that much fun as a casual gamer.

With Killer Instinct the characters are far more interesting, and there is a lot more to do aside from competitive play (and with the new ShadowLords mode you can play for a LONG time without ever going into multiplayer). Soul Calibur 3 also has loads of content outside competitive play as does Mortal Kombat 9.
My point is, there are better options out there. This would be something worth getting only if it is on sale for really cheap,  or if you're a diehard fan of competitie fighters. If you casually enjoy fighting games look elsewhere. There are better options.

Gorky-17 is a sci-fi horror-themed turn-based tactics game. Imagine Resident Evil 1 with combat system from Incubation. The atmosphere of the abandoned city is great and resembles STALKER series somehow, the turn-based combat is fun and varied with lots of status effect that can be inflicted on enemies. There are some easy puzzles and even some deegree of nonlinearity to the plot (one of the secondary characters can be saved or not, while the other one is killed no matter what you do). The leveling up system is lacking and I didn't see any difference when dumping points into a skill, but it's probably the only bad thing I can say about the game.
I'd like to remember what made the game popular in Russia at the time of the release. Russian version was more of an adaptation than translation - they changed a lot of names and plot details. For example, the main character trio became Russian, Ukrainian and Estonian who serve in Russian MES (Ministry of Emergency Situations). And then there was an official "funny" translation named Gorky-18, where they changed all the names and all the plot again, now adding a lot of humor of varying quality.
It is still fondly remembered as one of the first foreign games officially published in Russia. It was published in jewel cases without the manual (which was new for the time) and the retail price was equal or cheaper than the pirated CDs. Ok let me start out by saying that I love LOTR. I first read the Hobbit in the 4th grade back in 1987-88. I fell in love. Ive read the trilogy about 100 times..lol...and The SILMARILLION just as many times. I used to be obsessed and I still am to a certain point. With that said, I am a YUGE fan.
So let me say that I write this review with a biased towards LOTR. I will try to be as honest and brief as possible.
First, the game graphics and engine are AMAZING! Everything looks so good and each orc is unique. Images are crisp and detailed. The only problem that I enevtually realized is is that every area is EXACTLY the same but with different skins. It seems maybe the devs just got lazy? Or were rushed? There are no different shapes or buildings, just the same building with different drapes or different colored moss. Some minor detail changes here and there but nothing major or challenging. Looks amazing but gets boring after a while.
That brings me to second, the gameplay. At first the gameplay is really fun and challenging but once you master a few zones and level up, it becomes repetitious. Fun still but tedious none the less. Same challenges like kill x amount of captains, brand x amount of warchiefs, etc etc etc...They break up the monotony by throwing in different characters and creatures but your ealize its the same missions over and over with different labels. Once again, fun for a while but becomes tedious. Fun but feels like youve been there done that.
Fighting is cool, similar to Assassins creed and ROME. Enemy AI is hit and miss and once you learn how to fight and equip the perks, things get easy. Thats not to say that there arent some extremely tough captains and warchiefs, a few I still have yet to beat. Each one has its own personalities and strengths/weaknesses but once again after a while of doing the same missions the battles begin to feel old and you just want to get back to the main story.
Nemesis forge. Seems good in theory but then you just realize its randomly generated orcs. I dont think there is much depth to that system as far as different specs for each orc or anything. Seems like it just kind of randomizes what happens based on strength. Cool but seems more "gimmicky". Im not saying its bad and in the future Im sure it will impriove greatly but my impressions werent very postive. Kinda "so so". Still cool tho
The "open world" is exciting, at first, but after a while it feels like the same thing over and over again. Looks great but you want to take a boat across the sea to find something new.
Im roughly %75 through the game and now I just want to conentrate on the main mission with maybe some side missions if Im feeling like spending some time. At first all I wanted to do was grind away at captains and warchiefs but now Im kinda over it and want to see the story. Which brings me to...
The story. Really interesting if you are a fan of the LOTR lore. Much story and depth went into Tolkiens writing and WB did some justice to that by exploring Celebrimbors past. It is good but seems a little rushed. Over all I really like it but as always am wanting more.
I give this game a 3/5 stars. If they would have put more into actually changing things up a bit instead of just slapping new coats of paint on the same worlds, I would have probably given it a 5/5. I still really like this game and I hope they have changed a few things with Shadow of War. Thats why I am playing this game now because I am thinking of buying SOW and I wanted to brush up on things.
So thumbs up with a little rant!

For sure a wonderful game! It brings a lot of fun to a concept I havent seen done this well in a long time. The game pits you against angry mobs of orcs and other mythical creatures and does it with simplicity and fun!
The game starts with a short story about why the orcs are attacking and so on and so forth. However from there you start. Orcs spawn from a single (or up to 4 locations later on) location and have one goal. Reach a predetermined  "door" if you will on the map, and beat the heck out of anything that stands between them and the objective. If too many enemies pass through the door you must retry the level.
You can choose between two characters. A male character or a female character. The male character comes equipped with a shot gun and his own set of default traps to throw off enemies with. The female caracter comes with a wand that you can shoot either lower power bolts from faster or shoot charged up high damage bolts that also have a short ranged knockdown effect on enemies around the enemy hit with it.
The game offers new traps,trinkets, and weapons avalible to your character iin the spellbook. The in game store that uses skulls as currency that you obtain through beating levels. Everything is upgradable and it's always fun to see what kind of damage you can do with an uprgraded trap or weapon.
Co-op is the name of the game for the best fun in this game. Grab a buddy and you two can stop the orcs together! It's the same concept as playing alone except for that you get to do it with a friend. For me it return my mind to a simpler time sitting in my parents living room ripping through a game with a freind. It's great fun!
The game also comes with an endless mode in which enemies spawn in an infinite number of waves. It adds a lot of replay value after a somewhat short campaign. (maybe 5 to 6 hours).
Put aside anydoubt and pick up this game if you think it looks good. It's a great buy and will give you lots of entertainment especially with the three DLC pack bringing new levels and weapons. An easy 9/10 for me!

Basically tumblr in "game" form. And I use the word "game" very loosely here because most of it is an irritating and boring walking simulator that barely even qualifies as a game, let alone an adventure game as they advertise it. At least the soundtrack is decent.

That should be its own separate game on Steam, because it doesn't belong here with the rest of the trite bullsh.it that is Night In The Woods.
There's also a music rhythm minigame which is interesting. Soundtrack is the better part of this "game."
The anthropomorphic animal world is interesting. I'll admit, it has a cute charm that made me want to keep going. The visual presentation is minimal but functional and unique. It goes downhill now. The characters and dialogue... ugh. The suburban, trash millenial speak is grating to read. Also nothing turns me off more than seeing weak, loser and queer type characters in games (EDIT: OH NO HE SAID QUEER! YOU HOMOPHOBIC B@STARD). Doesn't make it any better that they're part of your crew instead of just part of the world. If you hate melancholic teenage drama as I do, you won't like NITW. Especially Mae, the main character. She is insufferable (although in her favor, I found the little notes she scribbles on her journal to be quite adorable.) Such a shame that its appealing visual art style, atmospheric charm and nice soundtrack is overshadowed by the godawful writing and endless walking that makes you wish you were using the time to play something else. Don't even get me started on the dream sequences. If I haven't changed your mind by now, the dream sequences will. They are utterly pointless. Take walking and talking, but exchange the talking for searching for hidden things you need to progress further and MORE walking with zero explanation. Sound fun yet?
I don't necessarily mind narrative driven adventure games, but honestly, point-and-click games have more substance than this. Those offer challenging puzzles that require effort from the player to solve. This offers... not much, if at all. When I said walking simulator, I meant it. Literally all you do aside from side distractions like band practice, is walking and talking. Carting your miserable kitty from one dumb conversation to another to take in some message about the rough life. This "game" exemplifies my biggest gripe with putting narrative first and gameplay second. Basically nonexistent gameplay and preachy, pretentious sad millenial self-pitying narrative that has my eyes rolling and mental energy exhausted from having to put up with it. Thought people play games because they want to escape real life, not get more of it. On account of this review being too harsh, let me say that I understand what they were trying to go for with the melancholic mood. I got in with the Autumn vibe, thanks to the music and the environment. But the tone of the narrative sounds so wallowing, lamenting, immature and frankly whiny that it's hard to take seriously. It more has me wondering why I shelled out $15 to suffer this. The writer(s) try so hard to make the player, no, user, think like them. Maybe I wouldn't have half as minded paying for this if I could at least relate to the characters, which I just couldn't do. I can't be bothered to care about any of them because they're so one-dimensional. No matter how hard I tried, how patient I was, Night In The Woods would not let me like it. It's like forcing yourself to listen to someone ranting about their life problems on you.
Usually I don't review games until I'm done with them completely. This is an exception because I don't count this as a game and it's so mind numbingly boring to get through all of it. I'm on Part 3 at the time of writing. I'll play more to see if anything changes my opinion, but doubt it. Didn't leave a good first impression and didn't get better by now. EDIT: I'm done now. Still bad. There's bare minimum player interactivity in the climax and the end is just not worth it. That's all I'll say without spoiling anything for those somehow still interested. It's anti-climactic.
EDIT 2: Upon review of my own review, I thought I should be fair. So since I don't consider this a game in the traditional sense, let's compare it with other non-games instead of holding it up to the standard of a traditional game. Like visual novels. Phoenix Wright. Zero Escape. Even from the perspective of a player who enjoys story more than gameplay, it still sucks. Both of those VNs I mentioned have elements of suspense and mystery that delivers actual tension and anticipation, as opposed to NITW (minor spoilers) giving you a severed arm, filler, filler, lecture, filler, lecture, then investigation. For me, good gameplay usually makes up for subpar story. An excellent story sometimes makes up for subpar gameplay. But a story that makes the player want to skip through the dialogue and no gameplay can't make up for anything. It's just s.hit. That's the biggest risk with "narrative first, gameplay second." NITW fails on that risk because it offers no satisfaction or reward for doing anything.
I could have just said "this game is tumblr, do not buy" at the top of this review and left it off there, but I'm so disappointed and let down with the "Overwhelming Postitive" rating that I made an effort to go on about why I found it bad. Also as I pointed out before, I really wanted to like NITW. Eh, I'm pretty sure most of that is people who don't play much games and/or tumblrites that banded to promote this. Or I'll let myself believe that. Take my word for it - if you like fun games, avoid this.

Should have read the reviews before buying, because you can pretty much get the same boring experience for free on YouTube than playing it yourself. This is definitely not worth the price, so if you're still interested after reading this, head over to YouTube and save yourself $15 or $20, whatever it costs right now. I want to like this game so much. The ideas behind Chess 2 seem so good. So far Chess 2 seems like a great Chess variant.
The problem is that this particular implementation just seems unfinished. You can play Chess 2 against a horribly weak AI. You can play live in 25 minutes a side games and you can play Correspondence games. Your rating goes up if you win and down if you lose (presumably based on your opponents rating).
The game looks nice and bar a few crashes, plays smoothly. But there is so much missing that you would normally take for granted.
No rankings ! You can see your opponents rating and yours in game. Out of game you see...nothing. No win/loss ratios. No breakdown of each armies win/loss. No leaderboards!!!!
You cannot challenge a friend. You play against random opponents only.
For a game that's supposed to be all about multiplayer this is just unforgivable.
There are no options. You window resize (unless you edit the game launch properties yourself). The music is nice but you cannot turn it down. You cannot even turn it OFF !
Your games are saved for replay. There's no chess notation. You cannot view your opponents or your own previous moves.
Even the Steam Achievements are just so boring. Again, just ... barely ... there.
Mind boggling. If this was early access I'd give it some slack as the core of the game is there and it is great. But in 2014 the total lack of any features is crazy. Especially when you consider the price.
Hopefully the game can get some much needed support and thrive but we will have to wait and see.

Major review change to properly reflect the long-ago addition of multiplayer with Steam friends - now Recommended.
This is a fundamentally ingenious and fun game, and totally worth the modern price tag - $10 for one copy or $15 for two - but only if you have Steam friends that will play it with you. I recommend it to anyone who's ever seen even a little fun in classic Chess, and I especially recommend it to people who are frustrated that classic Chess proficiency relies too heavily on the memorization of optimal, routine movement patterns.
With six perfectly balanced "armies," including the classic set of pieces, as well as a couple new rules - dueling and victory by midline invasion - the strategic possibilities are too multitudinous to pre-plan your matches, requiring players to put more effort into getting into their opponent's heads.
The five new armies are easy to learn and discovering their quirks is great fun. For instance, the Reapers have a Reaper Queen instead of the regular one that can teleport almost anywhere on the board but cannot threaten the King, while their Rooks are replaced with Ghosts that can also teleport anywhere but they can neither capture nor be captured (making them into the perfect blockers). You can actually play Chess 2 with an ordinary Chess board without needing any additional pieces (except stones for dueling)!

So here comes my opinion (I'm sure I will repeat things written before, so I try keep it somewhat short and formal):
Pros:
- Good, and suprisingly dinamic, yet quite tactical TBS combat system: team, but not classed based fights - each three of your main character can use any weapon you find during the game, and they can freely switch those tools-of-the-trade between each other, even in the middle of the battles!
- The setting is good (sounds and visuals fit with the game's concept very well)
- There is characther development: you can gain attribute points and level up weapon skills - not much, but just enough,
- Challenging but still balanced: For the first playthrough this game can be...., no, it WILL be hard and hars on you in the battles - there will be a lot of "Oh, shi..." moments-, but the items you find while exploring will even the odds from time to time. Paying attention for attacking angles, support items, damages types and constantly keeping an eye on the supplies is important.
- The story is pretty good too. Don't expect extra sides of originalty, but it does it's work to keep things interesting,
- Voice-over is okay.
Cons
- Low replayability: in every playthrough is the same, the same battles with the same monsters, everything is in the same place - basically it's a one-stop-gamer for most of the gamers.
- Voice-over is okay, and talking between the characters lets you to pick up little details about then, but not it just fits in every time. The voice actors fall of the character from time to time. The conversations only occur during the cutscenes and the beginnings of the battles, and sometimes are quite inconsequential (for example in an battle with a lot of enemies, the characters are sarcastical and and ♥♥♥♥♥ure, yet in the next fight with against only two enemy the got paranoid and scared of dying. Not a big problem, but makes the image look worse.
- Gameplay mechanics are sometimes inconsequental and has bugs (only one damage-over-time effect can be active, the enemy has electricity protection yet can be tranquilitized with a shocker, and theres a game crashing bug in one of the battles, so here's the solution for that:
- For me it's a bit short. You can play through the whole game with every area explored, every enemies slain, and every item picked up under 15 hours.
Overall, Gorky 17 is a fine survival TBS/point-and-click hybrid game with semi-isometric graphics in a horror-sci/fi setting. It's mixing the genres well. It has it's flaws, yes, but it makes up for it as well.
And also, I warn everyone to use discretion: If the game seems a little bit outdated, old, antiquated... well, it is. This game is originally came out in 1999, as the descprition says, in an age when Pentium III/IV processors, GeForce 256 video cards,  1280x1024 monitor resolution and DVD discs were the BIG things and the WinXP was still in development.
In the release year, this game was a fine product őf technology, but sadly stayed under the radar. However, up to this day this game still has a small, but sturdy fanbase, and three or four year ago there was an announcement of a sequel for this game under the name of Gorky 21. (sadly again, not much can be heard about it since then)
In my opinion, if this game had the random encounter system at least, and some random-generated terrain between the key locations. it would become a classic cult game. like the original Fallout series. Well, not exactly on the same level, but close enough.
All in all, I totally recommend this old, yet pretty and shiny pearl of gaming to everyone who won't turn down an old game, looks for a bit different TBS experience and likes if a game challanges them to weight and plan their every action,

*** When you start this game select the simplest graphics driver you have and select the zoggle to "not to allow zoom" and the game will run perfectly. Even on Win 8.1 + ***
Personally not a game for me, but if you like this kind of classic setting and turn based attack battles this is perfect for you.

This game is punishing. It can be brutal, agonizing, and downright cruel, and yet I can do nothing but give it my highest recommendation.
There are very few areas I can really find fault with. The worst parts by far (in my opinion) are any places with tight, easy to fall off ledges. Even though that's basically a quarter of the game (possibly more) and stands testement to how truly diabolical the level designers are, I still can't bring myself to hate any part of it. Carelessness is your biggest enemy, and one wrong step against even the weakest foes can result in death. That asside, if you can keep your composure and balance dodging, attacking and healing, this game is a treasure trove of hidden upgradable weapons, wonderful maps and gruesome, dark boss fights.
There is no happy ending. There is noone to be saved, no real storyline that you have to follow closely. Just a lonely fight against an unrelenting horde, trying your best to survive and push forward. This game, arguably the best from the "Souls" franchise, is perfect for anyone looking for a good challenge.
Just don't be surprised if you throw away your game controller several times before the end...
(Oh, an important/ more objective note: you will want a gamepad - USB wired Xbox360 controller is my preference. This game is not designed for keyboard & mouse, and really suffers for it if you don't own a gamepad. That's probably the biggest criticism I personally can think of, but yes, I am heavily biased.)

Punishing and frustrating, this game is designed to improve your threshold for rage quitting in a dark, undead setting.
I'd recommend getting DSFix at least to get decent graphics resolution, and some of the other more popular mods for the UI and PVP shennanigans. A controller is pretty much mandatory (I've hooked my PS3 one up and works well as an XBox 'lookalike') - K+M works, but is unbearable to me in this particular game.
A definite feeling of accomplishment as you bash your head through each stage and work out the tricks. Combat is more a tactical approach than a button-mashing fest - if you do mash the buttons you'll get swatted down pretty quickly. Very little hand-holding, if any, beyond some tutorial messages in the early zone, it reminds me of more old-school games where you were thrown into things, and progressing through the game feels more of an accomplishment as a result.
If you have high blood pressure it may not be for you.
Big penalties for messing up, but you get insane rewards, and some classes are very awesome!!! Awesome environments, mechanics, and awesome tactical game 9/10

State of Decay - Around 12 hours logged - I want to Love this game!  I give it 7 out of 10.  I recommend based on my review but read the Cons here to make up your own mind.  I might also say I'm tempted to go with a ten but the Cons in my opinion bumb me out pretty good so far with an emphasis on the game causing me to always get to the suicide scavenger point.  Cons:  Repitition of zombie bashing, car crashing and fetching.  At least make it more interesting to do these thing or find a way to lower the amount of repitition.  Random feel in the details of the game are missing where all farmers pretty much drive the same farm truck and all the new trucks either come in orange or brown. There is no looting of corpses which would make sense in this game including in obtaining weapons, ammo and armor. Many  visible items in the world would not be left behind by real survivalists. Ironically homebase needs beds and while I have a truck and see them in every home.  We are short on beds.  Perhaps put in a situation where players can stash stuff in the field for later pickup via mass transport or where another community member does the hauling.  Car collecting also requires a lot of walking to get them.  You should be able to have you companion return a car to homebase.  Changing between companions in the field would allow for more efficient looting.  Limitation in the use of vehicle space for hauling creates a unreal situation of excess fuel consumption and more repitition in driving/crashing.  Lacking the ability to save to recovery game at a prior point to a dead member of your community.  I understand the point of autosave but perhaps give people the option between autosave only, player save only or a combination thereof.  There is no easy method to gain trust, influence, recovery sleep or even stamina really.  All of these facilitate death by suicidal scavanging versus zombie play.   Base construction could be improved.  First base has tons of room but you are limit to building only two additions.  Might consider ways to upgrade the base to allow for more additions where there is room as something possible prior to relocation of homebase.  Controls for some items would seem confusing at best to a new player and perhaps some might go unlearned for sometime without a google assist. Weapon repair should be available in teh workshop.  I did not see that option.  Also item found should be useful in building things like table legs could be used to make tables ot bedframes.  Apparently people still must like you as a friend at the end of the world to help you scavenge for supplies to feed everyone.  lol  At what point do you just agree to work together for survival regardless?
Pros:  Originality, Nice infusion of various game types (Car Racing, Crash Derby, Survival, Zombie Bashing, Ninja/Theaf, Community, etc) Good feel on driving but why would classic sports cars feel more like a blimp than the old station wagons?  Cars in the game look cool but lack a real world randomness to it.   For a game that feels so real in many ways it drops the ball on things like this. Your fairly safe at homebase but with zombies climbing fences everywhere how is that even possible?
I've not played the expansions so I have no idea if some of these items might have been addressed there.
OK After figuring out additional controls the game began to become more reasonable.  However the expansions appear to simply be a repeat of the original versus carring over you last game.  What?  So now I'm building up again over the area I've already covered in order to open additional spaces?  I like this game though as it has my creative, how could this game be turned into a masterpiece, wheels turning.  I'll change to 8 out of 10 for now.  Moving it up because the controls eventually made sense but not liking the failure to continue between versions.  This of course amplifies the repetitive nature of the game.
Whats the point? I did not like this game whatsoever.

I usually enjoy very immersive, sandbox-survival games for their realistic attributes. State of Decay is NOT meant to feel immersive and actually plays more like a strategy game in the way it looks and operates. Often you're less concerned with the character you're controlling and rather the community as a whole. You have to worry about sustaining the base's daily needs and seeing what you build to better accommodate and fortify your community. Additionally, there is only a third person. Overall, don't expect to feel any immersion similar to DayZ, 7 Days to Die, etc.
My biggest peeve by far though is the HUD. It's in the way, it's huge, and potentially blocks the view of approaching zombies. The icon's for certain locations show up everywhere when scouting and walking around.
The game claims it's open world and you can do whatever you want but often the people within your base either talk to you about current missions or don't talk at all. You're often steered very strongly into the missions rather than doing your own wandering. The game does have a linear plot for the most part but it doesn't feel like I have any real freedom.
I think if I went back and treated it like a strategy / city building simulation I would appreciate it more.

This game is really not an RPG. It is a sandbox shooter with some annoying flaws. The keyboard controls are very awkward on the PC. I had to switch all the controls to the NUM keypad to get it so I could do a decent button mash. Button mashing is pretty much what fighting strategy amounts to. It's probably much easier to play on a console. The weapon system is very skewed; some weapons like shotguns are mostly useless in the circumstances you will typically encounter. On the other hand, one of the best weapons in the game, a wrench, is available from the beginning. Use a wrench; you won't need anything else.The sudden death save is  another Microsoft opinion design, you don't matter but Microsoft does. As with all microsoft products, they try to design you into corners you don't want to be in for their own purposes. Anyone who has studied typology can see their style in this. They don't have any business telling me how to play games. (compare to Bethesda) It sucks, especially because the AI will occasionally just pop a super horde on you that you cannot escape or beat, so you will lose characters, no matter how good you are, unless you are very lucky. This means that you must play the game only to win, don't become attached to any characters. Once you know the story, it takes about five hours (average) to win the game, and you don't need to level any characters up to win. Leveling doesn't help you much but you will max without bothering over the course of the game. You cannot go out alone on quests or looting. You must take at least one partner, but if you do, there isn't anything in the game that is very challenging. However, if you go out alone you will soon be dead, because although they claim it is possible to avoid zombies with stealth characters that simply isn't true in the long run. Sooner or later one will spot you and once one spots you  the AI starts stacking pops on you really fast. But the game is so easy to beat if you take companions this just makes the whole thing kind of stupid. In other words the game play is very unbalanced.
On the upside it's fun to kill zombie hordes with cars and the graphics are not bad, although they are not great either. There is an unlimited number of zombies. You cannot clear areas. Setting aside that we should suspend our disbelief in any fantasy story, according to my calculation based on the number of domiciles shown on the map, you will have exceeded the number of humans buried in the area since pre European times (prior to which we must assume only dust is left) many times before the end of a a typical game. And they'll keep coming after that, so don't worry you can smash them til you get very tired of it. Anyway, since I was hoping there was a good story to the game, I am disappointed with it. And never trust Microsoft !!! Always tell the truth: Windows 8 sucks. That's all I got ta say.

Behind all the pink and cute lies a deep game of intrigue. Nobles may be plotting against you, foreign powers might invade, assassins are out there and your people can revolt. There's a whole lot of skills you can train to deal with them and survive until you become a queen.
Contrary to popular belief, I don't think it's hard to reach coronation day, especially when the game tells you which skills you need to succeed at events. Once you're familiar with the fatal events and how to avoid them, you're free to experiment with different skillsets, make different choices and see how events unfold. And that's what the game is all about: experimenting to see all the possible outcomes of events. Only over the course of multiple playthroughs you'll realize who's really on your side, who wants you dead and all the stuff happening behind the curtains. After 30 hours I still feel like I'm only scratching the surface.
Play like a fair and just leader who's only interested in the benefit of the people, a tyrant who'll execute anyone who looks at you funny or a scandalous ruler who only wants to romance the female nobles. It's all up to you.
At the end of the day however, this is a visual novel/life-sim hybrid. None of the above will matter if you don't enjoy this kind of game. Try the demo first and see if you like it.
