Chess 2 takes the classic game of chess and adds in a bunch of new armies and it's own flavor of new rules. Chess players should feel right at home, as chess 2 still keeps true to it's heritage. Besides a selection of armies to play as, one of the most significant rule addition is the new median line. Any king that passes it wins, essentially adding a whole new win condition to the classic game of chess. Chess being an old as the hills game, the Sequel does a pretty good job at introducing new metas and strategies to really freshen up this ageless classic.
Visually the game goes with a realistic look. At first glance it may not have the visual impact of a more stylized game, but I think fans of chess will appreciate it's more sophisticated aesthetic. The pieces are well detailed with intricate trimmings and most importantly off all, the new pieces look like they belong in chess, and describe's it's characteristics well.
Though Chess 2's core is strong and enjoyable, it's not with out it's flaws. There are serious "quality of life" issues with the game. The lack of any sort of options, visual, audio, or even a menu is very odd. Even 8bit games have an options menu so I don't understand why Chess 2 doesn't. The game also focus on it's multiplayer. Though there is online play, there is no lobby system, no way to match with your friends currently. This is a huge over sight for a game like this. The devs did mention that they have an update planned for some sort of match making, which is great to hear, but it is missing on it's release so keep that in mind.
Overall Chess 2 is a wonderful game that will have veterans giggling like school girls, delighted at the discovery of new metas. For chess fans, this is an easy recommendation, but if you are just the regular gamer, curious to chess 2, with out more features or an options menu, it's always good to do more research.
Pros:
- Discovery of new metas
- Armies are interesting and unique
- Appropriate and detailed visuals
- New rules are enjoyable
- Still feels like chess, but new!
Cons:
- No options
- No Lobby
- Low on features

To Chess Players:
If you're more of a tactics player (short term captures and plans), you'll enjoy this game. Chess 2 (C2) is a much more fast-paced and unpredictable game than traditional Chess. C2 has 6 armies to choose from (there is the classic Chess army, but also new armies with unique units & movesets), and you can face any of them from your opponent, so games will have very diverse matchups each time. There are also 2 ways to win: Getting your king past midline and checkmate. This ensures games are faster and have less draws. But with the midline invasion rule, it is very "race-to-win"; there are less quiet moves, less subtle improving moves to a better position, less strategic play. Rather, its more just a string of tactical plays IMO.
Knowledge of Chess can help you in C2, but it will only help you so far. You can throw most chess rule-of-thumbs out the window, as there are new pieces with new rules. Controlling the center is good, but controlling the sides is also important as the king usually tries to flank to one side to invade midline instead of going into the center where he'll be mated. Castling early and often is actually a bad move. Fianchetto is waste of tempo, as bishops are on a better diagonal from their starting position. Knights are usually better in C2 because its usually semi-closed or closed positions. And because of that, rooks are usually worse pieces because the position is closed, but also because you castle less often providing less exits for your king rook. However, pawn majority in center is still important (if not even more important), and also the knight on the rim is still grim :-)
If you liked Chess because of same teams and starting off on even foot, you might dislike the 6 different teams. They are balanced, but are balanced in a bubble (as in they are balanced with respect to Classic Chess army, but some have advantage/disadvantage versus each other). It's a case of Perfect Imbalance (Two Kings army>Reaper>Nemesis>Two Kings). So you might dislike the fact that your army performs better/worse versus the enemy team, but it is is only slight advantage. But this provides opportunity for each game and opening to be very unique. Another factor in the game is the duel system (betting system). Whenever a piece is captured, you can bet against your opponent for the fate of the unit doing the capturing (that unit will also be removed if you lose the bet). This duel system was implemented for mind games, but it is only wild guessing IMO. It is like rock paper scissors, the player that picks his weapon by thinking 7 moves ahead is just as good as the player thinking only 4 moves ahead or 1 move ahead. Although there are limits to the betting system (you only gain betting stones by destroying an enemy pawn), and it is more complicated than I give it credit for, it is still for the most part an arbitrary system.
Overall, I would recommend C2 to chess players, because of its familiarity to Chess but also because it brings new life and something refreshing to it. The less you think of it as chess + new elements, but rather just a new board game with chess elements, the more you will enjoy the game for what it really is :) GL HF.

Although "more like Chess than Chess" is pure hyperbole, Chess 2 is still an excellent game.  It retains the strategic, thoughtful core of basic Chess while breathing new life into it. I came into this as someone who was initially interested in playing traditional chess, but didn't find it to be very fun due to the emphasis on memorization. I think it's more fun to think more "on your toes" instead of having to invest time up-front to memorize chess openings in order to enjoy the intricacies of higher-level play (just like how some people don't like having to memorize long combos in fighting games in order to really enjoy the game at even a novice level). Chess 2 really nails this issue, as well as fixing other issues that make it much more fun to play.
It's not really feasible to have an "opening theory" due to the many different possible matchups, so you actually have to think about the strength of different moves right from the start.
The midline invasion rule really helps to keep the games from dragging on and making it easier to win without having to figure out how to checkmate or end up with a stalemate.
The "dueling" mechanic adds a fun challenge of trying to predict what your opponent will do.
Overall, the experience of playing and learning this game has been quite enjoyable, and this implementation gives you a nice way to find opponents to play against that are around your level (using an ELO system), so you don't have to worry about being thrown into match after match with people who are much more experienced than you.

Chess 2: the Sequal is definitely a top notch strategy game.  While many are skeptical that the game is in some way anti-chess, I think it has taken the best elements of chess and improved them, and it has taken the worst elements of chess and replaced them.  There is no memorization, no two games that look alike, no mobility problems, no useless moves, and (almost) no draws.  It is just you and your opponent. I learned the game before it was developed to be on the PC, which is why my "hourage" is low and why I have early access.  IMO, it is really worth the buy, when compared to the price of an "ok" chess set, with just the regular rules and pieces, the price of Chess 2 is a steal.

Luftrausers is fast-paced bullet-hell dogfighter game; you are a plane and you shoot down other planes, missiles, ships and blimps down. Your objective is to survive as long as possible, taking down as many opponents as you can. Game is hard, death can occur within seconds of starting and your score is ranked online.
Moving left or right will change the direction your plane will face, pushing up activates the boosters, and trigger fires your weapon. There is no limit to ammo. Controls are tight, dodging bullets and shooting the enemy has you switching your boosters on and off. You take damage by being shot at by the enemy, flying into enemy planes or ships, and staying too long in the clouds or water. All damage can be repaired by not firing for a few seconds.
You start off with a fast balanced plane, accomplishing objectives tied to your loadout (you can alter the engine, guns and body) and levelling up will unlock new choices. The new body, engine and gun types can be mixed and matched for different combinations, each giving a different play style; turn your ship into a battering ram, attach heat-seeking missiles, drop bombs on enemies below or sink into the sea without taking damage. There are many combinations to try and they do a great job in stopping the game from going stale.
Default colour scheme is light brown, dark red and white; different colour filters can be unlocked (though none of them are to my taste). Music is very good and the sound effects have a nice 'oompf' feel to it.
If there is anything I would like to change is that a few more load out options would be welcomed and the cutscenes would be a bit longer.
TL;DR: hard but fun bullet-hell game. One map, but made highly replayable by combining different parts of the plane.

So first, some positive notes, because there was a lot about this game I liked and still don't regret playing it even though I can't personally reccomend the game to others. This game has some great design from the visual aesthetic, to the charming and haunting score, to the setting of the town it all occurs in. Next, the game had some great humor in it, which was really vital to the pacing and getting the player deeper involved in the characters and story. A lot of this humor is more for a younger, millenial-ish crowd however, so if you can't laugh at dank memes that mask depression or a lot of modern teenage lingo, a lot of the humor might not be for you.
Last, I, for one, adored the characters, but this tends to be a point of discussion for a lot of people. All of the characters have deeply intriguing and real issues ranging from mental illness to abusive pasts to bleak outlooks on the future due to their sheltered lifestyles. The dialogue in these moments is very real, and I find that refreshing vs the typical treatment these storylines get in a lot of Hollywood films or even some popular games (i.e. Sorry, I think To The Moon was insulting to those on the autism spectrum). By the end of the game, I did truly care for these characters and their issues and their resolve and what would happen to them. At the same time, I can understand the viewpoint that has been of much contention among reviewers. People either love these characters, or hate them entirely, and since your enjoyment of this game will very much hinge upon this, yes, some of the characters, particularly the player character, are terrible, trashy, cringy people at times. Some love this as it makes the character relatable. They make mistakes that we have made and it makes it easier to attach yourself to a characters issues when you see yourself reflected in them. However, I can see how some people would be turned off by this nature in characters so please, if you can't find a storyline involving real broken people with real issues living real life interesting; if you think a lot of the people who have these kind of issues are just whiny snowflakes (I'm not looking to debate this, I'm just stating viewpoints I've read in many other reviews and not judging anyone who has been through issues like this), please understand that you will most absolutely NOT enjoy this game.
So that's the bulk of what I liked as well as the main point of contention I see in a lot of reviews. So let's mention the parts that really held this game back and keep me from recommending it in the end. Most of the issues within the game stem from the narrative itself, as the game is a fully narrative experience, it's not about platforming or other aspects of the world. Sadly, the trailers do not reflect this, so I do feel slightly misled about how deep the world would be, but it's really just a walking simulator. I do enjoy walking simulator, narrative-led games a lot myself, but that's not what I was sold on getting. To this end, some of the minigames involved in the world make it clear that this game was set to be a walking simulator, and are painful to play through due to lack of polish in the controls and a general lack of idea of what is going on. This is slightly intentional, as you aren't exactly supposed to do good at any of these minigames anyway, but it shows a lack of polish and doesn't help the pacing of the story to have it slowed down by poorly designed rhythm and platforming sections. Along this line, the pacing itself is also major drawback of the narrative, particularly in the central plotline. There are some dream sequences that tease that player throughout the game to the deeper mystery of the characters and the town, but the pacing of these sequences is far too slow to keep the player intrigued, and then by the time you get to the end, it doesn't deliver any sort of reward for those punishingly slow sections at all. Sadly, this is the bulk of why I don't recommend the game, because the central plot line ends up being entirely unnecessary and incredibly dull and nonsensical despite what the characters go through in the rest of the game. If the game ahd been just about exploring the side plots that establish the characters and their issues, I think I would have enjoyed the game a lot more, but a large chunk of the time you'll put into this game is for a very poorly paced and entirely boring climax with no resolution. It's just plain bad storytelling in a game that is entirely based on the narrative experience of the player.
While there's a lot about this game to love, a lot of people will definitely feel like the hours it takes to get to the ending are wasted. I, for one, played approximately 10 hours to get to the end, and in the end I think about 7 of those hours were a waste and it could have been a much shorter and more enjoyable experience. This game just simply cannot be recommended, especially at a $20 price tag, as you most absolutely will not get $20 worth of fun, suspense, or mental stimulation from the experience, but it might be worth it to pick up at a deep discount of maybe $5 or so.

As far as the actual game goes, if you like simulating how most people would act in a survival type situation with limited resources, scarce ammunition, the elements, starvation/dehydration, wandering aimlessly for hours hopefully finding a house or spot that hasnt been looted, rampant paranoia, greed, barbarism, and the sweet sweet joy of finding a ranged weapon so you can have a brief period of relaxation before you let off one shot and everyone comes looking for you.
Then you sir/maim are a adrenaline junkie like myself that would enjoy prowling the beautifully rendered world of Miscreated.
Though not a true stealth/tactical game, the gameplay does reward sneaky patience, tactical thinking, as well as a healthy dose of cynicism. Most people who hate this game simply jump in and relate their ignorance of the world/gamplay mechanics to a broken/bad game and would probally trust a windowless van marked "free candy" in real life. Trust your instincts as to where you would look for loot and always play using a headset. Listen for the sounds of footsteps, rustling of the forests, distanct gunshots, and the sounds of a roaring car engine.
Before you play, study up the world map (not included within the game, unless you find a physical map) online and learn from the forums where to loot at the start and where to hunt people and you get geared.
I would recommend either the crossbow or recurve bow as mainstay weapon since they both are virtually silent and you can craft ammo from stuff in the wild (good luck finding any weapon honestly,lol). Nothing brings the fear than a poison or flaming bolt/arrow from out of blue from a bush to the back of some of the idiot bandits that roam the world looking for a easy kill.
And always pull a crazy ivan when you are traversing the world as you never know who could be stalking you (It might even be me)

In the end, I find this a buy for me and too all as well. I have heard that Orcs Must Die 2 is like Dungeon Defenders, but saying that is like comparing a milkshake to spoiled milk, it doesn't serve the justice this game deserves.

Let me level with you. Guilty Gear is an amazing game, arcsys makes the best 2D air dashing fighting games in the world. XRD is a fresh reboot, which throws out a lot of the complexity from the older games while maintaining the classic feel of some of the most iconic characters around.

XRD is a game that plays fast and aggressive while looking amazing.
However the PC port is extremely garbage. If you look around Dustloop, SRK, and the steam community you'll find lots of complains about frame rate issues.
I've got an amd cpu and an nvidia gpu, my friend has the same gpu and one model worse on the amd cpu. His game runs fine, mine doesn't.
Now, what happens is after a number of matches (about 10 or so) the framerate goes from a solid stable 60, down to 30 and the game becomes unplayable.
As I've mentioned, I looked into this a lot before refunding the game, this happens to all combinations of amd and intel cpus and also nvidia and amd gpus. Online, offline, it doesn't matter. For many people the game is just unplayable.
XRD is a fantastic game and I've loved it since the NA release on ps3, I'm just upset that I can't play with my pc friends.
For the sake of clarity I've tried a couple of fixes that were suggested online, both on forums and the steam community. I tried various configurations with nvidia control panel, in game settings, resets, game cache validation, re-installing the game, and nothing fixed the problem. Time and time again, after a number of matches the frame rate would halve rendering the game unplayable.

I was fortunate enough to be part of the beta test, so maybe some bias here!
I could talk about the game's polish all day (hint: reaaaally good polish.  I'm a particular fan of the music, but wow do the 3d pieces look amazing), but the most important thing is that it's just really, really fun.  Playing around with the different armies, improvising new strategies, trying out openings-- it's really refreshing to have this level of freedom compared to chess.
It's surprising, too, because usually when a game is designed to be really well-balanced (which Chess 2 is), the designer takes out most of the exciting stuff and you're stuck with a game that's really well-balanced, but not all that fun.  But in Chess 2 you have an army with teleporting pieces, an army with two kings, and an army where adjacent minor pieces share eachother's powers-- nothing is broken, but there's a ton of variety and a ton of experimentation you can do.
Midline invasion is a really underrated change, too.  It makes games way faster and more exciting, and it makes kings less weak as a piece!

As a long time follower of David Sirlin's games, Chess 2 does not disappoint.
I, myself, had the privileged of being part of the beta test group for this, and Chess 2 quickly became part of my daily routine. Being a chess enthusiast for many years, I quickly picked this game up and enjoyed it thoroughly. Its complexity is enough to keep me coming back, and its simplicity makes it easy enough for new players to learn how to play. (Yes, even for those new to chess)

Chess 2 was clearly developed with the intent of making Chess new and fresh again, and it succeeds completely at this prospect.  One of the most intimidating aspects of Chess 1: The Original is just the wealth of pre-established metagame that's been developed over the many long years it's been around.  With six (count em, SIX!) unique factions instead of just one, all the old material is completely thrown out the window and you have to learn Chess all over again, and that, I feel, is wonderful.  No longer is it about memorizing countless openings or having a wealth of unfathomable experience.  Instead, you play it like you would play a modern strategy game - thoughtfully pondering your own decisions and creatively coming up with your own solutions.  The midline rule also keeps the action tense throughout and prevents the more boring, drawn-out endgames of Chess 1; it feels like the way Chess was always meant to be played.
If you have ever been intimidated about picking up Chess before, now's the time to join Chess 2.  The sooner the better - joining in while the game is young will be an exciting opportunity to see it evolve, and to help shape the metagame and history of the game yourself!

This is a weird Polish turn-based squad tactics game. The graphics and mood are both like the original Resident Evils - dark, but cheesy. The game does a good job of keeping you off balance, not knowing who to trust, or how to survive each new horror you come across. Each boss is unique, and every few battles you'll fight a new type of monster.
Combat is a little weird. Weapons have distinct attack patterns - pistols can only be fired in four directions, while rifles can also be fired diagonally, etc. That restriction (and the weird camera angles) can make it difficult to make sure that you're on the right spot to be able to shoot an enemy, but you don't have to use all your movement at once, so you can adjust as needed.
Ammo (and healing items) are often scarce, but you also get some reusable weapons that can be used every few turns for free. Stupidly, this includes tasers that lets you stunlock some bosses (many are immune) to the point where they can't ever attack you or move.
You get to choose how your characters improve when they level up, but the choices are pretty basic. Increasing health is  mostly a waste because there's nothing that can one-shot you, and healing items just heal a fixed number instead of a percentage of your health. Max out accuracy for your shooters,
calmness for melee guys (so that they rage out and do bonus damage easier), and then go with either luck for bonus damage or improve your counter-attack chance. (Counter attacks are free actions, but you can't switch weapons or change your facing, so plan ahead. You can face your character by clicking on him). Make sure to save after every fight or event. There are some times when you blatantly should have been given a chance to reorganize your inventory but weren't, so just reload instead.
This game is very old and rough around the edges, but it often goes on sale for a dollar and it's easily worth that.

This game is punishing. It can be brutal, agonizing, and downright cruel, and yet I can do nothing but give it my highest recommendation.
There are very few areas I can really find fault with. The worst parts by far (in my opinion) are any places with tight, easy to fall off ledges. Even though that's basically a quarter of the game (possibly more) and stands testement to how truly diabolical the level designers are, I still can't bring myself to hate any part of it. Carelessness is your biggest enemy, and one wrong step against even the weakest foes can result in death. That asside, if you can keep your composure and balance dodging, attacking and healing, this game is a treasure trove of hidden upgradable weapons, wonderful maps and gruesome, dark boss fights.
There is no happy ending. There is noone to be saved, no real storyline that you have to follow closely. Just a lonely fight against an unrelenting horde, trying your best to survive and push forward. This game, arguably the best from the "Souls" franchise, is perfect for anyone looking for a good challenge.
Just don't be surprised if you throw away your game controller several times before the end...
(Oh, an important/ more objective note: you will want a gamepad - USB wired Xbox360 controller is my preference. This game is not designed for keyboard & mouse, and really suffers for it if you don't own a gamepad. That's probably the biggest criticism I personally can think of, but yes, I am heavily biased.)

SoD stands out in a sea of mediocre zombie games. Going in, I really didn't expect to like this game as much as I eventually did. Though a little rough around the edges it still offers up some solid and, often exhilarating, gameplay. Most of your time will be spent sneaking around scavenging for supplies (food, ammo, fuel, & medicine), managing/saving/assisting other survivors, improving your base with various facilities related to your survival (workshops, medical tents, sleeping quarters, etc.) and...running for your life. Zombies can be quite challenging in groups especially if there are a few 'special' infected mixed in. It's a good idea to always bring a battle buddy.

As for complaints; I would like to see more story/character depth, more and/or improved graphics options, and polished up combat. Long range gun play can be dodgy. Missions can become a bit repetitive, especially after several levels of Breakdown, but even an average mission can turn heart pumping if you find yourself surrounded, wounded, and on the run. Altogether, State of Decay is a fun mix of elements from the zombie genre that does a lot of things right, if not deeply. Well worth picking up when you can catch it on a Steam sale.

Great work done with this game and I'm looking forward to the next version and hoping for improvements in the arears where this game falls short.

Although it seems most people don't recomend this game, I say don't believe this game to be a bad game. Although its true what everyone says about this being very restrictive and scripted and very Call of Duty like, the game itself is still very fun
The story line isn't the greatest thing, but there are some super dramatic and epic parts that keep the campaign interesting. However the rest of the story line is pretty generic, but that doesnt really matter because the missions are fun enough that they could stand alone without a story line at all and still be really good on its own.
For the gameplay, some parts are scripted with the "Dog Fight Mode" which pretty much holds your hand and walks you through a dogfight, or just automates the flying so you can shoot. I can see why people dislike this feature, but I think it doesnt necessarily ruin the game because you don't HAVE to use it if you don't want to (although some scripted parts you'll be forced to use it anyway but that isn't very often), and sometimes the feature is actually useful because the game does get very chaotic and intense.(but thats probably because I'm a noob at flying games) Aside from the "Dog Fight Mode" thing, the rest of the gameplay is very immersive and fun with a great combination of stellar graphics and effects, and flying around shooting the crap out of things. (except for the helicopter parts, those were more annoying that fun due to bad controls.)
In conclusion, I must say that this is the first game in the Ace Combat series that I really played in depth, so I guess I did miss out on all the previous titles, and I wouldn't know how much better they were according to the veteran players. I can understand why fans of the series would hate this, but despite what they say, its still a pretty fun game.

Once, I had to travel to a quest on the other side of the map. I said to myself ''You cant make it there fast enough,you have to teleport !'' ... But seconds  later before pushing the fast travel button on the minimap, my eye spoted a lone caragor feasting on a squad of Uruks he had just killed. I observe his ferocity his ruthlessness the accuracy on his bites and  finally I decide that I had to tame him. I quickly drop on his back and I connect with him. He was mine. At that point I felt something weird, something that I havent felted before while playing this game a sense of warmth , of friendship. I knew how expendable caragors where in Middle earth..he would die if he got alone. So I took him under my care...
We had some good times together. We fought many battles, making ourselves quite infamous..Every Uruk was speaking about that Ranger of the Black Gate and his caragor friend. Our rampage reached the ear of The Dark Lord himself, made him tremple in his iron armor. But we made the greatest mistake out of all...we got ahead of ourselves and in the end, that terrible day arrived...
I was riding my caragor to some ''abandoned'' ruins to investigate some missing Ithildin symbols. By the time I was there I dismounted him and told him to stay close. I located the symbol on a 30 meter tall wall so I started climbing. The sooner I
get to it the sooner we will leave I thought. By the time I reached the top I was penetrated by a great scream for help. Oh no it was him! We got ambushed by a large squad of Uruks and about 3 captains - One of them HATED caragors so by the time he laid eyes on  him he got crazy. He started swinging his axes cutting his skin. I jumped down to help him and then he looked at me. He knew that if I stayed we would both die. He found a bit of strength left inside him battling the commanders and buying me enough time to escape. I looked at the eye of the despicable Uruk that killed him...his name was Bolg the Hungry. At that moment I swore that I will have his head. I spent days tracking him down and I ended up finding him and his followers taking a casual stroll. A great rage sparked inside me that made me rush towards him sticking my dagger in his back... His bodyguards tried to protect him but one after the other fell by my swift blade..they had a quick death even though they didnt deserve it. The commander was almost dead and tried to flee so I immobilized him with an arrow on the foot. I placed my sword on his shoulder moving it left and freeing his pathetic head from his miserable body. I noticed the fear on his eyes that it was the same with the one on my caragor's. By the time his head hit the ground reinforcements arrived only to find him dead and me gone..
After that I had time to mourn my fallen friend..
Today I am at the top of my league maxed out on experience and skills! Quite a warrior and a master of many many caragors. However I never forgot the one caragor that made me into who I am.

Night in the Woods is a lovely and quaint game that sets out to tell the story of a displaced young adult.
Every aspect of the game's visuals and sound do wonders to truly building a one-of-a-kind world.
The unique delivery of certain story elements through mini-games is also delightful (Perhaps my favourite thing). It feels stylish and immersive in its own unique way.
This game is a standout in so many ways, however, the overall narrative suffers in the later half of the game.
Either way, it's a profound game with lots of lovely bits throughout. The only problem I had was with traversal in the town (and consequently the dream sequences) in the game. Fast Travel or Sprint, anyone?

That said, if you dislike dialogue-heavy games reliant on you exploring a town and talking to its residents, then you likely won't enjoy Night in the Woods.

This is a very old game, from the 90's golden era of pc gaming.  Within its genera, it holds its end up well against many graphically superior games today.  It is a fun game and a good representation of gaming at that time.  Has some decent music too ("battle theme #2 player" is my favorite).  But I would note the following for those contemplating buying it.
1. I have windows 7 64-bit.  I had to use "software rendering" to get around a graphics issue.  Not all windows 7 users have to do this.  Has something to do with ffdshow maybe?  But this simple fix works fine.
2. there is one place in the game where it crashes, near the end, but this area is skippable and it is a long fight with no benefits at the end.  You may not even get the fight depending upon when you visit rooms in the last area.
3. recall that this was originally made for 640x480 monitors.  Scaling will be done either by your monitor or your gpu.   It is possible to turn this scaling off either via most monitors or your video card's drivers.  For example, nvidia has a "no scaling"  and "scale on gpu" settings which will render an uncaled 640x480 picture.  But interstingly enough I found this little picture almost impossible to play compared to the scaled version on my 27" screens.  So I went with the scaling.
With the sale, it is a cheap 30 hours of old style gaming entertainment.  For those who think it is hard, the trick is to look for all the boxes and hidey-holes to get first aid items and ammo and special weapons, and to fight smart.  That was part of the point with these old games (smart).  By smart I mean doing things like conserving ammo, using the proper weapon type at the proper time (ranged, area of effect, mele, and the all important negative buff inflictors), and tactics like figuring out when to close in for an attack, when to make the enemy come to you, what sequence your characters should attack in, plotting ahead by two or three moves in battle, and paying attention to the immunities and special abilities of different types of monsters.  You can't just do "combat shotgun to the head" in this game and expect to get through it.  In the end, like most great games, it is the special abilities that make all the difference in the really hard fights.  This game offers several negative buffs you can inflict on the mutations you will be faced with, so, whatever special weapon abilities a monster is not immune to, us it on them without reservation.
Good luck.

I've enjoyed everything about this game, but as im going to explain why, i'm afraid it will end up looking like the opposite,
Gorky 17 is flawed and it's nothing that much original either.
Its a turn based strategy adventure game with some rpg elements, back then it was probably the first time i´ve seen a game that mixes genres like this, but it didnt do anything i haven't seen before, and it was a fairly simple turn based game as well.
Its scarce in rpg elements, there arent multiple routes you can take, you wont do any moral choices, its fairly linear, and even the leveling up sistem isnt all the complex, it's also inconsistent when it comes to difficulty.
What it does right though, might be the reason why i choose to replay it after all this years and still find it so addicting.
For starters Gorky 17 is all about resources and tactical thinking, the game is easy as long as you are good at managing what you got, there isnt much ammo or health lying around and characters themselves become better with weapons after using them in battle.
winning isnt enough, finding the best strategy too waste as less ammo and life as possible, is just that important, you will have to know your enemies, know who too attack first and be aware of your characters limitations.

LUFTRAUSERS! Sorry, I’ve been told by publishers Devolver Digital that LUFTRAUSERS must only be shouted when mentioned. That is true, because LUFTRAUSERS is something to shout about.
LUFTRAUSERS is an indie arcade shooter by developers Vlambeer and the objective of the game is …to shoot everything! Presented as a 2D side-scrolling “wrap around screen” shoot ‘em up similar to old-old school games like 80′s Defender or 90′s Jetstrike your mission is to take to the skies and dodge, dip, dive, duck, dodge and finally BLAST anything that’s BLASTING at you! Enemies will come at you from all directions and in various forms. Ships, carriers and subs take pot shots from the sea and a menagerie of exotic planes (and a Zeppelin!) in the air that will engage in dog fights with you (or try and suicide themselves). As you progress things become more and more hectic to a dizzying degree as the amount going on at once escalates exponentially over 100 levels.
Thankfully as you play the game you complete challenges, level up and gain access to more and more aviation unlocks. In total 125 different combinations of weapons, armour and propulsion systems become available which vary wildly from thicker armour (which naturally gives you more protection, but then decreases your speed), guided missiles (that chase your target but only limited to shooting 4 at a time) or the more wacky “engine that fires bullets when you fly”. This diversity is a unique selling point of the game and getting the knack of each loadout and finding the best configuration to suit you or the scenario is key. For example I’m currently sporting an anti-gravity engine to stay in the air with minimal thrust, a laser which is less powerful than the machine gun but allows for constant damage over time and a light chassis to boost myself out of trouble …which is frequent.
Another plus is that the controls are minimal. No beefy manual on aeronautics or diploma for aerospace engineering required here lads! For the PC version of the game the up arrow gives you forward thrust, left and right turn you in a clockwise or counter-clockwise movement and ‘X’ fires your gun. Stop firing, and your plane repairs itself. Double tap thrust to give you a boost to (hopefully) speed you out of trouble. Simple? Well doing this under fire and the pressure of needing at times some pin-point precession of Maverick, it’s tough and times quite unforgiving.
Visual wise LUFTRAUSERS is presented (for the most part) in a sepia scheme. Images are simple and suitably retro, fitting to its heritage, while audio is catchy and 16-bit. The audible tone to indicate your planes damage and repair progress is a particularly nice touch as it allows players to not have to rely on a visual cue (such as a 100% bar) that could easily be distracting especially when so much is going on.
Overall LUFTRAUSERS is another great example of an indie title that I’m sure will be recognised for its achievements. It’s (Warning: Indie Game Cliché Alert!) easy to learn, fun to play, cheap (which is important in this day and age) and has a good re-playability. Recommended if you’re a fan of the genre or have the change and looking for something to while away your time with when not wanting to drop robots from the sky.

This game is punishing. It can be brutal, agonizing, and downright cruel, and yet I can do nothing but give it my highest recommendation.
There are very few areas I can really find fault with. The worst parts by far (in my opinion) are any places with tight, easy to fall off ledges. Even though that's basically a quarter of the game (possibly more) and stands testement to how truly diabolical the level designers are, I still can't bring myself to hate any part of it. Carelessness is your biggest enemy, and one wrong step against even the weakest foes can result in death. That asside, if you can keep your composure and balance dodging, attacking and healing, this game is a treasure trove of hidden upgradable weapons, wonderful maps and gruesome, dark boss fights.
There is no happy ending. There is noone to be saved, no real storyline that you have to follow closely. Just a lonely fight against an unrelenting horde, trying your best to survive and push forward. This game, arguably the best from the "Souls" franchise, is perfect for anyone looking for a good challenge.
Just don't be surprised if you throw away your game controller several times before the end...
(Oh, an important/ more objective note: you will want a gamepad - USB wired Xbox360 controller is my preference. This game is not designed for keyboard & mouse, and really suffers for it if you don't own a gamepad. That's probably the biggest criticism I personally can think of, but yes, I am heavily biased.)

I'd like to preface this review by stating that I'm not a fighting game enthusiast.
In fact, the only real experience I have with 2D Fighters prior to GGXrd is The King of Fighters XIII-- and I wasn't really a fan of that game. Despite my inexperience with the genre, I can say that
has salvaged my interest.
The characters in Guilty Gear are, well, ridiculous. From a sleeping boy who wields a weaponized bed to a British time traveler, the cast covers all the bases. Each fighter has a unique playstyle and, in many cases, a more peculiar fashion sense. Whether you want to fight with swords, sickles, anchors, flowers, billiard balls, or your own hair, Guilty Gear has it all. Another nice aesthetic are the palette options (skins) for each character-- all of them look great!
Although my arcade-fighter backlog isn't extensive by any means, I know that GGXrd plays great. The controls are simple, combos easy to pick up, and the fighting overall feels tight and responsive. Fights against NPCs seem fair with an appropriate amount of challenge. This means I can actually play Arcade and other AI game modes without the fights becoming too tedious or underwhelming.
Something that anyone, novice or veteran to fighting games, will notice immediately is the polish
GGXrd. While the character models are 3D rendered, they still manage to appear beautifully 2D. This effect really brings the game to life and allows for over-the-top battle intros and special attack cinematics.
The voice acting in this game is impressive, too. Having no original preference, I tried out both the English and Japanese vocals and ended up loving both. Each character's tone seems to fit so well, their voices emotive and packed with energy.
Xrd's soundtrack is also worth mentioning. From what I can tell, a lot of the BGMs were brought back from past Guilty Gear titles and given new life-- my personal favorite being May's
.
It's safe to say that
showed me how fun fighting games can be. Everything about this game prevents it from being just another bland entry in the genre. The characters, visuals, and music are never lackluster and they brilliantly show off the devotion that ArcSys has to their games.

An absurdist adventure game with Telenovela-style FMV cutscenes.
A deliberate throwback to the bad acting and weird plots from old adventure and FMV games, Damn Virgins features a wacky plot and colourful characters. You play as Xavi, one of seven losers who is just bumbling about his days and completely unaware of the evil plot where a crazed man wants to sacrifice them all to appease the Mayan gods.
Gameplay takes place mainly in two locations: your home, and a remote island. Puzzles range from finding a hidden key to solving a gear/block puzzle using the Mayan counting system... the puzzles here are really well designed, as is the overall level design.
Graphics are early 2000s standards: digitized versions of the main character and for the rest drawings. It all holds up pretty well, except in the cave section where it becomes easily unclear where you came from and need to go next.
Recommended for anyone who likes cheesy fun.

Damn Virgins is a prime example of a well thought out and executed indie game. I often seek out and play indie games for the very reason some people avoid them....because they are different! Most are not AAA studio games (this one included), which can be a very good thing.
Funky characters, goofy acting, humorous dialog (if a little juvenile at times), and mostly straightforward (and not too difficult) puzzles made this game a joy to play. Unlike one reviewer, I personally thought the decision to use Unreal Engine 3 for the graphics was a good choice as it gave the game a "throwback to the 90's" kind of vibe, just as pixelated graphics in games from studios like WadjetEye Games take me back to the 80's. If anything, I think they
to the immersion, not detract from it. I realize this is a personal viewpoint, but to expect AAA graphics from an indie studio is a bit unrealistic to me. Don't get me wrong....I like well done big-budget games with awesome graphics too, but this one doesn't need that to be a successful production.
The "decision point" in the game leading to two distinct endings was an interesting development. I especially liked the way the developer gave us the option to play the alternate plot path immediately after finishing the game, which led to different puzzles and cutscenes.
The only real con I ran into was the game had a couple glitches, one of which was game-breaking, but after messaging the developer via the game forum the problem was quickly fixed and I was able to continue on. I've never received that fast of a response from a AAA studio!
And although this isn't necessarily a con, I prefer being able to manually save my progress so I can revisit specific points during gameplay, but that option isn't available in this game. The auto-save and "continue on from where you left off" feature employed here is somewhat common, but I find it a bit restraining.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game, partly because I think the idea of sacrificing virgins always makes for a great plot premise....just maybe not
virgins!

A very arcade-heavy game.
If you like simple air-shoot-em-up-in-3D gameplay, don't need too much realism and if you're resistant to seasickness (flightsickness?) then this game is for you. All the airplanes and helicopters in the game are rather well modeled and look quite nice, explosions and other effects are mostly decent. The mission backgrounds/maps are rather well made and look quite nice from high above, even though they're not as pretty anymore when you're flying very low.
Gameplay, as mentioned before, is very arcade-like. Every plane carries several hundred missiles and the machine gun has unlimited ammo. Enemies fly seemingly entirely unburdened by what few laws of physics the game has, they have no limit to their maximum speed and just about most of them do a lot of turns that would just right out kill any real pilot. Mission design is mostly limited to "There's a group of planes there, kill them. There's another group of planes there, kill them too. There's another group of planes but they've got a bomber this time, kill the bomber first then the rest." and so on. Enemies seem to have a limitless supply of pilots and airplanes, coming out of nowhere, the story never even remotely ventures into the areas of "Where do they come from?" or "From where did they launch 120 air superiority fighters this close to Washington DC or Miami or Dubai?".
The occasional rail-shooter sequence as gunner of - OF COURSE - an M134 Vulcan mounted on a Blackhawk don't really make things better. And then there's the parts where you actually get to FLY a helicopter...
--- WORST CONTROL SCHEME EVER! ---
I will also mention the final bossfight. Now, I hate bossfights, I usually really do, not because I can't beat em, but I have no patience and no interest in unfair fights against entities with ridiculous scripted behaviour and massively overpowered stats that defy any logic and are usually only beatable because there's some ridiculous intentional flaw in their behavior patterns that allows the hero to win by exploiting it again and again.
This bossfight, is of course no stranger to this stupid phenomenon. The final boss is invulnerable until you have completed a series of headspinning useless sequences of automatically following him while shooting useless limitless missiles and machinegun shots at him. (See this video of the bossfight if you're interested:
This sequence tends to be extremely annoying, Akula (the boss) flys maneuvers which are impossible to follow and would with certainty kill any real pilot from G forces
he can do 180° turns on the spot at supersonic speeds (not joking).
Well... the story.... uhm... what story... ah yes. The americans are the good guys and saviors of the world, and you are the greatest pilot ever along with some of your friends (which are apparently aswell). Everyone else is either completely incapable of everything and the russians are (of course) the bad guys.
The story itself centers around some elaborate new form of city-buster-sized warhead which those russians have developed. It does the exact same thing as a nuke, but it can't be a nuke because that would invalidate the entire story, pretty much. (Oh the russians have nukes? That's NEWS!)
Dialogues are mostly rather flat and uninteresting. Quick time events are rather pointlessly strewn through the game and don't seem to actually do much mostly.
Did I mention that the russians are the badguys and the americans are the good guys? Alright, that's pretty much everything you need to know.
Well, all things considered, I cannot really recommend the game. It's nice to play for a short time if you want something arcady but it wasn't too much fun to play. Worth less than 5 bucks I'd say.

Once, I had to travel to a quest on the other side of the map. I said to myself ''You cant make it there fast enough,you have to teleport !'' ... But seconds  later before pushing the fast travel button on the minimap, my eye spoted a lone caragor feasting on a squad of Uruks he had just killed. I observe his ferocity his ruthlessness the accuracy on his bites and  finally I decide that I had to tame him. I quickly drop on his back and I connect with him. He was mine. At that point I felt something weird, something that I havent felted before while playing this game a sense of warmth , of friendship. I knew how expendable caragors where in Middle earth..he would die if he got alone. So I took him under my care...
We had some good times together. We fought many battles, making ourselves quite infamous..Every Uruk was speaking about that Ranger of the Black Gate and his caragor friend. Our rampage reached the ear of The Dark Lord himself, made him tremple in his iron armor. But we made the greatest mistake out of all...we got ahead of ourselves and in the end, that terrible day arrived...
I was riding my caragor to some ''abandoned'' ruins to investigate some missing Ithildin symbols. By the time I was there I dismounted him and told him to stay close. I located the symbol on a 30 meter tall wall so I started climbing. The sooner I
get to it the sooner we will leave I thought. By the time I reached the top I was penetrated by a great scream for help. Oh no it was him! We got ambushed by a large squad of Uruks and about 3 captains - One of them HATED caragors so by the time he laid eyes on  him he got crazy. He started swinging his axes cutting his skin. I jumped down to help him and then he looked at me. He knew that if I stayed we would both die. He found a bit of strength left inside him battling the commanders and buying me enough time to escape. I looked at the eye of the despicable Uruk that killed him...his name was Bolg the Hungry. At that moment I swore that I will have his head. I spent days tracking him down and I ended up finding him and his followers taking a casual stroll. A great rage sparked inside me that made me rush towards him sticking my dagger in his back... His bodyguards tried to protect him but one after the other fell by my swift blade..they had a quick death even though they didnt deserve it. The commander was almost dead and tried to flee so I immobilized him with an arrow on the foot. I placed my sword on his shoulder moving it left and freeing his pathetic head from his miserable body. I noticed the fear on his eyes that it was the same with the one on my caragor's. By the time his head hit the ground reinforcements arrived only to find him dead and me gone..
After that I had time to mourn my fallen friend..
Today I am at the top of my league maxed out on experience and skills! Quite a warrior and a master of many many caragors. However I never forgot the one caragor that made me into who I am.

Great game, best combat system i've ever used that isn't stupidly complicated but also isn't 'elder scrolls' basic
this is easily one of the few games i can comfortably give a 10/10 having bought it on all platforms (sorta, xbox was free) and played it to death across all of them, once you get a handle for the game's combat and get to know that like in real life you can't just get stabbed a thousand times and live to tell the tale. yea the pc port has issues but for one i don't really care about the 30fps thing, as fixing it with DSfix actually screws with the game's engine quite a bit so you can't make some jumps etc. and even when DSfix is installed the game runs without a problem if your pc can handle it (it's prettty poorly optimised to run above 30 so it gets unstable with some areas and draws more processing power than it really should, but i'm not holding that against it as it wasn't even intended to be accessed).
Don't get me wrong, the game is HARD to start with, and even now with something like 200 hours overall sank into it (rookie numbers i know) i have issues with some areas, enemies and bosses. however the more you play (without just getting stressed) the better you feel yourself getting till eventually those enemies that stuck you right at the start seem like a breeze as you backtrack through the area to speak to a vendor or grab a specific item.

This game, is quite honestly, the most fun game I have ever played. With the quick unlocks of new kinds of aircraft parts, the different gameplay styles that come with them, and the great dynamic soundtrack make this game a fun, epic, and unique game. In addition to lovely music, each new aircraft part can add new abilities, such as exploding on death, being able to fly underwater, etc. The flying controls are also excellent! You can turn on/off the thrusters and rotate freely however you want, allowing for the many parts of your plane to show off how they work best. For example, if you have a spread gun, heavy frame, and a superbooster, you would lead a ton of enemies in one direction, then cut the thrusters and fire backwards. Recommended: If you at all liked classic arcade side-scrolling shooters of old, LUFTRAUSERS is right up your alley.  It's a well-made side-scroller with high production values and excellent execution.
LUFTRAUSERS is a classic side-scrolling arcade shooter made by Vlambeer and published by Devolver Digital.  Vlambeer is a game development house that has a certain knack for having their game ideas ripped off by mobile developers, and there's very much a reason for that: they make simple, arcade retro games very, very well, with an imitable art style and direction.
At it's heart, LUFTRAUSERS is a side-scrolling shooter set in a sort of alternate reality at the birth of jet flight, full of all kinds of anachronistic references to old science fiction and a rich graphics style that fully realises and embellishes the genre.  The art style in general is very well-implemented, as is the sound design.  It all fits together very well.  The music design deserves special mention, because the in-game music changes slightly depending upon your choice of hull, weapon, and engine.  So very different choices of plane will result in very different in-game music and it is a way of adding variety to the game that hasn't been much used before.
The game mechanics are simple, but work very well.  The divergence from simple normal side-scrolling is the inclusion of a stall mechanic - when you are engaging the engine boost, you simply glide, which allows greater precision in turns at the price of losing altitude and slower forward momentum.  It allows for a high skill ceiling in the maneuvering and some truly amazing stunts.  Coupled with a variety of weapons, hulls, and engines that all act differently, the game not only offers a variety that keeps the game fresh, but also allows a player plenty of latitude to find a combination that fits their play-style.  The controls are responsive, and it plays just fine with a keyboard, though this is another game that definitely feels more authentic with a classic controller.
The enemies in the game are varied and become incrementally more difficult as you survive longer.  It starts as simple fighter planes, but progresses to patrol boats, jet fighters, ace pilots, battleships, and more.  On top of that, unlock enough and you can unlock a "SFMT Mode" that not only greatly increases the speed at which the enemy progression occurs, but also unlocks new enemies to fight, as well as affords new unlocks for yourself.
All in all while the game mechanics themselves are fairly simplistic, there is plenty of variety to keep you engaged and the production values for this kind of game are as high as one might have come to expect from Vlambeer.  if you like side-scrolling shooters, then I think you'll find a lot to love in LUFTRAUSERS.

Everyone is entitled to their opinion but I honestly don't know why this game isn't rated higher by most.  I think these devs have done a superb job of offering a solid entry into the crowded survival game field.  And they clearly remain involved in developing this into what could be an A-list title.
The graphics alone are worth the price of admission.  Sunlight, glare, moonlight, water effects, shadows.  All are rendered with detail and color.  On an Intel Core i7 860 @ 2.80GHz with 8GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB card, it runs beautifully at maximum settings, short of a little pop-up and tearing every now and then.  Tested out at lower settings, it still looks gorgeous.  Think Crysis or Far Cry without the need to kill everyone.
Beauty isn't always enough of course, but I think the gameplay is fun and exciting.  Once you get the basics down (and that's no mean feat), you start thinking strategically and logically.  Setting up camp gives you the opportunity to work later as the sun sets, but makes finding your way before sunrise a bit daunting.  Where to put supplies, tools, food?  What do you take to where and what do you leave for another time?  And for those who bemoan not being able to take everything with you, that's pretty realistic.  And the amount you ARE able to tote is generous (and maybe a bit unrealistic, but I'll take it.)
It was both exhilarating and scary when I finally left the familiarity of my first island and ventured to another that was thankfully larger, had more resources, and apparently something that hisses and bites me when I look for it (snake? insect?).  It's that type of discovery that makes me come back for more.
A major credit to the devs is offering a very easy to achieve save system (just build a shelter as soon as you can) and while it might not be as authentic as real life, where you have to live with your choices, it gives you the opportunity to explore options and ideas without frustrating you with permadeath.  That ultimately make it a more enjoyable as far as I'm concerned.  I play games to escape real life, not emulate it.
Many reviewers note lack of sufficient content and achieving everything that can be achieved but I haven't gotten there yet.  If I do get bored, or exhaust what it has to offer, and don't play anymore, I'd would still say I got my money's worth at $15.  Given that it's been lower on Steam sales, I think it's a bargain.  After spending 186 hours on The Long Dark (another EA title that can be thought of as limited but is tinkered with a lot and seems far from over), this is a great follow-up for me.  Like TLD, I often find myself daydreaming about what I want to or should do the next time I play Stranded Deep.
Nothing is perfect and my quibbles are that it would be nice to have an in-game tutorial or hints as to the mechanics,  and judging from some of the on-line tutorials I've viewed, I think the crafting system menu visuals were better in an earlier version.  I find the crafting menu in the current build harder to see and read.
I'm an older gamer who grew up with titles on disks and cartridges that were $50 and up most of the time, so when I see a worthy title on Steam that is EA and inexpensive ($15 is a little more than a first-run movie), I believe in supporting the hard work that devs put into it.  Usually it's a labor of love and innovation for them, so purchasing helps them continue to develop their vision.  The Beam Team has a great title here and I hope more gamers - particularly those who thrive on survival themes that don't include zombies and monsters - discover SD and give it latitude in their reviews.  I really think it deserves better review stats than you see here on Steam.

I got the game in a bundle without even knowing what it was, and I'm so glad that I did. I'm a meticulous person at heart, and organization is a personal passion. So when I started this game, with branching paths all over the place and all different unlockable story components and opportunities, I was in heaven. I've got a Word document saved right now, detailing the different paths and the effects of succeeding or failing each test. It's far from complete, and I'm certain there will be hours and hours of additional entertainment as I seek out the deaths, epilogues, and achievements that still elude me as I fill in more of my ever-growing chart of options.
Be aware, there's no such thing as a "perfect" game. I nearly drove myself mad attempting to raise stats in such a way that I passed every test. You simply cannot, and I think it's for the better. The game forces you to choose what knowledge and opportunities are most important to you and give up the rest or simply save it for another playthrough.
The artwork and different outfits are cute, and I appreciated that aspect of the game. However, if you do buy the game (and if you're anything like me, I hope you do because you'll have a blast), make sure you're doing it for the strategy and story element, since those are what truly make the game something special.

Isaac... such a strange game.
At this point in the game's lifespan, there have been many detailed descriptions of what makes The Binding Of Isaac so interesting.
It's unlikely I can explain its mechanics or appeal better than others, so here I am going to focus on why Isaac is worth trying. All I want to do here, is to convince you to give it a try if you're on the fence.
You see, even for the modern climate Isaac has an extremely weird and rather offensive sense of humor: poop jokes all over the place, routine references to dead babies, innumerable pokes at religion. On top of this, it's world is incredibly strange and distorted. After looking a little bit into the game, I could easily see someone being turned off by all this.
And once someone got past the game's ethos, it takes quite a while to get comfortable with the mechanics- personally I don't think Isaac is particularly hard of a game, but it definitely requires a lot of time to gain the skills to succeed without getting lucky.
As for its sense of humor, as irritating as it can be, depending on the person, it can be overlooked if you have the stomach for it, because Isaac emphasizes gameplay over anything else. It's perfectly possible to just play without thinking about the strange world and still have a good time.
As for the actual gameplay... today every other game seems to be some variety of roguelike, usually touting their difficulty. So perhaps the randomness and (sometimes annoying) challenge in Isaac is more accepted nowadays. But if this element was something turning you off of the game, it is perfectly feasible in Isaac to win the majority of runs, even with bad luck. Sometimes you get such an abysmal set of items that it's nearly impossible, but usually with enough knowledge of the game's systems and skill at dodging, winning is still doable. It takes a while - I remember when I was completely useless at the game and almost never could win, and I still could improve by a lot - but eventually it will happen.
Because one of the great things about Isaac is the way it balances systems and player skill. See, being able to dodge well or having really quick reactions helps, but so does knowing how to find secret rooms consistently, or how to optimize tarot cards, or how to pick the proper items when offered a choice between them. The more knowledge you have of the game, the better you'll do, regardless of how lucky you are or how fast your fingers are.
On top of this, Isaac has, in my opinion, some of the best systems I've seen in a roguelike. As I said player knowledge is rewarded heavily, but there are just so many areas to understand. Tarot cards, pills, secret rooms, item pools, devil/angel deals, curse rooms, item synergies... and there are hundreds and hundreds of permanent items, which can evolve such complex interactions late in a run. Out of the roguelikes I've played, it does the best job of making every run meaningfully different, yet also giving the player control (mostly) over how the run will turn out.
So, I would say give the game a try, even if it seems rather offensive or if you've heard people say it's annoyingly hard. Maybe it won't be for you in the end, but I think it's worth a shot if you enjoy games with random generation that nevertheless reward player skill and knowledge. Isaac has a truly massive amount of content, and the more time you're willing to give it, the more interesting of a game it becomes.

Here are just a few reasons I still enjoy every second of
:
Main Protagonists - When beginning
, the player has the option of selecting between two characters: an imbecile unnamed War Mage turned Miner who fans of the first game hail as the game’s protagonist and a seductress Sorceress who acted as the prior title’s antagonist. Obviously, these two characters-one being new to the ‘good guy clique-differ in both stature and basic weaponry, but playing as each of these individuals reveals another mark of comparison: their unlockable traps, weapons, minions, and skills are unique. For instance, the War Mage begins the game with a scattershot blunderbuss, tar traps that slow enemy minions, and a device to be placed on the wall that fires multiple arrows at crossing enemies; later in the game he can place panels that fling enemies (
-Neosho and myself), and other damaging traps. On the other hand, the Sorceress starts with a projectile launching staff that has the ability to convert orc forces into allies for a limited time, ice vents which freeze hostiles, and acid-spraying wall machines.
Humor - Though mostly from the War Mage than the Sorceress, the dialogue is very enjoyable. Whether a quip from the former villain to the witless hero or a pun directed after a combination kill by the player, each line may at least provoke a snicker from the player. There are also a few cinematic victory dances that may occur after a stage is completed, which is silly enough to be one of my favorite end-of-level treats out of any game.
Gameplay - As described previously, the player deters waves of antagonistic orc brutes using a variety of set traps, weapons, trinkets, and-if available-a partner. There is a loadout system implemented to where the player can only select a given number of traps at a specific point in the story; however, this ‘trapacity’ (do you see now why I am not permitted to make jokes? It should be court-ordered!) increases as the player progresses through the main campaign, and causes the player to select carefully before engaging the enemy. Each item retains its own unique upgrades, which allows players to partially dictate how they want to play. The usual shooter control layout is utilized (e.g. W, A, S, and D to maneuver, Space Bar to jump, LMB to use the equipped tool’s primary action) but there is no weapon zoom unless you are using the
modification for it; instead, the RMB functions your equipment’s secondary fire button, which-as an example when using the blunderbuss-fires a ball of energy that explodes on impact to damage and scatter hostiles.
Skull Currency System - As explained prior, the player has the option of purchasing upgrades to their existing items; additional equipment that can be purchased include character skins and new weapons and trinkets. Though the described system of ‘play your way’ intrigues me, how you obtain the in-game currency is even more interesting.
utilizes Skulls as a spendable asset, and are either dropped as a mark of achievement for scoring a high combination kill or for mastering a certain campaign level’s par, such as completing it within a given amount of time or not allowing any orcs into the Rift. This system is based more on performance than anything, which drives the player to achieve more advanced level scores and objectives for a more desirable Skull payout. It also entices players to attempt new trap and weapon combinations to try and best their previous scores.
Overall Feel - Whether orcs are flying due to a well-placed spring trap or are blown meters back by an enhanced blunderbuss blast,
melds the player together with an overwhelming sensation of hectic bliss. It is a purely indescribable impression that can be felt while playing either with a friend of solo. I honestly cannot exactly pinpoint single thing that makes this game as good as it is a cohesive punctuation of elements involving the thrill of every lightning bolt strike, every orc cartoonishly erupting in flames, every upgrade purchased; the game just feels right.
TL:DR - There is not much I can truly say against this game. I have an immense amount of fun whenever I play Orcs Must Die! 2, as it a truly unique gaming experience. From my perspective, players take the role of a comedic, naive sorcerer or sensible sorceress while attempting to prevent many orcs from reaching a rift using their upgradable weapons, equipment, and traps. I must admit that this game would be better to play with friends, but is just fine as a single-player experience. Have fun with this awesome game. Also, I will happily play cooperatively with anyone wishing to do so. Thanks for reading.

Before I say anything else, I have seen gameplay of this multiple times and I easily have collected over 25 hours in this world.
Alright, Night in the Woods. First thing that you should know if you are looking into playing this is that this game isn't for everyone. It's slow-paced, not much of an obvious plotline exists, and there isn't a whole lot of exciting (jumpy, fast-paced) things that are going to occur. However, if none of these things would distract you, I highly recommend it. The characters are sort of hit or miss in terms of how much you'll like them, but if you are already interested, I'm sure you'll enjoy them as much as I did.
There are many negative reviews on this game complaining about lack of story line, though this is completely false and they should not throw you off course. Night in the Woods is brilliant in it's form of presenting the storyline, as it shoves you into the middle of it and you are to learn more about the world and the characters by listening to their history. So in a sense, there isn't much a plot line in the present, but rather the characters reflect the story through conversations and their actions. Don't get me wrong, plenty happens in the present as well, including various things like Mae dropping out of college and the disappearance of Casey. There's plenty more things that happen, and going further in you'll find that the main story is following Mae's internal struggles. I believe the people who view this form of represantation were simply confused and unable to realize that this story isn't simply focusing on external conflicts but more so internal with nearly every major character.
Tl;dr, people who say this game has little story aren't really aware of the full picture and can be ignored in that sense.

This is probably going to be long. Just a heads up.
So, it all started out maybe a few months back. I heard of NitW coming out, but wasn't really interested in it. I watched a Starbot Dubs NitW comic dub, which got me a little more interested but not too much. Flash forward a few months, and my friend shows me Maebea. For those of you who don't know, it's the ship of the two main chars, Mae and Bea. Keep in mind I love gay ships, so I was kinda hooked. We were both furries too.  Flash forward to the Steam Christmas sale and Smissmas; I got a ton of money, so of course I blew a VERY small fraction of it on Night in the Woods.
It was the first of the 2 games I bought that I played. At first it was normal; Mae's everyday life was the same before she left from college, and I started to wonder when "Something's in the Woods," would happen from Night in the Wood's store page description, only slightly amused by the (spoilers)
.
And that's when Harfest happened. It took a gigantic turn, one that I only partially expected. It executed it perfectly; Mae only watched what had happened in horror, and as she tried to explain she was only shunted aside, portraying exactly what happens when something's wrong, but no one sees it until it's too late.
That's when those dreams started. And everything turned not into some college dropout's story; but the horror storyline which would only get worse. And yet, it was good. So good. Everything was so much more interesting, albeit confusing. As time went on, things started to get strange, and more confusing.
I finished the game. Now I was utterly perplexed, but I still liked it. It was a nice, fun game. I also did the Longest Night and Lost Constellation extra minigames.
But that wasn't the end. Something compelled me, told me to play it again and I would understand. Night in the Woods was the first Story-Based adventure game that made me want to play it again, to try another time, to try other routes, to answer my questions. Undertale, Bioshock, and the other games I played failed to do that.
Night in the Woods is a good game. The main spark that kept it was that everyone was an animal, but still acted like people; they didn't complain about their tail getting stuck, or their feathers falling off. Why? I don't know. But I only have a theory that they made them animals instead of people, to paint animals with the problems, instead of the norm of the humans having problems, and also to show that
.
So here I am. Playing the game.
I hope you do too.

Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor is essentially an open world Lord of the Rings game. It is perhaps an improved version of Assassins Creed. Definitely an enjoyable experience and fairly great all around.
- I would say that the main highlight of this game are the Uruk executions. They are so smooth and brutal. It is oddly satisfying to see dismembered Uruk heads fly in slow motion.
- Combat is quite fun and flows very smoothly; it reminded me of the Batman Arkham series combat style. You have a decent arsenal of weapons and abilities to play around with. The addition of quicktime events in battle also worked well. I’m usually not a fan, but it was well executed in this game.
- Since this game primarily endorses stealth, it is nice that you are given a variety of tools to assist with being stealthy. For example, you can quickly take down enemies, lure enemies, poison grog (their beverage of choice), shoot down meat to attract Caragors (vicious giant dog-like creatures), etc. It’s not my preferred playstyle, but the options kept me entertained.
- As you progress, the Uruk ranking system becomes more meaningful, especially after you unlock the branding ability. Suddenly you can battle their ranking system from within and force the Uruk to betray one another. Uruks also remember if they encountered you before and will act accordingly. If you ran away they will taunt you for your cowardice. If they killed you they will guarantee that you will die again. This dynamic makes Shadow of Mordor quite unique.
- I didn’t care much for most of the characters: very generic tragic heroes for the most part (not that I can blame them, considering their backstory). However, Ratbag and Torvin are great; two of the few characters that actually have a sense of humour. They made me laugh several times.
- Great attention to detail. Like the unique Uruk appearances and personalities, the runes on your weapons, or the addition of Ithildin. I especially like that the Uruk chant the Warchief’s name when he shows up.
- If you get the game of the year edition there are some nice extras, including two campaigns. I particularly enjoyed the Lord of the Hunt campaign because 1. you get to spend more time with Torvin; 2. compared to the main campaign, there is more variety to beasts/interacting with beasts. However, it is a shame that the controls don't feel as fluid when riding beasts.
- The world is fairly small, but in this case, that’s a good thing. Everything is fairly close by and you can unlock towers to fast travel to. You are always moments away from excitement. There are also skills and mounts that can help you travel faster so there is very little down time.
- Despite all the efforts to make this game quite diverse, i.e. different Uruk war chiefs with different weaknesses and abilities, different options to wreak havoc and kill Uruks, etc; this game still felt quite repetitive. Basically, you go from one point to the next killing Uruks, some of which are harder to kill than others.
- Often the cutscene audio was out of sync. Not sure if this is a mistake on my end, but I didn’t touch the audio settings before encountering this issue. I expect the default settings to work.
- For some reason Uruks will spawn endlessly. I find this a very strange decision on the part of the developers. Let me explain further. There are several camps in the game, naturally, they are full of enemies. If you are seen, an Uruk can raise the alarm, alerting the camp. Ok, makes sense. Here’s the issue: I don’t mind that I get seen, but I want to be able to win. Even if there are over 100 Uruk in a camp, theoretically you should be able to take them down one by one until you’re the only one left, right? Nope. They just keep spawning infinitely, and I don’t mean they only respawn when you exit and renter an area. They will literally respawn within meters from you only moments after you killed a few Uruk. I can understand that stealth is emphasized, but it shouldn’t be shoved down my throat. If I want to charge in head on it should be possible. More difficult, perhaps, but not impossible.
- It is a bit unnecessary that you must go through an unskippable cutscene every time a Captain sees you. This is especially obnoxious when a Warchief has several Captains as bodyguards and they tell you one by one how ugly you are (lol) or how they can’t wait to kill you. I enjoy their lines, but not the fact that the whole game stops just so you can hear them say it.
-
Overall, Shadow of Mordor is very well executed. Sure there are some imperfections here and there, but I still enjoyed playing it. I recommend you watch some
to see whether this game piques your interest. Personally, I look forward to playing the sequel. However, I hope that Shadow of War addresses some of the issues mentioned above.
