A game that takes place in the lord of the rings universe but contains some new features and some generic combat. Lets review of shadow of mordor in a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.
Pro:
Graphics are good. The world of mordor looks pretty ok on the first location but in the second location there is a lush pasture which is quite nice to look ate in a game dealing with the destruction of the realm of man or any non orc beings.
The characters sub characters are pretty decent. They are well modeled and well voiced leading to some nice conversations or in the case of ratbags...humor. Yes ratbag is a funny orc and that is pretty nice touch in the game.
The game is long. We are not talking about skyrim levels of long but there are quite a lot of things to do besides the main quests. Theres side missions that deal with mastery of the main characters weapons, conquesting the main lord of the rings villian's army, collectables, hunter quest, scavenger quest, and dlc. Though currently buying mordor grants the player the goty edition as the only version to buy but it still adds alot of value.
The game orc soldiers have stats or useful information. The main enemies in the game are no push overs, they require skill and planning to take down. The information for the enemies are gained from other orcs, captured people, or information laid out in the game. It displays the strengths and weakness of the captains which are a large variety. Doing the weaknesses really help out the fight.
The army arrangement is unique. The game has an army for the main bad guy, really dont know his name... Anyways the placement of each of the soldiers change depending on a variety of things like dying to a captain raises that captain up the ranks. That is pretty cool and shuffles the remaining captains around. If a captain is killed another will take its place in due time so there are plenty of opportunities to experience a variety of soldiers. If a regular guy kills the player then they can join the ranks if there is a spot open.
Most of the story is nice. Well to be fair the story that deals with the ghost guy's back story is pretty cool and very interesting to experience but the main character's revenge plot is nothing to write home about. Pretty generic and overall not interesting which is majority of the game. I put it as a pro because those small ammount of backstory missions really are what is the most enjoyable story moments of the game.
Con:
The main character is unlikeable. Other than his character design; his personality is not enjoyable. How can a person be immersed as a character with little to no personality than his sole purpose in this world is to have revenge. Now a plot with revenge can be good like in the case of john wick the movie but here with the lacking of any interesting personality, the character is too dull to enjoy.
Game breaking bug. Now this is a weird moment but when I started the game, there were no missions available from the start. Even after getting intel from an enemy the game would never place the missions on the map or in the game. It is a real bug and the only way is to restart all progress over again. I have noticed that in these recent reviews that there are repeating problems that are so easy to be solved.
1) Being Killed on sight (KOS) for no reason. This is something pretty common in open world survival games. In these games, the human race is practically the enemy. If you feel that being KOS is such a big issue, you have the option of a PvE server. With a PvE server you are able to learn the map, game mechanics, guns, etc. and are able to meet new people to play with. One tip I would recommend would be to not enter PvP alone unless you are skilled.
2) Taking too long to find loot. This is a game where you have to work to find your loot, it isn't just given to you. Personally, I have not found any problems with the loot system, it just shows that you have to value your arms and ammunition a lot more, and not just waste them on random mutants.
3) Being too quick to judge the game. In my opinion you really shouldn't jump straight into a full PvP server and expect to have a fun time. There are people who have been giving bad reviews for the game and they have played for 6 hours or less (excluding bad reviews from people who have played at least 10 or more) . Personally you should probably find someone to play with and someone to teach you about the game when you start out, if PvE servers aren't your thing.
There are of course, the cons to the game.
- Slow development times
- Long loading times (even if it is a large map)
- Glitches (I have not encountered that many bad ones, but you will notice them)
- Vehicles despawning after 2 days of inactivity. (This is something that supposedly should have players play the game regularly so that people don't hog vehicles. Personally, I feel that it is a chore to be logging in every day to check on my car so it doesn't despawn.
Personally, I feel that these developers should allow modding for this game, so the community may be able to create new maps or game modes that may create a better environment for new players.
If you truly do not like this game, I fully respect that. I feel that I had to get this review out because I see that most of these reviews are from players that have had a rough start to the game, and/or are very in experienced with this genre of games. I would just recommend trying PvE servers to start out to eventually play on PvP servers.
I wish current players, and future players the best of luck on their experience. You should buy this game not for what it is as of now, but what it will eventually be in the future. Regardless of the slow updates, developers are slowly making the game better in terms of optimization, and a bit more content such as new vehicles, map locations, etc.
Feel free to message me if you want to learn more about the game and /or play with me.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Vlambeer has always been good at creating really simple yet excellently controlling games, and Luftrausers is certainly no exception. Essentially, you have four buttons: acceleration, boost left and right, and fire. You do have a "health meter," which is represented by a white circle closing in on you before you eventually die, which can be replenished by letting go of the fire button and not getting hit for a little bit. Speaking of death, this game is pretty tough. It certainly has that arcade style quarter munching level of difficulty. However, death is only a minor setback, as it only takes two to three seconds to get back into the action after dying. An average run won't last you much longer than two or three minutes, though.
Another aspect of this game is the customizable ship parts. You can get up to six guns, engines, and bodies, each with their own respective weaknesses and strengths. It is these parts, as well as the challenges associated with each and every part, that make Luftrausers much more than the simple arcade shooter I thought it was when I first saw it. There is actually a remarkable amount of depth for such a seemingly simple shooter (yes, that alliteration was intentional). My biggest complaint about the game - and it may seem minor, but it caused God knows how many deaths - is that every time you get hit, there is a frame or two of pausing. It stacks up whenever you're trying to manoeuvre your way through a hail of bullets. This is probably an intentional programming thing, as a ninety-some-megabyte game should not lag an i5-3470.
Other than that, I really don't have any big time complaints. Also, SFMT mode made me cry in the corner out of sheer terror. I haven't completed all of the missions yet, and I still haven't unlocked the [Classified] as of the time of writing this, but I've gotten far enough into the game that I feel that I am able to give it fair enough of a review. For only one "big small" quibble, I give the gameplay in this game a 9/10.
Story: This is one of the times where I don't bother to review the game on story, since there really isn't any. Instead, I'll just skip on to the graphics and not factor in a score for story into the final score.
Graphics: One of the great things about applying a minimalist aesthetic is that it allows the artist to apply all sorts of subtle touches, and that's what makes this game great: it's filled to the brim with subtle touches that make it just great. For instance, when you're coming in over the water, how hard you're coming in affects the wake.Another subtle touch is the flames that come off of the aces whenever they are at low health. Overall, the pixel art in this game is just fantastic, and is definitely a good example of how to do considerable things with a minimal color pallete. For graphics, I'll give it a 5/5, 'cuz it just looks great.
Music: At its most basic level, there's only two songs in the game (the menu song and the combat song). However, in reality, there's about 126 songs in the game. How I can come up with that number is that there are 125 different ship combinations. Each part adds a different element to the base song. It's not a subtle thing, either; you can tell whenever a part you've put on changes the song, and all of them add pretty cool touches to the song. If you're switching parts every now and then, you most certainly won't get tired of the soundtrack. I know I didn't, and that's why I'm giving it a 5/5 for the incredibly dynamic soundtrack.
Overall rating: 9/5/5; 9.5/10. I can see why this game took so long to develop: there's a remarkable amount of polish to this game. Also, if you think $10 is too much, don't. The game really is worth the money (even more so on sale). It's very playable  and has that "I need to kill ten minutes so here's a game" appeal.

Until they implement a tutorial on how to use the time mechanic I recommend not even bothering with this mod. The mod makes use of the keys Q, R, & F to implement the aspect of starting, stopping, and replaying time, but that information isn’t made known to you upon getting into the game. They attempt to show you what you need to do through in-game video screens that display an example of two people working together in order to progress, but they don’t make the connection that the other “player” in the video is the past copy of yourself. My first impression of the video was, “wait, you need another person to play this?”
While I was able to get out of the first puzzle room, the second left me stumped as I was randomly playing with the time mechanic, but I really had no idea what I was actually doing and how those actions resulted in a positive or negative reaction.
Both Portal and Portal 2 have in-game tutorials to show you how the portal gun works and how to apply these basic skills to solve puzzles. This mod needs that because without showing the player how the time mechanic works you leave the player completely baffled as to what they’re supposed to do and unsure about why they’re not progressing.

One of the best versions of Counter-Strike (at least in my opinion).
CONDITION ZERO/TOUR OF DUTY
CZ adds new weapons, maps, auto-buy options, and even multiple singleplayer modes. It still has servers, and they aren't disappearing anytime soon; even if they were to, this specific version of CS has not only the option to add bots, but to also play the, "Tour of Duty" mode, where you customize your own squad from points earned from completing levels. These levels consist of your average Counter-Strike match but it comes with objectives that must be completed in order to win.
DELETED SCENES
Known as the "Deleted Scenes", it is a campaign complete with a story and voice acting that is very reminiscent of the original Half-Life, just with less headcrabs and more angery machete men. Deleted Scenes is an interesting experience, but it feels, "unfinished". It is still very playable, but it feels a bit buggy here and there but it is still playable from beginning to end. But considering these are, "Deleted Scenes", it is understandable that this part of the game would not be completely polished.
At the end of the day, this game takes everything from the original Counter-Strike, and just adds extra options and features, so I believe buying this adds on to a great experience that somehow is made even better.

A sequel to the venerable Counter-Strike, only this time with upgraded graphics, a singple-player campaign, and the introduction of a few new maps, essentially what Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is. I must admit, I was bewildered as to why such a game existed as it came in a Counter-Strike bundle I had ordered for £7 - which included Counter-Strike, Condition Zero + Deleted Scenes, and Global Offensive - so when I booted up the game, I was in for what I could only describe as the story mode version of Counter Strike.
The game presents Tour of Duty missions, each in their own unique maps, and gives you the ability before the fight to assemble a team, with each soldier having their own statistics which will affect their behavioural and combat abilities. Once you get into the mission, there are different objectives such as "Kill an enemy with a sniper rifle" or "Rescue a hostage" which compliment the gameplay and add a unique sidequest while you actively seek victory for your team you compiled.
Being the sequel to the exalted Counter-Strike, there is still a multi-player option available, just don't be surprised with the lack of active servers, for that you'll want to return to Counter-Strike 1.6 or go up a generation altogether.
Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is a polyphony of single-player and multi-player, with a wholesome single-player campaign which doesn't steer away from the game's core mechanics.
If you've never touched a Counter-Strike game before and want to have a go at one, you can't go wrong with picking Condition Zero as the starting grid to your Counter-Strike journey.

Nobunaga's Ambition: Sphere of Influence is a good game. It might be a tad over-simplified (streamlined?) for the strategy enthusiast, but it's easy to play and doesn't have a lot of abstract mechanics that could muddy the experience. It does encourage (well, basically require) delegating parts of your territory to AI control once you get large enough, which might be a turn-off for some people.
Being able to play out any battle in a Total War-esque battlefield is a nice touch, but it does feel about as rough as you'd expect for a non Total War game. It's functional and a nice change of pace though, and allows for outplaying the AI, as opposed to having to purely outmuscle/outflank them in the standard automatic overworld battles.
My main complaint is the tedium of building things and improving your provinces. Early on it's not too bad, if a bit time consuming and granular even at such small scale, but the rewards of a well managed province aren't overwhelming; after you've got one or two optimized provinces and expanded a bit you'll probably find yourself letting the AI make the decisions.
The wide variety of generals is quite nice, all with visually pleasing portraits, but the huge amount of events is something to call attention to. It can be fun trying to pursue the available events for your faction, to unlock special scenes and effects; there is a lot of intriguing Sengoku-era history in this game to be discovered, across most of the available factions. However, custom factions will lack access most of these events... such playthroughs will have a notable lack of personality and intrigue compared to a popular faction like the Oda or Takeda.
Ultimately, I had fun with the game. It's a modern take on the age-old Nobunaga's Ambition series, and it sometimes shows its age, but it's worth a play if you enjoy the series or have an interest in the period.

I've been a long time Ace Combat fan and I will admit that this game is not all that bad, but I simply cannot recommend it to people who are thinking that they're getting an Ace Combat game when they're purchasing it.
1.  The story
I'm well aware that story was never the strong point in Ace Combat games, sure, but they were at least charming enough that you could connect with them.  The story of this game was just too ridiculous to take seriously;  I couldn't help but roll my eyes and think "What.....seriously?" when the "motives" of the main antagonist were revealed (Won't spoil, but it's just STUPID).
2.  Helicopter/Gunship missions
They're kinda neat at first, but the more you do them the more you get to wondering "So when am I getting back into the jet again?".  Ace combat was always based around dogfighting with the best aces around, and these missions just felt completely out of place, like they didn't even belong in an Ace Combat game.
3.  DFM (Dog Fighting Mode)
It's kinda cool at first.  Makes the game very cinematic and gives you the feeling that you're the badass ace that you're supposed to be; only problem is that they take it WAY too far.  Some parts of the game are literally impossible to complete without it and aren't properly designated so you could be repeating a segment upwards of 10 times without knowing that you HAVE to be in DFM to win.  And I'm sorry, those ace fights where you're literally pumping 10-20 missiles into the back of some "Ace" pilot's plane?  That's not fun, that's just ridiculous.
4.  Replayability
There is none.  Sure you could go back and replay missions in the "Free Mission" mode after you unlocked them, but because of all the above problems it's just not FUN to do so.  All those new planes that you unlock after you beat the campaign are basically meaningless because the game forces a set playstyle on you with DFM.
Summary/TL;DR:  It was fun for the initial run of the campaign, but not beyond that.  Worth it if you're buying it for the sale, not so much otherwise.

Finally a zombie game that actually gets the point of zombies! It's not about shooting zombies - they're slow and stupid! No, it's all about the base - you know I'm right. You and your friends already know where your base is going to be if a Zombie Apocalypse happens - you've planned it in detail, worked out who you'd take, what to loot first.
Yet Zombie games are all about wandering around on your own, shooting them. Until now.
State of Decay places you in the midst of the Zombie Apocalypse and your onjective is primal - survive, by pulling together a team of other survivors with the skills you need, finding and modifying a base to fill your needs and keeping it supplied.
To make this somewhat more difficult, you have zombies trying to eat you. You have your basic Ready Salted Zombie, slow, stupid, endlessly hungry and more than a little squishy, especially around the head. But just to make things a little more tricky, you have a cavalcade of Freaks - mutant zombies with different patterns of behaviour to normal. And they are NASTY.
In any game about survival, it's important that however skilled you become, there is something that can kill you unless it screws up or you don't, and State of Decay provides these in a plethora of different ways. Zombies are attracted to noise, so fire your gun without a silencer, crash your car or have a companion who dies screaming and they will start homing in on you from miles away. The more zombies you're fighting, the louder things get and the more zombies come. The endless numbers can wear you down and as exhaustion takes its toll, the end is often close behind.
If not through a steady trickle of reinforcements, you might instead fall afoul of a full-fledged zombie horde, wandering the streets looking for warm-blooded food. Your location might be surrounded by them and fall under siege and yes, you do get to board up the windows. It keeps you safe for a while, until some gigantic redneck farmchild too large to fit through the door punches it through, drags you out and tears you in two. Flee and you might be run down by a speeding deceased member of the armed forces or a SWAT team agent in full body-armour and helmet, or pounced on from out of the blue by the swift and deadly animalistic Ferals.
Successfully combine your fighting and running and get clear and back to base? Don't worry, you'll probably still die from the Black Fever carried by bloated, ancient corpses in the mob - and by your companions, once they're exposed. Medicine is in short supply and medical know-how, even shorter - you either recover, or you die... and then come back for your friends.
If all that's not enough, you have the armed forces up to dubious things in the area, a former judge attempting to enforce the rules of civilized society in a world where there isn't one, a redneck family one banjo short of Deliverance, a doomed love affair and a passel of mis-matched survivors steadily driving each other insane. Suicide, murder and run-aways are all risks you'll run, along with drug addiction from the amphetamines you're jamming down your throat and up your nose just to stay on your feet.
Oh, and one of you might just be a serial killer.
State of Decay gives a proper nod to all the tropes of the genre. I haven't found any chainsaws, which seems a grotesque oversight, but you can spot the zombies who've been chewed through the chest by a lawnmower a la "Braindead". Look closely enough at the magazine racks and grocery packaging and see the order to OBEY from "They Live", Hedge trimmers? Check. Oar? Yup. The faithful rusty pipe of Silent Hill? Aw hells, yeah. Can you knock a Zed's head off by opening the car door as you drive past it at speed? Of course!
The base locations are also classics - a shipping warehouse, a posh walled manor, the local Church, a barricaded farmhouse out of town, an amusement park... all have their pros and cons and on the whole, are very well-balanced.
The main weak point of the game is characterization, with little more than a few lines of insight into one motivation of some of the characters, which appears in a dialogue when the character is getting to know you. In a game where you're expected to lose a few characters and switch to playing others, a measure of emotional attachment would really add to the atmosphere. Game mechanics, however, provide a surrogate reason to get attached to characters - after all that time training their skills, the loss of a character can bring a chilling feeling of doom, especially if they were the only one in your band of survivors with an essential skill, and the moods of your fellow survivors crash drastically after any loss.
While vanilla State of Decay's story mode is great fun, where it really comes into its own is with the Breakdown DLC. Breakdown sets the game to sandbox mode. You start with only your character (and Lily, your non-combatant radio operator) and build up a group and a base, accomplish certain objectives to unlock new characters or recruit other groups of survivors, play the level for as long as you wish, however you wish, then pick your six favourite characters, bundle them onto an RV with all your remaining gear and start the level again... only this time it's harder. And then you do it again, and again, and again.
Your characters can become pretty experienced like this, but only if they survive. The ratio of difficulty to character skill is very well judged, so no matter how well you survived the last x levels and how godly your characters are, there is always a definite sense that you are in much more trouble this time... without it ever quite feeling impossible.
The game has a few bugs, but they are mostly minor and don't crop up repeatedly, so they're not game breaking but you might lose a character or two to teleporting Freaks or your car suddenly flipping and exploding for no reason.
If you're looking for a Zombie Apocalypse simulator, this is the one you've been waiting for while you plot your survival strategies in the pub with friends. Don't forget to buy Breakdown, because the story mode will have you aching for the sandbox during those moments when the plot is demanding your attention and you want to ransack just one... more.. cupboard.

Pure garbage even by 1999 standards. Even if you get the graphics working halfway (Protip: choose software rendering), the mechanics are tedious and nonsensical. The only good point this has is that you can spam click through the near endless and stupid dialogue.
I gave up my fifty cents so you don't have to. You're welcome.

First off, the game has serious problems with graphics on modern computers and surprisingly, it's easier to run it on a laptop with an integrated graphics card than on a regular PC. When buying it, do expect it.
As for the game itself. Back when it was released in 1999 it was definitely a hit, however it has aged rather bad. The 3D graphics are clearly outdated - low res textures, low poly models, etc. Still, the general crudeness of the game somehow appealed to me so I decided to play it and finished it afterall.
Unfortunately, the gameplay itself is extremely dull. Once you get the hang of all of the game mechanics the game's only about fighting a vicious, unforgiving AI, which is rather easy to predict. Boss fights are oversimplified and often boil down to blocking/stunning the boss and hammering him/her down with every weapon available. The final boss fight is a complete joke and is probably the easiest of them all.
Finally, I was greatly disappointed with the plot and depiction of characters. Once the Great Conspiracy is revealed, it turns out to be a huge load of bullocks. It doesn't even qualify for a Z grade movie. Also, two of the characters totally drove my gears - Jarek Ovitz and Slavsky. I'm of Polish descent and Ovitz is NOT a typical Polish surname, nor is Slavsky a typical Polish name. Polish people are depicted in Gorky17 as strong, yet dumb and supersticious. Also, they have Russian accents and speak very bad Polish. I know the game was probably low-budget, but that doesn't excuse a complete lack of research on Poland and Polish people.
Honestly, I am super patient and that's the only reason I managed to complete the game. However, the game's not worth your time. There are other, better ones around.

I'll start off with saying this is a very hard review for me to write. I'm still not entirely sure whether I like OMD!2 or not.
I played through the base OMD!2 campaign with Kataztrophik. Playing games with others always makes for a better experience for me.
Unfortunately I found myself getting bored on more than one occasion. The maps all looked pretty much the same, the variance in enemies is limited, and I found the traps to be uninspired and mostly useless.
I'm a huge fun of TD games. They can be repetitive. The strategy in a TD game comes from playing towers/traps/units in best places, and finding a balance between upgrading and placing new units. Then there's the diversity. Do I need to deal with fast enemies? Maybe they're cloaked? Those ones are flying. Wait! There's a group that are resistant to a certain damage type! Oh no here comes the boss!!!
OMD!2 has none of this. You place a trap and that's it. You can sell it in build phases, but there's no upgrading as the level goes on. Therefore the only option is to spam defences everywhere with your spare cash.
The enemies in OMD!2 are very limited. It has some flyers, some high health hard hitting Ogres, some exploding Kobolds, some fast little buggers, Trolls that regenerate health and then the general mob. Even so they all seem pretty much the same.
The game just spams you with more and more mobs as the level progresses. You counter it by spamming more and more traps. There's no real strategy. Sure the traps filter out some of the bad guys, but you'll be doing most of the killing with your weapons.
This is where the game shines. The action gameplay in combat is pretty good. It's fluid and the weapons are fun to use. However, whilst this is certainly fun it offers nothing ground-breaking or unique. With the lack of variance of the enemy one faces it can also get pretty boring fast.
The biggest thing the game seems to lack for me, is bosses. There should be an epic fight against a might orc, the likes of which has never been seen before! There should be a dragon! A dragon would fit into the games style nicely, and there's no reason why there isn't one.
Overall OMD!2 is a mildly fun action game, with underwhelming TD elements. It's worth playing through the game with a friend, but there are better options available.
Bottom line: Good in short stints with a buddy.

Night in the woods did it's job in dragging emotions out of me throughout it's playthrough, its a damn shame they were mostly negative ones.
I'll quickly go over the positives in this game:
- The soundtrack is superb, i think each track is used perfectly for each situation you find yourself in and does a great job in relating what the game wants you to feel.
- Art direction keeps each setting interesting and fresh, with the scenery usually changing each day to keep it fresh. (I loved the dream sequences)
- For an interactive story telling game it has quite the playtime of around 20 hours if you want to go through both the Gregg and Bea plots and the bonus content, i've gotten more hours out of cheaper games but not from games of the same genre.
- If you go through events in different orders, dialogue will change accordingly, which is something I very much appreciate from the devs.
- With a game that's as Tumblr as this, im surprised at the lack of cancer from the community (so far).
As for the rest of the game, what the hell happened?
I was hooked within the first hour, i was completely enthralled in what i was going to learn about these seemingly interesting characters in the black hole known as Possum Springs, but after 7 hours of playtime and no plot i started to get a tad annoyed.
My biggest complaint is how dragged out the story is, if you want to re-visit and re-talk to everything you've discovered each day a playthrough will take you around 12 hours, this honestly feels like a cat got hit by a combine harvester and just because a doctor with parkinsons felt a pulse on what used to be a cat you've decided to keep the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on life support on the hope of it recovering.
I say this because interacting with MOST of the characters is completely pointless, and you'll probably ignore 90% of them on a second playthrough. The 10% who do hold any wait is usually due to an achievement. Even if you speedrun the game it still takes hours just for a hint of a plot (we'll get to that later).
Another complaint of mine are the godawful characters. EVERYONE is a stereotype or cliche of some kind, you've got edgy gothcrocs, get off my lawn grandpas, sport supporting bar dudes, the gays, closeted gays, schizos, tumblrites, old racists, mysterious introverts, spectrums, one normal guy, eccentric bookclub, etc.
I would of thought you'd get to learn anything about at least the main characters, but you get like one scene for each of them near the end-game. (Act one of a story is getting to know the characters, not the godamn epilogue)
The main characters are just draining, it gets to the point where im mashing my controller just to fast forward the dialogue since most of it is just filler until they get to the point. Every single conversation is just utter pain to get through.
Let me summarise most of the conversations in this game:
Spasticated greeting
MEME!
Stuttering
Question asked
Awkward pause
Another question asked
First question ignored and second question answered
Character has a stroke
Even longer pause as the player tries to recover their mental stability
Character you didnt even pay attention to adds to the conversation and is then ignored until developer remembers that they exist
Player cringing as they realise how many animation assets are re-used just for filler
Conversation abruptly ends with Mae staring into their soul or Star Wars OT edit
The characters themselves are just terrible people, Gregg is practically a sociopath who is hostile to anyone except his friends/mutual friends and thinks shanking his friends and committing felonies are happy fun times, Bea turns immediately hostile to anyone who doesnt pity her and/or tries to help fix her life, Mae is a genuine piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥who is so selfish she gets impatient if you take too long to mourn dead family member (and no, she doesnt get a pass just because she hates herself), and im pretty sure Angus' dead face matches his dead heart (also i believe he's the last thing you see if you're tossed into the pit).
Oh yeah, the pit, the antagonist of the game. After around 7 hours of doing nothing until you see a g-g-g-ghost (spoiler alert) you see a kidnapping, for some dumb reason Mae is fully certain she saw a ghostnapping because he could climb a fence well. So you spend the next 3 hours or so investigating sp00py shenanigans with your "friends" (the only one who seems to genuinely like you is Gregg). Then out of the left ♥♥♥♥ing field you stumble across a cult, at this point i thought i was hallucinating a plot for the game myself since it was so ridiculous it couldnt possibly be real, but it was.
I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not there was a murdercult kidnapping people the entire time, which the devs could of foreshadowed throughout the game if they could be arsed (and no, just because cults were mentioned a few times without any context throughout the game dont make it count as foreshadowing).
Anyway you apparently get shot at by the world's most quietest guns and fall unconscious for no reason, while your best buds ditch you because they'd rather play video games while you bleed out in some forest god-knows-where, then you get a confusing montage of scenes randomly stitched together with you teleporting around until you end up with the gang again and decide to take on the cult again.
Cue 15 minutes of crippled Mae limping around, 5 minutes of yadda yadda dialogue about feeding some pit god, the cult telling you to leave and then trying to stop you to leave and then you purposely trapping them down there to starve to death becuase you're such good people.
Anyway the epilogue then begins with you saying your farewells to every character you've met, even though dozens of people were murdered last night the town still seems fully populated (wouldn't it have been fun trying to figure out who was in the cult?)  and then you go to band practice which ends the game with some shallow cliffhanger that leaves far too many questions and too little answers.
Conclusion:
I'm pretty sure if this game had a plot and gave the characters actual growth then this would of been absolutely perfect, they nailed pretty much everything except the two things which are most important in an interactive story. Plot should of began at most an hour and a half in with that time spent getting to know the characters, then having the characters growing and bonding throughout the game instead of staying as two-dimensional archetypes who whenever show any legitimate emotion it's only for two minutes and is instantly forgotten about.
I just honestly couldnt give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about any of them.
TLDR:
Act one lasts 7 hours, act two lasts 4 hours, act 3/conclusion lasts 45 mins with a 15 minute epilogue at the end.
Characters are too reliant on archetype personalities and are exactly the same as when the game ends.
It's hard to care about the characters when there's no plot driving them and it's hard to care about the "plot" when the characters it's affecting are crap.

So people recommended I play this game since I'm a Monster Hunter fan..
- Gameplay: Combat has some similarities, but mostly when it comes to bosses. This game puts a heavy emphasis on bait-and-punish and counterplay. It will also expect you to take things slowly or be forced to learn by dying. I can't think of any death that I'd solely put on the game.
- Difficulty: Not as "omg impossible" as some people make it out to be. Yes, it's hard, but you'll learn as you play. Just make sure you go to the right place after you finish the tutorial, and not die 100+ times in the Catacombs like I did...
- Music: There was barely any, save for boss music. Barely memorable...
- Replayability: Oh man I feel like this is part of the game's draw. There's so much you can do with your character, so many weapons and spells to use... it just feels so good to try different things and do well. It's also close to impossible to 100% the game in a single playthrough, and you need to do a lot to understand...
- Story: The game won't give you much to go on. You'll have to make due with some vague hints from some NPCs or even equipment (yes, equipment). The endings won't help you understand what's going on. This was a real bummer for me. Thankfully there are tons of resources out there to help you connect the dots.
Overall, definitely an experience worth trying once, at least. As long as you have an average person's intellect and reflexes, you'll be fine. Just... make sure to get DSfix so you can fix the frame data issue.

If you like Terraria you MIGHT like this.
Starbound has many similarities between the two games, graphics and the game itself really (mining, ore tiers, cool weapons etc.) However, it really does feel like a spinoff of Terraria. IMO Terraria is a fully packaged game that has hundreds of hours to be played. Starbound felt it had a  hundred MAX (partially due to the main quest). I don't like the quest mechanic in the game at all, especially side quests as they repeated themselves insanely often (find friend, kill bandits, kill specific NPC). Main quest is literally scanning items and then fight a boss repeat. The story didn't feel amazing as it felt choppy with no "good plot" to it, mediocre at best but the characters are likeable. What I did enjoy about the game was the boss fights and combat. It felt unique yet similar with Terraria. The boss fights felt fun to play yet somewhat challenging with cool mechanics. I bought this game for $15 and I got about 20 hours of fun (like a dollar of fun per hour). I mainly found this game fun because I had my best friend play it with me as there are funny moments as you explore the galexy with aliens. BUT I don't think this game would be fun by yourself as it can be frustrating with some bad game design. Mild things that irritated me were holding torches does not provide light and NPCs that walk through doors would automatically close them. Also your ship is very uninteractive and was really hoping to have space battles of some sort. I hope they fix these two things above because I don't see the harm of adding them in and it was really inconvenient. I didn't download many mods to this game although I hear it's very fun. I don't think I'd want to play this game again. Honestly, I would only recommend this game if you're a HUGE fan of Terraria and are itching to play. Make sure you have some friends willing to play with you. If Terraria is a 10, I'd give this a 6.5.

This has been the best Street Fighter thus far IMO. I feel that this game requires more skill and thought processing than V. IV allowed players to be creative with their characters and the mechanics such as FADC, FA, and being able to link light attacks into Heavy attacks or medium attacks (and vice versa) gave this game life. I am aware that some attacks are like this in V, but not as much and a lot of combos start off with either st.mp or cr.mp to get everything going. I feel that V lacks the fidelity and still has a lot that needs to be worked on. Yes, IV had its problems (it still does), but guess what, V carries out some of those problems as well. But, everyone has their own opinions about both these games. I hope this review helps (or somewhat does) gamers who are trying to look for a good competitive and serious game.

Ok... so, I just finished the main campaign. And where do I even begin?
Should I point out how I think this game is just your avarage Playstation 2 GTA/action game... or, should I point out how this game only got its overblown hype, awards and attention because of nostalgia... and some references here and there to the movies.
This game is rich in its story; epic in its soundtrack and good-looking in its graphics... but is disappointing in its gameplay. Especially disappointing in its final-boss fight... if you would even call it ''a final-boss fight''.
So, in conclusion... can I recommend this game to others? No and Yes.
I can't recommend this game to everyone... just a handful of people. I can recommend this game to your avarage Grand Theft Auto/Action-fan... And of course, Lord of the Rings-fan. I can't recommend this game to people expecting a Witcher 2/Dark Souls out of this game.
In a nutshell:
+ story
+ graphics
+ music
- gameplay
- disappointing final-boss fight... all that build-up for nothing.
-The main-campaign is short.
The Arkham-style combat isn't engaging and the game mechanics are blended into the open world poorly enough to be immersion-breaking. The story is more fan-fiction than anything remotely serious.

Review:
This game is outstanding. However, don't compare it to Shogun:TW. The setting is the same, but the gameplay isn't. This game is more akin to playing Crusader Kings with a dash of total war battle mini-game.
The beauty of this game is the ability to plan on the overmap with vassals and retainers exactly how you'll invade territory. You can set routes of march for each independent army, set which provinces will support the other, order vassals to provide support to specific units etc and then hit "end turn" and watch your plan unfold. If you need to adjust your plan; you pause, make changes and go again. It's very well done.  The graphics for the units on the overland map are just like the graphics used in the Japanese TV series AOI Tokugawa Sandai. Youtube it. You'll see. @ 5 Minutes, 39 Seconds and 8m 45s
Though the game may seem daunting at first, it really is picked up rather quickly if you have a taste for grand strategy. You can micromanage every single castle, or designate provinces, assign regents and set the more tedious funtions of government to be delegated to your retainers. You can set a policy which is conservative, progressive or neutral. You can also set focus on Agriculture, Military or Crafts (commerce)
The game also has these intermissions with slide show animations about historical events that took place during the time, giving you, at least, a basic understanding of the situation in Japan at the time. It's great for the history minded, though are easily skipped if you prefer to.
You can create your own officers. Create your own clan. Form alliances. Absorb tribes, dominate vassals. Appeal to the Emperor for titles. It's ALL THERE.
If you love strategy and especially, if you love the history of Japan. This game is a no brainer.
Do yourself a favor and get it. Play the admittedly, boring tutorial. Then play on easy for a bit to get the hang of it. Really, there is a lot to do, but the game will prompt you when things need to get done. Once you see how it is done, you delegate to your retainers. Once you figure that out, (which doesn't take long) it's really easy to start dreaming big about how you'll become Sei-i Taishōgun!!!!!
Heeeet Heeeet Hoooooo!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

It's basically the japanese version of Romance of Three Kingdoms...and from the same company.
You can build towns, upgrade them, have some lvl of diplomacy and go to war, all in all pretty nice and solid. If you like japanese history or this kind of game in general, then this game is not so bad.
BUT....
...it's a massive click-fest. You wanna upgrade your castle ?
1. click on upgrade
2. click on the castle you wanna upgrade
3. click on the slot you wanna upgrade
4. click on the upgrade you want
5. click on the guy you want to do the job
6. click on the confirmation
... and you're getting kicked back to map, if you want to upgrade another slot on the same castle, you have to start from point 2 again. If you want to upgrade 4 slots in each of your 20 castles, you're clicking like made for the next 15mins+. Isn't much better for the rest of the game. You can automate at least some of that, but then you have to live with what the AI builds...which is usually crap. The AI built town ends up with 4ooo rice a year and a meager 2ooo soldiers....build it manually and you end up with 20ooo soldiers and still enough food.
Going to war..isn't overly enjoyable either. Click on the town, choose wether you wanna employ horses and or guns and done. You have 1 army. Armies can only move along roads...of course you canNOT built new ones. Tactics like comming outta the woods impossible.
So you send your army to fight, then watch numbers pop up above your army and the enemy until 1 army disappears. The only "tactical option" you have is attacking from 2 sides...assuming the enemy is on a crossroad and you can reach more then 1 road leading there.....
Playing the battles manually ain't any better. Every army is...1 army. All you can do is click your army and click where to go. Clicking on an enemy allows you to choose melle or ranged attack. Lastly you can use a skill (1 per officer in the army, 1 for horses, 1 for ranged), Those skills use a global resource that refills over time.
Choosing formations, the direction to face, laying ambushes or any other kind of remotely tactical gameplay....is not existent. At least Romance of three Kingdoms 11 allowed you to build armies with spears,pikes,swords,bows or siege engines, each having strengths and weaknesses....
The "historic gameplay"...is probably among the worst i had to endure in ages. The idea is nice and all but
You start out as Oda, the historic quest tells you to invade the province to the south. After crushing the counter attack you decide to continue. 40 years (ingame) later you still haven't gotten any history quests...and the game doesn't tell you anything. You have to search the net for posts telling you to only take the first castle. Because in a decade an event will take that castle from you giving it to the original owner..who will become your ally in another decade...and needs to be wiped out in yet another decade.
So you spend years (hours of gameplay) doing NOTHING just to not break the future historic quests.....and you still don't get them thanks to the "AI".
Like at some point an event allies you with Mino to the north...the next turn Mino marches a horde to attack the other Oda clan in your province. Problem is you are supposed to take that clan out in a historic quest a few years further. And you have absolutely no way of preventing them from getting murdered now. Your only choice is to hack/cheat/edit Mino, nerf-batting him to where he stops the attack. Then his neighbours start attacking him...and you need him for a historic quest as well...so you nerfbat his neighbours....then the neighbours neighbours....then.....
1 hour later you have nerfbatted every single clan on the map to oblivion (except your own) just to ensure no future quest breaks....and you can do the same again in half a hour....

This game always has me coming back for more. It is a top-down dungeon crawler where you play as little Isaac in his attempt to avoid his own imminent demise. Between the religious overtones and pop culture references, every item has its own personality and will change the playstyle of the whole run. The permadeath feature and fairly short game times, coupled with the plethora of items to unlock gives Rebirth incredible replay value. The game has also received several free content updates, it only keeps getting better.

Now, if you're scared of a challenge: ***run***.
This game isn't always easy. It can very easily be swayed one way or another, but it's fun alright. Each run is different, only being made the same by players inputting a seed from another run. There's a wide cast of items, enemies, and rooms to make each run different. Can the game hurt to play? Yes. I took a nearly two month break from it. But I came back for it. The game even has an active Steam Workshop and other modding communities to add more. You're buying a challenge with this game, but it's a good, mostly fun one.

State of Decay is a Zombie, Survival, Base Builder game that takes you for a spin in the world of a very recent zombie outbreak, bringing everything that entails with it.
In State of Decay you rely on your community to help you out as they rely on you to lead them, it's a game you can only go it alone for so long before needing the help of others, others you'll have to gain the trust of to get their help.
Like many other zombie games State of Decay has some out of the ordinary freak-mutation zombies that are relentless in trying to kill you and without swiftly responding to their arrival, make quick work of you.
Vehicles are a thing but if not used wisely you'll eventually find yourself making that supply run on foot as once a vehicle is destroyed, it's gone.
Maintaining your vehicles and equipment is a priority, supply runs will keep your people happy, you well equiped and things from getting out of hand.
While State of Decay lacks the realism experience it is still a great game that most zombie, survival gamers will love.

NOTE: I bought this on sale and I got all the DCL's with it.
This game is a lot of fun, why?
You start to play, get some story wich interested me and I had to kill an captain. Killing him was fun, so i decided to go hunt more captains.
I killed all the captains (execpt the mission locked ones) and then realised I had already about 15 hours in the game.
The story is decent, this game isn't really about the story, if you constantly do the story missions it is over in about 6 hours (bit of a guess, I did half of the story missions in 2 hours. but I had already played about 20 hours on another save slot)
The captains and warchief are at the beginning difficult, after a hour of 2 you can take most captains, not always easy but still fun because of the other elements that come to it, like is there a group of Uruks with you or are you alone with the captain and the intel of the capaint that either screws you over or you use to your advantage.
Later the captains become more difficult, I now hunt warchiefs, if they have 1 or more bodyguards and try to kill all of them, that can be very challenging as some can kill you in 1 shot (happend just a few times, so gather intel to know by which captain/warchief you don't want to get hit by). Even worse if they have no last chance, you get hit you die, this can sometimes be frustating.
Biggest challenge I had so far, 1 warchief with 5 captains at the same time. Died 3 times be at the end all of them were died and that felt really good when I got all of them.
About the DLC's I only recommend getting the free DLC's. Unless you like trail and error, then you could get the challenge and test DLC's, but be sure you like killing captains and warchiefs, they are about trying to get as much score as you can (you can also try to do elite version, with requires you to have done certain things, like in a certain time with certain score)
Do get the free DLC's, mostly Test of power (only challeng that is free as far as I now) and the power of shadow, this one contains extra runes that might suite your playestyle.
The bright Lord and the Lord of the hunt DLC's are 2 campaings, both are fun, but I don't think worth what they cost (9,99€), however. If your really like the game and want to get more for the game, you can buy them (of one of them)
The bright Lord is more difficult in fighint, but does have its advantage, not telling what because that would be spoiler, possible for the story as well.
The bright Lord campaing does give a bitt of story of what happend before, also has a small amount of colletibles (10 if I remember correctly)
The lord of the hunt campaing Is fun in a way that you get 2 new beasts and those beasts can do more things (or something else). This one was fun to. But I personally wouldn't buy 9,99€ for it. But that is to yourself
Also, little notes. When dropping from a wall or anything and you still face that wall but want to run another way. Turn around first, otherwise he might jump/climb the wall again. And, when aiming, don't always try to shoot trough little holes, the space some things take up isn't 100% accurate, with some you can with some not, doenst really matter mostly but is save you an arrow.

Ill start off by saying I honestly could not recommend this game at any price, even if it was free.
The game is just incredibly boring and one dimensional, there is no depth, there is no challenge, there is no skill, there is no fun. I cant even call the game a PVP game since there are so little players in the game, and when you do find some, youre either killed on sight, or they just run away, with the rare occasion of an actual interaction.
The game is primarily based on looting, pretending to claim it is a survival game. But dont get me wrong, there are elements such as hunger, thirst, and other staples to mediocre survival games, but they are handled poorly. Like I had mentioned, looting seems to be the primary focus, which is pretty poorly executed. Loot is rare, good items are even more rare, and exploration in this game is extremely unrewarding.
I have played quite a lot of survival games in my days, but this is one of the worst games in the genre Ive played (It ranks up there with games like H1Z1/Just Survive, The WarZ/Infestion Stories/Whatever its called now). For the devs to have sold over 780,000 copies, profiting at most $12,000,000 USD, there is no excuse to how poorly this game has progressed since 2014, and how basic and underdeveloped everything is.
I have played roughly 9 hours of this game, but that is more than enough time to realize that it was poorly spent. Nothing of significance happened in any of those times playing that would warrent me to play longer. If nothing happens in a 4 hour stretch of playing, nothing is going to happen in 6 hours, 8 hours, or more.
Oh, you can also forget about calling this a zombie survival game. It has mutants (which are just as rare as guns) who are too simple to be any fun to play with, more of a nuisance akin to DayZs broken zombies.
The environments in this game are more than lacklustre to say the least. Buildings are very poorly designed (massive empty rooms, houses that have no stairs to the second foor, no basement, overscaled rooms). They are copy and pasted in many parts of the map, so exploration is pretty boring after entering the same building for the 50th time. The map itself is pretty nonsensical with tiny towns spotted around, roads just ending out of no where, stuff like vehicles in seemingly random spots. One of my biggest issues with the map design is that the island at the northern sections of the map has massive invisible walls to prevent the player from moving any further. This is a massive turn off in any open world game, especially one that is based on an island (islands are used to solve the boundery issue in these types of games, preventing the player from reaching the end of the map). But rather than just letting the player go to the end of the island, they block them off with an invisible wall. Icing on the cake is that if you punch the invisible wall, it bleeds...
Overall I would give this game a 4/10, it tries too much to be like DayZ, and falls short of being its own game. It borrows too many poorly thought and designed mechanics from DayZ. Miscreated is just another poorly designed, hugely generic survival game coasting off the past success of games like DayZ.

If you're looking for another RPG maker game to add to your library then this would be a great addition.
Sprite work/Graphics:
First off I'd like to say I really enjoyed the character sprites. I always appreciate good sprite work and it's certainly present here, not to mention there's plenty of original item sprites and backgrounds from what I can tell.
I'm not super familar with all the DLC packs for every version of RPG maker, but I know for a fact there's plenty of original work here.
There were a few choices I felt were a tad odd, such as the icon for the dirty table cloth being a worn out cloak, but it wasn't enough to make me neglect all the GOOD choices that were made.
Sound:
The music was fitting throughout and I enjoyed the switch between silence and sound. The music that went along with the more lighthearted moments such as the ending was pleasing to hear as well. Also, I always enjoy when RPG maker games have sound effects for foot steps, and there was a nice variety here too.
Story:
Obviously, do not expect 20, 10 or even 5 hour's worth of game play from this. This is a short, sweet little game to take about an hour or so of your time.
Now, of course that isn't a bad thing. Some things are better being short and simple. I just think it's worth mentioning so you don't have heighted expectations for a lenghty game.
The story as I put it, was short and sweet. I won't go into great detail since I want this to be spoiler-free, but I really enjoyed the ending the most out of it. Which to be honest, is where most of the story takes place. You find some clues here and there, but all the real interactions take place at the end.
Biggest Complaint:
I didn't really understand the point of typing in the answers for getting into the dining room and a couple other spots? I was really confused, and then eventually realized it had no meaning. At least... I think.
I know in the bonus room you can say PUMPKIN at one of the spots to get a Dead End ending, but other than that, I don't get it. I felt like I should have needed to find a hint somewhere and actually give an answer, or this should have just been removed altogether.
I feel like this is more of a personal complaint, rather than a real flaw. And I apologize if I'm just missing something and there is more to it than I'm thinking.
Overall:
I 100% recommend this if you're looking for something cute to get into the spirit of Halloween, and/or if you just want another nice RPG maker game with some pretty appealing art.
Also it's good to note, it's FREE.
So there's no reason to not try.
I highly recommend supporting more creators out there like this, who are willing to put decent amounts of work into a game and not ask any money for it.
In conclusion, keep up the good work and emprovement for the next game you'll put out.

After 217 hours playing this game, here are my thoughts: if you're really into the history of the Sengoku Jidai (Warring States period) of Japan, this is an excellent game. As a strategy game, however, it's just OK. While you can personally manage the civil development and battles, you can (and eventually have to) delegate these to the AI. The real challenge and fun comes from the historical quests you get playing as the major clans in the different scenarios, where you have to achieve various goals to emulate actual famous battles and other events within specific deadlines. Yes, you can play as some obscure clan and lead it to greatness, or even create your own clan, but then the game just becomes a strategy game, and in that respect, Shogun: Total War 2 is the superior game with the same setting but without the "historical simulation" element. Another issue is that this game is a port from Japan, and as such is a lot more expensive than similar games and has some minor translation issues that cause confusion.
In sum, if you're a hardcore Oda Nobunaga fan who wants to simulate Sengoku history, pony up the cash and get this game. If you're just looking for a fun, straightforward strategy game of trade, diplomacy and conquest, get the Shogun Total War games instead,

So honestly this is a bit of a tricky subject for me. I don't hate the game but it's consistently disappointed me with how they choose to put it together, to allocate development time, and that sort of stuff. Honestly there's a lot to like in this game, but I can't really recommend it.
For starters, i have 163 hours logged on it but that's not really how long i've actually spent playing it. I've hosted a server and kept it running a lot for others several times throughout its development cycle, from early access to now. Really for a server host the hours i have logged are actually quite pitiful, especially when you compare it to Terraria.
So. This game is basically a grab bag of super fun theme park elements that don't have any real substance. You land on a planet and you dig through some caves and find some dungeons, weee! But then that's all there is to it, all the dungeons in this patch have felt pretty much the same and have neglected to surprise or challenge me even up through all the different planet tiers. They introduce super fun mechanics but don't challenge them at all.
The content is super short, which is a weird thing to complain about in a 15 dollar game I know but we are comparing it to Terraria here so it's worth mentioning. Not only is finding ores an uninteresting chore, it's also really easy. I just dig straight down in one part of the planet and i get a few, then i did straight down in another and get some more. The caves aren't interesting to explore, they're all super tiny with one chest in a really obvious place and then just a few ores laying around. Particularly when they're attempting a story of some kind it seems like a huge missed opportunity for environmental storytelling.
And it's actually kind of annoying because it seems like all they've done over the whole cycle is just add more shallow themepark elements. They haven't actually developed or put any new content in. 7 boring bosses if i'm being generous and counting that first crystal as a boss, and my memory isn't great but that might be like two more than they had when they first started early access a long♥♥♥♥♥time ago.
Speaking of which the story itself which is new from when i played in early access is really boring and generic. It seems so tacked on, it was more fun to be thrust into terraria and just imagine what could have possibly led the world to be this way instead of being spoonfed some off brand story about the darkness upsetting the balance and blah blah.
The bosses don't present a challenge at all really. It seems like I always win if my gear is good enough and when i do lose it's because something zoomed in off screen faster than i could respawn. Is my game's resolution too low or something? I'm spending half my time shooting at (and hitting) something I can't see.
The weapons are actually pretty cool, I don't have a lot to be a negative nancy about in that particular regard. I kind of resent how weird and inaccessible it is to try and get the particular weapon you want. Finally, an assault rifle! too bad im moving onto a new tier of planet immediatley, cant wait to sift through five hundred chests trying to find another. It's kind of a mess even if your base combat idea is pretty compelling to not have a clear upgrade path.
Sure I get that you want people to explore but this takes one of terraria's few problems of needing to roll a chest lottery to find a specific item you definitely should have for boss fights and taking it to extremes. If you're a novakid and you want to use guns it's not as much of a problem but that also feels pretty lame. There's no warning that says hey if you pick any species besides this one you're going to have to play craps for guns. god help you if you wanted to use melee but picked novakid
Also the metroid ripoff mechanic that's new is a cool idea but it's just not interesting. This is kind of a minor point but none of its mod abilities are useful except maybe skipping across water real fast. It doesn't even make you move faster than walking so what's the point? It was obviously just tacked on to give someone something to do.
Oh yea, and farming. It takes longer to set up a farm than it does to plow through content. I spent quite a bit of time hunting for cotton for my cotton farm and now i've moved beyond it already. I just purchased the next tier of armor so what's the point?
So if you just want a short, cute little pixel game in space with easy but somewhat time consuming gameplay then maybe you'll like starbound. The construction elements despite everything else are pretty solid so if you just want to build a base and a spaceship and collect pets then you should get something out of it.
But if you're looking for a game with solid gameplay and exploration elements, a challenge, or a successor to Terraria then you're going to be disappointed.

Look at the video for Luftrausers, where you can have a bunch of fighters chasing your plane, cut the engines in mid air, spin around, strafe them, and zoom off in the opposite direction. Yes, Luftrausers does let you be a crazy plane badass. Sadly, that's about the only good point.
The whole thing feels like an Iphone game, but brings almost enough excitement that it could qualify as a real game. Runs are short. You'll die within 5 minutes, easily. The score system is arbitrary and meaningless for the very same reason I cannot recommend the game.
Beyond the fighters, every other enemy simply takes too much damage to kill. By the game you have made the five or so passes needed to kill a battleship, three more have spawned, and they will ALL be training their sights on you while you try to kill the others. And you have boats, planes, subs, and jets to deal with while you're trying to ice these. The score system relies on a chaining mechanic and every single tough enemy takes more damage to kill than it takes your chain to drop, so you can only hope to play for score by hoping the RNG throws you a bunch of suicidal popcorn fighters and jets. The big bad blimp boss of the game is a total pushover unless you have to fight it while two dozen battleships also try to nail you from below but he may as well take twice as much sustained fire as you have put out since the game started to get him to show up and fight. The enemy variety is just tedious and sucks the fun out of the game beyond that initial rush where you duplicate the preview video's cool tricks.
Like an Iphone game, you can do three objectives each time to unlock parts to customize your plane and they're really the actual goal of the game as they block all the unlocks and provide you the only sort of direction you get beyond getting shot at. The plane parts are roughly 25% cool, 75% stupid, and share the same loose, uninspiring design as the basic game. Some change core mechanics in fundamental ways but they are not enough to save the game.
$10 for a tight arcade experience would be a no brainer but Luftrausers just does not have that spark that makes an arcade game fun. You won't come back to it months later to revisit the fond memories. It burns out too quick and does not leave much beyond the flash... Which is a shame as a lot of love and care went into the glitz and the flash and the style of it but a little more should have went into tightening the gameplay.

Crunchy. Fast. Addicting. Simple.
Much of the praise that you can attribute to Nuclear Throne is present in this arcade-style Vlambeer title, in which you play the role of a fighter pilot who flies a highly customizable jet. However! You fight a battle against insurmountable odds. A battle where your loss is inevitable. The question is, just how long can you last? How high of a score can you accrue?
Every game begins relatively the same, with you launching out of a submarine and having to destroy some enemy fighter pilots who fly slow and fire ocassionally. Then, you'll see some boats who'll shoot in bursts of three. Before long, your screen will be full of barrages of anti-air flak coming from battleships and streams of machine gun shots stemming from ace-fighters. Once in a blue moon you'll see space-ships with lasers and if you're good enough to kill enough enemies you'll be having to deal with a Zeppelin overhead which serves as the boss of the game. Each enemy you kill moves the difficulty up a little bit, meaning there isn't difficulty spikes per se...it's really a gradual thing. Hardmode (called SFMT) just cranks it to the max off of the bat and makes the playing field more even (read as advantagous) for the AI.
The controls boil down to the arrow keys and "x" to fire. Left and right are to turn your plane, while up is to accelerate in the direction you are facing. What's rather cool about Luftrausers is gravity. If you don't accelerate, you'll fall down to the water below and take damage over time for being submerged. Holding down x will allow you to fire indefinitely, but won't allow you to heal (which only happens when you aren't firing, thus potentially jeopordizing your combo). Your down arrow is only used for menus. This control set-up and gameplay style is remarkably simple, and equally so effective. Meaning keyboard users will find their frustration not in controlling the game, but rather from getting destroyed in SFMT mode like everybody else.
And the music, just superb. The game only utilizes one "song" but drastically alters what it sounds like depending on what parts you use on your plane. I forget which part (weapon, body, propulsion) changes what instrument (riff, bass, percussion) but it does and it makes each combination sound rather unique. The crescendo of the song, which remains the same regardless of loadout, is perfect for divebombing a pesky battleship while your own aircraft is ablaze and getting out of there.
To unlock parts and different colour schemes, you need to complete challenges. Like "kill x number of fighters with this part" , "get x amount of points" and what have you. Most are quite acheivable, some laughably so and others quite bloody aggravating.
Despite all the customization you can do, there are some combinations that are just infinitely more effective than others. To the point where you'll just want to stick to a select few load-outs. For me, I found that builds that combined speed with constant fire (the laser in particular for it's combo-friendly nature) simply worked the best. To the point where you are able to survive indefinitely by speeding horizontally near water-level and avoiding higher altitudes and major vertical deviation.
Some enemies rarely show up, namely the submarines (which have a microscopic chance to spawn when fighter-aces do) and the "secret enemies" (a fighter equipped with lasers and a sub with machine guns, also both tied to fighter-ace spawns). This wouldn't be much of a problem if some challenges weren't tied to killing 'em or killing 'em while at max combo. I've also noted that some challenges seem a tad broken, as the game sometimes doesn't track your killstreaks properly (kill x enemies while firing non-stop or without firing at all) despite the combo meter indicating the correct number.
And apparently there is some clear-save glitch out there that others have encountered. I don't know how it happens and I fortunately have not stumbled upon it.
Luftrausers is an enjoyable, sometimes frustrating experience that'll burn a number of hours away and have you hungering for that high-score. Its visuals contain a good amount of character, its audio is crafty and any Time Pilot fans out there will probably christen it as the spiritual sequel also on steroids. If you are looking for "story", "levels" or "dialogue", you won't be getting it here. This is an arcade experience and not-so-serious flying sim, not a bloody fairy tale.

Ignoring its title and separating it from the previous Ace Combat games does little to save it from its own faults. Ace Combat: Assault Horizon takes a step back from the interesting, if not corny world of Strangereal, and plays the Russian/American conflict card. This tired formulaic story is complemented by a downgrade in gameplay. Dogfighting is made simple, and boring, with the introduction of a near-rail-shooter experience that removes the freedom from flight and negates the need for skillful airmanship. It would be acceptable to have a “boss” flight lead require this mechanic, but every flight lead requires that you lock into dogfight mode; even if you land missiles on target, the game ignores the hits and will not progress until you put on your training wheels and go for the ride. The game does include a new diversity of aircraft with the introduction of helicopters and bombers, which if properly executed would nearly save the game, but bomber runs are not particularly fun and the helicopter sections are tedious and awkward. Overall, the game looks great graphically (although the graphical settings are sparse) and gives you a decently realistic flight simulation, but its glaring flaws make it just an okay experience. Personally, I would award 3/5 stars to this game and would recommend picking it up only if it happens to be on sale.

SINGLEPLAYER Pilot Difficulty REVIEW: I really really wanted to recommend this game. But there just isn't enough going for Assault Horizon for me to do so. The gameplay can get really fun and intense at some parts but in many other it can feel like a drag. Mainly due to the controls and game mechanics. The Dogfighting Mode (DFM) seemed cool at first and to be honest, I really thought it was a nice change for a spinoff game. What I disliked about it is that many of the dogfights (Including the final boss battle) that require DFM require you to wait until you have flown around exploding setpieces before you are allowed to actually damage the target. This can get very annoying and once you discover this you lose that feeling that you are actually using tactics to beat that enemy ace.
And then we get to the story by the highly acclaimed millitary writer "Jim DeFelice". Maybe there is something more hidden behind this dull, cliche story but even so, the story itself is a pain to get through. To sum it up: you get betrayed by the Russians who later turn out to just be revolutionaries in a against Russia. Then you work with the Russian loyalists to defeat the coup. Though the bad guy ace escapes with the superweapon to america so you follow him and kill him. The characters are another level of boring too. Most characters are your stereotypical cast: An ace who has a nightmares, a black man who seems interesting if only they dove into his story more, a cocky wingman, and a manly female. All of which are extremely predictable in the cliche things they do.
As a player of both AC 4 & 5, I tried to keep the comparisons to a minimum but even so, it is still hard to recommend a game with such potentioal when it's mechanics and story are so lackluster.
If you REALLY want to give this game a try. I would say go for it. It's not a terrible game and there are many parts that are really fun and thrilling. But if you are on the fence or expecting the top quality of it's predecessors, I would suggest waiting until the next numerical installment in the series.
