I will break this into sections and hopefully it doesnt read like a guide or something.
Combat System and AI: The combat system is essentially designed for use with a console type controller. With the conversion to keyboard and mouse the controls are inconsistent and less responsive. For example the plane controls use WASD and the arrow keys to emulate two control sticks, and the attack helicopter uses the mouse instead of the arrow keys. Furthermore the change weapon key is different between the two modes, and pressing the wrong key wastes precious seconds while you work out what is going on. The AI deliberately goes out of its way to focus you (even on the normal difficulty), especially when you are trying to complete the objectives assigned to you, 95% of which are timed, so it becomes extremely difficult to complete said objectives. You will often find yourself trying to evade 3 or 4 charged missiles when engaged in defensive DFM (DogFight Mode), and often the only way to complete any objectives at all is to target your attackers in offensive DFM at close range, leaving you open to attack from other opponents. Often too much will happen on screen at one time, so you miss opportunities to counter opponents in DFM or launch flares at a missile because you were too busy trying to shoot a guy down you just spent 2-5 minutes trying to get behind. The in-mission missile camera often prevents you from shooting down that one last guy as it follows your missile to the previous guy you just shot at, this can also take you out of DFM which is frustrating in the least.
Objectives and Missions: As mentioned 95% of all objectives are timed (either directly or having to prevent bombers or other from reaching a given point). Unfortunately it is almost always necessary to engage bombers in DFM at VERY close range for 15 or more seconds and continually throw everything you have at the target for the duration, as enemy health seems to regenerate if you go off and do other things, such as avoiding 4 charged missiles. This experience is utterly painful and downright cruel to the player, forcing them to focus on things other than completing their objectives (timed, remember).
DFM: DogFight Mode is almost always necessary to take down targets that just won't die to missiles in normal flight mode, and the AI doesn't pull any punches in DFM either. Often you will find yourself slammed into the ground in offensive DFM as the AI heads straight down and immediately breaks contact. If this doesnt kill you then you will be left with almost no HP left and be 1 normal missile away from restarting at a checkpoint, which are placed at the start of all objective CHAINS, meaning that unless each objective in the chain is completed perfectly at 100% then you will have to restart from the beginning of the chain. My head hurts just thinking about those restarts.
Plane Loadouts and Pre-Mission Briefings: Pre-mission briefings? Not in this game. What little that passes as a mission briefing is little more than a token gesture to advance the storyline, which is particularly bland. These cutscenes also do not tell you exactly what kind of hostiles you will be fighting and the relative proportions of each. All you are told is the GENERAL type of mission be it Air-Air or Air-Ground, and you will probably have to fight air targets in all Air-Ground missions using just the cannon on the Attack Helicopter, which is painful due to the mission conditions imposed on you at the time hostile heli's appear. So basicially you have to chose your weapons package completely blind. Even having just a small "this is what we are going to do in this mission" briefing would make this bearable and not complete guesswork. Most missions will not even have a cutscene before loadout selection.
Dont get me wrong I LIKE plane sims/action. But this is certaintly not it.
My advice if you want to own a game like this? Get HAWX, it's so much better.

I am one of those people who never seems to have a high luck role and loot usually sucks. This game, at least on all the servers I play on (yes, even 'high loot' servers) seems to give more loot when more people are playing, but I cannot say *better* loot. All that means is I must spend more time looting to get decent gear to protect and defend myself.
This game is a lot of fun with people, either as a clan or pure pvp, and I'm not a pvp person at all. But playing solo on an empty server is really only fun for a few dozen hours. Unless you are really interested in base building, the solo empty server sucks. You must loot blueprints in order to build anything beyond basic walls and doors, so you will definitely need to loot, but that is the point of the game. The crafting system is well done, I really like it, and the base building is tied directly to loot because you have to chop wood, craft lumber from the logs, then craft floor panels or wall panels and so on to create a wall or a platform or anything else. The recent update has added poles and a sort of gravity to base building so floating objects now fall.
Base building is not the sticky style like rust or others where the parts sort of click together, this game really makes you work for it. It's an OCD person's nightmare. You will have spaces between walls and objects that just aren't quite right together, it will drive you crazy, and you will spend hours trying to fix it. Eventually giving up you'll hop to a different server and start over, because as maddening as it is, you'll want to keep doing it.
This game is in development, and the devs are very active and responsive on discord. It's well worth the $20 and even better on sale. I only have 128 hours now, but will likely add another hundred alone, and if I find a good server to play on, that number will quadruple. It's a great way to waste time, but sometimes, playing alone, feels more like work than a game.

Given this game's reputation, you've probably already made up your mind about this one.
Dark Souls is a game that's all about attitude - because the game is literally about failure, both from a (limited) plot point of view, and from a gameplay standpoint. How you handle failure is the ultimate message of the game.
The point of the game is to help teach you how to overcome failure, and I believe the game is excellently designed to make that goal. But it doesn't hold your hand to do it, the effort has to come from you - because that's the entire point.
That fact is what's created the hardcore fans of this game, and the devisive detractors.
That isn't to say that if you give up on trying to enjoy this game that you're simply a loser that just can't git gud - there are plenty of subjective reasons for not enjoying this game as well.
But for me, this game is a masterpiece, and probably my favorite game of all time.

Dark Souls is a breath of fresh air. The video game market is full of games for babies who can't think for themselves, have all the time in the world to devote to meaningless tacked-on content, and need everything to provide instant gratification. This is bad for the rest of us. I thought I was burned out on video games for good until I found Dark Souls. Something just clicks about it. Every fight is deeply satisfying. Every action must be committed to. Every avenue through which you interact with the world is meaningful, and nothing you have to do is just for the sake of some lazy narrative the game forces you into. The player must work hard on their own to figure out why things are the way they are.
If I've made the game sound arduous, fear not. It is anything but. There is never a moment that feels unnecessary or like work, unlike many other modern RPGs. I think Dark Souls is the probably best game in the series (I HAVE NOT PLAYED 3), and probably the best single-player action RPG ever, at least that I am aware of. Dark Souls is less consistent than Dark Souls II, but this is not to say it is worse at all. The world is incredibly immersive, the good bosses really are amazing (despite four endgame bosses that are poorly designed compared to the high bar the game establishes early on), there are no gimmicks that require prior knowledge, and victory is incredibly satisfying, which is true in all of these games, but especially so in this one, as the interconnected-ness of the world gives the player a true feeling of progress. Buy this game as soon as you have the funds, but also be sure and install DSFix and use a controller.
THE FOLLOWING IS IMPORTANT IF YOU DO CHOOSE TO BUY DARK SOULS:
Make sure you use a controller. I normally hate them, but they are much better for these games, as there is input delay and a few really bad keybinds. The Xbox 360/One controllers are pretty intuitive, you can just plug them in and play, and I would imagine third party ones that can be acquired for cheap probably function in the same way. The game is much easier on the eyes if you install DSFix, set the resolution to 1080p and unlock the framerate. For the latter option, be sure and note that some people have problems with ladders, so you should make sure you toggle the framerate back to 30fps using the backspace key when you encounter a ladder. The game is perfectly playable at 30fps, but don't be afraid to play the game at the expected framerate for any PC game.

Gorky 17 (Odium in North America) is a turn by turn strategy game.
You will start with 3 guys from NATO and your objective is to rescue another team (Group 1) that HQ has lost communication with. The city is full of monsters and that's the game's main attraction: wasting them. As you can guess, the game's story is average.
The voice acting is okay. Dialogs are sometimes "funny" even though most of them are cliché, as are the characters. The team boss is Canadian and tries to help people and goes right to the point. Another guy is Polish, has a funny broken English and he wants to blast everything. And the last dude is French and is -- of course -- an unbelievable wimp. Well... all of this is not that great either.
During the combat phase, you will have trouble to see the tiles as they are transparent glowing green squares. It is also hard to visualize the opposition's move range as it has the same color and style. Also the overview is not isometric. Sometimes a weird camera angle prevents you from having a clear sight of what's going on. Crates and other stuff will block the view and those lovely glowing tiles. If you are not careful, you will end up clicking on the wrong tile and wasting a move. Or worse. In other words the combat phase is very clumsy.
When you are not shooting stuff, you are exploring the map. Every time you will spot a glowing crate -- which contains supplies like medpacks, ammo, etc. -- there will be a battle nearby. There is pretty much one crate per battle. Always. Whether the battle starts when approaching it or right after you emptied its content and went through a door or something nearby, a battle event occurs. Oh yeah I forgot: battles are scripted. There are no random encounters.
During this epic adventure, various people will join your team. It's all fine and all. Except that when they have to leave your awesome NATO team because they… uh feel like it or just because they die or whatever, they will simply disappear... along with all the stuff you gave them! Say goodbye to the shiny armor, handgun, precious ammo, etc. The inventory is NOT transferred to one of your guys. Save often, so that when they leave you can load a previous save, and empty their inventory.
But this is quite a problem as the ammo is scarce. The game is quite hard if you use firearms. The limited amount of ammo pushes you to use melee weapons. At first you won't have a choice but to shoot creeps. However, a taser and a tranq gun will help you freeze those turds for a couple of turns while you beat the sht out of 'em.
The taser among other weapons like the flamethrower, have unlimited "ammo". But, they have a cool down: like 3 turns to fire/shoot again. That means that when two of your goons have a taser or such other weapon, you will be able to keep a monster “tranquilized” forever. Just wait for the cool down to be over to tase the mofo again with the other guy.
So... basically a battle goes like this: analyze which scum to tase first, rush him with all of your guys, and melee him like a bunch of hooligans. Crowbar, baseball bat, axe. Yeah. The battles are hence, not very interesting. However there are some cool "weapons" like calling for an airstrike, an electric beam, and all kind of other crazy tools.
Let’s talk about bugs now. I had an inventory bug were a key item disappeared between saves. I had to restart the game as I couldn’t open a freaking door without it. Also the game cannot start on modern computer due to the old graphic "engine" -- if we can call it that way. However, fear not (or not that much) as there are a few different gorky17.exe builds in the game folder that you can try. Copy/paste/overwrite the original .exe with one of them and try to run the game. Disabling the hardware zoom is however pretty much always recommended.
On an old computer with WinXP and a crappy graphic card that has barely 3D acceleration, I had no problem running the game. It was flawless. However Win 8.1 x64 + GeForce GTX 770 the game crashed. Using the software only build + choosing software renderer was making the game super freaking slow. Even with my quad core i7 4770k. So I was back to my WinXP.
All in all I must have spent 10 to 15 hours of gameplay. Not that bad. But the overall experience was barely average. I’m hesitating whether thumbing this down or not. I had fun with this game. I wasn’t playing that seriously anyway and still ended up with shtton of ammo.
Hmmm… lets thumb it up.

“Long Live the Queen” is a life simulation game that’s reminiscent towards games like “Princess Maker” in Japan.
Primarily, the main goal is to have Elodie, the princess that the player has to “raise” and help her survive wars, potential threats, and ward off unwanted suitors before she could become queen at fifteen years old, who is considered as a legal adult in this time period.
There are different classes Elodie could take – such as, conversations, royal demeanor, animal handling, history, economics, faith, military, athletics, agility, and much much more! The more classes she takes, the more her skills will rise. The more her skills rise, the better she can understand certain conversations to progress the story along. Of course, it’s completely up to the player on what kind of queen Elodie could be just based on the choices made alone. There really isn’t an end to the choices to choose from!
One of the main things that brings people to this game is not just what kind of queen she would be but if she’s going to survive long enough to become a queen. There are various ways to die in this game and each one is actually part of the achievements – which is a unique thing about it since most games would try to prevent that from happening.
There is a way to avoid dying, of course, but the player has to make sure that her skill set for certain actions are pretty much almost completely filled up.
Another unique thing about this game is the mood system. For every mood that she is, there’s a penalty and there’s a bonus. Certain moods help boost up skills for whatever class the player chooses for her and others, well, not so much. There’s actually a penalty if the player makes Elodie take the wrong classes for a certain mood she’s in.
There are outfits the player can unlock, so long as that particular subject is pretty well-balanced. These outfits help boost up that particular subject, especially if she’s in a war, a tournament, or at the gala, although more often than not, they’re just there to change up from her boarding school uniform.
If Elodie does manage to survive to coronation, there are epilogues afterwards based on the choices that the player makes. They’re the literal result of what happens based on the player’s choices and decisions as a young fourteen year old girl trying to become a Queen.
Not only does the epilogues come in what happened to Elodie and her subjects (if they’re involved in any way), but they come in beautiful drawings that’s similar to stained glass on the castle walls.
But what do I think of it? I really enjoyed it! It’s a lot of fun and it’s fun to try to get the different endings and different deaths. There’s actually a checklist within the game itself to try to get all the achievements, deaths, and different epilogue stained glasses to try to vary the game experience up.
While it does seem that the endings are endless, there are a few problems.
Going over the game over and over, eventually, it starts to become extremely repetitive. Sometimes new menus and new choices pop up which could lead to different endings/results but eventually, the player might have to pass by that same choice and those same scenes again just to get to the choices that the player has to deviate from.
It’s a little bit of a bore but there is the option to skip the text so it’s really not that bad. Once new text pops up, though, it stops so the player can read it. There is the option to go back and re-do the choices but it doesn’t work all the time, so be sure you know what you’re doing in terms of choices.
The writing for the political intrigue is pretty basic for a life simulation game but, honestly, I’m not sure if that’s really a complaint or not. On one hand, the player would know exactly what to do in a situation such as that and it’d seem exactly as it is: too easy to figure out. On the other hand, it does give the player an opportunity to go back and do the other choice just for the fun of it and just to see what happens. It’s not really hard to get invested in what’s going on in Nova, the land this takes place in, but it’s just as easy not to.
The art is a hit or a miss for me. The character designs are simple, but one of the characters, Julianna the Duchess of Ursul, reminds me almost completely of Sailor Mercury of “Sailor Moon”. It’s a little distracting.
The backgrounds for the game are fine but, again, tend to be simple since the backgrounds don’t seem to change that often. There are places Elodie can go during the weekend, but there’s not a real immersion factor here although I’m sure that’s probably not intended.
Often, it’s hard to determine how old the characters are (especially the older gentleman who sends Elodie a necklace, customary for betrothal) but it’s clear when they’re supposed to be young though it’s hard discerning whether they’re a teenager or not if one isn’t paying attention to the dialogue.
More often than not, there’s almost unfinished feel with it. Granted, this game isn’t really meant to be something completely serious and, again as I mentioned before, it’s easy to not get as invested in it since there’s achievements for deaths. If you didn’t get the ending you want, it’s not like the game’s going to punish you – you’ll probably get an achievement out of it instead which could be beneficial if that’s what the player wanted.
The music for the game fits it although maybe not the splash song. It’s a piano version of “God Save the Queen”, the British national anthem but the rest of the game’s music is fine. Of course, if the player doesn’t want the music, they could always turn it off in the preferences.
As for the intrigue of Elodie’s mother’s demise, it’s pretty cut and dried. Based on the story itself when I got there, it’s so throwaway that her mother being dead might as well not have mattered.  From the way they alluded her mother’s death, I thought that this would finally get some deep stuff about the Lumens and why this world is the way it is (sort of modern but still in past fantasy/medieval) but it didn’t really end up that way, so that was disappointing.
Perhaps it’s best that way though – if the entirety for the game is simple, there really isn’t any rhyme or reason why anything else would be more important than anything else. If there is any real intrigue, it’s about some of the preferences the dukes and duchesses have for company. Other than that, there’s no real intrigue. As mentioned over and over, this is pretty much cut & dried. It’s a simple story for a simple game about simply raising a princess named Elodie who may or may not become queen.
It’s a fun ride, despite it all, and it certainly does have replay value even after the 100% achievements (epilogues, deaths, & achievements) have been unlocked. It’s not too deep and the art is cute although some people probably wouldn’t like it too much if they’re looking for a simulation with some depth to it. It is a fun game, though, and I’d recommend this to those who just want to try different things without worrying too much about the princess they’re trying to raise.

TLDR:  HOTAS (Saitek X45) won't work with this game.  Probably others as well.  Only playable with a gamepad, and a let-down if you want the classic Ace Combat experience.
As a long-time fan of Ace Combat since Ace Combat 4, I can say that this game really is a departure from the old, Ace Combat experience that most fans of the series have come to know and love.  That being said, when I played this game before on my 360, I thought it was still a fun addition to the series.  It could be enjoyable to someone newer to Ace Combat.
I got this game while it was available for free one weekend on Steam.  I wanted to see how it would feel controlled by a HOTAS, specifically, a Saitek X45.  I figured this would be simple; after all, Saitek made an Xbox 360 version of the X45 for special editions of Ace Combat 6.  After fumbling around the options screen for 30 minutes, I've determined that it's not possible to use the X45 with this game.
The default controls bound my throttle to an axis of movement the X45 isn't capable of.  For X45 users, it was the sliver paddle behind the throttle, usually used for rudder control.  Left and right were both used to yaw left and right, and up and down were used to throttle up and throttle down, except the paddle is only capable of moving left and right, leaving the plane stuck at max throttle.
So, why not just bind the throttle control to the X45 throttle?  First I had to learn how to control the menu, because each action I could perform was not listed as a key on the keyboard, but an obscure button from the X45.  Also, the mouse didn't work.  In order to unbind the throttle control, I had to press button 9 on the X45.  After trial-and-error, I learned that button 9 was apparently pressed when I switched the throttle into mode 3 (M3).  Then I selected to choose a key binding, only to have the game immediately tell me that the key I wanted to use was already in use, and needed to be unbound first.  After even more trial-and-error, I just unbound the entire stick and tried to bind the throttle.  That was when I found the source of the problem.  The X45 has several sliders on it that it uses to toggle modes.  The game was interpreting each of them as a button being held down.  The mode switch in particular was either button 9, button 10, or button 11, depending of if it was in position M3, M2, or M1 respectively.  Digital button presses could still be bound by holding the button down when selecting to set a binding, but all analog controls were overridden by the mode switch.
And that is where my biggest problem lies. Gorky 17 will always be a great game, with a very interesting story.
You start out in some dreary town, somewhere in Poland, and immediately you get the feeling something is very wrong here.
As you soon find out, things are going to hell real fast, and the enemy types leave you no clue whatsoever as to what exactly went down here.
This is the first thing that struck me as brilliant when it first came out, and it still does today.
where in most games you get a general idea of what you are about to face just looking at the enemy types (skeletons, zombies, wild animals, humans etc.), in this game you just get more confused the more of them you encounter.
Troughout the game you get fed some scarse information about what caused all this madness to happen, but you only get the whole picture near the end, in a very blatant exposition dump.
This almost seems as if the people that created this game ran out of time, or they simply didnt have any budget left to let the story come to a more natural, more fluid conclusion.
The variety of weapons, gear, and other items is very well done, and shows the tender care the creators had for this product.
While exploring and fighting inside the town, you encounter all kinds of NPC chatacters, all equally colorful and unexpected.
Some will even fight with you, turn into monsters, betray you, or help you out to find usefull stuff.
My verdict for Gorky 17 is that for its current price, its a no brainer to get it, great gameplay, great story, great game.
But beware, this game is old, and has no support whatsoever from its publishers, might not even work on your machine, and/or glitch out some times.
Pro:
Very atmospheric game that leaves you wondering right up tot he last second.
Good variety of gear and NPC encounters.
Cheap as dirt, especially with coupons or on sale.
Clearly a lot of care went into the game, even though the ending is a bit rushed.
Con:
The story could have been concluded more gradiently.
Old game, might not work properly on your system, or have glitches.
The voice acting (especially for the women) is a bit odd in places, although not bad.
Some fights can have fail states which you can not overcome (if you happen to have low health for example), save often.
p.s. A sequel would be very very welcome...

At first, I was not sure if I wanted to try Dark Souls, knowing its difficulty. I'm very glad that I ended up taking the plunge and trying this gem of a game.
First - the setting is wonderful. I am a big fan of dark fantasy, and delving into such an intricate, interesting world was and is a joy. The artistic design itself is excellent, and the medieval architecture and armor (elite knight armor, especially) looked wonderful. Flying into Anor Londo and seeing the huge city for the first time has to be one of my favorite moments from the game.
Second, the game respects the player. Yes it is difficult and it deserves its reputation as a tough-as-nails game, but the difficulty is not artificial. The game challenges you to improve, to learn from your mistakes, to see the flaws and failings of your enemies, and to be smart with how you approach situations. Very rarely did I feel like I died unfairly - they were usually a result of my mistakes and I knew exactly what I did wrong.
Third, the level design is absolutely phenomenal. From Software did an excellent job crafting a world that flows, with enemies in the right positions, with shortcuts to ease your later travels...everything felt like it was there for a reason.
Finally, the game is just fun. It's super rewarding to struggle with a boss or a difficult area and then conquer (whether through "cheesing" it or otherwise). PVP is a ton of fun and actually feels like it is a part of the experience and not quarantined off to a separate game mode.
I highly recommend this game.

I found Orcs Must Die! 2 to be a very fun experience. It is a 3rd person tower defense-style game, where the objective is to stop orcs from getting to a rift by utilizing various traps and weapons/spells. If you enjoyed the first game, you will definately enjoy this one as well- same orc slaughter, but more traps and weapons to use and upgrade. Orcs Must Die! 2 has a big upgrade system- you get "skulls" after each map to spend on upgrading your traps and weapons in many different ways. The better you do, the more skulls you get, and your upgrades persist thoughout all of the modes, allowing you to tackle the very hard modes such as endless and nightmare.
There is also is coop, which I think is a big selling point for this game. I just completed the story mode with my friend, and it was a ton of fun. Watching your combined traps massacre hundreds of orcs as they try to pass by is just so satisfying. As you get into harder levels, teamwork becomes very important as you try to hold the line against and army of orcs.
Even after you complete the story, there is still much you can do- endless mode (never ending waves of orcs, see how long you can last), nightmare mode (harder difficulty, but you keep your previous upgrades as I mentioned before), and many other modes.
There are a couple of downsides, though, that I will mention. First off, the in-game voice chat is downright awful, and overrides the steam chat so you can't use it. There is no way to turn it off, so my friend and I just made it push-to-talk, bound the key to something we never used, and then used skype or mumble.
Also, there really isn't much of a "story", it is not what this game's focus is- it is all about the gameplay. So if you are a person who is looking for a good story to drive you through the game, this is not it.
This game is not for everyone. If you don't like 3rd person action or tower/wave defense games, I don't think this will really change your mind about the genres. But if you have any interest at all in the game, I would definitely pick it up. It is very good at what it does.
Lastly, many of the levels seem to be made with coop in mind. If you plan to play though this game solo, you might have a difficult time getting through some of the levels.
Overall, this game was a blast to play with my friend. If you are looking for a good coop game to play with a buddy, I strongly recommend you try out Orcs Must Die! 2. Even alone, though, this game can still be a fun time. It has a light sense of humor about it that makes it all the more enjoyable, despite the fact that you are slaughtering orcs by the thousands!
Enough of a mix of mindless fun, mild strategy and action to give you enough entertainment for the asking price.  This is the only Tower Defense game I have played that I actually enjoyed.

So I sort of started writing a reply on the forums asking about the story and I started writing a review. And I figured it may actually be okay for a review so I'm writing it here:
As far as lore goes it gets the names right... and well I never came across a detailed story of how Celibrimbor was tortured to give up the formula for the rings of power so they did have some creative liberties. But there is the thing. Sauron tortured him to give up the FORMULA. In the story they say Spoiler:
As for the rest of the story. The Main character is your cookie cutout male hero without a personality. They propably wanted to copy and paste Aragorn and failed badly at it. The orcs have better personalities, which is why I played this game for as long as I had. The Nemesis system is the only good thing about this game.
Celebrimbor is better than Failed Aragorn. But I'm not sure if the devs got him right or not. He was tortured by Sauron so he may have turned out as he did if he ended up a wraith. But then again. Elves usually wouldn't encourige some ranger who was killed to raise an orc army to fight fire with fire. Then again you are fighting off evil so maybe... I'm just an intermediate in Tolkien lore. I think you'd need an expert to judge how Celibrimbor turned out.
There is also a Gollum cameo... thats it... not much to say. He didn't do anything except be gollum. Though tbh the appearance of Gollum did remind me that it is indeed middle earth not Theadas or Warhammer or whatever world is D&D set in. Seriously. This game has nowhere the feel of the Tolkien's world. Was this supposed to be Mordor? Why am I seeing pretty flowers, grasslands and rivers? What next? Bunnies skipping over mount doom? And aren't these orcs supposed to be an army? All I see are spare patrols and occasional warbands. And the forts are bearly protected with a random archer on watch. Heck they don't even do anything horrible to the slaves. "I know I'm a creature of Darkness and I could rip apart this human and feed on his guts. But I need to keep this PG12"
Speaking of Tolkien feel. In the movies and books, you had Epic battles. Heros against villains. Good against Evil. Armies of Darkness covered the whole fields with their corruption. Yada Yada. They were big what I mean to say. So when they told me that I'm going to raise an orc army to fight against another orc army. I was indeed excited. But when we finally get to the final battle its 5 of your guys against a small group of enemies + your nemesis. Granted I liked my nemesis. He was propably the best character. A randomly generated grunt archer that sniped me in a random fort. Yes. The best character for me is a nameless NPC given a randomly generated name and title. But Characters aside since I already ranted about those for a bit. The Battle was underwhelming and way too small to even be called a battle. But then again same can be said for the ending. As the game might as well have been over when my nemesis' head left his shoulders as what came after was so boring, rushed and generic I already forgot about it. All I can say is: The final boss is a quick time event.
So no I won't recommend it. It had a good system and it is my hope that some other developer will take this system and imprements it into a game with a good story and a good ending.

Luftrausers is an incredibly fun game which instantly throws you into the air to sink or swim. It's simple enough to grasp with minimal controls and easy to latch onto goal; if it moves, blow it up. It's a shooter, it's an action game, it's fun, and it'll have you hooked. If this doesn't make you want to be a Rauser pilot, I don't know what will.
Don't be fooled by the screenshots, this game is HARD. It appears easy, but it gets difficult fast. But unlike other games where ramped difficulty makes people want to give up after the first few tries, Luftrausers brings you back for more and more, giving you more options, more choices, more ways to kick some butt and blow stuff up. If you like a challenge, this game is definitely for you. You will spend hours with this.
What makes this game so delightfully addictive is it's simple elegance. It doesn't need to be decked out and fancy to be a really fun and difficult game. It's satisfying to achieve goals and relaxing if you want to kick back and blow off steam. The action is non-stop, the music is great, and the graphics are an awesome throw back to the days of Space Invaders. You become a part of this incredible world full of bullets and fire, and you will love every second of it. It's worth every cent, and for $9.99, you'd be crazy to pass up a game like this.

LUFTRAUSERS contains some of the most clever mechanics design and balancing you're likely to have seen for a while. Though there are only really three mechanics (Rotate, thrust, shoot), the way they fit together is stunning; releasing thrust is crucial for avoiding enemy fire, and you can only repair damage when you aren't firing yourself. The end result is both chaotic and balletic. Add to this a superb metagame, where you unlock new parts by completing micro-challenges, and it's hard to recommend this game enough.

This game has incredibly tight controls, insane enemy variety, ludicrous aircraft and panic inducing amounts of projectiles. What really makes this game an absolute beast is the indescribable music. Personally I wouldn't call this a true Ace Combat game. It's a complete departure from the feel of the series, almost like Namco's version Tom Clancy's H.A.W.X. It throws almost everything that you know away and builds a game that is barely relatable to the original series.
The game is set up by default for someone that has never played an Ace Combat game, which is a little suprising but is understandable given the huge differences. However due to this, the default flying style isn't as raw as the previous games untill you turn the control style to original in the settings. The hardest aces from the previous games become commonplace enemies in a sense, which the game's way to tell you to use Dogfight Mode.
Personally I enjoy dogfight mode a lot, however its a bit annoying how it is the most efficient way to take down most planes. It's also buggy at times, such as when you're chasing an enemy through very sharp turns, they shake you off, and you go smashing into the ground with no way of correcting your plane. I love the feel of intensity that DFM gives, but it needs a bit more work.
The missions were well suited for the game and had a good feel of intensity throughout the whole story as well, however I think the game could have been just fine without the helicopter minigun missions.
The story itself was awesome and I enjoyed it a lot, however, it's based in the real world, not the fictional world of Ace Combat.
Assault Horizon isn't a terrible game on its own, it's actually very good, but I wouldnt be caught dead telling people that it's an Ace Combat game.

Night in the Woods may be the best game I've ever played. It's certainly not a game for everyone, though.
***Spoilers***
- story
Night in the Woods is more a story in the form of a game than a game with a story. I don't know many other games whose focus lies so heavily on their story. The way in which you slowly learn about Mae and the other people in Possum Springs is one of the many strengths NITW has. There is a lot of exposition before anything actually starts to happen and at no point I felt bored or found something annoying or unoriginal. The story might not contain many plot twists but that doesn't mean it's predictable or stopping it from having a lot of mystery and unexpected turns of events.
In relation to the long exposition the ending appeared to be quite short to me. Since a sequel is planned I don't think this is actually a negative thing, though. And leaving questions open makes you start developing your own theories and keeps you engaged with the story after you finished the game so I personally find it rather difficult to find something I didn't enjoy about the story.
- characters
NITW's characters are very relatable. You may not have experienced the same events a character has to feel with them and to understand, or at least have assumptions, why they do what they do. This is mainly due to the incredibly well written dialog. While there is humorous small talk in the game as well, many conversations include people talking about their feelings and shared memories they have of their past.
Especially worth emphasizing in this respect is that Night in the Woods tries to capture a lot of different perspectives that so far have largely been ignored in many computer games. Three of the four main characters are queer, financial struggle is omnipresent for not only Mae and her friends but for the entire town, traditional gender roles are challenged, and people with mental health problems as well as religious and homeless people aren't vilified, to name some of the topics and social issues featured in NITW.
I really appreciate that, from my point of view, the game neither just shortly mentions these things being afraid of people not liking it because of this nor does it feel to me like it was meant to be played by someone to convince them of anything. Instead, my impression is that stuff like anarchy symbols are just there so that you can celebrate the game for having them if you want to, and this humbleness makes it even more enjoyable.
- soundtrack
The music is quite successful in creating a unique atmosphere of mystery, familiarity, and coziness that fits Possum Springs and its inhabitants perfectly. Some of it I find it to be a bit movie-like and a movie of NITW is something I'd definitely like to see! Some tracks are quite similar and not all of them a memorable but I think they're all original nevertheless.
- gameplay
This is the only aspect where I found something to criticize, even though not much. The dreams are relatively empty despite the great music and atmosphere. The only thing you can do is to run to the musicians and then back to from where you started. To have dialog in the dreams would perhaps destroy some of the atmosphere but there are other things that could be implemented to make the dreams more interesting. They're dreams after all, so it's a bit surprising that you have such limited opions in what you can do in them. One thing that I speculated could happen in Mae's dreams when I first played NITW was that you would meet other characters or dream of past events, e.g. in college or high school.
Some mini games and the climbing of buildings could also be a bit more complex in my view. Not every mini game has to be like Demontower but some more complexity e.g. for stealing pretzels would increase the suspense quite a lot.
- style
This is probably even more subjective than the rest but I think it can be said that the amount of detail is impressive. At the same time, in moments when simplicity is required NITW doesn't drown you with visual information. Something that sticks out for me is the variety of lighting without which the game just wouldn't be the same.
- conclusion
While being far from being perfect, Night in the Woods is a very brave game unlike any other I'm aware of. It's not a game where you win fights or solve elaborate riddles but a game where you are invited to explore a world and see it through the eyes of different characters. To amaze even more than NITW, its sequel will probably have to feature more perspectives, develop the characters introduced in its predecessor, and add complexity to its gameplay.

Night In The Woods is one big rollercoaster of expressions.
The game starts off giving off a carefree, colourful vibe, with fun things to do, see, and interact with. Yeah, it starts off pretty moody, with
but the first half of it is pretty positive.
The game suddenly gets more dark, with more and more secrets uncovering themselves, strange nightmares when you end the day, and more hints to what happens in the end. It constantly puts you in a feeling of dread.
And when you do get to the end, it's a whole mix of depressing, scary and upsetting.
The game no longer feels like it used to be, making you think "How did we end up like this?"
However, your friends are there for you, and you get picked up when it seems like all hope is lost. Even when you're at the darkest point in the game, where you have to face off with the main enemy, your friends are still there for you.
In the end, it gives a message about friendship, no worries and forgetting the past. That when you feel upset, or you're in a tight spot, your friends are there for you. That when you make a giant mistake in life, you just have to forget it, and look to the future. It's like a message to all teens and young adults out there.
The soundtrack is pretty good as well. Sure, it didn't impress me a few times when I was playing it, but sometimes it does the opposite of that and gives you enjoyment.
But there are 2 best things about this.
1, that when you finish the main story, there's still a heapload of content to play and check out.
2, it has the second least cancerous fandom i've seen! (i mean there is a few nsfw things here and there but honestly all fandoms are bound to have that)

I remember playing Nobunaga's Ambition all the way back on the SNES (which I was also addicted to).  The game has evolved quite a bit in graphics and gameplay complexity since then but the core gameplay is still nostalgically similar and quite addicting.
Graphics:
Awesome, I love it. The picturesque style of the portrait of the generals and gameplay footage fits in really well with the game.
Gameplay:
Good macro gameplay with interesting military and diplomatic options (a bit simplified compared to Civiliation series but has a low learning curve that even non-strategy fans can appreciate). On the extreme difficulty the AI can quickly expand out of your control and simply crush you if you aren't aggressive enough or build massive coalition alliances.
The micro gameplay (where you choose to take over the troops for micro-management during combat) is a bit disappointing and a step backward for the game compared to its SNES roots.  The main issue is that the troops move incredibly slowly and you are always on a VERY short timer for each round/year.  You can barely get anything done before time runs out and your combat options are very limited and simplistic (Total War series beats this game hands down in how well its implements the dual macro/micro gameplay). This is why I basically ignore the micro-battle options and just play the game at the macro level.
Replay Value:
High. You can play as any of 20+ factions starting in 7+ different time periods and scenarios.
Other:
I may be a bit biased for the game because I have a soft spot for Japanese Sengoku history that was started by the original Nobunaga's Ambition on SNES.
Overall: I really enjoyed the game and would recommend it to strategy fans, especially those who are interested in Japanese Sengoku history. I do find the micro battles to be disappointing.  Don't come into this game expecting Total War or Civization and you'll be fine.

Warning: this is my first time playing a

as a series precedes

Sitting between the tactically focused
series and the grand strategy behemoths of
and
,
manages to blend some of the highlights of both games into well realized strategy game with great production values. You will miss the scale of the battles of Total War and the complexity of planning trade/technology/resources from a grand strategy title, but this is my first time playing a game where I can see them both combined into an engaging experience.
Nobunaga's Ambition is partially turn based, partially real-time. The turn-based portion is at the start of every month. You have a “war council” and you get to plan all of the infrastructure/diplomacy/finances. This is much more substantial than the Total War franchise with an order of magnitude more lords, cities, things to develop etc. It really highlights the amazing map they have created of Japan. It's size and complexity makes it more akin to the grand strategy games like
, etc. You don't have quite the number of buildings, resources, systems of a game like Civilization, but it is so close you can taste it. And unlike the Paradox titles, the buildings, cities, districts are beautifully laid out in the map, giving you some feeling of accomplishment.
Once you are done setting your projects, plotting, buying/selling treasures, the month will play out in a real-time fashion. Here, your focus is moving armies around. The system is basic, but integrates well with the empire building. Essentially, each city will have conscripts that you can call to field (a number you increase as you develop your city) and they will be led by a lord that you assigned there. You will need your army to siege enemy cities/break enemy sieges. Once summoned onto the map, they will eat through their provisions which they can only refill by being next to your own city. The further your army needs to move or the longer it takes your army to achieve its goals, the more expensive the war is for you. If you can’t feed your army, be prepared to lose your holdings. It’s an elegant system which ties together a lot of mechanics in the game.
Onto the battles. On its own, it’s not anything to write home about. You are basically turning and moving giant crosses in hilly areas/areas with some defensive terrain. Each commander does have some ability to call to field, but this isn't really deep. I immediately thought the battle system could be better, more massive. What it does do though, is tie well with the strategic layer. Armies you sent to back up your frontline will join the battle you are controlling mid command. It’s really cool. And if you have enough units in the same area, you can engage in a “mass battle.” Basically, an all-in affair with every lord/army in the area. What a ♥♥♥♥ing awesome idea! If only the battles LOOKED as massive as the numbers keep telling me. You can, of course, zoom in to see some detail, but it’s just not detailed enough.
And the diplomacy is great too. Unlike a lot of other strategy titles, here it is tied to lords and gifts. Lords do a lot of things, like lead armies, build roads, build infrastructure. But you can also use lords to help create alliances, convince other lords to defect to your side (or just agree to not to defend against your next conquest). Lords themselves are important, almost everything you need to do in the game needs to be carried out by the many lords/nobles you have in your clan, so convincing other’s lords is good way to weaken your opposition. And keeping your relations happy by giving expensive gifts, marriage, or employing policies they would like is part of your challenge as a leader. It is a refreshing take on the frankly abstract nature of diplomacy in most strategy games.
To top it off, this is one of the best-looking strategy games out there. The production value is the highest I have seen in the genre. The heart of it is the strategic map which is absolutely bursting with details between the towns, the minor factions, the roads, the terrain. But on top of that, cutscenes keep you updated with the politics of the time. Fantastically drawn and filled with betrayals, plotting, and men of great ambition, they do a great job to immerse yourself in Japan’s history and gives more life to the lords you command. It's a nice change of pace from the spreadsheets of the Paradox titles. But the problem is that I failed a "story" quest (sometimes, you can be too agressive), I felt that something had went wrong. It doesn't handle alternate paths very well. Perhaps there is a way to integrate this more into the system itself.
Now, there are downsides. There is a repetitive nature to it, eventually a lot of the towns/cities start blending together. Some of the quests they put in do not tie well into the game (IE, an invasion force that you cannot see). I wish resources were a bigger deal in the game, it would be cool to have a particularly rich mining field to defend or to target and then develop. Trawling through factions after factions to find a couple of guys you can convert to your side each turn eventually gets dull. There are also some ridiculously powerful factions in the game. I understand that they wanted to create some challenge for the player, but it creates a wonky piece of Japanese history. The fact that you know EVERYTHING about your empire (down to 100+ point stats for every lord) does mean that the computer will never be able to sabotage you if you are paying attention to everything. This can get tedious. So it’s not perfect. But for all its faults, this is a well-made and well produced strategy game, and you will have fun with it.

There is something I'd like to note before I review. I do play this game regularly in hopes that some of these issues are fixed. This review and rating may be updated.
I love this game, which has some of the finest shmup action I've played. Beside the game play and the audio, for me, nothing else works. First off, I don't understand the decision the developer made with color scheme, more modes, more horrendous than the next can be unlocked to making it even more difficult than the last to identify enemies. A characteristic of this game that seems like a truely unnessisary hinderence. I'm really hoping there is a normal color scheme mode to unlock. Additionally, when you first load the game, you get the splash screen in wide screen, then in the game, standard. Black strips? What a tease, I can look past this small issue, only if it wasn't used a method to limit the firing range of the player and not the computer. Also with the graphics, I don't mind they are low res but it makes for difficult aiming without a line of sight or some other targeting method to see where you are shooting, this is critical when using weapons with a low frequency rate of fire.
Next, navigating the menu's are a chore and shouldn't have to be. When you have 'go to' screens set to buttons that change on you pending the menu screen you are looking at can get confusing. The menu settings can be changed way too easily and inadvertantly as the controls are too sensative with no way to turn them down or even have dead zones. And how the heck do you exit the game? Well, took me a couple games to firgure out but you have to navigate to one screen to exit the game or even get to the options, that screen being what I thought was the start of the game.
There really isn't too much more to this game and these intended unnessisary problems really do break my heart as I'm seeing a great game go bad. but If you are the type of gamer that can look past these problems, I do recommend this, but otherwise as it stands today, I can not. Maximum I'd give this a 6/10. That 6 easily could be a 9 or 10. Will update if game does.

Controls:

Graphics:

Luftrauser is a game of physical expression on a two-dimensional plane.
Luftrauser reminds me of three of my all-time favorite games from the spatial-awareness-shooty genre:
1. In Triplane Turmoil, momentum is everything - you have a narrow band of space between ground and sky, and your job is to occupy that space without getting shot down.  You have to maintain motion to keep from nosediving into the rocks, but a good pilot can stall into the perfect place to shoot their sibling's plane and pull out of the dive without taking damage.
2. Crimsonland is top-down bullet hell done right - the "bullets" are zombies, and the only long-term way to dodge them is by killing them.  The only way to kill them effectively is to internalize the dodging mechanics so that one half of your brain handles the feet, weaving around the monsters, with the other half of your brain working on aiming in such a way as to make sure that you can keep dodging a few more precious seconds.
3. It took me a few hours to catch it, but Luftrauser also reminds me of Uniball.  Uniball is soccer with spaceships, a weird futuristic air hockey viewed from the top down.  As a younger man I dedicated thousands of hours to playing online, but when bored I would even fire up the "single-player" mode without any other players, just to practice dribbling and moving.  Momentum is a huge part of the game, and I would practice shooting and passing while constantly spinning, limiting myself to only a few direction keys to force myself to use momentum with perfect efficiency.
Luftrauser is an arcade-intense game that asks you to dodge with one brain, use your other brain to shoot speedy bad guys out of the air (with MAX COMBO), and if you're really leet, gives you a spatial playground to express yourself in with all the spinning, stalling, and lasers that my childhood gamer's heart so deeply desires.
And also the soundtrack is super-awesome, the aesthetics are gorgeous, and the upgrades and goals are excellently crafted and all that other stuff.  But really, that's just the devs showing off after creating a beautiful Game.

At first, I was not sure if I wanted to try Dark Souls, knowing its difficulty. I'm very glad that I ended up taking the plunge and trying this gem of a game.
First - the setting is wonderful. I am a big fan of dark fantasy, and delving into such an intricate, interesting world was and is a joy. The artistic design itself is excellent, and the medieval architecture and armor (elite knight armor, especially) looked wonderful. Flying into Anor Londo and seeing the huge city for the first time has to be one of my favorite moments from the game.
Second, the game respects the player. Yes it is difficult and it deserves its reputation as a tough-as-nails game, but the difficulty is not artificial. The game challenges you to improve, to learn from your mistakes, to see the flaws and failings of your enemies, and to be smart with how you approach situations. Very rarely did I feel like I died unfairly - they were usually a result of my mistakes and I knew exactly what I did wrong.
Third, the level design is absolutely phenomenal. From Software did an excellent job crafting a world that flows, with enemies in the right positions, with shortcuts to ease your later travels...everything felt like it was there for a reason.
Finally, the game is just fun. It's super rewarding to struggle with a boss or a difficult area and then conquer (whether through "cheesing" it or otherwise). PVP is a ton of fun and actually feels like it is a part of the experience and not quarantined off to a separate game mode.
I highly recommend this game.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is an excellent follow-up to Robot Entertainment's "Orcs Must Die!" Offering new features such as co-operative play with a friend and levels with unlimited play, this game is definitely an improvement on its predecessor.  In this title, you take up the role of the War Mage, previously tasked with closing all magical rifts allowing orcs into his world and now tasked with protecting that same world from an orcish incursion alongside his old enemy.
Orcs Must Die! 2 plays as some sort of hybrid between a third-person action/shooter game and a tower defense title.  With good fortune, the game does this beautifully and seamlessly.  Levels are spent with players both working on building up their defenses and then taking upon themselves the challenge of killing any orcs that may have managed to survive through the vast and sometimes comedic array of traps that they've established.
If you enjoy third person shooter or action games and have any interest in tower defense, this game may be for you.  This game may also suit anyone wishing to find a shooting/action experience with a little bit of unique element implementation.  Anyone looking for a great game for two-player co-op should also look here.
Key Features:
- Co-Operative Experience (2 players)
- Tower Defense Elements
- Third Person Action/Third Person Shooter Elements
- Waves of Enemies
- Heavy Comic Relief
- Upgrades and Skill Trees
Time Personally Spent on Orcs Must Die! 2: 18 hours

This is a pretty interesting strategy game.  It's not Civilization, and it's not quite Crusader Kings II either.  There are aspects of both, but it incorporates unique gameplay elements to make it appealing to fans of those series.  You will fall victim to "one more turn" syndrome as you manage your army, forge alliances, and think about if you want to spend ten thousand bucks on an old pot.  The game is very logistics focused.  Wars can be won or lost depending on if you sent out your troops at the right time.  A lot of the fun came not from sending in a doom stack, but from navigating the terrain and predicting the what the AI would do.  There is also a fairly diverse diplomacy system, as the game is character focused instead of nation focused.  You can marry, capture, or execute officers each with their own unique skills and attributes.  Crusader Kings II fans should enjoy that feature, and you can even create your own officers.  If you are interested in the sengoku era of Japanese history you will probably find a lot to enjoy as well.  If not, it may seem a bit dense and strange, but I still recommend it to anyone.

This is an excellent purely story based game where decisions have REAL consequence.  Expect a challenge.  Extremely highly recommend at full price.
Full review:
INTRODUCTION
I have been considering this game for a while before getting it, finally picked it up in the best humble bundle I purchased yet for this game alone.  Do not be offput by the general public brushing it off as a dating sim, that is (or should I say can be) such a tiny aspect of the game I don't even really consider it while I play.
SO WHAT IS THE GAME ABOUT?
This game is about the struggles of a young girl about to become queen, as it says in the description.  Morethan that though, this game is about how your every move and decision is constantly changing and effecting the world around you creating hilarious, tragic, unexpected, and moving ways to live or die at every turn.  Atfirst the game will seem quite simple, but after your third, fourth, fifth....... death, you will realize just how deep the game can go.  The game's events are generally in a particular order, but those can change and diverge greatly and quickly based on what you choose.
THE GOOD
Choices and meaning.  This game does an excellent job of portraying not only that your choices mattered, but what each one actually meant.  This is extremely empowering to the player.  On the flipside, situations beyond your control, not because the game is unfair, but because of a choice you made... or didn't make, happen frequently and keep you on your toes.  You can feel like a god wielding magic user with all the military knowledge in the world, feel unstoppable as you crush armies with your will alone, but what happens when you get an unexpected gift?  Do you really know what it means?
THE BAD
Soundtrack.  That's about it.  It's a repetitive set of canned classical masterpieces in lovely midi form.  Beynd that, as long as you realize this is a text game where immersion relies on your imagination instead of clunky controls and flashy graphics, you won't have any huge issues.
THE INDIFFERENT
As far as things which I don't find good or bad, but worth bringing up there are two.  First is the artwork.  I personally find it well done, but not my favorite style.  All the male characters are to "kawaii" and some of the outfits are just silly, like a catsuit with a monocle.  Second is the difficulty.  While I welcome a challange, the game doesn't really lend itself to constant "save states" and it's usually better to start over every time you die.  While some people may not like the difficulty, I feel indifferent as the starting over is annoying since the first few events will be the same, but after that it is fun to see how the tiny change in your first 3 weeks completely changes the feel of the game.
IT'S FINALLY OVER
In closing, this is one of the best story driven games I have ever played.  I seek out games like this, such as A Dark Room (iOS), Indigo Prophecy / Heavy Rain (must play games for those who like story), and many other, less noteworthy titles.  Out of all of them though, this one may not be the absolute best, but it does do the absolute best job at giving the player power within the story, without giving the player power to control it like a god (I'm looking at you Indigo Prophecy).

I love Portal. I love Portal more than I love myself.
Portal and Portal 2 are two of my favorite games of all time- they got me into Valve's other games, which have come to join the Portal games among my favorites (especially Half-Life). Thinking with Time Machine, however, made me feel really unfulfilled.
Thinking with Time Machine isn't /necessarily/ a bad game- but I'm definitely not calling it a good one. At all.
Portal worked amazingly well for three reasons: great level design, a well-written script, and a unique mechanic. Thinking with Time Machine has only one of these.
The level design in TwTM is ABYSMAL.
Here is a list of things I would rather do than play test chamber 05 of this game:
*Remove my toenails with pliers
*Undergo open heart surgery without anesthetic
*Gouge out my eyes with a spoon.
The game contains no script besides a few captions at the beginning of the game, and turrets never really make an appearance. All the lovely charm of the Portal games, with cake and companion cubes and psychotic computers, is totally gone.
The "unique mechanic" is okay- but the tutorial is extremely vague, and makes you fail repeatedly in order to understand the game. More painfully, though, it grinds the pacing to a halt.
To explain my hatred for TwTM, here's a short list of ordeals I had to endure.
1) I spent ten mundane minutes playing a mediocre level. Just before reaching the elevator, the game abruptly crashed. Now, I've spent twenty minutes on that level.
2) Test Chamber 05 was clearly built while all the level designers were either out at lunch, asleep, or on vacation (possibly a combination thereof.) I put myself in inescapable situations that led to me needing to reboot the level more than ten times, and spent the entire time wishing someone would knock me out with a crowbar.
3) Many of the levels are built around accurate timing in an innacurate, buggy mechanical system. This results in having to redo monotonous tasks OVER AND OVER AND OVER.
If you hadn't noticed, I'm really, really, really mad about this game. Yes, it's free- well, actually, it's not. It's free to Portal 2 owners. You can argue it's like a free DLC, but Portal 2 already has some free DLC's that make this game look like Ride to Hell in comparison. The thing that bothers me most, though, is that this was on the front page of Steam. There have been VASTLY superior Source mods that didn't get nearly this much attention (Black Mesa, Blue Portals, etc.) if any at all. Yet this awful fan-made post-game addon got front page coverage. It may be unfair to compare a fan-made mod to a professionally designed high-budget game, but I really don't care. You get front page, you get critique.
I'm going to have to stop myself. I have more to say, but if I keep going, this will inevitably become pages long.
In summary:
Score A (assuming it's totally free): 7/10
Score B (considering it requires ownership of Portal 2): 6/10
Final Score: 6.5/10
Playtime: 1 hour
Verdict: on-par with mayonnaise.

I was a Street Fighter Fan of the first hour. Yes, I played the very first Street Fighter back in the days (and a couple of successors). I wanted to write that this game is only for fans of the series, but after the first couple of hours, this game is really disappointing, even though I do consider myself as some degree of fan.
The usual Street Fighter Looks. Super Flashy and in complete opposition to the Looks of the Mortal Kombat series. You know that, and you accept that, if you buy a Street Fighter game. However, compared to the first couple of Street Fighter titles, they have really exaggerated the exaggerations for this title. Not only in terms of saturation & flashiness, but also in terms of body proportions: While in the first couple of SF titles body proportions were still acceptable for comic standards, Chun Li' and Cammy's thighs are now double or thrice the width of their respective hips.
As usual for the SF series, the button combinations are at least medium in size and duration. Some special moves will be even long (half or full circle stuff). Supers are always long and/or complicated to execute. Very opposed to MK titles or Injustice with quick button combinations for special moves.
Within the first couple of hours, you are trucking excited as hell to have this huge roster of 44 characters. However, the more characters you play, the more frustrated you'll get, because at least 50% of them have the trucking same couple of special moves (i.e. some variation of hadoken, shoryuken or hurricane kick) and most of the supers are just variations of their special moves that hit harder. Why the truck would anyone want this? Capcom, spare yourself the trouble of reskinning Ken & Ryu 20 times and giving those reskins new names, instead give us 5 original, unique characters! Compared to UMvC3, this game is definitely a huge step back in the very wrong direction.
I don't know if it's just this particular version of the game, but is there really a story? I mean overall? Doesn't seem like it. Yeah, there are individual character backgrounds, but what you are being told is not even a story, but at most fragments of parts of seemingly totaly unrelated & different stories. In 3 words: The storytelling sucks.
This game has the worst storytelling of all games I have ever played since I started to play games in 1995. Even for the game standards back then this game sucks at storytelling, but for today's standards it's even more horrible. Especially with the character endings, I'd mostly go "What!?!?!?", "Seriously?!?!?", "That is so shallow..." or "How has that got anything to do with the pervious story fragments?"
This general trend continues throughout the entire game, be it the heartless, mindless, ever same and unrelated pre-match punchlines between characters (apart from one fight per character, where you fight your rival) or the equally unoriginal, lame post-match punchlines that the winner dishes only in written form. Especially annoying are Juri's and Abel's pre-match interactions when fighting Seth (the end boss): They are exactly the same as for every other character, even though Abel & Juri's previous story fragments clearly suggest a relationship with Seth. That is just plain heartless and lazy, Capcom.
The general game settings are not well done. It seems you can't turn off the damn subtitles, and you have to choose between either being able to listen to cutscenes or turning off background music, as cutscenes and background music were allocated in the same settings category instead of allowing to regulate cinematic & background sound seperately.
The online mode for this game is dead since the successor SFV hit the market.
I would like to say that this game is only for fans of the series, but it seems to me, it's only for real die-hard fans of the series. Complicated gameplay, massive lack of creativity in all aspects of the game (but especially character design & story) and therefore no replayability at all make this game a very bad one for me. I would not buy this again, and I will definitely not buy Street Fighter V now that I know Injustice 2 is coming out in 2017.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is an excellent follow-up to Robot Entertainment's "Orcs Must Die!" Offering new features such as co-operative play with a friend and levels with unlimited play, this game is definitely an improvement on its predecessor.  In this title, you take up the role of the War Mage, previously tasked with closing all magical rifts allowing orcs into his world and now tasked with protecting that same world from an orcish incursion alongside his old enemy.
Orcs Must Die! 2 plays as some sort of hybrid between a third-person action/shooter game and a tower defense title.  With good fortune, the game does this beautifully and seamlessly.  Levels are spent with players both working on building up their defenses and then taking upon themselves the challenge of killing any orcs that may have managed to survive through the vast and sometimes comedic array of traps that they've established.
If you enjoy third person shooter or action games and have any interest in tower defense, this game may be for you.  This game may also suit anyone wishing to find a shooting/action experience with a little bit of unique element implementation.  Anyone looking for a great game for two-player co-op should also look here.
Key Features:
- Co-Operative Experience (2 players)
- Tower Defense Elements
- Third Person Action/Third Person Shooter Elements
- Waves of Enemies
- Heavy Comic Relief
- Upgrades and Skill Trees
Time Personally Spent on Orcs Must Die! 2: 18 hours

Night in the Woods is a fun game in my personal opinion. I played it a week after it came out, and as i do  with most games, I was immediately critical of the game, as I am with most games. By the end of the game however, I had pretty much decided that NitW was my personal game of the year. That isn't to say that this game is for everyone however, so here are a few things that I would keep in mind if you're on the fence about it.
If you like:
-Story
-Long Dialouge
-Animal friends
-Mystery
-Fulfilling the friendless void in your life
-Music
-spending money on anything that has pets on two legs
-games that aren't exactly games
Then you'll probably love this game.
NitW is definitely not a game in the usual sense. You won't be engaged in any high tempo story with crazy abilities, but what it lacks in physical action, I personally think it makes up for in interesting and fun events. This game is really a graphic novel with a few minigames, as well as the fullfleged dungeon-crawler Demon Tower that you can play in-game. If that's a dealbreaker for you, I sadly have to say that you might not want this game, as a major criticism I hear (if this game ever gets any criticism), is that the main story is very low tempo, and that it only picks up at the end. If you love getting enveloped in a story with interesting characters and experiencing a world that feels lively and real, you might want to stick around. NitW definitely puts a lot of effort in selling the characters you take part in adventures with on each of the days that the game gives you, and as you progress further with them, you might just take a liking to them. Mae, the protaganist can come off as a bit hyper, which put me off at first, but I personally didn't find it getting in the way after maybe the first time. An important note though, is to remember to stick to one character more, as the further in the story you get in, the more the time you spend with a character, the more you'll experience from them. In my playthrough I switched between both Bea and Gregg and after the last event with Gregg I was a little confused as to what was happening as a lot of events that I hadn't played were mentioned. The one on one events were still great regardless, but it felt a little anti-climactic to me at the end.
The music is some of the best in my opinion. After my last meeting with Mr. Chazokov, I had already know this was going to be a great soundtrack. Luckily, I was not proven wrong, as many of the tracks are great. There is a lot of more ambient tracks that are great, but I personally prefer the more lively songs. This soundtrack has a plethora of songs you can come back to even after you completely finished the game.
Honestly if you've read this long and don't already own the game, go for it. It'll run on even the most busted of toasters, and it's even coming on the smartphone. Really, there's not many reasons why you shouldn't get this game to be honest.

I randomly picked this up when it was on sale, based on the cutesy look of the art, without knowing anything about the game. After playing it, I regret not paying full price.
The artstyle is beautiful. If this game was realistic, had 3D models for characters, or if it was humans instead of animals, then it wouldn't have been nearly as enjoyable as it was with this artstyle. Nothing ever blended in, everything was clearly visible and interesting to look at.
The game is so alive. The characters move and animate so fluidly. The leaves being pushed around by the character, the animals doing their own thing and the character scaring them, birds flying in the sky, trees swaying in the background. Paralax was used really well in this game and the world feels like there's more literal depth to it than the space you actually move on.
The music is catchy and never got boring. There is so much different music in this game. Every situation seemed to have it's own music. They are actually pretty good songs to listen to on their own too.
The minigames and non-platforming areas of the game never felt tacked on and cheap. They fit with the style and are fun and interesting. I often looked forward to them.
If more games in this universe, with the same gameplay and feel, are made, I would definitely buy them. It was just so much fun to be a part of this world.

Long Live The Queen is a solid simulation. In Long Live The Queen you control the activities of the Heir Apparent from the time of the death of her mother (the previous monarch) to her corronation. As is often the case, not everyone is pleased with the succession. The manner in which you handle yourself largely determines if they let you get on with it, or cause major trouble for you - of course some people just want you dead no matter what.
The only way to survive is to develop the skills to: survive dangerous encounters, make good political decisions, and generally avoid making a fool of yourself.  The game is pretty unforgiving, it takes a few playthroughs to get an idea of what you absolutely need to learn, and by when, but there's a good amount of wiggle room in there for agency in between. Once you find out why exactly certain things happen, you may be able to prevent certain life threatening events from happening in the first place - or alternatively welcome them, and knowing the challenges they pose, be prepared to meet them head on.
Overall, Long Live The Queen is an intriguing game, with a layered narrative that leaves an unusually large amount of space for the player to influence the unfolding of events and develop their character.
