There has become a large group of fans for this game who seem to appreciate the game for its willingness to kill the character and teach through trial and error.  It does these things well, but even if you find that sort of thing appealing I do not think it makes up for the many flaws of the game.
In this game your attacks are oddly placed on your triggers and bumpers (and you need to use a controller).  Instead of having a heavy attack simply being a held down light attack, it is on its own button.  Instead of having parry be a well timed block, it is its own button.  Blocking only works consistantly when you have your camera locked onto the target you are blocking, which is a problem because of the poor camera controls.  There is also a button dedicated to switching to using two handed attacks with your weapon.  The back button allows your character to perform gestures, and the start button brings up game menus but does not pause the game.  There is no way to pause the game.
This leaves you with R3, L3, A, B, X, and the DPad.  The dpad is relegated to switching your equipment and items on the fly.  A is oddly not context sensitive, but is a dedicated "interact" button.  X uses whichever item you have selected.  R3 is to focus the camera on an enemy.  B button is the only button with more than one purpose - it is bound to dodge, jump and run.  Tapping it will dodge backwards, tapping it while holding a direction will roll in that direction, holding it will allow you to run, and tapping it after running will cause you to jump - don't attempt to roll after running.
The controls are just poorly done.  I am not sure why there was any deviance at all from the standard control scheme of games like this, especially when it works so well.  Adding frustration to the bizarre control scheme is the use of a queueing system - if you push roll twice, you will roll twice in a row, despite it being a long time since you actually pressed the button.  This becomes a large problem when you run into the randomly occurring input lag, which my friends tell me also occurs on consoles.
The game also suffers from a terrible camera.  It collides with everything, making fighting near doorways and in rooms with low ceilings frustrating. It is too close to your character, and if not constantly babysat it will never point where you want it to.  As I wrote above, you are forced to lock on to targets with the camera to be consistant with blocking, but locking on with your camera just makes you unable to see behind you.  To juggle multiple camera locks in quick succession, you have to flick the right stick torwards the next enemy you want to lock on.  This works terribly, as you end up unable to rotate the camera properly while there are multiple enemies.
Between the camera and the controls, I feel like there is no enjoying the better aspects of Dark Souls.  They are truly atrocious, and so many games have done them far better.  It seems to me that a large part of the difficulty in the this game is just doing battle with the camera/controls.  These obvious flaws don't stop people from defending the game, but their defense of it amounts to "I can do it so you suck."  Well I imagine they could shove a broom into all of their orifices too, but just because they are capable of it does not make it a good experience.
Even were these problems not in the game, I think you really need to ask yourself how interesting a game based around observing and memorizing enemy attacks is. The combat is very clunky (or weighty, if you are talking to someone who appreciates it) and characterized by waiting for an attack you know you can counter.  Figuring out what is the best way to take on each enemy is almost never apparent, and usually involves trying random things until you find one that works.
This is certainly different from other games which have more active combat, and I think some gamers appreciate the uniqueness of this approach.  Personally I found this experimenting felt like a dull mechanic that artificially stretches the length of the game, and that combat felt incredibly boring due to how much time you spend waiting for your chance to attack.
I also see the game get a lot of praise for the combat being difficult, which I think is a very odd way to look at it.   Even if you are the most skilled gamer there has ever been, a terrible player with a guide book would be better than you at this game.  The only way to get through the game is to have prior knowledge of all the enemies and the areas.  People conflating this memorization with difficulty have apparantly not seen the videos of the game being beaten by blindfolded players, or by players using DDR pads, or guitar hero controllers.  The game has even been beaten by Twitch Plays like it was just another pokemon game.
Another divisive feature of the game is how it deliberately witholds necessary information from the gamer.  There is an NPC you need to talk to 3 times before he starts to sell what you need,  when the game does tell you what to do it is deliberately misleading (or straight out lying) to you, despite the bizarre controls the game only informs you of a few actions, none of the core gameplay mechanics are ever conveyed, most of the games UI and stats are unexplained, and some of the items in the game actually have completely incorrect descriptions - like a ring claiming it restores HP over time when it does no such thing.  This design forces the player to learn everything through a monstrous amount of experimentation, trial and error, and exploring.  I know some people like this feature, but I just felt like the game has no respect at all for my time.
I did not even scratch the surface about what a terrible port this is, absolutely requiring mods to play.  Without mods the game looks and runs terribly, but fortunately the modding community has been superb with fixing these issues.
I suspect that a large amount of the praise this game receives is due to it being many players first "hard" game.  They have nothing else to compare it to, and do not realize that a game that is hard like Contra is different from a game that is hard like Simon's Quest.  Dark Souls is like a modern Simon's Quest, but Simon's Quest still had better controls and a better camera.
If you are looking for a hard game that plays well, try Devil May Cry.  If you are looking for a brutal and combat heavy RPG, try Dragon's Dogma.  If you are insistent on playing Dark Souls, you need to get the DSFix mod and probably need a control mod as well, but I still would not recommend it.

This game was a disappointment, for what little of it i played. The design of the puzzles is poor at best. In most cases, you will face more of a challanged trying to get the mechanics to work properly (especially with the round cubes that refuse to stay put). If you came to this looking for more of portal, you will not come away happy.
Overall, the puzzles are simple, but the executing them is a bit of a challange. You will know the answer to most of the puzzles within a minute at most, but actually solzing them can take several minutes of tedious busiwork as you carefully run in an obvious and slow pattern to ensure you have time to solve the puzzles.
Also, gone are the portals (at least in the early levels). You have the portal gun, but you never need to use it. Portal-able surfaces are very rare and obviously marked, making any guesswork or experimentation a complete waste of time. In fact, the portal spots are so obvious, they actually give you clues as to how to solve some of the puzzles (because every surface that can be have a  portal on it is most likely used in the puzzle).
sound design ----- This portal randition isn't creepy like "Delapitation", it isn't creative like "Designed For Danger", and it isn't funny like "12 angry tests". There is no diologue, except some unintellegable speech from unknown characters. There isn't much in the way of music either. The sound effects that are in place are glaringly loug and annoying. The lazor sound effect is loud regardless of how close you are, and remains annoying untill you complete the level.
Graphics ----- Portal 2 was never a graphical powerhouse to begin with. It looks nice, but it's a little old. This mod is ugly by Portal one standards. It doesn't look good. The moments we get to see Chell as you use the time mechanic are ackward as well, since Chell was never very well animated. The game was made to be played in first person, but when we get to see Chell as much as we do, it gives off a very weird feeling.
Design ----- There are constantly a bunch of little things that bite at you. The loud and annoying sounds, the time travel mechanic being ugly and jerky (because a player is behind the movements), the overly large HUD reticule (the blue and orange oval is a lot bigger then it should be, and it gets in the way at times), the long puzzles that you know the answer to but can't finish quickly because of having to do everything twice, the lack of freedom with you Portals, and your lack of agency in general.
Conclusion ----- In portal, if you want to fall endlessly, make portals as shortcuts, use the portal as a mirror to get a look at chell when you "shouldn't" be able to, jumping long distances, falling, usuing portals to gain momentum, you can do that. You can make portals on surfaces that may hold no purpose, because you want to. You can screw around and try to break the game with weird portal jumps, you can experiment with various jumps, falls, and vantage points. There is usually one solution, but you can approach it from multiple angles and come to the conclusion at your own pace and in you're own way. All of this is missing in this mod. It doesn't feel like a portal game. It uses portal assets, but it doesn't have the same soul. It's free, so if you're curious about it, give it a try. otherwise, skip it or try a different level set on the workshop.

A really fun little indie title from one of the most proficient indie studios out there.
Luftrausers is a remake of an old flash game called Luftrauser (originally not Vlambeers game). The remake has enough new and fun content that will keep you consumed for the next week or so.
The greatest part about Luftrausers is without a doubt the combat. With the added gravity added to each airplane you'll feel like there's real weight in your Rauser when you're gliding through the air while shooting down a swarm of enemies. Added to this there's also a bullet hell feel to it where you dodge bullets and missiles while trying to get that extra score multiplier.
The game also has a dynamic soundtrack that changes with what parts you use with your Rauser. The changing music keeps the game fresh even though you've heard a similar track several times before.
The only negative that I can think of is that some parts (weapons/armors/engines) are a bit unbalanced and needs more work. It would also be nice if it was possible to crack down on the cheaters whom riddle the leader boards.
I'd personally highly recommend this game for all bullet hell, indie and arcade fans out there. The game is hard, but also so rewarding when you get the hang of it.

Luck will determine if you can carry a full score multiplier (and it's a big multiplier) because sometimes small planes and boats don't spawn often enough. The game derives its longevity instead through hiding the different plane parts behind missions, many of which only ask you be persistent than skillfull (accumulate X points over however many tries it takes).  You're going to notice the game's problems well before you get the last part.

Luftrausers is an action game where you fly an aircraft while completing missions and unlocking new parts. The goal is to get the highest score, by avoiding incoming rockets, planes and bullets. Kill enough enemies in one combo or reach a certain score and you'll unlock new parts for your aircraft. These parts might just help you get an even higher score. The parts are finely tuned and expertly balanced, so for example, increasing your damage might just make your aircraft fly/manoeuvre slower. You have to take things like that into account before taking off. You can adjust your engine, your weapon and your body and there are plenty of parts to unlock and use.
Luftrausers is a fun game with some good music that's probably best played in smaller sessions.

A subpar entry in a series of great games.
A few things you need to understand before buying/trying this game:
Ace Combat is not a flight sim
Ace Combat is not meant to be realistic
Ace Combat is primarily a console game
First off, the only graphics option is resolution, and that maxes out a 1440p. Even so, the game looks fairly nice, aside from the annoying static cockpit reflection in cockpit view. The story is a wannabe Tom Clancy USA vs. Russia, which is particularly annoying considering the previous games were set in a very interesting alternate universe with fake countries that are allusions to real life counterparts. Sure, the prewvious stories were corny, but you could get really into them. The story in Assault Horizon is both difficult to get into and corny.
Another issue in this entry is limited plane selection according to the mission. The game has a fairly large selection of planes, but it's wasted potential since you can only use a few each mission.
The music is composed by the same guy who was doing it since 04/5, so it is superb as usual. However, in this entry, the music is different from others in regards to their style.
My biggest issue with this game is that they wanted to attract new fans by making the game Call of Duty style with more emphasis on on-the-rails action than the freeforming fun of previous games.
I recommend all the other games in the series before this one, but Assault Horizon is still a decent arcade air combat game.
However, as an Ace Combat game, Assault Horizon fails in many aspects.
I recommend every previous entry other than this one.
Also, make sure you have a joystick/controller, as it is near unplayable otherwise, especially online.

You know, I was willing to roll with the new "dogfighting mode" where your plane pretty much flies itself as you simply control your speed and concentrate on lining up your reticule with the enemy to shoot them down. Why? Because no Ace Combat installment has ever been good with dogfighting and in turn in was never used. So I could kinda get behind that because if you wanted to play Ace Combat the classic way, just don't ever use your guns.
What I absolutely could not roll with is the lame controls and terrible scripted events which should have had no place in a game like this. Ace Combat has always been about jets. Now it has helicopters that control like COD. Seriously, they are exactly like COD. On top of all that, there are a unhealthy amount of quicktime counter manuevers to dodge enemy attacks and to turn tables on an enemy attacking you. My helicopter dodged a missle by doing a barrel roll (more like an aileron roll) after hitting the Y button in a scripted event. After I saw that I was officially done. It's not the lack of realism. It's the fact that none of this feels like flying. Putting in a ton of optional quicktime manuevers just made the game feel like I was just pressing buttons to win. It's not that it's too easy, but rather boring. It's not what Ace Combat fans were looking for at all which is the reason for all the bad scores it gets. I've never really been a huge fan of the series primarily because it is boring to me, and I can definitely see what Namco was trying to do here by changing up not just the controls, but the gameplay as well with the shooting and helicopter missions. I think games like Heroes of the Pacific and even Skycrawlers on the Wii are much more engaging and exciting to play. Fighting with modern jets has always been boring with your very unrealistic stock of missles.
In the end, this game was not good for fans of the series, nor was it good for new comers. Even at 5 bucks I wouldn't pick this game up.

In short, a 7.5/10. PROS: Great graphics, classic Ace Combat fighter action and great mission scripting. CONS: Takes away from original Ace Combat style of gameplay (more "Call of Duty" style, fast-paced action), plays better with controller.
I personally am a HUGE fan of the original Ace Combat series of video games. I have all of their games released for PS2, with "04: Shattered Skies" and "5: The Unsung War" being my favorites from Namco-Bandai's Project Aces team, but this game, in all respects was somewhat of a disappointment. Without a doubt, it's a very good and (to me) a recommendable game, it just lacks a bit where the old Ace Combat really shined.
The Ace Combat series in itself is very well-renowned as a combat flight simulator for the Playstation 2, and for many years, the Project Aces team were the best of the best on the market. No other video games at the time gave a more realistic sensation of combat flight. Assault Horizon really diverges from that original goal, however. As mentioned in another review, in this game, "Ace Combat" really becomes "Aerial Call of Duty". The game takes away from the realistic feel of flying the plane to bring in more action-packed and fast-paced gameplay. Features such as Dog Fight MODE and the addition of helicopter and gunship missions definitely stray away from the original Ace Combat. Other fans of Ace Combat on console systems will also take note of how impaired gameplay can be without a controller (joysticks are easier, and without them. the "free-viewing" mode allowing the player to look around the plane or cockpit becomes unusable).
But that is not to say it's a bad game. Mission scripting is as good as ever from the Project Aces team, and the visuals are without a doubt phenomenal. It's still an Ace Combat game. It's still very enjoyable.

In Night in the Woods, you play as Mae Borowski, a cat girl who comes home from college, only to find out that quite a bit has changed since her absence. Throughout the game, you explore Possum Springs and talk to the residents of your home town.
For someone who could care less for visual novels or walking simulators, the NitW
story was extremely compelling. I actually had a three week hiatus from playing the game because I didn't want it to end. The plot felt realistic and I was quite immersed through most of the game. Certain characters have backstories and the game encourages you to interact with them frequently to learn their personalities and morals. There is an underlying dread in every second of the game which heavily complements the theme of the story and it just makes it that much better. For as much fun and happiness everyone seems to be gathering, it's pretty freakin' depressing at times. The mood of a story can shift so quickly but smoothly, it catches you off guard sometimes.
To create indepth characters that have personality and don't act like lines of code is an incredibly difficult challenge. NitW blows through it easily. I have never felt so interested in a character who could probably just be an OC from a furry artist. All of the characters are animals, and the wildlife in Possum Springs are also animals, yet the game never dwells on it. Sure, the Mae's Dad will say, "Hey there, kitten," but you will never hear Mae yell, "Oh, look at meee! I'm a cat who hangs out with a bear, a crocodile, and a fox!" The dialouge may be a little cringy at first, it's like the characters are sixteen year-olds who just found out about the internet and texting, but you get used to it. Now, if you are a pansy who couldn't bear having your Christian ears defiled by a swear word, then you can eat♥♥♥♥♥♥ because Mae and her friends swear like sailors frequently throughout the entire game, but it's not Payday 2 level of excessive swearing
I really can't say there is much on the basis of gameplay, you've got the jump, triple jump, interact, run, look at♥♥♥♥♥♥ the simple things. Occasionally, you'll be called on to do a minigame of some sort, whether it is an illegal action or a music sequence. It gets difficult if you aren't a Guitar Hero master, which I am not, but to be absolutely honest, the music in NitW rivals Starbound's for my favorite soundtrack. It's more or so based on the player's preference on the artist: a garage band or an orchestra. I will say this, there are two running events that are very well executed due to the music, the story, and controls. They genuinely raised my heart rate from excitement.
I feel like the only people who could hate this game are people who do NOT pay attention to anything story wise. It is rare for me to be very invested in a game with limited replayabilty, but instead of trying to increase it's playtime, the developers spend time working on characters and the story. It's almost like someone put real effort and heart into a wonderful game.

Night in the Woods' narriative, like its main character, remains utterly aimless for far too long. Super Bunnyhop in his review said that the game relies upon the assumption that you strongly identify or at least know someone who strongly identifies with Mae's circumstances. Unfortunately, I don't think even that is enough to maintain the interest of most.

The plot is simple, you play as either an advisor to the princess or the princess herself, her mother just died and its apperent that she left a power vaccum in the land of the living. Elodie, the princess, in a simplified take on how royalty works is next in line for the then, but there's the catch, she's almost a year too young to take the crown.
The task here is to teach ehr the skills she needs to becoem a proper queen which includes such things as Animal Training, Art, Dance, Song, Running, Sports, Gymastics, Medicine, Espionage and Magic. Yes, Magic.
Along the way you must protect her form assassins, chocolates, psyco relatives, a commoner revolution, chocolates, a civil war, a forest that would make the Everfree pale in comparison, chocolates, sorcerers, chocolates, a sea monster and chocolate. Failure to do so will be a Game Over and will treat you to a humourous chibi carcature of the associated death. Her mood and wardrobe will determine how much knowedge she gets in a skill so any sudden mood swings will throw off your curriculum
The trick here is to know what skill are needed to avoid certain doom or pass checks needed to help her earn the crown. You will die a lot, you will save a lot and you will reload saves when you inevitably die a lot, primarely to chocolates, arrows, psycotic relatives, chocolate and the odd tentacle.
I'd give it a 10/5. If you like Visual Novels, Game of Thrones, A Song of Ice and Fire, Princess Maker or Chocolate then I do recomend playing this game.

Where to start... well, I stumbled upon this game by accident. I was looking for "Games where shields matter". This was a recommended entry so I gave it a shot. Almost immediately after starting I got horribly murdered by the huge Assylum Demon who gave no sh*t about my shield. After I got to Firelink I started to explore and I hit the Crestfallen Warrior who killed me, I respawned and he was right there again and killed me again and again until I wore him down. This is when I thought "WTF is this game?". But I stayed and played and got better and fell in love with Dark Souls. The game world and mechanics are so good that you forgive what a bad PC port it is. I mean, without an XBox gamepad (or mods) it is borderline unplayable. But the level design wins you over and so will the boss fights. The pure feeeling of joy when you defeat a difficult enemy is intoxicating. Firelink Shrine is a sort of hub area but it does not have to be. Bonfires are scattered all over the game world and you can level up at any of them. The only extra perk of the hub is that, as you free NPCs, they will move into Firelink Shrine (until you kill them or move on in their questline). The multiplayer aspect you will both hate and love as you get killed by invaders and have jolly cooperation with your friends (or random awesome people). Although the network code is flimsy and often makes it hard to connect to your friends without mods. There is so much more about the game but you know the basics and to truly know it you have to play it. And truly, for me, it's an awesome game I really REALLY recommend! \[T]/

Luftrausers is an arcade dogfighter game in which you shoot boats, jets, aircrafts and whatnots. A gamesession can variate between 30 seconds to 5 minutes (IF you got any luck surviving this long^^). It´s brutal, unforgiving, plain and simple but a hellish addicting game =)
GAMEPLAY
Simply put, you have to press 4 different buttons. And avoiding projectiles while flying. Oh and sometimes you needn´t to push a button or else you fly directly into another projectile xD But this depens on how you build up your aircraft. Bulky but slow with high firepower or fast with a melee body ala Kamikaze Joe? There are three different slots where you can choose your loadout: Weapon, Body and Engine. To discribe the gameplay of Luftrausers is a little hard so I put a playlist at the end of this review.
GRAPHICS
Graphics on the other hand are quite simple to discribe. 8-bit pixels with a stabile framerate of 30 FPS deliver fluid pictures of hate and enjoyment. Through unlockable color patterns the original 3-Color mode can be switched from psychodellic neon to simple black and grey and white. Every mode except the original made me puke and laugh at the same time but this lies in the eye of the beholder. :P
SOUND
Now this is what really stands out. Every game has a soundtrack but Luftrausers is a shiny example for how great and important good music is for a game. Every bodypart has its own "OST". I´d say industrial meets 8-Bit... I totally love it =)
For 9€ it´s hard not to recommend this game but after playing it for 8 hours only highscore hunting is left (maybe achievement hunting, but that´s not for me) I hope there´ll be updates with more equipment parts to play around with or maybe new enemies. For those who beat the normal mode AND defeated an enormous aircraft called "BLIMP" you get access to a new mode called "SFMT".. Even satan cries in his bedchamber after he played ten minutes in this mode xD

This game... IS RECOMMENDABLE! Please, try the game, if you like games like GTA, Mafia, Saints Row... Well, yea...

If anyone has played the flash game Endless Zombie Rampage 1/2 its like that. If you haven't and the screenshots aren't giving you enough information, its a top down arena style zombie shooter. You're running around outside of this house that is in the middle of what appears to be in the middle of BUTT**** NOWHERE completely boxed in as zombies come from the trees and the ground (literally digging its way out of the ground inside your house).
You start with a pistol and you unlock more guns as you get more kills. You build turrets to aid you in killing the masses of undead, as you progress, you'll "level up" which allows you to increase stats like overall health and health regen, increased weapon damage and reload speed, increased resource pickup and health gained from dropped health packs, and turret damage and ROF. When you kill a zombie they have a chance of dropping health, grenades, powerups, and scrap metal which is needed to build turrets, fortification, and to repair said turrets and fortification, occasionally the zombie dogs will crap all over the place and if you run over the "pickup" it slows you down. As you progress through the days, zombies get tougher and tougher and newer types of infected start showing up. To unlock weapons, you press the "i" key and you look at the chart, and you follow it. When you die and restart, no progress is saved. If you quit to the menu and start at say, Day 9, you start with your pistol and basically its like starting from Day 1 but you're starting from Day 9 so you fight the Day 9 horde with Day 1 weapon(s).

There are a lot of things that impressed me about Night in the Woods, the music, the art direction, the occasionally whimiscal and serious dialogue, and all those things that people have already said, like how relatable the characters are.
What really made it stand out for me was the depth of the writing.  It is entirely serviceable on the surface, and anyone can probably appreciate the experience just flowing through the story without caring about critical analysis, but digging deeper reveals a web of themes that connect everything together on multiple layers.  What might seem like throwaway lines in one place might end up being a relevant metaphor for something else later.  I wish I knew how they did it.
Alternatively gut wrenching and inspiring.  If you like games with a story, Night in the Woods is worth the experience.
It's hard to put how I feel about this game into words, but it makes me feel this sense of happiness and sadness at the same time?

It's linear as all hell, it's only ten or so hours long, and the main character can be downright punchable at times - but it is absolutely worth your money. Quite possibly the best written game I have played all year - or, perhaps, ever - and, should you have any experience with depression, mental illness, or just being a millenial in todays current world, you will almost certainly be touched by it. You should play it. For fifteen dollars, it's well worth any time or cash investments. You won't regret it.

A wonderful  game I played back in the days. Be sure that the graphics are dated, but this is not the reason you play this game.
The Game Centers around a NATO Command team that tries to uncover the mystery of the disappearance of another group.
While uncovering its secrets you roam a city that was designed with attention to detail and encounter enemies at different points of the map. There is a large variability of enemies and cool boss enemies.
The battles are faught in a round-based fashion, which is the aspect that makes this game so dear to my heart. Your group members (that change during the game based on its story) gain experience with the weapons they use increasing their effectiveness. They also level up and you can influence their attributes (like Luck, Accuracy, Chance of Coutner Attacks etc).
The maps are fight layed out using squares and usually offer some possibilities to retreat from enemies so that you are not standing too tight. They often also offer coverage or objects like explosives that can be used to your advantage.
The game is sometimes quite challanging because ammo can not be found in aboundance, so tactical thinking and choice of weapon is a must.
In conclusion I have to say that I can only warmly recomment this game to anyone who likes old school tactical RPGs and is not too put-off by the dated graphics.

Open-world fighting, sneaking and shooting - I haven't had this fun or been so immersed in a game in a long time. What's fun though is that the enemy captains (and warchiefs) are randomized, each with its own weaknesses strenghts so every battle against them will be a bit different each time. Adapting is a must through the whole game, but once you've adapted enough through upgrades and getting better runes you'll probably feel like the game has become... easy. You stop caring about your runes and just collect all the collectibles and do all the missions... which don't feel too fun after a couple of those. But achievements, right?

Upon intensive testing after the recent patch, somehow things improvise drastically (Also after reinstalling the game via a steam restore operation due to a need of reformatting, which yielded a reset system settings file for GGXRD). Also tested on another computer with an Asus R7 250X 1GB which performs exactly like the HD 7770 recommended at the store page & it does run like butter on it. Also seems to perform fine on a HD 6850, but there appears to be problems still with some systems, especially laptops for some reason.
To continue, I now get a smooth 60fps across all circumstances in an extended hours of play & the fight pacing is so fast it's like a different game at all. But of course, that's the GG we all knew & love. Thank you Arksys. With this, I wholeheartedly turn the direction of my thumb for this game.
Where to start, okay. Graphics. I'm never for one to care much about it but this game is glorious. 3D which are made to imitate handdrawn drawings can usually still appear 3D, but this game is a game changer in that field. For most of the time you'll be playing this, I bet your♥♥♥♥♥your mind would think you're playing a 2D fighting game though that's not the case. It doesn't only look like one, but is animated like one too! The devs sure knows how 2D animation techniques works & implemented it flawlessly with the 3D models (suffice to say, that's a damn hard feat).
Next comes the rule book. Basically, the tutorial. Older GG fans know the stuff, but even then this is the first time that there's an actual tutorial explaining what are stuffs like Roman Cancel, Gattling Combination & Dead Angle, their mechanicsm & how to pull them off & in what situation. There is also a challenge mode which is basically where you learn combos & what probable combo chains you can create with them. This also gives newcomers an opportunity to edge up to veteran GG players quicker.
The fighting in GG is also known to be very fast, as in this one & perhaps the fastest in the genre of fighting games, yet it can also get very technical & requires precise input if you're really thinking of beating people. As hardcore as it is, GG is also surprisingly easy to get into. Any beginner can pick it up & could play it pretty well after sometime. Yet it's of those kind which is hard to master. Real mean gattling combos can get very tricky to pull off but the payoff is tremendous as you could juggle or pin down your opponent given they're clueless on how to get out of your mean pushes, but of course- if your opponent knows what he's doing, he can also save himself in many different way, so no unfair edge there.
Characters are also very diversified in terms of gameplay. Characters range from melee to ranged attackers to other weird shenanigans & none plays the same. The only downside to this however it'd take a really long time if you want to master them all as GG is the kind of game where it pays to main a character of your own choosing & play using him/her almost all the time. So take your pick & train hard. And if you play with too many too much, others will surpass you in any given character.
I'd rant longer. But I need to go to sleep but including this & what everyone's saying, it's a great game, simply put. Some of us are luck to not/no longer face bugs with the game, but hopefully continued support is provided & they can fix the problem.
Recomended.

Nobunaga's Ambition is a light grand strategy game with combat focus that succeeds thanks to it's extremely clever design bypassing many of the genre's flaws. Micro and macro-management are balanced perfectly from the early game to the endgame.
Especially clever is the addition of mass battles, which makes controlling a lot of units and sending them into battle a breeze. A key to victory is to strategically move your battalions across the set paths on the map, catch the enemy in pincer attacks and attack their flanks. This leads to you commanding several units. As the game progresses there will be huge amounts of troops on the map, which would normally lead to a lot of annoying unit management. Yet, with enough units in one sector of the map, mass battles can be triggered. These put your troops in a Total War-esque real time battlefield, with your units placed in relation to their placement on the map. This not only eliminates the annyoing management of every single unit but also makes the outcame dependant on your battlefield skill, not only the size of your army.
Warfare is clearly the focus of the game, with much of the endgame often comprised of huge battles on several fronts. Thankfully this aspect is more fleshed out in NA than most other grand strategy titles. In this phase you will also delegate all micromanagement of your cities to the AI, whose course of pursued development you can easily adjust.

The game is good at what it does. It's not total war so don't expect epic combat. It's not crusader kings so don't expect game of thrones politics. The game is not even ROTK-style (which is a good thing compared to Koei's recent ROTK titles).
What I like about this game is how it replicates Japan's sengoku era. If you're coming from other grand strategy games, don't think all rules apply. You can't simpy transport all your troops from settlement A to B, that's not it works. You can only get X amount of troops from settlement X, and once the fighting is over, they are to return to their home (original) settlements. That's how it was in Japan. We're not Alexander the Great, where we can simply move all of our troops freely and expect the same soldiers to remain with us for numberous campaigns.
So yeah, I do like the differences in style of gameplay but not everyhing is perfect. The game might feel slow to some, especially if you're a passive player that likes to focus on building up. Most clans won't attack you unless you're right in the middle of the fray (e.g. Mori, Oda, Takeda, etc.)...well, from my experience at least. Once you start or are inviting into coalitions, things definitely pick up. This is the fun part of the game. I also thought creating a custom class and custom officer was managable and fun.
So yeah, it's a bit different but I enjoyed it overall. Not my favorite grand strategy game (even by Koei) but it's good enough for me to give it my approval, and more importantly, my time.

Grand Strategy is one of my favorite genres. And this game has quickly become one of my favorites games in the genre. While this series may be new to western audience, Koei have been making these games for decades, long before Total War or Crusader Kings etc. Thanks to Koei's strange aversion to making money, we have only received 2 games of this series localized for PC in the past 15 years.
Overall, this game, is one of two the most realistic and in-depth "ruler simulators" I have had the pleasure of playing. The other one is Romance of the Three Kingdoms XI from the same series, available in gamersgate. It may lack the court and dynastic politics of Crusader Kings, or the detailed strategic warfare of AGEOD wargames, or the graphical fidelity of Total War, but all gameplay areas combined, it trumps all other games.
Pros -
1. Character focus - Characters are portrayed with great detail, with RPG-like attribute and skills. Most of them are historical characters. Every bit of gameplay revolves around them, from development to diplomacy to warfare. Beautiful hand drawn portraits bring them to life. Large part of the gameplay revolves around making sure you assign the right man for the right job. Much like history, the fate of the realms is based on the abilities of its lords and officers. You can even create your own officers with similar details.
2. Provinces - You can distribute your realm into provinces and let your officers handle things. You can further set guidelines for the provinces, such as military targets, production priorities, assisting and supplying other provinces etc. This is both realistic, and prevents unnecessary micromanagement.
3. Realistic Command and Control - As said before, the game is a proper ruler sim. It does way with most of the "gamey" micromanagement as seen in games like Total War, and is more reliant on broad decisions that a ruler is supposed to make.
4. Multi-layer Development - You develop your realm in multiple layers - castles, their surrounding settlement (villages / districts), the roads connecting them, and strongholds in road junctions. You also set policies for your realm. There are five main resources that you need to manage - gold, manpower, supplies (food+), muskets and horses, that are used in development and warfare.
5. Warfare - Tactical battles are nowhere as "detailed" as Total War. But they are a lot more realistic. It plays out in real-time. Troop numbers are authentic. The army structure is true to feudal warfare, much like Crusader Kings. You also need to consider supply and equipment (though this part is not as detailed as Romance of the Three Kingdoms XI, where you have to consider food, morale and each individual weapon types). The pacing of the battles IMO is perfect for a game like this. The diversity and details of the character system spills into the battles, with your generals having access to multiple passive and active tactical options during battles, leading to very dynamic situations. Best of all though, as with everything else, you can choose to let your officers lead their battles completely instead of micromanaging everything.
6. Councils - The council system adds to the authenticity. Every month you hold a council, and decide on the development of your realm, diplomacy, scouting, exploration etc. At any point you are lost, your officers will suggest actions that you can take. And again, you can be totally hands-off and let your castle lords decide what they want to do.
7. Diplomacy and politics - This part is not as detailed as Crusader Kings, but with so much else to do in the game, I think its detailed enough. You can interact with other factions as well as the Emperor who is still the nominal head of the country. You can have marriage alliances, timed alliances. vassals as well as form coalitions against other overpowered factions. The diplomatic stance (friendly, in awe, wary, hostile etc.) and rating (% number, used for diplomatic actions) are independent of each other, which may lead to funny situations however. You can call for your allies and vassals to aid you in battle with specific objectives.
8. Tenets - Japan during this time was conflicted between the old ways and new. That conflict is represented here as well. All the characters, as well as your realm as whole, can be progressive, conservative or neutral. This effects how well your officers get along with you, as well as the development of your realm.
9. Customizable difficulty and complexity - There is a plethora of difficulty settings at the beginning of the game, such as how aggressive the AI factions are, or how harvests, manpower, troop strength etc. are balanced between you and AI factions. You can learn the game easily, then take on more difficult challenges. The massive degree of possible automation will help you cope with the great amount of things to do in this game.
10. Events / Historicity - Thanks to the game portraying a relatively short time span in history, it can play out in a lot more handcrafted way compared to the generic campaigns of Total War or Crusader Kings. There are many historical events, accompanied by text + image based cut scenes. You are even given a bunch of progressive historical objectives for your ruler to re-trace his/her historical path.
11. Graphics - This is a tricky one. The 3d graphics is old fashioned, like something out of 2005-06, but fully functional. The 2d artwork however, is exquisite.
12. Music - Last but not the least, is the epic soundtrack. Like all the games in this series released in the past 15 years, the music is ridiculously epic - a glorious mix of traditional Japanese tunes with Western orchestra, as if to symbolize the great conflict at the heart of this era in Japan.
Cons -
1. UI and intuitiveness - The UI somehow gets lost in translations. You may need to spend some time going through manuals and in-game help screens to understand all of it, because the UI can often be unintuitive and esoteric. The game is not meant for the simple-minded: P
2. Politics (especially internal) - Faction politics can be a bit random, with diplomatic rating and stance contradicting. Also lacks complex diplomatic deals as seen in many grand strategy games. Internal politics are completely lacking, except managing the loyalty of your officers.
3. Family / Dynasty - Family and dynasty are barebones. Characters can be "kin" and thus more loyal. You can also marry talented officers into your family to achieve that effect. But that is all there is. No treacherous vassals plot against you, no ambitious cousins or brothers to usurp your rule, unless through pre-defined historical events. Characters can give birth and adopt, but you do not have much say in their bringing up, as most of them are pre-defined characters of the era.
4. Logistics - I prefer the logistical depth of ROTK XI, where you have to manufacture and transport individual equipment types and then equip your soldiers with them. Here it’s much more "streamlined" for better or worse (worse in my case).
5. Tactics - I sometimes missed the tactical control I had over units in ROTK XI, or even in Total War. But as said above, I do however still believe the available pacing and depth of the battles is more suitable for this type of game, which allows you to focus on being a ruler instead.
6. Duels and Debates - In ROTKXI, your characters can engage in duels or debates to settle various issues. This is missing in Nobunaga's Ambition.
Well, this is already long enough. I will end it here. I may revise this later, to make it shorter and add in any other pros and cons I may have missed this time. Overall, if you are a fan of grand strategy and prefer your historical games to be high on history and realism, or have an interest in the Sengoku era, you owe it yourself to give this a shot.

For those of you that never got to try and enjoy Gainax's flagship series, Princess Maker, here you are!
Rather than playing as the father of the princess and raising her, you play as the princess yourself, attempting to survive childhood after your mother's death to be coronated the queen a few years later.  Conspirators, betrayers, and other nobles with agenda will be after you every step of the way and your decisions on what classes to take and choices made in dialogue have a chance to affect everything.  Don't let the simple nature of this game distract you from how deep and well-thought out this game really is.  If I had one complaint on this title, it would be the music.  Hearing an American theme-song to something titled 'Long Live the Queen' is a bit disconcerting...especially to someone from England...you know...somewhere with a queen....
There are no foxes, but its still a great game. Very dynamic and a ton of replayability.

State of Decay. Zombie survival. Main game, no DLC.
Awesome game with good story line but short, it was meant for the player to fully explore the region given to prolong the time spent on this game.
Missions are at first quite varied until it becomes a pattern after few hours, you will/not help some survivors, will/not help the neighbours around you, you get to train your neighbours for upcoming zombie attacks and a few more.
Storyline wise, it has that moment where you will feel rushed because of the situation you're in and push you through some of the toughest if not longest fight mission. Each character, especially the ones with you early on has some sort of agenda of their own and some are tightly knit together with the main story, as it will affect their growth as a character, but nothing to the point of being "Hardened" state.
But it is short as at, this time of writing, currently on 9.9 hours of gameplay give or take a few hours of being AFK, the main story quest isn't that much at all and can be blaze through with as few people and resources to get by. Most of the hours I spent through in this game are just resources management to have a stable outpost and to see what else the game has to offer.
Combat mechanics though are awesome and feel responsive to fight with the zombies but it has that quirkiness where sometimes you do get stuck. From melee to ranged weapons both are awesome but not sure if it has quite the selection to choose from but probably the standard for range it has; 9mm, shotgun shells, 5.56, and some revolver ammunitions as well.
Resource management are limited to the outpost you currently have and some limited modification you can put into it to further strengthen your companions and the outpost itself. From oil, ammos, building materials and food, you can scavange most of this either by yourself or call for someone to carry it over.
Reminder that this is just a review for the main game only and I haven't tested out the DLC which could provide even more gameplay, mechanics, characters' agenda and so on and so forth.
7/10 and Yes I recommend this game to those who like exploration/resource management to survive the infestation and also to those who like combat, could've give 8 or 9 if the story quest is a bit longer and more varied.

Starbound is one of the greatest indie games. Playing it for almost 120 hours in the time I made my review on it. I guess I was late to the party when the game's beta was released in 2013. But holy crap, I wish I knew the existence of such a game at that time. So let's start on what Chucklefish did good and "bad". Quotation marks matters.
Positive
- The story is a straight-forward one but not too undermining in most times and leads the expectations at the last stages of the game.
- The game is not making you focus on the story. You can basically do ANYTHING you want. Create a Death Star, a museum, a colony, terraform a world, it's all there.
- Monsters and the bosses' AI are snappy and don't derp that much in combat.
- Side scrolling combat done right.
- A lot of items and different types of collections for you to finish.
- Number of races that have different religion, beliefs, architectures and etc.
- Side characters like Nuru or Esther is written well and can be funny at times.
- ( Space is cool )
- Travelling in space is exciting and leads to more adventure in the long run.
- A great community with a reddit post that actually is active.
- Chucklefish communicates with the community in Starbound and applying some of their ideas.
- Legendary weapons are fun to use and can be used in any situations that you are currently in.
- Amazing soundtrack and worth the money to buy the OST.
- Mod creators have more freedom to create wonderful things.
and many more.
Negative
- Side quests are horrible and a lot of back tracking.
- Specific races are very hard to find and doesn't appear often in some of the planets that you would rather think that they will spawn there. FLORANS IN A TUNDRA BIOME.
- Sometimes Chucklefish diminishes expectations of most of the community.
- A painful death system, dying results in losing all craftable items, hence dropping them on the floor, and losing some credits.
- Some of the weapons are bland like straight rip off from Borderlands 2 Common Drops.
- Combat is a pain since the min zoom level is 2x and won't notify enemies that are farther if you just hold CTRL and move your mouse a bit. Nope.
- The Infamous Unskippable Esther Cutscene
MY THOUGHTS
Starbound is an 8 to a late 9. It's almost a 9 if it weren't for me using mods that make my personal negatives nothing. Overall, I would recommend for the sake of having it in your Steam library since it will definitely grow on you. But since some of the negatives have a great impact, including the side quests, in the vanilla game, hopefully Chucklefish will tweak it to be fun but also to be immersive.

You can expect every single enemy to run up your bum, without fail.
However, this game beats Terraria with its own forte; exploration. When you first start up the game, your given a flashlight, a broken sword, and a whole damn planet. I decided to explore the content of my new world ( which I branded as Tobias). I found villages, mysterious mushroom people, and a lot of birds. I made a house. I made a farm. A built a shrine for the gods of Tobias. Then, I found out that this is just one of millions of planets and experiences I could have with them. That is where that game shines.
If you're looking for a new exploration game to try, definitely pick up Starbound

If you liked Life is Strange then you'll probably enjoy this game. It's got nice art and a premise I really like but overall I think it fails to accomplish what it's trying to do. It's a shame because there's a lot of potential and it seemed liked they were going in the right direction for the first half of the game but then it falls apart. Since there's almost no gameplay, the story really needed to be stronger. I'm a big fan of these types of games but I think the style is going through growing pains and there hasn't been a game that's completely nailed it yet.
One glaring issue with these games in general is the developers seemingly can't help themselves inserting their political ideaology all over the place. There's nothing wrong with political themes and questions being asked in games but you have to do it very carefully for it not to be jarring. For instance, near the end of this game, there's a scene that's supposed to be intense/scary/shocking but suddenly there's this weird political monolouging that completely removes you from the game. You wonder why these characters are arguing this when they're facing mortal danger and possibly a Lovecraftian death god in the bottom of an abandoned mine.
Then we have the characters, who all seem to be backloaded with a lot of TragicPast TM. It's fine to do this with some of your characters sometimes, but not all of your characters, all the time. Characters can be informed by things that happened in their backstories but they shouldn't be a list of them. Good writing is developing a character by showing them doing something to inform the audience about who that character is. You can't just write a list of things that happened to a character and have them read it off to the audience and then expect empathy. There's way too much telling in this game and not enough showing.
Meh, there's a ton of things I could say more about this game but I guess overall I'd recommend simply because I think the more of these types of games get made, the better they'll get. I see huge potential in this genre and clearly so do many others. For these games to reach their full potential the writers need to stop getting so bogged down initial premise and focus on narrative.
Such a good game, it may not be perfect, but it has charm.

Over 9000 Zombies! is a stupid name for this game, however it's just a name and the gameplay here is very enjoyable.  This game is a great little hybrid of a twin stick shooter and tower/hoard defense. I was definitely mildly surprised at how much fun I actually had with this poorly named game.
In every aspect 9K Zombies is a simple game. The top down perspective allows for basic graphics, though things are easy enough to identify.  Objective wise things are also elementary; successive hordes of zombies spawn ever day/night cycle and it's up to you to blast them away using weapons that unlock as you progress as well as turrets/defenses you can build. Zombies drop grenades, health, and most importantly: scrap. The scrap is used to build turrets to help keep the Zs at bey. There are quite a few different ones to build and they have unique effects (Grenade Launcher, Flamethrower, Laser, Lightning, etc.).
All in all this game is quite fun, especially for being a simple game in 3 played out genres (zombies, twin stick, hoard/tower defense). My one main complaint is that the top down perspective + the crude graphics make telling the difference between a wall and the ground difficult in a few places.  This doesn't happen all the time so it doesn't impact the enjoyment for me. I've really been enjoying playing this game. For the normal $9.99 price definitely pass, it’s WAY too much money. Stick it on your wishlist and when it's on sale for $0.99 then absolutely grab it. While this game is good, and I enjoyed it, it’s not worth anything more that $1.99 imo.

Before reading: I bought this for £32 while on sale.
Short write-up: This games sits between Civ and Total War. It's an odd spot to inhabit, but also a fairly unique one too. The kingdom management/overworld aspect has similarities to Civilisation, however dig a little deeper and the officer management and diplomacy options add a huge amount to differentiate this title from 2K's flagship.
Officers can oversee development of your settlements, (an essential task that can become a little tedious as your clan grows - but thankfully can be given to one of your trusted retainers to develop automatically.) they also lead units into battle, conduct diplomatic missions, sow disharmony in the hearts of that one enemy officer who isn't too keen on his current lord and much more.
Battle comes in two flavours: the first is very Civ-esque and happens on the overworld, but without the turn-based element (little detail that I liked: if you march near other territories, armies will form and watch you from the borders until you're safely out range then they'll go home). This approach works fine if you have a clear numbers advantage. However, if the number of soldiers and officers is a little close then you'll want to take direct control. If you choose to do this then you are presented with a map based on the current location on the overworld and your units will respond to your commands directly. You'll have to tentatively scout for your enemy and then do your best to flank them.
Each officer has a skill that can be triggered in battle to either buff their unit/allies or debuff or harm enemy units. Most units can also opt to charge - a tactic that leaves the target unit in a state of confusion, which in this battle system is a very, very bad state to be in. As the game progresses and muskets are introduced, charging becomes riskier for the attacker as any units armed with firearms can 'release', which effectively counters the charge. TL:DR - Battles are pretty fun when you take control.
The sheer number of characters is mind blowing - each with stats and skills that can be improved and added to the more you use them. Keeping your chaps and chapette's happy is pretty important - this can be done with gifts (Feudal Japan as it turns out, was apparently full of very shallow people) or by offering your disgruntled officer one of your offspring to marry. You can recruit in one of three ways - find a ronin and pay him a small stipend to join (then immediately shower them with gifts/women so they don't sod off straight away), by convincing another lord's officer that you are in fact better than he is - making the officer jump ship, and finally: employing officers you defeated in battle. This doesn't always work and even when it does, the officers you gain are often not your biggest fan. If that particular method seems like too much hassle you can just execute them all. Or not. Your call.

I would not call "Night in the Woods" a video game. I would not call it an experience, either, though that isn't far off. I'd call it an interactive novel. No, not a visual novel like the PC-98 ones. A moving picture told like a storybook, which is illustrated into 60FPS fluid animation (the style adds to the novel feel, and I really really love it too), and through the perspective of a college dropout. Note: this game is barely related to "Life is Strange" even after all that. Calling it a video game would mean it designed for your fun only, which it is more than. Calling it an experience means it was designed for a spectacular feel, a 'lil too high for a fun young adult's life sim.
Before I get in-depth into the review, I'm gonna abuse the fact that you can get 2 free prequel games on the Night in the Woods official website for you to find out how this game would be to yourself, so that I'll be giving all *my* thoughts on the game and kinda alienating the reader. My thoughts only, sorry.
Oh, also, I have not played since March, and as of writing this review, the Weird Autumn update is all the rage. I also only played once, but I have been informed about how choices you make will determine your ending and people you meet, as well as side paths doing similar. (If you're detracted, I guess I'll say something which is a plus for a few people: I went into this game with less outside knowledge than most. I found out through a small community hyping the hell over this. If you need to know how oblivious I was, it took until a week before I actually bought this for me to find out this was a video game via GIFs. I thought it was a webcomic...)
So, if I call it a story, does it live up to their level of world-building? If I was to compare the atmosphere... it would be up there with Harry Potter's level of getting you into the thick. I even sometimes acted like a normal pedestrian: I saw a lot of the LPers in this game's hayday always use the running motion, but I would often walk in the town's streets, especially near Mae's mom. I feel like this was also a game where I would avoid triggering a small but slightly bad event like disturbing flying birds. I played the Longest Night prequel in a single sitting, and that was a 6 hour sitting that took up an entire day in-between school and sleeping for the next day's energy. Night in the Woods tells it's story very well: the entire thing's memorable, and makes it very relatable with many small, but well-known-to-many conventions, warm friends, warm interactions, etc.Those warm friends...
The main characters? A lot of people give crap to all but one of them, often Bea being crowned as the supreme friendsman, but all of them are great, lovable, adding to immersion and story, and oh my GOSH, do they compliment eachother damn well. The fact that they're all going to move sometime soon was the best excuse ever to make you do some crazy things that you wouldn't normally do just lounging around because it soon will be the end of the world(?). The locations all click, even if you aren't able to relate to it's basis, because of more characters conveying the mood by the state they have been stuck in because of the fall and their old-timey approach. I could go much further on with the smaller moments, i.e. choice choosing and some side areas you have to go to which are not related to the Possum Springs hub... but I will leave that to you. Oh also more side characters exist like Germ and that Q girl I forgot about and they're just as great infactGerm'sbestcharacterinNITW.
So, uh, gameplay. It's a game. Not a book. It isn't a giant cutscene that you press a few Dpad buttons to reach one and the other either. Okay, it kind of is. But it has enough gameplay to still leave it on a game. Most of it is a revolving cycle (until the last 2 hours of the game, really), which kind of makes sense: Wake up, talk to parents, go out and hop around Possum Springs, activities with friends, end your hyjinx, and go to bed. Repeat. There is no difficulty to it. Character movement is pretty nice, too: not notable, and a little unrealistic, but versatile enough for what the game throws at you. But, there isn't supposed to be difficulty to any of it. Not all games require a dying feature. The story makes up for it as-is.  And it's fun and relaxing! However, this would be repetitive. Thus minigames to the rescue!
They can be as lowly as... eating donuts and pushing some if you want Angus to eat anything, while you get important story exposition, and then you have the Harfest play which is secretly a choose-your-own-adventure and 4 da funzies, and stealing stuff from a Hot Topic ripoff by making sure you move while an icon is friendly... and I avoided the crowning jewel of them all, the band minigames! They're just Guitar Hero, come on. That doesn't mean they're fun; there's several fun ripoffs, after all. I am bad at all rhythm games. I also played this with a XBOX 360 joypad, meaning I had a diamond shape to deal with, and also not pressing another button accidentally while I reach for X and Y going from A to B fast. It was tough. And seeing the keyboard use 1234, that... that sounds way better.
Actually, from the looks of some other things they want you to do, this game really wants you to play with a keyboard rather than a controller. It requires some twitch motions and instantaneous response that a keyboard provides far better than a controller. All the power to them, really, if so, because I really, REALLY love when any developer abuses a keyboard to make a single set motion speed and twitch motions feel reasonable and actually make control superior to a controller. So... do that. Use a keyboard, and throw out your advanced silly joypad
So, it's good. There's one, major, glaring flaw to all of it, though (aside from it requiring a pretty beefy combo of technology to run, not counting the PS4 version, which it runs decently without said beefy power; shame I had a disconnect between my top and bottom halves of my display, though!): It isn't all that replayable. It's great while you have it, but if you played it with both routes, then yeah, you won't be able to play it in succession and still have some fun. The fun comes in the story, and the gameplay at the very core is just a giant point-A-to-point-B sidequest with some minigames thrown in. It's a good chunk of the reason why I've left it at 9 hours played (one playthrough) while I take the old gaming approach of playing a good game you bought over and over until you get a new one, often making me clock 38 hours and counting of a game like Jet Set Radio or 45+ to Cave Story: not even counting how I replay so many! By the time you've read such a long time of a great story but nothing else, you'll get a glad feeling for now know the whole story... but you wouldn't be able to read the story again as if it was fresh without waiting for a bit, something a game of moderate length and variability would be able to do easily and a story of any length not. Yes, the fact that it burns into your brain is the worst part about it. Certainly great while it lasts, though. Give it half a year and then you can play it again and have all the fun again.
So, final verdict? Get it as soon as you wish; if I was to compare it's effect, it would be very close to indie greats like La-Mulana, Cave Story, some of the better Sonic fangames/Mania, and probably have an effect, though not quite as big, still very noticable on a game, as Ico and Journey did on how story is handled (and the story being in your mind, too!). But, if you can help it, $20 is a *little* expensive for a game of this caliber. I would probably say when it gets to be sold for $15 is fine. In the grand scheme, though, a real story is a bigger slog, often of equalling length, and more expensive, so that, but it's being sold as a game, man. Don't let it detract from it's legendary friends + mood!!! tho.

Just like the route taken by many other franchises in the past decade, Ace Combat Assault Horizon is, sadly, what happens when a Publisher/Developer decides to rise the finger towards their loyal fanbase, and tries their hardest to appeal to a different, more modern mainstream crowd.
In the end and as a consequence, not only failing hard to get a piece of that pie, but losing the respect and support of those who were with them right from the beginning.
On the brightest side of things, there are twenty five different airplanes, three helicopters, and two bombers to chose from, each intricately modeled and textured, complete with beautiful, detailed cockpit views.
While the graphics menus are an absolute joke (more on that later), I haven't ran into any problems what so ever, everything works as it should, the framerate is stable, the controls are responsive and there are no visible glitches or problematic bugs typical of bad ports...
In an effort to not only simplify the game but make it more "edgy n'cool", the developers introduced a new mechanic  that goes by the name of Dog Fighting Mode (DFM for short), a mode that gets you close to the action, glues you to your enemy and takes literally up to about 90% of the control off of your hands, just so you may shoot him down with your suddenly increased aimbot like super accuracy.
As a result, DFM is nothing but an on-rails, scripted, nauseating (boy, that zoom in/out camera/field of view) joke that takes you on a quest you cannot possibly fail; It requires absolutely no skill whatsoever, providing no fun a result.

Such ain't "optional" either, since certain enemies can ONLY be taken down using said mode, and others can also glue themselves to you, forcing such mode on yourself.
...as if that wasn't bad enough, certain enemies will take you on a rather long scripted adventure (you'll notice those right away, they're bullet sponges) and can only be disposed of, once their fancy "scripted" event has come to an end.
For the first time ever in the franchise, we're given the opportunity to take control of an Helicopter (in fact, tree of them); This is indeed a breath of fresh air in the game, but unfortunately its implementation leaves a lot to be desired.
To start off, the shaky, in your face, zoomed in Third-Person camera, has got to be one of the worst I've experienced in a game, the levitating brick occupies almost three quarters of the screen and flies all over the place, making its best efforts to obstruct your view all the time;
Thankfully, there is a cockpit view, and even that has the bad habit of shaking in an exaggerated manner and zooming in every time you lock your weapons on a target.
...now, as far as Helicopter gameplay goes, it could be described almost as a modern generic Third/First-Person Shooter (only clunkyer) and in the air, which consist off gunning down waves upon waves of ground forces who oppose no threat whatsoever (as in challenge), occasionally dodging a missile or two (it's laughable), and maybe, face off another chopper one on one; Oh, and you cannot crash it.
Nothing too complicated... in fact, if you're expecting anything that requires even the slightest amount of thought, strategy and/or skill, you might want to look somewhere else...
Be aware though!
The game has the bad habit of taking the control off of your hands, constantly zooming into whatever goes boom;
Trying a little bit to hard to make people go nuts over rad explosions, I guess...
New to the series are too the Turret Sections, which consist of nothing but press right click for "awesome".
Unfortunately, there are no unique and/or interesting mechanics to the big guns themselves, they don't overheat nor do they run out of ammo, rate of fire doesn't vary from turret to turret neither does the ammunition they consume...
...and as an effect, these sections come off as simplistic, stale, repetitive, and nothing more.
It could be said they exist for the sole reason of instant gratification, and it wouldn't be too far of the truth, as challenge is kept to a bare minimum and all it resorts to, is: Everything you look at explodes and anything that hadn't exploded yet is inoffensive to your mighty immortality.
Which brings me to...
...the Health Bar of old, which is nowhere to be seen, and there is a reason for such;
Our friends at Namco, decided it'd be a good idea to borrow, amongst other things, one of the worst fads in gaming; The absolute ATROCITY that is regenerative health.
Yes, that's right, Planes/Helicopters fix them selves (you'll notice a red screen displaying Critical, Heavy and Light Damage at times);
But wait, this ain't over yet!
If that wasn't ridiculous enough, our beautiful flying machines now bounce of the ground as if they're made of rubber.
Together with "Invincibility Mode", such can be abused to no end...
...but boy, oh boy, there's more;
Amongst other fads brought to the table, is the poor implementation of either intrusive Quick Time Events (QTEs for short), that serve no purpose other than breaking the flow of the game, or QTEs that don't even have an impact on anything (yes some can be ignored completely)!
Some cutscenes are unskippable (thankfully those are very, very few and far in between), forcing you to "take control" of the camera, as in, moving the main character's head to look around, because apparently someone somewhere thought that'd be fun.
To add insult to the injury, not only is our main villain the typical evil Russian guy (because 'Murica, I guess) he's also called Markov; Doesn't this ring a bell?
Even the name is similar to an evil guy from a certain overly successful, yearly franchise that's been copied to the point of exhaustion for the past decade!
...it might seem like I'm nitpicking by now, but it's blatantly obvious who or what this game has drawn inspiration (or should I say lack thereof) from, there's even a boring, uninspired AC130 mission thrown into the mix, and a long boring one at that (actually, most missions overstay their welcome)! Who finds this fun and why?
While this game is properly optimized from my experience, the Graphic Settings menu is a joke, there are only four available options to "tweak", Antialiasing (can only be turned On or Off), Fullscreen, Vsync and Resolution.
On a side note, while the PC version contains all the DLC included, don't even get me started on how ridiculous and overpriced they were on the console version, which used to charge from $4, up to $6 for individual Painting schemes and Aircraft (Not sure if it still does)!
Boy have standards fallen low, uh?
Ace Combat Assault Horizon is a game that tries to hard to be the next big thing; Not only does it feel desperate, like a little kid yelling and screaming for attention, it also feels like a compilation of everything that is wrong with games, the industry nowadays and the mentality of those who Publish/Develop the games we used to know and love.
Therefore, earning an abysmal rEvo's rating of 2.5/10
I can't remember a single moment where I was enjoying myself; I felt suffocated in the middle of all of its "edgy" in your face exaggeration, mixed with boring, generic simplified gameplay mechanics...
It felt cheap, it felt empty and it felt outdated...
Outdated in the sense that the kind of game Assault Horizon is trying to be, has been copied and beaten to death multiple times in the past decade.
It's just not its unique thing anymore, and as a result you'll find "Assault Horizon's" core, in any other  brown, cinematic (edgy), military (or not), linear, scripted, simplified, over budgeted, mediocre AAA (triple A) game out there...
At the very least, the game's well programmed and functional, doesn't crash nor does it stutter around...
Fun little time waster, for its price i would reccomend, the game is fun if lacking in depth but again for its price whats to be expected.

State of Decay is an excellent zombie survival game. Maybe the one we have waited for.
Its only bad aspects are:
-Not enough missions/diversity in general you have few scenario missions that brings elements to the story (not bad by the way), but the rest are just related to supplies, zombie extermination, deliveries or allies to rescue so around 6 or 7 different  missions. The worst mission is the one for characters who are depressed: you go fight some zombies and after that everything is fine (horrible dialogues !).
-The gameplay is sometimes disturbing like every time you find supplies for your base, you are the only one capable to take them... even if you have other people with you or came with a pick up. Close combat is much more interresting than fire arms due to noise and ammo usage. Or vehicles wich become you primary tool of destruction if you consider the fact that you can horn to call all zombies of a large area or use it as a ram to kill tons of zombies (repairing cars is an option because you find quite a lot of them).
-Some bases are useless, so in general you will move 2 or 3 times and you will finish in the same place (no spoil here ^^).
-Zombies become not very dangerous when you master fights. Bases are not enough attacked and even if you save many people, you will never see more than a small horde attacking your base and involving 4 or 5 characters.
-Some locations could have potential like this army depot you can see near the main city, but you won't have missions inside such buildings. During all the game you will stay on the main map. Some  levels in buildings would have been great.
-Ally management is poor. You have to talk to someone you saved to play him or her and change his loadout and change again to your favourite !
Every character has skills you can upgrade when you play them. This is one of the coolest aspects of the game with combos and bases. The problem is when you ask someone to follow you, you can't ask them to stay somewhere or respect a certain stance (at least stealth is not too bad) and like i said they can't take a simple backpack...
-The end of the game is bad. In fact you've endured tons of fights and at the end... well it sucks.
-DLC are bad.
-The voice of the radio operator...
So to conclude, State of Decay is a nice game. You have to play it with few sessions to spare you boredom.
Be ware to check achievements before playing especially the one when you have to kill one of the infected survivors (to get it back even in a new game is a real pain).
And if you get a discount it's a steal.
