In short: this game isn't any '10-minute time killer' - it creates a sense of dedication in the player to improve. Worth every cent.
In LUFTRAUSERS, skill matters just as much as style. You are rewarded for playing well to the aircraft's strengths with large combos and/or survivability, but the game is not reluctant in the least to punish careless mistakes and exploit the plane's weaknesses from both above and below. The player is given plentiful options to craft their most favorable flight/combat experience, yet they must always be prepared to suffer the cons of their choices; frankly, the balances between Pro and Con in this game are commendable and always clearly stated.
The combat itself starts out quite simple with a few basic enemies to work with that are vulnerable to virtually any style. This acts as a sort of grace period for pilots testing new combinations. However, the game quickly works itself into a pilot's nightmare full of stray bullets, introducing new enemies in both sea and air. This steep difficulty curve, in combination with the mission system and various 'bosses', contributes greatly to the addictiveness of the game. New high scores give you a genuine sense of accomplishment and encourage the pilot to pursue other combinations that may help them reach even higher. All in all, LUFTRAUSERS is one tough survival test that will keep you coming back for more.

LUFTRAUSERS is not like any other flying shooting game - it has a "Roguelike" genre, but it's fun, way more fun than other Roguelike games. The biggest issue of Roguelike game is player often dies randomly with little or none character progression. You keep dying in this game too, but this game is not much repeative than other games. Players can try different kinds of plane builds, every build is combined with 3 parts: Weapon, Body & Engine. Each of them got unique attributes, so try to build your own plane & find set up suits you best can cost you hours.
Also, this game has a progress system that you can unlock different kinds of parts each time you raised to a new level. So it's not boring after died many times, at least an aim is set. The game progress is well balanced so you can get your new gear just before you are a little bit of tired, that makes you spend another 15 minutes to try your shiny new gear.
The last and the most important is LUFTRAUSERS also has awesome gameplay with simulated 2D physics. Each kind of plane has its own physical parameter. You can get these in *.json files under game folder, adjust them as well. Game control only need 5 keys(4 directions + fire) and it works just fine. I was a fan of Koei's Samurai Warriors series as well as Paradox games like Crusader Kings II and Europa Universalis IV, so I thought this looked worth trying out. And, boy was it!
Nobunaga's Ambition is a grand strategy game set in feudal Japan's "warring states" period where Japan is divided into myriad little states ruled by various clans. In the game you choose one of the clans, and are responsible for internal development (building up your agriculture, building new city improvements, passing new government policies and so forth), diplomacy (building up strategic relationships with your neighbors, trying to schmooze up the Emperor, etc) and of course, leading your troops on a conquering spree across the Japanese plains, trying to unify the wartorn land. You can play as one of the more famous clans like the Oda or Takeda and have an easier time of things or you can try your hand at a tiny, one-province clan like the Shiba.
I would best describe Nobunaga's Ambition as a cross between Crusader Kings, a Total War game, and a JRPG. It has the conquest and dynasty building aspects of Crusader Kings and the real-time management of massive battles seen in a total war game. But unique to this game are cutscenes and quests, with the occassional melodrama worhy of a JRPG. These are great, and what really sets the game apart. I think Paradox would do well to have these little story moments in their games. And if you are a fan of Samurai Warriors, it is also awesome to see some familliar faces.
Overall, I highly, highly recommend the game. It is a bit expensive at the time of this writing, but I believe it is worth every cent. You will get hundreds of hours of enjoyment and an infinitely replayable game.
What else to say, 30 years later and still fun, this is just awesome :)

I did this review after conquering Japan with Oda Clan in 1566 AD. In brief, this is an officer-centric war simulator. You head a clan of your choice and try to unite Japan as what Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Ieyashu Tokugawa would have done in the historical events. I have played Romance of Three Kingdom IV on PS and I can also say this game has alot of the game concepts similar to ROTK IV with updated graphics, more content and set in the Sengoku period. If you have played th Koei's ROTK series, this game should be a familiar face and a must buy. Comparing to modern good 4X or historical sim, this game lacks some of the info-rich interface features (mouse-over info, proper summary tabs), in-depth battles and complex diplomancy. The good news is that the sum of all parts is robust enough to provide a satisfying game-play without bogging down with too much info or excessive manual control. Here are some of the pros and cons.
+Pros+
-Fantasic artwork of the officers, staring hours into the screen is less tedious when you have your leaders and officers looking hansome and inspiring. Officer-centric approach make the game more human and helps in the immersion.
-Story Cut scenes are beautifully drawn and historical events presented in an appealing fashion
-Simple interface - easy to intepret once you overcome the learning curve which is not very steep.
-Simple but robust battle and diplomancy mechanics, dont be fooled by its simplicity.
-Provide a fair deal of automation and delegation of mundane tasks especially during med-end game if so the player choose to. (formation of province and auto-council)
-There are unlockables to lengthen the game-replayablilty, new scenarios, movie and officers.
- Create custom officers.
-Cons-
-Lack of in-game info like those in modern 4x games.
-Simple interface.
-Generic voice-over for officers, too few variations.
-English translation errors but it is better than no translation at all.
My recommendation:
One of the strengths of this game is the immersion into Japanese History during the Sengoku Period. Some of the officers and clans have rich back-stories which helps in making the game more fun and interesting. I suggest reading up on history to enhance your gaming experience. For a quick summary of the events during the Sengoku period, you can search "Extra History" on YouTube, you can wiki more after that. These guys on Youtube made an interesting 5-part series to aid you in understanding the back story, you would look at some of the officers in a different way after that. (like Akechi Mitsuhide)

i tried to keep this free of any specific spoilers, but my general thoughts and issues with it touch on how the story evolves so this review is more appropriate if youve played the game, or at least if you dont mind having a broad idea of the narrative
-------------------------------
unfortunately this is just another story thats 3/4 of a fantastic narrative featuring well written flawed characters, subtle portrayals of various themes, and an original use of the medium.. followed by 1/4 of a narrative with sloppy pacing, heavy-handed statements, an absurd direction, and most of all just a forced explanation that doesnt deal with what the story was saying in the first place.
why on earth would you focus a game on interactions between characters highlighting their own personal conflicts if you arent going to have them grow? especially with such a dramatic and interesting presentation regarding the main characters experiences - its insulting to any invested reader to place an arbitrary ending point based on a half-@ssed up-for-interpretation b plot rather than addressing the core and heart of the story.
yes 3/4 of this game is really REALLY good. but its strengths just prove that the writers/developers could have done better. yes, for 3/4 of the story you get to know some great "human" characters with their own problems and conflicts. But the rest of the game never tells you why you got to know them, why you should care, how this story impacted them. You leave with the same struggling cast of anthromorphic small town guitar hero rejects that you start with.
stories can end without closure, without a clear-cut resolution wrapped neatly with a bow on top. just ask Tim O'Brien. or David Fincher, if movies are more your cup of tea. but the reason why these stories work is because the emphasized themes and characters develop into something that pays off. even in mysteries without answers, thrillers without closure, war stories without endings - these stories move forward because of their characters, their themes, the world that exists within them. the conclusion should bring that somewhere - show what has changed from where it began. the exact details are somewhat vague, but however you interpreted them, this point still stands: this story spends a great deal of time introducing us to characters' inner demons, and personal problems, only to end by having its characters fight an external demon and solve a relatively impersonal problem. that is its finish line. artificial. and of course the implications are seemingly ignored, almost to a degree that feels like a plot hole. even the essentially LITERAL event of someone confronting their demons is interrupted by plot convinience and never fully approached head-on. i guess there are enough stories out there of abrasive people becoming more sensitive, of childish people maturing a little, of people who need help seeking it. i guess you dont need that. im sure some people dont change. but this story seriously made me think Mae and co. could do better. for as much time as Night in the Woods spends showing you its rather static characters in their rather static world, its a shame that it doesnt do more for them.
this game wears a lot of different hats, jumping from a character-oriented comedy drama, to an immersive visual masterpiece of a gaming experience, to a slice-of-life mystery narrative, to a few fun in-universe minigame concepts. for awhile, these ideas all feel well-executed, and thats because individually they are. but the thread that ties all of these things together is the central story featuring themes like small town culture, late-teens friendship, socioeconomic injustice, mental health, and existentialism/religion. and while yes these themes are good, and the storytelling involving them is good, in the end the actual plot never affects anything. theres so little in-universe development, the entire substance of it relies on just revealing things to the reader. it feels like a coming-of-age story that never hits the coming-of-age. the consequences of things are ignored, both in terms of how characters might change and how the story's world may be impacted. without any in-universe action, the entire thing just feels like an appeal from the creators directly to the player, from the writers directly to the readers.
everything this game says could have been said without without artsy dream sequences, without a a retro game-within-a-game, without an elaborate mystery narrative.. the ending is so hamfisted its point could be made without a story at all. a good book isnt filled with every cool idea the author has, its filled with ideas that function together and lead to something. omit needless words. yes, there's a lot of cool things at play here - and there are a lot of things about this game that can be enjoyed. but what do they do for it? how does this game function as a whole? why throw so many themes and concepts at the reader if your story and characters arent going to work through any of it??? perhaps the game itself explains this best:
i suppose if Night in the Woods really just wanted to portray this sense of meaninglessness without a fight, then it achieved what it set out to do. but there was a lot more potential in its characters, its world, its themes, and its medium. nihlism gives you a freedom to decide where your story is going, not an excuse to remain where you are. lastly, while depression is a very real problem/feeling, and a very powerful emotion and outlook, it is not a model for how to structure a story. at least, not a successful one. it is inherently unfulfilling. stories can end on a good note, on a bad note, on a mix of the two, and often that mix differs from reader to reader. but Night in the Woods doesnt end on much of anything, and it feels like the creators were focused on fitting in so many ideas that as a whole it is incomplete.

As the trend of seeing how far the concept of portals can be pushed conutines to live on, I sometimes question weather there is space for innovation in this now somewhat tired sub-genre. But Thinking with Time Machine, a recently released mod of Portal 2, proves that all you have to do is sprinkle a little pinch of time travel love to warrant another 1-2 hours of fresh, if somewhat short lived, portaling action.
Assuming you're already familar with the portal series, where test subject Chell faces a number of puzzles constantly supplied by the passive-aggessive GlaDOS, the game takes place after the events of Portal 2, where Chell is supposedly now free from the AI's torment; only to encounter even more of the aperture science facility, and in a confusing chain of events find herself trying to save the very being that wanted to trap her in a hell of never ending testing. The dicrection in which TWTM takes it's plot is very interesting, and presents a compelling theory about the aftermarth of Protal 2, dispite the player's somewhat limited exposure to it. The ending provides food for though about Chell's fate and how it is forever tied to aperture and GLaDOS. However, the plot is not the main focus of the mod, so player may give or take about the depth in which they immerse themsleves in this theory.
That would be the new time traveling mechanic introduced right from the start of the game, which challenges the player to think not only in portals, but also in time; sort of. It's more useful to refer to it as a hologram recording of you in the past; you start the time device, exicute the desired actions, and store for later use. It feels like a lonely version of the Portal 2 co-op mode, which is not to say it's inferior. It's a very elegent system, being simple to use and provides a new layer of consideration and forward planning to puzzle solving; although it does take away a sence of momentum a little compared to Valve's games. It also feels like most of it's potential is yet to be revealed, as the puzzles, in my opinion, don't quite get hard eoungh before the end of the game is met. I would think it'll be cool if this could be integrated into the commuity maps, just to see the public domain come up with it's own ideas.
As you may guessed by now, my biggest problem with TWTM is its length, as with the original Portal. I was surprized to have the game abruptly end before I just started to get into the flow of things. But on the other hand, this is a free addon in the end, so I'm honestly not entirely sure that comment is valid. I guess it depends on what you expect from mods.
In conclusion, I highly recommend you pick this gem up. It has the same pedigree as Valve's classics, and adds it's own spin on the concept. If you happen to have Portal 2 on you, get off this review and head over to store right now, because it's certainly wouth it.

Every once in a while you come across a game that transcends gauging its worth based on style or substance, and is instead just pure, visceral joy to play. Luftrausers joins that small party of games that is just so incredibly fun to simply experience that most traditional negatives it might have really do become inconsequential. I can’t really say anything that a thousand reviews before me haven’t already as it’s been near impossible to look on a game related site and not see people singing this games praises. But that’s certainly not without reason.
For the sake of argument let’s say this really is the first review you’ve run across (I pity you, go read someone else’s review, seriously :P); what is Luftrausers?
Short Version: A physics driven, bullet-hell, score attack, manic shooter with retro throwbacks but its own style. Go buy it.
Long Version: Luftrausers is an aerial combat shooter performed in the old-school style of arcade classics but with its own spin. That spin is basing its movement around climbing and diving physics, propelling high into the air only to release the throttle and let gravity carry you back down. Repeating the process over and over, enabling you to deftly navigate a maze of bullets being fired from dozens of on screen enemies at a time in a way that’s far more fulfilling than a traditional shmup.
Orient this around an amusing stylized art-style and a score attack set-up. The goal is to live as long as possible and kill as much as you can in the process. To add depth and longevity you unlock new weapons, armor, and engines that can be combined in dozens of different set-ups to change how you move and fight. Each part also has its own set of missions (such as reaching max combo, killing a certain type of enemy, or a certain number, etc.) that you complete to unlock further parts. Toying around with these various combinations adds some serious depth to an otherwise simple process, and injects a good deal of life into the already highly entertaining physics/gameplay.
Does it have some negatives? Nothing major that should detract from the experience for most people. For the sake of fairness I’ll pick apart two things that come to mind, but they really are minor when compared to the games overall quality. First the game could have benefited from a story mode. While clearly not necessary the style and humor the game does have on hand was a very solid framework for launching some kooky little tale off of. In the end the game still has a lot of life to it but a story mode would have extended that even further. The second and a REALLY small tick is that some of the missions to unlock new parts are infuriatingly luck based. Like killing a submarine at max combo when in all the thousands of enemies I’ve killed I’ve seen exactly seven submarines making a few missions like this frustrating. But both complaints are virtual non-factors in the face of just how good everything else is, but perhaps worth mentioning just to give you the full scoop.
In short Luftrausers is pretty much the perfect score attack game, and if you like the genre you definitely need it in your library as soon as you can pick it up.

Once I found it, this game became my go-to for the turn-based strategy genre. I have always loved this era/setting, but I can't just play Samurai Warriors forever. This game does a lot of things right: blending turn-based strategy with real-time combat, including diplomacy elements in a military conquest game, and allowing for a great deal of development of your land holdings. Not to mention that the game is very friendly to new or casual players, as you can choose to have the game AI make many of the decisions for you, and even have it 'demo play' for you to see how the game is played!
But lets get into the finer details. I'll start with the turn-based + real-time blending element. Each turn starts with a 'council' phase, where you make all your development and diplomatic decisions. During the council phase, time is paused. You then progress to the 'war' phase, where the real-time element begins, and you can move your units to attack your foes and claim new territory. You can still pause during this phase, and do some military-based diplomatic interactions as well. I love this approach, because it allows you to have more control over each and every battle rather than just taking turns hitting your foe and rolling a die. It doesn't end there, however, as this game takes things one step further and allows you to actually go to the field of these battles if you like, and directly maneuver your units and decide when to activate their skills! This means that you can often win battles where the leaders of your units are not as strong as your foes, or if your army is not as large. In the end, strategy prevails over luck.
Another aspect of the game that is done well is the diplomatic interactions. Each clan will have a different perpsective on you, depending on your size and distance relative to them, as well as being somewhat influenced by historical factors (or, at least, KOEI's depiction of the history of this era). Some allies may be harder to gain than others, but with the right amount of work you can turn any foe into a friend and do a great deal of manipulating the various factions in the game to act in your favor. You can even take this one step further, and form a 'Coalition' of forces to fight a larger foe, allowing you to direct your allies' attacks and time your moves so that no foe can stand before you for long.
Lastly, but certainly not least importantly, there is a deep system of development of your territory. You can improve the system of roads in your territory to speed your army along, build small forts to defend key chokepoints, or even build new settlements to artificially increase your own holdings. You also can develop both the 'city' and the 'castle' of each territory you control, and this is where the system truly shines. It is more than just building one of this and one of that, as each plot of land you build in a city can be upgraded along several different paths to provide different benefits. Not only that, but some of these upgrades will interact with other plots of land and improve their efficiency, so it is not just WHAT you build but also WHERE you build it! The castles have a similar variety of upgrades, each with their own effect, though they do not 'interact' with each other like the city upgrades do. This means that you can take several different approaches with each settlement, whether you desire them to each serve a separate purpose, or even if you want to change their purpose as the game progresses!
Overall this game is really very entertaining. There are a number of different historical scenarios already in the game, and the DLC scenarios can add to the fun as well. The one downside to this game is that it does stick pretty closely to KOEI's version of this era, so there's rarely a standard game where Nobunaga doesn't rise to power. Though I suppose the game is named after him. However, if you do happen to (somehow) tire of rising to power as any of the various factions across the various time periods, there is also an 'edit mode' in this game which provides literally unlimited replayability. The main aspect of this that provides replayability is that you can 'shuffle' the starting positions of the clans in the game, completely changing the flow of any era. On top of that, there are many more specific edits you can do to the game to re-balance it any way you like or to simply punish the last foe who bested you.
One other little note to make is that there are also 'quests' in this game, and many of them follow a more historical route. If you want to get to know the characters in the game a little better, or to know some extra bits of information about the events that took place, you can follow these quests to guide you through the game (and to get some achievements as well). Or, you can ignore all of that and follow your own path to victory as you see fit.
If you prefer medieval Europe to medieval Japan, then perhaps this game is not for you. Or, if you are not as famliar with this time period, or you don't enjoy KOEI's version of history, then you may be turned away by this game. But the variety of player-friendly options in the game make it accessible to players of any skill level, and even if you consider yourself a 'pro' at strategy games you can still set the pre-game options to make things much more difficult for you if you so desire. All things said, this game greatly stands out among its peers in the genre, and I'm going to be playing it at least until the next generation of strategy games around, and will continue to come back to it even beyond that time.

For thousands of years game creators have attempted to create strategy games that can replicate the battlefield experience. From pushing Pushing Blocks with Sticks (TM) to computer simulated grand strategy games, none have succeded.

Long Live The Queen is a punishing and addictive visual novel very similar to life simulators like Princess maker and Visual novels, such as DraMatical MurDer. Combining the best elements of both, you effectively play as Elodie, Crown Princess who's beginning tutoring to become Queen of Nova after the death of her mother. The intrigue system and diplomacy elements are heavy in this game, and if you slip up with any choices of lessions, you will die and it is that simple. It often feels like it'd be impossible to accomplish all the skill checks and that's exactly the point- without cheating, it's unavoidable to not fail at something here at least once.
That being said, sometimes failing has rewards. Not only are there achievements brought on by death, but you're actively encouraged to replay- Try your luck and see what you may get by working with Elodie's other stats. Adding the romances in is a nice benefit. Unfortunately, most of them are fairly boring and strictly political, but pursuing any of the female characters such as Briony, Alice or the few interesting male characters like Evrard can provide even more replay value.
Given the nature of this game, if you decide to look for help on any kind of Wiki or Youtube Tutorial, you're going to have a lot less fun with it because part of the challenge is doing it on your own and finding out what works. Reapplying someone else's technique can make it incredibly easy to beat them game, which makes it very short if you decide not to go for every achievement and possibility.
All in all, this game is not for anyone who doesn't like replay and not for anyone who doesn't like making choices and figuring out somewhat cryptic systems to achieve maximum results. If you do like being challenged with intrigue, carefully calculated skills and heavily differentiated play sessions, you will probably love Long Live The Queen.

Exotic trips to Africa for a spot of elephant hunting. Lavish parties were the dress code includes Nazi uniforms. At first glance the life of royalty is an easy one. Having recently played Hanako Games’ Long Live the Queen, I have however acquired some newfound respect for the monarchy. If this title is to be believed wearing a crown on your head is a perilous existence fraught with danger.
Long Live the Queen stars fourteen-year-old Princess Elodie who is set to become the Novan Empire’s queen, in forty weeks time, after the passing of her mother. Players need to ensure that Elodie survives long enough to reach the coronation date, which is easier said than done because EloDIE lives up to her name. With foreign nations threatening war, assassins waiting for the right moment to poison your candy and rival aristocrats plotting to usurp the throne it is safe to say that Elodie’s existence is as fragile as that of an Xbox 360 whose warranty has just expired.
A good chunk of the game revolves around picking Elodie’s weekly curriculum of studies. The classes you choose for her to attend will raise her proficiency in said field, which will determine her success or failure during key story events. If you aspire for Elodie to be a diplomatic ruler you could for example get her to study up on flattery, public speaking and composure. If you are the warlord type who prefers using force you could however get Elodie to learn military strategy, offensive magic and the use of weapons. How quickly Elodie learns a subject is dependent on her mood, which can be tweaked by selecting what she does over a weekend. Playing with her toys for example makes her more cheerful whilst forcing her to visit the castle’s tombs will make her feel afraid.
Gameplay wise Long Live the Queen feels like a visual novel. As the nation’s leader you’ll routinely be asked to make decisions on matters such as the kingdom’s tax rate, foreign affairs and how to punish criminals who are brought to the court’s attention. It’s fun seeing the consequences of your actions, although be wary of what you pick to do as one wrong move can signal a swift game over. Challenging a rude upstart to a duel will end in tears if your sword skill is low for example. Even something as innocent as choosing to attend a friend’s ball can turn sour should bandits ambush your carriage during the commute to the party. See, it’s things like that that discourage me from ever leaving the house.
My rating for Long Live the Queen would be three stars out of five. I had fun playing through the story as it is unlike most games on the market. I would best describe it as a simpler version of the Princess Maker games, which most Western players are unlikely to have sampled given that the franchise has not been released outside of Japan. Speaking of Japan the game’s visuals feel like they are emulating an anime with Elodie sporting bright pink hair and a magical girl outfit that wouldn’t look out of place in Sailor Moon. The artwork on show isn’t spectacular, but it gets the job done and looks more polished than some of the other titles in the Hanako Games library.
Despite enjoying the game I cannot give it a higher score as the story is fairly linear with your choices not having a huge impact on where the narrative goes. The game is also fairly short and can be bested in just under an hour (although you’ll probably need multiple playthroughs to suss out how to avoid dying via a process of trial and error.) Still there is some replay value to be had, as there are multiple endings to unlock along with achievements to earn, which will encourage players to explore all of the game’s content. Not bad for an indie title that costs around eight quid. Given that it’s available to purchase on Steam you might even be able to pick it up for cheaper if you are fortunate enough to catch it during their generous sales.

PROS:
*Good use of physics
*Unique "second character" mechanic
*Feasible achievements
CONS:
*Finicky mouse control
*Unique mechanic underused
*Projectile variety largely meaningless
*Not very "puzzly"
*Some potential slow-down in later levels
GAME LENGTH:
Achievement hunters should expect to be done in around 6 hours.  Those who just want to complete the game should expect to take around 5.
SCORE:
6 out of 10
I didn't expect much from this game, so I was surprised to find myself enjoying it as I played through the first world.  However, somewhere in the middle of the second world, I began to have nearly constant trouble controlling the power and direction of shots, as if the game were fighting me.  This is perhaps related to its mobile origins, but whatever the cause, it quickly spoiled my experience.
Unfortunately, by the end of the second world, I also began to tire of the game because of a lack of variety and puzzles.
There is some effort at adding variety:
(1) Different spark types
These include sparks that explode after three bounces, roll upon contact with a surface, split into two upon contact with a surface, burst into a cross formation after some time, or split into three immediately.  I didn't find that the exploding or rolling sparks were really any more useful than the normal spark, except in those rare instances where they alone could kill the enemies.  The cross spark's burst, being out of the player's control, was too unreliable.  And while the splitting sparks offered a chance to kill more enemies at a time than a single spark, it was not always clear where they would go after the split.  I am not really a fan of Angry Birds, but that game does a much better job of making use of its unique projectiles.
(2) Enemies who move, fly, or teleport
Since the enemies in games like this are really only targets, I don't expect much variety from them.  However, in what I feel to be the absence of meaningful variety in spark types, the lack of variety in this category stands out as well.  Moreover, all of the mobile enemies in this game are capable of moving through or behind walls where sparks cannot reach them.  This means that the player has to wait for them to come back out, which can make some levels tedious.  Perhaps the worst offender is the teleporting enemy, who can reach inaccessible locations
reappear in those same places again and again.  I once saw such an enemy reappear in the same place four times in a row, forcing me to wait.
(3) Obstacles like electricity, portals, spinning blades, and walls that open when a button is pushed
The electricity and blade obstacles destroy your sparks.  For the most part, they are used satisfactorily, though sometimes the delay between the electricity being on and off is too long and the blades are very rare.  The portals only really show up in the last world, so you won't get to deal with them unless you play to the end.  With the exception of maybe two levels, these are used satisfactorily as well.  The buttons, unfortunately, can be very frustrating:  once pressed, they can be pressed again, which turns whatever mechanism they operate back off.  When buttons are put in cup-shaped spaces, this often means that a spark that lands in the cup will hit the button, then bounce back and turn it off.  Managing to hit a button only once (or three times) in these cases always felt like a matter of luck.
(4) A second character who can catch the first character's sparks, then throw them
This was a very good mechanic, but it was under-used.  It should have been a more central mechanic to distinguish this game from others.
To recap, this game features a unique but underused mechanic, an underused or occasionally frustrating set of obstacles, a limited set of enemy types with a frustrating ability to hide, underwhelming projectiles, and few "puzzles" that take advantage of those projectiles' unique traits.
Additionally, the fourth world drastically increases the difficulty.  I aimed to achieve 3 stars on every level (awarded, I think, for completing a level with at least 2 sparks remaining) and had an easy time of it for the first three worlds, but then gave up on doing it on a couple levels in the fourth world due to its difficulty spike.  Some of those levels involved very difficult shots with no room at all for error.  Fortunately, there is no achievement related to getting all 3 stars in the final world, perhaps in recognition of this difficulty.
Speaking of achievements, these are all pretty easy to get.  There is only one that I had to "grind" to receive:  fail 100 times.  Since I was aiming for the 3-star achievements anyway, I knew if I would be unable to complete a level before I officially failed it.  It was much faster to simply refresh the level than to throw my remaining sparks and wait for the failure animation and screen.  This meant that, by the end of the game, I had under 5 of the required 100 failures.  If you are an achievement hunter and you play this game, remember to take the extra time to actually fail.
Finally, in the fourth world, I noticed that the game would occasionally hang as a result of all of the animations, particularly when portals and electricity were abundant.  I easily meet the recommended requirements for this game (as should anyone at this point), so this shouldn't have been a problem.
Overall, I give it a 6/10.

Cartoony artstyle is of course one of its best parts as well as the music (which you'll eventually get to play yourself in a Guitar Hero style mini-game).
There's a lot of surprisingly deep reflections around the life of a college student lucky enough to go out of his hometown vs the friends that had to stay there and work. I won't spoil anything but it gets really weird the more you go through it.
Be aware that the first couple days before Halloween will be boring as you'll basically just wake up, do your things with your friends and go back to sleep. But this is part of what the game is about - an "adult" that sleeps until 4 PM, does nothing the entire day, plays on his PC then goes to bed.
Unfortunately there's only one savestate and if you want to explore everything and unlock all achievements you'll have to play through it at least 2-3 times, which takes some time given there's no easy way to skip events or go faster. Luckily the latest Weird Autumn update brought dramatically decreased load times which was one of the most annoying things of the game until now, so going through multiple times it becomes way easier.
Probably not a masterpiece or as impressive as other indie adventure game, but overall enjoyable in the message it conveys.

I was pretty suprised but also almost scared when ArcSys announced that they would bring an actually current title to PC,  since up until now they just brought somewhat dated titles with ports of varying quality to steam.
Rest assured, ArcSys delviered a kickass port of a kickass game.
With GUILTY GEAR Xrd -SIGN- we have a topnotch Anime-Fighter just dripping with style. The characters and stages just look absolutely stunning and are beatifully designed and go along well with the astounding Butt-Rock soundtrack.
While Blazblue usually goes for a story mode for each character with multiple endings, Xrd features the sort of arcade mode you have come to expect from most fighting games and an actual watch/readable story of approximately 3 hours length.
There also is the so called M.O.M. mode where you have charcater progression with leveling and items and fight enemies with special stat-modifiers that includes items that you can actually use in combats, such as bombs and potions.
The diverse cast consits of seventeen characters that are all unique and play completely different, and thus I never really found yourself longing for more characters as I was already helplessly overwhelmed by the sheer diversety of each character.
As a disgrace to the human race in general and the gaming community in particular, I found solace in the fact that this game features some of the most helpful tutorials I've ever seen.
The game teaches you everything from how to execute special moves to spacing, punishing, wake up pressure, lenghty combos (which are thought in the "Mission" gamemode), blocking mixups and utilizing other various defensive options. It even teaches you how to handle abusable moves of the entire cast.
You want it, the Xrd tutorial got it.
There isn't a lot to say about the netplay other than "it's fantastic", and the lobby system where up to 8 people can play at once (in 1v1s of course, pls don't paraphrase me) is quite nice.
So in conclusion, this is an amazing looking game with an amazing soundtrack. It's amazingly deep from a gameplay standpoint yet amazingly beginnerfriendly due to the amazing tutorial (and the ArcSys combo system in general).
To top it of, the online is also amazing.
If you have any interest in fighting games in general you owe it to yourself to own this game.
If you haven't, you should really aquire some interest in fighting games or else you propably won't expierence this game.
And that would be a shame.

The duration of how long you can survive is far beyond the entertainment that the game provides for that duration.
The problem isn't the lack of content, it's how the game is executed.
To begin, i'll just say that there is (some) entertainment to be had. But if you think that you're going to get $10 worth of gameplay, I am here to tell you that it's likely to be false.
First games I played I didn't know the control to build turrets and ended up walking around just shooting stuff. I quit before I died on a couple of attempts because I got bored, I thought that there surely must be more than what I was seeing. I came back and checked the controls properly and learned how to build turrets. You can build a max of 6 turrets at a time, but you can build as many walls as you like. Just need a little patience and (PERHAPS) a little luck to get enough scrap metal to build some turrets and some walls...
So standing between 2 to 3 layers of walls. Within those walls I had a few rocket turrets and a repair tower to keep them in top top shape. I was just standing there firing my minigun and throwing endless grenades.
Every once in a while I would run out the top of the walled enclosure to top up my grenades. The biggest concern wasn't taking damage when I went for the unrequired grenades, not at all. My biggest concern was: How long can I stand here behind this wall and fire my minigun before I get bored?? ...About 10-15 minutes.
So the initial 25-30 minute build up was for me to realise I was just going to be standing behind walls shooting at enemies for another 20 minutes and nothing can touch me. A game that allows you to be invincible because of poor design so early isn't worth $9.99 as it was too easily exploited.
A game like Risk of Rain gets away with allowing you to exploit it because it introduces "game mutators" as such to change how you play the game. As soon as the game was exploitable was when it got boring though.. So the same thing applies, but it WAS a good game.

I'm about two hours into this game, and I really like it.  First, for those who are saying in various places that the color change option doesn't work:  You have to unlock color palettes.  The function itself isn't broken.  I'm on level 8 and have 3 color unlocks I think, along with 4-5 unlocks for each of the three parts of the plane (weapon, body, engine).
Anyway, what is this game?  Basically a rogue-lite version of an old-school plane shmup.  Rogue-lite in a somewhat similar way as Rogue Legacy, in that if you die, that's it - you're dead.  But, you carry over points for  level-ups and complete tasks to unlock new parts for your plane.  Your plane has three parts that can upgrade:  Body, Weapon, and Engine.
Body includes stuff like Armored (takes a lot of hits, but heavy and slow), Melee (no damage from crashing into things but lower health), or Nuke (go nuclear and destroy everything on the screen when you die).
Weapons includes a Cannon, Homing Missiles, a Laser, etc.
Engine includes one that shoots bullets to propel you, a hovercraft engine where you have almost no gravity, and an underwater engine where you take no damage from hitting the water (But still bounce out after a second).
The game itself controls well with keyboard or an XB360 controller, although the menu options are a bit weird.  Just getting to the options menu or quitting the game is a chore.
Graphics are retro, but nice enough, and I like the game's soundtrack quite a bit.
Pretty cool that you get it on PC/Mac/Linux and it should pretty much work on most PCs.  Ran great on both my desktop and Surface Pro.
Annoyances?  I'm not sure about longevity.  Game gets pretty damn tough as you go on.   I'd give this a very strong recommendation at $5, but for $10, I think you have to be down with the concept of the game to get your money's worth.
Last thing to say here is that the flight mechanic is super cool.  The way you can cut the engines and maneuver just feels sooooo good.  I find it hard to explain until you play it, but they absolutely nailed it.
So, yeah,  recommended game if you're a fan of the modern rogue-lite concept grafted retro-style onto the best controlling shmup I can recall.

Starbound is one of the greatest indie games. Playing it for almost 120 hours in the time I made my review on it. I guess I was late to the party when the game's beta was released in 2013. But holy crap, I wish I knew the existence of such a game at that time. So let's start on what Chucklefish did good and "bad". Quotation marks matters.
Positive
- The story is a straight-forward one but not too undermining in most times and leads the expectations at the last stages of the game.
- The game is not making you focus on the story. You can basically do ANYTHING you want. Create a Death Star, a museum, a colony, terraform a world, it's all there.
- Monsters and the bosses' AI are snappy and don't derp that much in combat.
- Side scrolling combat done right.
- A lot of items and different types of collections for you to finish.
- Number of races that have different religion, beliefs, architectures and etc.
- Side characters like Nuru or Esther is written well and can be funny at times.
- ( Space is cool )
- Travelling in space is exciting and leads to more adventure in the long run.
- A great community with a reddit post that actually is active.
- Chucklefish communicates with the community in Starbound and applying some of their ideas.
- Legendary weapons are fun to use and can be used in any situations that you are currently in.
- Amazing soundtrack and worth the money to buy the OST.
- Mod creators have more freedom to create wonderful things.
and many more.
Negative
- Side quests are horrible and a lot of back tracking.
- Specific races are very hard to find and doesn't appear often in some of the planets that you would rather think that they will spawn there. FLORANS IN A TUNDRA BIOME.
- Sometimes Chucklefish diminishes expectations of most of the community.
- A painful death system, dying results in losing all craftable items, hence dropping them on the floor, and losing some credits.
- Some of the weapons are bland like straight rip off from Borderlands 2 Common Drops.
- Combat is a pain since the min zoom level is 2x and won't notify enemies that are farther if you just hold CTRL and move your mouse a bit. Nope.
- The Infamous Unskippable Esther Cutscene
MY THOUGHTS
Starbound is an 8 to a late 9. It's almost a 9 if it weren't for me using mods that make my personal negatives nothing. Overall, I would recommend for the sake of having it in your Steam library since it will definitely grow on you. But since some of the negatives have a great impact, including the side quests, in the vanilla game, hopefully Chucklefish will tweak it to be fun but also to be immersive.

I've been with Starbound for quite some time now. I remember putting a distress beacon on my house, and being fried by space penguins. In my opinion, Starbound cannot compete with Terraria, as Terraria is far more combat oriented. If you jump in with those expectations, you might be left with a sour taste in your mouth.
Combat is somewhat lacking, especially with the namesake of a randomized universe; the creatures. In previous builds, the fauna on a planet had special abilities. Imagine my surprise when I walked up to a small dog, and it shot fish at me. But, that's no longer a thing in the Starbound universe. You can expect every single enemy to run up your bum, without fail.
However, this game beats Terraria with its own forte; exploration. When you first start up the game, your given a flashlight, a broken sword, and a whole damn planet. I decided to explore the content of my new world ( which I branded as Tobias). I found villages, mysterious mushroom people, and a lot of birds. I made a house. I made a farm. A built a shrine for the gods of Tobias. Then, I found out that this is just one of millions of planets and experiences I could have with them. That is where that game shines.
If you're looking for a new exploration game to try, definitely pick up Starbound

I'm a fan of the Dynasty Warriors Saga and most games produced by Techmo Koei - I'm sad to say that I didn't enjoy this game, Maybe it's just my lack of ability but It's not at all like I expected.

This game has quickly become one of my personal favourite games, I've previously played Koei's other game series including Bladestorm (both new and old), Dynasty Warriors (one of the first games I really played fully and have played every one since 2), and their Romance of Three Kingdoms series which could be compared to this. This is my first time playing any of the games in the Nobunaga's Ambition series and so far I've been loving it, its similar to total war games in a way, some things are more simplified and on the lower difficulties the AI obviously isnt that intellegent but they have custom options for difficulty that allows you to make the AI harder but not allow them to cheat in other aspects that a game would normally let them cheat in such as diplomacy, income, supplies, etc. There are also multiple things that can be done to help minimize the micromanagement as your clan increases in strength such as creating provinces, delegating cities so that development is handled by the lord of the castle, and a few others. There is also the option to follow along with certain parts of history through quests that you can choose to accept or decline as they come up in history, some people have mentioned issues with the AI interfering with quests by their actions but so far through Nobunaga's line I have yet to run into any issues caused by the AI. A few downsides that I believe would've been nice and that I had enjoyed in the ROTK series were actual castle defenses, battles near your castles are fought outside the gates with defensive turrets (if you've built them) and some log spear walls (both of which are destructable simply by ordering your unit to walk through them, it takes them a little bit of time however so it will delay your unit and towers will still fire while you are destroying them.) Diplomacy is also quite simplified through a trust system which just involves you sending an officer to them who will stay there till trust is at 100 or you order them back. One really interesting feature however is the ability to add up to 3000 portraits into the game to use for character creation. This option allows for many play throughs with different themed forces or even allows you to implement yourself into the game. The game looks very nice and isnt very demanding on your pc so low end machines should have no problem maintaining 30+ FPS which is very playable for a RTS game. Overall if you enjoy RTS games or have played any previous games of this series or the ROTK series then I would highly recommend the game, if you consider the price tag a little too high for the game then add it to your wishlist and hope for a sale (not that common with Koei games, but I personally don't regret my purchase of the game at full price.)

That this game doesn't review better is a sign of the times. Despite numerous setbacks over the years, Koei has still managed to bring us a fantastic experience that, in some ways, other key strategy games cannot match.
Only the proliferation of games these days has caused gamers to expect more and more.
Yes, it is not as deep and complex as Europa Universalis.
Yes, combat is simpler than Total War.
Yes, diplomacy is odd and easily exploitable.
However, let's consider what this game does extremely well, that other games don't.
AI and challenge! How many times have you spent countless hours in games like Galactic Civilizations and Civ5 only to find the AI has just been dinking around the whole time, leaving your expectations for an epic late game confrontation completely unfulfilled? For me, even an advanced game such as EU4 has done this to me repeatedly.
In this game, Enemy armies maneuver in a way that will take a careless player by sunrise. You thought you were heading to a face to face clash and suddenly the enemy god tier officer flanks you and wrecks you. Or on a larger scale, enemy clans form coalitions against you if you start to steamroll the map. Granted by that point it's not impossible to overcome, but I just spent the good part of a day fighting EPIC HOJO. It wasn't as one sided as it would have been in EU4 or Civ5. Hojo means business. Powerful officers and lots of resources all of which were brought to bear.
Thank you Koei for actually providing AI that makes all your preparation worth it.
Note: you can make officers that are so powerful that the game becomes trivial. I recommend against it - make some flawed and varied officers if you're into created clans. Also, playing as Nobunaga, Hojo, or Shimazu will result in an easy game no matter what. Good for beginners though.

As someone who was raised on the old Koei series, and loves just about any micromanaging strategy game out there, this game is pure perfection.
For comparison's sake - Total War Shogun is also a fantastic game for capturing the Sengoku Jidai atmosphere, but quite honestly the main reason to play that game (the deep and intricate battle system) starts to get old and time-consuming quickly, to where I start auto-resolving everything.  Sengoku, on the other hand, is so extreme with the political and economic management that it starts feeling more like work and less like a game.  Nobunaga's Ambition hits the perfect sweet spot between the two.
Even though the outcome will obviously be different than it was in history, I find myself constantly thinking that the flow of the game and the decision-making is as close to representative of what Nobunaga, Mori, Shimazu, Date, etc, went through in their day.  Watching the armies move during an allied or a coalition war is a sight to behold.  Development of the towns/castles is just detailed enough, and almost feels like a mini-game on its own.  Diplomacy is simple, lightweight, and extremely important to pay attention to on every turn.
Possibly the best feature in the game, and one of the most historically accurate, are the provinces.  You can only directly control so many castles, and the rest you must assign to separate and autonomous provinces.  Once again this system is simple and lightweight, but extremely deep on a strategic level.  You may find yourself completely re-arranging everything in order to keep control of the castles whose armies you wish to control directly, or even to take the load off of how many development/army commands you end up making each turn.
I hope this game does well enough to bring Gemfire back.  They just don't make games like Koei did anymore.

Long Live the Queen is the dark souls of visual novels. Don’t be fooled by the cutesy graphics and initial light heartedness you might feel from it, its a brutal savage man eating simulator.
The princess needs to manage the kingdom and survive until she becomes queen sound easy enough? It’s really not…
First you need to make sure to understand how mood affects how well she can learn certain criteria and it becomes rather difficult at times to decide which is the right way to swing her mood. At times it will lead you to wield great benefits in her education in certain skills like wall climbing or singing that you wanted to invest in at other times… you will give yourself negative bonuses that make the skills unappealing to touch with a stick.
The skills  you can invest in which will result in successes or fails during events depending on the circumstances, the good news however is that if you fail in one skill for a event another one can make up for it. For example having low composure might lead you to fall, but with fast reflexes you can avoid crashing into someone.
At times however you will find yourself flustered that none of your skills you spent time on actually helped you out in certain situations and will want to go back to an earlier save to invest points in the required skills  to see how the outcome changes which is why multiple saves can be very helpful in case you need to go back further to achieve a high enough skill.. especially to prevent a death that can occur anywhere in the game
Sometimes you are presented even a new option from investing points into skills that would not normally be available otherwise. For example knowing things about trade and mining can open up the option to invest in certain prospects presented to you.
Once you understand how to avoid the death flags and finish the game there is a lot of different endings, events, and deaths to be seen and experimented with. It is quite fun to replay the game and think you are better prepared only to be thrown into a new series of events because you invested in other skills.

A single player game where you are a community of survivors trying not to die in a recent zombie apocalypse.
Realtime Third person action/foraging game.
Summary
I love the game but it has its flaws, well worth the price.
The Draw
Permenant character death (the gear/backpack is recoverable from a dead survivor) and you control an individual but can call out backup from home or other survivor communities in a fight or to cart the heavy cargo home (optional escort quest or let them solo the risk).
Vehicles with decent variation (from sensible 4 door family wagons to 4 x 4 pickups and 2 door musclecars)
suprisingly threatening zombies. The standard zombies are dangerous in packs, special infected need specific takedown methods (bullet immune, boomer, tank/charger hybrid, stalker), which can encourage you to take the risk and bring a friendly NPC with you (unless its the tank hunt mission in which case it is certain death to the somewhat sluggish NPC character)
good map setup where after the campaign intro you can move to and fortify one of several base site options, the dlc provides an endless map escalation scenario (campaign map with an escape to make harder function), and a mode focussed on base defence and deep insertion rescue and harvesting missions.
moving around is kept dangerous, campaign map resources are finite so each reload full of (noisy) bullets is important, damaged mele weapons need to be swapped out for fresh ones before they break so they can be repaired overnight, cars though numerous and powerful can start to become limited later on if you crash to many times or get caught offguard while mowing down a horde.
the detriment
I had an issue with the storage box where it would force me ot take the 1st item selected whenever I opened the crate, gear is requisitioned by faction/fame points and taking an item out costa more than putting an item in. the bug lead to rare shortages of fame (when it pulled out a ranged weapon)
The combat is functional but clunky, the special moves/passives earned by capping player traits help but the basic mele and gun combat lacks depth. distractions, firebombs, grenades, etc help but
Lack of sneak options. Later on with a capable/levelled survivor I could manage a horde or 2 horde with manageable risk and careful use of a moltov, there were few opportunities where stealth felt like an option. quietly foraging a house in the middle of an infected area is one thing but every new house seemed to have 3-5 zombies you had to take out in the process, being quiet only prevents a roaming herd from getting in on the action (which tends to waste a sizeable portion of resouces to handle safely)
core gameplay is similar to dead island, assassins creed (fixed world, unimaginative mele and satisfying stealth kills) and system shock 2 (there's you and an environment and the aggressive hordes out for your blood, resources are limited and you need to get stuff done)

NOTE: This review covers the original release, not the Weird Autumn edition, as that's not out at the time of this writing.
This game is, on the surface, about a girl returning home after dropping out of college and finding weird stuff happening in her hometown. What it's actually about is existential angst, losing and finding your place in the world, holding on to (and more importantly being able to let go of) friendships, and life moving on with or without you. It gets into some pretty heavy stuff, but never pretentiously or heavy-handedly.
The writing is sublime. Mae, the main character, has got some problems, but she's ultimately relateable as she tries to pick up her life where she left it, discovering that her friends have all moved on during her absence. As you progress through the game, choosing which friend to reconnect with will affect the ending (there are two) and some of the cutscenes. The game needs at least 2 playthroughs to do all the events and see every cutscene, but it doesn't feel like a chore because you find yourself really wanting to return and spend more time with these characters that Mae calls friends. Mae's friends are all wonderfully complex, well written and (eventually) likeable. The story takes a darker turn about 1/3rd of the way through, but the writing never faulters. The little sidequests and minigames break up the gameplay, but always feel like they belong, never being jarring or out of place (though the difficulty spike for the song minigames may catch you off guard the first time through)
The music is wonderful and atmospheric, always reflecting the perfect mood for any given area or scene. The game's art direction and graphics are also fantastic. Simplistic, but with loads of character and personality. Even the random townspeople standing around in the background will look busy, or be having conversations you can sometimes listen to, all making the little town of Possum Springs seem really alive.
If I have any complaints about the game it's that there's no way to have every event in a single playthrough, and with characters as well rounded and developed as these you want to spend as much time with them as possible. I've purchased this game twice (first on the PS4, then on Steam when I wanted a portable version for my laptop) and even with that I don't regret a penny of it. Night in the Woods is an emotional trip, one I recommend to anyone that likes quirky games, good writing, or simply wants to fall in love with some tragically beautiful writing. It's my favorite game of 2017.
Literally my favorite story-based game of all time. I cried a lot.

One of the best games I have played in years. Highly immersive with a compelling set of characters and narrative-driven storyline, Night in the Woods is an experience that was so fun and refreshing to have. I would highly recommend this game if you enjoy a visually-stunning artstyle, incredible soundtrack, and witty dialogue.

One of the most ridiculously complicated fighting games ever made, with a ton of flaws to stop people getting in to it without thousands of hours of practice. Many of the problems with it have in fact been fixed in SFV, but sadly SFV is extremely lacking in terms of content as of now, so many people are stuck here.
So, why is it so bad, you ask?
Street Fighter fanboys will defend this nonsense until the end of the earth, and it's one of the most ridiculously stupid things I have ever seen.
The general idea behind one-frame links is that when you do an attack and want to follow it up with another, only the joystick's input is buffered. You cannot buffer the button presses, and instead, they must be pressed in a lot of cases, completely frame perfect on the second that attack frame ends.  Not only is this an incredibly needless execution barrier that keeps newer players out, it's also made worse by the fact the online has a hideous delay, making these frame-perfect links almost impossible.
These one-frame links are so bad, an in-game exploit known as 'Priority Linking', or 'Plinking', is commonly used in competitive play to increase the leniency of these links. You can tell you've got a needlessly complex game if even the professional players have to exploit the system to pull off their combos. SFV has in fact, fixed these frame links, and according to the developer, the minimum amount of frames needed to do a link has gone down to three.
This is perhaps the worst thing, in my opinion. You'll quite often be in a match and you'll be struck down over and over, not knowing how to counter a certain move. Do you block high, block low? How are you to know? The ingame move-list for each character doesn't tell you a damn thing about anything. Is this move projectile-invincible, does it break armor?
The only way to find out ANY of this is to look the information up on community wiki's, and considering how many characters there are and how many moves you need to learn the properties of, it's almost shameful that the game can't just tell you this.
Consider this a deviation with no real inpact on the game, it's more of a personal gripe. When the majority of your game is done online, it's not the best of things to have people taunting you and sending you invites to 'LOL YOU'RE BAD XDDDD' steam groups after every other match. Consider this because of the normalisation of Street Fighter as a game, tons of people play it, which brings in the majority of bad eggs that you see. But this kind of behavior is often seen at professional tournaments, too, which doesn't help to bring down the image of the FGC as a whole.
If you're considering getting into fighting games, I'd very much recommend you pick up Skullgirls to start you off. SF4 is not a beginner-friendly game, and has an enormous execution barrier that will stop you from getting the full enjoyment of this game until you're thousands of hours into the game. There are much better fighting games that you could be playing.
I only hope SFV gets more fleshed out as time goes on.

The time mechanic is great.  Honestly its more like playing co-op with a hologram of yourself than any kind of "time travel" but its a solid mechanic.  That being said, I think it was poorly designed visually, and in regards to the levels and puzzles.  The HDR lighting was used terribly and EVERY LEVEL is slathered in glowing, blinding white panels that you can't even use portals on.  Visually, those white panels are repetetive and boring.   Functionally, they are confusing.  They obscure the portal guns cursor ALOT.  And we are spoon fed "portal" symbols on the few panels which are portalable.  If we're playing this mod, we are veteran portal players.  Please don't be that condescending.  More things I find telltale of poor level design:  Floors covered in fizzlers with inane timers are far too prevalent;  buttons needlessly placed on ceilings; seemingly complex solutions, which would have made me feel really smart, only to disappointingly find out that the solution was to use myself as a holographic temporary puzzle cube for 60 seconds.
All in all, A for effort and more or less realizing an awesome idea.  I recommend it because I know exactly how much work goes into these things, and its free.  You should play it to form your own opinion.

TL;DR: Great game. Your options may seem limited, but they accumulate, and in the end you will desperately try to find the one way to save poor Elodie from yet another grisly death while also trying to figure out who wrote dirty poetry about you. Incredible replay value due to branching story.
In the game, you take control of Elodie, a princess whose mother has recently died and who is about to inherit the throne. She just turned fourteen, and you have one year to mold her into the queen she will have to be. Along the way, there are plenty of opportunities to die, which you should avoid - or not; there is, after all, an achievement for dying in 11 different ways ;)
You train Elodie by choosing classes for her, two every week, which gives her points in one of about 30 skills. During the story, skill-checks will pop up (binary choice, you either pass or don't, no luck involved) and inform you that you got/missed some information, succeeded in a task or will quite often leave you entirely guessing which influence your doing a good job at dancing at the ball had on the progress of the game - but that's fine, finding out is fun!
Additionally, you spent your weekends doing things around the castle. Some further the story, others change your mood, and your mood changes your skill point gain. This means that you WILL be rooting for Elodie to please become more depressed and lonely, because happy people don't learn to handle animals as well.
There are multiple ways to survive practially any challenge, and there are many secrets to discover in the story. I doubt you could find them all in one playthrough, or even three - there are just not enough weeks in the year to learn everything.
In summary, for such a simple little game, I had and am having a lot of fun trying to do different things and (still!) trying to find the stupid 2nd lumen crystal and, and, and ....

This game was really relatable to me, as I also had a similar situation with college that lead to anxiety and depression. It is truly AMAZING how accurately the game portrays your mental state, your interactions with friends and family, and how it changes for both sides with some time during this phase. Not only that it shows it, but it makes you feel the exact same void if you really get invested. I was truly impressed. The minigames were hit or miss, but
were, looking at you pumpkin head guy, pretty enjoyable and fun.
Not that the game doesn't have problems.. I felt like pacing was really weird, especially in the beginning. It's like the story progressed way slower than it should have and meaningful sections were a bit too far apart from each other because of that. That said, I still liked the first few chapters the most, as when the game starts to get into a different subplot later on something happens to the writing. I don't really want to spoil the plot, so I will just say that it makes aspects that shine in this game less meaningful and important. It seemed like they were trying to go too much into symbolism in order to multiply the strength of overall emotional impact, but with a much weaker writing it just kinda.. falls apart towards the end and leaves you feeling conflicted and confused.
This game is still a solid recommendation to anyone, especially if they are going through or already dealt with depression since that's when the game hits right home. I am looking forward to Director's Cut update and I will happily alter my review if this update fixes things I didn't like and focuses more on what game does best.

Ok so I love Koei and since Tecmo joined.... Nothing but good things (besides dynasty warriors 7).so I've played a few of the ROTK games and all of the "warriors" as a big total war guy I was worried the tactical aspects of this game wouldn't be able to hold up. I was wrong , the game is different , it reminds me very much of Dynasty Tactics which was a really fun game to play as you could play as slow or as fast as you wanted and there was a lot of micromanaging of cities and officers.
Graphics
Nice, the graphics are quite cartoony , aesthetically pleasing none the less and with the sheer scale of the map it really holds up. The portraits for all of the Characters are impressive and stick well to the description of the real life embodiments.The armies being displayed by the "jigsaw pieces" is a really nice and welcome feature.
Gameplay
Simple council where time freezes and you set what you want to be built and what policies you want to to follow for a few months until the next council. Once the council is over time will progress at a speed of the users specification , and armies will move buildings will build and Events will occur allowing you to see all of your policies in action. The battles are a total war crossed with Dynasty tactics style; realtime speed but in depth tactics for each general allowing ft an in depth battle system that's easy to learn. Now I've only played 5 hours st the time of this review and I will update this if need be but diplomacy seems to be the aim of the game ,enticing enemy generals to defect keeping alliances and making surrounding tribes (minor factions) support you, so far diplomacy is interesting and is the focal point of this games different scenarios.
Sound
Score is impressive , despite being modernised you can still feel the sense of traditional Japanese music , also my with the war drums before battle starts , the music doesn't feel out of place whatsoever and is in fact quite immersive!
I haven't listened to the English dub actors but the option is there for those who can only tolerate American. The Japanese voice actors are immersive and all fit the character they're meant to portray (good casting Koei)
Other
The game is made of custom scenarios , but you can play any clan of the time period and the scenarios are of decent length I've been playing for 5 hours and am still on the first scenario and I have no idea how longs left however with my knowledge of the time period I feel it'll be over within the next 2 hours
The custom Daimyo system is incredibly in depth , I've not fully tinkered with it but you can choose your family , traits and stats . You can also place your custom character in any of the scenarios as a Ronin (wanderer looking for a master) or a retainer , someone who is under the command of a clan instantly.
Overall
I'm really intrigued by this game and it's a nice breath of fresh air from Koei , the casual city management and intense battles make this game fun for any mood , I advise a strong knowledge of the time period or ancient warfare for full enjoyment out of this game. If you're a fan of Japan, strategy or just fulfilling games , then this game is for you.
I'd give this a game 9/10 for me I haven't found any major flaws and I'm having a great time , great product from Koei they've set the bar here!
I think from an unbiased point of view and. For someone who isn't a Koei fanboy/girl this game is probably a 7.5/10

Forget the minimum requirements listed, with some tweaking (see the forums), you can run this game on a toaster. I have an i3 2.2Ghz CPU, 1GB Nvidia 630M (yes, M!) and 4GB RAM running Win7 64bit and I have it running at 60fps, which is a must.
The netcode is actually pretty decent. I'm in China and I have managed to play people in Asia with 1-4 frame delay and I'm using WIFI!!
Roster is interesting. I will admit I was sad to see all of my favourite characters gone (Zappa, Jam, Johnny), but the new characters are unique, I especially love Ramlethal and Elphelt, and the returning characters are true to their previous incarnations.
Graphics are amazing. This is the new standard for cell shading. The animation is slick and maintains the style from the sprite based games and the stages look good.
The game system is the "usual" ArcSys fare; double jumps, air dashes, Roman Cancels, instant blocking, etc.
The mechanics are slightly toned down compared to Accent Core, but it's still a solid system. Remember Accent Core was evolved over many itterations to get as complicated as it was and this is effectively a "new" chapter for Guilty Gear.
Problems, there are a few. Ranked matches often don't connect, Lobbies sometimes cannot be joined. There is a memory leak. Some of the keyboard keys apparently cannot be bound (I use stick so I don't know details). Some problems with using certain resolutions (there are work arounds). The devs have acknowledged these problems and are working on a patch at the time of writing (playing launch version, no patches).
Why are you still reading this, buy it now.

Somewhat of an early review, but here we go. I've been looking forward to this port for awhile.
PROS-
-Stylish look. Keeps the anime artstyle that made the series true, but also uses 3D models. It's actually insane how crazy good these models look and how they apparently aren't 2d sprites.
-Fairly similar to other Guilty gear titles. It's slightly slower in terms of speed and it's not as technical, but these mechnical charges are extremely small.
-This is a port, and the port (for the most part) is great.
- Netcode is FAN-♥♥♥♥ING-TASTIC. It's seriously real good. I played over 40 matches today and none of them had noticable lag. Of course, I'm sure this could change with distance between players, but this is definitely one of the best PC fighting games in terms of its netcode.
- Challenging difficulty that makes the game rewarding to learn. Not incredibly easy to pick up and definitely hard to master.
-Pretty decent sized roster
-The rock and metal themes in this game are iconic and amazing to fight to. Makes fights even more entertaining
Cons-
-The only real issue I have with this port is a possible memory leak issue. Many people have reported issues with fps slowly dropping over time when playing the game. It seems to be related to dxinput controllers. I simply unplugged my fightstick while playing the game, and plugged it back in and got a stable 60 fps again. But this is still an unacceptable issue for a game that shouldn't be very demanding.
-The level of entry in this game is very steep. If you never played a fighting game, this one isn't bad to start with, but you'll be losing a lot (as you would with most fighting games anyway if you're a noob).
-The story is odd and non-traditional. It can be a bit offputting to others.
- No real options to go past 1080p from what I've read. Could be wrong.
- This version will be outdated soon, as GGxrd Revelator is coming out soon. I'm glad Arcsys Jp decided to finally get a company to port this game for us, but if they really want these games to do well, they need to make sure to keep them updated at a timely fashion just like with the console versions.
- Online is not cross play with ps4/ps3. Steam users only, which will eventually twindle, since fighting games aren't big on PC.
Overall, I think this is a great game. Amazing fighting game and I'm having fun learning it. I hope Revelator comes out on pc around the same time as the console versions. However, there are some port issues that hopefully get ironed out by the next patch for the game. Regardless, I still recommend this game, but please be wary of your purchase, since you might run into some issues due to shoddy porting. My experiences had a quickfix, but who knows what you'll run into.
