9.5/10. First off I don't think it's as hard as people make it sound, if you have a good walkthrough or you just know what you're doing and you look up the strats for the bosses it isn't that bad, going in blind is pretty tough though. But with proper preparation most the game (even ornestien and smough) aren't too difficult. One of my favorite things about Dark Souls is that although there is a certain order in which things should be done, in which bosses should be killed, there is often a way to access areas prematurely and fight bosses earlier then normal, often times a glitch isnt even require and most other times there's a glitch to get there early anyways. This isnt very useful for new comers like myself since fighting many bosses early will mean almost certain doom it makes the game feel very open and free flowing but not so much so that it feels pointless or confusing. I feel like it balanced linearity and non linearity perfectly for the type of game that it is, because total linearity is boring but total nonlinearity in a game like this wouldn't make much sense and I feel they did a great job finding the perfect middle ground where doesnt feel spoon fed but it also has enough structure to support a good difficulty curve and story developement. Besides that its gameplay is great and the story is interesting, the leveling system is good and equipment is much like game's linearness, has a certain order of progressively better gear that you will naturally get but you can get some really good gear early on, I used the same weapon throught out almost all the game and I got it pretty early, the catch is getting this better gear requires fighting powerful enemies, some of it isnt even garuteed to drop (mine was only a 20% chance drop from a powerful, non respawning enemy) and they require you to dedicate levels into certain stats (I did get a better weapon but I was never able to use it because I never invested enough levels into strength to use it effectively). The game isn't fully open world, there are some areas that are seperate but more than half the areas you vist in the main story are all in one massive map, none of which is computer generated, its all unique, each room different none of that cookie cutter crap, the map is big and it sews together beautifully in a really satisfying way. The one big complaint I have is it has some pretty signifigant glitches, infinite souls, infinite humanity, tons of boss and area skips, AI bugs or terrain oversights that allow for easy boss cheeses, tons of stuff like that. But just playing the game without looking up how to do any glitches you shouldnt really find anything big, it's only when you look for them will you actually find them, but they are there. Overall a really solid game. I would rate 10/10 if it weren't for the infinite souls glitch alone... its pretty broken and if you abuse it, it makes the game pretty trival since souls are both the main currency and xp for leveling up (essentially allowing you to buy whatever you want easily and massively over level with ease). I also didn't care for the PvP, that's not to say the PvP was bad just to say that I could never win it and the invasions right when I was about to reach the next bonfire were pretty annoying, but as I heard the PvP can be pretty fun if you know what you're doing and if you don't like the random invasions you can just play in offline mode like a coward (like I did).

I am very split about this game.
On one hand, its a perfectly functional game and I can totaly see why people would like this
On the other it does everything I dislike.
First of all, let me get this out of the way.
This game is not terraria. Terraria was about progressing your world and your base through hardships, building giant structures and killing extremely hard bosses for that single glimpse at your base and saying ''I did that. I alone have done this in a way that no one else would've''
What is starbound?
Its about exploration.
And this is a big reason why people like it and I dislike it.
The comparison between terraria and starbound is like the difference between don't starve's base game / reign of giants and don't starve: shipwrecked
Your base is temporary, something to use and replace in starbound / shipwrecked. You are the main feature of the game.
Though most people would like that, I prefer base building over exploration.
But. Do I like the game?
Yes, its a fun game on its own, I just don't like some of the parts that make it what it is.
Would I recommend the game?
Without a doubt, yes.

TL;DR: Great game. Your options may seem limited, but they accumulate, and in the end you will desperately try to find the one way to save poor Elodie from yet another grisly death while also trying to figure out who wrote dirty poetry about you. Incredible replay value due to branching story.
In the game, you take control of Elodie, a princess whose mother has recently died and who is about to inherit the throne. She just turned fourteen, and you have one year to mold her into the queen she will have to be. Along the way, there are plenty of opportunities to die, which you should avoid - or not; there is, after all, an achievement for dying in 11 different ways ;)
You train Elodie by choosing classes for her, two every week, which gives her points in one of about 30 skills. During the story, skill-checks will pop up (binary choice, you either pass or don't, no luck involved) and inform you that you got/missed some information, succeeded in a task or will quite often leave you entirely guessing which influence your doing a good job at dancing at the ball had on the progress of the game - but that's fine, finding out is fun!
Additionally, you spent your weekends doing things around the castle. Some further the story, others change your mood, and your mood changes your skill point gain. This means that you WILL be rooting for Elodie to please become more depressed and lonely, because happy people don't learn to handle animals as well.
There are multiple ways to survive practially any challenge, and there are many secrets to discover in the story. I doubt you could find them all in one playthrough, or even three - there are just not enough weeks in the year to learn everything.
In summary, for such a simple little game, I had and am having a lot of fun trying to do different things and (still!) trying to find the stupid 2nd lumen crystal and, and, and ....

LUFTRAUSERS is addicting, let me start by saying that. You customize your plane, take to the sky, and have some bullethell fun.
When I say it's addicting though, I don't mean it in a good way. It's addicting like heroin or crack cocaine is addicting, at it's core the game is barely playable.
The game mechanics are fine, really, they are, you fly around in a way that no pilot should never ever have to fly (i.e. cutting the engine off to make a hard turn, spinning in circles just to engage at the last second before hitting the water), shoot at boats and planes, and later, shoot at dirigibles and submarines. Let me start with that first one: I saw one review of this game that described the game's controls as "flawless." This is in no way the case since it feels like someone took a bullet hell, stapled that vector graphic Tank battling game to it and called it a day. In no way should anyone have to control like this in a bullet hell.
As I mentioned before, you can customize your plane, and this is neat. But this is where the game falters THE MOST. Most of the unlockable parts you, well, unlock, are absolutely useless. You can unlock a melee fighter body which can ram into thinks without even getting a scratch, but when you realize that this is a bullet hell you should be uninstalling the game. You can also unlock a few other bodies, but all of them are ♥♥♥♥ing useless with the exception maybe one or two. All of the other bodies basically cripple your plane in the hopes that you'll find the tactic fun or interesting.
The weapons I don't really have a problem with. They all have their ups and downs with the exception of missile, which no sane human being would ever use, but for the most part they feel finished and polished. It's such a shame the dev didnt take the time to ♥♥♥♥ing do the same for the other parts you can apply to your plane.
And then there's the amount of parts you can have. The game's store page boasts 125 combos to add to your plane, but when you factor in the undeniable truth that most of the bodies and engines are ♥♥♥♥ing useless, you're instead left with about 50 useful combinations. And, while 125 may seem like a lot of parts, YOU WILL UNLOCK THESE PARTS WITHIN AN HOUR, POSSIBLE EVEN LESS. THAT'S RIGHT, ALL OF THE PARTS WITHIN AN HOUR. I.E., THE BIG GOAL  OF THE GAME, IS ACHIEVABLE IN AN HOUR OR LESS. If they don't expand on the part customization section of the game, or at least improve what you get, I see no reason to even touch this game.
Also, you get to unlock color schemes for completing the entirety of a challenge tree. They're eyesores. And the names of these color schemes are the devs' names backwards. ♥♥♥♥ING. CLEVER.
The game's prequel was a flash game called LUFTRAUSER. With the tacked on S, it makes sense that this is not the only ♥♥♥♥ing thing that's tacked on. Don't buy this game.

As a game, Ultra Street Fighter IV is pretty good. The main thing I look for in a fighting game is gameplay, and USF4 mostly delivers in that respect. However, as a PC port, USF4 is disappointing. That doesn't mean you should write it off, however.
USF4 is the final entry in Capcom's line of Street Fighter 4 games. Before this particular entry was developed, Capcom made the stupid decision to saddle its PC ports of Street Fighter IV and Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition with Games For Windows Live. GFWL is DRM that no customer wanted; not only was it unnecessary, but it caused problems for many of the game's paying customers. When Capcom seemingly did the right thing by patching GFWL out of SSF4:AE's PC port, the game's netcode inexplicably took a serious hit. Online play became unreliable at best.
Not long after leaving GFWL in the past, Capcom announced that it would develop USF4, and that this update would be developed with Steamworks-based netcode. PC gamers had reason to believe that USF4 would have great online gameplay because it would supposedly be developed from the ground up without any GFWL integration. What PC gamers got instead was simply a patched version of SSF4:AE that still features the same broken netcode. Capcom promised to fix the netcode, butyears later, it has clearly failed to carry out that promise. With Street Fighter 5 having been released, it is unlikely that Capcom will ever fix Street Fighter 4's netcode for the PC.
What USF4's sorry state of online play usually amounts to is that internet-based games will be unplayably laggy. This problem occurs even when both of the players are in the same region and have stable internet connections. If you have the fortune of playing online without significant lag, the experience is compromised by the fact that the game does not support voice chat or even native texting.
The game isn't a total wash. You can have a good time playing with a buddy who's physically in the same room as you, and the single player arcade mode is mostly fun to play through. For me, the fun stops as soon as I reach Seth, the game's final boss. He's frustratingly cheap and you'll probably struggle to win more than one round against him unless you resort to memorizing his patterns and exploiting their few loopholes in a very contrived manner.
Seth battles notwithstanding, USF4's gameplay is solid. However, I don't like Capcom's decision to substite the SF4 games with a focus attack system instead of the parry system that was introduced in Street Fighter III. Although USF4's roster is large, there are many shoto clones, so the gameplay between characters isn't as diverse as your eyes may lead you to believe.
As far as graphics go, the characters look pretty good, although Decapre looks way too derivative of Cammy for a first time playable character who was hyped to the moon. (Thankfully, she handles completely differently and does indeed function as a unique character.) Most of the backgrounds are bland and unimaginative, but this has been a problem with every Street Fighter game since Capcom moved on from the Street Fighter II series.
I really dislike that game's music, sound effects, and especially its announcer. Sound-wise, the only thing I like about the game is the voice acting.
Bottom line, this is a pretty good game, but Capcom should be ashamed for promising to fix SSF4:AE's netcode, only to release this installment and have it suffer from the same problem that Capcom neglected to fix. Mainly for that reason, I disapprove of this port, but not the game itself. People who have friends who can play with them IRL will likely derive the most enjoyment from the PC port of USF4.

I was wondering when this was going to get released outside of Japan. Heh, maybe I should have paid more attention to the news. I would've bought this day one.
I am a long time fan of both the Nobunaga's Ambition, and Romance of the Three Kingdoms games. We're talking since the NES era. A friend showed it to me, and all I could think of at the time was, "what kind of names are those? How am I supposed to remember who's who?".
Over time, these games opened my eyes to a type of gaming I haven't seen before. Managing many aspects of a country/empire. Things most games at the time didn't do.
As time has passed, other developers have taken the leap and joined in the crowd in this niche. Which is great. Game series such as Europa Universalis Crusader Kings, Total War, if you like those titles, you will like this game.
Anyways, about this title specifically. Last NA game I played was Iron Triangle. That game is tough. Easy to pick up the basics with a strong clan on easy/normal difficulty, hard to master with a weaker clan on hard. This game is showing me much of the same.
They have expanded on the domestic aspect of it. You now have to focus on improving roads to both increase trade income as well as troop movement. Planning out domestic district expansion is also key. You have to figure out if it's worth it to choose the expansion upgrade, or one that exploits what you have on that tile, and passing up the expansion (ex. You can choose an option that lets you get additional farming in the next tile, or you can forsake that to focus on lowering the cost of purchasing horses). That was a very nice touch in this game.
In former games, there was essentially one city per province. Now there are multiple cities per province. Again that opens up a new aspect to the game. Do you focus on food? Troops? Income? Innovation? A lot of strategies to employ even on the domestic level.
I've barely scratched the surface so far, having played less than 4 hours currently, but I am really liking this title. If you're a fan of grand strategy like Crusader Kings 1/2, or Europa Unversalis 3/4, you should get this game. There is no multiplayer, but there is an abundance of single player. More than enough to warrant the purchase.
EDIT
I'm now about 15 hours into this game. There just seems to be a new surprise around each corner. Now I can build new fortresses in my provinces, thus increasing my harvest/income/draft pools even further. Enabling the option that allows maidens to become officers adds another dimension. Some of them are best used to seal alliances, or raise an officer's loyalty. Others, become better than officers, so why not let them loose on the battlefied?
As far as content is concered, this game is a 10/10. So much replayability, plenty of tweaking of options, and yes, make good use of the in game encyclopedia.

But over all it is a good game, that i would recommend to anyone that likes strategy games or japanese history.

A great game that lets you pick a faction and lead them, or even create your own (and your own character/links to families in game!), Nobunaga's Ambition: Sphere of Influence is another game in the great series of strategy games KOEI puts out. The politics, development, and management of everything is fun and addicting. I found myself upgrading towns, building new ones, setting policies and skipping out on battles just to micro-manage everything because I was enjoying it, experimenting with alliances and marriages and messing with officer's loyalty are all fun features in the game. As for combat in the game, it can be resolved automatically. General's abilities, unit's skill and abilities, and allies all come into play when auto-fighting. You can also manually do the battle, allowing some input and tactics in an otherwise hopeless situation, or simply just because it's fun. Unlike some grand strategy games, the game actually has a story you can follow too, given via historical objectives to complete. These are optionable and exist to add flavor and fun, and can be completely ignored if you'd prefer total freedom in how you rule and act.

Over 9000 Zombies is an understatement. There are a lot more than just 9000.
This game is an endless horde shooter that has progression. You can expand your array of weapons by shooting zombies, killing them, and gaining xp for your weapon.
I've played this game for 10.6 hours now, all of which has been single player, but Over 9000 Zombies would 100% be better with a friend. Playing Over 9000 Zombies alone is a lot more difficult because you don't have someone else watching your back or repairing the walls or turrets or building. I haven't played multiplayer, so I don't know if the difficulty is increased with more people, but I would expect that that would be the case.
There are a ton of different mechanics to aid you in your quest to survive as long as possible. Not only is Over 9000 Zombies a wave shooter, it's also a tower defense. Zombies will occasionally drop scrap metal which you can use to construct towers and walls, and as the waves get harder and harder, the towers and walls are a welcome help. Your decreased sight and light mechanics keep you on your toes, because you could turn around a corner into a mass of zombies at any given moment. Although Over 9000 Zombies isn't a horror game by any means, the darkness that surrounds you if you're at low health definitely gets the heart racing.
The graphics in Over 9000 Zombies are nice. The decorations in the background are fitting and help the mood and theme of the game. The developer made maps are all unique, with differing buildings and environments. A lot of the maps reuse the same tile sets, but the developer has made it so that it doesn't seem very obvious.
The Over 9000 Zombies workshop is one of the best features of the game. The community continues to support the game even though the developer hasn't really updated it (which is one of the only downsides). My favorite maps in the game are made by the community, which are all evenly balanced and not overpowered. The maps, both community made and developer made, are all a good size, not too big and not too small. Even in the later waves you still have room to move around and strafe your way through the zombie hordes.
The audio in Over 9000 Zombies is decent but not the best. The music is alright, but in my opinion it should be more fast paced than it already is. All of the guns have the same sound effect at different speeds, which gets bland very quickly, which is another downside to the game.
There is no story to Over 9000 Zombies, which kind of makes sense because its an endless horde shooter, but a little bit of exposition here and there wouldn't hurt. Perhaps a tutorial would be able to provide the exposition that is needed to have any sort of story, but there is non unfortunately.
A recommendation that I'll make for future updates (if there are updates in the future) would be for weapon customization. Eventually your weapons would all max out and would get pretty boring, so being able to customize your weapons would be pretty neat.
There are only a couple downsides to the game. The first of which being the lack of developer support for the past year. Perhaps the developer is working on a really big update which will push a ton of content into the game, or perhaps not. There has been no communication between the players and the developer. However, the Over 9000 Zombies Workshop will continue to add new content to the game to provide a fresh experience for old players. Eventually the game does become a tad bit boring, especially when you reach the final stages of weapon progression and when you have enough scrap to build the best turrets. The price tag is also a bit too much for the game in my opinion. Although the game is fun, it's not worth 10 of your hard earned dollars. If you want to buy Over 9000 Zombies, i suggest you wait for a sale.
In the end, Over 9000 Zombies is a great game for those who enjoy endless wave shooters with weapon progression. The price tag is a bit high and the developer hasn't released an update in over a year, but it's worth trying the game out for yourself, especially if you have a friend who is willing to play.

In the ever mountain of "early access" games that is starting to obstruct the view from finished games, Stranded deep is one which has had my attention for a while but like all public alphas, i stayed clear of for the first year.
Stranded deep even now is nowhere near complete. Which is a bit of a problem. The term alpha used to refer to a piece of software which is more or less finished but requires a large testing audience to discover any bugs. Nowadays it has come to mean a game which has been conceived, and the developers want you to start paying for it before it is complete, assuming they ever "complete" it at all.
Ranting about this "alpha" culture asside lets look at the good and bad points.
The idea of being stranded on a desert island is not a new one, but it is one which no developer has properly committed to before. All the otehr survival games which have been doing the rounds have something extra added, be it zombies or dinosaurs. The reason behind this is that a true survival game engine would have to be extremely complicated, as a real life survival situation would require you to use literally anything and everything available to you, including the very dirt that you walk on. Even today, consoles and computers would struggle to deal with the complexity of a game which focuses solely on survival in a way in which would be realistic. So to distract you from this, most devs throw other challenges at you to keep it fresh.
Stranded deep is something of an anomaly on this point because apart from sharks and snakes (both things which would likely be actual problems in this situation) the primary dangers that you face are starvation, dehydration, exposure. This is great news because it means we are getting closer to a proper survival sim which doesnt need added nonsense to be playable
there are some glaring issues which could easily be remedied. For example. The "intro" sequence is entirely unecessary, or rather, player control is unecessary, it could easily just be a cut scene. I suspect that rather more inspiration was drawn from The Forest which also has a plane crash intro. if you look at your body in the intro to Stranded deep, for some reason you are wearing tattered clothes, on a private jet. Something of an immersion breaker from the start.
Next is the draw distance. I use a high end rig on ulra settings and i still find myself paddling toward grey fog whilst the game decides whether or not to render the "closest" islands.
i could go on but i will end this review short by saying this
If you dont mind playing a game where you will spend most of your time sat in a life raft paddling blindly into nothing, hoping that the game engine will render the next chunk before you reach that ghastly seam in the skybox, then this is the game for you.
Stranded deep, much like many of the "early access" games, should not have been released until it was MUCH closer to completion that it currently is.

Pros:
- You get the build bases
- You need guides to craft more more structures and other things
- Vehicles work, from bicycles, cars, buses, trucks and you can store them
- You scavenge for the usual stuff, food, water, armor (there are levels of protection)
- There is a change of environment, rainy, sunny, night, day, tornadoes, lightning and thunder, radiation places
- You'll at least find a few people as you journey on the world (guaranteed for sure)
- There are pistols, rifles, assault rifles, melee, bows, tranquilizers, shotguns, snipers
- You can sack, tape, and handcuff people
- There are mutant like creatures, even a really powerful one that looks like The Thing from Fantastic Four, and a two headed two tailed dog lol.
- There are also wild animals like deers, wolves, squirrels, pigs, chickens
- For the most part amazing animations compared to other indie survival games
- SO much to explore, like seriously
- The game is comparitively easy to figure out where you are, especially if you have a photo of the map
- Has chat and voice around whichever area you're in.
- The graphics really are amazing.
Cons:
- Less love and attention from the publicity so population is going down but still enough that a few servers gets full
- Building needs some improvement in terms easeness when it comes to perfectly aligning building parts like walls and such and also crafting better
- You only have limited space of storage per base so you can't store much
- All the vehicles have the same inventory space no matter the size, only difference is how fast you can drive and what purpose it could give. (like maybe to help go on top and raid a base that has no roof, etc. etc.)
- Its alpha, there always are a few glitches and more refining to be done
My Conlusion:
The game is epic and amazing, sort of addicted to it at the moment. You really should play the game and invite your friends to get the game as well and have some good loving pvp, survival life.

Background: I have over 1000 hours in ARK: Survival Evolved.  But I play as a solo player, on a HARDCORE PVP server.  The toughest survival game I've found to date... but having over 1000 hours, and having reached a point where it no longer provides that challenge for me that the first 800 hours provided, I started looking for a more "realistic" alternative.
Which brought me to "Miscreated."  I did my homework... I watched many videos other people had made regarding this early access game.  I thought about it, finally decided to try it, having thought that I was going to find a more realistic crafting system with "real world" applications.  And believe it or not, PVP isn't generally an interest of mine.  I like helping people succeed, not kill people.  But in ARK in PVP, it's basically like "One Life; One Chance."  That's the level of challenge that attracts me.
I purchased the game.  I understand it is early access... but so was ARK.  Absolutely no hints on what to do, and (better yet?) it was dark where my character woke up.
I find a small house, purely by luck, and begin to search it.  And here is where the negative begins...
1) I can't break open the wooden doors or windows?  I can't use this crowbar I found?  Nor this baseball bat?  I can't set the building on fire??  I can't break the windows?  I can't rip up these window shades into their rope and wooden slat components??  Downstrike number one.  It was becoming daylight, but frustrated from lack of abilty to scavenge everything I log out, go to bed, and next day off to work....
2) Get home from work, spend a few hours in ARK maintaining generators and the like, and decide to try MisCreated again.  Log in to a whole new server, low population so I have a chance to learn before someone kills me - which I fully expect.  Next learned thing... can only carry 6 items.  So I figure out that I can craft.  I need 4 rags to make a rope, and another rag, and boom, I'll get some knapsack type thing to allow me to carry more stuff.  Spend the next 15 minutes NOT finding any rags, despite "seeing" hundreds of items that could have counted as a rag (the two tents outside, two sleeping bags, many beds, many tarps floating in wind, the car seats, etc etc.)  That's enough of that, I'm now up to about an hour total spent in this EA game, so I log off, bed, work next day...
3)  Try again after work... don't bother with ARK, see if I can find a daylight fresh server, and see what happens this time.  Spawn somewhere near a camp-like place.  Find a generator that I can repair, and using it turn on some lights?  Exactly how is that going to help me survive in a place where you really don't want to attract attention to yourself lest you bring massive death upon yourself??  So I then think, okay, I need a hidden base where I can operate out of... so I keep looking.  Now I've made a knapsack roll and I can carry more items.  I made rope with rags, 4 to be exact.  And then, walking around another part of the camp, I come across an army tent.  Set up.  With benches inside.  Not much else... but what is holding up the tent?  Stakes, wooden, and ROPE!  All combined, roughly 100+ feet of really really good rope!  Except...
YOU CAN NOT HARVEST THIS ROPE HOLDING UP THIS TENT?!?!?!
So, that's it for me.  For now.  I will check again in a couple patches.  You can keep my $20 or whatever I spent.  Use it wisely.  Give players the ability to 1: carry more up front?  2: scavenge EVERYTHING POSSIBLE, even if it's just wood fragments from this piece of plywood covering this window that's indestructable...
TL;DR: potential not yet realized

Well, first off I'd just like to say now, I WAS an ace combat fan prior to this game.
I played this game previously when I was a console junkie, on the Xbox 360 after loving Ace Combat 4 for many years on my playstation 2, Back then, i was expecting it to be just the same old lovable gameplay mechanics, just updated graphics and a new storyline based in a fictuous world.
I was wrong, on all fronts.
They brought in dogfight mode, or as I liked to call it, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mode, which held your hand through something that wasn't particularly hard to do in the first place in this franchise, which is dogfight. Now I remember Ace Combat 4 being unremarkable in the sense that there were very few moments where I'd actually have to break contact and fight off an enemy attacking from behind. But dogfight mode goes over the top with it, it happens too much, and suddenly in order to maneuver and engage a radar target behind me, I have to press a button rather than have the ability to, do it myself.
not only that but the sudden need to change the camera mode in third person, i don't particularly like 3rd person anyway, but suddenly I need to zoom in on my guns when I fire them, and the same with my bombs, too. okay, namco, keep taking those tablets.
I could no longer pitch and roll like in previous games, no, instead my turning was forced at a certain angle and my speed affected how much I turned, not exactly a wrong thing, speed does affect your turning, but it just felt wrong...
not to mention, suddenly your aircraft are like the T-1000 from terminator 2, they have regenerating health... HA! how laughable.
Next, the storyline was America vs Russia, oh dear, not only have they removed the fictional worlds I was used to in Ace Combat, but they've also jumped on this bandwagon? seriously?!
I won't say too much because, spoilers, but it feels like the aircraft version of call of duty in terms of the story, in fact most of the time it feels like story elements have just been ripped right out of Modern Warfare and applied in the most generic way possible to this game.
The characters were very obvious and quite frankly unprofessional at most times, there was the overly masculine edgy black dude, the pretty blonde girl who looks like the woman from Ridge Racer Type 4, who is so obviously into the colonel, who is this really edgy legendary fighter ace (apparently) who likes to say &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; and "damn" alot, then tell people to cut the chatter when he's the one talking. Then theres Guts, the overly enthusiastic dude who wants to impress his squadron leader. then of course there's the stereotypical vodka drinking russian dude who speaks with a russian accent, and you SO can't tell that he's a bad guy or something, because this game SO isn't obvious(!)
so the storyline annoyed me a little but I gave it a chance at the time, trying to find something to love in this game, along with that, your player character is no longer an enigmatic pilot who you only know the callsign of, and also that he/she only flies jets (the addition of helicopters made me want to cry)
so it's 2014, I feel like trying it again, following my departure from my Xbox and the entry of my PC.
by this point I wasn't really an ace combat "fan" anymore I got around to playing 6, and then I started using my PC more, realised that there was more fun to be had so I let ace combat gather dust....
I played this on the free weekend after i saw it advertised and old frustrations brewed up, the same criticisms above applied, only worse because of how badly this game was ported.
While I can say, for a 2013, game the graphics are quite good, but the options are horrific, you get to choose whether anti aliasing is on or off, and that's really about it.
not only that, but the menu isn't even mouse friendly, no, you have to use your keyboard/controller.
speaking of controllers, good luck finding a controller configuration that actually makes any goddamn sense! remapping the controller is a nightmare, and unless you know what button is what, you're going to find the first level a frustrating guessing game. I spent a good 20 minutes on the first level figuring out whats what.
oh and that tutorial level, isn't much fun anyway, its a hand holding bunch of nonsense in which you MUST do what the game tells you or you can't get off that screen or the other guy won't die.
in other words, this "enhanced edition" is a sloppy console port with upgraded textures... oooh wow.
Namco, if you read this... I'd play Ace Combat again if the next one had an option to turn DFM off, and just have classic ace combat controls, and gameplay on a carefully ported game. I'd gladly pay £40 for the next game if it were like that.
there's a point where a game can be innovated too much, and people reject it, and this is a classic example.
I wouldn't recommend it, purely for the fact it's a sloppily made game with too much hand holding going on.

And so, yet another series of great games falls into mediocrity. The best name I can come up with is: Call of Duty - In The Air

This game is very disappointing.
Let me start off by saying that i have been playing Koei games since I was a kid and played Noabunaga's Ambition on Nes. I have played all the RTK games from part 1 and up that had been put out in English so I was excited when this came out in English because Koei has  been skipping English releases of its war games lately and all we have gotten is DW crap.
Why is it disappointing ya might ask? Well its just a basic game, its like they took all the basics that a game like this needed. Sure theirs some fighting and some diplomacy and you can build in your cites but its all at basic levels.
The fighting is so limited all you can really do is pincer attack to in cress damage and use each officers one combat ability they get. Thats it, other then that you just mostly sit there and watch the troops run at each other until its over. No real "grand strategy" built into this so called Grand Strategy game. Pretty much every other game out there has more depth to its combat which is a real shame because this game has next to nothing else in it but the combat.
The only thing that has any depth  is the city building and  truth be told it don't have much to it either. Most cites start out with a few plots of land mostly set in groups of three and you can pick what to build on them. Crafts, farm, or conscripts and wach of these plots of lands can build a few different things that in cress what resources you get. If ya build the right stuff and have big enough city you can pick a "epic" type building for your castle that gives extra bonuses but nothing that special.
Diplomacy is pretty shallow, you end an officer to talk to a kingdom every turn to build up your trust and at certain levels you can ask for troops, ask for an alliance for a few months to a year and at 100% offer to marry the two clans together for an alliance that lasts as long as they stay married. AND thats it.... Yeah really thats it, nothing ever really becomes of the alliance you still have to spend trust to ask for help from each other and nothing to ever suggest two people from your clans are married or any talk of their kinds they have together. Recruiting an officer works pretty much the same way, you send a guy to talk to them for months till they build up enough discontent to turn on their current plan. At 40 they agree not to fight for for 3 months, at 80 they agree to join you if they faceyou in combat within a set amount of months and at 100 you can just get them to come straight over to you. Their is a thing with low end tribes where the clans oaround them can buy them off to pay for them to fight for them and thats it.
Family is just the same as diplomacy you have random kids and they grow up to be officers or of they are females you can make them officers or pick to have them be maidens to marry off. Theirs no real since of it being a clan or family at any point in the game. Just hey we are a clan... then a whole lot of nothing else about it, which is soooo disappointing since clans and family are such a big part of that era in japan's history.
Thats pretty much the game. Yeah thats it..... Even in the Nes  Noabunaga's Ambition had more depth, you could plot and hire nija's to assassinate people or set fire to their supplies or cause riots but in this one you can't do any thing else.
Why are their so many good reviews about the game with very little to say about it? Well people wana talk it up to get others to buy it, they want to show koei that their really is a market for other games besides DW in English and like me they was willing to spend $50 for a sub par game in the hopes that we will get better ones some day. But in all honestly the game is not worth it enless do you want to support other English titles, its just so lacking and boring in every area of the game. <shrugs>

30+ hours now.. and I have decide to do a review for this...

Each turn in this game is 1 month instead of of seasons or years make the game feel very slow at times but once combat is on.. it feels very fast at times...
Everything was done really well but it will feel very repetitive to any new comers of this game serie.
I have played over 30 hours now but i only unified less then 1/4 of Japan on my very first game. So this game will probably rack up the same amount of hours I have played for CK2 sooner or later.
There is a in game achievement system but it doesn't have steam achievement.
Price of this game is also very high like most japanese game that's landed in Steam store.
8.5/10 but I can only recommend to veterns of this serie and hardcore grand strategy lover... Since it's not very friendly to new comer of the serie and it's very pricey(and you won't get a 25% discount for a long time)...

This thing is a piece of freaking art, Monolith really impressed me with this game. It took me about 25 hours to complete the main story line, and it was such a blast. There was never a time where I felt that there was nothing to do, the world of Mordor just had so many things to complete, but it was never overwhelming. The controls were great, they gave you enough time to counter the attacks before you were hit, and the combat system was SO CREATIVE! If you want to go stealth, you can sneak up behind enemies and eliminate them with the help of your dagger, or you can play the sniper and hold right click to draw your, "Spirit bow", which slows time temporarily to assist your aim, and of course, you have the sword used for up close combat. But weapons are not the only source for combat, there is the wraith drain attacks, when near an enemy, you can hold e to do this wierd force-choke style attack that refills your arrows. There are two areas in Mordor: Udun, and Nurn, free for you to roam and explore. And there is the nemesis forge, the nemesis forge allows you to findout more about the Captains and Warchiefs, Captains are much more resilient and proficient compared to other uruks, they have special strengths and weaknesses which can be found out through the nemesis forge, and the Warchiefs are like the Captains of the Captains, like the Captains, the Warchiefs have strengths and abilities, but there are usually multiple captains in the area the Warchief can be located, there are only four Warchiefs in Udun and Nurn, but every time a Captain or Warchief is killed, you get power for it, which are used to unlock abilities, and other Uruks take the place of the dead Captain or Warchief. There are many other things I could cover about this game, but, i'd rather have you find out for your self. Oh yeah, the game and dlc is only like, 19.99 right now.

This game has too many flaws in it to be enjoyable.  This game isn't worthy of the title of Ace Combat.  I want to go in with an open mind but it just has terrible game mechanics.  From planes performing impossible moves to the dog fight not engaging at the correct time, this game can aggrivate even the most hardcore veterans of the Ace Combat series.  The development crew must have been a bunch of guys who grew up with COD and wanted to emulate it to the letter, with bad story telling and just making certain that there is an explosion every 3 seconds.
The story could have been a lot better, but the writers decided to go with the most severly ADD pilot I have ever met and to have no depth with character development.  They also wanted to go for the whole Russia is bad theme that COD has beaten to death and then some.  I mean I get the fact that from the Cold War, Russia has never got rid of their stigma of being evil, but I mean come on, lets see something more interesting.  The main villian of the series lacks a true motive for what he is doing, and, personally, they really needed to expand his backstory.  I got to say it was pretty boring when the AC-130 level came into play, cause I was spoiled by how good COD's version was (I will say that that was my favorite level in COD).  You would think that a game producer who focuses just on aircraft would have a better grasp on this.  I will say that the helicopter missions were definitly interesting and a breath of fresh air, once you died 20 times just trying to get used to the new controls.
The gameplay mechanics are another point in the game that actually hurt it.  The dogfight mode is intersting, but annoying when you lockon a target and face an invincible fighter plane, because the producers want you to go through their house of explosions before you can take him out.  Also I have had this little problem affect me multiple times, I will be in the dogfight mode and the enemy plane nose-dives into the ground, and you would think that that is one less plane I have to worry about. Wrong, because your plane will also quickly follow suit and explode, just because dogfight wants you to have the nose of your aircraft so far up the enemies exhaust, that you could just pull the fuel lines, that you also share the fate due to bad AI pathing.  Also while the cinematic following of the missles is pretty cool, it just detracts from the game and causes you to sit in your chair for an extra 5 seconds, while you could be shooting down the other guys who is in front of you.  Once you come out of it 9 times out of 10, they have escaped.  Also the quicktime events are dumb, they offer no, I repeat no, effect on the game, but their are about 3 out of 20-something quicktime events that will make you fail a mission.
The last major problem I had is that the game isn't that hard.  Changing the difficulty isn't really a test of your skill, like having less ammunition or the AI being smarter, rather it's just how much more that the AI can defy physics and perform outragious moves.  One example is the final dog fight and it has to be done in dogfight mode.  If you break dog fight with the enemy, then the enemy can perform some weird 360-180 backflip, with a double axial from hell and be right on your rear.  Sure it makes it harder but it is just something that isn't that fun to deal with.
The good thing about this game is the normal dogfighting, not that stupid lockon behind them crap.  It was a blast to relive the old system of using the IFF to track down targets and just shoot them down.  That was a method that proved your worth in the old games, where if you couldn't manually track behind your targets and tack them out with missles of guns, you were dead.
If you are a new flyer to the Ace Combat series and were either turned off or interested in the series, I recommend that you get a ps2 and play Ace Combat 5 and/or Ace Combat 0.  The reason is simple, the Ace Combat series is hands down one of the best jet fighter sims out there, and this version was just a disgrace.  Now maybe I'm a guy who just enjoys living in the past, but I can tell you that this game had potential but terrible execution.
Keep those skies clear.
(PS I don't like to put spoliers in my reviews, so I am unable to explain, in this already long review, certain key elements in the story that are just bad.  Also I don't really play multiplayer due to internet problems.  So my review is focused towards those who enjoy the campagin of games.)

I don't normally write reviews but I feel compelled to in this case due to the price tag.  This game is way too expensive by US standards for the graphics and overall mechanics in my opinion.
For someone that likes epic strategy and complex development decisions, I felt Nobunaga falls short; the mechanics felt clunky to me, and the graphics were disappointing.  Unfortunately there are also comparisons to this game being like Total War.  While the strategy elements are better here, for someone that likes unit tactics in battle, Total War is a vastly superior game; this game's combat mechanics (and graphics) are very simplistic.
I am not saying it is a bad game, but I would not pay anywhere near the retail price as it stands today at close to USD $60, or even at the recently discounted price of $48.  Given its development overseeas I'm not sure what the chances are of the price coming down, but I plan to wait for the $20 mark or less...

Pros:
+Ambitious and beautiful game

+Diplomacy seems to be multi-layered

+Has good combat mechanisms built inside

Cons:
-Not enough user feedback on your actions
-Gameplay doesn't get complex at all and becomes quickly very repetetive
-You cannot determine things like facing of your troops -> Way too simplistic UI
-Forces the story down your throat if you deliberately play as some minor faction far far away from Oda Clan
Nobunaga's Ambition is an overall a good game. It seems to include very complex succession mechanisms and character influences on your feudal fiefs. In that aspect it remotely reminds titels like CK2. However it doesn't seem to go all the way there when it comes to diplomacy.
What do you mean "seems", you might ask. Well the game does its best to hide information from you. It doesn't give you that many numbers, when deciding who to lead your castles or armies or wether or not it has some hidden effects somewhere else. And you even cannot decide which way your troops are facing while in combat mode. Everything is so automated that you don't feel like you are in control.
It would be reasonable to ask 60 eur from a PC title if they would improve UI when they imported this  to PC. Now it requires so much extra clicking to get that piece of information that you expect to find in non-existent tooltips. But as everything is so automated, you rarely need to know why things are folding out as they are. This game comes with a manual to explain mechanisms that you never get to actively use unless you really sit down and read it.
Its a good game but pricing is way out there. 30 eur would be more correct if the game wants to compete on its own price tag. It is not however a fully fledged and polished AAA product.

Part one: Gameplay.
Middle Earth - Shadow of Mordor is an open world hack 'n' slash/stealth platformer like Assassin's Creed and Batman - Arkham Asylum. Your primary methods of killing enemies are your sword, which is used in an attack/counter system, and your bow, which is used to snipe enemies in bullet time. Your bow has limited ammo which is regained through pickups and by draining Uruk. Which brings us to the next point, you have a variety of spectral abilities that supplement your powers including: A teleport attack, a stun, an area attack, an attack used to mount creatures, and the ability to brand Uruk and turn them to your side as sleeper agents, using them to bring down Sauron's army from within. I'd say the biggest selling point of this game is the Nemesis system. What is the Nemesis system? Okay, so there are 25 unique Uruk. 20 are Captains, and 5 are Warchiefs. All of these characters have different strengths and weaknesses, as well as some flavour text and their name that say something about their character and role in society. As an example, you might have Ratlug the Butcher. Maybe you interpret his name as meaning he is a cook? Or possibly more sensibly you think he is a skilled and brutal combatant. His motive is "Has gone 3 days without a fight. That's 3 days too many." This further reinforces his role as a ruthless killer. His strengths are Combat Master, meaning he can't be hit with melee, Immune to Ranged (attacks), and Immune to Stealth (attacks). So we're buggered, right? Wrong. His weaknesses are Fear of Caragor (A big cat thing) and Vulnerable to Beasts, which means he gets one shot by Caragor, Graugs (trolls on steroids) and Ghuls (zombies crossed with ants). So we ride in with our Caragor, he tries to run away, but then we pounce on him and rip him to shreds. Unlike every game ever, this boss, along with all 24 other bosses, required a unique approach to kill. You can also brand the Uruk captains, which will turn a portion of the enemies to your team, and unlock some side missions related to helping them climb the ranks of Uruk society. The generic hack and slashing gets repetitive, but not quite boring, after the ~15 hours the main game lasts for. Overall, I give the gameplay a 9/10, mainly down to a lack of palate cleansing quests and activities.
Part two: Story
This is mainly where the game falls flat. It is a generic plot where Talion (your character)'s family is murdered, and then he is murdered. He is brought back to life (unlife?) by the spectre of Celebrimbor (but he doesn't know that). You and him then go on a quest for vengeance against the Black Captains (the guys who murdered you) which are high-ranking servants of Sauron. You find an orc called Ratbag, who allies himself with you, and you help him reach the position of Warchief. Then you go kill the other Warchiefs, while also discovering artifacts that tell you more about Celebrimbor's past. After the other 4 Warchiefs are dead, you draw out the Hammer, one of the Black Captains, who one-shots Ratbag and then attacks you. You kill him. Then a lady called Lithariel takes you to a new map, where you help the Queen of the Shore free her people by unlocking the Brand spell and using it to take over all the Warchiefs in the area. It is then revealed she is possessed by Saruman, so Lithariel breaks her staff which frees her (?). Then you head over to the Tower, the second Black Captain. He is guarded by the Uruk Captain who killed you the most (Or Ratbag if you never died) and a small army of Uruk, which you dispatch with the help of your Branded Warchiefs. The boss fight with the Tower lasts about 2 minutes, all you have to do is stealth Brand him 3 times which is easy and underwhelming. Right after that you go to the Black Gate, which is guarded by 5 Warchiefs (The 5 Talons of the (Black) Hand) and a large army of Uruk, which you kill with the help of your 5 Warchiefs. Then you fight the Black Hand, who is actually Sauron, in an extremely easy series of 3 quick time events, at which point the game ends. There are two story DLCs, the first, Lord of the Hunt or whatever, adds more quests all to do with new beasts like the Caragath and and the Wretched Graug. The second DLC, the Bright Lord, is about Celebrimbor's conquest of Mordor after he captured the one ring. It adds new abilities, most prominently the One Ring, which gives invisibility and unlimited finishers for a duration. The campaign is based on branding an army of Uruk. It ends in an absolutely fantastic boss fight that is very hectic and chaotic that goes as follows: You start with your 5 branded Warchiefs and fight Sauron and a never ending swarm of Uruk. Then he pisses off and makes your Warchiefs go hostile, so you kill them. Then he comes back and brings them all back to life, and you have to fight Sauron and the Warchiefs all at the same time. When you kill Sauron, the One Ring slips off your finger and onto Sauron's at the very last moment, causing your capture, at which point you are murdered by Sauron. Overall I give the story a 6/10. Not very interesting, not very long, and completely non existant in the Bright Lord, but for the most part a tried and tested formula that gives just enough background to justify our protagonist's wanton slaughter of Uruk.
Part three: Overall.
Middle Earth - Shadow of Mordor is a game that does one thing very well and that is being a hack 'n' slash open world game. It is entertaining, it is fun, and it made me want to play the game for 14 hours straight (which I did). It offers a short, if deep, experience that while I thoroughly enjoyed, it doesn't quite reach the threshold of getting 1 hour of fun for every dollar I spend on it. I very much recommend it if you can find it on sale or have a fair bit of money to throw around, but otherwise I'd give it a miss. I am very much hoping that Middle Earth - Shadow of War will prove to be capable of providing me with a more lengthy gameplay experience.

This game is absolutely a must have at full price, let alone for when it often goes on sale for well under ten bucks.
The vast majority of my playtime has been in co=op and it has been a blast. The basic premise is so satisfyingly simple that it is hard for the game to fail based on it alone; Destroy as many baddies as you can, using a fairly large array of weapons and traps.
Figuring out different set ups for different outcomes is just as enjoyable as perfecting one and watching it wreak havoc. My friend's build style leaned more towards utter destruction, let his factory of traps do the work. I, however, enjoyed a more CC style of building. My assembly line of hell became a very effective tool at corralling massive hordes of bad guys until the path was bursting with orcs, then use the push-back glove to send a sea of baddies flying over the edge of the nearest cliff.
that is until we got into the DLC where we used the handy feature that allows you to complete refund all your currency (skulls, naturally) to change up our playstyles whereas I was now Mr. Death and my maze was designed to obliterate all creatures. the maps are well thought out and able to accommodate 1 or 2 players very well (can only speak for up to 2) and most details are considered. You don't often get into situation where you say "I wish this". this games does enough to keep you wanting more, but doesn't give so much that you feel like you're being pandered to or coddled.
If you like wave style games (CoD Zombies, GoW horde mode, etc), tower defense, or even puzzles (figuring out what works with what and where can be interesting) then you'll like this. It is just good ole fashioned fantasy orc bashing, done very well.

A sandbox zombie game where survival and scavenging is the #1 priority. You can build and upgrade a variety of homebases and then do missions from there. You must balance the need for materials to build essential areas like beds, a workshop or medical area with the groups need for food, gas, building materials and ammo. All the while there are sudden events that pop up like helping another survivor group or helping your group with killing a special infected.
The game is solid at its core with the only major gripes being how absolutely stupid the friendly AI is, and variety of the missions.
Some examples of incredibly frustrating AI in a 1-save-perma-death game include:
Friendly AI trying to tank a Big Un and instantly dying.
Friendly AI standing around during sieges, not helping.
Friendly AI not knowing to back up from choke points, preventing you from firebombing, grenading or using any sense of strategy.
Friendly AI finishing a mission, then walking straight home across a path of special infected or hordes, which kill them.
Because the game can sometimes be a tad cheap with car rollovers or hitboxes, especially with the Big Un's 1 hit kill, I wish that there was at least a single save point, but i understand the direction the game is trying to take. You can also get around this by saving a copy of the game file but a more user friendly option should be available.
90/100. A must own for people who love zombie survival and scavenging.

If you're a fan of zombie games even in the slightest, then this is the game for you. This game really hits home on how living in a zombie infested world should feel. If you don't forage for supplies, you die. If you don't keep up on your weapons, you die. If you are not meticulous about getting that last supply crate into the truck before the charging horde reaches you... You die.
State of Decay is a wonderfully done game in the way that it doesn't quite feel like anything else. The idea is that you're on vacation when SHTF and you have to rally other survivors you find to build an encampment to combat the infected. You have to make sure it has good walls, ample food and shelter, and most important of all.. Quick, easy access to nearby supplies. Everything in this game is Finite. You WILL run out of supplies eventually. Blow up too many cars, and you won't have any left to drive. You really have to want to survive in order to get anywhere in this world and this game couldn't have done it any better. There were moments where I had a horde just behind me. I'm 50 yards from the truck. Do I run for it or dart off into a nearby building to try and lose them? Do I drop the bag of supplies I just collected, or hope for the best? Fire off some rounds at the risk of attracting more undead? The choice is yours. This game is entirely open world and completely non-linear. Play how you want.
But you've been warned. How long will you fend off the State of Decay?

Luftrausers is surprisingly good. Incredibly good, even. You start it up for the first time and within a minute of playing it you'll be smiling broadly and wishing that every game could be as viscerally enjoyable as this one.
The controls have been honed to perfection. Simply flying around with the aircraft (is it called a Luftrauser?) is pleasing to the senses. Throughout the game, you'll unlock new parts that you can use to customize your plane, which come with both benefits and drawbacks. Here's where the true brilliance of the design comes in. Each part of the ship has its own instruments to add to the song that plays during the game, and each part has multiple missions that you can only complete with that part. So each combination of parts - and there's at least a hundred - offers a unique experience. To top it all off, every aircraft you can possibly assemble with these components has its own nickname, such as the Nightmare, the Tuberauser, or my current favorite, the Warturtle.
It's cheap, it's intense, and it's extremely challenging. If you like shooters of any kind, consider Luftrausers a solid purchase.

First of all, this game is NOT just a reskin of Terraria, both games are they're own thing, and have their own great qualities. Now that that's out of the way I'll get to the review!
~Introduction~
You start off the game when your the character you created was sleeping in on the day of his graduation. On your way to the event, there is an npc that gives you a short explanation of the basic control mechanics (should you need them). You can take your time and talk to the other npc's there as you desire. When you get to the ceremony The Ruin (I giant mass of tentacles and destruction) attacks and destroys earth in cutscene (that is unskippable; same as every cutscene). You barely escape as the sole survivor of the attack. Your ship then flies to a planet and you begin your journey to defeat The Ruin.
~Overview~
There are 7 playable races, all of which have their own armor's, ships, and blocks. They differences are only asthetic, with the exception of differently shaped ships. Once you fix your said ship, Starbound offers the level of space exploration that you would have hoped for in 'No man's sky'. You can pilot your ship to travel across auto-generated moons, planets, asteroids, and solar systems (which actually have a moving orbit around each other!). You can even interact with other ships that come and go. Some will be hostile, and others friendly; both have equal opportunites to collect loot! Every character has his own unique universe to explore. When you are in the games hub area, you are offered multiple npc's and stores that will provide you with abilities, items, and resources that progress you through the game, and allow you to play it how you choose. Some of these feature's include farming, mechs, furniture, customizable signs, fuel for your ship, food, and other misc. supplies that you may find useful in the early game. I found the main story to be a little lacking (however it is optional after you get your ship repaired). It consists of relatively short missions and a bossfight, followed by a tedious "clue hunt" for items related to the next mission area. The loot system allows you to both craft and/or find all the weapons you want, each having it's own selection. Among the different weapons are swords, hammers, daggers, axes, whips, spears, wands/staves, a variety of gun types, fist weapons, and more. All Armor must be crafted, with the exception of shields which can also be found. The multiplayer is exactly what you would think; you can join your friends whenever you desire, and explore any planet in either of your universes together. No complaint's there, however the interaction between your characters is less pleasing as when the hub changes during the story, these changes are universal (no pun intended) across all your characters. Meaning that after you complete the story once, some things don't really make sense. For example: You are being sent on a mission to recover an item that is literally sitting about 10 feet from the quest giver from the last time you did the mission. Like I said, it makes no sense. On a more positive note, the game has an excellent modding community, due to the fact that modding is relatively easy. I learned how to do it in about 2-3 hours. Installing the mods is even easier, as all you have to do is subscribe to any item on Starbound's workshop, and it will be automatically installed to your game. If you prefer to play vanilla, chucklefish regularly updates the game adding new content fairly often.
~Pro's~
Great Exploration
Well implemented Multiplayer
Ease of Modding
Active Modding Community
Low Graphics Load
Can be played however the user chooses
Open world(s)
New Content still being implemented regularly
~Con's~
Lacking/Tedious Story
Unskippable Cutscenes (can be fixed with a mod)
Some Logical Inconsistency
~Conclusion~
Just like any other game, it isn't perfect, but Starbound goes above and beyond to deliver a game that they feel is worth playing, and this is only added to by the excellent selection of mods. With great multiplayer, and vast amount of well done gameplay features, Starbound is definitely a game worth checking out!

SOM is the story of a man's journey for revenge on "the black hand" who murdered his entire family.
Visuals, Audio, Controls:
The Visuals are rather impressive similar to Assasin's Creed 2 standard.
Audio is good esp with the arrival of orc's war chief/orc taunts.
Controls is not fluid as compared to Assassin's Creed though either because of the in-game design object or overlapping of the same key functions.

Nemesis system is interesting like looking through Dating sites of orcs with stats.

Looking at the
franchise as an outsider it kind of seems like a cult, what with the fanatical devotion and passion it inspires in its followers. I’m happy to say, as a spectacularly average gamer who just completed his first full playthrough (took about 60 hrs), I now understand why that is. This is not your ordinary AAA game, polished to perfection with a carefully scripted path laid out for you. This is a game with solid RPG mechanics under the hood, a visceral combat system up front, and an expansive world encompassing the whole experience.
What surprised me the most about
was the discovery that, despite the difficulty you hear so much about, the game is primarily about exploration. The level design is honestly beyond any game I can think of. The world is massive, with dozens of intricate and diverse areas for you to explore and no loading screens separating it all. This is the only game I’ve played where all of the sprawling vistas decorating the skybox are actual physical locations you can go to, and it begs the question of why that’s so uncommon in gaming. As you progress you’ll discover shortcuts that allow you quick access back to locations it took you hours to reach initially, making travelling through previously cleared areas a lot faster. The ingenuity of these shortcuts will make you want to explore every corner and crevice that much more thoroughly, and really lend a sense of definite scale to everything. There’s also plenty of opportunity for sequence breaking (provided your skills are up to it), since
refuses to shepherd you in a particular direction, instead letting you discover the wonders and dangers of the world for yourself.
Combat is the other major component of the game and it’s simple to grasp but difficult to master. It demands careful management of stamina and timing, but is not as punishing as you might expect. The thing I really like about the combat system is that the enemies are essentially working with the same restrictions you are: they have limited stamina, health, and a clearly defined moveset. You just need to figure out how to exploit that. The hitboxes can be dodgy sometimes, particularly with some of the ridiculously massive bosses, but there is always a way to counter and make up for it.
And what about all the dying? Well, it is true that as a new player you’re going to die a lot. In
, death is the mechanic by which you gain knowledge of the area and enemies until you master both. It’s hard to take it too personally, because the loading screen is lightning fast before you’re deposited back at the last bonfire and it quickly trains you to find the fastest way back to the spot of your previous demise. It’s actually a very clever mechanic, as the game essentially trains you to speed run it.
The difficulty of the game is an interesting thing. While I don’t agree with the fans who insist “it’s not that hard”, I also see where they’re coming from. The challenge in
is very organic: it comes from careful enemy placement, environmental hazards and, of course, huge bosses. All of these things are easily overcome with experience (which you usually get by dying multiple times). Once you understand it though, it seems as natural as breathing and you wonder why it gave you any trouble at all.
if you’re an average gamer wondering if you should check out this infamously hard game, the answer is “YES”. This is a genuinely beautiful game with deep mechanics and it’s no accident that it has made such an impact on the games industry. Buy it now and join the cult of
.

Let me just start by saying that this is a suprisingly fun game. If somebody told me I would spend over 15 hours playing this game I would not believe it. This is a visual novel which means that you basicly play through a story making descisions along the way changing up the story everytime you play it through (which can take between 10-40 minutes). Depending on the path you take you will lead to different endings and a lot of them being... your death.
Throughout the game you will level up different traits, depending on what you choose to focus on different part of the stories will be easier for you to complete and changes your possible paths. If you fail a test it's not the end of the world unless... you die. And even if death comes a lot and often and forces you to restart it's acutally not frustrating, instead it works as a motivator to play differently next time.
With every restart you want to know what happens if you level different traits, completing a trait test you didn't complete the last time. For example, if I become a animal trainer will my pet dog become a great strong guard dog? Or will I be able to tame animals throughout the story? You want to know!
I do understand this game is not for everyone, if you're not a fan of slow/reading heavy games you probably dont want to get this. But if you get a chance to try it, DO SO. Suprisingly fun and of course you want to collect every possible DEATH achievement...

If you are a 20-something with existential nightmares and post-college anxieties then this is the perfect game for you! I won't delve too deeply into the plot but basically Mae is a college dropout returning home to live with her parents in Possum Springs. Upon returning home she quickly learns that everything she knew has since changed and everyone has moved on in one way or another since she left for college. In realizing this Mae's inner turmoil surfaces where she feels as if she is eternally stuck as a teenager and that her life is unmemorable and pointless. The plot circles around these feelings of inadequacy and goes in some unexpected and sometimes wild directions to expand on these concepts but saying anymore is huge spoiler territory. This game does an amazing job portraying that horrible feeling of growing older without growing as a person that many (including myself) experience today. I felt Mae as well as the other characters were incredibly relatable and I thoroughly enjoyed this short but wonderful experience. If you feel like performing some introspection or simply enjoy a well-written slice of life story with a bit of mystery then I would definitely recommend playing Night in the Woods.

I'm someone who likes 'walking simulators' and slow, meditative gameplay. This is the first time I've played a game where I've thought the pacing was consistently far too slow, even for me.
The gameplay itself can also become incredibly tedious. If you like to explore every part of a game and look for hidden areas and achievements you should prepare for frustration. If I like a game I will happily play it over and over again, but the repetitiveness in this game becomes mind numbing. It's like a mobile app that rewards you for checking in each day, but the reward is so low you'll wonder if it's even worth it in the first place...
And it probably isn't. This game punishes you for exploring, and not in the conventional sense: you'll waste so much of your time and be so aware of that wasted time that it may make you want to stop playing altogether,
The reason why I'm so harsh on these two areas is because I really, really liked the story of the game. It hit home harder, perhaps, than any other game I've played. Certain themes were genuinely difficult and even... slightly painful to confront?
In other words, this game is moving. Few games I've played can make that claim.
There are countless other great aspects to this game, including the stunning art direction, entertaining dialogue and chatacters, as well as a great score, so much so that it seems easier to focus on the negatives.
If I can recommend one simple way to hugely improve this game, I would say that movement speed should be massively increased. That way it doesn't become as tedious to walk the same route so often, and it doesn't become as crushing when your triple jump fails and you have to start a platforming section all over again. Other reviewers have also suggested a way to prepare a response in advance before someone finishes speaking like in Oxenfree (which is next on my list).
It makes me sad to say that I cannot recommend this game, at least, not while the pacing issues persist as much as they do. I'm aware that having your character do the same thing over and over is likely alluding to the pace of modern life, but there are ways to make this engaging too. Why do the something in game you could do in real life if neither provides any entertainment?

The concept for Thinking with Time Machine was pretty interesting.  You record yourself doing past actions, so that you have, in essence, one programmable test subject.  This would be pretty cool, but this mechanic is VERY limited in its use.  As opposed to Portal and its sequel,  which allowed you a lot of freedom with the portals, this game sort of lays out how you are supposed to be doing it.  That's another thing: the use of portals is also highly limited.  The portals are really just put there to help you with the time recording thing.
The game really has no tutorial mode, except for a few early levels.  These keep the player from becoming familiar enough with the mechanics that it takes a very long time to work out what you must do in the later test chamber.  This is especially frustrating given the difficulty of the test chamber.
Finally, the storyline of this is really poor.  With this new mechanic, you would think that they might include an interesting story about finding the Time Machine.  Nope.  The storyline is just that Atlas and P-body hijacked GLaDOS, and SHE tells YOU to go back in time to fix it.  Really, it was lackluster.  I know short, aesthetic Hammer maps that have a better storyline.  There is ONE part where the Borealis barges into your test chamber, but it's purely aesthetic and you can't do anything with it.
All in all, Thinking with Time Machine is a cool concept that was poorly executed.  I'd give it a 6/10: fun, but hardly as good as Portal.  This said, with some fixes and added features, it could be really good.

There are challenges on every map. These challenges vary on difficulty and the map itself. The game will go on until you finish all the challenges. I want to like this game REALLY hard, but I just can't. On the surface, it seems like everything you've been yearning for all these years, but it gets the finer aspects of a zombie apocalypse all wrong.
*For starters, this has got to be the most relaxing zombie apocalypse you'll ever play. The zombies are a nuisance, not a threat. In any number. You can take out entire hordes all by yourself, in melee combat, without taking a scratch. No skill required, just spam attacks. The game pretends to have a resource management aspect, but everything is so incredibly abundant - like, two orders of magnitude more abundant than what would start to vaguely resemble something approaching scarcity - that it might as well not be there.
*The combat is incredibly dull. Melee combat (no skill, just spamming buttons) is so effective that firearms are rendered essentially irrelevant. Before long, you'll start dreading being spotted by the zombies, not because they can end your life, but because you'll be locked in another repetitive mashfest for another several minutes.
*In what's perhaps one of the most wrongheaded game design decisions of all time, the authors decided to link resource consumption to real world time. So, if you do the entire game in one sitting, nobody has to eat ever, basically. Not that it would have mattered otherwise, because as already mentioned, everything is plentiful to the point of irrelevancy.
*The game is full of idiosyncrasies that throw you off. For instance, in one mission you're required to barricade a house in preparation for a zombie attack. The house has some 4 small windows that are barricadable, and one HUGE glass window that's not, no reason given. You think the game bugged out and start freaking when the zombies approach (at this point you still don't realize how little threat they represent), only to realize they uncannily ignore the huge window entirely. The game just doesn't consider it an entry point - real world logic be damned - and it doesn't bother to explain that to you. But no matter, now you've barricaded everything, and the mission doesn't end. What's going on? Oh, right. The game forgot to tell you, now that everything's barricaded, you have to get out there and fight them all. Which begs the question of why you're barricading to begin with.
*There's no actual simulation or emergent behavior going on. No matter how many zombies you kill, it's never going to make a global difference; more will be randomly respawned. Zombie and survivor migration, uneven resource depletion of areas, survivor competition, none of that is simulated.
*As a result of everything above, everything you do starts feeling like a chore. No gruelling life or death decisions, no tactics, no strategy, just♥♥♥♥♥♥that needs doing. Might as well stop playing now and go wash that pile of dishes in the sink.

Ultra Street Fighter IV is a great fighting game and a great addition to the Street Fighter series.  The final version of the Street Fighter IV series contains tons of characters, plenty of modes including an arcade mode (hint, hint, Street Fighter V), and a great fighting system.  New faces and old favourites come together for a fast-action favourite that is sure to please fighting game fans.
The only thing I don't like about the Street Fighter IV series is the lack of a multi-level Super Meter like in previous games like the Street Fighter Alpha series.  While this game does have a Super Meter, it requires the super meter to be completely full before being able to do a super move.  This means you have to charge up an entire super meter that would be the equivalent to a level 3 super meter in Street Fighter Alpha 3.  It is very time consuming just to fill up that meter, but there is also the new Revenge Meter where you can execute moves similar to super moves much faster.  However, this meter only fills up when your character is getting attacked.
Regardless, Ultra Street Fighter IV is an enjoyable game with an excellent fighting system.  I recommend it not just for fighting game fans, but for all gamers as well.
