This game was... a nice little suprise. I got this on sale for a whopping 99 cents, and wasn't expecting much. What I got was a fun and addicting little game.
This game will NOT be for everyone. It's an old school top down, very simple, zombie shooter. You start out on a map and simply have to survive wave after wave of increasingly difficult zombies. You pick up powerups from dead zombies, unlock new weapons as you progress, and level up via a simple but nifty little levelling system.
This game is for 1 to 4 players, COOP or online. You kind of need a couple of friends if you want to last a long time. I made it to about level 30 playing solo, but there comes a point where there are just too many zombies, and you'll need some backup.
It's a very simple game with simple graphics and gameplay, but it's actually good mindless fun. You can get most of the Steam achievements pretty easily, and it does get monotonous (Best when played in short bursts), but for 99 cents, is worth it. It only comes with a few maps, so I would suggest getting some more from the Workshop.
All in all? This game isn't for everyone, but I got WAY more than 99 cents worth of fun out of it.

Luftrausers is one of the most satisfying, enthralling arcade shooters to hit the market in recent memory.

This game is freakin fantastic.  Do you want a quick but addictive game that has you constantly saying "maybe just one more try" over and over again?  Then this is made for you.
Luftrausers is an arcade shooter in which you pilot a fighter plane.  The controls are incredibly simple: turn left, turn right, boost, and shoot, but that's all you need to feel like the world's coolest fighter pilot.  When you let off the boost, you enter a very floaty stall that allows you to turn more quickly to get those sharp turns and finely aimed shots off.  Using your boosters in combination with stalling to dodge bullets as they fly at you from all directions is one of the coolest and most gratifying things I have experienced in a game recently.
What makes this game really great is the ability to customize your plane.  As you play, you earn parts that allow you to choose your plane's weapon, body, and engine, all of which have wildly different attributes that greatly affect the way that the plane works.  This lets you mess around and customize your play style, which I find to be incredibly fun.  Each part has its own missions/challenges for you to complete (ex: Kill 10 enemies without shooting them).  These missions help you level up faster and earn more parts, so you are encouraged to keep changing things and completing different missions instead of just sticking to one plane and never changing it.
Let's see, what else is great about this game?  Well, the art style is lovely and the soundtrack is incredible.  What's even cooler is that different combinations of plane parts have subtle affects on both the art and the soundtrack!
So, do I recommend Luftrausers?  Absolutely and wholeheartedly!  This game is so addictive that it will have you playing for hours, and for $10, I think that's a great deal.
Still not convinced?  You can play a free version of this game here:
It doesn't have nearly as many features, but it can give you a good idea of what the gameplay is like.

As of June 16, 2017, the game is very playable, although there is some content that still needs refining and elaboration in order to finish it properly. This game on the whole does not quite measure up to Terraria for me, due in part to what appears to be a stronger focus on exploration rather than construction, but there are very few games that will do what Terraria has done, and Starbound is a very good spiritual successor in this line of 2D arcade ludological playgrounds. I commend Chucklefish, and hope they continue to make forays into this style of game.

I first got a copy of starbound a while back, and it had alot of potential in it's beta stage. Couple months ago, the 1.0 update released for starbound so I decided to give it another play and I have to say, the guys over at Chucklefish Games blew my mind. They managed to add so much more into the game, making the entire experience just that much better.
The story itself isn’t the most complex or mind-blowing, but the universe that the developers built to tell it in is overflowing with character and detail. Each of the six sentient races has a unique culture, architectural style, and ongoing conflict that must be resolved in order to save the galaxy.
Yet they weren’t vain enough to force us into it, so all of that story is optional. There’s nothing to stop you from going off and setting your own exploration or building goals in traditional Minecraft or Terraria fashion.
Overall, Starbound excels as a exploration and crafting game, as a 2D platformer with varied and engaging combat. It can feel overwhelmingly time consuming and punishing in the first few hours, but the freedom to uncover these small secrets of the universe and make its worlds your own is worth the wait, and the expert fashion in which Starbound binds all of its sides together makes it truly special.

One of the more unique and fun strategy games I've played. I've always been a fan of Koei's work in the Samurai and Dynasty Warriors series. While I've wanted to get into the series, I've made the mistake of using the older games as sorta my original starting ground and couldn't make sense of it.
Now I'm not saying that this game is casual, but it's definitely a lot easier to get used to how controls work now. Visuals are pretty, and it's pretty fun to slowly watch your towns grow as time passes and you become more powerful.
As for battles, granted I must admit I've not quite gotten the hang of it yet, but it's fairly complex battle tactics far as I can tell. And sometimes you do get lucky and overcome a bigger opponent and feel like the king of the world.
For the history buffs such as myself, this game really places historical knowledge more at the forefront unlike the Warriors series. The events telling the lives of different warriors and lords is always enjoyable to learn. And as for the CG movies and events, they're rather well done.
While it's not perfect, I feel comfortable recommending this game to near anyone who wants to try a strategy in general.

Why you should play Long Live the Queen:
1. You can dress up as a magical girl!
2. Even if you win once, there are a lot of different things which you might want to explore. The path I took meant I missed out on some interesting stuff, even if I won in the end. Replayability is great in a game like this.
3. There are a lot of ways to win (and a lot of ways to lose). Saving a lot helps, and the game is built in such a way that you can get feedback on what choices you should have made. And the game auto-saves for you if you forget to save at a crucial point.
4. It's a game which, on the surface, seems really easy, but requires a lot of strategy to work, especially if you're aiming for a certain kind of queen. It's not only what skills you want to invest in which matter, but your mood. You want a queen who can act like a queen? Good luck with that, because only 2 out of the 8 moods (excluding Injured and Neutral, which are hard to get) aren't negative towards that feature, and it's hard to get those said moods. Figuring out what skills you want to invest in and how much is crucial if you want to succeed.
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes interesting strategy games, and want to see how hard it is to be a princess.

Lets start by saying that by buying CZ you get three games. Multiplayer Condition Zero & CS 1.6(If you don't have it already) and singleplayer CZ Deleted Scenes. As far as I'm concerned, for multi, it's better to play CS 1.6. Condition Zero doesn't even look that good with "better" skins and textures. More people play CS 1.6 so it's easier to find servers too. Also, i think that overall, 1.6 is a better game. Now... it's worth very much to buy this for Deleted Scenes. Everyone who ever thought to themselves how cool it would be if CS had a singlep. campaign... you will wonder no more. You fly around the entire world, there is a mission on almost every continent. It's hard, but good, plenty of meds and ammo lie around so even on the hardest difficulty surviving shouldn't be a problem, rather a challenge sometimes. There are around 18 missions and all of them are good/great. To be honest I expected much less from Deleted Scenes and I was pleasantly surprised. I would recommend it to anyone who still enjoys GoldSrc games. Just remember to switch off that damn vertical synchronisation before you'll start playing. It's on by default, made me move like an elephant with all that input lag ;)
PS: If you decide to play on hard from the start, just remember to play it like regular CS. Don't rush, pick around the corners and obstacles alot and quick, reload only when safe, always aim heads, shoot mainly bursts or single shots, try not to get shot and this will be a walk in the park. Park full of terrorists that is. Also, after you'll finish all of the main missions, there will still remain few undone on the world map, bonus ones, be sure to finish them too, they are  interesting and a little different than the rest. Like "Run!" mission or "Miami Heat".

One of the best games in my library. This map is BY FAR much more immersive and realistic than Dayz's map. Dayz feels like you're limited to just one big forest and a couple of towns with no supplies left. However, in miscreated, it doesn't feel like you're limited to a tiny island, it feels like your limited to an entire country. From the enourmous and highly detailed city, to the comfortable little towns, to the forests, to a massive cave and underground system, to the huge military air base with guns and vehicles galore, Miscreated just nails the map like no other game I've seen before. Now to the community. I've heard a ton of people say that the community that plays this game is full of toxic roleplaying 12 year olds who only exist to joke about your mom. But from what I've seen from my 8.6 hours on record, this game is full of players who are willing to befriend you to make a team, and eventually you'll find yourselves at the top, with all of the weapons, bases, and teammates you would have ever wanted. The graphics in this game are more than amazing, and they surprisingly look good and run well on a potato like my PC. Let me just put it this way... This game is so ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful, my desktop background is a screenshot of the enourmous city from this game. Verdict: Whether it's on sale or not, this game is an absolute must have for all of you who love exploring a huge open world, befriending other players (or not) and surviving in the unforgiving world of Miscreated... It's a permadeath, so "unforgiving" shouldn't be a surprise.

I regret paying full price for this game for the following reasons:
First, a minor detail:  the game never saves your display preferences.  I need to go into the options to make it full screen with my monitors resolution every time I start playing.
This game is a real time / turn based hybrid.  Once a month, you go into council.  If you are doing something important, council interrupts.  It can even interrupt battles you are currently leading.  When this happens, you are given a set of menus.  Each month I find myself checking every menu.  I start with development, then move down the list in a very repetitive manner.  It gets to be a grind.
Battles are determined mostly by army size and officer.  That is because there are only three types of units, spears, horseman, and musketeers (eventually).  The quantities of each unit are based on the total army size, not any personal decision.  There are buildings that can make them better, but it really doesn't matter, because they all play the same.  Every army is a rectangle composed of people if you zoom in far enough, and they move towards other rectangles on a plain battle map.  Then the officers use abilities and one side wins.  You could use tactics, but most of the time I just let the AI handle it, because the sphere of the battle rarely ever encompasses all the units participating in it (a unit of 1000 with a unit of 10000 behind it could get slaughtered, and the battle mechanics won't always acknowledge the 10,000 until the 1000 is gone).
Historical events are a farse.  The game has no adaptability built in whatsoever, which is strange, based on how the events play out.  If you make one mistake (accidently take something you aren't supposed to, make an alliance with someone you are supposed to fight, etc.), the historical questline for the clan is completely derailed.  The longer the chain, the more difficult it is to prevent derailment, because even if you don't screw it up, the AI can, and often will.  Somehow you have to know what the entire questline requires before the questline starts.  An example:  the name of the game is based on Oda Nobunaga.  This questline can be derailed in about 1000 different ways.  Fastest way to derail it:  enticing a nearby officer who is spectacular to join you before you finish the first two quests.  If he isn't a part of his starting clan, your events can't work.  Also, this quest chain is very long, and you can't expand at all near the beginning.  Any expansion (including building fortresses) derails it.  The AI derails it on their own.  Events that are supposed to fire won't because a clan got wiped out, or it isn't holding the right province.  That would all be forgiveable, if the historical events didn't show that they can just manipulate the game to whatever shape they want.  In one Oda event, the Imagawa just take one of your fortresses, no fighting involved.  In others, clans spring up from nothing.  If they can do either of those things, why couldn't they adapt to what the player has done?
The building system is difficult to understand.  I only just figured out last night that castle facilities (which are labeled as equipment in the help menu), require specific development levels to work.  You can't know this easily because the help menu doesn't explain the build requirements outright (no other castle structure requires development), and you can't select the pulldown menu to see the choices (and the requirements), until you can afford one.  I found out last night that you can hover over a castle or fortress, and sometimes, if they might be able to make one, a list of possible facilities appears.
I could go on about how disappointing this game is, but I'll stop here.  There is very little community support for this game so far.  You can't even easily google things to find answers.  If you want a grand strategy that is very challenging, far more diverse, and has a Library of Congress level of community support, check out Europa Universalis 4.  800 hours in and I still don't feel bored with it.

Nobunaga's ambition: Sphere of influence is a masterpiece, essentially a product of over 30 years of development. There are so many wonderful things about the game, but for me, the biggest success it's how I actually learnt quite a bit (and started to become more interested) in this period of Japanese history and the key characters in it.
One of the most brilliant parts of the game is how it is designed to allow players to effectively set up automation. On the surface, many new players might wonder why certain things (the resource model, battle system, generation of troops etc) seem so different to other similar games. But play longer, and you'll realise the incredible design philosophy of the game. Many similar games suffer from ''big empire syndrome'', while Nobunaga's ambition is incredibly fun both for small and big empires - due to the ability to set up effective delegation. The game shifts from micromanagement of individual units and bases to overall management of provinces and grand strategy. This includes coordinating huge attacks (eg: 100,000 soldiers) from multiple bases and allies.
Another astonishing idea in the game is the design of alliances. Unlike many games, in this game a player would often truly help allies (instead of taking advantage of them or planning a backstep). Marriage alliances are permanent and coalitions can be formed, where allies help each other to take out larger empires. It is almost like a movie or real history, where an alliance of desperate armies unite to defeat the enemy. You can win the game with having active allies (instead of having to betray them and conquer their lands)
Similar to the Romance of the Three Kingdoms series, the other thing I really like is the ability to pick any clan in the game to play (instead of being forced to play one side). It's awesome trying to defy history, such as stopping Nobunaga from trying to conquer Japan. There are also many other features such as the ability to create custom officers, clans and change BG music settings.

Overall, I totally recommend the game - I would rank it probably among the top three games I've ever played.

Stopped playing during the tutorial level for two reasons:
1. In a high paced fast air combat game, is it REALLY a good idea to have a tutorial that freezes the game to display a message? I failed the first mission a number of times due to this.
2. Dogfight Mode - What the hell is this? A gross over-simplfication of flight mechanics to create a "YEAH EXPLOSIONS WOO" montage. I'm sorry, that's not why I play games, least of all flight sims, I don't want my hand held and the mechanics dumbed down to the point of infantile.
Also, Quick Time Events are a cancer that turns interactive video games into (in the words of Mr Yahtzee) "PRESS X TO NOT DIE" movies. Quick Time Events make up the bulk of maneuvers and avoidance techinques and having important aspects of a flight action game reduced to such simplistic levels is frankly painful.
Now, don't get me wrong, I'm no flight sim anorak, but the bit of game I experienced made me feel like I was largely watching a vaguely interactive movie. The flight mechanics themselves seemed fairly alright, but are heavily bogged down by unnecessary gameplay mechanics to oversimplify dogfighting to the point of being banal. Enemy on your tail? complete the pseudo QTE and automagically maneuver behind the enemy, rather than you know, actually using skill to outmaneuver.
Other reviewers compare this to COD in the sky, maybe that's true, but at least COD doesn't make you enter a CQC mode to shoot someone in the face at point blank range. Imagine how frustrating that would be?

My only tip to you if you decide do play is to stick to one of your 2 main friends from beginning to end to see all their scenes (since going out with them is what usually moves the days forward). I love Monolith. I've loved them since way back when they made Blood. They have always made solid games with interesting twists, such as F.E.A.R. and first-person slow-mo, and Condemned: Criminal Origins with its melee and crime investigation focus. They did it again with Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor.
Shadow of Mordor is a third-person action game that plays like a combination of Assassin's Creed and Batman: Arkham Asylum. In the Assassin's Creed vein, there is a lot of climbing on buildings, sneaking around, stabbing orcs, interrogating informants, and finding collectibles. Shadow of Mordor does all of these better than Assassin's Creed has in the past. The climbing feels better and it's more obvious where you can and cannot climb. The stealth makes more sense, as breaking line of sight gives a ghostly outline to show where you were last spotted. This makes following enemies seem less omniscient and not unlimited in numbers, while still presenting overwhelming amounts of enemies. The informants are also better done in Shadow of Mordor. Taking a page from the Arkham games, information on your particular target can be gained by grabbing a particular orc, instead of tediously following NPCs, or (even worse) innately somehow knowing everything about your enemy from the start. This last one is something Assassin's Creed has botched badly in the last couple games.
Taking pages from Arkham, the combat in Mordor is very much influenced by those games, with the same attack, counter, evade, and stun face buttons. It's a well-done imitation, and I found that my skills learned from the Arkham games translated perfectly to Mordor. Also taking a page from Arkham's books, the collectibles include bits of Middle-earth lore which makes them something that (as a Middle-earth fan) I want to collect, rather than just boxes to check to completionists.
What Mordor does that neither of those games do is introduce the nemesis system. You see, true to Middle-earth lore, Uruk-hai lead the orcs and they are nasty. They're mean, they fight each other, and power is the rule of law. In the game, there are around 20 Uruk captains. They all have unique names. They all have a unique mix of strengths, weaknesses, fears, and hatreds. For example, a particular captain might be invulnerable to stealth attacks, weak against fire, afraid of Caragoar (large four-legged beast), and a hatred of losing. This would mean that stealth is useless against him, and he will regenerate his health if you take his health down but not out, but fire will do more damage, and he'll lose all of his strengths and hatreds if he sees a Caragoar.
Controlling the 20 something Uruk captains are five warchiefs, with more power and unique attributes themselves. They also have bodyguards, which are Uruk captains. Taking on a warchief without accounting for their bodyguards is a good way to find yourself fighting a lot of powerful Uruk. But you don't know any of these attributes or command hierarchy from the start. You don't even know these Uruk's names. You have to collect intel to learn these things. You can go into these fights blind, but it's much easier when you know what to expect and who might show up. Later in the game, you can exploit the command hierarchy by turning bodyguards against their warchief, or turning warchiefs and captains against each other.
Reading this, none of it might sound particularly compelling, but it is so well done that it makes the entire game. The named Uruk must have thousands of lines of dialog because repeat encounters result in them bringing up things that I had done to them in the past. Where Assassin's Creed forced me to collect intel just to put me in the same sneak, murder, run away cycle, Mordor made intel optional, and made the unique Uruk attributes a way of forcing me to be creative with my approach. The nemesis system created stories in Mordor that few games can replicate even with crafted encounters. I've written up a great example of one of these stories involving Orthog the Crafty at my blog.
Despite all of these strengths, Mordor isn't perfect. In fact, where it is lacking is in the crafted story. You play as Talion, and, right from the start, your wife and son are fridged and you're killed by a minion of Sauron. However, you learn that Talion can't die because he's possessed by a wraith. The wraith doesn't know who he is, but his power keeps Talion from dying in his quest for revenge. The story isn't particularly bad in itself, but it suffers from too much fan service. You run into a handful of antagonists modeled accurately from their characters in the Lord of the Rings movie trilogy who seem to just pop up for no good reason. Or at least, not good enough reasons. It's a bummer, because I loved all of the collectibles and their stories and found them much more interesting than dragging out movie characters for the apparent purpose of saying "HEY THIS GAME IS LIKE THOSE MOVIES! REMEMBER THOSE?" It's the movie poster cover art on the latest print of a classic novel. Tacky and unnecessary. The game itself stands alone great without the ham-fisted cameos.
The game ends weakly, and leaves the doors wide swinging open for the sequel, and I personally cannot wait. Maybe they'll get the story right next time, but if they don't, I'll hope to make my own, better stories with an improved nemesis system. Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is one of those rare games where the gameplay mechanics create better, more interesting stories than what was written for it, and I hope that we see more of the nemesis system in these type of open world action games in the future.

This game is deceptively simple. There are three main components, emotions, skills, and events/decisions. At first it seems like one of those games where you just have to get your stats up high enough to get through. However, all of the aspects are linked. You need the right stats to unlock possible paths, your actions affect your mood, and your mood determines what skills you can level up the most easily. And there are many different viable options, each mood gives different bonuses and penalties to training, each skillset will unlock a different option, and each option has a different affect on your game. However, that doesn't mean it's easy to find options that will get you through the game. Having now clocked up over 31 days of survival and 20 hours of gameplay I thought it was a good time to get a review in the bag.
I’ve been playing Beta 0.21 for the past week or so now and I’ve been watching video reviews and gameplay for months. This game appeals to me because (besides my interest in the outdoors and survival) it presents a challenge that’s a far cry away from the regular FPS’s that I usually indulge my gaming appetite in.
I’m well aware that this isn’t a full game – it’s in beta. It’s very much playable but there are a lot of glitches and bugs! For instance, Stingrays don’t like sandbanks – they magically swim through them and into the scenery (so don’t go spearing them because you’ll lose it). On another occasion while messing around with Sharks in shallow water I got bitten and magically beamed some distance off the island and had to make a daring swim back to shore. Never the less, the game is very playable, very likeable and very addictive.
My machine runs comfortably with the settings on ‘high’ in terms of graphics, I’ve noticed no lag at all. Framerates are smooth and the resolution is turned up. Volumetric clouds are on and I’m still not having any dramas. I’m running an i5-4670 with a GTX 760 graphics card. There is some noticeable delay in some scenery parts loading when you ‘continue’ a saved game but other than that I’ve had no issues.
The gameplay is all first person and is very playable. There are some nice shadows, the water looks absolutely stunning and the textures above and below the water are all extremely beautiful. The atmospheric effects are very nice as how the environment works at night, during the day and during rain. I particularly like the shadows cast by environment objects when the moon’s out. The whole game environment is very visually pleasing. The draw distance is very low but I suspect this is deliberate to enhance the mystery in the setting and to further add challenge to the navigational element of the gameplay. There is no in-game map and you have to find a compass – I thought this was a genius element of the gameplay and really makes it interesting.
Having said that I’ve explored every single island and have figured out that the map is a 5 x 5 set of islands all diagonal to each other in terms of compass points (NE, SW, SE and NW). I managed to create my own map (pen and paper) using the compass and now find it easy to navigate from one side to another. The gameplay area is surrounded by a row of connected fishing buoys. I have tried travelling beyond them but it seems you simply go on forever in an endless sea of blue.
The controls of the game aren’t new – typical “w,s,d and a” format for movement with other buttons for inventory, actions and similar. All the keys are in close proximity to each other from default so there was no need to fiddle around with the control assignments before getting stuck in. The game is about survival so many of the tasks are monotonous such as collecting wood, collecting materials for lashings and similar activities. However, there’s a bazaar sense of achievement throughout doing all this. Building shelter, hunting fish and cooking them – there’s a virtual ‘manliness’ to the game that although apart from the very first few minutes, it lacks any story from what I can gather the mechanics and gameplay combined allow to you get lost in making your own story – the character you play remains nameless; I’m sure that’s not accidental.
This is one of the most fascinating and addictive things I think. I have come back to the game days on end because I’m thinking about getting those resources I spotted on the island in the bottom most corner or planning how I might actually kill a shark. The replay value even in beta is great. I’m hoping there is an ‘ending’ to the game such as being rescued but on the other hand I hope not. The simplicity and consistent goal of surviving (not letting your health, hunger, thirst or tiredness reach zero) of this game is where it’s pleasure lies. The four bars that represent your condition lend themselves to your style of gameplay. Full bars means I can explore, low bars means I have to make camp and start eating.
Although resources throughout the game (normal setting) are plentiful, there are times I have found myself scurrying up palm trees to grab coconuts to quench my building thirst which fastens the pace of the gameplay every so often. This resource management makes you become resourceful by nature and managing those bars effectively also delivers a satisfying sense of achievement. I find myself checking I have some kit with me before venturing off to other islands. This adds to the dynamic gameplay making ‘Stranded Deep’ more than just an exploration game.
The Shark sound effects are also very nicely done. When the prowling, finned beasts are in close proximity (regardless of being in the sea or not) a beastly, demonic tune plays to let you know. A nice touch that keeps you on your toes. The natural environmental sounds throughout also provide a perfect backdrop to the lush, tropical setting ‘Stranded Deep’ features the character in. You’ll find water life varies with location and depth of the water too. These sound effects only enhance the gameplay experience, especially when underwater. I get a genuine sense of dread when swimming and find myself automatically making a b-line straight for the shore when I hear the sound of approaching teeth.
I admit I was a little disappointed to have discovered the apparent linearity of the islands and that there were so few. However, the mechanics of the game; using an axe, building your own tools, the in-game character must have read a whole boat load of SAS Survival books and Ray Mears before getting on that plane!
There are elements of the game apart from graphically that need much refinement. I’m finding it next to impossible to find the various wrecks which are hidden underwater available to explore because the character simply doesn’t hold their breath for long enough. At times I’ve also found that the persistent thirst for blood by sharks around certain islands does interrupt the player’s micro goals of the gameplay too, such as exploring the waters. I’m hoping these will be ironed out as the beta develops.
I haven’t really played any similar games so there’s little benchmark for comparison. However, I’m loving ‘Stranded Deep’ at the moment and I’m excited that I made a small investment in a developing game and a developing world. If it’s this good at beta 0.2, I have high expectations for the full game release!
If you’re contemplating buying it, you won’t be disappointed. Just be prepared, it’s far from perfect, there are glitches (many of which you can take advantage of) and issues but the experience is none the less entertaining, enjoyable and leaves you with a strong sense of achievement and curiosity as to what really lies in the deep.
Great game, massive well done to the developer(s) – looking forward to seeing more!
Edit: Having written the review above I've discovered the "cartographer" and the growing community of island developers. This really has changed the playing field. You can edit existing islands, create new ones and download custom made maps (the best part) and islands. The game really is worth getting just for this!

First of all, this game is NOT just a reskin of Terraria, both games are they're own thing, and have their own great qualities. Now that that's out of the way I'll get to the review!
~Introduction~
You start off the game when your the character you created was sleeping in on the day of his graduation. On your way to the event, there is an npc that gives you a short explanation of the basic control mechanics (should you need them). You can take your time and talk to the other npc's there as you desire. When you get to the ceremony The Ruin (I giant mass of tentacles and destruction) attacks and destroys earth in cutscene (that is unskippable; same as every cutscene). You barely escape as the sole survivor of the attack. Your ship then flies to a planet and you begin your journey to defeat The Ruin.
~Overview~
There are 7 playable races, all of which have their own armor's, ships, and blocks. They differences are only asthetic, with the exception of differently shaped ships. Once you fix your said ship, Starbound offers the level of space exploration that you would have hoped for in 'No man's sky'. You can pilot your ship to travel across auto-generated moons, planets, asteroids, and solar systems (which actually have a moving orbit around each other!). You can even interact with other ships that come and go. Some will be hostile, and others friendly; both have equal opportunites to collect loot! Every character has his own unique universe to explore. When you are in the games hub area, you are offered multiple npc's and stores that will provide you with abilities, items, and resources that progress you through the game, and allow you to play it how you choose. Some of these feature's include farming, mechs, furniture, customizable signs, fuel for your ship, food, and other misc. supplies that you may find useful in the early game. I found the main story to be a little lacking (however it is optional after you get your ship repaired). It consists of relatively short missions and a bossfight, followed by a tedious "clue hunt" for items related to the next mission area. The loot system allows you to both craft and/or find all the weapons you want, each having it's own selection. Among the different weapons are swords, hammers, daggers, axes, whips, spears, wands/staves, a variety of gun types, fist weapons, and more. All Armor must be crafted, with the exception of shields which can also be found. The multiplayer is exactly what you would think; you can join your friends whenever you desire, and explore any planet in either of your universes together. No complaint's there, however the interaction between your characters is less pleasing as when the hub changes during the story, these changes are universal (no pun intended) across all your characters. Meaning that after you complete the story once, some things don't really make sense. For example: You are being sent on a mission to recover an item that is literally sitting about 10 feet from the quest giver from the last time you did the mission. Like I said, it makes no sense. On a more positive note, the game has an excellent modding community, due to the fact that modding is relatively easy. I learned how to do it in about 2-3 hours. Installing the mods is even easier, as all you have to do is subscribe to any item on Starbound's workshop, and it will be automatically installed to your game. If you prefer to play vanilla, chucklefish regularly updates the game adding new content fairly often.
~Pro's~
Great Exploration
Well implemented Multiplayer
Ease of Modding
Active Modding Community
Low Graphics Load
Can be played however the user chooses
Open world(s)
New Content still being implemented regularly
~Con's~
Lacking/Tedious Story
Unskippable Cutscenes (can be fixed with a mod)
Some Logical Inconsistency
~Conclusion~
Just like any other game, it isn't perfect, but Starbound goes above and beyond to deliver a game that they feel is worth playing, and this is only added to by the excellent selection of mods. With great multiplayer, and vast amount of well done gameplay features, Starbound is definitely a game worth checking out!

Advice/IMPORTANT INFO for people completely new to fighting games:
My "experience" in "fighting games" is limited only to the Super Smash Bros. games, and I can tell you that the sheer number of mechanics in this game is intimidating (50 parts to just the tutorial!!). For this reason, I must say that the learning curve is pretty darn steep. This game is NOT for players with short attention spans (e.g. immature CoD/CSGO players, casual players in general). The controls will feel wonky and unintuitive if you're also coming from Smash Bros. because the mindset you have to adopt is COMPLETELY different. It still feels that way, but given the gameplay videos I've seen on YouTube, I really think that the effort will pay off in the end.
Optimization/Graphics:
The game runs at a locked 60fps (because button timings need to be very precise with only a few frames). It seems to run well for most people, but for those on lower-end systems (like me with Intel HD graphics), you're going to need some tweaking in the files because the graphics settings in-game are more of a hindrance than they are helpful. Once the tweaking is done, the game should run very smoothly. In my opinion, the tweaks don't take too much away from the overall look because of the brilliant art style and cel-shaded graphics.
Music:
It's good and makes sense for this game, but as a rather completely new player, I don't want to hear the same song over and over again when I'm struggling my way through the 50-step tutorial. Highly polished Jet action, with a thin Single Player and fun Multiplayer. Well worth the money when purchased 75% off.
Great fans of the series may consider this a spin-off rather than a 'classic' Ace Combat game, and they would be right. With  the addition of Dogfight Mode the creators clearly tried to make a more visceral, cinematic experience, and they did succeed in that regard. Only after playing this game did I realize that the previous iterations in the series often reduced you to repetitive battles against large collections of HUD indicators, but here the designers have tried to get the action as in-your-face as possible. You can see what you are fighting, what your weapons are doing to it. The camera shows your plane in all it's glory, missiles launching, bomb bays opening and guns firing. This is the best-looking Ace Combat yet.
Complaints about this game being the Call of Duty of the series mostly stem from the storyline, which hits all the appropriate but tired old cliche's. The story is set in the real world rather than the 'Strangereal' alternate reality of previous installments, seemingly to make the story more realistic and relatable. But it is sadly not exploited to the fullest. All characters and factions could as well have been their Strangereal analogues, making the choice to do a standard 'America vs rogue Russians' setup all the more puzzling. The only real benefits from this new setting are the locations (beautiful renditions of several cities) and the use of proper markings on the aircraft. Otherwise, both setting and story seem underused yet at the same time conspire to make the Singleplayer Campaign dull and the characters (while animated and voiced acted well) undeveloped.
As far as equal gender representation goes, a grand total of 1 (one) woman is present. She may be considered part of the main cast and is portrayed as a strong, mature female person amongst the group of male characters. Sadly she is the playable character only once during the story, and in the end is reduced to the 'female admiration reward' without the writers even bothering to introduce a proper romantic subtext.
The multiplayer is what will ultimately redeem this game for many people. It is well designed and fun to play, the designers clearly made a good effort to make this more than a simple tack-on deathmatch with a couple of maps. Multiple modes are available, and there are rankings, call signs, aircraft and perks to be unlocked. Certainly one of the best mutiplayer modes for a flight sim I've ever seen.
Even if you already own this game on console (as I do), the improved graphics, added planes and skins and the ability to use a proper flight stick make this worth it. If you still need ancoragement, think about this: the game, when discounted, probably costs less than all the DLC you would need to buy for the console version to get the same content.

The game is great, and there's a lot of reviews already, but I thought I'd give it a go , from a point of view of a CK2 player.
- Compared to the centuries spanning CK2, NA:SoI focuses on a sort period of time, the Sengoku free for all following the fall of the Shogunate.
- Like in CK2, Historic positions are hugely imbalanced. You CAN start with a small clan surrounded by huge ones, and you'll be crushed, as is logical.
Similar to CK2 demesne limit, you can't rule everything directly, but the game is very generous, allowing you to manage everything in a given radius from your homebase. It is not until you reach a huge size that you need to resort to regents.
However, you also lose controls of the armies of your regents, being only able to give them general directives like "Stay put"/"Attack this clan"/ "Support this province"
The economical management itself is pretty straightforward: develop a mix between crops/cash/soldiers and improve your infrastructure. The "Auto council" does a good job if you feel lazy.
Like CK2, Officers are at the heart of the game, but in a different way. Almost all actions require an officer to perform it, so you need a pool of retainers to conduct your armies and develop your realm.
Each officers has stats (War vs Economy) and a loyalty rating. In theory, low loyalty officers can betray you if bought by a rival clan (up to defecting with their castle, if there were alone in there), but in practice, it's merely an annoyance.
Don't be afraid, no retainer is going to try to plot to assassinate your heir or launch a full fledged rebellion.
You can play a marriage game too, , in order to secure permanent alliances or make a promising officer you kin. But you will never inherit land that way
Japan is in the middle of a civil war so might makes right. You can attack anyone without any casus belli.
The only thing is that the Emperor can force a 6 months truce if someone bribed him enough.
Likewise, you can abdicate and choose your successor anytime you like.
No surprise, NA:SoI is much more detailed and tactical than CK2. Even without going into Real Time mode, the mechanics of NA makes war very interesting.
- Armies can only travel on the roadnetwork, and a maximum of 3 armies can fight at a single node:
This "simple" mechanics is enough to demonstrate the importance of chokepoints and an efficient road network. A strong fortress at the right place can defend access to a whole region.
- Supplies. Soldiers leave base with 120 days worth of supplies and refill at each friendly base. This makes it very difficult to rush behind enemy lines and attackers may have to cancel a siege if it's progressing too slow.
in constrast with CK2 dynamic generic events, events in NA:SoI are both historical and tightly scripted.
Playing to recreate history makes it very awkward, since a moderatly competent player will significantly outperform history and will then need to wait for the "correct" date while refraining from expanding too much.
Some quests are also "unnattural" in the sense that they make you do things that would be suicidal.
Still, any fan of Japanese history will want to trigger Honnoji's Incident and others shattering events.
I'd never tought I'd say that, but NA:SoI makes me long for Paradox's UI. :)
For a game that relies so much on retainers, the interface for sorting through them is a nightmare, with information inconsistently split on several tabs.
Long story short, the game needs an officer search engine ...
Worth.

Through a retro styled theme,
does what many other zombie survival games can't. It brings thrills and fun into the realm of an already bloated genre that verge on impossible, annoying, complex, or expensive. For the low low price of $1,49, and for a two-pack no less, you will most certainly be entertained for long periods of time. Take a step back into the late 1990s. Experience gaming through its purest lens. This is honestly a great little title that you can play with any friend.
Don't let the term "zombie survival" and "low price" detract you from picking up this game, however. Where games like
and
are more prominent and come to mind, this game - of course - doesn't compare. What it has, though, definitely makes up for what it lacks. There is a huge amount of content that is offered: a vast amount of options in terms of guns and turrets. Various enemies that you have to adapt to; many maps as well. Strategising comes down to a "T" if you really want to master the game and get all the achievements.
There is also a Leaderboard, where the best players have survived over 300+ nights. Challenge yourself in this aspect and, in the end, see why this game will give you all the bang for your buck.
+ Custom maps!
+ Day and night cycle
+ Leaderboard challenges!
+ Various maps to choose from
+ The soundtracks actually aren't that bad
+ You can't go wrong with a retro styled game
+ Shoot, shoot, and shoot - that's all there is to it
+ Achievements and trading cards are always a bonus
+ Good soudtrack that doesn't take away from quality of game
+ Simple graphics and sounds effects makes for great gameplay
+ Multiplayer option offers even more fun with friends at a cheap cost
+ Very straightforward, no tricks or gimmicks when it comes to a zombie survival game
+ Easy on the computer; hardly any lag despite there being tons of things going on at once
+ Ability to come back into the game as long as your friends survive (MP). It isn't too easy where you aren't punished, however - if you die, you have time added on to your spawn time, so it is both forgiving and punishing
+ Huge collection of weapons to upgrade, customise, or utilise; for such a cheap game, you would think that your options would be more limited, but no.
truly impresses with the amount of content offered

I have a really hard time recommending Middle-Earth Shadow of Mordor. It has too much Ubisoft formula without even being an Ubisoft game, the nemesis system is interesting at first but not very thought out in this entry and large parts of mid-game story progression are simply grindy without being noticeably fun. Between all the collectibles, way too many uninspired NPCs mixed with very few noteworthy NPCs basically leaves Shadow of Mordor with solely nice optics and a good working combat mechanic. Pretty much everything else, and everything else being lots and lots of content is mediocre at best.
Shadow of Mordor does some things right but it is absolutely incapable of gripping the player in any way whatsoever. Just a mere week after playing the campaign I have forgotten 90% of all NPC interaction as well as story progression, as it is entirely irrlevant to the game except for a very few major plotpoints or unique character appearances which are also way too few in number.
Shadow of Mordor is by no means a bad game, but at what it tries to do, it fails miserably. I have played far worse games, but with many of those I ultimately ended up having way more fun than with Shadow of Mordor. This is also most likely the reason why it sold so miserably on release, even although critical reception wasn't too bad.

I love Monolith. I've loved them since way back when they made Blood. They have always made solid games with interesting twists, such as F.E.A.R. and first-person slow-mo, and Condemned: Criminal Origins with its melee and crime investigation focus. They did it again with Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor.
Shadow of Mordor is a third-person action game that plays like a combination of Assassin's Creed and Batman: Arkham Asylum. In the Assassin's Creed vein, there is a lot of climbing on buildings, sneaking around, stabbing orcs, interrogating informants, and finding collectibles. Shadow of Mordor does all of these better than Assassin's Creed has in the past. The climbing feels better and it's more obvious where you can and cannot climb. The stealth makes more sense, as breaking line of sight gives a ghostly outline to show where you were last spotted. This makes following enemies seem less omniscient and not unlimited in numbers, while still presenting overwhelming amounts of enemies. The informants are also better done in Shadow of Mordor. Taking a page from the Arkham games, information on your particular target can be gained by grabbing a particular orc, instead of tediously following NPCs, or (even worse) innately somehow knowing everything about your enemy from the start. This last one is something Assassin's Creed has botched badly in the last couple games.
Taking pages from Arkham, the combat in Mordor is very much influenced by those games, with the same attack, counter, evade, and stun face buttons. It's a well-done imitation, and I found that my skills learned from the Arkham games translated perfectly to Mordor. Also taking a page from Arkham's books, the collectibles include bits of Middle-earth lore which makes them something that (as a Middle-earth fan) I want to collect, rather than just boxes to check to completionists.
What Mordor does that neither of those games do is introduce the nemesis system. You see, true to Middle-earth lore, Uruk-hai lead the orcs and they are nasty. They're mean, they fight each other, and power is the rule of law. In the game, there are around 20 Uruk captains. They all have unique names. They all have a unique mix of strengths, weaknesses, fears, and hatreds. For example, a particular captain might be invulnerable to stealth attacks, weak against fire, afraid of Caragoar (large four-legged beast), and a hatred of losing. This would mean that stealth is useless against him, and he will regenerate his health if you take his health down but not out, but fire will do more damage, and he'll lose all of his strengths and hatreds if he sees a Caragoar.
Controlling the 20 something Uruk captains are five warchiefs, with more power and unique attributes themselves. They also have bodyguards, which are Uruk captains. Taking on a warchief without accounting for their bodyguards is a good way to find yourself fighting a lot of powerful Uruk. But you don't know any of these attributes or command hierarchy from the start. You don't even know these Uruk's names. You have to collect intel to learn these things. You can go into these fights blind, but it's much easier when you know what to expect and who might show up. Later in the game, you can exploit the command hierarchy by turning bodyguards against their warchief, or turning warchiefs and captains against each other.
Reading this, none of it might sound particularly compelling, but it is so well done that it makes the entire game. The named Uruk must have thousands of lines of dialog because repeat encounters result in them bringing up things that I had done to them in the past. Where Assassin's Creed forced me to collect intel just to put me in the same sneak, murder, run away cycle, Mordor made intel optional, and made the unique Uruk attributes a way of forcing me to be creative with my approach. The nemesis system created stories in Mordor that few games can replicate even with crafted encounters. I've written up a great example of one of these stories involving Orthog the Crafty at my blog.
Despite all of these strengths, Mordor isn't perfect. In fact, where it is lacking is in the crafted story. You play as Talion, and, right from the start, your wife and son are fridged and you're killed by a minion of Sauron. However, you learn that Talion can't die because he's possessed by a wraith. The wraith doesn't know who he is, but his power keeps Talion from dying in his quest for revenge. The story isn't particularly bad in itself, but it suffers from too much fan service. You run into a handful of antagonists modeled accurately from their characters in the Lord of the Rings movie trilogy who seem to just pop up for no good reason. Or at least, not good enough reasons. It's a bummer, because I loved all of the collectibles and their stories and found them much more interesting than dragging out movie characters for the apparent purpose of saying "HEY THIS GAME IS LIKE THOSE MOVIES! REMEMBER THOSE?" It's the movie poster cover art on the latest print of a classic novel. Tacky and unnecessary. The game itself stands alone great without the ham-fisted cameos.
The game ends weakly, and leaves the doors wide swinging open for the sequel, and I personally cannot wait. Maybe they'll get the story right next time, but if they don't, I'll hope to make my own, better stories with an improved nemesis system. Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is one of those rare games where the gameplay mechanics create better, more interesting stories than what was written for it, and I hope that we see more of the nemesis system in these type of open world action games in the future.

Whilst this is a nice attempt at something clever, the chambers feel like they are 80% tutorial levels for the purpose of tutorialing the capabilities of the time-loop mechanic and 20% actual chambers.
of the actual chambers, the difficulty curve is very odd. the 3rd from last chamber was a real annoyance due the tasks necessary to execute the solution rather than the solving of the 1st 1/2 of the chamber. for the 2nd half, the inclusion of an uneccessary button made it harder to solve (note: if you just ignore the ceiling button it will save you a lot of time). the 2nd last level looks like something was missed out as it can be solved without the need of the time mechanic after the 1st part. the last chamber was very fiddly, although it felt to me that it was demonstrating the true potential, requiring you to do a syncronised ballet of tasks between yourself and your time-loop'd copy (i actually was feeling "so is this how the rest of the levels will be like, but then the game had no more levels to offer. a real shame).
there's a hinting of a possible story going on, although due to the low number of levels, it doesn't really get explored. in particular, why are you running this gauntlet of puzzles? why is chell trying to get to the goal that she is working towards.
of the gameplay mechanics themselves i was dissappointed that the portal gun had a very definite second fiddle role to the time mechanic, rather then playing an equal role. i don't believe there was ever any use of momentum puzzles for example, and most of the time you were basically either using the time mechanic with occasional portal placement or just not portalling at all.
the visuals are very nice, i particularly like the new take on familiar apperture objects like the doors and the chamber number plate, but found the square buttons that replace the standard round ones to easily be confused with box-only buttons from afar. the reuse of the same skybox on every map was a dissappointment as it reduced the feeling of progress + caused some visual impossibilities due to the placement of windows, however this was offset by the clever stacking of chambers so you could see bits of old ones and upcoming ones through windows.
being able to see your feet - i could take or leave this, as you really don't find yourself looking down all to often. the real shame is that the time-mechanic's data pad actually shows you what your copy is doing from first person perspective, yet because of how the character model has been implemented, it means that you can only see this neat effect if you are looking down, which is impractical when trying to move about and solve puzzles (yes i realise that it's more realistic that way, since focusing on an iPhone whilst trying to walk down a street and not bump into anyone is tricky enough, but i'd say that this is a case where better gameplay should trump realism). if they made this part of the hud instead, i could see it becoming an integral part of more complicated puzzle solving events, allowing you to sync up actions better when you can't see your copy directly.
overall it's a very good attempt for a mod, especially one dealing with such a finicky mechanic in nature. i would like to see more levels involving the use of the 2 chells working in tandem (though with leniency for timing of course as lining up the recorded actions with your own is tricky enough as is), maybe some interesting double portaling play involving momentum.
i look forward to see what more is put out, either by community or by the mod team. i'd imagine almost any normal co-op chamber could be a possible candidate as a single player chamber for this mod.
tl;dr:
-nice idea
-nice visuals
-could incorporate more portalling / momentum in the chambers
-short and inconsistent difficulty curve
-has potential
-needs to have more maps/chambers

State of Decay suprised me, as I expected a cheap, stereotypical zombie apocalypse game. However, what I got was not, and was very enjoyable.
Note: I own none of the DLC
State of Decay has a good story, interesting game mechanics, and overall enjoyable gameplay. It allows you to upgrade, move, and interact a home base, recruit survivors (whom you can then switch to), and run over zombie hordes.
While the perma-death feature worried me at first (I absolutely hate perma-death), it encourages using all of your characters available, to keep them all at average, and not focus on one or two, only to have them die and you have to retrain some new survivors.
Some of the quests are linear and repeat often (Hunt down this zombie, clear out this infestation), but there are quite a few unique and interesting quests that heavily affect your group of survivors, and the world as a whole.
Good zombie game, would recommend. 8/10

Dark Souls has a reputation of being a hard and punishing; it worries me that people who haven't played this game think it might be too hard and would miss out on a genuinely fun game.
Dark Souls is not hard, it is challenging; the game has never felt unfair and I've never felt like I've died without deserving it. But I don't want to focus on the difficulty of the game, because I don't feel that the game's difficulty is what defines it.
Dark Souls is an incredible RPG with outstanding level design. I've never played a game that feels more rewarding to level up your character and aquire new and unique weapons that become more and more powerful as they scale with how you level your character. There are a large amount of possiblities on what weapons you choose and how you upgrade them to suit your own playstyle. There's not a more satisfying feeling than having a second encounter with an early game boss and absolutely destroying them after you've leveled up since your first encounter. There's so much variety in playstyle that is completely up to the player which keeps me coming back to multiple playthroughs with different playstyles and classes.
Dark Souls has some of the best level design I've ever seen in the game. Every location connects to another which connects to another which circles back to where you started. It really contributes to immersing you in what feels like a huge world with all sorts of different environments. You can easily get to any area in the entire game from the starting area which makes the game feel less tedious and mundane. For the most part, the environments look incredible and it's always exciting wandering into a new area, not knowing what new enemies and hazards could come next. Although one of the few things I dislike about this game is the environment of the early game, which feels somewhat samey and boring. However, once you get past that, the game opens up into interesting and dynamic landscapes and some of them have literally left me with my mouth wide open in awe (not even kidding my mind was blown).
I'll keep this section short because to be honest I haven't really dove very far into the world yet; but the lore for this game is fantastic and has so much behind it. The game doesn't force complex story down your throat and try to make you follow their narrative. You can pick up a good amount of very cool lore just through the world itself and interactions with NPCs. And if you are really captivated, then you can dig in deeper and find mind blowing stories behind characters and locations.
Is this game challenging? Yes. Will you die a lot? Yes. But don't let this game's reputation prevent you from experiencing a genuinely fun and well-designed game that stands as a landmark in the RPG genre.

I'd just like to get this out of the way: yes, I like Dark Souls. In fact, I love it. I think the only one I didn't outright love was 2, mostly due to the relatively bland enemy design when compared with the other games. Even 3 had monsters that would sprout out into horrific nightmare fuel abominations, but 2 was mostly knights in armor or standard humanoid figures with weapons. By this same reasoning, Bloodborne was probably my favorite, though it does lose points for not getting a PC port, something that would greatly fix the loading times.
So why don't I recommend this?
Because this port is sh!t. Like, impressively sh!t. Locks itself to 720p at 30fps and is basically unplayable with a mouse and keyboard, unleass you're the sort of person who rebinds every command to find the most optimal keys to lay commands before starting every game. Even with a controller, the framerate and the sheer number of graphical glitches I've experienced turned me off before getting through the first level. It's just simply unplayable.
Go buy it on console. Seriously. It's just a horrible port, but everything else is great. And while you're at it pick up all the other games as well. The learning curve's fairly steep, but it cements that feeling of accomplishment you get when you finally break through the barrier you've been up against for the last 3 hours.
EDIT: To those who may already own this game or are determined to get it working, I have had it pointed out to me that there is a mod called DSfix that can get it working. Having tried it out for a bit, I can say it does dramatically improve things, though you'll need some time, dedication, and a light-to-decent amount of tech literacy to get it working. Even then it has its issues; I'm searching now to see if there's anything else that would help. Still, while I recommend the console version still, if you are determined and can work with mods, feel free to work towards that. (Thank you to Wilserien for the information regarding DSfix.)

So often has Dark Souls been discussed, it's difficult to say anything new. If nothing else, I simply wish to add my voice to the chorus of well-deserved praises for the game.
What I will add is a couple of rebuttals to common criticisms. First, I found the Prepare to Die Edition port completely serviceable. It's nothing amazing, to be sure, but I found it perfectly playable unmodified with a USB controller. "Essential" mods like DSFix and PvP Watchdog are certainly worth exploring, but if you don't want to go to the trouble you can still absolutely enjoy the game.
Second (though this is well-known among the community), the game is not as absurdly difficult as it is often made out to be. If you're hesitant to try Dark Souls based on rumblings about how "insanely hard" it is, I encourage you to check it out. It's more that the game requires patience and perseverance to learn - moreso than many other games - than that it's unfair or excessively difficult. With willingness to apply yourself and search for tips on things you can't figure out yourself, I do believe anyone can get through this game. And really, the satisfaction of success, on top of the incredible lore, level design, and combat, make it all undoubtedly worthwhile.

Jeez, where do I even start?  Night in the Woods is the story of a young college dropout, her crazy collection of friends, her town full of weird but wonderful neighbors, and also a very very VERY bad thing.  Several, really.  Mae Borowski is a heck of a character, and following her on her crazy and "eff the police" antics has a joy to it that makes you quickly grow to love her.  Even as the story - which you help create through choices - takes its many twists and turns, you just can't help but root for her.
This game is clearly a labor of love, with even the most minute details given all the care and attention that a programmer can give.  Possum Springs isn't just a setting, but with all the people and events, it almost becomes its own living thing.  The more you explore the town, the more you discover about its history, and the more you end up WANTING to explore all the strange little nooks and crevices.  I myself spent more hours combing over the rooftops and tunnels than I did actually following the main story, and my time was more than rewarded!
All in all, I definitely recommend this game.  A fun little adventure with a great moral to the story, Night in the Woods is sure to keep you hooked right up until the very end.

Street Fighter 4 (Vanilla) -PC-
Street Fighter 4 brings the franchise back to its glory days of 2D fighting action. It has brought me more joy than Virtua Fighter, Tekken, SoulCalibur all combined.  Street Fighter 4 is just head a shoulder above any other fighting game on the market. The game is simple enough for anyone who played Street Fighter 2 back in the day, but with all new combos, moves, and a gauge super move system, Street Fighter 4 is easily the best fighting since in years,
To be fair, I've always been a Street Fighter enthusiast. In my youth I was so captivated with all the memorable fighters like Ken, Ryu, Blanka, and Chun-Li and have always stuck with me. I loved the simple back stories and how they all came from different parts of the world and how it affected their very different fighting styles. Throughout each one of these fighters lives, they were directly affected negatively by the villain Major Bison. They make M. Bison out to be such a powerful merciless tyrant.
In Street Fighter 4, All of the original fighters reprise their roles. Some time has passed, but M. Bison is still up to no good. There is also a new cast of characters, 23 playable characters in all. This includes all the original 8, the 4 original bosses, 3 from Super Street fighter 2, and bunch of new ones I’d never heard of. Needless to say, there are plenty of characters at your disposal.
Street Fighter 4’s play style feels very natural for a seasoned veteran and newcomers alike. Pulling off special moves and short combos can be learned in a just a couple of minutes. Then learning in which situation exactly to use these combos can take much much longer. For more advanced players, there are some really crazy combos you can pull off. The game features a training mode where it will show you all the different combos, starting with easy ones and moving on to the more complex. The training mode it pretty huge and there’s one for every character.
And as fighters should, your characters are thick and have a sense of weight to them. The artistic style is a mix of cell-shaded cartoons and brilliant realism. It blends nicely to bring the game to life and to strike a chord with the nostalgia of past Street Fighter iterations.
In battle, there are 2 gauges present: the first gauge fills up as you take damage, the second fills up at you cause damage to your opponent. The “take damage” gauge can be released to perform a super attacks. This attack is a once a battle attack that can really sway the favor of the battle. This attack can be blocked or dodged if you sense it coming, but each characters attack is different and will come at you from a different direction or timing. The second “do damage” gauge can be used several times during a fight. When used, it will enhance your current special attacks to make them stronger. I found the whole gauge system very fun and it brought some spice to the action.
To unlock all of the characters you’ll need to beat the game with almost every fighter. I found myself spending hour after hour battling the computer for this means.  Its very rewarding to unlock new fighters, but I do with there was an easier way to get them all.
The online mode is where the game really shines. Playing against the computer is one thing, but going up against a real person in another story. After spending some time against real opponents, you’ll soon realize that your small set of moves and predictable  jumps will easily be countered, resulting in defeat after defeat. I was very hyped when I heard Nobunaga's Ambition : SOI was released on Steam. I had been very fond to NA series, even though I had only played the NA : Iron Triangle series on the PS2. After quite a decent play time, I decided to make a quick review. Note that I hadn't played other mass strategy games such as Total War, etc. ,  except Sid Meier's Civilization 5.
You should buy this if :
1. Are very interested in everything about the Sengoku Period.
2. Have loads of time to sink into this game.
3. You are proud of the Oda badge on your steam profile !   XD
I'm comparing NA : SOI to NA : Iron Triangle ( IT ). SOI have many improvements and new features compared to IT, but has major flaw in its battle system.
Improvements:
1. Game Concept
SOI has a much more enjoying game management by introducing the Council Phase every early month, which is much more sense in ruling an empire. This phase is where you carry out strategies ( diplomacy, survey, incite, etc )and town developments ( agriculture, crafts, etc ). After this phase is known as The Battle Phase. The Battle Phase is very similar to the previous NA series.
2. History telling
SOI narrates Sengoku Period in very detailed and interesting. Its CGI are very beautiful, the actors scripts are also really enjoyable to read.
3. Quests and Events
I was very thrilled with the brand new Quests concept. At times, there will be objectives for you to complete before deadlines such as capturing castles, gaining diplomatic points, or even attempting to employ Hanbei Takaneka which was very funny. Upon completing the Quests, rewards are given and some quests changes the world.
4. Defined Battle
You actually get to completely control your units in a Battle and Mass Battle. This simple Defined Battle can actually turn the tides even when withstanding greater foes. The environment during these battles are also very picturisque and enjoyable.
5. New Policy Concept
Policies allow you to determine your government form, either militaristic or economical, or somewhere in between. Each policy have their own merits and demerits which are makes the game very diverse. Policies utilise the " Innovation " system, which have the Progressive, Neutral and Traditional stage. Most policies can only be enacted when their requirements had been fulfilled.
Flaws:
The only major flaw in NA : SOI I can point out is its battle system.
1. Army Composition Too Simple
Your units are basically infantry and archers. They can be equipped with horses and muskets, giving them " Charge " and " Release " tactics respectively and some officers benefit these equipments ( Nobunaga, Shingen, Shigehide, etc ). This mixed army compositon in turn make battles repetitive and boring in a long run. It would be more interesting and challenging if unit type was the absolute unit type ( Only Infantry, Only Archers, Only Dagoons, etc ). So I would place Infantry in front, Archers in back, all that kinds of formation instead of head-on fight and still win.
I guess siege units were removed from this game? It's very dissapointing because siege units bring strategy diversities. Back in NA : IT, I used to enjoy blasting enemies with cannons from afar !
2. Technology System removed
In NA : IT, each clan have their own specialty in technology (Oda with muskets, Tokugawa with Infantry, Sanada with Engineering, Mori with naval, etc ) . But this was removed in SOI, making each clan somewhat similar, repetitive and greatly reduces the replay value of SOI.
3. Officers Multitasking ?
I noticed that Officers in SOI can carry out both political and military tasks. Example is that while Toshiie was busy battling the Azai, he can still build roads from Nagoya which was quite far away. Comparing to NA : IT, an officer who is engaged in battle is not available for political tasks.
Bugs:
The only bug I encountered is when changing your clan's daughter ( maiden ) name. The GUI got all messed up after changing the name. I was super lucky that I had just save that time after a long battle of Oda with Takeda. I'm using Windows 8.1 .
I guess that's it for my quick review. Overall, NA : SOI is very enjoyable to play and I'm looking forward for more NA series, and restore the Technology System , just like or even better than in NA : IT !

Played this game for half an hour and had 2 crashes since.
I love the aperture setting in general, and this does it fairly well. I dislike the use of tiles which now just is confusing(I mean, I could shoot portals at white tiles, why can't I now?), plus the shiny effect on it isn't any better. It looks like consuela cleaned it around 50 times.  The buttons and doors however look stunning and are very Aperture-sciency.
The time machine itself, does not. The fun thing about portal and all it's devices, buttons and what-not is that they are all somehow feasable in the real world. This, however, is not. It's literally just a tablet which spawns yourself out of nothing with the actions you have just recorded. Not only that, but it can interface with it's surroundings and you can jump on yourself, but you cannot collide with your standing self, because then you can just walk through yourself. This whole mechanic makes very little sense, plus it ♥♥♥♥♥ on the whole space-time paradox. Remember how Cave johnson told you not to look at your past(or future) self? Yeah, I think it's clear.
Then it's mechanics, the usage of the time machine is confusing and not explained at all. There are tutorials to the side of some things, but the screens plus tips in the video's(which are done very well, might I add, they fit the Aperture science vidoes really well) are too small to actually be viewable, making the whole time machine thing more of a guess work rather than actual game mechanic.
Then to the part where I went, in GLaDOS chamber, where Atlas and P-Body are also present. Those two robots are having a conversation in some robo-gibberish language. I got the subtitles to that, how in the hell am I able to "hear" what they are saying? The room design there is also bad, there are 4 doors and only one of them is actually open for whatever reason. Portal dealt with this issue very well by giving a dialog, or placing something in front of the door, to make it clear. Not only did this add character to the whole environment, it made it clear that this was not the place to go. Not the case here.
Then we come in GLaDOS emergency control room, where Atlas and P-Body disappeared from out of thin air. This room suddenly has the 70's Apertue science look to it, except for a single device. Not only that, but where is the red phone? This red phone is an integral part of the whole environment there, and is talked about more than once in the whole universe.
Not only that, but the location of the room where you are in, plus GLaDOS' chamber is physically impossible. From the ending of Portal 2 you are sent upwards out of GLaDOS' chamber into a field. This is where TWTM starts. From this point you have only moved upwards via elevators, making this room physically impossible to be there.
And then we go to the game itself. Had 2 crashes in half an hour. Tool tips(like you are getting when zoomed in) show the string instead of the actual text.
Overall this game is rather clear that it is not Valve's. IOn the half an hour of playing, I encountered way too many plotholes already plus the game itself(from personal experience, and seeing it here on the community board) seems to be incredibly buggy.
It is that it is free, so there is no harm in checking it out. But due to it's quality(or better said, lack of) I cannot recommend this. I will (maybe) pick it up at a later time and hopefully get further on it, and will update my reccomendation accordingly.

LuftRausers is basically a really focused arcade game. It doesn't do a lot, but what it does, it does really well. The game plays kind of like Asteroids except there is constant gravity pulling you towards the water. The customizable Rauser is pretty cool. You pick a weapon system such as a machinegun, a continuous laser, spread shot that pushes you back, homing missiles, etc), a body (high health but low agility, you take no ramming damage but have little health, drops bombs but slow health regen, etc) and an engine (heavy thrust but poor turning while thrusting, near anti-gravity, no damage entering the water, etc) and then you just fight nonstop waves of enemies trying to rack up as many points as possible. Each combination has its own nickname and each part has little achievements tied to it too.
The gameplay is pretty frantic, as the sky quickly becomes filled with enemies and bullets. Thankfully you can take a decent amount of punishment before dying (unless you're using the melee part) and you regenerate health whenever you're not shooting.
The variety you can get while building your Rauser is impressive, a few of the builds I liked was a Rauser equipped with a heavy, slow firing cannon, the melee body, and the water engine. I'd just dive bomb ships and fire the cannon just before I rammed the ship and plunged into the water, even the battleships can't take too many hits from that. Of course, if I timed it wrong I'd fly right into their gunfire and be blown apart (melee body can take 2 maybe 3 hits from full before dying). Another cool Rauser I had success with was the Beam Laser, Bomb Body, and "Original" balanced engine. I'd just zip around dodging enemies and bullets and slice ships and planes to ribbons.
You don't have to grind too much for the parts either, I think I've basically unlocked almost all the parts (except one special one for each section I think, the padlock symbol looks different than the one for the rest I unlocked) in only about 2 hours of play I'd say. One additional neat thing is that the music changes depending on your parts selection. Its the same basic theme every time, but different parts use different "instruments".
