I played this game early on and from memory I purchsed this in early access so this review should be read with that in mind.
Early on you crafted armor using the previous tier of armor as a requirement this has changed as the game updates.
Getting lucky and finding a gun in a container was a ether extremely helpful or just more random junk however being on a more difficult planet did improve your chances of finding something useful. I have not played vanilla recenly but there are ways to craft, find or purchase something useful if you are willing to put the time in.
Bosses were a case of gather materials for armor, weapons & the summoning item and then run around trying to dodge most of the attacks while attempting to defeat it with whatever you had on hand or being clever and tring to box in the boss for some easy hits before the box was destroyed. Now the game has a main quest / adventure / story that leads you to each boss, maybe getting some intresting loot along the way and some bosses require a specific technique to efficieny defeat.  This was something lacking early on that has now been fixed.
Seeing as I prefer to build up a single planet - if said planet does not have any unpleasent weather or enviromental hazards - venturing off planet for resorces not avalible on that planet the ammount of biomes in early access was fairly limited (having said that I never got very far in vanilla because something frequently prevented my progression). The wiki at the time showed a reasonable number of biomes spread out over a semmingly infinity number of planets but eventually the biomes became repetitive. Now the game is expanding whats in the, well, space between planets and adding in other interesting looking content.
The general enemy creatures always looked alien and thats an excellent fit for the game but early in development anything that flew was potentional death incarnate with nasty, high damage projectile attacks and if it was an enemy that remained on the ground you have better be careful about approachint it if there was more than one of them just in case it was a predator. Now everything that moves is not out for your blood the split second they detect you - some are passive to you and will ignore you unless to attack, flying creatures are not 100% hostile ether. But like minecraft or, a better comparison, terraria more dangerous creatures come out at night which makes sence from a realism perspective - real life predators have been known to hunt at night to make it harder for there chosen prey to detect them.
The enviroment can be just as dangerous then and now - the starting planet generaly has no serious surface hazards, may have hostile & non hostile non player characters and fairly weak creatures that after gearing up can be defeated an a single hit from a well equiped player making resorce gathering fairly fast & easy. If the game decides to mae things difficult for you then you may have to deal with lethally low temperatures, fire rain that burns your character if you are caught outside, heavy rain that causes flooding and meteors that annihilate eveything... maybe not at the same time if you are lucky - that was before your ship gave you some warning of what to expect of a planet before beaming down.
I ended up solving the limitations of the early versions with some content added by mods from some talented people / teams. with the way the game is going I'm impressed with wbats being added and may give it another go in vaillia later - thats saying something as I rarely go back to games I have finished.
If you have enjoyed terraria / minecraft and similar sandbox like games then you will enjoy this otherwise wait for it to go on sale for what you consider a fair price and purchase it. If you know what you are doing, get lucky with drops & play vanilla then I would expect the game to last around 10 hours but if you add in some mods, spend some time exploring and maybe invite some friends then it could last for 100+ hours.

It's an overall good game, and once you get past a certain point it becomes a lot more enjoyable to play. I got the game a long while ago, when the main quest was just to go to other planets, and it's certainly improved since then.
While being kind of similar to Terraria, I really don't consider them to be the same game. In Terraria, you build a base, in this, you explore. I think the main comparison people are making is that they're 2D platformers that involve digging.
Pros:
-The questline now is actually exploration-based rather than resource-based, and isn't overly difficult.
-There's a LOT more to do now beyond just finding resources; miniquests are honestly pretty fun and a good break from the main quest, and you can actually upgrade your ship now.
-Going to other planets is cool and now relatively painless. Getting a crew member on your ship who can upgrade the fuel efficiency makes it better.
-The armor progression and upgrading your worktables is neat and a driving force for me. After a certain point I stopped doing the main quest and focused on that.
-Pets are automatically obtained and can be interesting. Still had to look up how to properly take care of my pet, though.
-Intergalactic space market. The whole space theme is right up my alley. Also, the cities with different races is cool.
Cons:
-The main quest, while being more in-depth than before, is still kind of boring after the first two steps. Each individual part is pretty much identical to the last, just in different areas.
-A good majority of the beginning is just digging for resources. After a while, you get a stash going, but you can't do much but dig until that point.
-Kind of loses its appeal after a while, given those last two points. I'd enjoy it more if there was a more interesting goal, and I feel like the actual end goal of fighting the Cthulu dude would be something I'd more actively go for if I wasn't already bored with the questline before it.
-Multiplayer exists but is sort of a pain if you want actual co-op. It'd be cool if there was an option to operate on the same ship, but so far, you can only teleport to other people's ships. I like the party system, though.
All-in-all, really liked it, but got kinda bored. Certain aspects progress fast and other aspects progress too slow to keep up with them.

This is basically Dark Souls: The Visual Novel
You play as Elodie, a 15 year old girl who tries to get ready for her coronation but is stopped by LITERALLY EVERYTHING because everyone is out for her blood. Bad situations happen and if you don't have the right skills raised or pick the wrong choice, she dies a horrible death. Spoiler: You're going to die many times.
Save. Save a lot.
During the game, there are a variety of skills Elodie can learn, which can range from being a prim and proper princess, to learning magic, to having knowledge of someone's forecoming death from a wilted flower. Elodie's mood affects how quickly (or slowly) she learns these skills, so you can make her go play with her toys for some cheer and isolation, or tell her to go to her mother's tomb for some good ol' depression.
You can die from literally anything here. Poisoned chocolate, arrows, tentacle monsters, and magic are just a few examples of how a young girl's already traumatic life can and will get worse. The good thing is, with enough of Elodie's spilt blood and some rage, you'll find a way to counter all those damn death flags and be crowned queen.
Once you beat the game once, you can try another method of making it to the end because there are many ways you can get there (or die on the way there). You can rule with an iron fist or try to be a pacifist. You never get the same ending twice.
This game is fun, challenging, and playing dress up with Elodie isn't too bad either.

Not as good as Transport Fever, but still alright
Firstly, Train Fever is years older than Transport Fever, with Transport Fever having besides trains, trucks, buses and trams also airplanes and ships, campaign, more refined goods production, other features, and a reworked game engine of theirs. Nevertheless, Train Fever seems to be on sale a lot cheaper, I still play it to pick up the last few achievements I don't have, and I find it itself still enjoyable after around 50 hours of game-play (and 90 hours of Transport Fever game-play).
As the product description says it is a modern-day Transport Tycoon, but it has some differences in terms of game-play mechanics, with on the downside being that it has no AI faction whatsoever nor any multiplayer.
In regard to other differences, one is about how passengers and goods behave, with in Train Fever there being a so-called "20 minutes rule" - which means that if a passenger or piece of raw material/goods doesn't reach final destination within 20 minutes from house starting point, then they/it disappear on that journey (or do not even start the journey). Those 20 minutes are in game-terms 20 months, with info screen showing how long it takes i.e. a train to make a full forth-and-back journey. So if there is a single train with capacity of 50 units of oil on a line with round time of 6 minutes, then that means that the maximum capacity of delivery within one game year is 100 units of oil. (And due to that it usually not advisable to set a line to wait for full load as it worsens that round time.)
And another difference is about how industry behaves as in that i.e. oil well doesn't start producing unless there is demand from an oil refinery which doesn't have that demand unless there is demand for goods from a town - which simply means that one needs to have both an operating line for delivery of goods from refinery to town, and a line for delivery of oil to refinery, established before the oil well begins producing at all.
Mentioning those differences may sound from me as if it were a very complicated game, but just mentioning it a bit in detail as to save eventual reader/purchaser time digging in tutorial texts or forum about why their line is not functioning while perhaps used to that Transport Tycoon game-play where a coal mine throws out as much coal as a train can take.
Other than that, similar to Transport Tycoon it does have town growth if supported, and one can similarly quickly end up having various train tracks independent of each other with plenty of overpasses and tunnels or having plenty of train tracks in some kind of network while playing around with rail signals to make it work so no train does get stuck. So if you are into that kind of stuff then you are probably going to enjoy Train Fever. However, if price is not an issue then you may want to look at Transport Fever, which is improved in several aspects.

If you like old school Koei strategy games, you will love this.

This is a pretty awesome KOEI strategy game. It's actually very difficult, but feels rewarding when you do conquer your rivals. Like other KOEI strategy games, there is a heavy focus on personnel and on making good use of your officers. However, this game is a bit different from other "ruler only" KOEI strategy games because you can also play as a vassal clan. The game gives you a wide array of options for acquiring new officers, developing your lands and managing diplomacy. I can praise KOEI on a lot of other things as well. For once, they actually decided to release an English dub for one of their strategy games, and it's actually awesome. Additionally, this game is a translation of both the original game Nobunaga's Ambition Souzou and its PUK (expansion pack). It's the first time that KOEI has localized an expansion pack for one of their strategy games. The localization is also overall pretty good. There are a few spelling errors here and there, but nothing serious. As a PC game, this title is also better than all of KOEI's other English deliveries. The load times are practically non-existent, the game runs beautifully and it has not crashed on me once even though I tend to experience crashes with a lot of other video games. Finally, the options for customizing the game are amazing. You can edit all sorts of things and create your own unique characters/clans.
It's worth mentioning that the scope of this game is enormous. It seems like there are four or five times the number of bases that existed in Iron Triangle. Moreover, due to the way troop mechanics works, it's actually not so easy to conquer the land quickly. The large array of scenarios in tandem with the length it takes to progress through each one means that players will have hundreds of hours of potential playtime on their hands.
The best thing about this game though (at least for me) is the fact that Koei included a huge array of historical events, some of which even have cutscenes. These historical events sometimes manifest themselves as quests that allow you to relive some of the historical drama of this period. Oftentimes you will have to make a tough decision about whether you want to follow a historical questline or go off and do your own thing. +A very useful PDF manual (file name: Nobu14PKManual) that I found to be very useful even after the prologue.
What's there to hate?
-Battles can be a bit lacklustre with limited options of skills/variance (only horses/muskets/spears/bows), compared to RoTK with duels, siege units, traps, etc but this is Nobunaga's Ambition, not RoTK after all.
-Quests can be confusing where you might make a wrong move in hiring some officers/conquer some lands etc that might stop the quests from continuing. E.g. accidentally killing Saito Dosan too early stopped my Nobuhide's scenario quests from appearing anymore lol.
-It drains your time and energy. Seriously it does. I started on a Friday night and ended up still clicking for one more turn on a mind-numbing Saturday 10AM. Continued clicking till my wife came out.
-You will probably create your entire family into the officers creation mode. I have added my niece and sons into the list, and I was even creating my father-in-law as an opposing clan. Decided not to when I saw my wife's face as I asked for his name.
Summary:
I am loving it as a big RoTK/Nobunaga's Ambition/Genghis Khan/Koei strategy fan and I will first-day purchase or pre-order this anytime all over again. For others, you might wanna read up more and check the game play before buying, not everyone can appreciate this beauty :D

LUFTRAUSERS is a game near impossible to not admire at least a little bit during play. The combat is simlpy something to behold, as you zip across the sky in a beautiful, brown, bullet-filled sky while all hell breaks lose around you. It's a spectacle arcade SHMUP, and an extremely good one at that. It's really hard to not overplay how much fun the flying and shooting is in this game, it gives such an exhilarating and engaging feeling that's hard to find at this calibur. The game is recommendable on this aspect alone, the game is a prime example of a game that's just fun to play, you don't need any other motivation.
Unfortunately, that's really all there is. The customization is limited, and a lot of the parts are kinda lack-luster in comparison to their counterparts. For example, I think the homing missiles, the cannon, the collision body, and bomb body are all utter garbage, their drawbacks all outweigh their benefits, and there are clearly better weapons. After for playing for just a few ours, the dominant strategy effect takes place and I see only three or four combinations worthy of my time. Randoming is fun as well, but a lot of the time you'll just get a back combination and die before you get anywhere really exciting. The names for each combination and mis-matched music tracks are really neat, but the novelty wears off as each match lasts just a few minutes. The missions are over in four or five hours and the SFMT, although gloriously hectic, gets a bit more frustrating than fun pretty quick. At the bottom line, the game sadly gets a little repetitive about four hours in.
It's just that the game is so amazingly fun to play. Everything feels, looks, and sounds fantastic, it's a great experience. The price is a little steep for a game that gets a little old only four hours in, but if you don't mind fighting the same same seven enemy types over and over and over in rapid succession with stunted progression just for the sake of it, the game is simply and utterly fantastic.
This game is addicting like crack. Too much fun.

Let me state I've already played and completed this game when it initially came out on the xbox 360. I've always been an ace combat fan so I'll admit to some bias in that regard, along with a love of military aircraft in general.
That said, this itiration of the Ace Combat series, while fun, full of adrenaline, and still top notch in visual quality as you'd expect, I still felt the new Dog Fighting mechanic took away from some of the imersion.
In previous titles, dog fighting was as you'd imagine, difficult. Trying to follow your target while staying in range for your main gun and leading the target so you actually hit. While at the same time making sure you did not crash into anything. This, obviously takes some skill and practice, which I felt was a good challenge to the game.
Assault Horizon however takes the burden of piloting and has you focus more on the target. Now it's a matter of making sure your crosshair is on target for your main gun or missles (whichever you prefer) and the plane is essentially on auto pilot after the target. You can change your pitch and angle, sure, but you are certainly only following the target aircraft.
This was more a design decision to add cinematic fluff than anything else. That hollywood sequence of flying just underneath a crane while at Mach 2 is undeniably impressive and enjoyable for most. But after repeated intervals, it begins to feel cheapened.
This is certainly a good game for those new to the flight combat sim, or new to Ace Combat in general to get a feel for series. While I wish they kept the old dog fighting mechanics in this, it does allow for a lot of 'wow' moments when you do pull them off.

Ace Combat Assault Horizon... where to begin.

If you've played the past games and have loved the sim style, then avoid this game, as its now focused more to an arcade style. That coupled with a lackluster story have me dissapointed in Assault Horizon.
If you're new to the Ace Combat franchise and are looking for cheep and easy arcade sim, this game might be for you; but buyer beware, it might not be worth it even then.

It's an overall good game, and once you get past a certain point it becomes a lot more enjoyable to play. I got the game a long while ago, when the main quest was just to go to other planets, and it's certainly improved since then.
While being kind of similar to Terraria, I really don't consider them to be the same game. In Terraria, you build a base, in this, you explore. I think the main comparison people are making is that they're 2D platformers that involve digging.
Pros:
-The questline now is actually exploration-based rather than resource-based, and isn't overly difficult.
-There's a LOT more to do now beyond just finding resources; miniquests are honestly pretty fun and a good break from the main quest, and you can actually upgrade your ship now.
-Going to other planets is cool and now relatively painless. Getting a crew member on your ship who can upgrade the fuel efficiency makes it better.
-The armor progression and upgrading your worktables is neat and a driving force for me. After a certain point I stopped doing the main quest and focused on that.
-Pets are automatically obtained and can be interesting. Still had to look up how to properly take care of my pet, though.
-Intergalactic space market. The whole space theme is right up my alley. Also, the cities with different races is cool.
Cons:
-The main quest, while being more in-depth than before, is still kind of boring after the first two steps. Each individual part is pretty much identical to the last, just in different areas.
-A good majority of the beginning is just digging for resources. After a while, you get a stash going, but you can't do much but dig until that point.
-Kind of loses its appeal after a while, given those last two points. I'd enjoy it more if there was a more interesting goal, and I feel like the actual end goal of fighting the Cthulu dude would be something I'd more actively go for if I wasn't already bored with the questline before it.
-Multiplayer exists but is sort of a pain if you want actual co-op. It'd be cool if there was an option to operate on the same ship, but so far, you can only teleport to other people's ships. I like the party system, though.
All-in-all, really liked it, but got kinda bored. Certain aspects progress fast and other aspects progress too slow to keep up with them.

This is probably the best indie game I have ever played. with over 200 hours of playtime I still havn't felt like I've done everything in the game. and compared to the first game it's a bit less pollished but certainly gave the possibility's we where missing in OMD1. co-op among other things is simply a blast in this game, and for a large part the reason why the replay value is so high. but lets break the game down a bit and see what we've got.
The Game itself:
OMD2 works on the same basics the first did, beating the braindead matter out of the endless army's of orcs in it's ultraviolent road runner cartoon comedy style. But now with much more cake and sprinkles added. it's basicly how OMD1 shouldhave been. we now have endless mode, co-op, And a much bigger arsenal of weaponry to play around with. it actually felt more like an expansion pack then a part 2. but certainly one that was worth paying for. it just has all the features that it missed in the first incarnation. the only thing missing, is a level creator. but thats not a complaint, thats a sugjestion for part 3. If they ever make one.
Our Weaponry:
I like it when I can fully Automate my level into a perfect killing machine where I can sit back and watch the slaughter. So simply put I like "TRAPS" and a large arsenal of traps I got. aside from my nitpick that the Swinging Mace of OMD1 got nerfed like a hammer hitting a pack of butter, but to be fair the thing was overpowered. the majority of traps are a lot of fun to work with. Toss em, Burn em, Slice em, Shock em, Melt em? you've got all the options possible. and after 200 hours I still havn't tried all of the combinations.
Now our Arms,
I was surprised but I actually became a fan of the Blunderbus in comparison to the crossbow. even in part one I would rather run around like an idiot with the blade staff, and after I noticed they made the crosshair even more narrow for headshots then in the first game I was done with the arrow shooter. not that it's a bad weapon. it's just not my weapon of choice. Also I'm a big fan of the sorcceress wand. which had a lot of variation in it that makes it a formidable weapon. her normal attack for the speedy weak types, a charge attack for crowd controle and even a charm beam to stall and damage the bigger threats.
Level design:
This is where the game is kinda flawed to some extent but also in a rather unavoidable way.
most of the story mode levels where designed for 2 players, to also make the levels challenging for co-op play. This makes playing some levels in single player a downright stress bomb. especially the horrific upstairs/downstairs. which is a gruelling level to play solo in my opinion. it's not bad to design a difficult stage, but there has to be a fair chance to complete the level without feeling forced of being dependant on another player to complete it. nevertheless all of them are still possible solo. but the co-op designed stages just feel less fun on some accounts.
Gameplay:
I care nothing for graphics. let me just get that out of the way. because it doesn't matter how pretty the game looks if the controls are crap it's worthless. and OMD2 luckily remembered what was so good about it's predecessor. the controls are solid, fast, and fluent. some of the best responsive controles I've ever had in a game. 9 outa 10 times I feel it's my fault I died, not the game. the only arguement is that some of the death's caused by pittfalls can by a bit unforgiving. just sticking my toe into a hole is not a vaild reason for my character to die in my opinion.
Weapons menu:
I thought i'd mention this seperatly from the gameplay since it doesn't concern the game in the mids of action. OMD2 uses Skulls, you get Skulls either randomly while playing or by simply finishing a stage. You can uses these in your weapons menu to upgrade your Arsenal, making things cheaper, stronger etc. the game even cuts you some slack and allows you to respec this skulls after each stage at your leagure so you can prepare them in a manner better suited for the upcomming stage.
In every way, the menu works. it's easy ot use, and I can rearrange the weapons in my own preffered order. my only problem with this is that I have to click on every weapon to see if I maxed the weapon in all of it's fields. This system works. but I wouldhave liked a way to see which weapons are and are not fully customized.
Music:
It's like i'm listening to instrumentals made by Rhapsody on Fire. the fast pased gameplay and tone of the game matches the music perfectly. it's classical, it's metal, it's threatening and just gets you pumped everytime the orcs barge their way through the gates. and in contrast to many people that like the soundtrack of the game. I dont hate the credits track. "Can I has Credits" is in fact one of my favorite tracks of the OMD OST.
In overall:
The game has a few bugs but nothing worth mentioning.
So having a score above 80 is something it more then deserves.

I often do not write reviews but this game is amazing, if not one of the best games I have bought on steam in terms of Grand Strategy.
First if you love Japanese History or wish to learn more about it then this is a great game for such (In terms of events and facts the game provides). Second if you want to have a long save that is enjoyable throughout then I recommend this (I'd suggest starting as a clan such as the Hojo, Amago or Ouchi for starters as they are the strongest).
I've done two playthroughs. One as the Satomi (a small clan which often is crushed when used by the AI) and the Takeda (a hard starting clan because there are two stronger clans South of your land).
With the Satomi game it came to a standstill because I had all of the east and required a mere ten more castles plus Kyoto to become Shogun. Where Nobunaga Oda held most of the West par Shimazu land. With only us three factions and none able to break the other it didnt seem anyone was getting anywhere.
My new save I took over Japan fully. Even though I became Shogun and could enact a ''No More War'' Policy which would win the game for me anyway. I thought to myself ''Largest army... Best Generals.... Still got my orginal ruler...'' and continued to conquer until Japan was united.
The main thing is in this game is to make sure Oda Clan does not expand. If they do and Nobunaga takes over then you will struggle and end up like my Satomi as he becames all too powerful.
Good things:
Ending is amazing
Game overall is easy to grasp after 5 hours
Tons of clans to play, so if you finish one you can pick another
Good for learning
Nobunaga is a monster to face in battle
Bad things:
Religion has next to no affact in this game which is a huge dissapointment for me
No Ikko Ikki (as far as I have noticed)
Your not able to check your rulers age
Would be nice for a family tree. So I can see who is in my family (Not all sons have the last name as ruler making it slightly harder)
Overall I rate this game 98/100. Only issues is no family tree which would of been somewhat good and useful and lack of religion affacting clans.
To those who buy this game have fun ! I know I will continue to do so.

Quick review followed by a story
Have you ever played Total War: Shogun 2 and thought "wow this game would be great if the A.I. wasn't horrible" or "Would be good if this game was challenging without just being A.I. army/agent/♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ diplomacy SPAM"?
Well Nobunaga's Ambition has you covered, focusing mainly on the Map-based this time with polished gameplay  (I hate using this word) and A.I. that makes sense. It also gives much more information about the time, giving you visual novel style information about different clans, people and historical events which is an unexpected joy, making the country feel more alive.
There is still fights between clans, these are not as good as aformentioned Shogun 2, but you cannot just abuse the AI and win when it is 10 to 1. In this game it is much more simplified, but difficult (watch let's play vids for a good look before buying), every loss will affect you, every win will make the game hard later on as other clans start fearing/admiring you.
TLDR
Want an great strategy game that focuses on the Sengoku Jidai where there is plenty of detail and a game to waste plenty of hours, try out this.
Story time
After downloading the game, I started out the game playing the 'tutorial' scenario where I lost the first battle and was booted back to the Main Menu. Annoyed at this, I started the second scenario, focusing on the events of Nobunaga's father, Oda Nobuhide, Stating off in my small province of Owari, I started playing with the features, slowly building my towns and my armies. After 1 hour of messing around, I started to attack a single clan, winnning a province and stroking my ego. Choosing to follow historical missions of the time for the daimyo, I eventually came to fight the Imagawa and the Saito. After securing allies, I attacked with my petty force of around 3000 with my allies force of over 10,000, I defeated the Saito, caputing the daimyo and coverting him to my side (a real prize).
After defeating him, I made my way south, attacking the next enemy, over the next 5 hours, I took that clan down to one base (not with frustration or Save Scumming, but with fun). Once they were no longer a threat, I started to regroup and attack the nearby TAKEDA clan because every time I play a game about this era, I always attack them. Well turns out that was a stupid idea, continually being defeated by their strategy and my poor logistic handling. When I finally got a truce, I had only taken 1 province and it was continually being attack from a northern enemy clan, trying to take it without success.
Leaving 10,000 troops there, I pulled back and began focusing on the last Imagawa base I had ignored, putting together another 10,000 to try and take it. There was a catch however, on the other side of the Imagawa were the powerful Hojo clan besieging them, so I smashed their army in the side, taking the castle without loss. HORRIBLE CHOICE IN FORESIGHT. For the next hour or so was mainly diplomacy and building, making the Takeda neutral and I could ask them to lead a hand if needed. Then THIS HAPPENED, Oda Nobunaga appeared as an officer and straight away informed me that 40,000 Hojo troops are comming my way. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ 40k? I have 10k left at home and 10k at the north, how can I do this? The enemies came thundering across their land, besiging my castle that I had taken, smashing my armies and forcing me to ally with an enemy clan of the hojo and requesting the Takeda (who were close) to give me a hand.
THIS is where the game started to shine for me. Losing battles against them, I realised something, I still had 10k forces north to use and they were close to the hojo, but on the other side of the clan, So I had an awesome idea. I got those 10k soldiers to storm into their land, besiging 3 castles at once. The enemy AI came to realise what was happening and pulled some of the forces back to defend when suddenly the Takeda forces showed up at two sides, blocking the force of  about 35k.
With MASSIVE AMOUNTS OF TROOPS IN ONE SPOT, the game stopped and told me of the 'MASS BATTLE' mode. "What is this?" I replied before clicking this. Entering a battle with 40k soldiers, equally matched I had a battle with the enemy. Eventually winning, the Hojo were in retreat, the 'spine was broken'. Seeing this other neutral clans started attacking the hojo, becomming a land grab.
That is where I am up to after playing 20 hours. Still have the of Japan to go. ^_^

This adorable game is tagged as a visual novel, but it's a bit closer to a puzzle game (kind of an optimization problem).  Every turn (week) you decide what skills your princess needs to train.  Most weeks something interesting happens.  Sometimes something happens that can result in your fledging queen's death, but that cruel fate can be avoided if she has been properly trained.  There's another part to this, though: Elodie's training is directly influenced by her mood (bonuses to military and weapon skills when angry; who would've guessed?).  So in addition to managing her training you need to manage her emotional state to ensure she's receptive to the sort of training you want her to have.
Like any puzzle game, the puzzles are static.  Once you've discovered how to avoid eating poisoned chocolates the first time you'll have a pretty good idea of how to do it on subsequent tries.  This is kinda cool since you can learn how to win, but it limits replayability.  Even so there are a LOT of branching paths offering moderate replayability.  I've had a good deal of fun with it, and I haven't come close to winning (though I've already died in five different ways!).

The mechanics are quite simple, you have different moods you have to balance and these moods give you different bonuses when studying. You get to study two skills a week, from obscure and ultimately useless ones like "Animal Handling -> Falconry" to more useful ones like "Military -> Strategy" and "Courtly Manners". It would seem almost impossible to tell which skills are more useful until you get a couple playthroughs under your belt and learn the sequence of static events and paths that your choices/performances take you down. Fake example just to avoid spoilers: You know there is a battle coming up in Week 20, but a royal ball coming up in Week 10 and if you fail that then all hell breaks loose. You would most likely want to train skills for the ball first to impress nobles to keep them happy and still have ample weeks to train for the upcoming battle (that may not be revealed to be happening until Week 18). This insider knowledge gives you almost a required advantage as being blindsided by events can often end in your untimely (although amusing) demise. Make new saves often.
I would recommend this game for cheap during a Steam sale. Initially, during my first playthrough I wanted to say that it was worth more than a few dollars but there are two key things that prevented that. First, although it would appear as if events are random to some degree, all of them are static. This isn't necessarily a problem since they play out like branches of a tree as you progress through weeks (the first few events are always the same but choices eventually branch out into hundreds of possible combinations). Although there is eventual variety of outcome based on choices you may have made at the start of the game, and some of them have a greater degree of impact than others, they all feel pre-determined, albeit outlandish at times.
This segues into my second reservation about the game and really the two points could be summed up into a "This game isn't unrestrictive but pretends to be" argument. My second problem with the game is that it feels too short, i.e. it has a timely ending. The 40 weeks (read: 100 or so decisions made by me) were just enough time for it to really feel like the world was about to react to the character I guided or vice versa. It was just enough time for the plot path I ended up traversing to thoroughly♥♥♥♥♥♥me off and make me want to switch to ruling with an iron fist and transforming into a cruel leader bent on revenge.
In short, what I really wanted was a dramatic unfolding story with random events that could carry it much farther. I was impressed with how many possible combinations they had in the 40 weeks, but would have traded half of those combinations for the game to even double its length. Ideally, this game would go on forever, like some sort of visual novel crime-drama strategy sandbox extravaganza. I'm glad I didn't bother paying attention to any of the dozens of dukes and dutchesses and their names because the end came too quick for any of that to matter much.
In summary, LLTQ is a fun game to sink a few hours into for relatively cheap but falls short of its potential in that it isn't quite a visual novel version of Total War or Civilization without the combat. Its replayability depends on your mood toward short playthroughs where it could have cemented its replay value with more depth per playthrough.

I should note that I haven't beaten the game yet - this is merely my take on what I've experienced of it so far.
Night in the Woods is first-and-foremost a story-driven game. You play as Mae Borowski - a 20 y.o college student who drops out in her first year and returns to her childhood home of Possum Springs. The game undoubtedly takes heavy inspiration from Scott Pilgrim - from its main character to the quirky dialogue, even to the group's cobbled-together garage band that only seem to be able to attract a single supporter to their rehearsals! Even the art style is reminiscent of SP - it's got a colourful and recognisable style that really is a delight to just look at.
Most of the game consists of platform-style exploration akin to an adventure game, speaking to people in town and discovering new dialogues and details. The standard exploration is also mixed-up in these sections with a host of minigames - these help to add variety to the gameplay and spice things up.
In some ways, it's less like playing a game and more like playing an interactive graphic novel. But the story it tells, I feel, is a more personal and sentimental tale than SP, with the main themes explored including childhood, growing up and all it entails, relationships, personal responsibility and mental illness.
The comparisons that some people have made to Stephen King are also apt, as the game deals with some familiar themes and tropes from his work (don't want to spoil anything here). The story of Possum Springs deals with the heavier themes of deindustrialisation and the disenfranchisement of American Rust Belt communities. Possum Springs itself, despite the beauty of its rural, autumnal location, is a total dump of a town - economically-deprived, stagnant and soul-sucking for the likes of Mae (but it's still home). It's a setting that may be all too familiar to some players.
There's also the to-be-expected generational battle between the conservative-minded elderly and the more liberal, rebellious youth that Mae and her entourage make up. In places, it skirts the realm of the political but not distractingly so and anyone choosing to dismiss the game on this note would be missing the point entirely (and doing themselves a disservice).
If this all sounds a bit heavy, I should note that it's not a total downcast slog to play through. The game expertly balances its disturbing and sombre moments with plenty of humour, wit and downright hilarious moments, mostly brought to us through Mae and her friends.
The characterisation is excellent - Mae and her friends are memorable, well-detailed and, in many cases, laugh-out-loud funny. The moments we share with them feel unique and special, and we're really brought into the world through their perspective. As with the setting of Possum Springs, the characters are also extremely relatable. I guarantee everyone can recognise at least one person they know in real life in these characters. The writers really captured the millenial 'spirit' (from its anger to its joys) in an extremely compelling way with Mae and co.
The dialogue is fantastic, containing a wit and incisiveness that I didn't even know I'd been missing from games. The way the narrative is framed is also excellent - and there's a constant undercurrent of suspense and intrigue as we try to piece together the mystery of Possum Springs. It's a genuine pleasure to play something so well-written.
Soundtrack is also great - very themative and varied.
The main gripe I have with the game is the sense of repetition in places. In some ways, it plays to the game's advantage, giving an impression of the staid monotony of life in Possum Springs. That said, searching out new people to speak to and new things to discover never got boring - but I won't deny that I found some of the backtracking to be quite tedious at points. While I love the aesthetic of Mae's dream sequences, having to repeat the same sequence at the end of each day quickly wore on me. Replayability may also be an issue for some, though I understand we will be getting new content for the game next month.
Ultimately, those are only minor detractions. I'm still enjoying the game's story, atmosphere and characters too much for these gripes to dampen the overall experience.
As I said at the beginning of my review, I've yet to finish the game. It's still possible that it goes downhill and culminates in an awful, terribly-written ending that manages to undo all the good things I've said about it. In which case, I will return to edit this review. But from what other people have said about it, I don't think that's all too likely, and my experience with the game to date has been one of joy.

Ace Combat Assault Horizon (ACAH)
I really dig flight simulators, especially flight simulators of military aircraft.  I'm a fan of Microsoft Flight Simulator and am also a fan of the techno thriller genre from Ace Combat series or the great Tom Clancy HAWX games.  Yes, I get that Ace Combat (or even HAWX) is scarecly a "flight simulator", but I also frame these flying games in the realm of flying exotic (and highly classified) aircraft on a console or PC.
The Good:  Flying military aircraft on highly classified if not outright impossible missions.  The developers here did an outstanding job of replicating the aircraft inside and out!  You even fly an Apache and as a gunner on the side of a Blackhawk.  Graphics during the cutscenes are awesome!  Even shooting down some of the enemy aircraft are eyecatching events with the oil splattering and aircraft breaking apart.
The Bad:  Why the developers strayed from a winning formula is beyond me.  It would seem that they tried to combine a flying game with a fighting game (think Afterburner meets Mortal Kombat).  There's only one way to destroy certain enemies and that's to engage them up close and fly low to the ground with the cinematography of a Braveheart or Gladiator swordfighting scene.  To escape some of the missiles, you need to pay attention to two arrows lining up.  Basically, they tried to hard to make this game stand out.  Controlling the Apache or the Blackhawk gunner was clumsy.
The Ugly:  Interesting story...from what I know of it.  The game play is awful!  So awful, that I couldn't trudge through it and get immersed in the game.  It pains me to say this as I love these types of games, and wanted to love this game so much as I've loved the other Ace Combat games.   The voice acting (or the script) needed work but it wasn't terrible.  Like other flying games, even the good ones, your missions require you to fly against a numerically superior air force.  Thankfully, your aircraft carries a numerically superior amount of missiles.  IMHO, this "numerically superior aircraft vs you and your missiles" theme leads to repetitive and quickly boring gameplay.  It didn't help that some of the missions dragged on adding little if any value to the overall story!
It breaks my heart to do this, but no....I cannot recommend ACAH.  If you get it for free, then maybe.  But no, I can't recommend this game especially since it doesn't even approach the standards of Ace Combat Fires of Liberation.

Now that GG XRD -Revelator- is out, this version is pretty much obsolete, so to those of you that haven't bought this game and were waiting on a sale, I now recommend you just buy the new version instead, as for me I am personally not shelling out another 60 bucks just to get the Balanced Changed verison with additional characters, considering they will most likely release a 3rd installment with everything included and more balance changes down the line anyway, this never ending cycle of selling a balance update packaged with minor amounts of additional content really needs to stop :/
If you've been playing this series in the arcades since early 2000s like me, then I highly recommend you change the audio to Japanese as soon as you boot the game up before doing anything. As far as I can tell, the game runs flawlessly: No tearing, Good response (at least locally), even when V-sync is turned on. Graphics are eye candy for what I'm used to a GG game having, new mechanics are great (albeit a bit cruel at times to execute :/, but I expected as much...). I also love how much more useful roman cancels are, adding even more depth to the already expansive combat of the series. Honestly, the best part is, the game has yet to crash once on me (though Arc has a good rep when porting over their fighting games from console to PC compared to other publishers)...
The only gripes I have with the game is the fullscreen resolution is currently one level lower than my monitor's ratio, so it has black bars at the edges of the screen which really bug me, and I am unable to fix atm (though from what I read, this issue is being addressed...), and that the Final Arcade boss, although challenging, is the weakest Guilty Gear Arcade Final Boss I have faced by far, examples from the previous games I played on normal:
-Guilty Gear X Dizzy made me continue like 30 times before I beat her.
-Guilty Gear X2 I-No was a bloody nightmare, which took me a whopping 50 tries before I got her strategy down, I can still only 1CC her with specific chars.
-Guilty Gear Xrd Ramlethal Valentine... Continued only once... Tad dissapointing but, still a fun boss...
Overall I HIGHLY recommend you buy this game, especially now while all the DLC is free for the 1st month...
-9001/10, would buy again (and I probably will with Revelator around the corner, lol...)
*EDIT*  12/13/2015
So after playing arcade with a few more chars, I discovered that apparently, the final Arcade Mode boss changes based on who you are using. Needless to say, this seems to make the final boss fights (least in arcade) even weaker than in previous installations due to them feeing far easier (since I already know what to expect, and that's honestly the only reason Ramlethal managed to beat me the first time around...). So if you want a challenge in arcade mode, then crank up the difficulty and use a char you suck with, cause that will at least make the arcade mode enjoyable...
One more thing, unlike in other Arc system fighting games in the past (at least when GG and BB are concerned), the story mode in this game is more of a Visual Novel than anything else, you literally will not fight in it's entirety, but rather be a spectator... so if you are going in expecting anything more, you will be dissapointed. Sadly, this game also has the 2nd smallest roster (including unlockable characters, only making it fall behind Guilty Gear PSX by 1), and while the amount of content included is short and sweet, and the online component may give it a few more bits of longevity, just know that compared to the last installment released, Guilty Gear XX Accent Core + R (which is also available in steam) you are getting far FAR less for your money. Just be wary of that before you do decide to buy into it (in all honesty, due to this game being pretty much a ground up project with a new engine, I can somewhat forgive the lack of characters and content compared to older titles. This, along with the sequel being released very soon may also explain why they reduced the game's price on launch...)

Last night I was sitting on Mumble with mah bois, when a friend brought up Xrd's graphical style. I went "yeah, it's great, it looks like sprites but it's 3D- it's on Unreal Engine, you know...too bad it's only on PS4 or whatever". Imagine my surprise when he corrected me and told me that not only is it coming to Steam, but it's
. I didn't believe him at first and hectically checked the store page...there it was, just casually sitting in the new releases category as if it wasn't
to have an ArcSys game released on Steam, and especially before it has drifted off into complete obscurity. As a European in particular, this is as if Christmas had come not mere 3 weeks, but 3 years early.
So far I've played through and enjoyed the first ~25 challenges of all characters and played the advanced tutorial, which is pretty great and I'd say comparable to the advanced (and widely praised) tutorials in Skullgirls. They really teach you how to get around stuff that newbies often have trouble with, like zoning, ground to air anti-airing with normals, and so on- probably my favourite feature of the game. There is a mode called M.O.M. that seems very similar, if not identical, to Abyss mode in BlazBlue games; I'm not sure how close they are, I don't bother with that stuff, but it's there.
The game has some teething issues, like titles all still being in Japanese and the HUD resolution only scaling to 720p (which is getting fixed), but it runs quite smoothly (alt-tabbing is super fast, as well, which is a real blessing), it obviously looks great, and from what little I remember of the older Guilty Gears, it's pretty close to its heritage with some innovation. FromSoftware makes incredibly good games that will both punish and reward you for playing them. The difficulty of their environments and enemies is astounding, but the way they are designed are both beautiful and captivating. Dark Souls is probably the best example of this. The map is so finely crafted, so exquisitely fluid. The mobs are all challenging and fun to combat (except the dogs, of course).
Despite my high praise of this game, I cannot suggest the PC port of the game at all. Because this was FromSoft's first port of a Souls game to PC, it suffers from some of the worst optimization I have seen in a PC port. Even after spending hours tweaking the game with various tools, I couldn't get the game to run fast enough to be playable.
As such, if someone were to ask me if they should buy Dark Souls on the PC, I would suggest they purchase Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin or Dark Souls III. As it is, this entry in the series just isn't functional enough to be worth buying.

Hello all.
This is a long review, with your classic pros / cons and a final verdict. For those of you looking for a quick read, feel free to skim through or simply skip to the verdict at the end of the review. I hope this helps!
A player's summary:
This game is a survivalistic - type open world environment. The scene is set on Orca Island, a small patch of land surrounded by the infinite blue, yet holds dense concentrations of buildings and woods spread throughout the map. You spawn in with clothes on your back, a flashlight in your hand, something on your head, and shoes on your feet ... or maybe it's flipflops. You " goal " is to have the " perfect life ". You want to gear yourself up with weaponry, cool clothes, grab a vehicle and get established on a nice patch of land.
----------
Pro's
-----
- Addictive.
Starting out, it's an instant winner survival game. Spawning in, taking your first deep breath, filling those lungs with that Miscreated air, you take in the lovely scenery and wonder how quickly you'll be killed after taking your first step. With a large, decent - rendered open world, there's plenty to explore and do.
- Customization.
While there's no immediate character customization ( aside from choosing a gender for your character ), the game does offer quite an immersive character customization through items. From 3 different camo's with multiple patterns to hoodies, ballistic helmets, gas masks to my personal favorite, bright pink running sneakers, this game has a lot to offer.
- Diverse weaponry.
There's quite a few weapons in the game, from your .357 revolvers to .45 and .9mm sidearms to 7.62 and 5.56x45 rifles. Throw in a few crossbows, longbows, assorted knives, crafted bats and weapons to my personal favorite: a baseball bat wrapped in barbed wire titled " Her Majesty".
- Fluid combat / movement system.
With first / third person viewpoints, and decent movement mechanics, the game fit moderately well into the survival - game industry. Sadly, you can't go prone.
- Vehicles.
This game has quite a few vehicles, ranging from multiple colored sedans, armoured trucks, and ATV's to full - fledged buses ( The " Party Bus " - Aptly named if I do say so myself ), military transport trucks, and police cruisers - yes, the sirens and the lights work.
- Time cycles / weather.
The night / day transitions are moderately smooth, aside from the minor issues here and there ( graphically - wise ) the night, day, and weather visuals are graphically well done with audio to match.
__________
Con's
-----
- The updates / bugs.
While this game has relatively frequent updates, ( once a month or every few weeks ), they prioritize the wrong things. For example, players pushed the developers early on to introduce vehicles to the game - which were full of bugs. After patching the immediate bugs, the developers now focus on adding new content, rather than refining and fixing existing content. A recent example ( 9/30/17 ), being rather than fixing bugs such as while interacting with any given object, and the game crashes you will loose large portions of your items upon return, the " Ocean bug ", where somedays you will simply spawn in the ocean upon logging in reguardless where you logged out and be forced to drown to return to the game world ( swimming to shore will result in being stopped a few yards out by an invisible wall, effictively trapping you in the water ), and more, the developers decide to release new vehicles and items, resulting in more bugs. A recent on where I had been out and about looting for more gear, my current gear / inventory with items that I valued at around 80 hours loot time ( I value items in any game based off of the time it takes to acquire said item ), and suddenly I was attacked by a pack of wolves. No big deal, I had my trusty Mk18 rifle with around 500 rounds - oh, then my screen goes black. Not completely, I can still see my HUD, composing of my health bar / status bars, I can see the chat box, etc but everything else is black. End up dying, and spawn in ( of course ) on the other side of the map. I sprint back; of course my body's despawned by the time I get back. This happens all too often.
- The interfaces / crafting system.
While the interface isn't as bad as one may be led to believe, it's generally very time consuming to craft anything ( simply navigating to your crafting interface for base parts for one ), and interacting with your gear during combat is a nightmare. The crafting system is decent, with a diverse selection of items to craft - only you need to find the blueprints first. Ever heard the saying, " It's like looking for a needle in a hay stack, but more like a crumb in a f***ing ocean! "? That's quite an accurate quote reguarding finding your *important* blueprints. Walls 2 ( allowing you to build the largest walls - 3x4 ), storage ( allowing the construction of the larger of the two storage boxes ), gatehouse ( crafting a gate and a frame for allowing passage of small vehicles through walls ), etc are among the rarest loot drops in the game.
- Mutants.
There are a few varients of mutants, to save you a trip to the wiki I'll list them all here:
Small:
= Average sized mutant with a shirt and jeans. Moderate speed / damage.
= Average sized mutant with shorts and a needle for an arm. Moderate speed / high damage.
= Average sized mutant completely nude. High speed / moderate damage.
Large:
= Large sized mutal completely nude. Nicknamed " Brutes ". Moderate speed / extremely high damage.
Misc:
= Mutant multi - headed dogs. Enough said. High speed / low damage.
= Wolves. Roam in packs. High speed / moderate damage.
Most of the AI are buggy, unpredictable, and quite frankly, bad. They will get stuck on vehicle roofs, etc.
- Lack of consistent gameplay.
This means that up until a few months ago, the game was completely player - run: meaning that ALL Miscrated servers were contracted by players through
( which holds a monopoly on all Miscreated servers ). This means that if no players paid the rediculous price of upwards of 40 euros ( $50 USD+ ) every month, you could not play Miscreated, even after purchasing it for $20 off of the steam store. Due to this fact of server prices be outlandish and absurd, and the server hosting is unstable and connection is weak. Chances are, the server you are playing on will be shut down in a matter of days, or if you're lucky and it's a new server, it'll be gone by the end of the month. If it lasts longer, it can be shut down on you at any point.
__________
Final thoughts.
*Please note this review had to be cut short due to maxing out the word count. I didn't touch on all points of the game, but I've tried to cover the main points.
This is quite an enjoyable game, and for those looking for a quick survival experience, or if you're new to the whole open - world concept, it's a great game to start out on - if you don't mind loosing your items frequently or being killed often. For an " early access " game, it's decent. But may I remind you that it's been in this state for nearly 4 years. Yes, they warn you of bugs and character wipes, but is this game really being worked on? Do the players really get their money's worth? Is there this many bugs and issues with the game, yet it's been out for 3 years, and nearly being considered " complete "? Questions you'll have to answer for yourself. My verdict: It's not worth your money in the long run. You'll become invested in this game, as it's addictive and fun for a few quick hours of gameplay, but soon you'll become frusterated with the rough mechanics, bugs, nonexistent lore, among various other issues.
This said, I do hope this helped some of you decide on your purchase of this game. If you have any questions, please feel free to send me a message and I'll try to get back to you as soon as possible as once again I had to cut out quite a bit to fit this all into one review.
You all take care.

Like a lot of people I have a bit of a split opinion on it.
Lets start with the time travel mechanic. It's a very interesting mechanic that is executed pretty well. It does what you expect it to do. When you stay on a button the button gets pressed. When you push a button the button gets pushed. It records where you aimed your portals so even if you can't fire the portal somewhere at that moment your past self will attempt to fire and the portals will apear if your past self can fire them succesfully. Your past self is still affected by things like emancipation grids if they are active at present. Simply put, what a co-op player can do your past self can do.
There is 1 mechanic that gets introduced that is not very fitting though. This mechanic is the ability to jump onto your past self when your past self is crouching. All it does is allow you to get some height to get over obstacles. Something that did not need to be introduced seeing how it's only used to jump over obstacles that have been made high on purpose or reach buttons that are put high on purpose.
This brings us to the puzzles. They are underwhelming. The first room uses a screen in the room to tell you the time machine buttons. The problem is that the buttons are very hard to read. A simply pop-up that shows the button and it's function like in the normal game would have made things a lot easier. Especially seeing how the buttons are not the only instructions that are on the screen.
The few rooms after that room are pretty well constructed. They introduce you slowly to the functions of the time machine. The increase in difficulty during these rooms is about the same as portal 2 assuming you played single player portal 2 all the way through.
But then there is GLaDos room. This is where things start to get bad. In GLaDos room you're expected to use a control panel that never gets introduced to leave. This control panel is hidden in the envoirement behind a door. One of the problems is that there are several other doors that you can't interact with. Other than the text on the door there is no indication that you can interact with it and the text looks like cosmetic text with no meaning at first glance. Another problem is that the panel has multiple buttons on it but no clear indication that there are multiple buttons. It looks like a single interactive object instead of an object with several buttons.
After that room the difficulty is pretty much all over the place. The first room after it is a pretty reasonable difficulty but if I remember correctly the room after that uses magnetic recepticles on the ceiling. You can also get stuck in that room by doing what you get taught in the very first room, using your past self to hold down a button, if you record over you holding down the button. A few rooms later on the other hand all you need to do is press a button to move a cube past some emancipation grids. You only need the time machine for the first button. after that you can just press the button, get the cube and move it past the emancipation grid. And then there are some rooms that simply require you to be as fast as possible and that barely involve any thinking.
The portal gun, just forget about it. There are only a few rooms in the mod that use it and you never need to use it more than a few times. There is exactly 1 part in the game where you actually have to fling yourself and that part does not use the time machine. There is a lot of missed oppertunity for puzzles that really feel like co-op puzzles. Oh, and your portals disappear every time you play your time machine
The story is lacking at best. There are only 3 story segments including the ending and opening. The opening is promising. The second segment is avarage and the ending is simply confusing and nothing more. And I don't mean confusing in the I don't know what just happened way. I mean confusing in the why way. As in why bother adding a story if you're not going to give it any closure.
Last we have a very strange subject. The astethics. The mod goes for a simplistic futuristic look. Seeing how I have a similar taste in astetics I don't mind the change from the portal 2 look to much. At least, I wouldn't if it was done correctly. The problem lies in that white square panels are used to provide light. You see the problem? Large white square surfaces that are  all over the floor, walls and ceiling. A portal gun being in your posesion that gets barely used. A recipe for confusion. And that is exactly what it was. You can barely recognize portal surfaces because they look almost exactly like the lights. This makes some puzzles very difficult to solve. Especially because even when you do recognize the surfaces the lights do not make it clear whether you need to use your portal gun on other parts of the puzzle.
All in all this is a mod that needs some serious work. The portal gun is mostly useless, the jump mechanic is unneeded, the difficulty is all over the place, you are expected to recognize and use elements that you've never been introduced to and you can barely recognize portal surfaces if at all. Safe yourself the hour of your time that this mod would waste and wait until the developer(s) update the mod to the point where it's playable and has a fair difficulty.

After playing for a while on the scenario where nobunaga became a daimo, i have finally face my 1st true test where my alliance is being ganged by 2 of the largest clans. I realised the following:
- This is a very complex strategic game where strong alliance, right buildings built, efficient resources management and and even luck (i had famine event during harvest month on both my cities when i planned for an offensive which i had to delay for a year) play a part in expanding and survival of your clan.
- Build more fortresses to increase income and troop count.
- Set policies to boost your clan
- increase diplomacy with as many clans as possible (+20 helps with gold income +40 allows you to summon help)
- I am facing the current adversity of 2 huge clan ganging up on me from the east because i was focusing on the west and naively thought they will not ally to attack my alliance.
-building relationship with the shogun and bribing the official for higher ranking post
-Battles can be settle automatically in the strategic map by AI or in a tactical format controlled by player
In my opinion, the battle system is very flawed. After so many battle in tactical form, i have yet to get a hang of where tactical movement and placement actually works.
For example surrounding a single enemy unit with 3 allies will see the same amount of troops losses on both side. having horses and musket does not seem to improve damage other than having the charge and release tactics. Using them placed the unit uncontrollable even after enemy in front had lost and retreated.
Another example is in an arrow battle, my unit with superior general and 3 times more troops takes more damage than a weaker opponent facing each other both with musket.
That means battles will most likely be the force that has higher troop count will win although not always true. (I have lost or win with more or less troops before but do not expect any significant victory using a lesser force)
The only times that i saw any difference are the tactics used by various units. However the tactic bar(command bar) increases so slowly which limit tactic usage to change the battle. Both side starts with the same amount even when the troops count are different or number of general/units are different. This means a smaller force can cast the same amount of tactics as a much superior force.
This is unlike ROTK 12 which has faster regeneration of tactic bar and troops movement placement are important. In this game it feels non-existance.
Tactical battle map are small and maneuvability is havoc when you want to aim an enemy unit but is near to another. Mass tactical battle map feel the same small size as normal battle and there is hardly any tactical movement to be made like flanking and sending decoy which could be made in ROTK 12.
For those who played koei ROTK games, this game battle system is more like ROTK 12 than to ROTK11 due to it being real-time. And i prefer the battle system of ROTK 12 than this game.
For those who played medieval 2 total war, the battle system in this game is nothing like total war. This is due to the fact that there is only one type of unit and medieval 2 has many different types. Therefore do not expect it to be the same or even better.
However I will still recommend this game for its strategic part of the game, story, orchestra music, pleasant graphic, difficulty of the game and the complexity of game. There are many more reasons listed out by others and given my hundreds and hundreds of hours playing ROTK games, this is a potential hundred+ hours game for those who have the PATIENCE to conquer japan. If not I would recommend skipping this game as learning the basics and the tutorial will be more than 2hr and you can not accomplise and gain any satisfaction in a short term.

Here we go again, another zombie shoot 'em up. When will the zombie thing end? Probably when it stops making money. Either way, I doubt this will stop any time soon, until then, let me present Over 9000 Zombies!
Gameplay: 93/100 A-
Gameplay is simple, using ASWD to move around, use your mouse to aim and fire your weapons and granades. It's solid and responsive. My major issue more has to do with the design of the game when it comes to colors and characters on the screen, making it hard to see, but that's for later. Everything is done at the bare minimum, from the menu screen for building walls or turrets to finding resources for upgrades. The learning curve isn't high, but the difficulty ramps up fairly quickly, especially if you're playing alone, but at no point did I rage quit out of frustration. My normal reaction was "I wonder if I can get further this time?"
Audio: 100/100 A+
The sound effects are clear, the guns sound like guns, but the true shining jewel of this has to be the single looping 15-minute track full of electro-punk rock goodness. Having not listened to this kind of music in years, I quickly fell in love with it and truly added to the gameplay and kept your blood flowing, much in the same way how the music picked up in Half-Life 2 when things were getting intense.
Visuals: 87/100 B+
Over 9000 is a bit of a sight for sore eyes, while it isn't harsh, thing can be a bit clearer in design, unit/item outlines or highlights would greatly improve the game on a visual level, but it isn't a deal breaker since not seeing a power up isn't usually the end of the world, it would just be nice to have bit more indication of where things were.
Content: 84/100 B-
There isn't much at first, but there is a map builder. Weapons are unlocked over time and there is a wide variety of turrets you can build along with enemies with different attacks
Multiplayer: 89/100 B+
This is where the fun can increase tenfold, just like in Left 4 Dead, having friends around increases the chaos and that's good for a game built on frantic decisions. But once again, the design is what holds this area back a bit as things get cluttered really quick from either game effects, zombie guts, or other players, but it could also just be the map I'm playing on. Anyways, bring a friend to the apocalypse if you can.
Design: 79/100 C+
Alright, the design of the game is very basic, almost too basic, as the colors and sprites end up blending together all too much for my tastes, but this doesn't have much to do with the old retro style, just a poor design using the retro style. Besides that, most of the game works well because of it's simple approach to everything. No, you can't customize the controls, but there are only a literal handful of buttons you need, why would you want to customize them?
Performance: 100/100 A+
Being the game that it is with its pixelated style, it pushed my 2GB graphics card to the max just so that the game could run smoothly. Sure I could have turned off the advanced PhysX Effects and bloom visuals, but whatever. I'm kidding of course, any computer should be able to play this game just fine with no issue whatsoever.
Verdict: 90/100 A-
Yes, it's not the first of its kind, nor will it be the last, but one thing is for certain, it is a solid game that sucks you in if you let it. You can't just play one round and call it quits, you have to keep going until you just keep going, like the first sip of a new wine, the first two glasses are strange, but by the third, you can't stop and it just goes down smooth. And just like wine, it's best with others around to enjoy it with you - Cheers!

Night in the Woods is a narrative driven game done right.  Not to say that it doesn't have its faults, but I feel that the game did the dialogue system and choice branches very well.  This is something that the giants of this genre, namely Telltale, still fail to do well with.  They often forget that the character you're playing as doesn't always have to be a direct self-insert of the player.  The dialogue choices didn't always boil down to nice, mean, or neutral.  Sometimes what was said wasn't what the player might want to say, but simply a selection of what the protagonist might say.  The protagonist is their own character, not a fill in the blank.

Though I found the dialogue and a few characters a little unrealistic, I think the main story was both captivating and ,at times, relatable.  The feeling of dropping out of college and not knowning what to do with onesself is something I've experienced.  I felt that this was presented in a pretty realistic way.  The mystery itself was quite interesting and didn't end up being a letdown like the godawful third act of Firewatch.  All in all, I enjoyed this game a lot.  I'll probably give it another playthrough at some point to see what scenes I missed out on because of my choices.
