Don't let the lore scare you away. It's difficult, but not impossible and you learn a little more with every session. A fantastically three dimensional story and commendable commitment to a realistic drama can have you fall in love with a world that changes every time you play depending on your choices. Yes, you'll die. It's normal. The point is to experience the story, and reflect on the suffering death sentence of a young monarch in revolutionary times carrying the sins of her nation on her back.
Gameplay involves turn-based choices to keep your kingdom happy, all the while growing in stats as a person and managing emotions to avoid becoming emotionally crippled. I personally fell into the roll of Elodie all too quickly, identifying remarkably with her fears and willfulness. I let my emotions dictate my actions from time to time, imprisoning a man I should have just executed because I identified with him after feeling guilt for previously executing a woman I somewhat pitied. I debated marriage for ten minutes without touching my mouse, truly contemplative of the sacrifices I could make for my nation and heart. I felt a genuine giddiness when my cousin recovered from her snakebite, and true fear when I was finally assassinated 33 weeks in by a furious archduke in a public stabbing during international festivities thus sparking war.
This was my story. One of my many stories. Yours will be different. Buy this game today, and fall into the role of Princess Elodie.

A Visual-Novel type RPG with a punishing yet fun brutality as you're flung into a world where everyone is out to kill you through no fault of your own. You play as a fourteen year old princess with pink hair, and while that does seem to turn some people off, I compel you to give this game a chance. It is incredibly intricate and very addicting, but the best adjective I think should be applied to it is
. We, or at least
, tend to associate immersion with games where you
the player character, typically first-person games, where you see out of the eyes of the protagonist as if they were your own. This game is very unlike that, but somehow made me feel more a part of the universe than any Call of Duty could.
If you actually know what you're doing, this game is pretty short.
And that's the whole point: you're a fourteen year old girl suddenly thrust into this seat of immense power and responsibility, with the lives of thousands depending on you, let alone your own.
It's a difficult juggling act, as you balance regality with intrigue and strategy and personal capabilities.
In my final winning playthrough, I became this ultimate uber-awesome juggernaut, with maximum magical ability, financial and strategic military genius, all while being a master archer and swordswoman. But because I invested so much time in those abilities, I was completely deaf to current events, history both foreign and local, and internal and external affairs of all kinds, so when a dude comes up to me after my big tournament and yells about how the blood of his family is on my hands or something, I have no idea what he's talking about.
And that's the real beauty of the game: you're
to make monumental decisions that will shape the future of your entire planet, all while being completely uninformed.
Of course, I don't have to be, and on an earlier playthrough I didn't read a page on naval strategy and bulked up my spy network and learned all about the current politics and events, and stuff played out differently because of that.
But the thing you have to learn is that nine out of ten options lead to your death.
I said that when played properly, the game is actually rather brief. But it took me nine hours to calculate a winning playthrough. And I mean
; I actually did a lot of math and experimentation to locate the best overall course of action and determine which activity to perform week-by-week on the small scale, so maybe that time too is a bit shorter than average.
The game isn't randomized, so if you do the same actions in two different play sessions, the results will be exactly the same, so the secret to success is really just iteration and trying every possibility with the foresight of what will happen in the future; something some games try to shy away from but that works wonderful here.
Long Live The Queen is agonizing in its difficulty (especially because it seems to trick you into thinking you're doing well when in reality you've just dug yourself into a hole you won't notice until it's far too late), but while some games can be downright soul grinding and make you want to punch a wall, every time I failed here, I never ceased having fun. It shares that quality with Super Meat Boy in a way, but I think LLTQ actually does it a bit better.
But even though you fail and die,
, Long Live The Queen always seems to adequately reward you when you do eventually find that correct course of action.
I fought that Ion or whatever guy at the end of my tournament like twelve times. Sure I won most of them, but got stabbed and bled out in a good handful too. In one iteration I tried to fight with swords but would inevitably fail and had to learn to use staves instead. But that one, final playthrough where I actualy won the whole game I found a new, third option (aside from accepting the duel or declining) where I epically burned his body to a crisp with my newfound Sith Lord fingertip lightning, as said some clever little dialogue. That alone was just so rewarding to me, and when later I finally beat that invading king with a magic Spirit Blade which combined my Lumen-abilities and my skill with swords by decapitating him, I was just so pleased. The imagery alone is worth twenty bucks: me, a cute little innocent fourteen year old girl with pink hair, blocking every one of his attacks with a combination of carefully cultivated reflexes and magical training until I make a split-second decision to conjure a blade of light and slash the man who terrorized me in (not)countless playthroughs before down like a vine blocking my path to the palace.
Another major point I have yet to really touch upon is the gravity of your actions.
I'm a big fan of Dragon Age and Bioware, and very much like actions with repercussions and ripple effects.
I think this game may do it a bit better.
Every one of my actions and decisions, no matter how small or uninformed, seemed like it made an impact, and the final epilogue presentation felt very rewarding as the future was shown as shaped by me.
And I only scratched the surface.
I still had a plethora of achievements and choices and scenarios unplayed and unmade, and several different angles I could of taken for every event. There remains so many options I didn't have access to for everything because I didn't invest in this one thing or try this tactic, which provide future options I didn't realize they would, which makes this game have high replayability, even though I'm going to shelf it for now after that long, nearly ten hour run of playtime.
Long Live The Queen is incredibly rewarding, immersive, fun and actually ridiculously original, at least to me. It offers an experience like no other I've come across, and I would recommend it to any that thinks they can make it to coronation.
Just buy it. A game everyone should own.

Up front, my playtime represents a comprehensive playthrough of the base game to include all collectibles, side missions, and several achievements.
If you're a fan of games like Batman (the combat is very familiar), God of War, Mark of Kri, and Conan, but want a dash of the "open world" then you will feel right at home here. The combat is great, the controls are smooth and intuitive, and the way you can shape some of the military hierarchy within the ranks of Uruk armies is a refreshing system that makes the game interesting and unique to its genre. The duality of the main character(s) is implemented very well and the game makes good use of the strengths they have to offer. The period in which SoM is set is also pretty interesting and fans of LotR will be absolutely giddy inside playing this. The collectibles and dialogue all made me want to watch the movies and read the books again. The minor downsides were that some of the missions did feel repetitive after awhile, primarily the outcasts ones where you are rescuing slaves over and over. There are 24 of those if I recall correctly and they never really change. They are optional though. Combat is a blast and you are given a variety of tools with which to dispatch your foes. This was great fun but also meant the game was never really much of a challenge and by the end I felt absolutely godlike.
I spent somewhere around $7 on this game while it was on sale and received the GotY edition. I highly recommend it even at full price and am looking forward to playing through the additional content.

A game that will be enjoyed by some and passed by others.  It is a VERY slow-burn style of game.  Player population is thin, so there may be long periods of time where youll encounter no one, even on a fully populated server.  This is by design, however.  Due to the very slow nature of gameplay, it is understandable why some may not like this game.
Difficulty wise, this game is merciless.  There is minimal UI.  There is no 360 no scopes.  Everything has to be earned and defended.  You're given nothing but the clothes on your back.
Most people will play kill on sight, but there are some servers are that frown upon that behaviour, but to be frank the constant threat from players are what make tbis game enjoyable.  Never knowing their motives is an exciting aspect.
Still has bugs and exploits that can be abused (it's in early access, what do you expect?), but fortunately the developers are very active is smoothing them out.  The only real complaint I got against this game is that ammo and gear are WAY too easy to find.  For a game that is about post apocalyptic scarcity, this doesnt make much sense.
Overall, I enjoy this game (and games like it).  This has the most compehensive gameplay (if not the most feature rich in comparison to competitors).  Could use more features beyond additional items and locations, but what it has meshes together well.  A solid early access title and I look forward to the finished product if it ever gets there.

Overall Rating - 9/10
Graphics - 8/10 : There is nothing stand-up amazing about the graphics and there is nothing bad about them. They are more than solid. They do the job but there is enough there to actually make you think the game is pretty. The artwork in cutscenes is splendid to look at. The best part for me is the castles and how detailed districts look.
Sound - 6/10 : Meh. The songs are a little repetative and loud personally. They do not really provide any ambience and I found myself turning off the music itself. Voice acting is brilliantly done and there is a good range of voices that make characters feel different, which is good.
Gameplay - 10/10 : Halfway between EU4 and Total War. It doesn't have as in depth a battle mode and it doesn't have as in depth a grand strategy mode but it is a brilliant balance. It doesn't feel "light" on mechanics. It has a nice spectrum of things to keep you busy each turn. The battle mechanics are a little clunky but it doesn't subtract from it.
Replayability - 8/10 : Much like EU4 and Total War, there is a lot of replayability in so much that you have access to all of the different nations from a variety of different starting points but it isn't that different an experience. It is repetative but if you play games like EU4 and TW it is the same situation as those games. There are feats to accomplish but these aren't linked to steam achievements which is a little annoying.
Price - 7/10 : Considering games like EU4 and TW, the price point is a little higher than you would normally expect but it isn't overpriced per-say. If you like these types of games you will most definitely put more than enough hours in to make it worth it and if you compare it to a game like EU4, if you include all of the expansions, then it is a pretty good deal.
I would really like to see it get some proper expansions or mods possibly in the future. This type of game in the European setting would be amazing.

If you enjoy Total War series but find the neverending battles eventually bog things down, this is the game for you.  I played it on a "budget" PC with integrated graphics and it ran silky smooth.
The character system seems deep and kingdom organization is very addicting.  The kingdom management succeeds because it's focused on scarcity.  You have limited money, limited vassals, and limited "labor" (action points).  Population helps build up action points and is required for a strong military.  Investing in the economy is important, even investing in roads, building new castles, fortifying key points.  There are so many choices but they are structured in a simple way that is not overwhelming.  Your characters increase in stats as time goes on and gain new traits.
The battles are also great.  They are smaller in scale than Total War, and they play quicker.  However, this also means the computational demands are a fraction of Total War series.   You lose some of the interesting decisions of Total War, such as specific units to produce, precise formations to employ, etc, but I found myself usually auto-rolling those battles as they drag on forever.  In Nobunaga, I am excited for the battles.
The menu UI is very logically laid out.  There are a few options that could be confusing at first, like transferring vassals, but the game walks you through what each action does.   Speaking of options, the game has a great set of options both in terms of difficulty (even specificying how you want the AI to be more difficult) and for graphics/what not.
The translation is very thorough, with some good localization here and there, like the dialogue in the Tutorial.   There was only one or two points where I felt the wording could be improved significantly.
I paid $50 for it at launch but, knowing what I do now, I would have easily paid $70-80 for this game and been happy.

I played the NES version as a Kid and I put more hours into the Romance games than anyone should ever admit to - so when I saw this I knew I had to get it. While I didn't set my expectations very high....  the tutorial pretty much doomed my opinion.
I don't believe I've ever played a tutorial which did a better job of turning me off from a game than this one did.  The tutorial shows you how to do about 5 basic acts within the game, so that you can have some idea how the game's interface works.  Sounds good right?   If that's all it did, that'd be fine.  But it also includes dialog between your character and someone advising them.   If you want to actually read the descriptions of what it is that you are doing - you click your way through conversations that take dozens of clicks.... click click click click click...     Otherwise you have the option of hitting the skip conversation button which fast forwards through it all - revealing just how ridiculously long the conversations are without telling you much.
After forcing myself through the tutorial - I decided to give the game a shot.   To be honest, it's not bad.  In fact it would probably be just fine if it weren't for the fact that there are so many other games out there.   As it is, the game feels as though I have to go through far too many menus and clicks just to accomplish basic tasks.  Nothing is so encombersome that I can point to it and say "AH HA!", but it still feels .....   Heavy.
TLDR: I found the game too much of a Clickfest to truly enjoy the game that exists here.      4/10

Surprisingly fun single-player missions. Part of the fun in this game is just dealing with your incompetent bot teammates who don't always behave... properly. Also, Turtle Rock rules! (Particularly Mike Booth. He's the guy responsible for most of the programming behind Valve's bot systems used in CS:CZ/CS:S/CS:GO as well as L4D/L4D2/TF2. That guy is awesome.)

If you don't know what this game even is, I'm not surprised. This is mostly a hidden thing that a lot of people don't know about, so I'm going to tell you exactly what is Counter-Strike: Condition Zero.
If you buy the game, you get Condition Zero and Condition Zero Deleted Scenes. Both have a singleplayer campaign, but the Deleted Scenes is more of an actual singleplayer story with voice acting and characters that help you, while Condition Zero itself has a singleplayer (there is a multiplayer that I'll talk about later) where you use points to hire more professional bots to complete missions. First, I'm going to tal kabout Deleted Scenes.
CZ Deleted Scenes is as I stated earlier, a singleplayer Counter-Strike campaign mode with story elements that create a plot that you're a soldier and you have to kick♥♥♥♥♥to get to your objective. There isn't just one story, there's a LOT of them. It kind of reminded me of COD (atleast the older ones, I haven't played any of the newer ones) where you'd play as different characters fighting in different battles, except you don't get switched back and forth, each mission you're a different person fighting different people working with different comrades. You fight in a diverse amount of countries around the globe like Russia, United States, Germany, Japan, etc... All of the weapons from the original Counter-Strike are in CZ but are re-modeled and work differently in Deleted Scenes, like they're more accurate. They also added in a few more peices of equipment like the RC Bomb, which can blow holes through walls in specific areas, a radio, where you can call backup (also in specific zones), a blow torch, where you can blow off locks (once again in specific zones), and finally an optic camera, where (in specific zones, of course) you can basically see through objects. I also love the voice acting in Deleted Scenes, it's not because it's good, it's alright at most, but I just love how bad it can be. None of the characters really sound believable at all, and they really don't get a grasp on what's going on, a lot like the scientists from HL1. But the voice acting may not be good, the writing is actually good. I particularly liked the mission where you'd infiltrate a Russian military base undetected, and while you're doing this you can listen to a few conversations, like how this guy won't trust his buddy with his lighter anymore, or like how it's super cold and how if there was an intruder that they could throw isicles at them. I think if they could've gave them better voice actors, I think that the dialouge would be perfect. Now the gameplay. I'd have to say I absolutely LOVE the gameplay in Deleted Scenes, it's Counter-Strikish but as said before the weapons are a lot more accurate, which makes sense because presmuably you're trained on how to not have a ♥♥♥♥ing bullet go 60 meters off of where it came out of the barrel. There are different kind of enemy NPCs, some of them are suicide bombers, some of them run up to you with knives and try to stab you,, snipers, assault teams, etc... It's linear, but there are a lot of places in your path to explore and easter eggs and loot. All in all, I give Deleted Scenes's campaign a 8/10.
Now it's time for the actual game. Condition Zero. Condition Zero not only has a multiplayer, but a singleplayer campaign where you get points for completing missions and you can use those points to hire more skilled bots to be on your team, you can choose the difficulty of the bots on the enemy team, but as far as I know, the difficulty you set does not affect the bots on your team. I think it uses every default map in the original Counter-Strike. Also, you only play as CT just like Deleted Scenes. There's not exactly any story, it's just that you have to stop the Ts from defuing the bomb or keeping hostages bla bla bla Counter-Strike things.
Now it's multiplayer. The multiplayer in CZ is actually good. It's like your typical early 2000s game, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t matchmaking, all community servers, and a good mix between comepetitive and casual. It's not like CS:GO where you're paired up with 4 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ just to have an entire enemy team made of hackers. And while hackers are a problem, they actually get banned by admins and people who are way better than you (called smurfs in CS:GO) aren't a problem because you can just leave and find another server with people that meet your skill. I'm not the best at CS but ♥♥♥♥ing hell I have almost 1,000 hours on CS:GO and Im still in Gold Nova because of how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t the hacker thing is. I liked being able to leave the game without having to wait 30 minutes to a ♥♥♥♥ing month to play the damn game again. CS: CZ really feels like Counter-Strike, not a cash cow with a community more toxic than the air in China where hackers make up 50% if not more of the that toxic community created by a sellout company (because CZ actually wasn't made by Valve, CZ was made by Turtle Rock Studios, and Deleted Scenes was made by Ritual Entertainment). I want to be able to play with real legit players that are at my skill or slightly higher or slightly lower. None of this would be a problem in CS:GO if there was 1. Not a ranking system. 2. No matchmaking and 3. A good ♥♥♥♥ing anti-cheat. In CZ I don't care that much if I die because it's not going to matter, Im not in a ♥♥♥♥ing tourtament where I could win thousands of dollars, Im in a ♥♥♥♥ing normal match in a game.

This is an unexpected gem. Years ago I would have laughed at the idea of narrative games but Night in the Woods makes a strong argument for them being my favorite genre. It doesn’t really tell a story so much as it places you into a small town with many stories and big problems (the biggest might be in your head) then allows you to experience and shape them.
Nothing in handed to you, it’s a complex story (or set of interconnected short stories) which you’ll have to make sense of yourself. Dialogue and characterizations are stellar. The people in this game feel like real people I have known, or were. By far the best writing I’ve seen in a game.
Like many narrative games it can feel like a walking simulator at times, you will spend a great deal of the game holding down the thumbstick to the left. The repetition of the game is intentional and I feel well implemented, daily activities with a few surprises here and there. Each game day ends in a little adventure which is often a minigame or a choose your own adventure style dialogue tree. This really helps breakup the periods of people just talking to each other.
While I loved the story of Gone Home I do agree with the complaints that it was too passive. Night in the Woods shows narrative games how to tell a compelling story while still containing gameplay.

Both games in the Orcs Must Die series are like stacking dominoes, spiked dominoes that explode into acid or fire. Both are delightful exercises in meticulous trap placement for a payoff of blood and gold. Try it yourself in the demo!
But before you do, let me elaborate on OMD2's upgrade system. Traps/weapons are upgraded with skulls, and these can be obtained in two ways: by completing levels for a one-time reward of up to 5 skulls, or by achieving repeatable feats (i.e. killing 1000 orcs, beating 5 waves in endless mode). To upgrade absolutely everything, you'll need 1651 skulls, but ultimately you'll only need a tenth of that to max out all the traps you can equip at one time, give or take a dozen.
Furthermore, this game has a supremely player-friendly feature: unlimited respecifications, or rather the ability to get back all the skulls you've spent and the freedom to reinvest them in whatever traps you want to try next. Players are free to upgrade any trap they like for an outrageous strategy, and can easily redistribute those upgrades for a different strategy!
If you have played OMD1, then OMD2 has another new feature: Multiplayer. You can now co-operate with one other steam friend to tackle the orcish hordes. Both of you can only carry half as many traps, but the benefit of a second player more than makes up for it, as you can help each other with setting traps and assisting in combat.
, there is no match-making system, so if you want to enjoy OMD2 as a co-operative experience, you'll need to find a loyal steam friend who has (or will have) the game as well.
All in all, this is game is a satisfying, whether you're on your own or side-by-side with a loyal friend. Mind you, do note that this game can get a bit time-consuming, so make sure you've got sufficient free time once you get started on it.

In general, this is just like the first game, but with a more fleshed out upgrade system and the addition of the much requested co-op mode.
However, as someone who five-skulled all Nightmare levels from the first game, I found there to be a massive difficulty spike towards the end of the campaign in this sequel. You can tell how much the developers emphasized designing with co-op in mind, as you're playing levels that seemingly require you to be in four different places at once.
It's still an enjoyable (albeit overly challenging) game if you're playing it solo.

Street Fighter IV is a game that truly requires skill (unless you play the crappy 3ds version). If you want to get good at the game you must have lots of dedication and time and patience to finally start winning. performing combos can be complex as well as defensive strategies. The music in the game is also pretty good. They have remixed versions of the character themes which sound pretty nice, Especially Adon's theme and Akuma's/Gouki's theme. As for the graphics, they are pretty unique with the less catoony but non realistic paint brush styled characters with fairly decent and non muddy textures. The online runs pretty well since my review of the game and does not hiccup very often for me. Did I mention you can even download mods? Every match is always different and you will continue to learn things about how characters work, game mechanics, and how some people's playstyles work. You will constantly improve even if you lose, and don't get down if you lose because EVERYONE loses. All in all, it's a very good game for 30$ and I highly recommend it.

I conditionally recommend this game. Things to keep in mind when I say "conditionally":
- I'll share my silliest gripe first: I'm pretty sure the trailer should say this is "digital heroin" not "heroine," but it doesn't look like the developer will ever re-create their trailers, so that cute typo stays with us for the ages.
- On the topic of things never changing, Transport Fever has stolen its thunder, but that's to be expected when quasi-sequels emerge - it has been almost three years since this title came out, after all. This does mean you're going to live with the game's quirks without much in teh way of changes, so you'd best be getting this on a good sale!
- There are persnickety background rules. Fail to deliver within 20 minute? Your passengers spontaneously disappear. If you can't accept this, don't read any further, go find a freeware copy of the original Railroad Tycoon instead.
- The interface is the gaming equivalent of working with SAP or any other program with minimalist UI. You have to adapt to its quirks rather than vice versa. The developers, to their credit, finally added a dialogue to let you see your old saved game names so you can over-write a prior save if you like doing that sort of thing. I originally used 1-letter saved game names because there was no way of clicking and selecting your old saved games. This, plus finicky track laying mechanics, are prime examples of the challenges you used to, and still deal with, respecitvely.
This review started off as a comment to the discussion boards asking whether this game had any life left in it. I started with the following anecdote: I hadn't touched Train Fever in 11 months, but the introduction of Transport Fever inspired me to go back to this game and a world I had paused on. It's still great fun, but a source of occasional massive frustration. I built a small junction of tracks which confused the heck out of the pathfinding - of course this led to all passengers abandoning my profitable mainline route because it appeared to not exist even though the trains still knew where to go!
Absolutely bizarre - I realized I had a problem when my $30M cash stockpile began crashing to less than half that (I was distracted by other side projects connecting spurs).
In the end I destroyed the buggy junction, rebuilt that chunk of mainline and re-created the entire route. This interface issue actually brought a bit of a challenge back to the game, as I had inadvertently created my own "rescue your company from your own sloppiness" scenario.
Compared to the original Tycoon games I miss a bit of the challenge from fighting real competitors on the map as opposed to the imaginary cargo transport forces and the tyranny of the automobile stealing your customers, but all-in-all, it's still an addictive timesink. And the graphics are average to gorgeous depending on how you admire the world, so that's a plus too. Did I mention the free DLC adding North American vehicles makes it especialy awesome, given the number of Canadian transit vehicles? That's a big plus too.
This is a fantastic transport tycoon game and I have had a lot of fun with it. Only issue is that it is a very demanding game so check the system requirements.

Yeah its a long term Beta, Beam Team Pty Ltd is an independent video game studio based in Brisbane, Australia.
The team consists of two developers, Ben Massey and Sam Edwards. That's two guys, not a dev team army like some games, so if you are interested in survival crafting games, with massive quantities of content and weekly updates, this is not the game for you. What you do get for your money is a slowly expanding game that appears to be crafted by people who care.
Theres no cannibals, dinosaurs, or zombies to kill you ingame, only snakes, sharks and poisonous fish, and as multiplay hasnt been added yet, you can play at your own pace without fear of hoardes of school wagging kids destroying your shack while you are not there. A map editor is included for builder junkies like myself. While this game is a long way behind the forest, rust and others of that ilk, it is as i said, being made by a small but enthusiastic Dev Team.
If you are looking for a completed bugless game, go away, this is not for you, I dont want to see your whinings in the forums. However if you actually understand what an Early Access game is, and enjoy relaxed open world survival games you might enjoy this game as much as I do.

I am giving this game a thumbs up, and I want you to hear me out on it.
This game is one of the most beautiful survival games I have ever played. Yes, there are bugs and glitches that drive us all insane, however, you can't deny that it is beautiful.
Now, here is where I think the game is seen negatively and why I believe the reviews here are mixed.
I think the developers were trying to please two audiences by having PvP and PvE. I don't think PvP works with how this game is designed. I have read so many reviews on here where people are upset because they spawn in and immediately die. If you were in an apocalyptic world trying to survive why would you kill each other? I get it, PvP but does it work? You get a handful of players in PvP that want to team up and survive, but then you have those players who just want to kill everyone off and not even communicate with anyone on the server. This reminds me of The Division and why it flopped so soon. If you want to go shred through players and win a “chicken dinner” go play PUBG or H1Z1 those games are designed for this type of player.
The hours I have played in this game have been spent in a Whitelisted PvE server called 'The Sanctuary' The name is true to the experience. I fell in love with this game because of how the game is played on this server. You are in a world where you are trying to survive. There are rules in place to keep the game experience pleasant. The best part? No floating bases. A community that plays together and has built relationships with one another because they want to survive together. We help each other find loot we need, help build bases, teach new players how the game works, etc. Every single player matters. If you die, you better believe we send everyone out to help you get your loot back. That's what it's all about.
On whitelisted servers you can find a place that works for your play style. It’s very difficult to find a server with an admin who stays on top of their game. One who doesn’t play favorites, who has rules in play to make the game easy and comfortable, who boots people because they are breaking the rules, and who has trusting moderators. I’m lucky to have found that place.
I really wish everyone could experience this game that way because I believe that's how it is meant to be played. I love Miscreated so much and want to see it be successful. I hope those of you who read this found this helpful and if you didn’t I understand, to each their own. Happy gaming and thank you for listening.
Cheers,

I'm reviewing this game from the point of view of someone who's a fan of Paradox Interactive games series (Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings, etc) and also enjoys the Total War game series.
I've have no past experience with Koei strategy games, but needless to say, this game instantly caught my attention. Historical Strategy games that are anything more than wargames are few and far between, and this one looked really well done, and its made by a developer with decades of experience on this genre.
Most of the gameplay would fall somewhere a bit closer to Total War than to Europa Universalis. The turn-based aspects, and the way you improve each holding, are very reminiscent of the strategic portion of Total War games. The character with attributes, traits, loyalties and such also greatly remind of that series, and in a good way. The game pacing is akin to that of Europa Universalis (besides the fact that this one has turn-based elements).
The combat, despite looking slightly like TW, is very simplistic. And that's not a bad thing, it goes nicely with the game flow, and the mechanics that guide combat are tied to many other aspects of the game.
The game also has (historical?) quests for each clan in each campaign, giving a pretty nice incentive for replayability. Those remind me a little bit of the main campaigns from the Hegemony game series.
Speaking of the Hegemony game series, this game also has a Supply mechanic that is very reminiscent of it. Troops need supply, and they need to refill it periodically - you can't sustain a long distance war forever.
All in all, this seems to be a really solid game for those that enjoy Grand Strategy games.

If you have only ever played the Total War series of games the first thing you need to do is wash all expectations you have away based on your experience with TW and make a vow not to compare them. It's apples and oranges and both can be equally awesome in their own right.
The strengths of Nobunaga's Ambition: Sphere of Influence as I see them are in its kingdom management gameplay, its fidelity in relaying historical events of this period in Japan, and the level of detail put into characters that inhabit the game. When managing your kingdom (or Daimyo-dom?) your various castles and towns have districts within them that you can upgrade to improve their perfromance at generating a resource (gold, provisions or conscripts) for your clan. There may be special locations in the area that if found further increase a given districts production. You can also add more districts to most castle/town areas after certain requirements are met. Add to this other infrastructure options such as road upgrades, fortifications, fortresses (not a typo, both are a thing) and you have many options on the way your clans lands look and play.
If you have never played a KOEI game and are a history fan, shame on you. Once again KOEI brings to the table a level of detail and polish on relaying historical events in the prescribed setting at a high level. If you like to read and enjoy story it is very likely you will find this aspects of the game entertaining. Unless you are a scholar in Japanese history of this period you will most certainly learn a few things. They also explain why certain characters did what they did in the context of the period.
Speaking of characters, they are what drive your clan. They have four abilities (Leadership, Valor, Intelligence and Politics) which are used to complete various actions in the game. They also have (up to 20) traits that give various benefits based on the action taken. Characters can gain traits through events while playing and you can also create your own characters and assign traits to them as well.
Lastly, combat can be handled at the macro and micro levels where in the former you joint point your forces at a target and let them handle it and in the latter you can direct units individually on the field, use leader special abilities and make other tactical decisions in a "real-time pauseable" environment.
Very happy that KOEI decided to release this game in english. I hope they continue to release updated versions of their other non-Dynasty Warriors catalogue as well. If done at this game's level of detail and polish they will be well worth the money.

This is a really good strategy game. There are many aspects to the game. It runs in monthly turns. Military orders may be given during the turn, as the month passes by. Deploying and moving troops is possible. Of course, during the Council phase which occurs in between turns, military deployments and movement orders may also be given.
The economy aspect of the game is pretty neat. You can do all sorts of economic things. These include increasing your economy (agriculture for provisions, crafts for gold, and conscripts for troop increases), construct special buildings in city districts, change city district types (food, cash, troops), build new districts once city population increases, improve defenses, increase road size (impacts troop movements and city populations). There are a few more things as well, such as building a new Fortress (small city).
Diplomacy is cool. You can improve your rating with another clan, persuade minor Tribes to your side (they give troops in battle or special income or you can even have them join a nearby city, increasing that city's population), give gifts to Clans (makes them friendly for a few months) or Officers (officers improve their loyalty), place a Lord at a castle/fortress, or even marry people to gain loyalty or alliances. If anoth Clan is at 40+ diplomacy you can request troops from them. Neat.
Military battles play out on the strategic map. Optionally if there are enough troops engaged you can control the troops directly, similar to the Totwl War series. Personally I use the strategic battles as I prefer them. When you surround a castle/fortress you need as many troops as that location's defense has in order to lay siege and capture.
A Castle has a larger town than a Fortress fyi.
There are a few more things you can do, such as hire ronin as leaders. This game has many things to do.
Anyway, this is a pretty neat wargame. Good game.

An unexpected delight, Long Live The Queen is a darker than expected, addictive click through story game with plenty of paths to keep the 100% completionists occupied for quite awhile. The game is drawn in a frilly girly style, but that only seems to add to the deadly events in a madoka magica kind of way. Though this game is far from horrifying, it's still dark in nature and you should go into this game expecting to die. Many times. But dying is half the fun.
I got this game as a gift from a friend and it isn't the type of game I usually play, but as far as visual novels go this one had me hooked and clicking for hours trying to make it through the game without dying while at the same time trying to be blessed by cats or become cruel enough to become an evil minion for a dark wizard. The sheer number of branching paths gives this game high replay value. While there are some set in stone events that will always happen regardless of your choices, your previous choices will affect the different routes you can take to overcome (or utterly fail) the situation.
It is not a game suited for people who like high action games or novels with deep, moving storylines, but I would definitely recommend it for people who want a time killer, a light hearted yet twisted fairytale, or want to test the waters to see if they enjoy visual novel style games.

An interesting mod, that is for sure. But my thoughts on this one are kind of neutral. These are the times I wish there was a thumb kind-of-in-the-middle rating. Because this mod has both good and bad qualities.
It's gunna be a long one, prepare yourselves!
When I first started this up, it looked great. It has a well-made feel to it, the maps look good and it doesn’t have any sloppy corner cutting or anything like that. You can see straight away that the graphics are an interesting twist on the usual lay out of the testing chambers that we know and love. There are some differences in this mod, the panelling surrounding the chambers are dark a lot of the time with very bright, almost back lit ones, to contrast.
It starts where Portal 2 left off, so I suppose it acts as a kind of “Portal 3 – What happens next” kind of thing. Obviously putting in mind that this isn’t actually officially what happens in the storyline, just a kind of “what if” experience.
The concept in general is very interesting and when I found this on Steam I was really quite excited to play. It gets straight into it and you get your new-fangled technology pretty quickly. One thing that bothered me is that you aren’t exactly welcomed into this new experience. There is no real tutorial on how to use your “time-machine”, you’re pretty much just thrown into it. Admittedly because of this I was wondering about a little while trying to figure how to work it. Old lady with the remote style. Not exactly a gripping start to a game/mod.
After faffing around for a while I realised that a screen in the first room with an animation playing on it, showing you what to do, actually had teeny tiny barely readable instructions on what keys you should be pressing to record, stop and replay you’re past self. First thought being, “Why couldn’t they just put those instructions on screen for a second or two?”
Once you get started the new game mechanic becomes quite enjoyable to play around with. It’s new and unseen in the franchise before so it is pretty nifty when you get used to it. The whole game kind of has a “co-op mode for one person” feel to it. You run around making a copy of yourself to help you through the puzzles. Which is quite interesting, but on the other hand it makes the portal gun feel kind of useless. There is always next to no panels you can actually use the portal gun with. Throughout the whole thing you don’t really use the portal gun that often and it just made me think it was a little pointless to actually have.
And with that, it brings a kind of change to how the game feels as a whole compared to portal 1 and 2. The other portal games are very much focused on the use of momentum and force to get around and solve puzzles. Whereas this is more… running around and hopping on your own back to get around and solve puzzles. Not really the same feel.
Story wise, I’m not even sure if what this has counts as a story. It makes several references and has a little dialog along the way, but ultimately I think this game was a lot shorter than I expected. I expected it to go into and explain what it was trying to get at as you progressed, but it just kind of… ended. Leaving me with “wut juss happen” kind of reaction. I still don’t think I understand what it was trying to get at…
…But all judgements aside, this mod was made by a few guys with a bit of spare time on their hands. Mods, in my opinion, never really have the highest of expectations. It’s a nice little add-on kind of experience for any major Portal fan. All in all I would say it’s worth a go. It’s free and you have nothing to lose.
TL;DR : It has good and bad qualities. No real tutorial, “what?” kind of ending and pretty short. But interesting new game mechanic, nice twist on usual graphics and an interesting concept.
Really good mod, good continuation to the story a bit short though.

A feel-good game that is relaxing and immersive in terms of its storytelling and timeline progression. The characters within the game are great - each one has a different personality that at least someone can relate to. Likewise, the art in this game is pretty unique and nice. The mini-games that you partake in usually fits well and does not cause any discontinuities in the overall comprehension of the storyline. I have only done two playthroughs of Night in the Woods, but it was nice that each of them felt different in terms of the storyline and in terms of what you learn regarding the characters that you interact with. In addition, the soundtrack for Night in the Woods is great and enjoyable even on its own.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone interested in a relaxing storyline with relatable and cute characters. Also, while I am not saying that this game is exactly like Undertale, I think that if you enjoyed Undertale, you will most likely enjoy Night in the Woods as well. Finally, with the release of the "Weird Autumn Edition" (a free DLC which essentially added more story and content to the game), I can definitely say that Night in the Woods was one of my favorite games of 2017. Thus, I fully recommend Night in the Woods and I believe that the game is worth trying out!

If you have been a fan of the NA and/or ROTK series by Koei, much like me, you will most likely enjoy spending countless hours trying to unify feudal Japan under one clan's banner in Nobunaga's Ambition: Sphere of Influence. I've been a fan of NA for almost a decade now. Having spent hundreds of hours playing Lord of Darkness, Rise to Power, and Iron Triangle. I patiently waited for the day Koei would release another one of these titles in North America. The wait was really worth it. Sphere of Influence surpass previous titles of the series in many way, although it falls short in some areas that made the series good in the past like certain feature they added or remove that I did not like (i.e. removing officer stipend, Naval battles, etc...), and city/fief building along with some other aspects of gameplay has been simplify. Sphere of Influence however kept the core aspect of what fans love about the previous titles and is a solid good title to reintroduce fans of the series in West to Koei's strategy/historical simulation games as it delivers feature rich engrossing gameplay, taking and/or enhancing certain good aspects from its previous two english titles, such as improving on and adding more depth to diplomacy, along with adding a few new features that greatly improve the game like clan quest events. Although the battle mechanics and tactics seem good but lacking sometimes, it does not take away from the satisfying strategic gameplay element that made this series fun to play in the past, If you have enjoyed the previous Nobunaga's Ambition and /or Romance of the Three Kingdoms titles you'll likely find yourself enjoying spending hours on end planning, building, scheming, and taking city after city as you struggle and fight other clans to unify the land under your rule. Nobunaga's Ambition: Sphere of Influence is a great installment to the titled series and a good game to get new and old fans interested in the genre for possible future titles. If you are interested in historical strategy simulation games then you should definitely buy this game as it is easily a 8.5/10 game. Well that's all the time I have to tell you about my thoughts on Nobunaga's Ambition: Sphere of Influence as I will now be spending most of my waking hours playing this game.

State of Decay is living up to its name in every sense of the word, and I am absolutely in love with it. It's probably the best zombie survival game out there. It has almost everything right, and for a zombie fan, it is definitely 10/10. It is not a game borne of this Golden Age of tutorials and hand-holding. This, rather, is a bleak scramble for survival, and one in which the zombies are all but guaranteed to win. Also,keep in mind, a zombie can never be too dead.
State of Decay is an open-world zombie survival game, but what’s not obvious right away – and glorious once you plumb its depths – is that it’s a full-blown role-playing game. A fantastic one at that. Switching back and forth between one of several player characters, you’ll travel across the multi-town desert region recruiting new survivors, searching vacated shops and houses for supplies, and managing relationships with the people you encounter – both those in your party as well as other humans you’re not aligned with.
Decay’s only other missteps are minor. The plotline is engaging and sets up a great finale, but it falls a bit short due to a lack of tough choices, such as the ones you had to make in The Walking Dead. And while it may seem unfair to criticize a game for nonexistent features, you can’t help but daydream about the fascinating possibilities and adventures that a cooperative mode could’ve laid bare – especially when State of Decay’s creators have publicly stated that they originally planned to included it and hope (not “plan,” hope) to still add it via a post-release patch.
In short: Tense, frightening atmosphere; great settlement gameplay; character system.

The Game:
Guilty Gear Xrd is a 2D anime fighter in the same line as Blazblue, Arcana Heart, UNIEL, etc. Or rather they are in the same line as it, considering how long Guilty Gear has been around. Xrd -Sign sports a roster of 17 character, 12 which are returning veterans. The 5 new characters are all somewhat more gimicky than the veterans but are a nice addition and fit in well regardless.
Game modes include standard affairs like arcade, versus, and training modes, as well as a challenge mode that has specific trials for each character that help you learn them ala Street Fighter 4 or Blazblue. It contains a story mode, which is about a 5 hour long anime more than anything else, as you don't fight in it. MOM mode also makes a comeback but has been heavily revamped. Instead of being a straight survival mode where you collect medals and healing items, its more of a conquest type thing  where taking on one hexagonal challenge opens up more and it keeps branching out as you colelct medals to buy items and upgrades for your character. Mission Mode also makes a comeback, but instead of just being a fight with certain conditions attached to it like "Only the 5th hit in a combo and above deal damage" it just puts you in a situation and asks a task of you that you have to succeed at more times than you fail.
Of course there is the online aspect of the game. I haven't been able to get into any ranked matches unfortunately but player matches have worked wonderfully. The lobbies try to replice an arcade environment, having up to 4 boths where players can fight and spectate at. Ther weird thing i syou have to pick your character before you confirm the fight with the other person, which is weird, but not too bad. Ive only noticed a bit of latency and lag when a lot of people are coming and going from the lobby at once, otherwise its been a very steady experience, especially with friends.
The Port:
Game runs absolutely great and looks gorgeous. Haven't had much trouble online with the randoms I played, a little bit of latency here and there as people came and left the lobby but nothing bad. When playing with a few friends in a single lobby, it was perfectly fine with no hiccups.
Points taken off I guess for some of the UI being a lowres, not that I reall care about that. Also some people report the FPS taking a nosedive after a long session due to memory leaks, most notably on AMD products. I myself use a 6850 and fx-6130 and have had no issues regarding that. I played about 3 hours straight online with friends while recording the game at 60fps and still had no issues. And the final thing to note is that trying to configure the keyboard controls are a pain in the butt. I use a stick but my friend uses keyboard and he has trouble configuring the arrow keys for movement instead of wasd.
There is an ongoing argument about whether this is a  PS3 port or a PS4 port, but I honestly don't think it matters. it has all the same content and really only a few UI elements are noticeably different upon being pointen out, though ASW and Shini on twitter did say patches are to come. Otherwise the game itself, characters, stages, effects, etc, look completley on par with PS4 and in some situations better in comparison screenshots, and thats before any sort of downsampling or any sort of texture filtering through Gedosato.
Considering how well optimized it is and having all the content of the PS3 and PS4 version, save one superfluous overworld lobby system everyone hates, I think it definitely gets a solid 8, even in the face of the previously mentioned issues. Its an above average port and way better than I had anticipated from ASW.
Overall:
The game itself is amazing and marked the return of Guilty Gear as a major player in the Fighting Game Community and the port itself is very solid. I have a very midrange, soon to be outdated, computer but it handles the game perfectly fine at max settings and at my monitors resolution. The online has been a solid experience so far as well. There are a few issues with the port that will hopefully be ironed out as mentioned above, but otherwise its hard to get better than this. For the discounted $24 with free DLC or even the full $30, I heavily urge you to try it out.

Please take note that I am new to these post-apocalyptic survival games.  Never played Rust, DayZ and such.
I really recommend this game.
Miscreated is probably the game that makes me the most nervous.  It's hard to describe as I don't like it but at the same time I look forward to playing it every day to reproduce this "state of discomfort".  E V E R Y time I enter an house, my heart is pumping and all I want is to loot it as quickly as possible so I can get out and go hide in the bushes (/chicken).  If you are in an house and you hear some footsteps approaching, you're usually in for some trouble... also, the nights are really really dark.  You start with a flashlight but you have to be very careful with it as it gives your position quite fast.
Hiding around became an art for me in order to survive.  This game is really unforgiving if you are playing alone like I am.  If possible, try to make reliable friends with whom you will be able to loot and fight/defend together.  I'm playing on a well established server so venturing into any town usually mean you'll cross another player.
I just started (about 40hrs into the game) to explore the base building side of the game and it's quite awesome.  I would recommend that you do it as well as fast as you can if you ever start.  You can put some additionnal storage in there for your weapons, mats and food.
Take note that there are many different kind of servers.  I'm playing on an official one but I know that they are a lot of customs servers out there.  Some with specifics rules such as "no kill-on-sight" or ones with a more RP aspect where you need to interact/talk before shooting ... depends what you are looking for really.
As for the graphics, they are really beautiful.  I think the game is well optimized for its "early access" state.  I'm still running with an i5-2500k (OCed to 4.4) and a gtx 970 and I run everything to the max.
So yeah, I recommend this game!

Early impression (7 hours at the time of writing)
I have never played a Koei strategy game before to this was all new to me, but I followed the fun (if long) tutorial through to the end and started an easy campaign as the Oda on the "Birth of Nobunaga" scenario, I then proceeded to play faaaaaaar longer than intended this afternoon.
I had a blast. Coming from a Shogun 2 total war fanatic standpoint, this provides a very different experience, that somehow sits between a Paradox game like CK2 (or Sengoku) and something a bit lighter like the total war series.
Battles are automatically fought out as the month progresses and you can dip in and try to turn them in your favour if you want to. There are some great positioning based mechanics at work here that make positioning your forces or paramount importance to victory, attacking from different directions and defending or bypassing choke points, are both important things to understand, and provide a lot of enjoyment.
Management of your "Officers" is a huge part of the game and I'd say this makes it more like the aforementioned Paradox titles, land management is also important, and takes up much of your time.
There is a fun internal and external political system to maneuver and this allows you to do some very fun things like forming coalitions against powerful enemies and calling friends to fight for you, you can even mediate peace between two antagonists!
Ahh! so much I could write, but to save you reading a truly monumental wall of text, I'll say this:
If you:
Like Paradox grand Strategy: This could be fun for you, a little less fiddly, a little less in depth and Byzantine, but still plenty to do and the war management system is superbly good even without zooming in for the battles.
Like Total War: If you really only play for the tactical battles this may not be your cup of tea, it is undoubtedly a lot simpler and very strategy heavy by comparison. For people who like the strategy side of it or are balanced in their interest, this is well worth a look, go check out a lets play or two.
Sengoku Jidai\Japanese history fans: This stuff is catnip for me and I loved following the historic quests, learning new things about the events and personalities of the era and loved many of the realistic touches. Simply superb!
Graphics- not bad, pretty at times
Sound- great soundtrack and other ambient\Ui sounds
Strategy gameplay- Deep with lots do do and lots to think about
Tactical gameplay- Simple but fun diversion with good impact on play if you opt in to it
Performance- Ran flawlessly for me, minimal loading times
AI Performance: I really couldn't say. Easy is just that, I hear its competent on higher difficulties
Localisation- Pretty good though not without a few easily overlooked errors
Multiplayer-None, so don't buy it if you want that
Controls and UI- not too bad, takes a little getting used to and vassal management takes a while (might be missing something)
Overall: Great game I will be playing for a long time to come if my first impressions hold true- Ay Ay Ooooohhhhhh!/10

From Tecmo/Koei comes the original conquest game series Nobunaga's Ambition, a game about conquering Japan as a daimyo and the historical events that happened in that time.
As the game starts you can chose to make your own clan or play as one of the historical clans.
This means you can follow history befitting your clan or chose to defy history such as with the death of Nobunaga, Imagawa's failed battle and ambitions to take the capital, or seeing a victor between the legendary battles between the Takeda and Uesugi clans.
The games is very similar to a Total War but very easy and its more about positioning than certain units beat other units and Crusader Kings 2 which is more about taking areas and making sure that they obey you.
If you have played TW or any paradox game you will enjoy Koei's games as they are very strategical and very different from other strategy games.
I suggest if you do get the game do the tutorial to learn the basics and then play small single province clan just to learn the ropes until you are confident, I myself made the mistake of playing a larger clan after to tutorial and learned 2 turns in that i had more than just the main castle and 3 years in that I actually had 4 small castles and not just the 2 I could see from the main castle.
Finally to add Koei/Tecmo took a gamble to see if the west once again would like to see their games in English and if enough people are willing to show support for the game then Koei/Tecmo might release some of their other games in English like the new Romance of the Three Kingdoms 13 which is slated for release at the end of this year or bring some of their old games to an English crowd.

This is easily the best game I've played so far in the Nobunaga's Ambition series. The systems such as historical events, and  the dynamic choice of how you'd 'like' to fight your battles makes the game flow very quickly, and makes executing what were once arbitrary and hard to find events so much easier.
The only things I feel are truly missing from the game are a more complex technology system like Iron Triangle had, and potentially more portraits for create an officer such as some of the much earlier games. These are minor flaws, and over-all this game functions FAR better than older Nobunaga's Ambition games.
One of the best minor additions is the concept of loyalty based on type of ruler, and it makes it harder to keep rulers or other offices you acquire that are opposed to your liege based on a set of modifiers. However, you are indeed more likely to keep officers as long as you maintain a relatively strong and consistent force.
Easily my favorite KOEI game yet 8.5/10

Here's the deal. Koei has been making these two grand strategy game series called Romance of the Three Kingdom and Nobunaga's ambition. You're placed on a large map of China and/or Japan respectively and you take control of one of the historical warlords in the period. You're given control of the finances, diplomacy, and the military features of the realm and you're given the huge task of reuniting a tortured land and placing it under your control.
However, for the longest time American and Europe gamers have been given a raw deal. Koei has always given us the raw game, 1.0, without any of the accompanying DLC in the Power-Up Kit. This happened time and again during the Romance of the Three Kingdoms series and continued throughout the Nobunaga's Ambition series. This is DLC that added additional features to the game. Features such as new cities, new officers, foreign nations interfering positively or negatively for your faction, enchanted items or magic that change the way battles are fought. All sorts of cool stuff which never made it to us American gamers. We got the base game and that's it. If you didn't like it, you had to either pirate the game or you were out of luck. And even then, the pirated games were poorly translated.
This time, the situation is different. The game itself comes prepackaged with all DLC in the Power Kit enabled. All sorts of stuff has been added to the game since it has been released and with this special edition release, you essentially get all of that for free. The only thing you'd have to pay for is for additional starting scenarios, even these come free if you take advantage of their special release. And honestly, they're not really needed. You're getting such a good deal with this game already. Additional scenarios are just icing on the cake.
The game itself brings tremendous depth. Each individual officer in the game has their own set of skills. Some may be good at martial arms, others may delve into politics. Some officers may be good at everything, others nothing. The factions are divided in power between the castles and the stronger fortresses which protect their fiefs. Fiefs that can be improved by talented officers to produce more food, gold, and fighting men as time goes on. This will consist of most of your early game. You will want to build up your fiefs as quickly as possible. You won't be able to take over the land if you cannot bring an army to the field!
In addition to an army, the game introduces a new wrinkle in the form of tribes. There are many factions fighting over the land of Japan, but in addition to these there are several neutral 'tribes' that simply want to get along in a land divided by war. Each month, you can dedicate officers and a portion of gold each month to compete with other clans for the loyalty of this tribe! The higher their loyalty, the more they will do for you, such as providing gold and resources and helping you out in battle if you fight near their location. Eventually, if their loyalty reaches 100%, you can even get them to swear their complete loyalty to you and assemilate their tribe into one of your cities, giving them a significant boost to your population along with all the bonuses that it entails. Sometimes, the leader of the tribe will join you as an officer, giving you another asset to help improve your lands domestically and spread your influence abroad.
Diplomacy makes its return in two forms. Traditional and covert operations. On one hand, you can use diplomacy and give gifts of gold and unique items to other forces in order to secure good relations with them. Better relations secure longer alliances, measured in 6th months, 1 year, and 2 year, and even permanent agreements if you have a spare daughter for a marriage alliance. Others are more brief, such as requesting to borrow troops from an ally temporarily to give you that edge in a key battle. If you gather enough allies, you can even organize a large coalition with the combined objective to take down a faction that has grown too large to take on alone. But beware! Friends today may become enemies tomorrow. Treat your friends well so that they will always return the favor.
Covertly, you can send officers into enemy territory to try to convince an enemy officer to betray his lord. These operations sometimes take years to complete, but they are very much worth it, and can sometimes be the tide you need to turn a battle, sometimes even a war, permanently into your favor.
Wars take a while to get to, but once you do it is clear this is where the game has its focus on and where it shines the best. Everything you have done up until now comes into account. The number of your troops that arrive on the field, your allies and their proximity to the battle, the weapons and equipment your soldiers are equipped with, the amount of food you take with you, the tribes you have gained loyalty with and whether they are close to you or not, the location of the battle, the decisions you make during the battle and the deployment of your troops. Literally everything has a factor of whether you win or lose the battle and what you can do afterwards. Sometimes you will win a costly battle, but find yourself unable to follow up the victory because you have lost too many men and you cannot conduct an effective seige safely. Sometimes you have conducted bad diplomacy that has surrounded yourself with enemies who quickly jump on your now weakened clan, resulting in a game over! The wise lord who triumpths over his enemies conducts his operations cautiously, taking advantage of every opportunity he can get! As the Art of War dictates, he secures himself against the possibility of defeat and takes advantages of the opportunities his enemies present to him. If you do this, you will be successful.
Finally, the world itself is an active, rapidly changing world. Events that shake the land will strike at random, such as earthquakes or tsunamis. Eventually foreigners will come, bringing along their religions and advanced technologies. This introduces muskets to the game, which Nobunaga historically used to bring a large part of the continent under his control. If you can take advantage of this technology early, it can bring you a huge advantage. There are other events that can effect you as well, such as story events that can change the very fate of your clan, but I don't want to spoil too much. You'll have to find that stuff out for yourselves!
The game in general is for the patient, calm types who like to sit around and plot global domination. The depth this game provides and the strategies you can take to bring yourself both victory and defeat are endless. A single playthrough can take several hours for a single faction...and that's if you never make a single mistake or lose a battle...which you will. There are certain things out of your control and even the wisest general cannot see everything outside of his domain.
If you have the patience, the intellect, and the courage to dedicate yourself to a strategy game of epic proportions, this game is for you.
If you want a game that provides quick satisfaction for minimal effort, go play Call of Duty.
That is all.
Also you can marry officers to cute maidens to make them part of your family. Their children will later on become your own officers and even the heir to your clan if you're marrying off your sons. 10/10 would ship couples again.

I have no idea why there are so many negative reviews. I think the game is excellent if only people paid enough attention to it. It might not be as complex as other games out there but then again there aren't any new games that offer the Transport Tycoon and Railroad Tycoon experience. The game is much closer to Railroad Tycoon 3 than Transport Tycoon, that's where transport Fever comes in. Fair enough if the game was a developing bench for Transport Fever but I actually see nothing wrong with that, besides if Transport Fever is so much more complex then I am happy I am getting trained on Train Fever beforehand. Industry is pretty basic and you don't get the stock exchange from Railroad, never like that anyhow.
I have purchased the game on 80% off, so for me this is a massive bang for my buck. The graphics are great, the trains are great and in addition you get a few trams, buses and trucks to go alongside them.
For anyone that loves transportation simulators and don't want to buy Transport Fever get Train Fever at a fraction of the cost and enjoy it, I have for so many hours. Th game comes with the USA vehicles and a few Mods.
I shall give my words of wisdom for anyone looking to play the game. If you start the game at the earliest time, 1930 it will take around 20 years before you see any upgrades coming up. This gives you time to build-up your connections or you can start the game in 1950.
TRAINS:
When connecting town, try in the beginning to connect the closest town together. I have actually made a full circle of the map by connecting one town to the next as and when I could afford it, not by creating a full circle map and a train going from town to town which might have been better but also very costly unless you have infinite money. Then at the end I connected any leftover towns in the middle to one or two of the early connected towns. It is also a good idea if you can start placing train stations when you can afford, no need to connect them but have them placed so the towns grow around them. I have reached 2010 and I have only used the first platform length, doesn't seem to affect the trains even if longer.
BUSES/TRAMS:
To be honest I didn't have much luck with buses/trams, they seem to bring low income if at all, especially within the same city. I have had a few buses/trams connect two closer cities making a steady income but nothing to shout home about.
If you use buses and trams make sure you upgrade all the roads used for your routes with BUS LANES. Even better if you can go for the wider 4 lanes roads as the first lane is kept for your vehicles (trucks, buses, trams) and the rest for traffic. This will help them getting stuck behind slow moving cars.
TRUCKS:
These little things brought me the mos profit early on. Check each city, see what their goods needs are, the more and unfulfilled requests the better. If the factory producing the good is in between two cities great, set up two different routes so it produces good for both cities. Easier to start with Wood or Oil as each factory only needs 1 resource, the Ore factory needs 2 (coal and iron) so more costly for you to run. Take a Saw Mill and Forest, pause the game, place a truck stop by the Forest, 2x truck stops by the Sawmill and truck stop in the City, try to get the stop near the Industrial area, when you switch on the colours and good lanes, bottom right hands side, the blue buildings. If the city demands 40 Goods then start with 4 trucks, 4 transporting wood, 4 transporting goods. I always started with 4 or 5 trucks even later in the game. This is why I have said to place 2 Truck Stops by the Factory, at one stop you drop the goods, at the other you pick up the goods, if you use the same stop for two lanes you can end up bottle necking as the trucks wait for goods produced.
Same for a 2 resources factory, 5 trucks bringing 1st resource, 5 trucks bringing 2nd resource, 5 trucks taking goods to town. You can use the same stop for resources as the trucks will just come in drop resources and go, but good should have a separate stop as truck can queue up. Try to place them so the truck bringing the resources don't get stuck behind the ones waiting.
ROADS/RAIL:
This is where the game has a bit of a fail. There is no way to upgrade a road once a rail track has been placed on top of it. Make sure when you go over any roads with a rail track stop a few meters before the road then continue placing your tracks, stop a few meters after you pass the road and continue with your long track afterwards. That way when you want to upgrade the road, you can just delete that small section for the rail track passing over the road instead of a costly track running for miles, tracks with bridges or tunnels can cost you millions to lay down, too costly to delete just to upgrade one tiny piece of road which can bottleneck your trucks, buses or trams.
Good thing is that you can upgrade your rail tracks once electric and high speed track become available without having to delete your old track. Same for the roads, as long as there is enough space for them and not going under rail track they can be upgraded.
ALWAYS ALWAYS have your 4 lane roads with BUS LANES, as I mentioned before, your trucks, YES the TRUCKS, buses and trams will use those bus lanes but local traffic will not which means your trucks will fly by all other traffic and not get stuck behind slow moving cars. However, all your vehicles will use that 1st lane, be it bus lane or not, therefore they will get stuck behind the slowest going vehicle. Best to use separate roads if you intend to use vehicles with different speeds.
INDUSTRY:
I would imagine that later in the game you could start using trains to transport goods but I think trucks will still be better. They cost less than the trains in initial pay and maintenance, not to mention that a truck will leave as soon as it is full up but a train with 4 5 wagons will stay there until full slowing production down. If you have a train with 4 5+ wagons going back on forth between stations without maximum load what is the point.
The industry is based on demand and supply, so if you stick 2 trucks of 10 cargo hold each on a route, both the resource supplied will be 20 production and the good produced. If you stick 5 trucks it will be 50... and so forth hence why a train is really not a great idea. Frankly speaking I could have 2 3 trucks doing my journey as they are fast enough to do full trips and handle a production of 200 but the industry will only see my 3 trucks assigned to the route so it will assume I can only deliver 30 goods/resources.
Also avoid trying to supply one Factory with two of the same resources, let's say wood from two Forest to one Sawmill. On of the Forests will just stop production and you will lose money on it.
If you supply multiple towns from 1 factory the goods production will go up and therefore the demand for resources will also go up so your forest will start producing more, just make sure you add 1 2 extra trucks.

I have a love-hate relationship with this game
There are some extremely annoying bugs and poor implementations of some features. Things that I can think of at the top of my head:
- The way that vehicles are guided through intersections is a pain in the pineapple, and often unnecessarily causes delays of 20+ minutes. This is especially annoying early in the game, and/or on hard mode.
- The terrain is extremely difficult to deform, given the limited and pretty much broken tools available.
- Vehicles never change lanes/tracks, but instead their routes are absolutely hardcoded. This means that, for example, a train will not choose the best available platform at a station, but instead wait until its designated platform is free.
- The amount of money analysis tools are very limited, and overall vehicle management is pretty much non-existent.
As frustrating as it is, this game is beautiful, addicting, and super satisfying. If you like OpenTTD-style games, and if you have a lot of patience (or no patience at all, but you like trains and stuff) then I recommend this to you.

A top down shooter in which you try to fend off massive hordes of zombies in waves (or days). 'Over 9000 Zombies' basically is a tower defence game but without the actual tower defending.... if that makes any sense. The focus this time lies on keeping your character alive. You can run around the map, salvage scraps and pick up grenades. With the scraps you're able to build defences and turrets to help you in your aid. Obviously every wave you will have to defeat more and/or more difficult zombies. There are several different zombies like fire spitting zombies (or bombs?) and zombie dogs but you will also gain new weapons like shotguns, rifles etc.
The first 6/7 days are easy to survive and completing a wave takes quite a long time. During that time you will be doing the same thing (killing zombies...) over and over again that, combined with the pretty bad graphics, might be a bit boring and/or cause you an eye strain. I have not yet played this game in co-op but I'm sure it would be the most fun.
Overall 'Over 9000 Zombies' is a neat little game, although I would not recommend it for the current price of 7 euro.

This game definitely falls short of what I have come to expect from the Ace Combat franchise. You are forced to use a no skill dogfight mode that only requires you keep you're target within a circle on the screen and fire missiles. There are a few levels, such as the helicopter gunner ones, that have you "on rails" for the entire time. These are tedious and can't be completed until the action sequences run their course. It's also no longer set in a fictional world, which destroys the suspension of disbelief that made it so you don't question the unbelievably huge aerial battles. You are also given regenerative health on your plane, which means that if you take damage you can just play conservatively for a bit and not have to worry about being shot down. Overall, I would say this is definitely the weakest offering of the series. I bought it at a mid range discount (~$15), and feel that was still too much for this mediocre game.
