Just by the name alone, if you ask any of the long time fans, they'll tell you what they think at the drop of a hat.
Having played through the campaign fully, I can see just why this game was made. The article I read prior to playing the game comparing it to a certain hyper-popular first-person shooter cemented my opinion in stone already. One part of me wants to like this game, but the other part screams at it in disgust.
Ace Combat Assault horizon is a frank departure from the series established bizzaro earth in which it takes place in the more familiar setting of our world. It seeks to establish a cast of loveable characters from the outset with plenty of dialogue inbetween missions.
While the game certainly stands on its own as a certifyable Ace combat game, it definitely has the feel most fans of the series have come to expect, but has a flawed core that sours the experience.
From the core, it tends to lean to hard on its own gimmicks to draw in new players, and it shows in the gameplay, the addition of Dog-fight Mode is a sort of,"On Rails" mode to help new players take on enemies.
its an easier to control help-to-kill method, and concurrently show off the much touted,"Aircraft Gore" as defeated planes spiral and tumble helplessly with much unnecessary amounts of oil, flames, and debris splattering on the screen, and an unskippable dramatic camera to show you your kill in gruesome detail as it suspends you from play. Counter DFM, is a feature called,"ASM" which is initiated in the same way as DFM is. ASM allows you to turn on your persuer and take THEM in DFM.
As a whole, the usual Ace combat control scheme is bogged down by this new control addition and a step back from the tight controls many have come to expect from the series. the timing required to pull off the ASM is far more strict and leaves  you more vulnerable than outmanuvering your opponent and mashes itself in your way, and many of the mission components require you to use this DFM to complete some objectives properly.
Many of the games enemies seem to have been made with this mode in mind as they all zoom and boost impossibly out of your reach if you decide to engage them in any other form of combat other than DFM, I saw this mostly on the "required" targets and seemed to me as a way to railroad the player into using it at expense of artificially lengthening the game time.
Moving on.
From its mission structure to its characters, it tries real hard to make Ace combat fit within the confines of the modern game while still leaving a bit of salt from the previous games to flavor it.
In the end, AC:AH Feels short, shallow, and unmemorable, nevermind the technical issues that mar it.
the choice to cast the title in the current modern world left the game with a bland pastel of identity to draw upon let alone the suspension of disbelief to hold, the characters have no origin, we know nothing of why the characters have the motivations they do, they cast off the primary reason for conflict and instead leave a revenge plot with no plausability for its existence.
The story for me wrapped up in 8 hours, accounting for deaths and failures due to awkward DFM controls along the way.
To draw some comparisons between this and one of the previous titles, some of the titles had branching mission structures, and depending on how you play, or what you do, the story unfolds in a different way, giving some area of control and feeling of detail.
The mission structure of AC:AH is linear, the missions are short and there isn't any replayability in them as most missions are roughly 5 or so minutes long.(they can drag on because the game wants you to rely on DFM) The details of each mission are traditional for the Ace Combat library, in fact, as far as to say, they don't use any of the more interesting mission structures that the previous titles have. It goes to highlight the limited scope the modern world presents from a reality standpoint.
From what I gather from this game, it was made with multiplayer in mind, (Singleplayer is just one long tutorial) and I'm sure it does it acceptably, but doesn't warrant me trying as coming away from the singleplayer, left me a lot more sour than sweet.
As a fan of the series, I'm dissapointed that Project Aces had to push out a title that was more than likely a cash grab to monopolize on the current trend of modern military shooters, not of their own volition, but by their parent company.
The good I gather from the game is, that I hope any form of success has made Bandai-Namco think strongly about porting previous Ace combat titles, and developing future numbered games to the PC as a viable platform.
This review isn't supposed to be to complex or properly formatted or well worded. but it does get across a number of gripes I have with the game, and goes to highlight what happens when game companies try to,"Follow the leader" instead of doing their own thing or doing something new.
TL;DR: As a fan of the series, steer clear (but I'm sure I don't need to tell you that), but if you're someone who wants an arcade-y flight game to kill some time online. look no further.

I was expecting Nina to utter "Why do I even bother?"!
There was again a plethora of riddles (logical and illogical) and I've found it a bit refreshing actually, that half the game seems to have mundane, every day objectives. When we get to the grand ideas and plots many games (as well as this one) lose their charm.
The dynamic between Nina and Max is better in this game. As their relationship is already established from the previous one, we get to see how it evolves. Oh, and Max has become way more handsome! :D
What I didn't like was the casual misogyny. Of the 4 women in the game, 2 were playable characters (Nina and Sam), the 3rd (Katharina Jordan) was described as a "bimbo" from Nina, (also Sam mentions another "bimbo"), and the 4th (the police officer in Paris) as "average in all respects", and "ugly". Way to go Nina for your stance towards other women!
Also, breaking the 4th wall can be fun, but Nina kinda overdid it. Too many references that we're playing a game. We know we are, so enough already...
All in all, it is a more than decent game, and I even liked it quite a bit more than the first one.

I'm a sucker for mystery, conspiracy and/or secret society stories, and that is what you get here. The story isn't fully fleshed or in any way intricate, but rather a bit shallow and simplified. One can't help to think that they could've done a lot more to get a more fully story told, but I still found it entertaining enough.
It's an old game now, and it shows through looking at the characters, several backdrops and the cutscenes. Several are a bit blurry and low on detail. However, some backdrops looks a bit sharper. Anyway, it probably looked damn good when it came out, and it doesn't look half bad today. That is acceptable.
The voice acting is overall ok, but it lacks a bit emotion and suspence. There are several tongue-in-cheek comments from the main characters that sometime works and sometimes don't. It is hard to tell at times if the game takes itself seriously or not.
Figuring out the puzzles in this game was entertaining enough, with proper clues given and mostly quite logical solutions. Sometimes, though, they felt a bit cheap and out of context. The locations you go to are also mostly interesting.
The game as a whole seems based on a good foundation, but a bit rushed and inconsistent. The coincidences within the story is a bit too much to swallow. I'm sure it is probably based on time and budget like most others. Either way it is still entertaining enough to enjoy if you are into these sorts of things.
I also played the first in the series and enjoyed that one as well. There are a few references to the previous game but you certainly don't need to play that one to enjoy this. It is a whole seperate storyline.
I can absolutely recommend this game for fans of point'n'click adventure games and for people who like a bit of mystery. If you're not into these types of games to begin with, it is probably not going to change your mind.
I rate it 6/10, because it has aged a bit and has that thin storyline. If I had played it when it came out and rated it at the time it might have been rated a bit higher.
As always. If you are looking into buying this, don't base your decision on this review alone. Others-, any your opinion might differ from mine.
Happy gaming :o)

So you're this guy (or girl) who has to defend the rifts from orcs who are crawling through because some guy was like "Hey, even though you closed those in the last game (late spoiler warning... oops) they should actually be open. Silly geese." So there you are, armed with a few tricks like a rocket launcher and a shotgun fighting wave after wave of orcs. Good thing the orcs drop money each time you kill them so you can buy more stuff to help your fight against orcs and orc accessories.
That's basically the game in a nutshell.
The cool thing about this game, though, is that you can carry a certain amount of towers at a time and can play with a friend(s?). So you can your compatriot can together end the horde. That's fun. That's cool.
Where the game really shines is the customization options, though. It's because you unlock so many new hotbar slots that the game gets interesting. You can make decisions about which towers are ideal for this map and the screen that lets you change your hotbar tells you all the enemies that will be coming during the mission. Do you really want to bring the tar over the spider web this round? Or do you even care about slowing them down this round when you can mow them down with a thousand* dwarves? Do you want to bring just one weapon for yourself? Do you even want to bring a weapon for yourself? That slot could be used as trinket or something... Just all the possibilities. I think I'm a  sucker for possibilities. Games that have a ton of possibilities tend to be the ones I enjoy the most and this is no exception.
If you enjoy tower defense games at all, or even if you don't and just enjoy Sanctum or TF2's MvM Mode, this game will be right up your alley. This game is just fantastic for a game of that sort. MOBA? Tower Defense? I'm not sure of the category. I guess that's irrelevant anyway, but this game is a solid purchase if you didn't get it from the humble bundle ages ago.

Not only that it possesses such depth (both story and gameplay wise), but it also represents a rare blend of mind-bending strategy and beautiful visuals.
- The art style of the game is a story of its own.
- Unlike the original Banner Saga, Factions is a purely pvp experience.
- The combat is turn-based and it is very well done.
- Strategically, every battle is like a tree - each branch represents a unique path and there are    quite many to choose form!
- The game is very complex and the more you play, the more new layers you start to discover.
- It feels like chess, but is much more fun.
- It is very well balanced and for each team lineup there is a counter lineup - you only need to find the right one!
- The music and the sound effects blend in very nicely and provide a calming ambient between and during battles.
- The community is small, but very warm and polite - you trully have a feeling like you are in a mead hall.
If you are a fan of good turn-based strategy, complex mechanics, beautiful visuals and good music to accompany it all I highly recommend this game to you and if you aren't, give it a try, it will be worth your time :)

This is good. Real good. If you're a fan of Koei's Romance of the Three Kingdoms series then you're going to like this. Even then, based on the 4x and real time battle mechanics, if you're a Total War fan, you may enjoy this as well.
Essentially, you choose one of several scenarios and choose one of hundreds of different playable characters (not counting the ones you can create yourself) and attempt to unite Japan during the Sengoku Jidai period. Yes, yes, I know, isn't the Warring States starting to get a bit old? Well, this is actually a very refreshing take on it because it's a story driven experience where you receive Historical quests that creates an interesting world in Feudal Japan (as Koei is apt to do). You develop your nation, starting with just a city, using your officers and as you grow economically, you build up militarily. You attack neighbors, convert their officers and make alliances where needed to ensure victory and further grow the amoeba that is your clan. On top of this, the atmosphere of the game is absolutely beautiful, with thriving immersive cities that actually grow visually as you develop them. You just built Stone Walls? Well you actually see Stone Walls on your Castle now.  I will say, the UI can be a little troublesome at times but if you take your time and play the tutorial, you should be able to pick it up rather quickly. There are also a metric tonne worth of actions you can take as compared to ROTK games. As a fan of Koei's Strategy games, I was pleasantly surprised to see this and I'm glad to say I have not been disappointed. Highly recommended!
Update: 3 hours in, no crashes, very good optimization as far as I can tell. AI can be ruthless. Take your time building up. Updates will continue as I notice things.
Gameplay Impressions:

UPDATE: I added a short FAQ at the bottom of the review, it is a good tl;dr if you have a quick question.
If you have ever played any of the romance of the three kingdom games, or nobunagas ambition games you must get this game!
However chances are you haven't since those series dont have many titles localized in english.
This game is quite similar to Europa Universalis in my opinion, but with many different mechanics. The combat however is somewhat more like Total War then like Europa. And there is just so much to do in this game! I think both players who aren't new to hardcare strategy games like Europa and more casual players who play the odd Civilization, Total War, or Dynasty Warriors Empires games will very very much enjoy this game.
I haven't experienced any bugs yet which is nice because a lot of the other koei releases as of recent havent been great for pc. From what I have gathered this isn't a port since it was made on pc first which is also great.
The create/edit officer this time around is very very indepth! I am still working on my first officer an hour in and am not even halfway done!
Personally I love the theme of this game, it has very beautiful artwork and music. The historical theme is very epic and has some really cool back story to it too. You can play from a historical scenario, or play the fictional scenario and do things your way. A lot of fun options to play around with to really make it your own when you start a new game.
While not as indepth as europa, this game comes close but is 100x easier and more visually appealing. The combat is a lot more indepth then Civ 5 as is the diplomatic aspects of this game as well. The game is very easy to pickup once you get into things!
You get to command units of thousands of troops led by unique officers who all have their own cool ability and tactics that can be used to put interesting strategies into action. You can even search for hidden roads and stuff to help you plan battles ahead of time.
Between managing diplomacy with neighbouring clans, fighting a war with another clan, trying to entice an enemy officer into joining my clan, developing my states and teaching my officers new abilities I am having a lot of fun! This was a well spent $60, I would definately recommend this to all my friends.
PS - For those of you who are curious this does come with the Power Up Kit (if you don't know what this means, in simple terms it's just more customization options and such)
EDIT: I wanted to update my review a little to answer a few questions.
1. How is the performance?
From what I've read people are managing to run this on older system, I have a completely overkill computer so I'm not sure myself what the minimum requirements would be to run this game  however I have yet to run into any sort of lag or buggyness, I expect this game to be well optimized since it was made for the pc first (so not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port for once, thank you koei). PS I am on windows 10 64bit, i5 3570, 8gb ram and nvidia gtx 970
2. How is the combat system?
Ok so I've said it was totalwar like, but that was a bit vague right? So not everyone has played total war so I will try and explain without comparing to total war. So combat seemed rather straight foward at first, it was like the classic rotk system where you kinda just sent your platoon out and watched them mindlessly kill each other. However things like passive skills, active abilities (which sort of activate randomly and can easily change the tide of battles)  and stats like INT, VAL and LEA play a important role to winning battles. There was one thing that bothered me, instead of being able to freely move units wherever on the map, they are tied down to board game like routes called roads (roadwork can be done to improve travel speed). I was wondering why the combat felt like it was built on bogged down rotk mechanics. Then I saw this little button that would pop up over an units when they are enganged in battle, clicking it takes you into a war map with all currently engaged units that is more akin to the combat system of previous nobunaga's ambition games. This is where you can freely control your units, choose when to use your officer abilitys, use terrain advantage (barricades, turrets, etc) or even choose to seige the base (if nearby one) instead of enganging in direct combat. In this mode I have both completely wiped without dealing any casualties to the enemy officer, and have won impossible (etc 7000 vs my 3000) battles with the use of strategy. There are a lot of cool abilities and you can choose to engange in melee or ranged combat here. Horses can be used to charge the enemy with great speed and a high chance to confuse them, muskets can be unloaded which can also confuse the enemy, and you can use any of you adjucant officer abilities as well (depending on how much "control" you have over your unit).
3. How agressive is the ai?
There is a agressiveness setting you can change before starting your game, I have it set to high, so when I send units out the neigbouring states immediately send units to my border and draw close when I send them out to fight. Some times it is a bit frustrating, because often after taking a fort or so, it is immediately attacked by another clan, while I was still new to the game I lost many newly captured forts like this. It was quite annoying, this lead to me to start planning more intricate strategies involving split attacks, attempts to form alliances etc. What bugs me though is how handicapped you are if you decided to play the game starting with only 1 fort, you dont have enough labor to make any facilities and you are lacking in nearly everything, it's too expensive to endeavour in any kind of diplomacy. So here i found my self resorting to underhanded tactics (waiting for others to war, etc), and submitting myself to another clan (with this I get an ally and foreign income).
I hope I've cleared up most of the questions here, if any of you have other questions feel free to ask, I will try and update my review with answers to your question!

Starbound is a pretty good game, it's what No Man's Sky should have been, except, cheaper, and better in all ways. Despite being a 2D Sidescroller, it still managed to be a better game, because Graphics are not everything. That being said, there are major flaws with the game, but it still makes this game a good one nonetheless.

Starbound is an incredible example of a game which, somehow, managed to get worse with every patch. I bought into the hype and bought the game the day preorders became available. When it first became open for play, it was pretty alright. Clearly early stages of development, some weird bugs and balance issues, but nothing clearly horrifyingly wrong. Concerns began to raise nearly immediately with the first update, however.
Going mining was about as exciting as it is in any game of this genre; you stand there, drooling slightly, holding MOUSE1 and slowly moving it over the blobs of Craftium. However, on desert planets, ore would often spawn inside the piles of soft sand that collapsed when disturbed, dropping the ore and sending it tumbling down. This was AWESOME. Find a big cavern of soft sand, give it a whack, and ride the wave to the bottom, getting all the ore funneled into your backpack, with the risk of a too-far fall, being buried, or ending up hopelessly lost. You know, cool things that make exploring exciting.
This was deemed Too Fun™ and was removed. Mine from stable rock, plebian. Ore doesn't spawn in soft sand materials, and if it does then it gets destroyed instead of dropped.
But okay. At least we could explore for the ores using the various movement abilities we'd probably found by then, zooming around, swinging from dual grappling hooks, spamming dash techs in the air to dangerously hurl ourselves so fast the game couldn't keep up and risk slamming face-first into a cliff or monster. You know, cool things that make exploring exciting.
This was deemed Too Fun™ and was removed. Dash techs are usable once in the air and consume energy, grappling hooks can no longer be dual-wielded, and walking backwards is now slower just in case someone was enjoying that too.
At least combat had potential for depth. With a combination of varied melee weapons, a wide variety of guns, and monsters that actually used abilities instead of trundling at you mindlessly to inflict contact damage, this could be pretty good once it was expanded on, making a new planet and new depths of caverns dangerous, faced with unknown opponents. You know, cool things that make exploring exciting.
This was deemed Too Fun™ and was removed. Melee weapons got token boosts like "can aim," while guns were slammed into the ground, spit on, and followed up with actions best not described in a public setting. Guns now consume MASSIVE amounts of energy for damage that lightly irritates the target, and if you run out of energy you get locked out of doing anything at all until it fully recharges. Oh, and movement techs use the exact same energy pool. Monsters? Making them do things was interesting, so naturally now they need to just trundle blindly forward to deal contact damage instead of using attacks themselves.
Well... hey, at least we have base building, right? We can find rare stuff, break down interesting materials, set up a nice camp somewhere with a farm for supplies... Nice rewards for going out into the universe to find things and show them off to friends. You know, cool things that make exploring exciting.
This was deemed Too Fun™ and was removed. You want those cool dungeon materials? Better go find the block making them all invincible first. By the way, it's buried way down there past the impossible-without-mobility-boosts lethal obstacle course. Your reward for getting to the end is a mobility boost that sure would have been nice to have 2 hours ago! Farm for materials? Ha, nope. Crops do not grow if you aren't watching them, because that's how plants work.
They also need an exact amount of water. Too little and they die, too much and they die. Of course the systems that automatically water plants for you need hours of grinding to make and don't work if you aren't looking at them.
Well, at least Starbound has progression and quests! Things to do! You actually have goals to work for beyond "Get more stuff to get more better stuff faster." The whole universe is open to explore at your whims, wandering planet to planet just to check things out, sometimes even hitting that infinitesimal chance of going to a planet someone's already been, so you can check out their cool base or vacuum up the garbage they didn't want without dealing with the traps and static spawns yourself, or the risk of going to a planet way above your ability to handle it, with powerful enemies, dangerous environments, and materials you can't figure out how to claw out of the dirt. You know, cool things that make exploring exciting.
This was deemed Too Fun™ and was removed. Planets now have hard locks gatekeeping them to ensure you play only in your corner of the sandbox. Finding someone else's planet involves them explicitly telling you where they are. Environmental hazards are nullified entirely by shoving an Anti-Interesting Upgrade into your face. Quests consist of finding an ultra rare material that you need to upgrade your lacking equipment to actually survive bumping against a squirrel which then immediately eats your leg, so that you can make a spoon for their coffee.
As the spectre of bad gameplay design looms larger and larger with every patch, this may also cast doubt on the game's actual core programming, and you would be correct in your assumption that it is coded as masterfully as it is designed. Memory leaks are so bad that services which rent multiplayer servers didn't allow Starbound. Running it yourself for only 3 or 4 people total will lead to a hard lock and crash as your computer's memory is flooded with garbage code in a matter of hours. Large servers are lucky to last 30 minutes.
The game stutters and struggles to load chunks (the sections of the world itself, for those unaware of the term, which are not all present at once to cut down on loading screens and make the game run faster. In theory). In addition to the memory leakage likely being the primary culprit, it turns out that there was never an optimization pass done on the graphics. The final step of a 2D sprite-based game like this is often "flattening" the images. This takes the file, consisting of many individual sections that make it easier to work on, and turns it into a single cohesive image rather than (random number) 30 fiddly ones that stack on each other. Flattening not only reduces the filesize of the sprites considerably, it also makes it easier on the system to render. It only needs to produce 1 image instead of 30. Since it is rendering 30 images per entity, anything more than a player and a single monster chokes the system's resources, causing lag and pop-in. When you're zooming as fast as you can, that's a lot the game's trying to do at once, which is why sometimes you go hurtling off into the void when half a second ago you were on solid ground in your motorcycle.
How in the world did all the horrible grinding not get addressed? How did these now-glaring gameplay issues get finalized and sent on? Turns out the developers don't actually
the game, they just /admin the materials they need and call it a day, which includes just having the best equipment to speed things up.
Never, ever buy a game unless you will be happy with what you receive in return right at that instant. Assume the developer goes out of business 4 seconds after you buy the game. Even then, always remember: It can get worse. It can always get worse.

This game was gifted to me by a very generous person during its open beta. I have never been more proud to watch a game grow from its bare bones into a rich universe full of so much to do and cultivate a community of players with endless creativity.
Starbound is cute indie sidescroller that offers so much more than what's on the surface.
Fans of voxel or other indie sandbox building games and those new to the genre alike have something to love in Starbound. A rich story full of adventure and lore leads the player through space to save the very Universe from total annihilation, discovering secrets of different species, history, and badass weapons along the way. Randomly generated dungeons across the stars add a bit of spice to space exploration, allowing players to test their mettle against hostile space ships, dungeon guards, monsters, and booby traps!
The game encourages players to create a world of their own, whether planetside or in space. A tenant system exists for player-created colonies and offers rewards as "rent" that get better and better as the player builds in more dangerous areas. And for those who prefer zero gravity and asteroids, newly updated features include options to build a modular space station after exploring space in your very own customizable mech. Farming, fishing, and hunting provide food aplenty and players can collect recipes to become a master chef and satisfy their hunger with the finest interstellar cuisine. Science junkies and engineers can create in-game masterpieces with the game's wiring system that go beyond simple functions like on/off elevators and lights, and add unique flair or security to your builds!
There is so much to Starbound for players to explore and enjoy. Whether you're quest and goal oriented or prefer to take things at your own pace, if you want to battle in an arena or work your green thumb in a vegetable garden, it's an experience you can make your own. Chucklefish is an active game developer in tune with its players, often responding to player concerns and feedback, and opening the game up for easy modding. And the player modding community might yet just be the biggest draw to the game! Players have added endless amounts of new content for the game, providing hours upon hours of replay value. You can visit the steam workshop and find mods to improve your game UI, mechanics and graphics... or choose to add mods that completely change the way your universe is generated and add new systems, vehicles, buildings, vanity, lore and playable races to the game.
To be certain, with Starbound at your fingertips, the Universe is yours to mold and enjoy however you see fit.

I had high hopes for Train Fever, at first glance it has everything you could want from a new Transport Tycoon/Railroad Tycoon game: Nice graphics, plenty of vehicles, growing cities and industry.
Visually Train Fever is nice. I have had some frame rate issues with every computer I have ran it on (including my new PC, which can run Just Cause 3 and Fallout on max settings), but the game remained playable from that perspective.
The economic side of the game is the first big let down. There are far too few industries and given it takes time and patients to get them even remotely profitable, there really isn't much incentive to bother.
What really kills the game for me though, is the track building and routing. It is incredibly tricky to build a bridge over a road for instance. To get double track working properly is also much much harder than it should be.
To be fair, the developer had released several updates (including to the interace and trackbuilding) but none have made the game worth playing for me. The time spent on their free (cosmetic) update- the American scenery was appreciated, but would have been much better spent on the gameplay.
The release of Transport Fever rubbed salt into the wound: improvements that should have been made to Train Fever were implemented there instead. It would have been nice if the developer had put the Train related improvements into Train Fever as a gesture of good will.
To put things into perspective, Railroad Tycoon 3 is a comparitavely challenging business simulation with dozens of industries, a basic version of the stock market and far more interesting maps. It beats Train Fever in every aspect apart from graphics and was released back in 2003 (and work on my Windows 10 machine).

The characters all seem very flat to begin with but expand into having some real dilemmas that flesh them out more than most games ever manage. What else do you have to do on a weekday night waiting for the unevitably better Ace Combat Infinity to release on PlayStation Network in full, glorius English? Oh. You want to buy this game.
Well Ace Cobmat Assault Horizon is a very special game. You fly around in a plane that autopilots you towards your enemies while all you do is sit back, gun, and shoot missiles. This game basically wants you to enjoy the explosions happening around you and make you feel like some badass pilot, but in reality you're occasionally tilting your stick, holding down one button, and when you hear the right sound you want, press the other button.
Let's get down to the meat. You're a pilot who's scared of dying or something so he pisses his pants everytime he's about to die, but also tries to stay badass. He doesn't know who the ♥♥♥♥ he is and you'll lose track of his internal conflict after the first mission because he barely talks about it again until the end of the game. Some Russian group is up to no good and you got to beat them up. So pick your plane out of the preset "please use these planes because they don't break the mission" list, then you're off. Oh wait, that's not every mission. Some missions require you to be in a helicopter that can take collisions into buildings and other missions make you be the machine gunner on the helicopter. That's cool but it's not Ace Combat.
Ace Combat is about jerking off to people calling you the legendary beast or having some Spanish guitar in the background strumming a catchy chorus while you ejaculate over the screen to some female saying that she doesn't want to fight a war. In this game, you're Beef McTruckHam fighting for the greater American good with some heavy thrashing music in the background every other level.
Levels get frustrating as you may get annoyed by the DFM system and end up not holding a button long enough to shoot something to death. Other times you get distracted by optional enemies during a sudden timelimit. This game gets frustrating and you'll probably only replay 3 or 4 missions.
So should you buy this?
Yeah, but don't treat it like an Ace Combat game. Treat it like you're playing Call of Duty in the skies, because that is what it'll ever be.

This game is an absolute bargain!
Firstly, I'll go over the improvements over the first game. First of all, we have the skull purchase system. After you comlete a level, based on an array of criterea, you are given a skull rating. These skulls are all added to your tally. You may then head over to the shop and spend these skulls on whatever you choose! This shop includes tons of traps, a large number of weapons and a good number of trinkets. Trinkets are new too, they provide passive and active bonuses, but normally do not directly affect combat with the horde. You may think that with that much content for this price, everything is just a reskin. Nope! There are tons of new traps, all varying dramatically from eachother. The weapons are all viable in their own ways, I haven't found anything to be straight up the best. Basically, tons of content that will leave you "staying for one more minute to get that next trap". Also, nothing is too overpriced, so there is very little grinding. Three levels max will get you that new piece of expensive gear to try out. By the way, some items are locked so you have to unlock them by beating a level. We don't want you getting the good stuff too soon! Finally, tons of upgrades! Every trinket, weapon and trap has a nice line of upgrades to further customise your play. My personal favourite trap is the haymaker, a spinning bar that comes down from the ceiling to deal damage and push the orcs around. I upgraded it to make it literally throw the orcs up into the air, sometimes to their deaths, which just makes the game that much more fun!
Secondly, CO-OP! This is easily the best part of this game, now you can join in the orc slaying action with a friend! It is perfectly balanced, with all "money" earned being evenly split between players. However, always keep an eye out for that bonus skull that sometimes pops up after killing an enemy. Both players can see them, and me and my friend have had great races across the map to get us one step closer to that expensive weapon. Everything is better with friends, and Orcs Must Die 2 is exponentially so.
I'll cover the rest on this paragraph. First of all, we have a new character, the sorceress. She has unique traps of her own, unobtainable by the classic War Mage, but he has his unique traps too. With some very interesting and often humerous dialogue between the rivals, it provides a great bit of story telling without drifting from the main content: killing Orcs. Another great addition to Orcs Must Die 2 is the secondry fire. Every weapon has primary and secondry fire modes, with the secondry providing a nice effect at the cost of a bit of mana. I'm pretty sure you can upgrade every weapons secondry fire, so you can find what fits you and make it the best it can be!
Overall, It's just a blast. Especially at the £6 it is during this Holiday sale, you really can't go wrong with Orcs Must Die 2.

Banner Saga 1 & 2 are great games by themselves. This game, which is s multiplayer pvp format of the game - is an abandoned project only used to promote BS 1 & 2 these days. With all my respect to the developers, who are but a small team with a great vision for character and style, I can by no means justify a completely abandoned product as this one while it still allows players to invest real money in game. The only news and update notifications you will see are regarding the other 2 games. Most recent news notification ( which regards to bs 1 and not this game ) is from 2014.
It is understandable that plans not always work out, but responsibility has to be shown when this occurs and in this case - 1. real money purchase options have to be blocked and 2. formal developer notification as to the state of the game has to be made.
Game has great potential. In fact, so much more than bs 1 and 2 can ever dream to have - as it is not based on AI but on human inteliligence which is ever creative, ever fresh, ever challenging. Hence endless potential and replayability.
But putting aside the peculiar decision to forsaken it for the sake of much more limited projects ( personally spent almost 300 hours in this game vs 12 hours in bs1 which I didnt even care to finish ), I can not but criticise the ignoring tactics of the developers not having the integrity to at least admit and apologize for turning their back on this game.
Unfortunately I have to say - do not go near this game until Stoic acknowledges its state and has the integrity to either announce their plans for its future or announce their lack of and stop selling real money packages for a dead, unsupported product.

Another great installment in the Secret Files series.  There was one major improvement over the previous game that I enjoyed:
- Running.  Finally the opportunity to move quicker across scenes.  It automatically kicks in when the player has to traverse at least half the screen but I'll take any improvement over slow walking
Graphics have improved slightly over the previous game.  The character models are animated a bit better now although they still suffer from a lack of expression.  Given the smaller studio, it's not a deal breaker.
Voice acting has larger discrepancies as far as quality goes.  There are vastly more areas where it looks like the actor tried to act funny but it comes off as a bit trying too hard.  There were still areas where the dialog/writing was actually quite apt and I laughed out loud at the jokes.  The major issue I had with the voices was the change from the previous game.  The main character's voice deepened quite a bit.  Granted I overall like the new voice actess, she comes off more dry; the first game's actress, while grating at times, actually had better emotional projection overall.
It's still one of the shorter adventure games I've played but one can still see the love and effort the developers put into the game.
Overall I enojyed the game and it's a welcome addition to anyone's adventure collection.  Still recommend getting it when it's on sale as for the price, I do enjoy Telltale games more than this.

This is a good mod. The time machine works very well, and is executed very well. You solve Portal like puzzles with the twist of the time machine. There's no dialogue whatsoever and you should find yourself immersed if that's your way of working. There is one thing to make sure of: BEAT PORTAL 2 BEFORE YOU PLAY THIS MOD. THE INTRO CONTAINS SPOILERS OF THE ENDING CUTSCENE OF PORTAL 2. Other than that its a good time.

Not at all what it could have been...
While this game is the first Portal 2 mod to be released on the Steam page, and not the first unveiled, it can be seen that it only got there by cutting corners. (Not with the corner cutting machine). This game brings forth great concepts, and great custom content, yet the "game" itself, is incomplete! The game contains more bugs than my grandmother's attic, its graphics don't even compare to maps on the Portal 2 workshop page, and the flow and style of the game is practically nonexistent. Here's one example: The portable surfaces are the same shape, size, color, and brightness as the lights on the walls of the test chamber. Instead of leading the player, the gameplay system follows a pretty consistent pattern of "spend a long enough time in the room and eventually you'll happen to find the right solution." So many loose ends, logical inconsistencies, that needed to be tied up, but weren't, lead me to believe that this mod is still in beta. And yet it's released on the store page! Why!? Granted, I didn't waste money on this, so I shouldn't complain, but imagine the onslaught of garbage that can tumble onto the Steam store page, as every inexperienced person with a Portal 2 idea, decides to make a mod without knowledge of how a game should be made. Not a good sign for the future. My advice: If you're going to make a game and release it, form a team, and read articles on game design. Half of the creative process is research, and game design is above all, an art form. A lot more work should have gone into this "game".

I speak as someone who is still pretty amateurish at fighting games in general.
It's a fine version of the game with all the characters and costumes (finally. Thank goodness Capcom has decided to make future content in SFV unlockable through gameplay). You can play (in versus) every version of your character,
so that's a neat touch.
It's probably one of my favorite 2D fighters.
I think that although the game has a great challenge mode to teach you how your character works, I feel more
can be done to educate a player as to how combos work.  It took a while to understand all the uses for a character's force move. It's important to me that a game describe itself fully before some guy bodies me using an overall well known
tactic that is essential to SF4 unbeknownst to me .
More could have been done on the lines of tools for a player to explore the game such as hitbox displays.
I see no reason why this wasn't added, as it's an essential aspect of the game for anyone who wants to
actually get invested in the game. There does exist an external tool for PC users that can bring this functionality,
but it doesn't make sense not to add it.
On a visual standpoint, it's very nice looking, although the character models tend to have varying accuracy
with their drawn art from the select screen. Everyone looks....puffy. I dunno, it's something I can't put my finger on, but
although it's functional for the game and easy on the eyes, it's not stylistically interesting to me.
Ryu looks stupid, I'll just say that. He looks so much better in SFV so far.

Speaking of which Capcom should get third strike on PC, just putting that out there.

My only regret is that some characters I love to play as such as Dudley are not yet confirmed for the
next game.
The true test is yet to come, which is whether or not we'll be playing this when SFV comes out. I don't see it standing the test of time as SF3 did due to it's excellent game mechanics preserving it with competitive functionality and overall depth of play. USFIV is currently one of the most balanced 1 on 1 2D fighting games with a good fighting system, good amount of characters, moves and game modes. SFIV is a 2D fighting game like most of the previous Street Fighter iterations. It has various characters which increases the chance of some that may catch your fancy. There is even more characters in this ultra edition which is an upgrade to previous SFIV versions. Fighting speed in general is normal compared to other 2D fighters which leaves a good open window for command inputs in-between. This PC version have a decent system settings and controllers compatibility other than x-input (xbox 360/one based) devices and keyboards. For all characters the fighting system has 6 main buttons, blocks are done by holding back, standing, crouching and jumping attacks, throws, dashes, wakeup delay, characters get stunned after certain amount of attacks taken, a 2 stage charge attack (called focus) for each character which strength varies by the duration pressed, characters have special moves and there is extra bar (called super) which has 4 stages (bars) and can be used for having ex version of some specials by using one bar and a super which consumes all 4 bars, there is finishing move bar (called ultra) and each character has 2 ultras which can be selected individually or together, focus then dashing can be used to link some attacks (called focus cancel) and can be used to cancel an active attack for defense and backing up. Attacks are categorized into high, medium, low, overhead, throws, some characters has command throws also and fully charged focus is unblockable. All non-normal attacks will chip the health bar when blocked and can finish a round. All characters have taunts which can be disabled before matches.  Arcade mode acts like story mode with few (1 or more) still images with narration as prologue and a small animated clip as epilogue with rival battles before the boss battle that has special before and in match dialogue. There is versus mode for local or computer battles and also there is computer versus computer matches. Training mode is on normal quality with ability to record actions for the dummy and can be locally controlled or computer controlled and all bars are modifiable, there is challenge mode which is a series of combos for each characters. Online multiplayer is decent now but with less players than the consoles versions as there is no cross platform multiplayer, all online battles have voice chat, there is ranked battles, online training, room battles and tournament like rooms with one active match at a time and all can be open invitation to all or friend invitations and in rooms you can set the number of slots for which type. Online battle can be selected to start and halt current offline matches when found, this applies to arcade and training modes. Online and versus matches replays can be saved although in limited amount and you can watch some matches for high ranking players and some recent replays for others all can be viewed by region or characters. There is a ranking system for your overall points and your character points. You can be unique online by having an icon, a title and a vs screen message and all are pre made. There is different customs for each character and a lot of them are unfortunately available as DLC.
Pros:
Easy to pick up and learn but hard to master.
A very balanced fighting game.
Big selection of characters that a lot are totally unique with either English or Japanese voices.
All characters versions are available in addition to omega versions.
Ability to have different playing styles, strategies.
Community, as there is a lot of player made material for every subject.
Competitive real life tournaments.
Almost endless shelf life for a fighting game.
cons:
Lackluster arcade/story mode.
No Tutorial mode.
Stages default BGM is mostly boring except for a few ones.
No visual upgrade from 2008.
Price is high for an upgrade.
DLC is overpriced and cannot be earned in-game.
Mastery require too much training for any character.
No time attack or survival/endurance modes.
Offline and online play variety is limited.
Some online modes are almost abandoned.
Need to manually adjust some settings in graphics card options outside the game for optimum performance.
No official list of all combos or official in-depth guide, also no technical visual assist in training for hitboxes and moves recovery and active frames.
Only icons, titles, default custom colors and taunts are rewards for playing.
I hope this is a fair review of USFIV on Steam.

EDIT: A few paragraphs down is a review I wrote when I was halfway through the game. I'm leaving it here as a reminder of how good it felt before getting to the crappy second half. The game becomes utterly boring once you get the ability to mind-control orcs---which sounds like a cool ability, but it just means you don't get to do any more fighting and assassinating. Which is just as well, because at that point the fights and assassinations have become so easy that they're boring themselves.
Perfect example: The only mission I really had trouble with was one where I was specifically not supposed to murder someone. I kept accidentally killing him with the loose controls (or one of my minions, or just a random beast killed him). REVIEW OF FIRST HALF:
This game is a sequel to Batman: Arkham City, except it takes place in the Lord of the Rings cinematic universe, except it's bizarrely dark and edgy and violent. That sounds like a dumb idea for a video game, which is why it's such a surprise that it's actually good. If you liked the Batman games, you'll like this. The whole experience is very polished, and the procedural content gives the game a very organic structure.
The IP:
As a fan of the books and the movies, this game felt like fan fiction to me-- the story in this game doesn't feel like anything Tolkien would've written. The dialogue is full of weird references or quotes of lines from the books/films. For example, we run into Gollum pretty early on, and he immediately calls us "Master" and offers to guide us somewhere. Fanservice as gratuitous as it is self-defeating.
Overall, the way the IP was used didn't delight me, but it didn't bother me either. This game expands on the lore, showing what was going on in Mordor around the time Sauron was rebuilding Barad-Dur. It's a neat facet to explore.
The Setting:
We're in Mordor instead of Gotham City. Instead of thugs and supervillains, we're fighting orcs and... meaner orcs. (Bit of a lost opportunity--I would've loved to see the Nemesis system in a superhero game.) The baddies have a lot of personality, and the voice acting is on the better side of average. I do wish they used actual British voice actors instead of Americans doing fake accents.
The environments are actually nicely varied: I was afraid it would all be a grey-brown blur, but there are some interesting places to sneak/fight/parkour your way through.
The Mechanics:
Combat is nearly identical to Batman, though slightly more forgiving. The same goes for the stealth, actually, since the absence of guns makes it easier to deal with enemies once they've spotted you. All the grappling on gargoyles stuff is replaced by parkour climbing, which works quite well for setting up sneak attacks. Bat-gadgets are replaced with wraith powers, which are pretty neat.
Here's the big difference, though: In Batman, every encounter was usually either a combat encounter or a stealth encounter. In Shadow of Mordor, any encounter can be defeated with stealth, combat, or (usually) a seamless combination. I defeated one tough encounter by charging into enemy lines, picking off a few of them before they could surround me, running away, climbing up a ruined castle tower, taking a few potshots, and diving back down into the melee. It was nuts, and I had to disengage and re-engage like 5 times before I cleaned up the area and got to pick up all that sweet loot.
You can choose how to approach each encounter, but you also need to pick your battles. There is a penalty for dying, so you need to know when to run away. And if you do get killed, you get to plan a perfect revenge on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who did it.
I also appreciate that the orcs sometimes run away from the player. If only the goons of Arkham City had that much respect for the Batman.
The Structure:
The overall structure of Shadow of Mordor is very open. Of course there's a story quest with clear objectives, but you always have multiple side quests to pursue. There are always bosses to go hunt down and fight--some of them are wandering certain areas of the map, some of them are in specific missions, and sometimes they'll sneak up on you... all of them are (seemingly?) randomly generated, and drop random loot, giving this game sort of a Diablo feel.
The collectibles in this game are just as pointless as ever, but I've enjoyed completing them as I work my way through the game world. It's not like the Riddler trophies in Arkham City, where I kept saying "I'll come back and do that later," and then never ever came back to do them. Maybe it's becuase there are so few in each zone, and the game gives you very clear indiactions of your progress.
The Wrap-up:
I'm not even halfway into this game, and I'm very impressed. TLDR: This is a good game. Hopefully it stays this good throughout the full playtime.

What a shame.
In an attempt to revitalize a series that didn't really need it, Namco and Project Aces wound up just dumbing it down and ripping out any charm it had in the process. The game certainly looks quite nice, it is too bad you won't get to control it half the time you're playing.
The game seems intent on forcing you to watch Michael Bay-esque explosion and destruction setpieces, through the use of a new "feature" called Dog Fight Mode. I'm not sure what the intent was here, but what they did was made roughly half of the enemy fighter pilots in the game nearly impossible to shoot down by giving them an infinite amount of flares that recharge instantly, an apparent invulnerability to gun fire, and twitchy flight patterns that their aircraft should not be capable of performing.
All that is to force you to activate Dog Fight Mode, a glorified Quick Time Event. It takes control away from the player (pretty much always a sign of a bad game design idea) and instead lets you nudge the plane around slightly on a preset path, with the goal of firing missiles when a circle turns red and lining up the gun sight with the enemy. It feels incredibly janky and unsatisfying.
Even then, the game will pull impossible stunts and prevent you from killing the enemy jet until you fly past whatever dumb falling crane or explosion they want you to see. Because god forbid we have these things trigger naturally, that might actually be satisfying for the player. No instead the developers decide you have to see THIS exact sequence of events EXACTLY like this.
Rather than having a goofy flight game with solid mechanics in an absurd setting, they went with a boring real world setting and broke the mechanics so they could shoehorn in an unwanted feature that does nothing but effectively force you to view cutscenes. I was hoping that I would be able to avoid using DFM entirely, but I guess I'm not allowed to have fun.
I went into this trying to have an open mind about DFM, but the fact that the game forces you to use it is unacceptable. I honestly did not expect them to do wrong one of the few things that Tom Clancy's HAWX did right, that you never have to use the gameplay gimmick. And even as far as gameplay gimmicks go, Assistance Off is more interesting, creative, and enjoyable than DFM.
In conclusion, if you are an idiot who likes games where you push a button occasionally to watch complex cutscenes instead of actually performing those actions and think yet another story about Americans and Russian terrorists fighting each other is exciting, you might like this. Otherwise I cannot recommend it.
Port the PS2 games to PC instead Namco, there's money in that.
In any case, I'm going to see if I can mod this game to remove DFM altogether and try to salvage something out of this mess.

Spoiler: The queen doesn't live long at all.
Got this game through the auction; way more enjoyable than initially expected.  In a nutshell, this game is an anime version of Dark Souls innocuously portrayed as a loli princess simulator by the cover art.  If watching a blank slate pink haired preteen girl die repeatedly while trying to come to terms with common sense on her way to coronation sounds great, this might be your VN. The game is more gruesome, political, and dark than the initial art style suggests.
Death is addicting, and it can be infuriating trying to clear the game; the world just keeps giving surprises when least expected.  The infamous chocolate end that many other reviews allude to is just one out of eleven ways to die; some methods of death (as well as 39 achievements and 24 epilogues) are extremely obscure and it takes a lot of hours to unlock all of them.  Some playthroughs (i.e. hours) will be spent optimizing stats to trigger a specific flag.
Branching story implies there are multiple ways to play this game.  You can behave in a benevolent manner fitting of a queen and win hearts through diplomacy and fairness.  Or you can be a tyrant and quash the inevitable rebellion.  A stalwart warrior who crushes armies with might or magic?  Or maybe a darkened Elodie who succumbs to power, whose name is never in Novan history spoken again.  Or will your legacy be the first queen to establish hospitals and sponsor the printing press?  Many ways to play, many endings to experience, many achievements to collect, and many ways to die.  How will you play Elodie?
Pros
+Cute characters
+Music
+Branching story (keeps OCD people occupied)
+Execute peasants for laughs
+Abuse the maid
+Tons of political drama, backstories, and hidden motives (allies in one playthrough are antagonists in the next).
+Elodie can become evil
Cons
-Needs good planning skills
-Takes a long time to complete
-Some achievements are crazy difficult to get (few guides exist)
-Need to have a habit of having dozens of savefiles

This is a very excellent game, I really enjoy it.  I love watching my empire sprawl across the map, never to be tamed.
Unfortunately, there are a few gamebreaking issues.  The game is called Train Fever, though the best use of your resources is with trucks delivering cargo.  Busses are cool and work in conjunction with trains well, but they bring in very little profit, if done right.  Cargo trains can bring in loads of profit, but are unstable.  It is hard to balance the correct number of cars and how much the factory produces.  Long distance cargo runs are not profitable.  The train maintanane cost outweighs the profits, or the factory/factories will not produce enough to make a train worthwhile.  Often times, neither factory on the lin e will increase, even though both are getting all their goods shipped in a timely manner, resulting in profit loss as the train gets older and becomes obsolite.  Trucks work better, with very tiny maintanance costs, and can therefore better serve the cargo industry.
Passanger trains are another matter.  Connecting 2 nearby cities with a single train works well and is very profitable early on, but this is train fever.  That means we want to see some trains running around.  So you improve your tracks, and have 4 cities connected in a loop.  Guess what?  Unless you get newer, faster trains, they aren't going to make a profit.  So now it's in the 1950s, and your loop is profitable.  So let's expand, shall we?
Except passengers don't want to go, which doesn't make sense.  A distant, far off city is now accesible for a short train ride, but still no one does.  I have three train lines, one is a loop of four cities.  The other two use that same loop, but also add 2+ extra cities in a bigger loop.  The first line is the most profitable, because for some reason the simulated citizens DO NOT like to go very far.  Anyway, enough ranting.
Other than that, the game is very fun, and I would definately recommend.  It could use some work, but I still play it and it makes me happy.
Then there is always that dude who jumps off your train mid-transit.

First lets talk about the graphics in this game, they are 3D with an anime style similar to the popular series Abunai sisters, but the design in Guilty Gear Xrd puts their own twist on this by making it not a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥to look at, I love the look of this game and I can't help but when a KO in this game happens but put a screen shot of the lovely camera angles that show.
I heard that the only reason that they changed the graphics to 3d was to have a alway availible goto model now to save on the budget on sprite development and never have to worry about them showing age for a long time, but if them making great looking anime styled models with lovely backgrounds is them trying to save the budget I want to see what they can do when they're spending it all.
Makes me wish there was a mod to move the camera in battle behind you, I wouldn't even care how much harder it would make the game I just want to see it and take more screen shots of this gorgeous game.
In my opionion the game is really fun, cast is very varied in what every character is capible of and what they use to get the job done and it can also be said that fighting no 2 players is the same since everyone seems to find something else great about the character to use, just when you think you've got that characters play style down.
From the Roman canceling, rejects, faultless blocking and even more it seems like there is way to much content to get used to at the start but online there are always beginner servers to get a hand in with playing others who are not yet themselves that good at the game.
For a first fighter this could seem a bit like too much but it's really not a bad choise because it means if you're into learning a game inside and out it would be a like being a kid in a candy shop
Now to get to some of the negitives of this game.
The story mode really is just talking the whole time with not a ounce of game play in it and the animation for such lovely 3d modles doesn't due much justice, it's like seeing static VN portraits in 3D and this really shows as an issue when you see fights in story mode look like they're played through micro soft power point.
Next is the online in this game, it's functional if that is a thing to call it but you'll constantly be kicked from rooms that claim good connection and then somehow get into that 0 connection room you clicked by mistake, also the online matches after the patch in this game have lead to a few times the game just crashes.
The patch claims to have fixed the ranked mode in this game but it turned into the same click their name until the game gives up and lets you play that it was before, combined that with the crashing now online and I don't even want to play ranked from fear of being called a rage quitter.
Then we get to the main issue that I've have had with the game and how well it runs, going by having task manager in the side while running the game to check on it I seen that the specs post patch from pre patch are a good 150% higher and it didn't fix the issue where as the game is running the specs of the game slowly but constantly go up leading to eventual lag on the menu of all things, but here just opening and closing the game seems to reset it.
this is something I really want arksys to get into fixing because the game seems like otherwise it would be able to run really well on much weaker machines.
It may look like I dragged way much longer on the negitives then the possitives here but when you get past the problems that come mainly in the online and the story mode of the game what you will find is a great fighting game that if you are a fan of the genre you will not want to miss by miles.
Over all the possitives of having a great and closer to the current version of the game come out on PC overlap the negitives but in the future I hope they at least figure how tofix the current online.

I'll need to be updating this review as I play. As of this writing, I'm now about 30 hours into the game.
This was my review about 2 hours in:
"This was awful. The most difficult enemy to overcome is the controls. This game is to fighting skeletons as QWOP is to running."
^ that was while using an xbox controller. The combat takes a long time to get used to, and until you've done it a lot it feels incredibly clunky and unresponsive, and simply trying to look at the right enemy and swing your weapon feels like a chore at first.
but I got used to it.. and found it very satisfying once I did. Of course I had to look up how to actually backstab and parry online, because there are some very unintuitive caveats, but yeah, in the end, it feels very satisfying.
Since that review, I'm changing my recommendation from No to Yes, but with a huge caveat. People always say this game "doesn't hold your hand" or "hand things to you" and you might think that that's a good thing, but... well let me explain:
It's a game of mazes and traps, but the worst mazes and traps aren't so much in the environments you traverse and the enemies you face, they're in the decisions you make, and in a way that can be very, very unfun.
The first example of this that I encountered was immediately after the tutorial, when I didn't see the "right" way to go, and wasted a lot of time trying to go the "wrong" way. This was my bad. If I'd explored meticulously enough, I'd have seen the thin path to the "right" way and noticed that the enemies were easier to fight.
The second was in the UI. When looking at your character stats, the UI tells you that you can press Select to see explanations. When looking at items, however, it doesn't, but you can. The first time I saw the items stats screen, however, was while talking to a merchant. The stats screen looks the same, but you cannot press Select to view explanations while talking to a merchant, so when I pressed Select as an experiment and it didn't work, I concluded that you can't press Select to view item stats explanations. After all, it says you can for personal stats but not for items. I didn't know what some of them meant for the next 20 hours of gameplay. Git Gud... right?
There's an important elevator that should save you a lot of time early in the game. The first time I walked into it, it didn't work. Later I learned online that it should work, and when I tried it again, it worked. There was never any indicator that it had started working, and you never have any reason to believe it should be a functional elevator.
You do a thing and get an item to teleport you back home. You can either use it, or decide to walk. If you use the item, you'll never learn of an NPC that just appeared from nowhere on the way back.
There's a really nondescript locked door in a location that you'd otherwise have no reason to re-visit, but it's the only route to the second part of the first quest. What you know of the quest is that you have to do something up above in (Location Name) and down below, in (Location Name) but your only indication of the location of (Location Name) is "above" and "below". Well there's a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of "below" in this game that you can access from the very start, so I went to the wrong "below" and spent maybe 10 hours on it, clearing it, before I looked online and learned of the door. There was never any indication that I was in the "wrong" "below" and there was never anything to draw my attention to the nondescript locked door, which, by the way, was located way above.
So when you hear that the game doesn't "hand anything to you" expect that this means, basically, everything. It doesn't hand to you a bunch of what the controls are. It doesn't hand to you a hint of where you're actually supposed to go. You'll often be presented with options but you were never "handed" any clue what they might possibly do, so you're choosing blindly.
It does, sort of, hand to you a really heavy-handed, sparse story. At least so far. I've seen only the bare-bones of what you would call a story, and it was delivered by NPCs basically expositing story at me, plus a cutscene at the start. The worldbuilding is amazing and unique, though. Enemies, environments, lore, etc, all very good and fleshed out if you're looking for it. I think people confuse worldbuilding and story though, when they say the story is so good. What story-like progression there is has been so slow and confusing.
EDIT 70hrs in: Finally beat the game. Once I got the right upgraded armor and weapons, and a good level, actually defeating enemies became practically trivial. This game is like a puzzle game, where you have to do certain things in certain orders in order to progress, except unlike a puzzle game this game provides almost zero clues as to what the thing you need to do is, when you need to do it, or really whether you need to do it at all. It'll just leave you flailing about uselessly wasting your time unless you look everything up online. There's practically no chance you'll actually get to experience the story without looking it up online. Even paying very close attention, reading everything you see, talking to everyone you see... you'll get maybe 40% of what there is available to get (which isn't much) and the rest is only accessibly if you just happen to do the right things at the right times in the right order, either because you looked it up or because you just got lucky.

TLDR: A low-quality point and click game with an awful story, terrible voice-acting and puzzle design that averages on poor. Only really recommended for those that loved the original game or are really desperate for an adventure game; and only then on a sale.
Long story: You play as Nina and Max once more, but after they have apparently broken up. Nina bumps into a guy minutes before he horribly dies, only to find that she has gotten his luggage by mistake. Cue secret sect which threatens the world and you have the makings of the most cliché story ever. Now, there is nothing wrong with a cliché story, as long as the details make it come alive and the characters make it memorable. Secret Files 2: Puritas Cordis does not do that. The story is awful from the start until the very end. It does not seem to know whether it wants to be a more serious game (like Broken Sword which is seems heavily inspired by or is trying to mock… I don’t know which) or a light comedy… but the “if this was a computer game” jokes clash badly with the scenes where we are supposed to believe Nina is scared or feels guilty. It’s all a mishmash of different tones. This may in large part be due to the horrific voice acting. Some of the side-characters are fine, but the ones for Nina and Max are atrocious. Nina’s voice actress does not seem like she could hit a right intonation if it bit her in the throat. She butchers every half-decent joke the script throws at her. Max’s actor instead seems to have been told “speak slower… and douchier! No douchier!” The only saving grace is the fact that you can skip dialogue and cutscenes; if not for this I would not have finished the game at all. However, this still means that you’ll be skipping most of the dialogue and whatever atmosphere and hilarity they were trying to convey.
The puzzles then. Some of the puzzles not related to items are actually quite nice. Nothing too challenging, but good fun. The item puzzles are a bit more problematic. They are often obtuse or suffer from the same adventure game logic as other games in the genre (i.e. many puzzles should have been solvable with other objects), but that’s okay if not great. The real problem is that the game loves throwing a ton of items at you, but rarely explains your goals very well. This means that you are almost always combining items without any clue or reason why, and you’re forced to try them out randomly at whatever spots are available. It was exceedingly rare for me to feel like I was actually planning my actions in any logical sense. For example, on the boat you are supposed to build a European monument, but while you are given some cities from which you can build, you are given no examples of monuments from those cities. Maybe you know them all, maybe you don’t. Personally I had not visited the city from which the correct monument was from and only built it by randomly combining items. No thought, no plan required or even encouraged. The game is full of that kind of thing. The worst of which is probably when you are supposed to get a street cleaner to clean the street by getting him wet. *SPOILER* You do so by getting an alarm to go off which makes a guy run there, which makes his friends drive by and miss him, which makes them turn up on the bridge, into the puddle which makes the guy wet. *END SPOILER*. The solution would be fine, if there was any indication that this is what would happen if these events were set in motion. Instead the only reasonable way to figure it out is by doing everything possible with your items at the different locations and hope for the best. That is not good puzzle design.
I will not compare Secret Files 2 to the original game, because frankly I don’t remember it that well (though if I’m not mistaken they liked to drown you in items there too), but I did like it well enough to want to try the sequel… but only if it was on sale. Apparently I did not like the original so much that I thought the sequel must be worth 10 Euro. And I was right, it isn’t. In fact, I’m not sure it is worth the 2.5 Euro I paid. It’s not an awful game. Puzzlewise it is a very standard adventure game, not special in any way. It just happens to be coupled with a boring story and main characters which are either bad in of themselves, or are just made so by their horrific voice-actors. Anyway, I can’t recommend the game unless you are deeply in love with the series or desperately want an adventure game. But even then, there are definitely better ones out there.

Ultra is one of the best fighters I've played, hours of fun whether you are an experienced fighting game player or new to the genre. At times I feel as though the game could potentially be a bit more fun with some added game modes such as a ladder mode, especially for players who prefer single player, although I do recognize that this is not a theme of street fighter games and might not seem appropriate with the arcade mode.
The tutorials and training sections of the game are really useful, but sometimes I feel as though they don't go into enough detail in regards to teaching certain game mechanics like focus attack dash cancelling, which is an important mechanic in this game. "Skullgirls" for example shows hitboxes and hitsun in the training mode, and gives tutorials in a wide variety of the game's mechanics, which I feel would really benefit Ultra to new players.
