EDIT: A few paragraphs down is a review I wrote when I was halfway through the game. I'm leaving it here as a reminder of how good it felt before getting to the crappy second half. The game becomes utterly boring once you get the ability to mind-control orcs---which sounds like a cool ability, but it just means you don't get to do any more fighting and assassinating. Which is just as well, because at that point the fights and assassinations have become so easy that they're boring themselves.
Perfect example: The only mission I really had trouble with was one where I was specifically not supposed to murder someone. I kept accidentally killing him with the loose controls (or one of my minions, or just a random beast killed him). Afterwards, I told one of my minions to just go fight the enemy boss himself, which he did, and won.
The last bit of the game basically beats itself. The final boss is two QTEs in a row (sounds like a joke, not a joke). Words cannot express my disappointment.
I'm still recommending this one, but just know it gets a lot worse after you leave Udun.
REVIEW OF FIRST HALF:
This game is a sequel to Batman: Arkham City, except it takes place in the Lord of the Rings cinematic universe, except it's bizarrely dark and edgy and violent. That sounds like a dumb idea for a video game, which is why it's such a surprise that it's actually good. If you liked the Batman games, you'll like this. The whole experience is very polished, and the procedural content gives the game a very organic structure.
The IP:
As a fan of the books and the movies, this game felt like fan fiction to me-- the story in this game doesn't feel like anything Tolkien would've written. The dialogue is full of weird references or quotes of lines from the books/films. For example, we run into Gollum pretty early on, and he immediately calls us "Master" and offers to guide us somewhere. Fanservice as gratuitous as it is self-defeating.
Overall, the way the IP was used didn't delight me, but it didn't bother me either. This game expands on the lore, showing what was going on in Mordor around the time Sauron was rebuilding Barad-Dur. It's a neat facet to explore.
The Setting:
We're in Mordor instead of Gotham City. Instead of thugs and supervillains, we're fighting orcs and... meaner orcs. (Bit of a lost opportunity--I would've loved to see the Nemesis system in a superhero game.) The baddies have a lot of personality, and the voice acting is on the better side of average. I do wish they used actual British voice actors instead of Americans doing fake accents.
The environments are actually nicely varied: I was afraid it would all be a grey-brown blur, but there are some interesting places to sneak/fight/parkour your way through.
The Mechanics:
Combat is nearly identical to Batman, though slightly more forgiving. The same goes for the stealth, actually, since the absence of guns makes it easier to deal with enemies once they've spotted you. All the grappling on gargoyles stuff is replaced by parkour climbing, which works quite well for setting up sneak attacks. Bat-gadgets are replaced with wraith powers, which are pretty neat.
Here's the big difference, though: In Batman, every encounter was usually either a combat encounter or a stealth encounter. In Shadow of Mordor, any encounter can be defeated with stealth, combat, or (usually) a seamless combination. I defeated one tough encounter by charging into enemy lines, picking off a few of them before they could surround me, running away, climbing up a ruined castle tower, taking a few potshots, and diving back down into the melee. It was nuts, and I had to disengage and re-engage like 5 times before I cleaned up the area and got to pick up all that sweet loot.
You can choose how to approach each encounter, but you also need to pick your battles. There is a penalty for dying, so you need to know when to run away. And if you do get killed, you get to plan a perfect revenge on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who did it.
I also appreciate that the orcs sometimes run away from the player. If only the goons of Arkham City had that much respect for the Batman.
The Structure:
The overall structure of Shadow of Mordor is very open. Of course there's a story quest with clear objectives, but you always have multiple side quests to pursue. There are always bosses to go hunt down and fight--some of them are wandering certain areas of the map, some of them are in specific missions, and sometimes they'll sneak up on you... all of them are (seemingly?) randomly generated, and drop random loot, giving this game sort of a Diablo feel.
The collectibles in this game are just as pointless as ever, but I've enjoyed completing them as I work my way through the game world. It's not like the Riddler trophies in Arkham City, where I kept saying "I'll come back and do that later," and then never ever came back to do them. Maybe it's becuase there are so few in each zone, and the game gives you very clear indiactions of your progress.
The Wrap-up:
I'm not even halfway into this game, and I'm very impressed. TLDR: This is a good game. Hopefully it stays this good throughout the full playtime.

This isn't a puzzle game. It doesn't feel like a puzzle game, and it doesn't play like a puzzle game. I recognize it was a free game, so oddly enough, I went easier on it, ignoring some missing or errant minor details, but I still have major gripes about the game. The time-travel mechanic is limited, and can't really produce many puzzles that are difficult, although it does apparently warrant the creation of a whole bunch of menial tasks. None of the puzzles felt like I accomplished anything after I beat them because they were too easy. Some puzzles took longer than they should have; once I figured out the solution, which never really took more than a quick glance, it took forever to actually perform said solution.
One major flaw was with how the levels were designed; that white light square texture on the walls were used WAY too much, thinking that I could place portals on them only to find out that most of them were red herrings. There was one puzzle that was particularly damning, a room where I had to get a ball and a cube from one to another, both activated switches required to get between them. My first instinct was to shoot some of the walls with the portal gun (because everything was a white square, big surprise), to no avail, so I figured that this puzzle didn't require the portal gun. I ran around both rooms for ages, stacking all kinds of things to get from one room to the next, only to find that I was totally stumped. I gave kudos to the author for actually making a difficult puzzle. I went online to find that, oh, yeah, one of the white squares you CAN put a portal on. So now I want to take that kudos and shove it up his♥♥♥♥♥
Honestly, if you're still curious, I can't hold you back because it IS a free mod. But of you're like me and are just looking for something to tithe you over until a big game release, then just pass; it's wasted space on your storage drive.

If you like the combat and art style of The Banner Saga, then you will find joy in Factions. Matches consist of ranked or unranked "friendlies" where you compete against 1 other person using a set-up of the classes found in the original game - Varl and Human. Each match earns you Renown (should you win) and the ability to level up your team, much like was done in the game.
I've seen some reviews commenting on the lack of people on the server, or matches hard to come by, and I write this review mostly to say that I haven't had any difficulty finding a match. In fact, I often see a lot of the higher level (by +2 levels) matches popping up looking for an opponent.
The beauty of the team system is you can level some favourites but also have a team of lower level so you can try out different play styles without waiting longer than a couple minutes for an opponent. I imagine a lot of this relies on the time of day you are looking, but the community is quite active and with TBS2 shortly being released, I see even more people coming into Factions.

I came to this game from a background of  RailRoad Tycoon 3  (Released 2003)  9.99 USD on Steam
Railroad Tycoon 3  is getting a bit "long in the tooth" and I was hoping for an upgrade. While Railroad Tycoon 3 is not as pretty, in my judgement it is a superior game to Train Fever (and its sucessor Transport Fever) in many ways.
Railroad Tycoon 3 has no signals and these are an improvement, it did have water towers and maintenance sheds that are absent from Transport Fever. Growing up in a railroad town spoiled me but I'd also expect a turntable.
Railroad Tycoon 3  has no mechanic for returning empty freight cars for re-use. This game has them but unlike real world railcars, almost all wagon types are for a single commodity only. e.g. Why aren't coal hoppers and iron hoppers interchangeable?
Railroad Tycoon 3  has a robust economic game with 30+ commodities in 1,2 and 3 deep production chains. Transport Fever has maybe a dozen commodities.
Railroad Tycoon 3  had the ability to buy stock in your company and learn about the benefits (and dangers) of margin buying - no such thing exists in Train Fever.
Railroad Tycoon 3  had a more robust undo ability for laying rail.
Railroad Tycoon 3 had 66 Historical Locomotives rather than the 45 offered in Train Fever.
Railroad Tycoon 3  had debt that changes as to rates making refinancing something that must be contemplated
Railroad Tycoon 3  had the ability to start (or buy existing) industries and businesses so as to further develop your transport empire.
Railroad Tycoon 3 had AI Competitors that may require that you buy them out in certain scenarios.
Railroad Tycoon 3 had AI Competitors based on real world people who played roles in the development of the Railroads. You got a bit of history with your gaming.
Railroad Tycoon 3  had economic cycles that affect supply and demand. Nothing like it exists in Train Fever.
Railroad Tycoon 3  had 20+ scenarios that really encourage you to explore the intticacies of the game . Train fever is pretty much sandbox only.
Railroad Tycoon 3  had overview maps that made spotting industries and resources (and the demand for them) much clearer than anything offered in the "fever" games.
Railroad Tycoon 3 had  the ability to build water towers and maintenance barns and the need to consider such things.
Railroad Tycoon 3  had well laid out Train lists that show at-a-glance status information that you cannot see as easily in the "TF" games
Oh Yes... Transport fever offers planes and boats as well as rail and road transport. Unfortunately the basic UI and AI challenges that were handled so deftly in the antique Railroad Tycoon 3 are still handled somewhat poorly in Transport fever.
There WAS and still is a lot of room for improvement in both games. Neither addresses switching engines. Those little workhorses that set up the long trains that we see crossing vast distances.  No marshalling yards are supported.  No telegraph service (an integral part of the US Railroads)  is modelled.
Transport Fever LOOKS like a great game. I just wish that the devlopers paid more attention to what had gone before and incorporated some of the "things that worked" into their game design.
I've played Train Fever quite a bit and once you get used to the demand driven economic model rather than the supply/price driven model used in the earlier game. It can be fun. But I do get a bad case of the "mightabeens" every time that I start to compare th game with its predecessor.
Now the discount offered to Train Fever owners  for the improved Transport Fever" brings the price down to $30 USD.
The discount is going to have to be much deepr than that before I add  planes and boats and ignore the other shortcomings of the game.
BTW... there ARE a few things that the developers could have done differntly that would have improved my rating:
1) Track laying - Same day undo - allow any track laid to be demolished (on the same day) at no cost. This would somewhat make up for the lack of a real in-game track planning mode.
2) Enable ESC as a means of bringing up the main loading menu. The current method wastes time and screen real estate.
3) Make it easier to reload a saved game. I'm not sure whether this has been fixed in Transport fever but it required actually quitting and restarting the the game in Train Fever.
4) Options should also be available via the escape menu. If one wishes to turn off the game sounds or something similar one has to quit Train Fever. Why was music the only one that can be silenced in-game?
5) If you're going to do windows DO WINDOWS. Windows should be resizeable. Scrollable left and right as well as up and down. Cut and paste renaming should be enabled as well. Allowing for longer names would be good too. Default names suggested based on terminals would be great.
6) Put a confirm on save game deletes. It was far too easy in Train Fever to delete the latest save game if one generally deletes a few saved games at start up time.
7) As with any simulator with economic aspects, graphs would be nice. Or even improved statistics on trains. 5 and 10 year running averages of revenue expenses profits, passengers.
The graphs on cities in Train fever were there and useful but could be greatly expanded on.
8) How about a column on the industry list as to whether or not it's using a transport line. It's in the individual window so why not on the list?
9) Signals are important in this game. They should be easier to see whether zoomed in or out.
10) The Manage lines window should be sortable on Time, et al
11) Station list should be sortable on cargo
12) A button for next on line or next should be available in the vehicle details window
13) The Mouse zoom feature should be more granular (more interim steps)
14) A Trainopedia feature would be great.
15) Towns list should show Goods needs supply and a few more details that are now only viewable in the city windows
16) Commodities should be easier to see on a fully zoomed out map.
17) If this game were look more like Railroad Tycoon III as to GUI features, it would be great.

•	This is the first ‘Transport Management’ game I have bought in a few years (I was a big fan of the Railroad Tycoon series) – the game doesn’t disappoint – the graphics are very good and for the most part the interface is intuitive.
•	This isn’t a game you can pick up and play proficiently after 5 minutes – the game has a steep learning curve. I recommend watching a few YouTube tutorials before you get started (there isn’t a ‘guided start mode’ – which is ridiculous for such an in-depth game).
•	 The interface itself could defiantly benefit from being optimized (more ‘sorting’ and ‘apply to all’ required).
•	The placement of roads and rails is somewhat infuriating at time and there is a well reported ‘bug’ / ‘feature’ that prevents certain roads from being upgraded.
•	The game itself is divided into ‘eras’ with different vehicles becoming available when certain dates are reached – as a new player you aren’t able to jump into a ‘modern era’ without first playing through the early eras.
•	I haven’t experienced any crashes or glitches in the game.

Last March I discovered Vlambeer's Ridiculous Fishing and it became my first essential smartphone game.  What makes it so compelling is that the game starts simple, yet tough and the proceeds to reward you with dozens of neat perks to slightly break the game urging you to greater depths and new areas.
Luftrausers has the same formula and it's freaking brilliant.  It controls not unlike an old Lunar Lander game.  It's tough to fly and in addition your being shot at from every direction.  But it suddenly rewards you with great plane customizations ("parts") that break the game is slight, yet brilliant ways.  An engine that shoots bullets behind you, where you're not aiming.  Armor that lets you not take melee damage, at the expense of health.  An armor that explodes when you die, killing everything on screen.  The combination of the "parts" is up to you.
In order to nudge you into trying new parts combinations there are a progression of missions for each part, and that's why you'll keep coming back for more.
Vlambeer has once again shown that they are masters.

It's hard to review this game. The main reason why is because it's difficult to even really call it much of a 'game' to begin with. It's more like an interactive story where you actively walk around a small middle-America town.
Night in the Woods is worth playing if only for the world-building, the art style, and the characters. If your goal is to analyze it's gameplay, I'm sorry to say, but beyond the occassional roof-jumping and moving your hand/paw to grab things every so often, there isn't much in the way of gameplay at all.
However, if you are the type who is not bothered by this at all and are willing to play through it, then NiTW will offer you a very compelling story and general perspective on a colorful cast of main characters and even interesting side characters you will meet up with repeatedly.
Pros:
-Good, storybook-esque art style and smooth animations
-Good world-building
-Soothing soundtrack
-Compelling, 3 dimensional (heh) characters with flaws and motivations
Cons:
-Practically non-existent gameplay (if you are expecting any at all)
-Story itself is pretty slow and the ending feels out of place compared to most of the rest of the game
-Repetitive runninjg around town each day if you're looking to talk to everyone and achievement hunt
I may have sounded harsh, but I do actually really enjoy this game. It's just that it doesn't feel like a game at all.
I'd give it an 8/10

I'll need to be updating this review as I play. As of this writing, I'm now about 30 hours into the game.
This was my review about 2 hours in:
"This was awful. The most difficult enemy to overcome is the controls. This game is to fighting skeletons as QWOP is to running."
^ that was while using an xbox controller. The combat takes a long time to get used to, and until you've done it a lot it feels incredibly clunky and unresponsive, and simply trying to look at the right enemy and swing your weapon feels like a chore at first.
but I got used to it.. and found it very satisfying once I did. Of course I had to look up how to actually backstab and parry online, because there are some very unintuitive caveats, but yeah, in the end, it feels very satisfying.
Since that review, I'm changing my recommendation from No to Yes, but with a huge caveat. People always say this game "doesn't hold your hand" or "hand things to you" and you might think that that's a good thing, but... well let me explain:
It's a game of mazes and traps, but the worst mazes and traps aren't so much in the environments you traverse and the enemies you face, they're in the decisions you make, and in a way that can be very, very unfun.
The first example of this that I encountered was immediately after the tutorial, when I didn't see the "right" way to go, and wasted a lot of time trying to go the "wrong" way. This was my bad. If I'd explored meticulously enough, I'd have seen the thin path to the "right" way and noticed that the enemies were easier to fight.
The second was in the UI. When looking at your character stats, the UI tells you that you can press Select to see explanations. When looking at items, however, it doesn't, but you can. The first time I saw the items stats screen, however, was while talking to a merchant. The stats screen looks the same, but you cannot press Select to view explanations while talking to a merchant, so when I pressed Select as an experiment and it didn't work, I concluded that you can't press Select to view item stats explanations. After all, it says you can for personal stats but not for items. I didn't know what some of them meant for the next 20 hours of gameplay. Git Gud... right?
There's an important elevator that should save you a lot of time early in the game. The first time I walked into it, it didn't work. Later I learned online that it should work, and when I tried it again, it worked. There was never any indicator that it had started working, and you never have any reason to believe it should be a functional elevator.
You do a thing and get an item to teleport you back home. You can either use it, or decide to walk. If you use the item, you'll never learn of an NPC that just appeared from nowhere on the way back.
There's a really nondescript locked door in a location that you'd otherwise have no reason to re-visit, but it's the only route to the second part of the first quest. What you know of the quest is that you have to do something up above in (Location Name) and down below, in (Location Name) but your only indication of the location of (Location Name) is "above" and "below". Well there's a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of "below" in this game that you can access from the very start, so I went to the wrong "below" and spent maybe 10 hours on it, clearing it, before I looked online and learned of the door. There was never any indication that I was in the "wrong" "below" and there was never anything to draw my attention to the nondescript locked door, which, by the way, was located way above.
So when you hear that the game doesn't "hand anything to you" expect that this means, basically, everything. It doesn't hand to you a bunch of what the controls are. It doesn't hand to you a hint of where you're actually supposed to go. You'll often be presented with options but you were never "handed" any clue what they might possibly do, so you're choosing blindly.
It does, sort of, hand to you a really heavy-handed, sparse story. At least so far. I've seen only the bare-bones of what you would call a story, and it was delivered by NPCs basically expositing story at me, plus a cutscene at the start. The worldbuilding is amazing and unique, though. Enemies, environments, lore, etc, all very good and fleshed out if you're looking for it. I think people confuse worldbuilding and story though, when they say the story is so good. What story-like progression there is has been so slow and confusing.
EDIT 70hrs in: Finally beat the game. Once I got the right upgraded armor and weapons, and a good level, actually defeating enemies became practically trivial. This game is like a puzzle game, where you have to do certain things in certain orders in order to progress, except unlike a puzzle game this game provides almost zero clues as to what the thing you need to do is, when you need to do it, or really whether you need to do it at all. It'll just leave you flailing about uselessly wasting your time unless you look everything up online. There's practically no chance you'll actually get to experience the story without looking it up online. Even paying very close attention, reading everything you see, talking to everyone you see... you'll get maybe 40% of what there is available to get (which isn't much) and the rest is only accessibly if you just happen to do the right things at the right times in the right order, either because you looked it up or because you just got lucky.
Dying is actually fun. 10/10.

Everything is worse here: The graphics, the story, the music, the puzzles, the characters, and - holy hell - the voice acting! Literally some of the worst acting and voice direction I've heard in my life. You know you're in trouble when you constantly want to gnaw your mouse-clicking hand off while being exposed to yet another lengthy and supremely annoying internal monologue delivered with a warbling vibrato.
And the jokes - don't get me started on the "jokes". The quips in this game are so embarrassingly bad, the fourth-wall-breaking references so completely out of place that they soil the whole tone of the game. Puritas Cordis doesn't seem to be able to decide whether it's supposed to be taken halfway seriously or as a complete farce. Every other character you run into spews nothing but sarcasm at you, and the main character positively oozes sarcasm from her every pore. You can't have coherent dialogue when everybody's sarcastic! Even the puzzles are, for the most part, insane. Gone are the relatively coherent and logical puzzles of the original - You need to be on some pretty heavy medication to come up with the solutions to a few of the crazier brain-benders in here. Avoid if you value your sanity.

If you’re reading this, chances are you’re either a legal guardian whose little ones are huge fans of Nemo, Dory, and Marlin (Finding Nemo (2003), Finding Dory (2016)), or are a parent whose kids might just be fans of oceanic creatures in general, which makes them especially awesome, to say the least. (And if you’re here because your inner child is interested in this or just because you like sea turtles, don’t worry, you’re still awesome.)
Turtle Odyssey originally came out in 2007 and is a children’s game for kids aged 5 to 10 by the Russian developer and publisher Realore Games. When Ozzy discovers that his shell has been stolen, the little turtle sets out to get it back only to discover that three magical artefacts have disappeared as well.
The game is a sidescrolling Jump’n’Run platformer, built similar to the style of the games circling around Nintendo’s loveable little mascot, Super Mario (1983 ongoing). Ozzy the turtle walks on the bottom of the ocean (yeah, I know, just roll with it), collecting coins, and defeating enemies by jumping on their heads. The characters in Turtle Odyssey are adorable in design, the controls easy to figure out and remember, and it takes about four hours to finish the whole game. So, it’s perfect for children, or is it?
This little game, only 9.9 MB in size, is loads of fun, but has a few setbacks. It doesn’t work under Windows 10 and requires Windows 7 or lower to run. I played this game on my toaster, an old 32-bit Windows Vista toaster (with an Intel Core 2 CPU, 3070MB RAM, and a GeForce 9500 GT graphics card), so I had no qualms whatsoever, but households with more up-to-date hard- and software might find this to be somewhat of a hurdle. Turtle Odyssey also let’s players switch between controller and keyboard on the fly, has fully rebindable keys, and the menu is fully navigable with a mouse. That would awesome if it weren’t for one little thing: The game has trouble identifying gamepad inputs.
I tried Turtle Odyssey using an old, wired Microsoft Xbox 360 gamepad and the directional recognition didn’t work properly. After tapping a direction, little Ozzy sometimes kept on walking left or right and at some point jumped around the entire time, even if I had already released my fingers from the gamepad. This forced me to revert back to playing with the keyboard, which I don’t think children who play this, will want to do. My suggestion here would be to unbind all controller keys and use 3rd party programs like Joy2Key or XInput Plus and see if that helps. The controls on the keyboard are very responsive, but don’t feel as tight as in the game with the plumber.
The most important questions when considering buying a game for kids is if they’re going to like it, how long it will keep them occupied, and how easy it is to get it working. Turtle Odyssey does have quite a bit of replay value and each of the regular stages also contain secret areas with lots of treasure to discover. The game also does a marvellous job in explaining all game mechanics and enemy types and once in a while some cool background info on turtles pops up on screen. I really liked that.
So, are they going to like this? Generally speaking, yeah, your children will probably enjoy this. But please do keep in mind that I had these problems with the controller, so if your child loves to play with a gamepad instead of a controller, this might become problematic.
With all that said, I would love to try out the two sequels to Turtle Odyssey and hope that Realore Games was able to fix the controller issue in them.

It's not bad if you're playing to reach Day 10, after that it just becomes an (easy) grind-fest. I made it to day 27 (12th place on the leaderboards for kicks) before I gave up. Once you get a powerful enough weapon, you can just stand there and hold the mouse button while using your other hand to feed your mouth with chips.
I can see this game getting a lot better, but:
Nays (as of now):
- I found very little use for most of the weapons, there's a lot, but you'll probably never use them.
- Items that give you temporary stat bonuses don't last long enough/aren't very interesting, I couldn't justify picking them up.
- Block placement is fun, but I never seemed to be able to collect enough resources to build more than 8 blocks at a time.
- Music starts to get annoying, it's not a bad track, I just wish there was more than NUNUNUNUneeeNUNUeeeeeNUNU...
- You can't be bothered to look at the UI early on, it's very small and should be more noticeable.
- The cursor/crosshair is also difficult to spot, I never know where it is after blinking.
Yays:
- The A.I works very well, I can see there is some AGGRO involved.
- Bullets don't simply go straight, there's some realism.
- Hit testing is spot on for walls/structures.
- Various mobs, the game is not limited to zombies.
- I don't regret paying $4 for this.
Basically, this is Bird's Eye Serious Sam, but the weapons will eventually need some major balancing.
Wants:
- Map Maker, especially for a tile-based game like this.
- More items: fences, mines, det-bombs, bla bla.
- Bosses, bosses that don't like it when I spend that past 3 hours camping in my 7x7 structure.
- Leveling and more stats... Make this game better than Diablo 3!

Update 25 November 2014:
I've had to change the review to a thumbs down due to the latest updates to the game:
The good part of recent updates was that they removed the guns being unlocked permanently feature and they are now unlocked each time you play as you would expect in a permadeath game like this.
The bad part of the update is what they did to the map: It used to be a fairly large, varied map with multiple buildings, water and so on; now it's just one tiny map featuring one building and there's no water.
This is something that happens with early access games sometimes and I really don't like it. Valve say that you should be careful with EA and only buy games if you want to play them as they are now. Well now you can't even bank on things staying the way they are when you buy the game: they can get worse, as is the case here.
Some of the videos on the store page still show the old map which is very misleading for new customers. The videos have always been misleading in other ways too: showing glitchy video effects that are not present in the game, despite in some cases appearing to be. Also at least one of the videos rotates the screen but you can't rotate the screen in the game, they are actually rotating the picture to give this misleading impression.
edit: The dev has said the large map won't be coming back:
"We had to make some design decisions about the size of the map, mostly because the sort of zombie survival game that this is, is the sort where you barricade yourself in a build and fight off an overwhelming swarm. Both a large and small map were tested, but because of the spawn mechanics and the way the swarm operates, I had to choose either a small one or a larger one, and the small one just played better in my opinion."

Some positive but mostly, best character and aspect of the game:
-Backstory is fricking amazing. LoTR is a international iconic franchise for a reason. The story from the franchise is enough to give any new game/movie/book/etc. a huge start just because the universe is already so detailed. But the one thing no game nor movie ever touched was about WHO exactly made the rings? They only ever showed/said that it was an elf king who made the rings. This game starts you off as a useless character whose story means nothing. Literally yes, Talion's story is rather irrelevant and is only there to carry the "detective aspect" of who the elf wraith is in that sense. Otherwise, his story is really just there to push the agenda of killing Uruk's and all those major VIP characters. So he's a good vessel for the story.
-
They could have done more with Talion's character if there was more content and a better writing team that made an effort into making his interactions with characters such as The Deserter and leader of the Outcasts (which is a great backstory in such a short amount of words and they did nothing with it yet acted like they built some "bro" thing out of it. Which they didn't, not even close), Lithardriel (girl who protects her witch mother) who winds up getting killed with her mom the moment we stop looking. And do note, Talion's family just died and they make Talion already give sexy eyes to some new chick like a few days later. Wtf? At least the elf has a clue "What of your family?, "Your wife and son?". Anyhow, the mother was well done with a very interesting backstory. Too bad we get to see roughly 2 minutes of her and then she's meaninglessly killed off.
-
Torvian was the best character written in this game after the elf. He lives, one of the only two to do so, has good voice acting, has a good meaningfull backstory, useful to a section of the main story, and has plenty of content involving him. Do note this is because there is a whole DLC about helping him kill some warchief Uruk's who use beasts to rule Mordor.
-
Continuing on with Talion, useless story, vessel for the real story, the end. So, exluding Talion, we are left with Celebrimbor who the game IS REALLY ABOUT. He starts as a wraith bound to Talion who doesn't remember anything (supposedly). We find out this is and isn't true. Eventually, through Talion's story. We come across Golem, yes that Golem. I believe they should've left his character out of this. Since there actually is a time issue involving him being there and things he said. For example, in the movie Golem is tortured into revealing that he knows who took the ring from him. Bilbo. This was said at the same time the movie took place. Why would he say Bilbo has it if this elf King says it's his and Golem believes he has it and never finds out if he does or doesn't? That's a flaw in the writing team matching it to the lore of the existing universe. (yes I'm a nerd, sue me)
-
But excluding the writing flaw there, it's through Golem that we find out who Celebrimbor is. He is the ring maker. Which is a huge lore explosion and story arc. A creative and beautifully done one too. Do note Celebrimbor has many dialogue remarks in this game involving items/places. For example, the towers were build in the DLC dedicated to him via the Uruk's.  Of which, he makes comments about. He also makes comments about Golem being connected to him in some way. This is a early hint that they are connected because of The Ring. Continuing on, skipping all the way till the end. Summarize every memory sequence. We then know that he was an elf king that had his family killed in the same manner and by the same "person". Which adds a touch of intrigue to Talion's boring story. After we cross the sea to fight the "major boss" over there, which was extremely easy. We find out that Celebrimbor is not cursed to Talion. But chose to be connected to him, which prevented Talion from dying with this family. This also means Celebrimbor is still very much wanting to finish Sauron this whole time as his motive.
-
Now that it's the end of the game. Terrible "ending boss fight", but we see that Celebrimbor in wraith form can be manipulated via Sauron. At the end after temporarily beating Sauron, Celebrimbor admits defeat and says that death is calling them both since Sauron can not be defeated. This is where Talion has his finest moment, he says "could you live for eternity in death knowing you could have stopped him?". This line signifies that they both believe Sauron is undefeatable but together there is a possibility that they can defeat him. It also is just a good one liner to begin with. This ques the end and a sequel.
--
Bright Lord DLC-
Continuing with the Celebrimbor backstory above, this whole DLC is about the events before Shadow of Mordor's base game following Talion. Furthermore, how Celebrimbor got to be connected to Talion to begin with. You get to play as Celebrimbor, which was freaking awesome, and all his special abilities that are only his to use in the dlc AS WELL AS getting to use the One Ring in all of it's glory as something more than just a cloak that Harry Potter's dad stole and made into a blanket. Due note, a downside to this DLC was it takes place on the same playable area that the base game is located in. Celebrimbor starts with a full memory of him being betrayed by Sauron, who gave him the gift of a magical crafting hammer (which is why Sauron was called "Bringer of Gifts) in return all he had to do was make Sauron a magical ring. Once he made Sauron the ring, Sauron ordered an attack on Celebrimbor and his family. All of which were captured and Celebrimbor was forced to make the ring even more powerful than agreed upon. In the main game, the furthest memory we get to see is Celebrimbor editing the ring then taking it and jumping at Sauron with his sword in hand. "LuL" In the DLC, this happens but follows with Celebrimbor continuing into Mordor with the ring with his motive to build an Uruk army and attack/challenge Sauron. Which is a great backstory, and start to the DLC filled with the great back and forth magical banter between Celebrimbor and Sauron. Of which, between the two. Celebrimbor's voice actor nailed the strengh of the words. He sounds more fierce than Sauron. Which is fitting considering who Celebrimbor is. The story takes place accordingly. More warchief missions, for the same reason as Talion's story. To build an Uruk army to fight Sauron. Not really pleased about it, was hoping for more meaningful missions. We get at least the one challenging mission there is, The Sauron fight. Sauron was easy if you use the ring, but the 1 v 5 against the captains was a pain. In the end, you lose but find out that Celebrimbor chose to be connected to Talion in his desire to beat Sauron now with another in with the same motive. Celebrimbor is easily the best and main character to this game with the most story.

While State of Decay has it's issues it's also a very grand visualization of a sandbox zombie survival game. It is the most human approach to a game of this genre, it isn't some badass 'shoot 'em up' where you run around and decimate the zombie faction, but a weighty survival game in an ever changing environment. After a certain point the flow of 'goals' begins to slow, but the primary goals of this game are coded in human instinct. Do I have enough food for today, or should I stock up on building materials? Do we have enough ammo to fight off the impending horde? These are questions you will become all too familiar with. It's such a change of pace from other zombie game, this game causes you to be incredibly cautious. The permadeath is a prime example of where this game derives it's difficulty from. It isn't difficult in the sense that you can't kill the zombies. In fewer numbers they are especiall easy to take care of. The game is difficult in the sense that it is challenging, and you genuinely have to think about your next moves if you value your survivor's life. While it can end up being frustrating, permadeath is one of the most human aspects of this game. This game is easily a fan favorite, but the niche catered to may be too small for expansion. I'm sure Undead Labs can make a follow up while still creating enthralling lore, which is more than I could say for a majority of the companies pushing out games today. I still find myself enjoying every second I play this game. 9.5/10 Easily one of the best games in it's league.

This Zombie/Survivor is a breath of fresh air to the genre.  It's not a mindless zombie shooter nor is it an insane duct taping chainsaws to a kayak paddle crafting game.
Pros
- The game adds a lot of thought into the game like having to hunt for resources which might be difficult depending on what you need
- Combat is enjoyable, with melee being the primary focus and limited firearms that is realistic aka you can't mow down a horde of zombies with a single pistol
- You swap through characters, each with different benifits and perks with varying strengths and weaknesses.  No superheros here
- Your character gets tired from staying up and doing combat, you can't just have one guy running around doing everything
- Choices have consequences, wrecking a car means its always wrecked.  Getting a member killed means they are killed for the rest of the game.
- Decent sized map with vehicles to make it less tedious
- Vehicles that you get to essentially play demolition derby against zombies
- You have a community that you are trying to run which will have it's hiccups.  This adds to the realistic overall scenario as in; people will get sick, get mad, get depressed, become mean, etc... and you'll have to make choices on whether or not that person is a risk to your community.
- Also dealing with a community, you may want to go hunt for supplies but one of your survivors may have wondered off and you should probably rescue him over getting supplies.
- Ton of play hours and unique scenarios
Cons
- The Lab canceled on it's initial plans to make a multiplayer mode
- The storyline isn't a rendition on Shawshank or anything but it's okay (still more than L4D)
- Vehicles aren't the biggest focus during development, it's no GTA but still useable.  The new expansion added cargo space in the vehicles which was a HUGE bonus to both realism and utility (this is a pro)
Overall, it's a fun game and for under 20.00$ it'll bring you a lot of fun.  They added a kind of "survive" mode that forgets about the story line and the resources replenish after a certain amount of time, so you have the sandbox survive feel.  Especially during these holiday sales of being under 10.00$, you'll feel stupid not buying this now.

If you are a fan of some flash games like "Last Stand:Union City" where you wander around to stay alive, then State of the Decay is a "fleshed out" 3-d version of it.
Although it's fairly constrained to using melee and small arms, it would feel someone overpowered to be carrying military grade weapons.
It maintains the tension of scavenging with the possibility of being overwhelemed in large numbers. So always be mindful of the crowds of zombies that could be nearby.
I look forward to a future iteration which improves on this formula with more weapons, character leveling, items, options, and building details.

Ace Combat Assault Horizon is a fun game, but don't play it if you're looking for an ounce of realism.
The game plays more like a movie than an actual game: The camera regularly focusses on your kill (especially if you were in DFM, Dog Fight Mode). Although this does give it a awesome experience, it can get frustrating at times. I personally find it fine if used SPARINGLY, and that is not the case here. I've had to learn to pull up when I get a DFM kill just to make sure that I don't hit the ground. It's cool to see your target disintegrate piece by piece and finally, when it is destroyed, break into a million pieces, but sometimes you do wonder how you yourself weren't killed by that same debris.
Realism is chucked into a garbage crusher and then thrown out the window. This game is even less realistic than HAWX, and thats saying something. Planes throw impossible manuevers. I even belly scratched my plane a few times, once right out of recovering from a stall (noob mistake, I know), and didn't get killed by it (just critical health). I also rammed my chopper into the side of a building a few times with no consequence besides stopping abruptly. Your health pretty much recovers like in Call of Duty, it doesn't stay at a percentage for the entire mission.
The game has some interesting "features" like DFM (Dog Fight Mode) and ASM (Air Strike Mode). While these are cool in theory (and can be fun in practice), they are way overused in the game. HAWX had AOS (or something like that) which was completely optional to use and you were only forced to use them in setpieces. Here MANY of the targets can ONLY be destroyed with DFM (DFM is the main culprit that makes the game feel more like an action movie than a flying game). Like I said, they can be fun and they make the dogfights very intense (and fake), but their overuse is frustrating.
Technically, it's beautiful. Good graphics (I'm not a good enough judge to say great), awesome music. Interesting story line; not awesome, but not useless either. Missions are challenging enough and far from boring, but any experienced pilot will find most of them to be a breeze. Controlls are easy enough, although I couldn't survive with standard flying game controlls. It's almost as if it was designed around a mouse (which makes sense since its a PC exlusive). It is cool that you fly other aircraft/roles (ex. a Apache attack chopper or a bomber. Not fighter bomber, BOMBER), but some of these levels LITERALLY feel like a bonus level of Call of Duty.
Despite all the above, Ace Combat is a very fun game to play. GAME, not FLYING game (nevermind flight simulator); you feel like more like an action hero than a pilot. Many reviewers very aptly described it as "Call of Duty in the skies". I found it a fun distraction, but I didn't feel even an ounce of real flying. It is worth getting this game for the action or on sale if you want, but don't come looking for a flying game.

-Missiles have been gimped, bringing their range from ~5000 (in the PS2 games) to about 2000.
-Machine guns have been buffed, making them a better option than missiles in most cases.
-Dogfight Mode is unavoidable.  If you want to kill certain enemy aces, you need to give up control of most of your plane and play something that feels an awful lot like a mini-game.
-On-rails helicopter missions where all you do is point and shoot. Also unavoidable.
If AC4, AC5, and ACZ are your jams, I wouldn't pick this up.  It's going to bother you.  Oddly enough, I think that Strike Suit Zero comes the closest on PC to replicating that PS2-era Ace Combat gameplay.

A great game for those who love to simply explore and survive, without needing combat to have a good time. Hence, the cons section of this review applies less to me and more to potential buyers who may expect something different.
Pros:
- Beautiful graphics, even without the settings maxed out. Little quality is sacrificed if you opt for more performance.
- Genuine sense of tension, especially early on. Attempting to manage supplies and avoid dehydration- you can come quite close to death if you aren't careful. Also applies to the unpredictability of the ocean and the ominous music that plays whenever a shark is near.
- A few navigational realisms that are both nice details and occasionally useful i.e flocks of birds (or bats at night) that help signal when you are nearing land and/or what direction land is in.
- Fun for those that enjoy experimental building, making forts and such, building and decorating even beyond what you need to.
- Not heavily combat oriented. This is a downside for some. I genuinely enjoyed it. Many survival games also play around the objective of avoiding and killing a range of enemies. In Stranded Deep, the environment is your main enemy with sharks being a mainly avoidable threat.
Cons:
- Achievements are not currently functioning and may not ever. Not a large problem, though disappointing for achievement hunters.
- Development is slow. Not personally a problem for me, but the game may be lacking for some.
- Has it's share of occasional bugs, as with anything.
- Currently, it is what it is and little more. If a simple, fun game with elements of exploring and building is enough for you- you'll enjoy it regardless. If you're looking for more depth and things to do, this isn't the game for you.
A final thanks to the youtuber Robbaz, whose video series on this game got me hooked in the first place, and also to the dear friend that gifted this to me <3

LUFTRAUSERS is a challenging arcade shooter that makes you fight to beat your high score. There's no deep story or hero with a traumatic past here. Just you gunning down countless waves of scum who deny you the right to the skies.
Here's a video giving you my first impressions of the game. Although given how short it is, you may be able to consider it a review.
For those of you who want a short and dirty summary, I'll break it down for you with pros and cons.
+ Challenging gameplay. There isn't a point where you'll ever be bored with how easy something is.
+ Great replayability. No game will ever play the same, especially when you throw in all the different plane parts into the mix.
+ Lots of different playstyles. You can fly everything from a plane that spearheads through destroyers to a meaty clunker that fires a laser and poops bullets.
+ Smooth, responsive gameplay. Nothing feels clunky and everything responds when you do it.
+ Every shade of yellow you can find is here. Bask in its yellow glory! (Though you can change the scheme when you level up, but why?)
- Extremely short. After playing 3 hours, I've practically done everything in the game.
- Some of the weapons just aren't as good as others in my opinion. The homing missiles seem to have a lot of trouble hitting their target, even massive destroyers that barely move. Limiting you to 4 at a time makes it even more frustrating when they don't hit what they're supposed to. The cannon is similar, as it only allows one shot at a time, and if you miss, you have a lot of downtime between shots. And in a game as fast-paced as this, missing happens often.
- Sometimes enemies just don't spawn and come after you. It makes it hard to bump up combos and get more points, allowing the more interesting enemies trying to gun you down.
- Sometimes the game can be cheap and send 3 destroyers at you at a time with a few ace pilots to boot. At that point, you're just not gonna live with the amount of things on screen.
All in all, I recommend you pick this game up when you want an excellent time waster. Even when it goes up to 10 dollars, it'll still be worth it. But if you don't like the fact that it is so short, feel free to wait until it goes on sale. You won't be disappointed either way.

Now, a successor has arisen, and it's called "Over 9,000 zombies". Weapons, turrets, walls, thousands of zombies to kill, an expansive map, far surpassing it's predecessor.
But unlike EZR,
In EZR, you got a breather. A chance to go to the store, go to bed or go back fighting, but it was a break in the day.
In Over 9,000 zombies, your only solace is death. You get a minute between waves, where zombies no longer spawn, then it's back to the frantic shooting, dodging, and repairing that is O9Z.
And I for one, wouldn't have it any other way.

ignore the time in game as i'm still playing to get the other endings to this game. that said, this has been quite an interesting little game. It has it's pros and cons but it's not too bad, but to be clear i should go through the pros and cons.
pros:
- the story is quite humourous at times
- the music isn't bad, if a bit repetitive at times though
- the artwork is very well done, from the character to the backgrounds
- the biggest of the pros, the game is well built (more on this in a second)
- multiple paths to take (outside the death endings)
Cons:
- there is a fair amount (almost too much) trial and error to be had
- the correct training towards an ending is not really made clear or is logical some times
- it is a touch too short (i wasn't sure if this is a pro or con, i'll explain that too in a second)
now to my more 'flowing' review and explanation of some things. first a disclaimer to those wondering whether or not to buy this game, this is more of a "training" sim along the lines of princess maker (and it's hentai counterpart) or true love '98. the thing about these types of games is that it is impossible to get all endings in one play through, the idea is to focus in each playthrough on a set of training you, the player, think has the highest priority and see where you end up (or in the case of true love '98, who you end up with).  these games aren't for everyone as they require ALOT of trial and error to get the ending you want.
That said, there are a few areas that are good and a few that are bad. right off this is a well built game, i've played a few games like this before, some had great artwork and music, but you could tell the programmers couldn't give two craps about if the scenes function correctly resulting in white screens from misprogrammed code not making an image appear correctly, the wrong image showing up or double images showing. so it appears these guys at least had the basics covered. however there are a few faults. the music, while nice, repeated one too many times and became annoying after about an hour of play. Next the length of the game itself is way too short. now i'm mixed on this because i get the idea is that the player can experience a different set of choices (and ending) quickly. But at the same time there is no reason why the game couldn't stand to beef up each story path with a bit more content and story parts. I mean, so far i've completed at least 3 endings (going to work on the to serve evil ending next) and honestly there's not much variance between them outside a few changes between whether you focus on magic or not. I've played other games with similar gameplay that had the same idea of branching paths that still had robust stories to them (the aforementioned true love '98 being one of them).
that said though that's really the only major issues i had with the game. as for a recommendation, if you've played this style of game before or have the patience to try, i'd recommend it, it's just quirky enough with enough content to keep you occupied for a bit. However if you have no interest in this style of game play or are used to other sim games where you just follow the story to a multiple choice point then i'd take a pass on it.

Some positive but mostly, best character and aspect of the game:
-Backstory is fricking amazing. LoTR is a international iconic franchise for a reason. The story from the franchise is enough to give any new game/movie/book/etc. a huge start just because the universe is already so detailed. But the one thing no game nor movie ever touched was about WHO exactly made the rings? They only ever showed/said that it was an elf king who made the rings. This game starts you off as a useless character whose story means nothing. Literally yes, Talion's story is rather irrelevant and is only there to carry the "detective aspect" of who the elf wraith is in that sense. Otherwise, his story is really just there to push the agenda of killing Uruk's and all those major VIP characters. So he's a good vessel for the story.
-
They could have done more with Talion's character if there was more content and a better writing team that made an effort into making his interactions with characters such as The Deserter and leader of the Outcasts (which is a great backstory in such a short amount of words and they did nothing with it yet acted like they built some "bro" thing out of it. Which they didn't, not even close), Lithardriel (girl who protects her witch mother) who winds up getting killed with her mom the moment we stop looking. And do note, Talion's family just died and they make Talion already give sexy eyes to some new chick like a few days later. Wtf? At least the elf has a clue "What of your family?, "Your wife and son?". Anyhow, the mother was well done with a very interesting backstory. Too bad we get to see roughly 2 minutes of her and then she's meaninglessly killed off.
-
Torvian was the best character written in this game after the elf. He lives, one of the only two to do so, has good voice acting, has a good meaningfull backstory, useful to a section of the main story, and has plenty of content involving him. Do note this is because there is a whole DLC about helping him kill some warchief Uruk's who use beasts to rule Mordor.
-
Continuing on with Talion, useless story, vessel for the real story, the end. So, exluding Talion, we are left with Celebrimbor who the game IS REALLY ABOUT. He starts as a wraith bound to Talion who doesn't remember anything (supposedly). We find out this is and isn't true. Eventually, through Talion's story. We come across Golem, yes that Golem. I believe they should've left his character out of this. Since there actually is a time issue involving him being there and things he said. For example, in the movie Golem is tortured into revealing that he knows who took the ring from him. Bilbo. This was said at the same time the movie took place. Why would he say Bilbo has it if this elf King says it's his and Golem believes he has it and never finds out if he does or doesn't? That's a flaw in the writing team matching it to the lore of the existing universe. (yes I'm a nerd, sue me)
-
But excluding the writing flaw there, it's through Golem that we find out who Celebrimbor is. He is the ring maker. Which is a huge lore explosion and story arc. A creative and beautifully done one too. Do note Celebrimbor has many dialogue remarks in this game involving items/places. For example, the towers were build in the DLC dedicated to him via the Uruk's.  Of which, he makes comments about. He also makes comments about Golem being connected to him in some way. This is a early hint that they are connected because of The Ring. Continuing on, skipping all the way till the end. Summarize every memory sequence. We then know that he was an elf king that had his family killed in the same manner and by the same "person". Which adds a touch of intrigue to Talion's boring story. After we cross the sea to fight the "major boss" over there, which was extremely easy. We find out that Celebrimbor is not cursed to Talion. But chose to be connected to him, which prevented Talion from dying with this family. This also means Celebrimbor is still very much wanting to finish Sauron this whole time as his motive.
-
Now that it's the end of the game. Terrible "ending boss fight", but we see that Celebrimbor in wraith form can be manipulated via Sauron. At the end after temporarily beating Sauron, Celebrimbor admits defeat and says that death is calling them both since Sauron can not be defeated. This is where Talion has his finest moment, he says "could you live for eternity in death knowing you could have stopped him?". This line signifies that they both believe Sauron is undefeatable but together there is a possibility that they can defeat him. It also is just a good one liner to begin with. This ques the end and a sequel.
--
Bright Lord DLC-
Continuing with the Celebrimbor backstory above, this whole DLC is about the events before Shadow of Mordor's base game following Talion. Furthermore, how Celebrimbor got to be connected to Talion to begin with. You get to play as Celebrimbor, which was freaking awesome, and all his special abilities that are only his to use in the dlc AS WELL AS getting to use the One Ring in all of it's glory as something more than just a cloak that Harry Potter's dad stole and made into a blanket. Due note, a downside to this DLC was it takes place on the same playable area that the base game is located in. Celebrimbor starts with a full memory of him being betrayed by Sauron, who gave him the gift of a magical crafting hammer (which is why Sauron was called "Bringer of Gifts) in return all he had to do was make Sauron a magical ring. Once he made Sauron the ring, Sauron ordered an attack on Celebrimbor and his family. All of which were captured and Celebrimbor was forced to make the ring even more powerful than agreed upon. In the main game, the furthest memory we get to see is Celebrimbor editing the ring then taking it and jumping at Sauron with his sword in hand. "LuL" In the DLC, this happens but follows with Celebrimbor continuing into Mordor with the ring with his motive to build an Uruk army and attack/challenge Sauron. Which is a great backstory, and start to the DLC filled with the great back and forth magical banter between Celebrimbor and Sauron. Of which, between the two. Celebrimbor's voice actor nailed the strengh of the words. He sounds more fierce than Sauron. Which is fitting considering who Celebrimbor is. The story takes place accordingly. More warchief missions, for the same reason as Talion's story. To build an Uruk army to fight Sauron. Not really pleased about it, was hoping for more meaningful missions. We get at least the one challenging mission there is, The Sauron fight. Sauron was easy if you use the ring, but the 1 v 5 against the captains was a pain. In the end, you lose but find out that Celebrimbor chose to be connected to Talion in his desire to beat Sauron now with another in with the same motive. Celebrimbor is easily the best and main character to this game with the most story.

This is one of the most fun games i've played in recent years. It has very fun combat mechanics, pretty good stealth mechanics, and of course... The Nemesis System. The Nemesis System is one of the most innovative and one of the best mechanics that has been introduced in a video game. You can keep playing for hours and hours just hunting down your targets, every target is randomly generated so you'll be unlikely to meet the same target again except if you haven't killed them.
Middle-Earth: Shadow Of Mordor is a part of the Lord Of The Rings Universe. It is set in Mordor (The Orc Wasteland of Middle-Earth) sometime after the Hobbit movies and before The Lord Of The Rings Movies. You'll play as Talion, A ranger from Black Gate. Him and his family have been killed by The Black Hand Sauron. But then he gets Reincarnated by the help of a wraith, Celebrimbor (who was killed by Sauron) he is the "elf" Who made the Ring Of Power. Together they seek vengeance against the Dark Lord. Overall i think the story is OK its not that great and at the same time its not that bad either. The characters aren't really that memorable, the villains are just plain villains. BUT you can make a bond with your most hated nemesis and thats one the things that i really like about this game. Gameplay FIRST Story LATER.
Like i said, this is one of the most fun games i've ever played. The combat system is fun as hell, the stealth mechanics are really great, and more. The game does have a skill/leveling up system and its pretty good, but in my opinion you can get OverPowered too quick. The map is ok, dont expect it to be detailed or huge like The wither 3 and R* games maps, but its a map that you can have fun with the combat, the nemesis system and so on and so fourth. There are collectibles that you can collect and activites you can do such as freeing slaves or powering up your weapons. There are more things but overall those are my opinion on the gameplay of shadow of mordor.
Overall this is a Pretty good f%$#&n game. If you're a fan of the Lord Of The Rings Universe you should definitely buy this game. even if you're new to Lord Of The Rings, BUY IT. Its really one of the best singleplayer games i've played in a few years. Sure the story is not perfect, but who gives a S%#T. The gameplay is what matters here.

State of Decay is basically at its core is a single player, third person 'Zombie Survival' action game, with sim like management elements.
When you start off you're in control of one guy who, with his chum, gets lost while hiking. If, by some miracle you dont die, you'll never see the more interesting mechanics of 'State of Decay', which is that when you die, you take control of a different character instead. You dont respawn. This makes choices matter a whole lot more than in most games, as you always have something to lose when going out to get supplies with a band of survivers.
You also have to manage the survivers health, morale, supplies (and inherantly, the shortages that will occur) and generally look after them. Characters will get tired over time, and you'll have to swap out the playable character for a bit while they regain thier energy.
This brings me to one of the games more annoying mechanics. Even when you're not there, the game world is still moving, albiet at a slower pace. Survivors can die, run away, starve, and generally things can go bad fast when you arn't there. While it's a cool idea, I found it just became annoying to patch up the band of survivors, turn off the game, only to find that someone had been killed off when I came back.
Gameplay:
Controls are reasonably responsive. Sometime it feels a little sluggish and the jumping mechanics are a little floaty, but it's all servisable, and doesn't impact the game a whole lot. You have the options of melee weapons, or guns when dealing with the undead.
Combat is passable; nothing more. You'll find yourself spamming the attack button as your character losing stamina while the zombie you're wailing on continues to suck the durability from your weapon.
The game really punishes you (which I love!) for trying to take on large groups of Zombies, as you'll find you'll be quickly overwelmed.
Guns are also an option, but are loud, crude and are in limited supply. Usually a last resort unless you have a silencer.
In conclusion: One of the better surval sim games out there.

Night in the Woods (NITW) is a very unique game. As you're no doubt aware, the praise for this game has been overwhelmingly positive. The funny thing is that with a lot of games, that seems to throw people off. Maybe they think the game gets more praise than it deserves, or that the fanbase is toxic, or some other reason. Let me state now that I strongly believe all the love NITW has received is completely justified. Sure, this game won't be for everyone, no game ever is. But the love and care that went into NITW is clearly visible when playing the game. Actually, I don't think "playing" is really the right word. I think it's more so that you experience it.
There are hundreds of reviews that go into detail about the plot and premise, so I won't bore you by repeating it all. Let me just say that the concept of NITW had me instantly hooked, and I essentially couldn't stop playing until I beat it. And then I played it again. And then again. I was kind of addicted haha! The world, story, and soundtrack are excellent, but it is the characters that make this game truly extraordinary. They are so damn likable and so damn relatable that I even nominated NITW for a Steam Award. The category I made was: The "Most Relatable Characters" Award. To summarise, if you haven't, please give NITW a go. I strongly believe that like me, you'll be pleasantly surprised.
P.S. I played NITW offline, that is why I only have about five minutes on record haha!

So I love this game but I can't play it. :(

As for the question: "Should I buy it?", the answer is "Not anymore, because it just got a much better sequel."
Don't get me wrong, in the last two years the game got a lot of support and a massive free DLC, but it still hasn't fixed its most glaring flaws.
1. The interface is atrocious all the time, and counter-intuitive most of the time. Several useful options are buried deep in the awkward multi-tabbed menus, and some are absent entirely, like adding more platforms to an already-built station.
2. Gameplay is simplistic by design, and worse yet, it's badly explained. Besides supplying factories with raw materials, you're never explicitly told what effect your transportation efforts have on the cities and why.
3. Game balance is odd. Early game is usually a breeze, particularly if you focus on the obvious choice of passenger transport, but if you slip in late game, you're done even if you quickly go for damage control.
With the release of the sequel I mentioned, called "Transport Fever" and priced similarly to this game, I strongly advise you to give this one a pass.

I strongly recommend trying the original flash game before buying:
This sequel essentially extrapolates the original's gameplay into various goals while existing in a singular world.
Ship components are unlocked after completing these goals. The patterns of enemies remain roughly the same, with the exception of boss-esque appearances.
The core gameplay is phenomenal, but the lack of variety comes as huge a disappointment. What about a mission-based system, or campaign? Different missions with combinations of the enemies. One level could be entirely naval-based, another strictly dogfighting ... the list goes on.
To conclude, if you enjoy the original flash demo, go for it, but don't expect much more than the challenges and ship mods.

I have played a few visual novels before. And Long live the the queen feels more like a whole game than say a visual novel + a game. That being the game does a good job making the visual novel part into more of a game expereience than having a game stapled on to it.
That said the relationship between the player and the protagonist is quite different. Many times before in other VNs I feel like I need to gauge the protagonist emotions, skill sets, and personality when it comes to decision making, or sometimes all that information is displayed out via the story but doesn't really let the player be involved other than branching story arcs.
Long Live the Queen is different in that your knowledge of the character's mood, personality, and skills are yours to create and yours to maintain.
For those who are not familiar with VNs I think this game is a more interactive version of a VN versus the VNs +stabled on game mechanics. I have just gotten through my first play through and the idea of finding other story arcs in Long Live the Queen feels much more exciting than other VNs because rather than memorizing dialoge tree just to get through everything, you have to manage the numbers so your mood and lessons can get to where you want.
The first run I got I was having a blast! I was totally immeresed in the story... until I got killed by chocolate. After that you just want to move on from the death and just play again.
This is where my critisism comes in. As much as you want to just sit down and relax with the story... you can't you have to backtrack and make preperations to survive not just 1 step ahead but 5-10 steps ahead. That moment when you are a viewer or the immersion of being with the character is broken because now you have to get technical.
Now this is both a good and bad thing.
Negatives first

Because once you get about a third of the way through you start the realize that the game is out to kill you, like really out for your blood! It's enjoyable enough for the length of the main game (25hrs on my playthrough), but I'm not keen to delve into the DLC for more of the same.  Be aware that the difficulty peaks early, then the game gets steadily easier as you develop your abilities and attributes, since no new enemies are introduced past a certain point.
Ultimately, I'd recommend the Batman: Arkham series over this for the combat, or the Assassin's Creed series for a stronger story... but if you've played all those (and Mad Max) and want something similar, or just *really* like Middle-Earth, then you should find Shadow of Mordor to be reasonably fun until something better comes along.

Street Fighter 4 has been very fun for me. Playing online and then practicing in training mode afterwards is what I do most.
Sadly it doesn't have any single player mode worth mentioning, and is very focused on execution.
I still like it a lot, playing with friends feels great.
The netcode let's me play with my friends in Canada with little delay.

The Good: If you're not picky about the backgrounds and screen resolution, you can practically run this game on a toaster. (e.g. my laptop) If you happen to be one of those lucky folks who owns something a little nicer than a toaster, the game looks great on its highest settings, (which I have seen before) especially when you consider its age. The different post processing options for character models are nice too. Omega mode is ridiculously broken, in the fun kind of way, as is Edition Select. Ultra itself is quite possibly one of the best examples of fighting game balance I've ever played, especially considering the size of the roster. Multiplayer is still going strong. I'm able to find matches at just about any time of day I choose to boot up.
The Bad: Netcode can be....spotty. One minute no lag, next, you're underwater. Overall though, it's bearable. Also, the bars next to people's names almost never seem to be very accurate as to how good your connection with the other person is here on PC. Which is a little irksome.
The Verdict: Not a bad port at all, certainly better from what I hear than the travesty that was the PS4 port. My hours in game should speak for how I feel about it, especially when you consider I only bought it about five months ago. (Already owned it on 360, but that's....out of my reach for now.) Worth picking up, especially right now while it's on sale. Won't really teach you much about how to play V though, given the way that's looking so far.

Night In The Woods is another game in the vain of Life Is Strange, The Tell-Tale series, etc. Which primarily uses lines of text and dialogue over actual gameplay to convey a more meaningful story without the distractions of micro managements and other nuisance's that games with more traditional gameplay implement.
However Night In The Woods makes its themes and morales more relatable than Life Is Strange or The Tell-Tales Series. For one Night In The Woods doesn't add anything to the main character that any normal person can't relate to. Not many people can relate to the problematic consequences that come with time travel, being convicted for the murder for your wifes lover, being a secret werewolf in a secret world of fairytales,etc.
Instead it presents all its principle characters as an aspect of life, without spoiling much, Just know that there's a character in this game that anyone can relate to without feeling as if some aspect of them is just to unrealistic that completely turns you off.
This is a game that sincerely cares about its characters and the world they inhabit, if you've got time to play Life Is Strange or any of the Tell Tale games than please give this game a try, its worth your time and money.

The story was ignorable, the sound was whatever. The graphics were alright.

The graphics are good, except for ground textures, which are what you would expect from games of this genre – low-resolution and blurry. But there's a plenitude of 3D buildings, the jets and helicopters are well crafted, explosions look nice, and even characters don't look bad at all.
Fighter jet gameplay is simple enough and shooting down enemies while in DFM (dog fight mode) is very satisfying. The only problem is that the HUD (heads-up display) can be a little intrusive, with too much information on screen. This can prove distracting at times, especially with the amount of dialog going on.
Helicopters are absolutely dreadful to control, however. Luckily there are only a couple of helicopter missions in the campaign, and they're far between.
As a side note, I might add that the game can be perfectly played with mouse and keyboard, but was clearly designed with a gamepad in mind.
The story is utterly forgettable, but I reckon it is not the selling point of this game, so it can be safely ignored.
The sound effects are decent. On the other hand, the soundtrack, while not bad per se, is very repetitive and does not go together well with the action.
Lastly, multiplayer is fun, even if few people bother with it due to Games For Windows Live.
Overall, a solid game.
UPDATE: Since the writing of this review, Games For Windows Live has been patched out of the game.

Luftrausers isn't a dogfighting game. Yes, you're in a plane and you're shooting down planes (and boats and blimps), but what it really is frenetic aerial bullet hell chaos. But what makes Luftrausers so good, besides the action and stylized graphics, are the controls. Your plane is insanely maneuverable, able to turn on a dime, reach top speed in a moment. That level of control makes a difference.
It's one thing to weave between some bullets and return fire. It's another to swoop into a dive, deftly plummet through a hail storm of bullets, take out a projectile-spewing battleship, and pull up so close that the water's surface is flared up by your thrusters.
It's one thing to shoot down some planes. It's another to maneuver your enemies into a tight cluster, cut your thrusters, and shoot the planes pursuing you while your momentum carries you in the other direction. (And it helps that just activating your thrusters is so satisfying, thanks to the awesome fwhoosh sound effect)
It's fast, it's hard as hell, it's addictive. The music is great. The visuals are simple, yet suit the game perfectly, displaying all the information you need to know without cluttering the onscreen spectacle. Each new part you unlock feels different, a new tool to master, Luftrausers isn't the most complex game, but it's certainly one of the most addictive and satisfying I've played in a while. I'd say it's up there with One Finger Death Punch, in terms of a simple experience that's laser focused on delivering finely tuned fun gameplay. It's the kind of game where I'm instantly restarting upon defeat, to improve my skills, complete missions, unlock new parts.
