With over 100K positive reviews between this game and its predecessor, my two cents probably won't persuade you if you're undecided.
That said, I'm happy to give context: The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is the revamped version of the previous edition. It's a rogue-like twin-stick shooter that calls upon classics like Zelda with a grimdark sense of humor layered over. A celebration of the grotesque and morbid, Rebirth puts you in the reigns of a small child, naked and alone, in a battle of life and death against the nightmarish manifestations of his abusive mother and her ilk. It's a little more complicated than that, of course, but that will be for you to discover.
The crux of the game, more than the story, though, is the infinite replayability. This was true of the original version, but Rebirth even more so. Everything is random, from the levels down to the items, so no one run will present quite the same scenario without using a seed. Tear effects, or the changes to Isaac's (the protagonist's) combat abilities, now have more ways to combine, and there are more items, in general, to discover and experiment with. New enemies also make an appearance, bosses included, in addition to new obstacles and room types. Completing the game and hitting certain milestones reward more items and bosses for the engine to roll.
Last but not least, a host of quality of life improvements show in this installment. Save games, multiple instances, and general UI features provide a smoother experience. Not including a new couch co-op feature that allows you to be not-so-alone, with one player acting as a baby follower while the other controls the central character.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth and its predecessor both enkindle a type of willful determination to persist in the face of adversity that few games provide with such clarity and enjoyment. You will likely struggle, and you will inevitably fail, but failure is not only acceptable, it's by design. The point, and what makes this game so compelling, is that failure is rarely disheartening, as it feels well within the player's power to do better next time with a failed run or one hundred under their belt. I recommend Rebirth, and hope you find the same sort of compelling experience that I and thousands of others have.

I've played a whole lot of zombie survival games, so it's rare that I see anything new in these sorts of games that I haven't already seen dozens of times. Over 9000 Zombies doesn't really bring anything new to the table, but its straight-talking no-frills approach to the genre is laudable. You're plopped down in the middle of the hordes, and told to shoot and build your way to victory. There's a bit of tower defense going on too, through which you can put together a base to keep the undead back, and then hope for the best. My video playthrough can be found here:

While not quite a review, here is an overview and first impressions video. This was recorded 3-4 hours before officially going on Early Access.
In it you collect scrap metal, grenades, health, and new weapons from fallen zombies and enemies. You can use the scrap metal to build turrets and barricades to try and survive the hordes of thousands of zombies. It actually seems to work quite well, though right now it does have a few good and bad points.
-Surprising amount of content so far.
-Music is nice and has good production value, gives good energy to the fights.
-Vast numbers of enemies and explosions going on. Tons of carnage in later days.
-The Map needs more variety or randomness, right now they are just a few main areas that just work flat out better than others.
-The difficulty curve can be unforgiving if you don't plan.
-Maps needs some sort of tile smoothering or filtering to make it feel less sharp.
Those are just some of my thoughts, so far it plays nice and actually pretty fun. It's certainly quite full for an early access game these days.
Edit: I had said that the grenade launcher stops working. What I didn't think about was it using actual normal grenades as ammo, and it appears to use one grenade for a full magazine. So thats not a bug.

After a little over 850 hours, I think it's time for a review.  Been playing a little over a year.  I've had a great time with this game.  There are things that need improving, but the bugs aren't as bad as people let on.  I think I can count on one hand how many times I've died to a game bug.  For EA, I believe that's pretty good.  The game has improved and things are getting a lot smoother.  There are regular updates.  Many of the recent updates seem to be the base for adding future survival elements and optimizing.
The stuff you need to know:
This game does not hold your hand.  It can be hard.  If you want to feel like you're really lost and trying to make it in a post nuclear world, this is it.  You do not spawn with a weapon, food, map, etc.  There are no name makers, mini map, location markers, crosshair overlays...nothing.  AND that is a good thing.  This game forces you to think and think hard.  Think about routes of travel, think about your base layout, think about how you should approach other survivors (if at all.)
The weapon mechanics are pretty good.  I've had my most intense batttle moments of 25+ years of gaming in Miscreated.  The chance of losing all your hard earned gear makes battles super intense.
Looting isn't as hard as others would have you believe.  Ther is ample loot once you learn where to look, and lean to not go running full speed into a building.  Someone will kill you in self defence.
This game can be lonely playing by yourself, but not in a bad way.  That said, it is so much better with a group of friends working together to survive.
There are PVP, PVE, and RP servers.  Special rulesets like PVE and RP/No KOS servers are typically whitelisted, but you can get added to them.  If you look, you can find your place in this game.
Highly recommend.

Great game. Really surprised how much I enjoyed this one. A huge open world to explore, survivors to take care of, needs to cater to, and hordes of zombies. If you enjoyed Day Z, but just want to play something a little more 'fun', you'll love this.

I want to like this game so much.  I have always BADLY wanted to see a game set in some dire circumstance, scrounging to survive, supply and build up your "Fort" and the people within.   Finding survivors, finding supplies, openly exploring, etc.   Zombies or not, the concept is what I wanted.  Unfortunately, there's too much here that misses the mark.  The controls/menus are really not great (PC port being a huge contributer to that).
Permanent Character Death being mandatory, not optional was also a pretty big turn off for me.   Inability to save and reload from a save if you mess up.  Yes, I understand that that is part of the game by design; that you can't save and reload on a whim, that actions have consequences, but I bet I am not the only one who doesn't find that enjoyable.  I would much prefer to see that as an option, a "hardcore" mode maybe.
Another annoyance, I can't let my character sleep?  I have to have one in play at all times?  THAT is a bad idea.  I first picked up the game and quickly learned that you can wear out your group.  So, I had a bunch of "tired" people, no one was rested and able.   Could I just sleep it off? NOPE.... seems like a logical part of the game is just not there.  Again, its that survival aspect, but this isn't fun, it is just tedious.
But the real nail in the coffin was the persistent world.   If you don't play the game often, the game progresses without you.  Walk away from the game for a week and your team falls apart, uses up supplies, and become lost.  WHO THOUGHT OF THAT IDEA?!  Good God! What a terrifically bad idea!  There's many other shortcomings here and there that just make the game enjoyable to try, but not worth sticking with.  I appreciate what Undead Labs tried to do with this game, and I hope they release State of Decay 2, with a little more options and less punishments.
I suppose there are gamers out there that enjoy the unforgiving aspects of the game, but I also think it turns off many players as well.   This game was SO CLOSE, but it had to have that sadism/masochism unforgiving component to it.  SURVIVAL Horror indeed, but in being so punishing, it makes it less fun and enjoyable.
I was hesitant to Not recommend this game, as most of my dislikes are simply personal taste, and has nothing to do with overall game quality, which overall is decent (clipping aside).  But the choices in this game, to make it a true grind and punishing.... its just a bit too much to keep my interest.

Looking really forward to Transport Fever, i decided to pick this up to get a bit of a taste.
After a number of extremely frustrating hours, i have given up. I cant take this mess any longer. Being a huge fan of games such as TTD, Railrood Tycoon, Simutrans and the likes, i figured i should give this a shot. Unfortunately, all i ran into was frustration and subsequently, dissapointment.
The basic idea of the game is simple: Starting from the 1850's until the modern era, you have to connect towns with one another, provide transport inbetween and the production of goods towards the cities. Growth of these cities is impacted by how much goods they process and transport capabilities. Unfortunately, it does neither very well. Whereas previous games of this genre have had a lot more possibilites for transport, you're limited only to trains, trucks and the odd tram system. While this wouldn't necessarily be problematic if it were well fleshed out, you're stuck with limited options and vehicle options. Often at times, you're only making a trade-off between 2 different vehicles or simply just picking the most modern one you've got - and there's no differentiating passenger needs either. Goods are divided between ore, coal, wood and oil - with only 3 different production lines. To be blunt, it's extremely basic.
But even if that were functional, i'd still not be all too negative about it. The game itself suffers horribly from bugs. Thankfully, i haven't had a crash-to-desktop thus far, but that's all there's to be said. Sometimes, factories or other locations producing goods are simply not making any resources, with absolutely no explanation whatsoever. I looked up on the forums and guides if there was any explanation, but all i found was 'yeah, it's a bug'. Nobody can tell. Roads (and especially rails) are annoying due to the fact they don't connect well with high ground - even though it should be possible anyway - making for an extremely frustrating experience to actually get a connected line - and god forbid you're going to want to electrify your roads/rails, because it's torture to get that right, you're often better off just demolishing them as a whole and re-electrifying existing lines.
In-game speed options are limited to only 4x speed, so if you want to pass the time a bit, i often alt-tabbed and browsed the internet a bit before jumping in 20 minutes later. Why there's no ingame high-speed option, i have no idea.
Overall, its only redeeming quality comes from the somewhat pleasing aesthetics. Cities grow exponentially, depending on their use of transport and supplied goods, which is quite satisfying. The game's also highly moddable, and there are plenty of assets and mods to be found online. But to be honest, that's all there's to be said about it.
I'm still looking forward to Transport Fever anyhow, but i'll be very skeptical. Train Fever is a mess. I hope they'll do it right.

Well, I bought this game on a special promotion and since I am an Ace Combat veteran, I had to get it. I was a little nervous about buying an Ace Combat game for the PC and it appears that I was rightly so. This one is not your typical Ace Combat game. There is a new dogfighting mode, helicopter piloting and door gunning. My first challenge was to get control of the game. The jet fighter was easy enough (grab my PS2 controller with pc adapter, plug in and configure), but for the helicopter and gunner sequences, that controller didn't cut it. I had to configure my Belkin n52te controller in concert with my mouse to accurately control the helicopter and the mouse was really key to being effective with the gunner sequences. Once I got a handle on the controls, the fun began.
Flying the jet for me was pretty much a blast from the past. Machine guns, missiles, special weapons, etc... all there. DFM (Dog Fighting Mode), however, was a new one on me. In the past, there were enemies that were better than the other ones and if you killed them, you got medals and such. Well, on this game there are lead targets and the only way you can take them out is by following them until you can activate the DFM and shoot them down. There have been mixed reactions to the DFM, I personally have no problem with it and it does come in handy in many situations. Also, you can BE engaged by an enemy in DFM. In this instance, there is a little button that can be pushed at the right time that will perform a dizzing evasive manuver that will put you behind the plane and you then have your chance to shoot it down. Pretty sweet to me, I like it. Also, the other new feature is flares. Someone fires a missle at you, deploy flares and turn to evade. Simple enough. The jet fighter sequences are definately enjoyable.
Helicopter flying is a different story. I HAD to get my n52te and mouse to fly this thing effectively. There was no way that my PS2 controller or my keyboard was going to cut it on this one. I had to be able to turn, hover to the left or right and be able to fire at the same time. That was too much of a challenge for a PS2 controller. So, once I got a handle on controlling it effectively, I had fun with it. There is your turrent gun, rockets and air-to-ground missiles. Once you learn how to control the helicopter well, it is just as enjoyable as the jet fighter sequences. And the dialogue from the helicopter pilot will crack you up on occasion. :-)
Door gunning is fairly simple. You have a set of cross-hairs that you put on the enemy and shoot. Right mouse button zooms in. Shoot all enemies. Shoot, kill, kill, kill, shoot, kill, kill, kill. The mouse will assist you with more accurate shots than the keyboard or controllers will. Once you get into it, you'll love it.
Overall, this is a successful game. The controls took a lot of getting used to, but once you got the hang of it and customized the controls to your playing style, you'll love it. Buy it with confidence.

This game can be very decieving in both the game itself and what you expect of it.  Upon looking at it most people think "Oh, princess maker but cooler looking."  It would be better to think of this game as medieval politics simulator but with a whole lot more death.
The basis of the game is that you are the 14 year old princess of the kingdom of Nova.  Your mother has just died leaving you to become queen in her stead.  As you are only 14 your father is techniquely leading the kingdom as you are groomed for command, but he is awesome enough to let you make EVERY DECISION IN THE KINGDOM ON YOUR OWN AS EVERYTHING TRYS TO KILL YOU (even the chocolate).
The gameplay is straight forward, and will remind you quite a bit of princess maker, but remember the goal isn't to make you a pretty princess.  The goal is simply survive until your coranation.  Each week you choose two subjects out of a large list to study from and get points in those subjects.  That is half the game right there.  The other parts are choosing weekend events, managing your mood and surviving.
Long Live The Queen tells its story through text given after every week of class.   THE STORY DOES NOT CHANGE WITH EACH PLAYTHROUGH.  In the text you will be given skill checks on how many points you have in a specific subject.  For example when someone tells you there is a snake at your feet, you have the option to 1) Look down   2) stand still       If you choose the latter you will be given a check on your composure skill.  If you suceed the check you will hold still and the snake will die.  If you fail your friend will be bitten by this extremely poisonous snake.  While this check does not lead you to die it is a reminder that people are trying to kill you.
Checks like this are all throughout the game and one of parts of the game that turns people off is that you will have to play the game multiple times to know what is coming and to prepare for it.  This does not ruin the game but makes it soooooo much more gratifying when you finally, avoid getting killed by all the plotting nobles, survive the civil war you started, kill the foreign conquerer in your realm, survive the peasant uprising, and FINALLY are declared Queen.
There is also an emotion system that I wont even go into here.
All in all Long Live the Queen is a game that is underated and misunderstood by many, but is a great game where you can learn something new about the story almost every playthrough and once you get the hang of it, you will find yourself loving your loli queen.

Permadeath alert!!! As a child of the coin-op generation I grew up with the reality of permadeath. Protecting your digital ambassador became all consuming and, when death finally arrived, failure resulted in a great deal of physical abuse directed at the controls in your hands and the surrounding cabinet.
It has been a long time since a game has evoked a level of anger, frustration and loss at the death of a sprite but State of Decay took me right back to my childhood.
I'm not going to comment on graphics or gameplay or on bugs or dodgy controls (actually I will comment on the last two - I've seen no real bugs and the controls seem fine). Nor does the strength of this game lie in it's setting. How could it? The zombie genre has been done to (un)death.
The true appeal comes from watching the consequences of your actions and sitting helpless whilst you witness your character being torn to shreds for the first time. It is then that the slow realisation sets in that there is no going back.
The game is currently on offer. At less than four quid what have you got to lose?
For you gamers out there of a certain age... even if this is not your normal choice of game, take a chance - you won't be disappointed.

I would hate to make a game these days... People are just a bunch of whiny b1tches anymore... Miscreated is amazing. I can't believe all these bad comments. Everyone has their own opinion. I get it, but some people are so toxic, and talk so much crap though. I don't know how game developers do it.. Anyway. about the game.. I have tried every survival game out there & compared to miscreated they all suck. Miscreated is hands down the best one out there. Plus.. it's cheaper than most.. I'm blown away by the bad reviews.. The entire world of miscreated is just absolutely stunning & beautiful. For being a fairly large world, it is pretty amazing that they can make it look so good & detailed, and have it run well at the same time. Everything... is detailed.  Too much to explain but It truly feels like walking around in an apocalyptic world. Not like a bunch of games where the buildings look neat until you try to go inside and find that you can't actually go in them, Or, others where you can go in only to find an empty bleh looking interior. Not on miscreated. Everything is detailed & beautiful looking. On top of that there are some really neat things you can do in this game, and so many funny moments. My first game of miscreated I found a big town.. seen some people typing in chat something about meeting at the tents. Thought.. hell, I'm gonna go find them and talk to them. Didn't know my way around at all but I seen some big warehouse looking things. Thought maybe that is the tents. Went over to the building and went inside. It was a large warehouse with only one door to get in or out. As I was looking around two guys came running in the only door, put there guns in my face, and told me to put my hands up. These guys were fully decked out in camo, big duffel bags on their backs, and M4 rifles with lazers on them.. I was like oh ♥♥♥♥... After a little direction from my adductors I hit the correct key to put my hands up... then they tied my hands behind my back, took my clothes, said see ya later, have a good day buddy.. and left me. I was stuck walking around with my hands behind my back in my underwear... lol.. After that I was hooked. It is these kind of moments that just keep me coming back to miscreated. The game is not perfect. It can be frustrating at times when you die & you lose all your stuff only to respawn spend 20 minutes or so to finally get some good stuff, just to get shot & die once more.. It's tough sometimes. But, then you have one of the many many great encounters that I have experienced only on miscreated, and the game is just so freaking fun & awesome. It has a steep learning curve, and I think some people get turned off before they ever learn the game well enough to make it enjoyable. You don't have a map so you have to explore & learn the world, learn the gun spawns, and learn the game. It is brutal until you do. It helps to start off in low population servers, and it helps to look up a miscreated map online & use that map along with the street signs in game to learn to navigate your way around.. Eventually you won't even need anything, but it will take a while to learn. It is also a lot better if you find other players to team with. Not only is it funner, but it's safer, and you will learn the gaem faster. If people shoot at you... don't just stand there. Run, zig zag, and get the hell out of dodge. Or shoot them back. Don't trust everyone you meet. Actually don't trush anyone. We all started as that noob who was constantly getting ganked & killed, or having people mess with them. After a while you won't die nearly as often, and you will be one of those guys with duffle bags, M4's with lazers, and all that. That's when things get really fun. There is a lot of PVP in this game. It's just the way it is. The dev's have been working on the mutants & ai, and they are getting to be more of a threat. They can screw you up "especially the wolves" but there aren't really enough of them to be big threat. Some people don't really like pvp, so they might not get into the game. At least not the way the game is now. The dev's are very active, and update pretty regularly. Actually very active for being just a small dev team. I would hope, and I believe that at some point down the road you are going to have hordes of mutants in the cities, and there is going to be a lot more ai so they will be more of a threat. I look forward to that, but it's not a deal breaker for me.. I personally enjoy the pvp. The gun fights are sometimes fast & unexpected or other times they are slow and tactical where patience is important. You can actually hide in bushes or similar. It's not like other games where people can turn their graphics settings down, and be like oh look... a guy standing in those twigs. Nope. Not in miscreated. Not saying you can't notice someone in the bushes in miscreated, but you can hide... very well. This makes for some very tense gunfights. All in all. If you are on the fence about this game. It's most certainly worth the $10 "when on sale", or the $20 "when not on sale". I would pay even more for it myself, so I think the price is absolutely reasonable.

I'm torn, like really torn.
I have enjoyed Ace Combat for as long as I can remember.  From going to the arcade and sitting in the, awesome at the time, faux cockpit living out my fantasies of being a fighter pilot to playing Ace Combat at home with my friends on Playstation 2.  Ace Combat, to me, has been the hands down best arcade style flight game for a long time.  Yes there were some weak games in the series, but there wasn't really anything else like them (maybe Hawx, but I have to imagine there's a reason only 2 of those were made while every other Tom Clancy game gets sequal after sequal).
Now for me the best games in the series are the PS2 generation, I'm talking Shattered Skies, Unsung War, and Zero (Zero being imo the best game in the series, for story, presentation, and just sheer variety of jets).  Nothing beat going against the Yellow Squadron at the end of Shattered Skies, or being able to command my wingmen in Unsung War, or going aginst the aces of Zero.  Yes, the playstyle could get repetitive, some could even compare it to Nascar in the sky with missles, with all the constant left turns and all, but the variety of missions, the awesome stage design (chasing enemies through canyons and going all out Death Star style on giant miltary bases and destryoing giant fleets of ships just to name a few), and the insane balls to the wall story telling (Demons of Razgriz, do I have to say anything else?).  Ace Combat was  game that seemed to know what it was, first and foremost an overtly arcade flight sim (and I use the word sim very lossely).  That doesn't seem to be the case here.  Let me explain.
As I stated Ace Combat has always featured crazy fictional storylines about nation against nation all out air combat.  That's not the case here.  Once again we are "graced" with the classic tale of crazy Russians doing crazy things.  Now I don't want to spoil anything, but I will say that the story, like so many others, is about revenge.  I know, real original right?  Now there have been a lot of comparisons to Call of Duty, and as someone who has played both Ace Combat and Call of Duty, I can say the comparison is apt.  There is a lot to the story that invokes thoughts of the current Call of Duty campaigns.  Once again, crazy Russians, doing crazy things, based around revengs.  I don't know if all of these game developers are delving into the same writing pool, but it sure seems that way.  The story overall, for all of it's cliches, isn't what I would call bad, but it's not what I would call good either.  Rather I would call it forgetable.  I want to say that it is a good lead in, as motivation, to the missions you play, but honestly, you could probably drop all of the cut scenes and still get the jist of what's going on.  Not that it would matter to much.  Needless to say, don't come to this game for the story, you can find the same thing, but better, in just about any movie about flying from the 80's (Top Gun, Iron Eagles), and that's not saying much.
Gameplay wise is where things start to get divisive though.  Before Ace Combat was about skill, to a degree, having to keep up with your target, know when to fire missles so they would have a better chance of hitting, being able to stay in close for guns range, etc. but now that seems to have been circumvented in place of scripted action that's what many would describe as being "on rails".  Assault Horizon introduces Dog Fight Mode, or DFM for short.  Ini DFM you can engage enemies in scripted (though not to be fair, not all the tim) "on ralis" segments usually not being allowed to shoot down an enemy till you have gone through some cinematic moment the game wants you to see.  Sometimes this is a plane crashing into a stadim, as seen in the demo, othertimes it's till a plance decides to counter you, engaging you in a back and forth DFM challenge.  This can become quiet tedious, especially as the game progresses and it forces you to use such more and more.  For those that want to avoid this, I hate to inform, I don't think you really can.  There are portions of the game where it is not even possible to shoot the enemy down till you engage them in DFM and then follow through the cinematic at which time the game will actually make your weapons begin to do damage.  This, as I'm sure you can guess, get's rather old.  Thankfully though much of the previous combat does remain.  As I stated you can still engage enemies without the use of DFM and these engaements feel the same as before, if not even better, as the enemy seems to be a little bit smarter this time around, and that's not a bad thing in this case.
What is a bad thing though, is the friendly AI.  They are useless.  I don't say this lightly, but I don't think I have ever seen such horrible AI before.  I mean that.  All I'll say is this, there is a level in the game, about mid way through were you are tasked with destroying a target, you have at this time multiple aircraft in the air with you, friendly and hostile.  The friendlies task you with targetting particular aircraft informing you that they will take care of the "escort craft", they don't.  Not at all.  Nothing is more frusrtrating then seeing the sky filled with friendly aircraft only to watch them fly around not going after a single target as they tell me not to be concerned.  These targets are all over you at this point, not being concerned isn't really possible.  Especially considering it's impossible to destroy your targets without engaging the other aircraft.  oh, and did I mention you were on a timer?  Yeah, there's that.  Like I said, horrible AI.
I won't even get into the helicopter sections, this review is already long enough.  I will just say this, they aren't as bad as you may have heard, but they definettly aren't good either.  They are once again forgettable; like most of this game to be honest.
I don't want to end this by doing nothing but bashing the game so I will say this, the game looks good.  It does.  It's hands down the best looking Ace Combat game.  The ground textures are still laughable, but what do you expect?  The aricraft though, beuatiful.  Also, the aircraft selection, it's good.  Granted there has been better in previous games, but what can you really expect?  It's not like there is a whole lot of modern jet fighter today.  Some of the missions were alright, but nothing to really write home about, but nothing to seriously decry either, they were just, well, forgetable.
And I guess that about sums it up, a forgetable game.  Like I said I'm torn, I really wanted to like this, it's Ace Combat, but sadly it's not.  It has the name, but none of the feel.  I'm pretty sure that JSAF may honestly be better, and that's saying something.

If you've never played a souls game before just like me, then this game is going to be very difficult to get in to. As long as you stick to it until you're at a comfortable point (you can become stronger faster than the game can get harder), the game opens up so much to you with its amazing lore, enemy designs, visuals and music. Every now and then, the game will throw something at you that makes you question your actions, and it can get pretty emotional at times (cough cough Sif and Priscilla).
While the positives far outweigh the negatives later on in the game (once you're familiar with controls and tactics), there are a few drawbacks that can make the game clunky, frustrating and difficult for the wrong reasons, giving off the wrong vibe to new players like myself. I personally think the camera is the worst offendor of this, ocasionally getting locked into a wall during a tight squeeze (Capra Demon fight, getting cornered by Smough's enormous belly, etc). Another thing to note is that the hitbox detection can be pretty annoying, mostly notable in the Iron Golem's grab attack. You could be 2 meters away from his swing, yet you'd snap into his fist and get killed for something you easily would have dodged if the game wasn't built like this.
Negatives aside, the game holds up well even after the years it has been out. Many Souls players seem to favor this one over the others. Highly reccomended, but hang in there for just a few more hours and you'll be hooked.
Also, the game is much better off being played at 60fps with the DSFix found on the community guides. However, some bugs can occur because of the uncap on the frames, such as clipping through the floor when sliding down ladders (very rare) and the occasional jump being impossible to make, as the jump distance is cut by about 20%. This is easily bypassed by hitting backspace in-game to put the game back into 30fps and back to 60 at any time.

Fair warning: if you plan on playing this game as it is on Steam, do yourself a favor and install DSFix in order to fix some issues with it (this is a really crappy PC port of an XBox game, link to DSFix here:
and probably get yourself a controller (unless you want an extra challenge, as the controls of the game aren't conducive to a mounse-and-keyboard setup).
That being said, this is a fantastic game for both old-school RPG fans and people wanting to get into the explosively famous Dark Souls series. If you feel intimidated by its "Prepare to Die" tagline, please don't be; though there is a fair amount of dying and a great deal of challenge with the game, the controls are fairly intuitive and easy to grasp in a surprisingly short amount of time. Should you need help understanding stats, the game even has a handy help tool for you to use. Those who enjoy the combat will find it challenging as well as rewarding, and those who enjoy the lore will find themselves overwhelmed by a world lying in ruins, long past its prime and filled with cynical merchants selling gear as well as noble knights and other characters descending to their own ruin in spite of their skill in combat.
Perhaps one of the most unique aspects of the Dark Souls series is its multiplayer, which I would describe more as "social" than anything else. Interplayer contact is organized by giving players access to an "IP pool" of sorts that increases as the play session goes on, meaning that players have access to more messages from other players, more summon signs, and more opportunities to invade and be invaded as they continue playing for a session (making online play more immersive for long sessions). There is close to no control over which IPs the players come into contact with, so if you prefer solely playing with friends or want to give friends priority in the IP search, there are ways to go about achieving that which can be found online. Interplayer contact is based on which of nine covenants players belong to, which each place emphasis on different aspects of online play (such as PvP, PvE, and Co-op). These covenants are what make the game's social nature function, and allow for unexpected encounters and additional challenges for players.
Since it contains difficulty settings, Dark Souls is still accessible to people who may not consider themselves very good at action-RPGs or video games in general. Don't let the tagline scare you, and allow yourself to be immersed in the dying realm of Lordran and all it has to offer. Praise the Sun my friends! \(^-^)/

Finally, after 54 hours, I beat it. At last. I have quite a few things to say.
I did love playing this game. I adore the level design, the brilliant lore and worldbuilding, the fantastic realisation of some very solid themes of death, glory, the juxtaposition between the majestic and the macabre. I love it on a technical level: while it's not a graphical masterpiece, when you compare it to another action-adventure RPG from the same year, Skyrim, you can see pretty clearly that Dark Souls is much better in terms of graphics (and in terms of almost everything else in my opinion). The sound design is utterly wonderful: careful silences, grand themes, tentative moments of quieter, more somber pieces like Gwyn's theme or the Moonlight Butterfly. And of course, the combat. The combat is slow, deliberate, everything feels weighty and impactful, it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to get good at but once you do you really start to feel the flow of the enemy attacks.
For about two thirds of the game, I was enamoured. I climbed Undead Berg in awe. I trudged through Blighttown with grit and determination. I wandered through Darkroot Garden, loving the mist and the mystery. I dashed through Senn's Fortress after dying in it for the dozenth time. I ended up going back to the Undead Asylum, and fighting the Hydra in Darkroot Basin (which I found... horrifying, utterly genuinely terrifying for some reason) then the one in Ash Lake (my favourite area in the game, just such a numinous indescribable feeling
. And then I plowed through Anor Londo, and met O & S.
This is where the game began to turn for me from an enjoyable feat into a frustrating grind. It was so hard to beat these two that I opted to go back and beat Pinwheel just to get the Rite of Kindling (hilariously easy boss fight by the way
). Then after O&S I went down to the Tomb of Giants, which was maybe the peak of the endgame content for me. Expertly crafted usage of lighting, and a healthy level of challenge. But Nito was kind of a pushover, and it was then I started to realise that the combat system, especially when it came to bosses, is kind of... overly repetitive? For about 80% of enemies, especially in the late game, the best way to fight them is roll through attack, circle strafe around and hit them in the back. This was the Nito fight in a nutshell for me. And every Silver Knight, and Black Knight, and Quelaag and Bell Gargoyles and Taurus and Capra and the list goes on. It wasn't easy, but just kind of boring.
And then I went to the Demon Ruins, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I ♥♥♥♥ing hate the Demon Ruins. The visibility is horrible, the frame rate is bad, the bosses are easy as hell to cheese and if you don't they're incredibly frustrating. The entire design of the area is gross and unappealing to the eye, and not a single regular enemy is unique or interesting (except those many-eyed cone things, those were kinda cool). I don't even know if it was a bug or something but those dino things out in the lava between the boss fight and the bonfire (I could never make out what they were supposed to be because the lighting was so bad) almost never attacked me. And then there's the boss fight.
.
Things looked up a little later though. I enjoyed the Duke's Archives and New Londo, though the former was quite frustatingly hard
and the latter a little short. I loved the Four Kings though, really creative and visually striking.
And then, Gwyn:
One more gripe: the overpowered nature of the lightning spear you pick up in Senn's Fortress (and lightning in general). Almost no enemies in the game have a high resistance to lightning: most are weak to it. So getting a pretty strong spear part way through the game that most enemies are weak to is a bit ridiculous. As long as you have a different weapon for the few encounters where lightning won't win out, this spear seems like an extremely obvious way to go. Put it this way: this spear at +2 was stronger than my Uchi at +8.
Overall though, the early game is more than enough to earn my recommendation, and although the late game is shaky it does have its moments. Dark Souls is well-deserved of its praise, and I would still regard it as one of the finest games I've ever played. It just isn't perfect, and I feel like I should say that to anyone thinking of going into it

So you put together a team of viking and giant warriors and fight short tactical turnbased fights and tournaments to get renown, wich is used to buy more space for warriors or upgrade your warriors. You get matched against players with the same combined level of fighters, resulting in very even matches.
The combat system is identical to the banner saga, with  the only exception of some small changes to the abilities of some units.
Though I strongly recommend the game, there are some issues that you should know before playing.
First of all it is a player vs player only game. There is no training mode or single player, if you want that you have to buy The banner Saga (strongly recommended as well).
The second major issue is that the game seems kind of forgotten by the developers, there are memory leak issues that cause lag, and updates are close to nonexistent.
The third issue is that most player quit due to the first two, or the fact that the gameplay changes very little over time, resulting in very few players online at any moment. This of course can cause painfully long periods of waiting for a match. This is also to some extent caused by the matching system, in wich you may be unable to battle anyone at all if you don't have enough warriors to put together teams of different levels (ironically happens predominantly to new players).
With those things out of the way, this is really fun and challenging game for you tactics fans. The turn system is different from many other games and is of extreme tactical importance, and to me the number of classes and restrictions are enough for a large umber of tactics and combos.
Adressing the issues: The first becomes a non-issue after like four fights. The community is great and everyone are excited for new players and will help you get started.
The second issue is bad, but in theory if more people play it the devs should work more to upgrade it. It will also likely get a boost after the release of newly announced TBS2.
The third issue is the hard one. I personally don't think its boring, just as I dont think chess is boring, even if chess hasnt got any upgrades or new skins for decades =). And remember that many quit because there are too few players already. what kind of logic is that? But I won't judge anyone who played the game for a year and a half, waiting for someone to fix  the lag and crash issues, and stopped playing when nothing happened.
Try it out though. it's Free! and fun!

I dreaded to play this game. I was watching the alpha/beta development of this game for a little while, and while I liked a lot of what I read about it, looking at the content didn't look 'refined' enough.
The gameplay is not anywhere as smooth as I had hoped and it's hard for me to get past the pre-rendered animations for literally every action. In the beginning I was watching my npc friend attack a zombie and you could see when each attack animation would create a 'stutter' between the next attack.
Right in the beginning I watched a zombie trap it self climbing up a ledge, clipping back down, then repeating over and over again.
The controls as a whole feel awkward to command and execute, with a lot of fine mouse sensitivity just to execute bulky, long animation sequences.
The camera doesn't zoom out very far at all either. For an open world zombie game, your field of view  feels kind of narrow and your character takes up a good size on the screen.
The gameplay is nothing like Left 4 Dead, but more like a more arcade gamestyle of Dead Rising with  a Dead Island feel.
You do get vehicles in this game though, and they handle really nice. They drive with a good weight to them, rather than the sometimes glidy feel of running around in the game.
My biggest gripe about the game is all the heavily scripted actions, which doesn't work when the combat generally tends to be just button mashing, making your character attack at nothing a few times to catch up with all the times you mashed the attack button.
I don't know how much can be improved upon with patches and this first game is rather bumpy in a lot of ways and would only recommend to buy on sale, I could definitely see this turning into a worthwhile series. The gameplay is unique and interesting enough that it can definitely be worth expanding on.

I'll keep this short for anyone scanning the reviews and seeing a whole lotta 'positive reviews' here: Ain't worth your damn nickle or dime. Not even on sale.
This game isn't worth your money in a lot of ways, but if you're the kind of person who loves repetitive, bland, uninteresting loot-grab games, maybe you'll like this too. Thing is, though, most of your gameplay revolves around finding the exact same pre-fabricated dungeons and houses in the exact same places scattered around same-y looking planets. Don't ever bother your time with trying to find loot underground as it is much easier to scan the surface collecting loot that way (underground loot isn't even better, unless you're trying to find those 'challenge' rooms which give crappy loot most of the time.)
You're railroaded down a tier progression path and the story mode. The story mode dungeons start off interesting but quicky lose their weight and worth because they can't possibly be tuned for the utterly broken♥♥♥♥♥combinations of loot you can get rather easily. AI is stupid and will follow you to the ends of the earth unless you manage to break contact long enough in a way they can't follow.
Mining is a slow, arduous process that has to be upgraded to work faster. Find chips scattered in the pre-fabricated houses I'm sure everyone here has looted for the sixtieth time to upgrade the tool. Your tier progression often follows mining for an ore and smelting it, almost nothing more. If there's anything extra to make a bar, it's just a tedious waste of your time.
The game has a lot of moddability, which means I can mod out these horrible quirks of the game- but you can't mod out the horrible combat. Combat has been reworked several times. Each time, it gets even more tiring to fight an enemy, to what we have now, where enemies take many hits to kill and are often spawned with ANNOYING quirks... such as temporary invincibility, and, floating through walls.
The texture work, however, is nothing short of amazing. Tiles tend to mesh well together. Building can be fun, but only if you're even capable of finding cool stuff to build with. See, you can barely craft any tiles until you find a recipe for them, but most tiles don't even have a recipe. That means looking through a whole bunch of planets to find the pre-fabricated building to tear the blocks away from! Yay!
If you're going to get this game... exclusively use a creative tool to mod in blocks and build. Anything you make in this game can look beautiful. I just wish the game was as deep as my college debt.

First impression: Mobile tactics game for beginners (not (yet?) available on mobile).
It's tactics because you command up to 10 units, turn-based, with predetermined battle outcomes and a predictable AI. (There is no multiplayer.) It's mobile because the maps are small and the interface is huge and the windowed resolution is fixed at 1280x720; space is optimized so you can play it on your phone. It's for beginners because games often last less than 10 turns (did I mention the maps are small?), and I managed to beat the achievement missions including mission 20 of the human and monster campaigns (they have 20 missions each) after completing the tutorial, skipping the rest -- well, all except monster mission 19, which requires careful counting so the AI splits up the way you want, which is too much micromanagement for me right now.
Each side has 6 units types, with HP, walking range, attack range, attack and shield; at the beginning of your turn, your shields regenerate, then you move and attack with each unit, and then it's the opponent's turn. You need to plan your moves in advance, and, in many cases, predict where the AI is going to move so they step on traps properly (you need to stop on a trap or it won't trigger) or split up into smaller groups. There are 9 tutorial levels and four campaigns of 20 levels each; two campaigns are fully unlocked once you complete the tutorial.
I did complete the human campaign and found the difficulty a tad uneven, but since all of the levels are unlocked, that's not really a problem.
If your looking for "my first tactics game", then Monstro will do decently; if you want a casual tactics game with more tactical depth, try
.

I think I’ve never played a game as
. This game is best described as a mixture of turn based tactical battles with a puzzle game, in the sense that you have to find the correct way and order to take out the enemy units or complete a certain objective without getting your troops killed.
The story of the game is presented to you in the form of an introductory cutscene and via little text windows at the beginning of every mission. The game takes place in Ludus, a place where monsters,mythical creatures and humans live in peace but once in every hundred years the Skygods summon some sort of floating islands, with perfectly shaped squares, in order to humans and monsters fight among themselves for the amusement of the gods.
The gameplay is pretty simple and easy to understand but, however, this doesn’t mean that the game doesn’t offer a challenge, it is quite the opposite. On each mission you’ll have control over one or more units, and usually your objective is either to slay all enemy units or to eliminate a certain enemy. The loss condition, of course, is not to loose all your units. Sounds simple enough, right? This is where Monstro: Battle Tactics really shines, it takes a simple and easy to learn gameplay formula and makes it challenging and hard by turning the fights and the levels themselves into puzzles of some sort. What I mean by this is that you’re able to move your units as you see fit, but most often the not, if you don’t plan ahead and find the correct order to attack and which enemies to go after first, you’ll end up loosing pretty quickly. Still, no need to worry about restarting the level since the game kindly offers you an “undo” function.
The game adds some variety to this by putting you against different types of enemies with different stats and by putting down some traps and movable and destructible walls. Your units also have their own stats, and some might even have specializations which increases a certain stat of a given unit. It is also in this sense that each mission is somewhat of a puzzle, because you have to compare your units stats with the enemies and figure out if you have what it takes to take the enemy down before it takes you.
Despite the cons I’ve mentioned above, Monstro: Battle Tactics manages to keep things varied and interesting enough to make me want to keep playing it. As someone who has never really delved much into tactical RPGs, I must say I like the way this game mixes some aspects of that genre with some light elements of puzzle solving. Therefore, if you’re a fan of light puzzle games, turn based strategy in general or are just looking for something unique with a twist, I recommend you check this one out!

Going to start this review with a question: Are you okay playing a game that is basically just walking around a small town and talking to people? If not, then this game is not for you, leave now, play something else. But if your answer to that question was yes... then you are in for a treat.
Night in the Woods is essentialy a game about its main character, Mae Borowski, and chances are that she will remind you of someone you know (or maybe yourself!) because she is such an incredibly written lead. She feels genuinely human in a way that makes you forget that she's a cat, in fact you'll forget that most of the cast are just an assortment of zoo creatures becuase they all feel human. They all feel real.
And just about as much care that has gone into making the cast has gone into writing the story, which I won't write too much about here because I don't want to spoil it. It starts off slow and it goes off in a bit of a weird direction, but you have my word, it's very very good. (Short summary: You play as a sad cat college dropout who has just the best friends and you all hang out and have a grand old time... and then spooky stuff starts happening)
Also, this game is gorgeous. You can probably turn any frame of your time spent playing it into a very pretty desktop wallpaper.
But yeah, if you have the patience to walk around the same area for about 4 hours (which it does for a purpose!), then Night in the Woods will be one of the most powerful and engaging games that you will ever play. It's my favourite game of the year so far. I highly, highly reccomend it.

AC:AH handles like the usual Ace Combat formula with the bombast and overzealous scripting of the latest Call of Duty games thrown in. Numerous times the game uses it's on-rails Dogfight Mode (DFM) or it's even more restrictive cousin Airstrike Mode to force the player to fly under -that- collapsing smokestack or -that- inexplicable jumbo jet, completely irrespective of the direction or location in which it was initiated. Allies/enemies vanish and materialise as the mission scripting decrees, or are completely invulnrable until they become a later mission objective. The DFM is also lacking in options for the player; you can just hold MG and accelerate and watch the pretty colours.
The (apparently) mandatory AC-130 level, the door gunner sections and the helicopter gunship bits, I'm afraid I can't speak fairly on them. Generally I slogged through them until I got my jet back, and certainly wasn't taking notes, other than to say the ground /building textures weren't designed for hovering that close to them.
The story is, well, the typical "US saves the world from someone who wants specifically to attack the US" fare we've seen everywhere since CoD 4. The comms chatter and recurring callsigns that has always made allies seem interesting is still there, but sparser and sandwiched in between asking for help and spontaneous bravado. The sense of edging along with a ground war is missing from the AC formula too - your team can hop between continent as if on an extended holiday, and the sense of bring under threat suffers. I didn't feel much attachment to the callsign either; Warwolf's leader is no Mobius One. As good as the real-world setting is, I feel Strangereal is a better setting for these games.
I'm giving it a negative rating, but that's not to say a bad game. The combat is wonderfully involving in its freeform state, with an excellently majestic soundtrack (Kieki Kobayashi et al doing what they do best), a great selection of planes and enough variation in weapon loadouts / handling / mission objectives to keep it fresh. There's some character to all four members of your flight, as well as the allied squadrons and land-dwelling elements, and even the traditional objective-dispensing AWACS operator has some colour to him.
In summary, what's good is most of the parts I liked from AC's 4 and 6 (you can even get the Estovakian fictional superplane from AC6, in original Strigon Squadron colours), and the parts i disliked were clearly taken wholesale from CoD and grafted around the Ace Combat experience. People looking to get the thrill arcade digfighters give would do well to look at JASF (interesting story idea there) or look to play Fires of Liberation.

XRD is an amazing fighting game, one of the best; and now it's on PC.
Guilty Gear is a game where there are a lot of system mechanics, along with some really unique character designs. The strong universal defensive system mechanics along with the way the tension/super meter works creates an exhilerating, fast paced game with a strong focus on offense and momentum.
The PC port runs perfectly fine, with some anti aliasing and the "standard" resolution options including widescreen. The options menu is kinda sparse, but because it's an unreal game you can do a lot of ini editting to really lower the graphics if needed.
The netplay is delay based, and having the PS3 version of the game, the PC version is as good if not slightly better. (This might be because 99% of PCs are on wired internet, as opposed to PS3s) Ranked Mode suffers more lag then the player match rooms. Although unfortunate they didn't fix it, this was an issue on the consoles as well.

Theres a reason why this game is only half-jokingly referred to as God's Gift.
Praise be.

I am very sad about this game because I see it as a missed opportunity. Firstly it is written for LINUX as well as windows, which is a HUGE plus for me. Secondly when it starts I can see a window "pygame" flash up, which I assume means it is developed in python, which I also personally like a lot. The artwork is good as well, although I don't care too much, although other people might.
The bad part, and the reason I can't recommend this, is simply the gameplay. You get to work through a few scenarios which let you make decisions to keep your crown and survive the dangerous world of a child queen leader. So far so good. But once you die and restart the game the exact same scenarios happen again, only minorly changing depending on earlier choices. The idea seems to have been to make the game make you restart once you fail. the ultimate goal being to get through the game once. The problem with this is that most of the death scenarios happen in the end of the game (but they still depend on earlier choices). So when you play the game for the first time you have no choice but to restart the game from scratch every time, change one decision, and then see what happens later. It's a lot of very unrewarding clicking. In my opinion this could have been much better if events were much more flexible than static, but even with the static structure this game could have been much less clicking and more fun to play. Sadly, this game isn't.

The pvp portion of this game is terrific.  I've never played anything like this game before.  The artwork and sounds are fantastic.
What's lacking is the community population, which is miniscule.  And also the lack of additions to this stand alone game which could benefit mightily from the introduction of new races, classes, levels of combat etc.
With the community being so small it can be difficult for a newer player to advance and not get discouraged because there is some learning that needs to take place and understanding of sound tactics.  Also more advanced players will have more advanced units the longer you wait in the queue there can be some lopsided matches that are drawn.
Main Pro's to the game are the utterly classic and beautfiul energy that was put into the game and setting.  It feels very immersive by itself.  You can also use numerous different compositions competitively.  There are numerous different styles that can compete from agressive surge forward teams that hard-charge, to sit back and play tank defense shield break and counter puncher style, and utilize also trap layers and debuff archer builds.
The game is neat, adult and children friendly.  A game like this either appeals to you very much for its core style that you enjoy, or you might not get it or dislike the lack of updates.  While there are similarities between the board and chess.  They aren't remotely similar.  You can arrange your units pre-battle like stratego, but also left/right and up/down.  You can put your group in a knot on the front lines to crash your enemy on turn 1 or spread them out on the back of the map so you have distance and can get your bearings if you want to play more cautiously.
A very nice feature to this game is that you can constantly modify, at no cost, the point distribution in 5-6 categories for each unit type between battles.  You can experiment each battle to find what works best and/or not to your liking.
This game is very underrated and doesn't deserve all thumbs down.  If this game had updates at least every 3-6 months it would have a much larger community and would keep people coming back.
I'm very appreciative of the developers introducing this game for free.  I've since purchased the main storyline game which is fantastic and plan on purchasing Banner Saga 2 once it releases this Winter.

When I first bought the game a few months ago (Actually around the beginning of the year) it was actually pretty fun, but now it really kinda sucks. Their "updates" have actually seemed to have the opposite of the desired effect and made the game worse. The game has barely changed since I first bought it and the changes that have happened have mostly reduced the enjoyability of the game. It's still quite beautiful but that is the most the game's got going for it after the first hour and a half of playing. Stranded Deep has loads of potential and many different directions that the devs could take that would greatly improve the game. I think I'm done playing it for a while, as many features are lackluster now. BUT, I still have high hopes for this game so I'm definitely going to be waiting it out for each update to roll around.
Also a few offhand thoughts:
-I haven't been able to find any more of those giant rusty sea fort things, which were actually pretty awesome when introduced.
-(Directed towards the devs) Why did you guys get rid of the interactive plane intro??? It was a much better intro to the game than just "Oh, we're on a plane. Now it's crashing." Is it purely because you wanted to get rid of the knife and lighter or??
-I like to listen to my own music while I play games and the walking sound effects made that very difficult. For some reason the walking sounds have been tied to the master volume instead of the effects volume. Along with that, they're louder than any other sound effect in the game and since they're tied to the master volume I can't turn them down without also turning down everything else and I would really like to still be able to hear the ocean behind my music
-Lastly, the player shadow is super derpy. I'll say that it's not too much of an issue as I've gotten some decent laughs out of it, but the two biggest things are that it looks like you're a weeaboo who is about to do that anime sprint down the convention hall (your character has their hands/arms really far behind their back and spread far away from the torso), and when you drink Coconuts your character's shadow inserts said Coconuts into their chest instead of holding them up to their face.
I you want the game and/or are interested in it I would say to put it in your wishlist and wait until it goes on sale because in its current state it's definitely not worth the full $15USD (it was when i got it, but as I said the quality has seemingly declined). The devs announced to have it complete in 2015 and here we are only a month and a few days from 2017 and it's barely changed.
At one point I actually refunded the game because the updates had gotten so bad, but as seen now I have repurchased it and I'm hoping that that's not a mistake.
I still "recommend" the game, but will be giving it a thumbs down in the hopes that the devs will take more notice. When played in very small portions every once in a while (every few weeks or so) it's still a fun game and I'm really putting a lot of faith into the Devs to make the game better. Please don't let me down by 2018, if you do, my review won't be nearly as forgiving as this one.

I saw this game and I passed by it as nothing, another short indie game that would not be long enough to be worth my money, but one day, while scrolling through the many game reviews on youtube, I saw a review for this game. I watched it and they said it was amazing, so I finally decided to give it a try, and it was and still is my favorite game I have ever played.

First things first: This is not a clasic turn-based rpg, let's just get that clear (I have no idea what that other review is talking about). This is styled very much like those games but there is no character progression, no army/party building, no skills, etc. TBS game maybe, rpg definitely not.
This is really a puzzle game using some mechanics from tactics style games. Think of it like playing challenge mode in chess games. There is a board setup and you basically have to figure out a strategy to solve it.
General graphics/audio: Very barebones, you basically get to toggle fullscreen, lighting & shadows (I have no idea why in the hell anybody would turn off lighting and shadows unless they were trying to run this on a rig from 20 years ago), music and sfx. The game is locked to 60fps but I'm not even sure 60 is necessary considering what is happening.
Story: Somewhat amusing story which I did not expect at all. I don't mean an actual plot because there is barely a story, there aren't really characters and stuff but the overarching narrative basically makes fun of tactics style games. Every couple of centuries sky-people who aren't really sky people go into a world where everybody is getting along and just makes them all fight on these square floating islands for their amusement. It's accompanied with little bits of text at the start of every level that are somewhat amusing.
Gameplay: Very straightforward tactics-style mechanics thrown into a puzzle. Units move on a grid, they have basic stats and attack stuff, enemies have movement preferences and if you mouse over them it shows exactly where the enemy will go. Some boards have a very specific way to beat and is basically trial and error. Most of the time a wrong move will ruin everything and you gotta restart or hit the turn back button. One mechanic I'd definitely recommend turning off is the one where when enemies attack your units it pauses the game and you have to click for the attack to go through. Since you can't press the turn back button this serves no real purpose, units move  quickly and there's no actual need to see when the enemy attacks, if it does and you didn't know it was coming odds are you f*cked up.
My main complaint would be the weird difficulty curve(?). With most puzzle games you expect it to start easy and then slowly and consistently ramp up until it is ridiculously hard. With Monstro the difficulty goes up and down, every once in a while you hit a hard level but in between them are levels that are not only much easier but also don't require a specific way to solve (a lot of the easier ones just require you to gather your guys up and wait for the enemy to walk in and get slaughtered).
Overall: Would recommend as a casual strategy/puzzle game. If you are looking for a new Tactics Ogre/Final Fantasy Tactics then this is definitely not for you unfortunately. There is decent enough value for the money, The first Human wing took me about an hour and there is a monster wing and a ++ wing for both races.

First of all, I didn't play the first game.  Secondly, I'm a big fan of traditional tower defense games.  This is definitely not traditional.  You're placing traps in a 3D world and you are a "wizard" dealing damage along the paths of that world.  It seemed like a no brainer to try but a few reviews had put doubt in my mind about the difficulty of the game.  In Orcs Must Die 2 you can play co-op to better deal with the multiple paths the orcs can take.  The reviewers hinted that finishing the game on the later levels is impossible without help.  At first, it seems overwhelming.  I too was starting to believe it was impossible.  The great thing about this game is you can improve the gear and traps you have at your arsenal.  You can replay levels, play endless levels to earn "skulls" (in game currency) for use in acquiring more traps or improving your inventory.   Eventually, with the right strategy and the right traps, the levels go from impossible to a cakewalk.  You feel that sense of accomplishment like you built an impenetrable fortress and laugh at the Orcs for even trying.  I definitely recommend this game for those who are into tower defense games, and yes, you can beat the game solo.

If you've never played a souls game before just like me, then this game is going to be very difficult to get in to. As long as you stick to it until you're at a comfortable point (you can become stronger faster than the game can get harder), the game opens up so much to you with its amazing lore, enemy designs, visuals and music. Every now and then, the game will throw something at you that makes you question your actions, and it can get pretty emotional at times (cough cough Sif and Priscilla).
While the positives far outweigh the negatives later on in the game (once you're familiar with controls and tactics), there are a few drawbacks that can make the game clunky, frustrating and difficult for the wrong reasons, giving off the wrong vibe to new players like myself. I personally think the camera is the worst offendor of this, ocasionally getting locked into a wall during a tight squeeze (Capra Demon fight, getting cornered by Smough's enormous belly, etc). Another thing to note is that the hitbox detection can be pretty annoying, mostly notable in the Iron Golem's grab attack. You could be 2 meters away from his swing, yet you'd snap into his fist and get killed for something you easily would have dodged if the game wasn't built like this.
Negatives aside, the game holds up well even after the years it has been out. Many Souls players seem to favor this one over the others. Highly reccomended, but hang in there for just a few more hours and you'll be hooked.
Also, the game is much better off being played at 60fps with the DSFix found on the community guides. However, some bugs can occur because of the uncap on the frames, such as clipping through the floor when sliding down ladders (very rare) and the occasional jump being impossible to make, as the jump distance is cut by about 20%. This is easily bypassed by hitting backspace in-game to put the game back into 30fps and back to 60 at any time.

Fair warning: if you plan on playing this game as it is on Steam, do yourself a favor and install DSFix in order to fix some issues with it (this is a really crappy PC port of an XBox game, link to DSFix here:
and probably get yourself a controller (unless you want an extra challenge, as the controls of the game aren't conducive to a mounse-and-keyboard setup).
That being said, this is a fantastic game for both old-school RPG fans and people wanting to get into the explosively famous Dark Souls series. If you feel intimidated by its "Prepare to Die" tagline, please don't be; though there is a fair amount of dying and a great deal of challenge with the game, the controls are fairly intuitive and easy to grasp in a surprisingly short amount of time. Should you need help understanding stats, the game even has a handy help tool for you to use. Those who enjoy the combat will find it challenging as well as rewarding, and those who enjoy the lore will find themselves overwhelmed by a world lying in ruins, long past its prime and filled with cynical merchants selling gear as well as noble knights and other characters descending to their own ruin in spite of their skill in combat.
Perhaps one of the most unique aspects of the Dark Souls series is its multiplayer, which I would describe more as "social" than anything else. Interplayer contact is organized by giving players access to an "IP pool" of sorts that increases as the play session goes on, meaning that players have access to more messages from other players, more summon signs, and more opportunities to invade and be invaded as they continue playing for a session (making online play more immersive for long sessions). There is close to no control over which IPs the players come into contact with, so if you prefer solely playing with friends or want to give friends priority in the IP search, there are ways to go about achieving that which can be found online. Interplayer contact is based on which of nine covenants players belong to, which each place emphasis on different aspects of online play (such as PvP, PvE, and Co-op). These covenants are what make the game's social nature function, and allow for unexpected encounters and additional challenges for players.
Since it contains difficulty settings, Dark Souls is still accessible to people who may not consider themselves very good at action-RPGs or video games in general. Don't let the tagline scare you, and allow yourself to be immersed in the dying realm of Lordran and all it has to offer. Praise the Sun my friends! \(^-^)/

Finally, after 54 hours, I beat it. At last. I have quite a few things to say.
I did love playing this game. I adore the level design, the brilliant lore and worldbuilding, the fantastic realisation of some very solid themes of death, glory, the juxtaposition between the majestic and the macabre. I love it on a technical level: while it's not a graphical masterpiece, when you compare it to another action-adventure RPG from the same year, Skyrim, you can see pretty clearly that Dark Souls is much better in terms of graphics (and in terms of almost everything else in my opinion). The sound design is utterly wonderful: careful silences, grand themes, tentative moments of quieter, more somber pieces like Gwyn's theme or the Moonlight Butterfly. And of course, the combat. The combat is slow, deliberate, everything feels weighty and impactful, it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to get good at but once you do you really start to feel the flow of the enemy attacks.
For about two thirds of the game, I was enamoured. I climbed Undead Berg in awe. I trudged through Blighttown with grit and determination. I wandered through Darkroot Garden, loving the mist and the mystery. I dashed through Senn's Fortress after dying in it for the dozenth time. I ended up going back to the Undead Asylum, and fighting the Hydra in Darkroot Basin (which I found... horrifying, utterly genuinely terrifying for some reason) then the one in Ash Lake (my favourite area in the game, just such a numinous indescribable feeling
. And then I plowed through Anor Londo, and met O & S.
This is where the game began to turn for me from an enjoyable feat into a frustrating grind. It was so hard to beat these two that I opted to go back and beat Pinwheel just to get the Rite of Kindling (hilariously easy boss fight by the way
). Then after O&S I went down to the Tomb of Giants, which was maybe the peak of the endgame content for me. Expertly crafted usage of lighting, and a healthy level of challenge. But Nito was kind of a pushover, and it was then I started to realise that the combat system, especially when it came to bosses, is kind of... overly repetitive? For about 80% of enemies, especially in the late game, the best way to fight them is roll through attack, circle strafe around and hit them in the back. This was the Nito fight in a nutshell for me. And every Silver Knight, and Black Knight, and Quelaag and Bell Gargoyles and Taurus and Capra and the list goes on. It wasn't easy, but just kind of boring.
And then I went to the Demon Ruins, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I ♥♥♥♥ing hate the Demon Ruins. The visibility is horrible, the frame rate is bad, the bosses are easy as hell to cheese and if you don't they're incredibly frustrating. The entire design of the area is gross and unappealing to the eye, and not a single regular enemy is unique or interesting (except those many-eyed cone things, those were kinda cool). I don't even know if it was a bug or something but those dino things out in the lava between the boss fight and the bonfire (I could never make out what they were supposed to be because the lighting was so bad) almost never attacked me. And then there's the boss fight.
.
Things looked up a little later though. I enjoyed the Duke's Archives and New Londo, though the former was quite frustatingly hard
and the latter a little short. I loved the Four Kings though, really creative and visually striking.
And then, Gwyn:
One more gripe: the overpowered nature of the lightning spear you pick up in Senn's Fortress (and lightning in general). Almost no enemies in the game have a high resistance to lightning: most are weak to it. So getting a pretty strong spear part way through the game that most enemies are weak to is a bit ridiculous. As long as you have a different weapon for the few encounters where lightning won't win out, this spear seems like an extremely obvious way to go. Put it this way: this spear at +2 was stronger than my Uchi at +8.
Overall though, the early game is more than enough to earn my recommendation, and although the late game is shaky it does have its moments. Dark Souls is well-deserved of its praise, and I would still regard it as one of the finest games I've ever played. It just isn't perfect, and I feel like I should say that to anyone thinking of going into it

I cannot recommend Ryzom highly enough.  It is unique in every way.  Every typical MMORPG mechanic has been given a novel twist and the science-fantasy setting is different from anything else out there.  (There are other science-fantasy MMOs, heck you can call WoW science-fantasy, but Ryzom does it differently.  Essentially, instead of sci-fi elements being added to a fantasy base, fantasy elements are added to a sci-fi base.)
It's one of the few surviving sandbox MMOs.
Roleplay is emphasized and supported through live storyline events where actual human beings basically DM the event and player actions matter.
This is a game that was created with love and you can tell: it's flawed and a little rough around the edges, but the whole experience brings a certain sense of wonder and enchantment.
If you're fond of Planet Explorers, you might find some familiar feelings in Ryzom.
I'd still be playing if I hadn't burned out so hard.
