While some of the visuals and graphics are stunning, and the story is somewhat engaging despite flat-as-cardboard acting performances, the gameplay is jerky, unresponsive, confusing, and.. well, horrible. It fails to deliver any of the excitement that is promised and is frankly just a boring, frustrating mess. It is exactly what you should expect from a console to PC port. A piece of unrealistic eye-candy that does about as much justice to modern air combat as the movie Pearl Harbor did to the battle it is named for.
The controls totally ruin an already bad game. Even though I had selected keyboard/joystick setup for my PC play-through, the functionality of both are a total miss as the support kept bugging out, and the game seemed to keep forgetting the controls that I had mapped for functions. Helecopter control was the absolute worst I have ever seen, even worse than the console version, if you can believe that. The "tutorial" system is still the most intrusive, unhelpful piece of flaming MiG-15 wreckage ever, and doesn't even display the proper keys to be engaged (it displays the gamepad controls left over from the console version). The infamous dogfighting mode is still like fighting in a tunnel and does not give you any sort of freedom of flight movement that is needed on close combat. I couldn't even adjust my rudder to bring my gunsight down onto my banking target. The gunsight (determined by my aircrafts seemingly on-rails AoA) refused to line up on any target despite my constantly trying to wrestle the controls into place.
In the end, the PC port of this game is even WORSE than the console version. I had intended to play this all the way though as I did on console, but after the 3rd mission I found that I was totally unwilling to stomach this "game" again in an even worse version. Uninstalling now to make room for games more worthy of a place on my SSD. The only upside: This silly thing cost me less than a burger at Carl's Jr. (I'd rather have the burger).

Ace Combat was an OK game with a relatively boring story line.
While some might perhaps appreciate the warbirds, I can't say that the selection was amazing, nor that your average coinesseur would be impressed with the selection. The music and sounds were alright, but again, nothing to write home about. As a flying game, this isn't going to be taking back any medals in that department.
My main gripe is with how short this game was - playing for only a couple days, with maybe 30-45 minutes of cutscenes, the majority of that time was spent re-doing annoying parts of missions - not so much annoying due to their difficulty or finesse so much as due to dumb, brokenness of the game itself. After a couple short battles in which you learn the basics of gameplay (read, you learn how simple it is to play), you are introduced to the game's cast and go on a couple, mildly interesting runs to quash some rebels. You quickly learn who the bad-guys are, and from there, its mostly predictable "go kill this there". Hardly any character development, no interesting fights, a lot of 'more of the same' dogfights. Well, almost.
There were a couple levels which were really enjoyable, like the bomber levels and the rail-shooter helicopter level - and the helicopter level at the end. Unfortunately, nearly all the action was spent spinning in circles, auto-locking the enemy in a warbird. But each one of these levels had no other level like them in the whole game - maybe development time was limited, but it didn't feel so much like a game as a prototype experiment with a couple test modes to play. And most of the air-levels were 'more of the same' ones - chase flocks of 'bandits' around, in a methodical manner, take them out one by one, while your team sits around getting maybe one kill for every five that you get. Your team, which usually consists of a single air squadron that, guess what, flies around in circles. This got so bad, the final level feels downright anti-climactic, since you end up just in another 'more of the same' fights, with less actual birds than in most of the rest of the game - or at least it seemed that way. Sure, at least you get to go one-on-one with your archnemesis, but beyond that battle being difficult, the game finishes with a weak wheezle. I kinda think the team fired their game designer, because I don't see much evidence that a game was designed at all, and its not just some bad jet-fighter simulator.
So is it any good as a simulator then, perhaps? Maybe, the actual flying seems to work ok and you can pretend to fight other jets. Five stars there. But the mechanics, as mentioned are somewhat broken. First off, very annoying, you cannot turn off hints. If, for whatever reason, you need to redo part of a level, or even if you just want to replay that level, you must have your fun interupted for 5 seconds by instructions written for a five year old. Yes, yes pressing that button might be helpful. First time's good, 10th time, not so much. Not to mention, the instructions given are garbage - they are simple enough, but given the highly actionable nature of the game, it would be much better to give a visual representation of the maneuver and let the player practice than to present a paragraph of text which doesn't mean a whole lot to someone in the middle of a battle. Though, as I said, they are pretty simple anyways, and you will pick them up during play, but better to scrap the instructions as they are entirely in my opinion.
There were also a couple of quirks in the game; in the second bomber run, after your initial bombing streak, when you switch to guided penetration missiles, the game will run you through one of its 'guided runs', and then confusingly position you so that you can't see any of the targets, as well as start you out going too fast. Yes, its relatively simple to fix this, but its a 'guided run', why on earth is it like this if you're going to force me into a pseudo rail-shooter mode? Its not even like you need to alternate height. Secondly, in the same level, actually, during the ICBM chase mode, if you fail to catch the missile the first time, you will be autospawned and given 3 seconds to figure out what to do. Given the instructions 'catch the missile' and the results for failing to do so 'it is out of your altidue range', it is in no way obvious that 'accelerate at breakneck speed after the missile' is the solution. Finally, again, in the same (poorly desinged) level, in the third section of the first bombing run, the solution is a bit at random, as the vehicles will change direction at random, and sometimes escape, yet they count towards a failure. Not technically a bug, and as there is a solution, its just challenging and not broken, but wondering why you keep failing that run despite carpeting everything the first three times, is a bit annoying.
All in all, it could have been a better game - fix some quirks, add a bit of depth and storyline, and this could have gone from 'OK game' to 'Good Game', but its nowhere close in my books.
For the price that I got this, 7 bucks, I'm out no more than the price of a bad film at the theatre, but I'd still not recommend it unless you have nothing better to do or play. And that's pretty unlikely.

When I heard the news that Guilty Gear Xrd -SIGN- was coming to PC, I was a bit skeptical. I am a huge fan of fighting games and didn't want this to be a horrific port. ArcSys dashed out ALL doubts I had. While I can't yet speak for the online portion of the game, the offline / single-player experience is as smooth as can be.
For $24 (as of this review), you get the full game (obviously), but you also recieve ALL DLC for no additional charge (at least that's how it was for me :p). This includes 3 additional characters, all costume colors, and all system voices to change the announcer voice to that of your favorite character! The game also has MAGNIFICENT art style (in my honest opinion of course). The game's music is also fantastic (and as a side note, the creator of the game is also the composer for all the music. How cool is that?!).
The only "con" I have is that when you play the tutorial or challenge mode, the onscreen inputs change from the keyboard's keys to the Xbox buttons every couple of seconds (if you're using a controller / fightstick). But this is a simple fix as the game has an option to switch the input display from the Xbox / keyboard buttons to the abbrieviations of the attacks as they are called in the game.
So even though this review isn't really an in-depth one, I can honestly say I recommend this game to anyone looking for an anime game, (or in my case) a new fighting game to play. 10/10
****EDIT****
After looking up information about the PC release, I have now found out why I have access to all of the DLC. For the first week of this game being on the steam store, you will get ALL the DLC for no extra charge.

I'm not going to say I'm the best or godlike at this game; I'm certainly not a Momochi, Xian, Infiltration or Daigo, but I don't believe I'm the worst either. This game has been my lifeblood for the past 5-6 years from Xbox 360 to PC. That being said, I'll miss this game when Street Fighter V drops and/or everyone inevitably moves on.
I'll say this much: never before has a game exuded so many moments of pure saltiness out of me, and never have I been so happy to get back on a game after some training room practice an hour to, at most, a day later. From the bodyings of my friends and me getting duffed by them to the intense, pure hype tournament moments from the professional players that are, quite literally, world warriors, the Street Fighter IV series from Super Street Fighter IV, when I started playing, to Ultra, has been worth every penny I've spent on it.
It can be frustrating if you're new, though, due to the execution barrier, so if you don't have time to put into the game to practice your spacing, execution, punishes and whatnot, you're going to get blown up, have a bad time, and will most likely quit within a week. If that's the case, just wait for
. That one's supposed to draw in newer and younger people alike.
Also, as with all games, some characters may be a bit stronger than others. With 44 characters, that's to be expected. However,
Player input was taken into account for this iteration of the game, and all characters seem, at the very least, viable to play at a tournament level and win with. So, don't be afraid to pick your favorite and have some fun.
That's about all I've got to say.
If you're used to Street Fighter, come from 3rd Strike or something, and you somehow don't already have this, get it. If you're new and looking to get into the game, get on that
when it drops.

I already own this game on PS3 where the base game was $30 on sale and I had to buy all the extra content which came out to be about $60 total. If it was a 1:1 copy of the ps3 I would already say this is a steal.
Gameplay:I feel that the game might not be as refined as streetfighter but amongst the anime figther sub-genre GGxrd should be the mold used from now on. The controls are fluid, the action is fast and the specials have that cinematic punch which makes them feel amazing when well executed. Even for a casual player like me the gameplay is challenging yet enjoyable. Unlockables aren't content blocks yet rather minor avatar cosmetics or sounds (aside from the unlockable characters which are already unlocked as of now).
Graphics: Old sprite based games look like poop when upscaled to 1440p and above. Even modern 2d sprite based fighters aspire for the 720p-1080p range. This game looks great at any resolution and it runs SMOOTH on older hardware (60 fps easily). Somehow they got the game to almost always have that distinct anime look without the jaring animation transitions which many cartoon graphics games have.
Price: The game just came out on PC even though its been out for over a year on console. Many publishers would market their game at $60 because its new to the platform regardless of when it originally came out. The $30 price tag is extremely fair for getting the game and all the DLC content that consoles have.
Conclusion: Arc System Works is starting to become one of my favorite game developers. Now that they publish their own games on PC we are getting high quality releases with full content at reasonable prices while the game is still relevant. I'm hoping they look to further break the trend of price gouging on fighters by releasing the next installment, -Revalator-, for a discounted price for owners of GGXrd -Sign-.

Aaah this mess and what a mess it is.
Back when The Banner Saga: Factions launched there was so much talk. Talk about ripping off the kickstarter backers (which they weren't ripped off they just never bothered to read), talk about the lawsuit for use of the word 'saga', talk about how the game was so perfectly balanced that it risked becoming stale.
Now no one talks about The Banner Saga: Factions anymore.
Looks like that last one came true.
First of all this is a mini-game, a subgame if you will. The point of this game is solely to PvP so do not confuse it with the main product and likewise this review is for this game not the main game itself.
TBS:F is like a game of chess...With only 4 pieces. But wait, each of those pieces come in 3(4) flavours so their is variety!
Except not really. Confused? We gotta go deeper Leo!
You have your typical 3 classes, you know Tank, damage dealer, how does it go again? shield smasher? Yeah thats it. Whats a healer?
Now without sounding like an instruction manual every unit has 2 bars, a health bar and an armor bar. armor reduces damage but the lowest amount you can do is 1hp. Be warned however that losing your armor is a big deal and a low armor or armorless unit will be cut down in short order! This makes games very methodical. Do you snipe hits for 1 damage each trying to score an early kill, or do you whittle down armor and then deal devastating damage to quickly mop up and win? Afterall their are no healers so every match is a war of attrition!
It works out really well and I can't do it justice with words alone, it is a simple idea that could have gone really badly but here it is balanced
.
Of course not all things are created equally in any video game and this one is no different so what sounds like an awesome and rivetting gameplay experience ends as a battle of patience as a losing player with 1 archer can still run away and then pick your remaining units off and trust me, they will. So every team has archers because being dumb doesn't pay off on the battlefield and most matches become mirror matches. Remember when I compared this game to chess? Imagine introducing a new piece into a game of chess. Imagine the sheer balance upset and new tactics that would bring to the table?! This game suffers that exact same issue because the balance is so fine, it is too fine and very easy to upset that balance.
So what happened?
It stagnated, what did you expect? A competitive game needs a lot to keep the crowds coming back. Look at DOTA, new champions every month is it? Streetfighter, new iterations just about every 2 years. This game? Not a damn thing since release.
The music is fine as are the sound effects and honestly who even gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥ The music has to be great for people to sit up and take notice and here it is just above average. But the art, this game is graphically a piece of art. Playing this game is like visiting an art gallery it just looks so good!
But you play a game to be entertained (usually) and this game is fleeting fun. Their is fun to be had don't get me wrong but when you decide to shake it up a bit and really get into the game you will realize their isn't much more to it to explore, what you see is what you get. So I can't recommend this game.

This game started as a massive frustration to play. I played OpenTTD and Train Fever for the first time in the last two weeks, and having never played any transport management games before I was quite surprised to find the much older OpenTTD far superior..at first. My first impression of Train Fever was that it was in an alpha state with too many bugs and missing or poorly designed issues that could have been resolved with more time in development and testing. However I stuck at it and after a 5 or 10 hours of effort I became a little more familiar with the game's ethos and foibles, and am really enjoying it.
Pros:
+ Graphics are fairly good
+ Frame rates ok but become slower the larger your network becomes
+ Fills in a much needed gap in the train management genre
+ Addictive management elements
+ Large amount of very detailed models
+ Vehicles slowly introduced in a historical manner as the years pass
+ Demand must be met before supply can be achieved is good for realism
+ The whole system you set up is interconnected in a realistic way, any problems in the demand/supply chain are of your own making. There is a wonderful 'butterfly effect' to your actions so you have to think carefully before you cancel your old routes/vehicles.
Cons:
- Cargo appears to 'walk' on its own which was annoying at first and initially made no sense why it would walk and ignored my routes. After a few hours it became evident what I was doing wrong and what the game mechanism trying to do, it became very useful in identifying what cargo was doing.
- No good tutorials. This is a massive problem as you then have to spend a lot of time on the web searching for basic underlying game mechanisms. Compare this to Transport Tycoon where you have to do the same but at least with that game you end up finding useful information and climbing up the learning curve in an interesting way, whereas with Train Fever its more of a frustration.
- Menus are a little cumbersome. Some features like the ESCAPE key just don't work to close individual menus, meaning you have to click DELETE to close ALL menus which is annoying.
- Laying track and roads could be better.
Neither here nor there:
- Cannot demolish some roads without mods, but enabling mods to bypass them would kill steam achievements. Conversely I guess it adds realism to how you would lay track, but I feel the game needs to emphasise a little more that it wants to encourage you on the realism aspects - otherwise it just seems like the game logic is being weird. Again a tutorial would have solved this.
In conclusion, the game is definitely worth buying if you like this genre, but be prepared to spend a few hours being frustrated at first climbing up that learning curve, it then becomes very enjoyable to play.
When Transport Fever is released I suspect it will surpass this in every way, Transport Fever may still be worth playing if the price is dropped as otherwise just wait for Transport Fever. I recommend playing Train Fever however as you will appreciate Transport Fever even more!

I feel like this game has a great deal of potential, however it is limited by a few major blocks.
Respawning and then corpse despawning. I tested starving to death at my base location. By the time I made it back to my body (about 15 minutes) it was gone, and only my hatchet remained.
I understand a game that has consequences for death, I do not have issue with that. However to die and have to completely restart the game, that sounds a bit extreme. Sure you can place a storage box, but it only has 10 slots in it. You are going to be required to then stash items around in the world and unless you host your own server for $$, you are going to have to deal with people stealing or perhaps the game just crunching those items.
The base building is interesting but I would like to see this with a snap grid. I like that you can easily place and pick up structure item, but not having a snap grid is frustrating.
I also am very against not having a local host or single player option. I have no desire to play on public servers and have my♥♥♥♥♥♥wrecked while I am at work (yawn), or have to pay $1 per slot to host a server so I can play with a select group of friends. I understand a major focal point of the game is PVP, but it's also survival and I'd rather survive against the NPCs than PCs. Co-op vs PVP, the eternal struggle.
My biggest gripe is that the trailer for the game is about 80 times more interesting than the actual game is. I see it has a lot of potential but I would not recommend it, even as a joke, in the current state.

The Banner Saga: Factions is easy to pickup, but offers incredibly deep gameplay. The real strategy comes in deciding on the composition of your team, and whether you are going to play defensively or offensively, focus on ranged or melee, have one or two powerful units or spread the ranks of your team evenly.
I've played games that are outright brawls, and games that have been about cautious manuevering trying to outflank the other team. I would recommend giving it a fair try over a number of days as durng my first few hours I almost quit because the combat seemed too chaotic and I didn't appreciate the nuances.
I really like the variety of classes, and love that some of the classes I initially regarded as weak have become my favourites. In fact I would say there are no weak classes and any unit can be good if you use it appropriately.
This game is not in any way pay to win; each side builds a team of equal level based on character rank, so battles are evenly matched. So for instance a rank 6 team could be 1+1+1+1+1+1 or 0+0+1+1+2+2 etc. The payment options just allow you to build that team faster (or even instantly with enough purchased renown), so that does not give any advantage within a skirmish.
I thoroughly recommend this to anyone who likes turn based tactical battles where skill is the overriding factor.

A Foretold Affair is a very uniqe Otome Game, and I instantly fell in love with it.
It offers three different love interests (male, female and agender) and each one of them is quite adorable in their own way. You decide which one is your future spouse at the beginning of the game, as you see the marriage in a vision of your future. However, even though your marriage is foretold doesn't mean you haven't go through some hardships until the day finally comes...
- The wiritng is very well and it's easy to get attached to the characters (including the MC)
- It has a very beautiful and atmospheric soundtrack that suits the mood of the game
- The characters and background are lovely as well
- The wold of the game is unique, with their own society and rules (even though the main focus lies on the relationships!)
Even though the main story stays the same, your choices pretty much alter the dialogues, so it offers great replay value, at least once for every love interest. So the game is quite lengthy.
You can easily see how much love and effort the developer put into this game, and it deserves much more love and attention. If you are a fan of otome games, I would recommend this game.

On the one hand, the art, story and characters are excellent. A lot of time and effort obviously went into this project. There were some minor bugs and typos, but nothing too distracting. Completely worth the money.
On the other hand, I could never quite get a handle on the MC, Buffalo Seer. Sometimes I loved her, sometimes I couldn't stand her, sometimes I was just... confused. She kept zigging when I wanted or expected her to zag. Also, the route setup felt strange; as the game went on, there seemed to be less and less interaction with January, which made me very sad. A Foretold Affair is an excellent and entertaining story where the romance is flipped on its head: rather than wonder who you'll end up with, you have to convince the person you KNOW you're going to marry that this is for real, all while dodging bounty hunters and traversing a floating island in the sky.
The characters are all entertaining and have great personalities, and, in an interesting twist, there is no restriction on the kind of relationship you can have. Whether you represent your main character, Seer, as a man, woman, or gender neutral, you can have a relationship with whichever of the three love interests you want.
The art style fits well with the steam punk theme of the story, and the character designs are great.
The music is great, and really works with each scene, helping you get into the mood of the story every step of the way.
Overall a great experience so far, and I'm eager to go through each route and see how things play out!

If you like Terraria and space-age games, then you'll love Starbound. This game is very short but fun, and it encourages you to go and explore different planets to advance the storyline. The bosses are a bit challenging, but once you know how they fight, it isn't that bad.
Once you've finished the tutorial quests, you're free to explore the galaxy. You have the option to build structures around different planets, transform barren planets into forests, and mine deep underground for those sweet loot. I choose to build. Along with building, you can also turn those structures into settlements and have people move in. You can benefit a lot from having a small town, as well.
There's a bunch of cool races you can choose from, so you aren't limited to just humans. I have taken a liking to Novakids. The races can range from Japanese Fish People to Medieval Robots, and that's not all of the races. There's also birds. All of the characters in this game are unique and very fun to talk with.
Or, if you don't care about building and exploring, you can always make music. Starbound gives players instruments that are hidden across every star, and you can use them to play your favorite meme songs or play something classical. Group up with friends, and you can start your own band.
But wait, there's more.
Even the main menu's music is beautiful. The game has a variety of calming music when you're exploring the planet, and it makes you want to explore some more to listen and relax. I actually want to sit down and have the game on idle as I study or draw to the music. If it wasn't for the gameplay, I'd use Starbound as an excuse to play music. But, as I said before, the music encourages you to explore.
The game's not also about fighting. You can also fish and dig up for fossils, or tend your own farm for food to help you survive. The more you advance in the game, the more items you can get.
And if you aren't into those and prefer being fashionable, then there's always that option. Your character can dress up and can still be powerful. Or you can ignore the story completely and just play dressup in this game. Nobody is going to question your choices.
Overall, I'd rate this game a 9.8/10. The story is a bit short, but everything else is amazing.

==========
... Ryzom was designed and developed in 2002/2003 and released in 2004. As Internet connections were very low bandwidth then, in comparison to the present day, it was decided that, to minimise the bandwidth requirements, Ryzom would use UDP instead of TCP connectivity. This reduces the bandwidth considerably but in recent years unfortunately some routers and some ISPs have taken to dropping UDP packets because they are not a high priority. As you are experiencing so many disconnections and the client hanging frequently, I suspect that you might be having this problem. I would recommend that you check your router settings and allow all UDP packets and also speak with your ISP to find out whether they are dropping UDP packets as a matter of course.

After playing this game over a couple times and finally beating it, thanks to a guide on the discussions section, I've come to realize that a lot of your skills don't really matter in this game. There are certain scripted situations of the story that require you to have a certain skill at a certain level, otherwise, you're forced automatically into a bad end.
SPOILERS AHEAD
This makes your skill choices seem very narrow and selective on other playthroughs of the game. In the end, your skills don't really matter and you don't really get enough time to develop the ones that would help you pass a lot of the skill checks in the game.
Skills aside, the game is pretty fun. I turned my character into a angry warmonger (only for her to die in the spoiler scenario above) that crushed a rebellion. The art design of the characters, save for the main character seem to be a little mediocre and just creepy at times. (The king's mouth reminds me of the "That makes me moist" old lady meme.) The lore and characters of the game are pretty forgettable, save for a couple recurring characters (notably the main character), as they thrust the names of random kingdoms and people you have yet to meet (if even meet at all) with lengthy titles at you from the very start. Being married or single in the game doesn't really matter, and doesn't seem to really affect the game much, if at all. It has the potential to be a really good game, but in my opion, it doesn't quite make it and ultimately left me feeling unsatisfied.
Bottom Line:
Do I suggest you buy this game? Unfortunately, no. It has a lot of potential, but in the end, it falls flat of my expectations for such a game.
For those of you who want a simple pros and cons list of this game from my personal opinion, here it is:
PROS
A lot of skills to develop.
Its fun trying to get the main character in the right mood to develop select skills faster.
Its satisfying when you DO pass a skill check during the story and it influences it a bit.
Unlocking costumes for each skill set is interesting.
The main character is super kawaii desu-desu.
The "morning" classes remind me of a portion the Totino's commercial by Tim and Eric:
CONS
A lot of skills to develop and not enough time to fully develop the majority of them.
Forgettable characters and kingdom names/lore.
Linear story the requires certain skills developed otherwise unavoidable dead end.
Choices in skill outside story-related skill checks don't really matter.
Somewhat mediocre-feeling character art design.
Lumen is important to story, yet can be easily overlooked due to choices at the start of the game.
Doesn't fulfill its potential.
Not enough tentacle monsters.

While those interested in the burgeoning zombie survival sandbox genre have no shortage of titles to partake of, those seeking a solo experience have been left with few options, particularly on the PC. Multiplayer games inspired by the Arma 2 mod, Dayz, seem to be popping up everywhere but the appreciable potential for a singleplayer game that focuses on PvE rather than PvP has on the platform gone unfulfilled. State of Decay looks to cash in on this opening, offering up a sizable chunk of game world populated by zombies, AI survivors and lots of loot-filled buildings to scour. While there are more than a few rough edges in State of Decay and a lack of the heart-stopping tension found in Dayz, there is an engrossing and enjoyable game here with a lot of things to do given the low cost of entry.
The start of the game sees you fighting zombies and completing simple fetch quests for a small group of survivors garrisoned in a ranger station. You are introduced to the combat and looting mechanics, but these only garnish the more engaging aspects of the experience. Soon you find yourself entwined with a larger group of survivors holed up in a church just outside a small town. This will serve as your base throughout most of the game as you earn the trust of fellow survivors, fortify your encampment and go out in search of supplies. Ensuring the well being of this group of survivors is ultimately what keeps State of Decay moving forward, as it provides good incentive for you to engage in the gameplay tasks which without context would be fairly banal.
After the opening sequence of the game, the constant flood of missions that you are informed of via radio chatter take a back seat to exploration and looting. Ensuring that your group of survivors have enough food and medical supplies will be the most pressing issue, and can be remedied by searching through houses which may contain zombies, supplies or occasionally survivors who can be convinced to join your group. You can climb tall objects and 'survey' the surrounding area, revealing locations of interest. Once inside a building, objects which contain items must be searched, and this takes several seconds to complete. Whether you try and sneak around avoiding combat with the walking undead, quietly scavenging what you need, or go in swinging to clear a house of its decrepit occupants before searching for goodies remains entirely up to you. You can radio home to request an AI survivor come out and pick up the supplies for you, but this requires clearing a location of all zombies first.
If you decide to clear a location of zombies before poking around for loot, the combat is functional but uninspired. With a melee weapon you swing away until either you run out of stamina, the zombies' heads explode or your weapon breaks. If you manage to knock a zombie down you can finish it off with a brutal swing of your chosen instrument of death, but most of the challenge lies in ensuring you don't get surrounded or backed into a corner. Firearms are straightforward and satisfying to use, although ammunition isn't readily available and firing a unsilenced weapon will attract nearby zombies, meaning they are best used only when the situation gets out of hand. Sneaking around zombies is a viable method, particularly when dealing with larger groups, and can be accomplished by takedowns from behind, distracting zombies with objects or using firearms with home-made silencers that only last for a set number of shots.
The zombies themselves shamble around convincingly enough, at least until they get stuck in the terrain which happens all too frequently. The undead will hop through windows, climb fences and grab you from behind as they endeavor to end your life. Special zombie types eventually start showing up, which range from the bullet-proof SWAT zombies to ones that explode in a cloud of poisonous gas when killed to hulking beasts that charge like bulls and sponge up a lot of firepower before going down.
If you do get killed, which happens very infrequently, rather than reverting to an old save you will start playing as another survivor in your group. It is in your best interest to keep survivors alive for as long as possible since you gradually gain passive improvements to a character over time, such as improved stamina, melee damage and increased health. If you are out and about with one character for too long, their maximum stamina will be decreased until they go back to the base and rest. When you do this, you will take control of a different survivor, meaning you will end up playing as many different characters throughout the game.
While the explorable area in State of Decay isn't huge, you can enter and drive vehicles left lying around which are all conveniently unlocked with keys in the ignition. Driving a car feels responsive and light almost to a fault; if you crash into an object at speed your vehicle will go flying in some pretty crazy ways. Running over zombies is a very effective way of killing them, although cars will become damaged in the process. Zombie hordes roam the streets, and running into them at full speed will be as damaging to your vehicle as it will be to the shambling flesh-eaters.
The amount of time you spend on State of Decay is linked directly to how invested you become in the well-being of your survivor group as well as your tolerance for repetition given there is no real end to the game but the random objectives start repeating. It takes a good amount of time and scavenging to fully upgrade your survivor camp with an infirmary, vehicle-repair station and watchtowers among other fortifications, but if you don't buy into the well being of your AI dependants you will struggle to care enough to go through the trouble of collecting all the required materials.
If you have been looking for a zombie-themed survival sandbox but don't want to contend with bandits and hackers in online games, State of Decay will scratch that itch. The lack of tension in exploration is vindicated by fairly complex mechanics surrounding the well-being of a group of survivors you must watch over. State of Decay succeeds in its ambitions and despite some rough edges provides a compelling open world experience.

This is the game you want if you are looking for a game with great combat that is endless. The game's story doesn't really even cross your mind when playing, I spent hours killing Captains and Warchiefs alongside branding them to fight along my side.
The game's Nemesis System allows you to either kill Warchiefs / Captains or Brand them to join your side. It adds hours.

Get the full bundle on sale.
The main campaign seems rather short; you can plow through the entire game pretty quickly if you avoid the extraneous side quests. As I write I'm not quite 30 hours in and I've been putting off the final quest for a couple hours already.
There are extra game modes, none of which immediately appeal to me, but I may end up trying them. They also look like extraneous side-quests though, so I don't entirely see the point.
That said, it's not a bad game. If you've played the Arkham series, it has similar combat, but much faster-paced (enemies will tend to invade your space much faster than the goons in Arkham do, no milling around waiting to see if countering is convenient for Mr. Wayne no not yet okay I'll give you a couple more seconds). Ground finishers are tough to pull off because enemies will often try to hit you during, and even the upgrade that makes them quicker doesn't always help with that. It's far more active. There's also enemies outside the main melee who will throw spears or fire arrows at you and it's very possible to get overwhelmed.
It's not a bad thing, though. It fits with the game: you don't want to attract the entire army because you will die. Which is fine; the captain and warchief system makes things more interesting. If you get killed, you don't reload from checkpoint; the person who killed you gets a promotion and a power-up, and the orcs fight each other for dominance. You then have to take them out, and they get replaced. It allows for some fun self-imposed challenges such as trying to take out as many of them as possible. The achievements help give some ideas about that, too, and I'm no achievement hunter.
Ultimately it's short but a lot of fun. You can pick it up while waiting for your pie to cook, play a bit, and then quit out without losing any progress.
There are some weird issues with lightning turning the landscape rainbow-colored, which made me worry my graphics card was melting, but apparently that's... "normal".
So there you are. I wasn't impressed when this game came through the queue but it was better than I expected it to be.

I have always been a huge fan of the Ace Combat series, but this game is a huge let-down.  I will disagree that the DFM system is necessary to take down the Target Leads like many of the other reviews have stated, but the enemy forces the mode far too frequently to be realistic or to make the harder difficulties even remotely enjoyable.
Attempting to bait enemies away from a furball is next to impossible unless they are not a main target.  Main targets remained locked together in a mess on one side of the battlefield and you are forced to go into it to get anything done and that results in constant missile dodging and lock-ons from the enemy and being forced into DFM by two enemies at a time at every moment.  The AI pilots on your side are useless and pretty much never get kills or even assist in combat, unlike in HAWX.  Their only purpose is as a distraction for the enemy and they don't even do that well.
In general, I enjoyed the game up until the obvious betrayal of the Russians.  Many reviewers have said that the storyline is forgettable, but, again, I would have to disagree.  While predictable, the story should interest anyone with a good understanding of military and how warfare is engaged in.  The multiplayer seems to be where this game shines and what it was intended for, because I am completely finding the campaign difficult to enjoy solo.  Perhaps in co-op it would be more fun.
A patch to the AI is definitely necessary to enjoy the campaign in this game.  Fortunately, playing multiplayer seems to feel like a much more realistic combat scenario than the BS you go through in the campaign storyline.  I will still recommend this game to people.  On lower difficulties, the game is fun and worth going through, but since higher difficulties are necessary for some of the unlocks, you won't be able to get everything like that.  Multiplayer will be a rewarding experience all around, though more people need to buy into the game so that there is more population available for multiplayer.

Note:  As of this review, I've not played the single player version, The Banner Saga.
This game is a very simple turn-based brawler.  In terms of pure mechanics, I'd say it plays like a stripped down X-COM: EU/EW, minus perma-death.  Or like viking flavored chess.  Of course, both of these examples are simplifications.
I really enjoy the balance of the gameplay.  Even though it's pure PVP, I've never felt cheated, which IMO is unusual for a competitive multiplayer game.  There's only a limited stock of different units, part of why the game is so balanced.
On the other hand, limited unit type means limited unit variation, which is unfortunate.  I've come to understand that besides not including enemy faction units (the dredge) from the single player, there is at least one more viking unit missing.
Additionally, you earn Renown (your currency and XP) at a slow rate, clearly to induce you to go to the shop and spend real money.  However, paying doesn't grant access to anything that anyone else can except for skins and extra renown.
While I've spent a shameful amount of time on this game, I have a proportionately substantial team to show for it and I haven't paid a dime.  Unlike other F2Ps where I wondered "Well what was the point?" when I finally logged off.

It's free.  It's balanced and fun.  It's rewarding and beautiful to look at.  I fully recommend giving it a try.

Playing Night in the Woods, I'm reminded of a literature class from years ago, where-in the instructor commented on ancient Greek mythology and plays - Namely, catharsis of spectators through the tragic.
Night in the Woods isn't necessarily tragic - Tragic things do happen, but so do hopeful things.  And humorous things,  And depressing things.  It's sad, and uplifting, and delightful in all of the beautiful darkness that plays out through the 12 or so hours of play (I've only played through once, mind you, and though the end result is generally the same, there's a few A/B paths you can take that influence ending dialogue - I'm waiting for the Weird Autumn edition coming December 13th.)
It is also wonderfully, wondefully cathartic.  There's a peculiar familiarity of a small town on the decline and well past its prime, inhabited by rose-tinted elders and outward-looking youths, and the aimless uncertainty of the young adults protagonist Mae and her cadre of associates, that just resonates with at least this player.  Enough good things cannot be stated about this game and its "hits too close to home" conversations, subject matter, and content (barring elements of the latter half of the game, fortunately!)
And of course, there's the utterly sublime soundtrack - There's seemingly a unique song for every screen.  Every. Single. Screen.  And more oft than not, even the ones you're not partial to you can at least recognize as being -good.-  Plus the songs Weird Autumn and Die Anywhere Else are both ridiculously apropos to the game content and make for excellent fan covers.  The soundtrack is also an excessively worthwhile purchase.
In fewer simple words, Night in the Woods (and its soundtrack) is a wildly enthusiastic five out of five.  Ten out of ten.  Two thumbs way, way up.  And so on.

State of Decay is a 3rd person post apocalyptic zombie sandbox survival game in which you lead a group of survivors in an end of the world all hell broken loose zombie world. I have not played other "hardcore" zombie games like Day Z, but I will say this is a very fun game. It's got an arcady feel to it in the driving around department, but I will say it also has a more hardcore like side to it. You have to balance alot of stuff, between scavenging supplies, doing missions, and other things that roll along those lines. Did I also mention that some of these things are timed and you will barely (or won't at all) have the time to do them all? Don't fret too much, all the ones you don't have time to due because they expire are not part of the main plot and these missions are randomly generated (which also mean replayability). Also you have to get enough materials to keep your base going. I can't say what happens if you run out, probably nothing good. Another thing is perma death, your character dies and you have to use another one. Bringing me to my next point in this game, there are alot of charcters, and you can use (control and be that character) all of your survivors as a fighting/gather mechanism. Another thing, there is a HUGE amount of guns in this game. There is probably a number somewhere but this game has many guns you can use. This doesn't mean that you will find them easily, it just means that your chances of having ALL of the same gun won't happen, although I have found having 2 of the same model of gun has happened a few times. You have many diffrent types of ammo, .22 .40, 5.56, 7.62, .50 just to name a few. Ammo is no easy thing to find, especially when you have alot of people using the same ammo type. This is strictly a single player game, there is not planned (nor do I think there will be) a multiplayer or a co-op. Also the game doesn't stop when you stop playing it, you'll log back on the next day and find out that your survivors have been busy surviving while you have been doing stuff in the real world.
A few possible negatives, I suppose the lack of multiplayer may be a bit of turn off to some. Alot of dialog is reused, but isn't noticeable for at least a few hours of gameplay. There are only about 10 or so voice actors so that kind of falls on the last point. If your a perfectionist that has to get everything and do everything right and do it 100%, you may be disapointed. You simply won't get to do every single mission before it expires, sooner or later you will die with a character, you will fail a mission, although I will say that is part of what makes this game unique.
All in all that's essentially as much as I can think of at the moment to put into a short(ish?) review of this game. My personal 10 cents is that this is a really fun game that you should pick up, whether you wait for a sale or just buy it and (if you want) all the DLC, that's up to you.

State of Decay is a delightful game to play. It does have replay value when it comes to the main story, Lifeline, and Breakdown. Now I do have a few complaints, however, but my overall view on the game is still good.
The first and foremost complaint would be that there is no co-op. Of course what they did do for it as a substitute is use the in-game AI characters as your partners (the player can ask another member from the home base/community to come watch your back). I do like that idea, but they could have had the option to also have 2-4 player co-op.
My second reason would be that there's not really any sort of dynamic weather system in the game. It would of course add to the atmosphere a little and make it seem slightly more like a realistic world, but the overall game is, of course, not a simulator. I just think that, in my opinion, dynamic weather would make the game a little more interesting in a way. Like the rain could affect the zombies somehow or the rain could cause some flooding down in Marshall. Or perhaps some snowy, cold weather that affects everyone. And fog which affects how far you see, so you can't see your enemies (zombies) coming as soon as you want.
And the final reason would be a gas system. You know, for the vehicles. And I know in Lifeline there is a gas system for the generator, but that's only until you upgrade it into a solar powered generator. You, as the player, probably will use cars a lot throughout the game, so why not add in a gas system? Because how I see it, gas looks like the last resource you'll have left over that you'll have the most of.
Now that's all I have to say about this game. And those reasons above don't really ruin the game for me and make me hate it, I just think it'll add to the experience and make it better. (Well, perhaps not the co-op for some because some people might have some troll-ish friends that'll like.... bring hordes to you, or leave you to battle with the mutated zombies, or even make sure you have to go a long distance just to get a car.)

Very little to do, the AI (particularily the pathfinding) is essentially broken, no ability to control vehicles or lines in any way beyond stopping or starting specific vehicles, your control over track/item placement is sketchy at best.
A nice illustration of the AI issues is how trains treat unavailable sections of rail.  If you segment your rail into sections like normal, only the section with the other train on it is seen as unavailable.  This is fine.  You build a parallel rail with a crossing immediately before or after the signal for the blocked section, your trains wont divert onto the parallel line, because they are programmed to drive straight up to the edge of the blocked section of rail and simply wait for it to become available again.
Its made even wierder by the fact road vehicles and road lines automatically adjust themselves to available roads, so the engine would be capable of making the trains divert, they just decided not to.
But yeah, at that point there is literally nothing you can do other than building an entirely seperate other line for each train, which isnt that big of a deal in game since you have more money than you can use, but it is just obnoxious.

You've probably heard all the negativity about this game by now. How DFM ruined the game because no skill is needed; a casual QTE click fest that dishonors the Ace Combat franchise. I wouldn't know because this is the first Ace Combat game I've played. But you know what? I haven't had this much fun flying since Strike Commander. A very immersive experience. And yes, I got shot down often while learning the controls. This game requires skill, perhaps not the kind of skill required of the other Ace Combat games, but skill nonetheless. I'm not a hardcore flight sim enthusiast by any means, but I've done my fair share of simulated flying, from biplanes to X-wings.
This game is not playable for me with keyboard and mouse in the dogfight sections; a gamepad is required. I use an old PS2 controller connected to a USB adapter with buttons remapped by X360CE. In the doorgunner and helicopter section, keyboard and mouse worked the best for me. Yes, I found them fun too. A minigun that doesn't overheat is just what I wanted for mindless shooting fun. The graphics in the gmae are decidedly not cutting edge, being rather low-res in parts, but it all looks perfectly convincing in the middle of combat.
I'm knocking out this review before the current sale ends in case someone needs to have another opinion before making a purchase. I thought about it all weekend, watching a ton of gameplay videos on YouTube. It was a lot more fun playing the game myself than watching those videos.

At first glance, this game seems to be your run-of-the-mill girly visual novel, however this is not the case. Long Live the Queen is,  in my opinion, is a fun and almost addictive simulation/strategy game, inside a visual novel. You do not have to be female to enjoy this tittle, the plot and choices are far from girly (I doubt many little girl games have assassins, treachorous family, and murder). Just because the main character is female and has pink hair doesn't mean the game is only female oriented, it's like saying Tomb Raider is for preschool girls because there's a GIRL!!!
As for gameplay, the mechanics are easy to learn, picking classes to earn experience in certain traits (like swords and history) and then having to use these skills in scenarioes. You can play as a loved queen, or just like a character from Game of Thrones, either being beloved or feared by all. Unlike a dating sim, failing these scenarioes wont lead to a "bad date" but instead lead to revolutions, lack of trust, and even the main character, Elodie, DYING. And you will die a lot in your quest towards coronation, each death avoidable, if you invest in the propper skills. Of course there are visual novel/dating sim features, like you can pursue a bachelor (or a couple bachelorettes), but the main focus of the game is on alloting skills to survive the year before your coronation.
Do not let the cute girl fool you, Long Live the Queen is a game that will satisfy either gender, giving you a strategy game with MASSIVE replayability and the art style and body of a visual novel.

Ultra Street Fighter IV is not a game for everyone. It is a very hard game. A few hundred hours is the basic learning curve for essentially being a beginner. That being said even for people not planning on being competitive there's a lot of content just in the combo system. It's satisfying working towards just doing combos in themselves or eventually beating your first opponent online. That being said, this is where the true nature of this game comes out.
USF4 Is a game of competition and self-discipline. This game will appeal to yourself if you always strive to improve. There will be an unlimited amount of times you will frustrated and convinced you hit a brick wall. This game is about gradual improvement, a constant cycle of finding new plateaus and satisfaction of overcoming them with practice, hard work and intellect. This is a personal game, you shoulder all the blame for losing in a competitive setting. If you are prone to rage-quitting then this game will quickly be deleted from your hard drive in anger.
Pushing past this however, you see the evolution of play and how you express your personality and play style as well as who you are playing against. It's oddly intimate in that you can recognize someone solely based on their movements, actions and decisions. In every game it is you against another person, another individual wanting to get better and improve, wanting to learn from you as you learn from them. This is the addicting part of USF4 and Fighting games in general, your best friends are always your enemies and you push each other constantly. Nobody will ever truly be satisfied in being "good enough", and that's all the reason you'll ever need.
Economically speaking it's the best ratio of purchase price to play time I've ever had and will probably ever have. Something like less than 2 cents per hour? Highly recommended. 10/10

Ultra Street Fighter IV? It's the same game as SFIV when it first came out with minor tweaks to the system and more game modes/characters. It can be really fun to show off your skills with the character you practiced with.....if you can pull them off. Now there are some really good players that just never stop pushing buttons, never allowing you to get a hit in otherwise but they are few and far between, the hardest part about pulling combos off isn't the good players, it's the link timing. 'LP, LP, MP, special move' is pretty basic but to pull it off, you need to be PRECISE! If you are a single frame early or late then LP will not link into MP, making it extremely difficult.
This isn't a button mashing game and you'll discover this really quick after you are beaten by a 2500+ player point person. That being said....
Player points: The points obtained by winning ranked matches reguardless of what character you use. This is basically your skill points. No you don't spend them on anything, it's just a badge saying how good you are compared to others.
Battle points: The points obtained by winning with a character. If you win with Ryu, your points go up with Ryu. Same goes with every other character.
Let's say you're a beginner, well this game is pretty old and with SFV still in development and the beta being out, most people are concentrating on that instead or just completely stopped playing USF4 all together, moving onto bigger and better things, leaving just the good players. What I'm saying is, if you're a beginner, you're screwed because all of the people who have played this every day since beta (most have 2000PP+) are still playing.
All in all it's a fun game and I recommend it but just know that you will lose an awful lot if you aren't familiar with the controls.

A new fever is in the works, it's called Train Fever!
Not really...
Train Fever is a game developed by Urban Games and published by Gambitious Digital Entertainment and it's mostly like the classic Transport Tycoon Deluxe and OpenTTD, only... it's not as good
Train Fever is a fun game to play, although I don't know why they just called it Train Fever as you can also add buses and trams but anyway, however, the game is very clunky and sometimes annoying. The train tracks to place them onto the landscape can be the most annoying bit of the game, this also includes bus stops and tram lines
Also, the game can be very annoying with the transport AI. I built a massive train system and thankfully it worked very well and made a lot of income, however, when I requested a train to go into a depot, it completely went onto a different line and completely ruined the train service (just like the Tube) and everything stopped making the game compeltely unplayable...
Another thing which bugged me was the level of difficulty. The game is not easy and you would end up bankrupt immediately if not selective. Of course I understand that the game has to have some challenge but you can fail instantly if you muck up something
Train Fever also gives you absolutely no tutorial, it just throws you into the game and makes you read a long boring tutorial... no. Also, when placing the train tracks especially, the game's framerate chugs like hell, so much so, I have to stop and wait for the game to regain the framerates to make it even playable. Also, the game freezed for a couple of seconds to autosave which can be annoying
However, the game does have a fantastic level amount of detail. From the trains, to the house, people and cars and landscape, this also includes the sound effects, especially the train sound effects. The music on the other hand, isn't that great
I knew that the developers wanted to make a very good Transport Tycoon game but did not manage completely but tried. Thankfully they gave away free DLC which takes place in USA and they are developing a sequel to Train Fever called Transport Fever which I have high hopes for
Train Fever is a mixed bag when it comes to purchasing, I am in the middle when it comes to recommending it or not. I highly suggest that for this game you check out some reviews and gameplay videos before considering purchasing, but overall, Train Fever isn't that bad!

Excellent game, a little short thought. It adds an interesting new mechanic to Portal, whereby you are your own partner in coop tests.

While this mod features some cool ideas, the execution is terrible.
First, you're not controlling time as the title suggests, but merely a clone of yourself whose actions can be played back at any time at the cost of resetting portals. It's basically a single-player co-op experience, but without the ability to switch between characters.
Second, one of the primary mechanics is to jump on your clone as if it was a platform, which sounds good in theory but ends up being very time-consuming since you can't just croutch but must also rise up while recording, and then timing your jumps to get on and off your clone. Doesn't sound like a big deal, but you have to do it constantly, and it doesn't work in a natural way.
Third, the level design is awful, barely using any portal mechanics, waiting all the time to make sure that you can sync up with your clone properly, not having the various elements stand out from the background (e.g. a touch screen set at an angle behind a non-interactive keyboard with pixel-wide switches on it), and wasting a lot of time doing chores instead of figuring out the solution.
Fourth and finally, this game is riddled with bugs, including Z-fighting textures, placeholder labels in the menus and even getting stuck. I can't even imagine what it was before the bugfixes. This mod feels like an alpha at best, not a finished game.
Honestly, if you want to play more Portal 2, stick with random maps on the Steam Workshop.

A well made and smart puzzler. The new time travel mechanic takes a while to understand, but new ideas are introduced slowly, and the game is paced in a way that allows you to practice each one quite a lot before more are introduced. As a nice touch, markers are placed where certain actions are performed (placing portals, pressing buttons, picking up/dropping cubes), and they count down to when the action will happen, which really helps with timing. You really get a great feeling when you create a long sequence for your past clone, and the two of you work together perfectly. And that's without factoring the absolutely gorgeous new art style that's been implemented!
However, there are a few minor annoyances i had. Mainly, pathfinding was a issue, especially on the chamber in which
where i spent many minutes wandering around trying to figure out where to go. And even when i'd finally found the way and got the to main room, i spent another couple minutes walking around trying to figure out where to go next. There is nothing that tells you to

The timed puzzle in Chamber 6 got frustrating very quickly, as on many attempts i would be running towards my portal as the timer ran out, the only reason i managed to solve it was because the door jammed and stayed open even though nothing was on the buttons. At first glance, this game seems to be your run-of-the-mill girly visual novel, however this is not the case. Long Live the Queen is,  in my opinion, is a fun and almost addictive simulation/strategy game, inside a visual novel. You do not have to be female to enjoy this tittle, the plot and choices are far from girly (I doubt many little girl games have assassins, treachorous family, and murder). Just because the main character is female and has pink hair doesn't mean the game is only female oriented, it's like saying Tomb Raider is for preschool girls because there's a GIRL!!!
As for gameplay, the mechanics are easy to learn, picking classes to earn experience in certain traits (like swords and history) and then having to use these skills in scenarioes. You can play as a loved queen, or just like a character from Game of Thrones, either being beloved or feared by all. Unlike a dating sim, failing these scenarioes wont lead to a "bad date" but instead lead to revolutions, lack of trust, and even the main character, Elodie, DYING. And you will die a lot in your quest towards coronation, each death avoidable, if you invest in the propper skills. Of course there are visual novel/dating sim features, like you can pursue a bachelor (or a couple bachelorettes), but the main focus of the game is on alloting skills to survive the year before your coronation.
Do not let the cute girl fool you, Long Live the Queen is a game that will satisfy either gender, giving you a strategy game with MASSIVE replayability and the art style and body of a visual novel.

Long Live the Queen is a fantastic game/visual novel. There are many reasons to love the game, and not many reasons to hate it.
Despite reading the Steam page and watching the trailers/seeing the images, there may still be some confusion to some on what exactly the game is. LLtQ is a hybrid between a visual novel and a raising sim. Visual Novels are easiest explained as choose your own adventure books with images. A raising sim is what it sounds like,  a simulation of raising a child. The concept of LLtQ is that you are Princess Elodie, who's mother has just died. You need to take up your mother's mantle, and attempt to survive until coronation.
The game usually takes multiple attempts to beat for the first time, and it is very much trial and error, as the player needs to figure out which skills to prioritize and what decisions to make. The real fun of the game, however, is exploring all of the possibilities after you have beaten the game. There is a ton of intrigue happening around the world Elodie lives in, but Elodie can't learn all of it (or even very much of it) in a single playthrough. Which is why in your early attempts you will most likely die. You will make what seems to be a reasonable decision, but die since you were unaware of the implications your actions had because of some specific knowledge you would need to know in another playthrough. It is almost beautiful how everything that happens in the game has a reason, and how all of the characters have hidden motivations that you need to figure through multiple playthroughs and deductions (as some motives require reading between the lines).
Even after 64.5 hours, I still sometimes stumble upon things I didn't know existed in the game. I can't recommend this highly enough.
tl;dr: Buy the game. It is awesome, and has so much detail.

Best $10 I've spent in a while.
For a visual novel, LLTQ has a TON of replay value. It plays a lot like Princess Maker, but a fair bit more dangerous, because you can (and likely will) die before your fledgling queen gets her crown. The different skills Elodie can learn provide a huge number of variables for the game to interact with. There's different ways you can win, but trying one path (excelling at social events) will make it difficult to excel at another (repelling an inevitable invasion) due to the fact you have a limited time to train her.
This is definitely a strategic game, but not at all action-oriented. You make choices and read the results, and adjust your choices accordingly, at the next scene or the next play-through. It isn't nearly as random as some of the negative reviewers seem to think, though. Events do happen at more or less predetermined times, either by time of year or in a chronological series, but WHICH events occur are going to depend on Elodie's skills, current mood, and previous actions.
If you're ok with point-and-click play, lots of reading and cute anime graphics, then definitely pick up this game. :)

Long Live the Queen is part visual Novel, and JRPG. The gameplay is making choices and reading the events that unfold as princess Elodie survives multiple trials and events leading up to her coronation as Queen of the country. The first thing you should know is that it is unlikely that you will survive the first time around and I highly recommend saving regularly.
In this game, the story progresses week by week with an event occuring each week and a choice of classes to raise certain stats. How elodie handles the events and choices are determined by the stats; for example if she receives a necklace from a neighbouring lord; if she has enough points in court manners she would know that wearing it would mean she is pretty much willing to marry him and you get a choice in how you want to proceed. If you don't have enough points however, she will obliviously put it on and feel great because some nice guy gave her some nice new jewelry. These events and what happens in them will then effect future events and then the story progresses based on the stats you raise and the choices that they give you.
Raising the stats is also part of the gameplay, you have a mood meter which tells you what mood she's in and depending on the mood, she would learn certain stats faster (e.g. When she's depressed she is more into animal handling and improves the stat much faster while she will learn conversation skills slower). Her mood can be effected by the weekly events and you can make changes to her mood through choosing how she spends her weekend.
The game has quite a bit of depth to it and finding new story paths or to just find out what happens if you pass a skill check is quite enjoyable.  The music is quite nice at times though there isn't that much variety and the amount of art is a bit lacking for all that happens, however it has a very involved gameplay and story which is fairly engaging.
Yes, it is a fairly challenging game and you pretty much win by remembering what happens and replaying it, but the amount of story and lore behind it and the sense of success when things go well makes replaying it still quite enjoyable (the function to skip dialogue helps too).
I wouldn't say this is the best game ever but its a decent game and I enjoyed it. Its definitely worth a shot if you are into visual novels or maybe into rpgs.

Hey, "Night in the Woods" is probably one of the best written video games of all time. It is uncomfortably relevant in ways that games never are. The setting is a small American mining town crumbling in economic decay after the closing of the mine. Long standing businesses are struggling to stay open or are empty skeletons haunting the landscape. Everyone works at the handful of chain businesses that have swooped in since Mae, the main character, left for college. It's a world instantly recognizable.
Also recognizable is the character of Mae. Her thoughts are relatable, her actions are actions many of us remember doing ourselves. Like many of us, there's also something deeply wrong with Mae, and she won't talk about it or deal with it. She is struggling with a mental illness. She's become self destructive, and even though you are Mae in the story, you can't help her until she wants help. The helplessness of her mental illness is made real for you. The normalness of her in every respect destigmatizes her mental illness. She's just like anyone and she has a mental illness.
Where the game really shines is that despite all this doom and gloom, this hardship and strife, the characters are capable of joy and fun. They are clever and funny. They aren't defined by their struggles, it is only one aspect of who they are. The script is full of quotable lines and fun little gameplay moments that highlight the fun the characters are having together.
There's also the promise of an unspeakable supernatural horror if you're not already down.

If you like Terraria and space-age games, then you'll love Starbound. This game is very short but fun, and it encourages you to go and explore different planets to advance the storyline. The bosses are a bit challenging, but once you know how they fight, it isn't that bad.
Once you've finished the tutorial quests, you're free to explore the galaxy. You have the option to build structures around different planets, transform barren planets into forests, and mine deep underground for those sweet loot. I choose to build. Along with building, you can also turn those structures into settlements and have people move in. You can benefit a lot from having a small town, as well.
There's a bunch of cool races you can choose from, so you aren't limited to just humans. I have taken a liking to Novakids. The races can range from Japanese Fish People to Medieval Robots, and that's not all of the races. There's also birds. All of the characters in this game are unique and very fun to talk with.
Or, if you don't care about building and exploring, you can always make music. Starbound gives players instruments that are hidden across every star, and you can use them to play your favorite meme songs or play something classical. Group up with friends, and you can start your own band.
But wait, there's more.
Even the main menu's music is beautiful. The game has a variety of calming music when you're exploring the planet, and it makes you want to explore some more to listen and relax. I actually want to sit down and have the game on idle as I study or draw to the music. If it wasn't for the gameplay, I'd use Starbound as an excuse to play music. But, as I said before, the music encourages you to explore.
The game's not also about fighting. You can also fish and dig up for fossils, or tend your own farm for food to help you survive. The more you advance in the game, the more items you can get.
And if you aren't into those and prefer being fashionable, then there's always that option. Your character can dress up and can still be powerful. Or you can ignore the story completely and just play dressup in this game. Nobody is going to question your choices.
Overall, I'd rate this game a 9.8/10. The story is a bit short, but everything else is amazing.

This JRPG is a dumpster fire. It has a potentially interesting base for the combat system, which it calls a "Free-turn Stamina Battle System." Basically, you get turns equal to the number of alive and action-capable party members you have in the battle, and may distribute them freely among your characters. This is balanced by everything, even basic attacks, costing SP.
Unfortunately, I wasn't a big fan of the game balance or how the system worked even so, being as how it generally broke down to playing as normal (or just ignoring one character) in most cases, but ultimately even if it was better, this game would have squandered it both by not having many options available for your characters until late in the game (like, until almost the end game, characters will only be able to wield one physical element, or one magical element and suck at one physical element... and enemies have varied resistances that it is useful to overcome), the game being horrifically grindy, and how it basically doesn't have a story at all, except for a vague sequel hook.
As such I have to say this is recommended for no one at all.
(I didn't complete this game because it was terrible, but I decompiled the game to look at the mechanics and my friend shinichizio did complete it, so I feel comfortable saying it doesn't get better after when I stopped, and also with my choice not to play any more, ever.)

Starbound is truly as incredible as so many others claim it is. The sheer vastness of everything you can explore, collect, build and do is staggering, and can allow for someone to literally play it for 100 hours without running out of new things to do or try. Once you get a hang of the mechanics and how the various aspects of the game interact, the only limit to what you can do will literally be your imagination.
Do you want to cave dive to find treasure and precious minerals on a volcanic world? You can do that. Do you want to build a metropolis colony on an ocean planet, covering the entire thing from end to end with modern structures? Add a zen garden room to your ship, or maybe an indoor pool? Build a full ranch completely enclosed in a green house on an arctic planet? Dress your whole crew in top hats and capes? Starbound lets you do all of that. While the mission levels can feel a little tedious at times, the game doesn't require you in any way to do them. Finish the game through the storyline or don't; you'll still be able to construct a tower made entirely of mushrooms in the middle of a desert.
Also, the soundtrack to this game is the best I've ever encountered. Period.
