Ryzom is a Free Trial for a subscription only sandbox MMORPG.  It worked, sounded ok, played ok, looked ok.
I don't like this game, but i guess someone might like it.
For more info:

Ryzom is 12 years old and it shows.  The game is beyond stable.  (I don't know if Steam supports it, but the game works great on Mac and Linux in addition to Windows.)  I haven't had any crashes in over 250 hours of play.  The character/mob models look clunky and the landscape polygons seem over large by 2016 standards, but the game is colorful and vibrant.  My 6 year old computer handles the highest settings just fine with FPS to spare.  The community is the most mature, helpful and pleasant I've ever seen (and I've played 30+ MMOs in the last 20 years).
This is a great game for MMO players who like to take their time and invest effort in a game.  In game money is really not a concern -- spend 30 minutes a day and in a couple of weeks, you'll have more cash than you know what to do with.  As a side effect, there are no gold spammers.  The thing that will take time is leveling up the skill trees.  There are 63 trees in total.  F2P can take most of these trees up to 125 (some are not available until skill 150 or so).  Subscribers can take each tree up to 250.  People have managed to max out every tree, but it takes years of dedicated game play.  Take a look at this excellent web site,
, if you want to see the trees and a whole lot more about the game.
This is a great game for MMO players who like to craft and enjoy harvesting their own resources.  Every useful piece of equipment is player crafted or player craftable.  Sure, there are vendors who will sell you basic items in a pinch, but they are virtually useless next to what the players themselves can make.  The crafting (and harvesting) system is deep and complex.  Advanced players get involved in caring about the season, time of day and material statistics to make the best gear.  The end game revolves around acquiring materials so that you (or a friend) can craft the best gear.  Gear lasts a long time, but, eventually it breaks and you need to replace it, so, that in and of itself becomes the end game.  (This is not the huge treadmill it sounds like, these crafted items easily last for hundreds of hours of game play.)
This is a great game for MMO players who want to group with others and enjoy the social aspects of MMOs.  Sure, you can level each skill by yourself if you like (OK, maybe not healing).  You can also walk from New York City to San Diego, but why would you?  The game encourages duo-ing and larger groups work equally well.  Working by yourself, you might be able to get 5 levels in a skill in a night.  In a group (even a duo) you can easily do 20.  It is up to the player, of course, but getting a group is as easy as saying something like "lvl 200 healer looking to train" in the universal chat channel, so why wouldn't you?
This is a great game for MMO players who like flexibility.  Every character can train every skill.  There is no tank/mage/melee dps/healer class.  Every character can fill every role.  Every character can rez (in combat too).  There are no builds.  It is impossible to "gimp yourself."  You can even change roles in the middle of combat -- the most you have to do is change gear.  You can cast that heal spell in heavy armor while holding a sword and shield, but it is going to take a quarter of your power bar and yield a crappy heal.  Swap into light armor and put on magical amplifiers and that same spell will take 1/20th of your power bar and yield a very strong heal.  So, as with everything else in life, there are trade offs, but they make sense and provide a great deal of flexibility.
This is a great game for MMO players who want to PvP on their own terms.  All PvP is consentual.  You can play the game for years without ever having to PvP.  It is there if you want to PvP,  In addition to the PvP zones, guilds control outposts which other guild can contest -- leading to scheduled PvP.  A guild can call on friends (individuals and other guilds) to come help them attack and defend outposts.  There is usually at least one battle a week which will leave the server buzzing for days afterwards.
This is a great game for MMO players who like a challenge.  The game will kill you.  The game does not coddle players.  Aggressive mobs lurk behind trees and under bushes.  They call friends.  They will chase you quite a ways (no, this is not EQ, they won't chase you all the way across a zone).  Better still, different types of mobs will come to each other's aid.  So, if you attack that flappy thing over there, not only will his buddies come beat on you, but that four legged mutant cow thing will probably want a word with you too.  (Death has a penalty, but it is relatively minor.  Most of us just harvest for 3 or 4 minutes to get rid of it.)
This is a great game for MMO players who like diverse abilities.  There are eleven different melee weapons (1 handed, 2 handed and "close" combat weapons).  There are four different ranged weapons (pistols, rifles, machine guns and grenade launchers).  There are dozens of different spells: elemental (acid, cold, etc), DoT, Defensive Affliction (sleep, madness, fear, etc), and Healing (health, power and stamina).  The various spells can be combined in various interesting and flexible ways.  They can be combined with AoE "stanzas" to make AOE versions.  They can be joined together to make double versions (double fireballs anyone?).  They can consume your health rather than (or in addition to) the normal power resource.  There are millions of valid combos and people are forever editing their abilities to best match their current situation.
This is NOT a great game for players who want instant satisfaction, want to strut around and wave their epeens everywhere or want to bully others and be jerks.  This is a slow, methodical game.  You can max out your skills, but it is going to take a while.  If you want to get to the end game quickly, it isn't going to happen, so this is not your game.  If you like to prove how great at PvP you are, you won't be able to do it quickly and you're going to find that the consentual PvP gets in your way, so this is not your game.  If you want to bully others and be a jerk, the community and the active CSRs won't tolerate it, so this is not your game.  If you want a respite from these fools, this IS your game.  Give it a try, it's free.

For the TL:DR crowd this MMO  is well over 12 years old where the original game company went out of business, sold the game and the current caretakers still want you to pay a $100 year subscription.
I remember the first time I encountered Ryzom.
I was 18 years old, working part time in a local retail chain in the electronics department.
I remember when the original discs came out.  Being the only one at the time fluent in DOS, I remember because we just had a customer come in wanting to know how much disk space the new Lotus for DOS took.  You just had to type DIR in the command line to see how much room it took.  I tell you this to give you a time frame for how old the game really is.
The graphics are from 2000, 16 years old, they are still playable but not going to impress anyone today.  The game was in development for over 5 years before it was released.
Sound and what little music there is are both okay.
There is no NPC chat all the interaction is with text only.
The population is very low, and is all French.  I do not have a problem with people speaking French but it does me no good if I can not find someone else who speaks what I do English.
I have the English tab open and for the past 2 weeks, over 40 hours or so the only chat or players I have met have spoken French.  So much for me joining a group or doing team stuff.
Now back to my story, I remember picking up a trial copy of the game when it first came out, the 21 day free trial period.  This was because the game only had the full subscription payment model when it first came out. At that time I played a bit until I got to one of the earliest magic quests, go destroy some jugs with your magic spell on the training ground.  Then I encountered the famous 1 foot high fence of shame.  Almost everyone is familiar with it.  You can not jump in the game and had to walk around the back of the pit to destroy the jugs and complete the quest.  Even today you still can not jump or dive while in water.  I remember thinking, well that is kind of stupid, maybe the game is not finished yet.  You can not even jump in the game, this is something they should have caught early on in Beta.  Needless to say I did not pay the $100 a year sub back then either.
I like the open world sand box aspect of it.  As others have mentioned it is similar to Morrowind and the Elder Scrolls. I have most of that series and found them all on Ebay full game for under $10 each.
I like the crafting aspect of the game, that was my favorite part in the old game Masters of Magic and the old RPG game Evil Islands.  Still have the original floppy disks of those games and play them today with the help of DOSBOX.  If you like open world sand boxes I recommend those.
I am currently at level 24 in all four of the main skill categories, Magic, Harvest, Fight and Craft.
I am off the training island and on the mainland.
I have even taken the time to swim to all the 4 main cities for my race, hoping that they might be different then the starting capital city for my race.  Spoiler alert, they are not.
I have my tiny bag full, even the armor on your body and the weapon you are carrying counts as being in your bag.  Right now I play for 15 minutes a day only, that is long enough to kill a few monsters or harvest a bit.  Then you have to run back to town and sell everything.  I am currently at my max items for sale 128 so I am not able to even sell any more items.
As a free to play player I can buy a single mount, if I can afford it to increase my bag size.
Then I log off and have to wait a full 24 hours to get enough of my goods to cycle through and sell in order to free up enough space to go "play" again the next day.
So yes, I have seen and played through the tutorial and seen enough of the game world to write an honest review of the game this time through.
The main problems I have with the game is it is very old, probably close to 18 years old including beta and early development time.
The original game company went out of business, sold the company.
They made the entire game open source, the code, the artwork the graphics the sound.
Basically it is an abandoned game.
What that boils down to is there will never be any more new content added to the game.
The current people you are paying your yearly sub too did no work on the project, they are just basically a group of old players that picked the game up on auction in bankruptcy court for a song and a dance.  You will never be able to jump or dive in Ryzom.
If they ever do decide to unlock the entire game and make it free to pay or $10 for a buy to own pay model like many other games have gone then I will recommend the game because it is fun to play.
As it stands now you get the 21 day free trial aspect of the game where they took off the 21 day time limit or you pay $100 a year subscription to unlock the game.  You can only play up to level 125 the subscribers can play up to level 250 so twice as much.
If you ever do buy a subscription that account can never go free to play, if you later on decide to quit and just play for free.  Also the free to play player can only buy a single mount to increase storage and bag size the subscribers can buy a mount, 3 packers, buy an apartment and do guild stuff.  The subscribers earn twice as much experience as a free to play player and some other things I forgot all of them.
That is my two main points here, first the $100 a year sub for a 16 year old unfinished MMO.
Second the game is not truly "free to play" as the wording on the store page suggests, the bag size, apartment, mounts, only deposit items in guild can not remove, can not participate in the PVP fortress battles and half the levels are locked out.

Long Live the Queen is part visual Novel, and JRPG. The gameplay is making choices and reading the events that unfold as princess Elodie survives multiple trials and events leading up to her coronation as Queen of the country. The first thing you should know is that it is unlikely that you will survive the first time around and I highly recommend saving regularly.
In this game, the story progresses week by week with an event occuring each week and a choice of classes to raise certain stats. How elodie handles the events and choices are determined by the stats; for example if she receives a necklace from a neighbouring lord; if she has enough points in court manners she would know that wearing it would mean she is pretty much willing to marry him and you get a choice in how you want to proceed. If you don't have enough points however, she will obliviously put it on and feel great because some nice guy gave her some nice new jewelry. These events and what happens in them will then effect future events and then the story progresses based on the stats you raise and the choices that they give you.
Raising the stats is also part of the gameplay, you have a mood meter which tells you what mood she's in and depending on the mood, she would learn certain stats faster (e.g. When she's depressed she is more into animal handling and improves the stat much faster while she will learn conversation skills slower). Her mood can be effected by the weekly events and you can make changes to her mood through choosing how she spends her weekend.
The game has quite a bit of depth to it and finding new story paths or to just find out what happens if you pass a skill check is quite enjoyable.  The music is quite nice at times though there isn't that much variety and the amount of art is a bit lacking for all that happens, however it has a very involved gameplay and story which is fairly engaging.
Yes, it is a fairly challenging game and you pretty much win by remembering what happens and replaying it, but the amount of story and lore behind it and the sense of success when things go well makes replaying it still quite enjoyable (the function to skip dialogue helps too).
I wouldn't say this is the best game ever but its a decent game and I enjoyed it. Its definitely worth a shot if you are into visual novels or maybe into rpgs.

Underneath the cutesy graphics is a brutal tale of intrigue not unlike what could be found in a regular game of Crusader Kings 2. While it is perfectly possible to lead young Elodie to be crowned without finding out the darker portions of the story, it is in repeatedly trying out different skill builds and unlocking different paths through the story that the complexity of the games shines.
But unlocking the dark secrets can be very tedious. The thing is, the game is in effect just algebra. There is no element of randomness in the game. Either you have trained enough to pass the skill check or you have not. Each event is triggered by some flag that was previously set earlier in the game. Each choice or event will affect the mood of Elodie by a fixed amount. In fact, much of the game is in mapping out exactly how many points are needed to pass, when particular events trigger, and their effects on Elodie's mood in order to maximize the skills trained.
I recognize that eventually, I will have figured out "optimal" skill builds and choices for each particular ending I want. But ultimately? I consider this game to be no different from a well-loved book. And I would recommend it to anyone who would like to read the story of a little girl forced to grow up too soon.

This is a visual novel with many branching paths and multiple endings.
You play the role of Elodie, the new Queen of Nova. Your mother unexpectedly passed away, so you're only 14 years old,  completely unprepared, and everyone is out to get you. You'll face jealous nobles, aggressive foreign kingdoms, assassins, bandits, disgruntled peasants, lunatics, power-hungry men who seek your hand in marriage (to rule through a weak queen), evil mages, and unkillable monsters.
You may also find friendship, romance, adventure, or unlock your magic power. But mostly you'll just be trying to survive (yes, hiding in your tower and refusing to go outside is a viable survival tactic in this game!)
Your goal is to make it to your official coronation (in one year) and your odds of success are slim.  I probably died about 20 times before my first successful game. The game is very much like the "Princess Maker" series in that you have numerous skills to develop over time, but you'll only be able to specialize in a few. What skills you train in determines what choices you can make and in some cases whether you live or die.
But in Princess Maker it's expected that your princess will survive to the end of the game and it's all about answering the question, "What kind of princess will I create?". By contrast, in Long Live the Queen  the question you'll probably be answering is, "How will I die this time?" Unlocking the many possible deaths is an optional challenge that is supported with Steam achievements!
With multiple skills, multiple choices and multiple endings there is a high degree of replayability.
My main criticism is that Elodie's mood affects her training efficiency, but there is no easy way to consult what kind of mood bonus you're going to get when you do your weekly training. Eventually I just wrote out the bonuses on a piece of paper and consulted it when doing my training, but it seems like that should really be included in the game.
It's a small quibble though, and overall I quite enjoyed Long Live the Queen. If you're a fan of visual novels, the Princess Maker genre, or choose-your-own-adventure books then you should give Long Live the Queen a try. Buy it if it's $5 or less.

State of Decay is quite possibly the ultimate zombie apocalypse game.  There are games that deliver better combat, there are games that have much more extensive crafting, the games that sport better survival gameplay…  But I do not believe you will find a game that blends all the best elements of Zombie survival games so well and to such a great effect.
To top it off State of Decay has a number of features that are either completely unique or at least very rare (could only be found in one or two other games).
Here is an incomplete, but telling list of what you will find in game:
1.	Combat both melee and ranged
2.	Stealth gameplay
3.	Vehicles (for travel and to use a weapon)
4.	Open World and rewarding exploration
5.	Storyline and side quests
6.	Crafting and base building
7.	Team management (recruiting, stats, equipment)
8.	Survival - scavenging for resources, basic needs such as food and medicine, mental health concerns (people getting scared, depressed)
Does the game have faults – of course it does.  Visuals are hardly cutting edge, there are bugs, there is somewhat annoying savegame system (intended to be something like “iron man” except it can easily be circumvented and everyone I know does), there are some less then satisfying missions, the randomness of resources can sometime make your early game unusually difficult.
… But in the end you will be hard pressed to find better thought out, better balanced and more complete Zombie survival experience.

While the game may sometimes look and feel unfinished, if you invest your time in it, it can be a thoroughly enjoyable experience.
Construction can sometimes be a bit frustrating, but with some perserverence, you can learn some 'rules of thumb' to help you out. Also, the UI can be a bit awkward at times, and sometimes, vital information is hard to access or just missing completely.
Sometimes - especially during the early post-release days, it felt more like a beta than a finished product, but patches have been released since then that fixed several of the issues that the game had. But to be fair, this game was developped by a very small team (only 2 programmers until the launch).
This game takes some effort and commitment to get in to, but once you do, it's truly rivetting and satisfying. If you don't mind the getting used to it and the occasional rough edge, I'd say that this game is a worthy successor of Transport Tycoon Deluxe, but still has plenty of potntial to do even better. Overall, this game is a big ball of awesemoneness wrapped in several layers of awkwardness.
Anyway, here are some hints to get you started.
Hints:
+ For your first game, start off with a flat small map. This is good for learning the basics of the game.
+ Grow your towns with frequent passenger service and goods delivery.
+ Do not deliver more goods to a town than it demands,
+ Passengers and goods will only make their journey if it takes 20 minutes or less of real-time to complete.
+ The journey-time not only depends on how fast a service is, but also how long someone has to wait. It is therefore a good idea to keep the frequency of the services high to reduce waiting-times (eg. when changing from a bus to a train).
+ Building a track close to another track double-tracks it. You can build any number of parallel tracks this way.
+ In the forums on the official website, there are many hints for how to do those things you wish you could do but can't. Also, there are many video-tutorials on YouTube.
+ It is possible to mod and add extra content to the game. There are plenty of downloadable third-party mods and enhancements, including new rolling-stock, buildings, decorations, maps, and even gameplay-enhancements.

Great Tower D game that doesn't leave the player just watching towers shooting, players need to combine their traps and their own weapons to beat levels or last as long as possible in endless mode. In single player you have 10 slots in co-op you have 6 each, allowing players to cooperate and go through levels by combining strats.
The thing this game holds over Dungeon Defenders is players don't have levels, you gain skulls which you use as currency to buy new traps that you can use in maps. So you don't have to worry about matching levels, just 6 fully leveled traps will do, because you can refund your traps for the full amount of skulls, so there's no need to tell a friend to hide in a corner while 4 other players do the work and just have him/her sit there and grind for exp which is EXCESSIVELY boring and what turned me away from Dungeon Defenders and nearly made me avoid this title, thankfully this game avoided that problem.
There's a variety of weapons, traps, trinkets that you can mix and match to make a range of fun traps to hit the orcs with.
Great art style, voice acting and humor added in with traps that also amuse. Have an acid covered flaming orc launched by a spring trap, bounce off a wall and into a pit the whole way he screams.

Ryzom is a great game with one of the best online communities I've ever seen. The crafting system is deep and character development is limited only by which skills you choose to level; there are no classes to limit you. The combat system seems simple at first but like the foraging/crafting system, has enough depth to it to make for interesting PvP for those so inclined.
The tiny starter island (Silan) does a good job of teaching you what you need to know to play, but the *real* game begins when you finish your lessons and go to the Mainland where there are far more opportunities, no matter what type of character you are trying to play. Hunters have a wider variety of prey, digger/crafters have better mats to dig, casters get spells that are unavailable in Silan... in short, Silan is only a glimpse at what Ryzom really has to offer. Any review based solely on a short time spent in the tutorial does this great game a disservice.
However, it's not for everybody. The graphics are a bit dated, the mechanics take more than 12 seconds to learn, and you can't get a maxed out character without grinding. If you are looking for a simple game with lots of eye candy that doesn't make you work for rewards, then Ryzom is not for you. But if you are a gamer that doesn't mind spending a few minutes learning who can tolerate graphics simple enough to run on a five-year-old laptop and is okay with not having things handed to you on a silver platter just for existing, it's well worth a look.
There are very few MMOs (RPG or otherwise) that I stayed with for more than a couple of months, but I've been playing Ryzom for about four years. If something is good enough for me to stick with, then it's good enough for me to recommend the game to others. So here I am, recommending that you give Ryzom a try.

I played Ryzom for a while back in the days, and play it again since it's available on Steam reminds me all the things that make me love this game. So I wanted to share my experience.
First of all, the universe is so compelling! The graphics may look a bit oldish, but the artistic direction is just stunning. The different feelings you may experience when traveling these unique landscapes can really move you. It is full of life, from the fauna to the weather and to the seasons.
Next, comes its community. For sure, Ryzom deserves to be called an MMORPG. Here, you will always find someone to help you, to hunt, to travel, to find something you are looking for, and so on. This is not a nowadays so-called MMO where you can just play solo. The force of Ryzom comes from the fact that you need the others players to progress, and that makes it a deep social experience. May you be shy at first, no worries, someone will propose its help soon, and friendships will come.
Another important point about the community is the roleplay. A lot of events are organized, by both players and event teams. This engages you so much.
Now, let's talk about the gameplay.
On one hand, I have to admit, the fighting system is a common one. But still, it's pleasant to play with. On the other hand, there are a lot of gameplay features making this game very deep and challenging to master.
First of all, the class-less design: this allows you to experiment with whatever you want. Want to be a master fighter? There are tens of weapon types, with their own skill trees. And not to mention, ending only one skill tree is already a challenge in itself. Want to mix some range weapon skills with healing skills? Do it, nothing will stop you combining the talents you have. What keeps it balanced is the equipment you wear. Don't think about doing magic with a heavy armor and a sword in your hands. You will have to put your light cloths on and your magic amplifiers to be efficient.
And about the peaceful activities: again, the harvesting and the crafting systems are very deep.
Harvesting won't consist in picking up some resources spawning here and there each 2 hours or so. Instead, there are dedicated skill trees which will allow you to gather rare resources. Also, you will need to learn where to harvest, at which time, and how to harvest efficiently. And every harvester has its very secret receipe that they may share with you.
Next comes the craft system, one that I never saw anywhere else. Here, the possibilities are endless. Creating the perfect sword will take you "ages" of research to find the receipe. The statistics of an object all depends on the statistics of the materials you use and their genuine combinations.
With all these activities, you will see that, everyone needs each other. You need a better axe? You will need a good crafter that knows the ingredients. You will need a harvester that will find that rare wood bark. You will need a team of high level fighter to kill that rare beast that will drop those very sharp claws. You need to harvest some rare materials that only appear once each winter at mid-night, deep under ground in the prime roots? You will need a team to protect you against the fierce kitins or against other player that want it too.
There is so much more to say, but I hope this review will make you want to come by on Atys.

I'm going to let you in on a little secret. I love flying games. I love them to bits. I relish the speed, the adrenaline, the viceral sense of the bits of metal that rocket past you at mach 2 as you riddle another plane with bullets. Ace Combat Assault Horizon offers all of that and that is why I like it.
Ace Combat has a long history that I have never experienced; so you will not get any comparisons with its predecessors from me. Instead I will tell you exactly why this game is awesome and why you'd do yourself a disservice when not playing it. Let's start with the obvious; the mental presentation. Stuff is literally thrown at you. You are experiencing a barrage of unyielding terror and excitement all at once. The game runs overtime to get you the best angle on the action. The camera will cut back from the action to show you the minute details of your enemy's plane as it disintegrates when you unleash a flurry of bullets and missles at at. If it wasn't enough, the game might just give you a front row seat and follow the missle as travels toward its mark.
Not exciting enough you say? Lets talk about dogfighting; the bread and butter of any aerial combat game. Initiation a dogfight in this game requires you to close the distance. A quick button press initiates the special pursuit mode that hooks your plane to your target and the pulse pounding chase begins. Your plane broadly follows the target, but the goal is to keep the crosshair in the center at a insane speeds to make your lock-on kick in faster to shove your deadly missles up his rear end faster. Your mark can escape though. By swaying and dodging, or by hitting the brakes hard and leveling the craft at the right moment you might find yourself being chased. Even then, if you can react fast enough you can instercept his manouver and rivet his plan as he flips in front of you. Everything is carefully accentuated with flares, scratches, explosions and other effect that really make the game's catch prase seem like the real deal: "Make metal bleed"
The story mode is a wee bit short. And by a wee bit I mean seriously short. One day is all you need. You do get some variation in missions and vehicles. Such as flying an Apache Helicoper, B2-Spirit Bomber or a DC-130 gunship, but the real kick comes from flying the many jet fighters. From the F-14 all the way to the latests supersonic machines. Multiplayer allows you to test your skill against other pilots, or cooperate in thwarting the CPU from bombing major cities. The only real problem is the general lack of players. So if anything, this review should have convinced you to shell some cash and come fly with me, cause I can use a few wingmen.

6/10 - The Harvester's Guide to the Galaxy
I've come back to this game for the 4th time now (I still own my disc from the orignal international launch).
For better or worse, nothing has changed.
Harvesting is still a unique experience, crafting is still fun (especially trying to craft a color-matching set of armor) and combat is still challenging.
But the quests are from the stone age of MMOs and the landscape has a lot of barren and uninspired places, the towns and settlements being the worst. And while the water itself looks nice enough (you can swim but not dive), everything underwater is barren land with not even plants or rocks.
Apart from the landscape the graphics haven't suffered that much over the years. The character animations are all natural looking and don't leave much to be desired and most mobs animations are quite convincing too. Harvesting effects couldn't look much better imo but the magic effects are a bit bland and combat effects are minimal - which makes for better FPS on older machines in return. The weather effects are also quite nice for an 'old' MMO.
Ryzom has a unique way of letting you create your own combat, magic, crafting and harvesting 'ablities' from actions, effects, upgrades and restrictions. Everything can be done as long as it's balanced. For example you can create an all-out attack that is very precise and powerful but eats up a lot from your stamina pool so you won't be able to use it often during a single fight. Or a 'pulling' spell that doesn't eat up a lot from your magic pool (called sap) and has quite a long range but is weak and has a long casting time in return. And when it comes to crafting, you can choose to imbue your object with a big bonus on your life, sap (spells), stamina (combat) or focus (harvesting) pool - or a small bonus of each. This versatility however has to be acquired with skill points that are earned in actually crafting something and also from crafting quests. Not a new concept but it works well (although it can become a chore some times).
Luckily there is no inter-dependency in Ryzom. Every character can harvest all the materials needed and learn all the crafting plans (kind of blueprints) for every single piece of equipment on his own. Specialisation still pays off, because it would take an unreal amount of time to train everything to the maximum. The system is simple but effective: If one wants to be a fighter in heavy armor wielding a two-hander, he can buy the blueprints and craft the weapons & armor  with a HP bonus - and if one wants to become a battle mage, he can buy the plans and craft armor pieces and amplifiers (gloves that increase spell efficiency) with a bonus to the sap (=magic) pool.
It is also possible to 'enchant' weapons so that spells and effects can be cast from them but it's quite complex and it doesn't pay off in the beginning to put a lot of time and skill points into it.
The AI has features no other MMO yet offers, like non-predatory animals walking over to you and watch you (out of curiosity) or large herds of animals moving across the map in natural-looking patterns.
Personally I can deal with all of Ryzoms minor flaws but there is still a BIG one - the inventory and shop mangement is terrible. Comparing items efficently is practically impossible and although there are filters both for inventory and shops, there is no way to sort anything - except for the games own enigmatic way.
It will be fun again for some time but it will not last for long I'm afraid.
Still I would recommend everyone to give it a try - if for nothing else, than just for the challenge of it. Surviving on Ryzom is not so much difficult but complex.

Honestly I can't see I've been this hooked on a game in a long while.
The Binding of Isaac is a rich blend of offensive, disturbing, original, meaningful, thought-provoking, and addictive.  The story line is incredibly screwed up, yet I find it so perfect (sorry Christianity).  I believe the only reason for the age-limitation is because of this dark plot.  Nonetheless, I am a fan of the bold decision to completely present the creator's personal controversial thoughts on religion.
The gameplay is simple yet rewarding and replayable, as there's an abundance of characters, items, endings, and floating babies to unlock.  The bosses and items provide such a high replayability-value.  You just never know when you'll come across the famous Brimstone item and incinerate the crap out of all of the headless children in your path.  As you get deeper into the game, even more possibilities are available.  I can really appreciate the thought put into everything within the game.
The music is also pretty neat.  Each level has its own theme, and the same thing applies for each of the final bosses.  And there's A LOT of 'em.
My only complaint is the endings.  Don't get me wrong, its a brilliant reward for completing a run, but the artstyle for the endings feels much too "glossy."  I enjoy the art ingame, but the cutscenes don't feel adequate for the horrifying scenario that every ending presents.  I personally feel that it should feel darker and more "sketched," kind of like the image you can see on the Steam store when scrolling through games.
That's about it.  Great game.  Don't hesitate to give it a shot.

LLtQ is a good game. Good, but not the best. It suffers from some repetition in that a good portion of the time you invest will be spent attempting to figure out which combinations of choices you make will lead to each ending (and avoid death in the process). The save feature cuts down on this a bit, but if you haven't had previous experience with this type of game, then you are going to be doing a lot of backtracking and starting over. On the other hand, if you know the trick to playing this sort of resource management game, you can easily earn your crown with a half-dozen deaths or less, and in just a couple of hours. The multiple endings add replay value, but you still face the same issues mentioned before. I found the art, UI, and story to be sufficiently engaging, but the music felt somewhat generic, and the $9.99 price tag seems a tad high. I would say buy this when it is on sale for maximum bang for your buck. In the meantime, if you still want to play a game like LLtQ, try the Princess Maker games. They are much more in-depth and have an RPG element to them as well.
Overall, I give this game a 7/10 - good enough to own and play, bad enough to be a little picky as to when you get your copy, and put it off in favour of better games.

Long Live The Queen is an excellent and essential entry to the "Idol Raising" genre of simulation games. Long Live The Queen deviates from your typical fare of Idol Raising in that you are grooming a young lady not for stardom, but for ruling a kingdom. The paths you can take and the chances for personal growth in Princess Elodie are vast and varied. You can, up to a point, end up playing vastly different games each time you play. What is a smart way to survive one point in the game could be disastrous in another.
The solutions to problems can be both fairly straight forward or way out of left field. A singing voice which through most of the game had been useless, can save your kingdom. The character interactions are satisfying and also heavily rely upon your stats, opening or closing both friendly and romantic options in people. Long Live The Queen allows you to not only play as a straight princess, but as a bisexual or lesbian one, even as a polyamourous one. You can also chose to ignore romance entirely. Aside from romance, on the platonic side Princess Elodie can turn most anyone wo appears into an ally, or an enemy who will attempt to kill her.
A satisfying experience all around, Long Live The Queen is a complex but not terribly long game if you're looking to just beat it once. It's strength lies in the sheer difficulty it takes to survive and the myriad of endings.

For an experiment, I decided to make a LP where multiple people debate and choose what to do at every prompt. The name "Dark Souls of VNs" was never so deserved.
Taking inspiration from the Gainax series of games "Princess Maker", Long Live the Queen will make you think. A lot more than most games in the genre. Any wrong turn can ruin, or even end poor Elodie's life and make you feel like an♥♥♥♥♥
Give it a shot if you want a non traditional VN.

The Banner Saga: Factions focuses on what really matters in a turn-based tactics game: the combat. Factions largely abandons the virtual dice rolls that define so many other strategy games in favor of basic math skills. Its clever two-stat system creates battles where the most skillful player wins, and when I pull off a move several turns in the making it’s rewarding in a way unlike comparative strategy games. Even if it stumbles in a few places, like the stingy way it doles out its in-game currency, tactics-minded players looking for something different should definitely check this out.
The graphics is wonderful and the gameplay is very nice and fluid with deep battle and leveling system.
What does bother me a bit is the fact that, altough you can earn money (which is called renown in this game) only by playing the game and unlock everything, it is a lot faster and easier to simply buy renown for real money, but that's very expensive for a F2P game (20 Renown = 1$, one battle lasts 30-40 minutes and can bring you a max of 12 renown, usually much less). This is a small problem, but it's not nearly enough to push me away from this great game.
Altough you can "speed up" the process of unlocking areas, the game is definitely not pay2win (the only things you can buy are cosmetic items like different colored clothes or shinier weapons that do the same ammount of damage like normal ones).
I really would pay for better cosmetic items, too, because I want more of this art. Inspired by the artist Eyvind Earle, the 2D art style of Factions manages to be striking without pushing my computer to its technical limits. It oozes style, with backgrounds that feel straight out of a Disney movie – if Disney made movies about bloodthirsty Vikings, that is. The strikingly well-done animations help seal it, making every ax blow, collapsing body, and movement a pleasure to watch.
Good game, you should try it :)

It is hard to really pin down the overall feel of Night in the Woods. It is a charming piece of art. It is a game, but you are not here for gameplay or action set pieces, you are here for the story.
This is a game about characters, about their hardships, and what drew me in was, how relateable a lot of those hardships are. Most of the problems faced by the cast are real life problems and that is what I find so endearing. It is a virtual culmination of the broken promises of a generation.

Night in the Woods is a game that can change the way you live your life.
Tl;Dr : Simple fun, engaging story, attaching characters, rewarding exploration, best adventure game I know.
While testing this game, I litteraly could not find a single con for the game, while the amount of pros is overwhelming, and in all senses Night in Woods is THE example of a well made adventure game for some main reasons.
Not unusual for an adventure game, NitW revels in its simplicity: the controls ? move, jump, interact, cancel. And yet it transforms some of the most common parts of life into what can only be called pure fun. Not because the game makes them fun but because they're already fun in real life. You wouldn't usually think of it, but jumping* is decently fun, playing with a ball is fun, talking to people is fun, but you don't think about it, and yet that is what the whole first two parts of the game are made off as you go around the day to day life of Mae.
The game also highly rewards exploration, with a map that clearly received a lot of care and attention, and many objects / characters who'll receive some form of evolution depending on your interactions with them. This makes that you will not be able to see everything on your first playthrough and you will need atleast two of them to see all of it, thus spreading the lifetime of the game to about 20 hours minimum (I am at the beginning of my second playthrough).
As to the narrative, NitW has several plots, none of which I will detail, however the first string follows the evolution of Mae, her friends and family as well as Possum Springs, the second follows the background / the lore of Possum Springs, the third is more lovecraftian and manifests itself through dreams, the fourth only comes into the game in the third and fourth parts, and relies on intrigue and an awesome ending. Each of these captivated me to the point where the game started haunting my thoughts all day long until I finished it, and even now it left its print, which does lead me to the final paragraph.
At the end of the game I did feel like I'd learned a lot, first of all over the life in ex-industrial / mining american cities, second of all over how to enjoy your life better and last of all over some progressive issues, these along with the graphics, music and story will have you leave the game with a sense of fulfillment that in my honest and big experience, I have never met before. And this is why I conclude by stating that this is the best game I have ever played.

This is one of those games that is never going to escape it's troubled beginnings. There have been some pretty major bugs that have plagued the development of this game and the fledgling developer has done a respectable job at addressing these. At it's core, this is a deep game with a super-steep learning curve and some frustrating interface/gameplay issues. So why is this getting a thumbs up from me? Because despite this, there is still a game that has absorbed me and has given me 80 hours of gameplay.
It's totally sandbox; you're on your own and just poking around with the game doing whatever you want with little other than profit and loss to guide you. But sometimes that's what you want, to just fiddle around and not have some corny derivitive quest thrown at you, or feel as though the goals set by the game are railroading you (pun intended) into playing a type of way you don't want to play.
Big tip: always start with bus routes, get several towns running, then you can start playing around with trams or connecting up compatible industries, expanding until you have enough to start laying track. It's about feeling when you're ready to expand into the next big step, being cautious and backing off if something isn't working.
But, this game would benefit from so much that would take the guesswork out of all this. The developers have obviously tried to go for a more intuitive feel to how you play a transport game, moving away from things like catchment zones when placing stops and the like, which should translate as more realistic: people in real life will travel as far as they need to for public transport, it isn't a binary 'I'm 100 metres away, I'm good to go. I'm 101 metres away, I'm not going that far,' but this does mean that you have no real sense for how far apart stops should be, whether you're bogging your system down with too many stops or missing out chunks of possible passengers because it's quicker to walk. But, in the end, as long as you're making money, who really cares about digital people having to walk a mile to work?
The simulation is broad and develops impressively over time, but again has some issues. Watching towns grow and develop over time is fascinating, although growth tends to often be counter-intuitive, with roads appearing almost randomly. Although you can place roads and have some control over the development of settlements, the lack of accompanying features and relatively minimal feedback into the transport part of the game, besides the ability to add a shortcut to complete a route or upgrade roads to improve speed, means there isn't much reward for getting into this too much.
All in all, the game is playable, albeit with its own little eccentricities. The game is more of a relaxing pass-the-time style than quest-driven adventure through the decades. But, as I've said, it works of you like that kind of game.
The developers are starting fresh with a new game rather than patching and updating this one, which tells me several things. Firstly, they've learnt a lot from this game and have listened to feedback and know that to try and put in all the stuff people want and correct the mistakes that the game has grown up with would be huge and likely game-breaking. But, it also tells me that they are still passionate about this game: they could have done what some many other developers have done, gotten as far as they could with their first attempt and then gone in a different direction. But they haven't. They are building on what they've learnt and starting fresh and in the world of game development, taking years to develop your first game, which is good but bogged down with virtually insurmountable problems, is the easy way to bankruptcy. So, I'm still happy I paid for this game, supported whoever is behind Urban Games, and I'll be there to support their passion for making the right game that they've always imagined when Transport Fever is released.

Wow. A friend recommended this game and it turned out to be an incredible adventure. The level of challenge is akin to classic roguelikes in that monsters are fierce and there is a constant tension throughout the game. However you always have the tools (or arcade strategies) to overcome every situation if you are resourceful enough. Most frustratingly, for a very skilled player all deaths can be averted. Sadly, I still die plenty of times.
The levelling up is exciting and the 'skill' tree is well-balanced. You can vary your role although the game does tend to reward certain play styles.
At a deeper level, the game really is an exploration of your personal character. You are repeatedly asked two key questions: Will you quit? If not, what will you change? Ultimately you realise you can improve and prevail in spite of tremendous frustration.
The storyline was hard to follow (however it becomes clearer as you replay it) and to truly understand the questlines I suspect spoilers are necessary. I'd recommend this for anyone who loves a 3D RPG and is prepared to develop their playstyle because walkthroughs will not solve it for you.

Starbound is truly as incredible as so many others claim it is. The sheer vastness of everything you can explore, collect, build and do is staggering, and can allow for someone to literally play it for 100 hours without running out of new things to do or try. Once you get a hang of the mechanics and how the various aspects of the game interact, the only limit to what you can do will literally be your imagination.
Do you want to cave dive to find treasure and precious minerals on a volcanic world? You can do that. Do you want to build a metropolis colony on an ocean planet, covering the entire thing from end to end with modern structures? Add a zen garden room to your ship, or maybe an indoor pool? Build a full ranch completely enclosed in a green house on an arctic planet? Dress your whole crew in top hats and capes? Starbound lets you do all of that. While the mission levels can feel a little tedious at times, the game doesn't require you in any way to do them. Finish the game through the storyline or don't; you'll still be able to construct a tower made entirely of mushrooms in the middle of a desert.
Also, the soundtrack to this game is the best I've ever encountered. Period.

It's a fun game, isn't easy, but you won't be pulling your hair out, or taking a hammer to your computer. Once you finish the levels, you can have some fun in the sandbox mode, which is exactly what it sounds like. You are in a box of sand, only unlike most games, you get to move the sand. You have an assortment of vehicles, which is a pickup truck, a flatbed with side guards, a crane on a flatbed, an excavator, and your dozer. They feature full control, which is rotation, elevation, bending, length, and your attachment (bucket or claw). With that, you can make just about whatever you want to in the dirt, such as tunnels and circuits for your pickup truck. Overall, I would recommend this game to a friend, and the price is right for the "budget players".

Long Live the Queen is fun in a way. I'm not giving it a negative review because it isn't... and I'm sure it appeals to the people who like putting cute girls in different uniforms, but Long Live The Queen's gameplay is pure, sheer trial-and-error. You spend your days in the castle, developing skills and learning how to be a good queen. Of course, Elodie can't be good at everything, so you have to pick which skills to develop and which to leave alone. This is all nice in itself, if it weren't for the fact that the game keeps killing Elodie in more and more contrived ways, and every time this happens, it's because the player didn't develop some kind of obscure skill enough. Which means you have to - and this is no exaggeration - play a few weeks until you die, then load your save again and gear all your skill points toward preventing that death. You need to do this every time. What's the point of playing a game if I have to die over and over again and can only prevent it by save-scumming and using foreknowledge?
Decided to train Elodie to work with falcons rather than dogs? Too bad, because for some reason a high Dogs skill is all that can prevent you from being poisoned. It gets worse. You get challenged to a duel, and since you've got a good lot of skill points in swords, you confidently accept - only to see Elodie getting run through because whoops, the game decides to test against Athletics instead! I went to assist my troops to fight a naval battle, but did you think the game would check my (almost-maxed) Naval Strategy skill? Nope. Instead, it tests against Climbing and Meditation. Naval Strategy isn't even checked once. It does check against swimming, but haha, did you think being decent at it was enough? Nope, sleepy time with the fishes for you! Get challenged to a duel? You die because your Composure wasn't high enough and you, for some reason, decide to charge the inhumanly powerful mage that just obliterated your father.
Yeah, Hanako Games, I know replayability is a good thing, but try doing it in less cheap and lazy ways next time. A game like Vlad the Impaler, which gives you choices in crisis scenarios and then tests against your stats, does it right. Your game, which railroads crisis situations and then decided to test against a single skill, does not.

So I picked up Night in the Woods a long time ago and just didn’t touch it. I don’t know if I was afraid it wasn’t going to be good even though I was so very excited to play. Everything about the game seemed so cute and stylish to me yet still I left it to collect dust in my steam library. On another note my steam library is where good games go to die. Anyway I finally forced myself to play and boy was that one of the best decisions I’ve ever made.
I went into this game knowing nothing, I’ll be honest I saw a cat as the main character and I was sold. I think this game is best enjoyed when you don’t know anything about it. That being said this is a review so I do need to talk about it. The story starts with Mae Borowski returning home after dropping out of College. I will give you guys some back-story, I am also a drop out so I instantly had empathy for the main character and that definitely skews my opinion. She goes on to have a hard time because most of her friends have their lives and she doesn’t know where to fit. I feel like the feelings of all the characters are expressed well and it reflects my own experiences quite well. I don’t believe this story is for everyone but I do believe that it has got its own charms that I think most will enjoy. The way the characters talk and interact reminds me more of when I was around fifteen to seventeen but it still gives you the feeling of friendship. I think it’s best if I don’t talk about the plot as it’s much better experience then whatever I could write here. I will say I was satisfied by the ending.
This game plays fluidly and there was never a point where I found myself standing still wondering where I go next. It’s a world that allows itself to be explored and almost invites you to. It never feels like the text options trick or deceive you, what Mae says is what you expect her to say. There were times where the jumping did frustrate me but I’m awful at platforming so I do feel if I’m being objective I shouldn’t deduct points. I did appreciate that you could choose who to hang out with on each day and that affected the story. I enjoyed the mini-games but I did think some of them went on a little longer than necessary and there was no way to skip them. Some of the mini-games also felt like they were sprung on you out of nowhere but I feel like it didn’t negatively affect my enjoyment of the game.
This is a game that is beautiful and stylish from the music to the world design. I fell in love with it. The world design truly communicated that feeling of a small town which I’ve never experienced. Each place I chose to explore intrigued me and really gave me the same reminiscent feelings Mae would have felt. I adored the music, it was something that teetered perfectly between whimsical and dirty kids in a grunge band. I feel like each song was lovingly made with the scene in mind and the feelings they we’re trying to communicate. All over this world felt complete as I was exploring I didn’t have any questions and I when I did the game answered them in one way or another.
I can’t tell whether it’s the lovingly crafted world with how it looks and sounds or a story where I felt real empathy for the main character. Everything about this game I love. Every character reminded me of people I met when I was a teen and the stupid shenanigans we would get up to. This game truly deserves to be bought at full price and played with no distractions. If this review can convince one person to buy it I’d be happy.

AT A GLANCE:
A rare sort of game that elegantly combines disparate genres to create a memorable, unique experience that will stay with you long after you finish. The colorful cast of woodland hipsters may get tired, yet you'll keep coming back to see what you missed or just to experiment.
IN-DEPTH:
There are games with style over substance, and games with substance but no style, NITW is sublime because they are one in the same. The flatland visuals are the essence of its play, and its quirky off-beat story would not have worked any other way. It's just one of those pairings like the cookies and creme of an oreo where you can't have one without the other.
The real magic of the game is in the writing. With Undertale, I was constantly frustrated with how "wrong" choices could forever knock my game off track and ended up re-starting several times. With NITW, I never felt that pressure. I would play through the story one way, live with my mistakes and then try to do it all differently the next time. I was well rewarded. Instead of minor tweaks, the wild story branches show you only fractions of the whole. Replays are a must, which might bore you if you're not into the chracters.
How could you not be, though? I guess if you're not into music, or not into art, this isn't for you. However if you want to get to know a gang of slackers, ala Scott Pilgrim, who get into wild adventures, you'll relish every moment.
A lovely soundtrack, a story that can suck you in, and characters that seem to come alive.  I can't wait for the Weird Autumn edition.

I really felt that
had come home to roost when I heard about the PC release - finally, this well-thought fun series could shed its technical limitations and esoteric (albeit charming) control scheme.
Sadly, this version (i.e the one included with the day one release) falls short. First impressions are weak indeed, with no keyboard control over the camera (and this being totally essential for even the first mission), and a highly limited soundset(simply put, the engine noise loop is too short and rather grating when it's the only sound in the world).
After connecting a 360 Pad to enjoy the controller support (which is indeed global, sufficent to select a level and navigate the limited options) things improved somewhat, the responsive controls very reminiscent of the mobile version. Also reminscent of the mobile version, however, is the very limited draw distance - keeping track of your surroundings when away from buildings is a bit of a challenge, though the authenticity of the minimap is welcome!
I'll curtail this review and give you some basic ups and downs.
UP:
Physics are pretty solid and the vehicles feel like the chunky toys they're modeled after.
Still has some of the charm from the small-screen editions.
Nice, relatively readable UI font (Think of the Wip3out font only you can actually read it).
Cross platform! Any game that runs on Linux is very welcome!
DOWN:
Very weak and limited sound set.
Limited fun without a controller.
Small selection of levels and no free-play option (nor is there a level editor).
No configuration except from the most basic and essential (The stick configuration bent my brain at first, Turning on left-stick steering really helped!)
360 pad is not really a precise enough controller. I would love to break out the twin joysticks and set the game up to use them, but alas this isn't a supported option.
In summary:
I feel like this is still a tech demo, and that it's swinging above it's station somewhat in price. Wait until it's 50% off and I'd say you've got a game that will provide a few hours of entertainment (with the sounds turned off and some music in the background), at least until you've beaten all the levels and had some fun plowing up the biggest clay-ball you can in the dozer.
I wish I could be more middling on my appraisal of the game, so take this to be an "it's okay" review, rather than an outright positive one.

Game is quite like terraria, and loving terraria I have mixed feelings about this game. For those who have played terraria, ill compare this game to it towards the end. Putting aside the fact that one of the artists that worked on Terraria left Re-Logic and stole all of reds ideas for a sequal to terraria, This game is weird. The first few moments are awe-inspiring as you look around the first world and wonder what the hell all of the things at the top are and what the hand mechanics are and the beautiful world; its great. But the game kinda goes downhill from there.
You go on and dig for materials and weapons and realize that the weapons system is weird (Only a few magic, butt ton of guns and an alright amout of swords) (also the names are waaaaayy too long to say in a normal conversation) and then you get to your first boss fight. And. its. awesome. the whole way there is creepy and dark and unsettling and when you first get to look at the boos its terrorfying and the bossfight is great because its not just something you pump bullets into (although this is weird becuase the whole game revolves around that)
But thats all that was really memorable for me. I remember another bossfight where it was a plant or a spider, but the game gets kinda repeditive. (go to a new world, get the ore, fight boss, Repeat) And unlike terraria, its very linear. you go from bossfight to bossfight. And the worlds system is super cool but it works against my primal urge to have a house. Sure, you can say that your ship is your home, but its not the same, you cant build on it. If you play with more that one person, then it gets annoying to get all the ore and you end up just choosing which ship to upgrade, becuase you cant get enough uprgade things for both.
In terraria, I remember the first time i defeated each boss, it was thrilling and adrenaline pumping- because it took me a while. With this game, it felt kinda easy, and the three options in the creation menu leave me wanting, (Game way too easy, game too easy, F*** you this is impossible) If there was a "meh, but enjoyable" option, i would chose that. I do recomend that you play this game with someone, as it makes it more difficult and more easy (you have to feed 2 people and get everything for 2 people ect.)
TL;DR: Game is a little repetitve especially towards the end, but it is enjoyable. 7/10

Long Live the Queen is the kind of game that takes the visual novel genre and makes it into something that's both frustrating yet fun. Similar to the Princess Maker games from Japan, the goal of the game is to aid Princess Elodie into Queendom so that she can continue looking after the realm. You do this by making decisions for Elodie and deciding which classes she should attend (2 per week) in order to polish her into a tru gem. Of course, it's not as simple as that.
The story has multiple endings and many twists and turns which often evolve in the death of our dear Elodie. Commoner uprisings, magical wars and coups are all parts of what you have to avoid running into whilst hoping that along the way someone doesn't try and trick Elodie into eating poisoned chocolates.
The game is fun with a lot of decisions but can get frustrating after seeing Elodie stumble at the same hurdle over and over again. Gameplay is literally using a mouse to pick decisions but the interactivity of the story makes up for it. The additional clothes for Elodie are a nice touch. If you're an achievement hunter there are plenty of achievements to be found, and as there are different storylines there's a lot of replaying that can be done with satisfyig conclusions. Towards the end when you have almost 100% it can get tedious going through the same story again and again, however.
Overall this game is great in any collection and not just for girls. :) Long live the Queen!

Wow. A friend recommended this game and it turned out to be an incredible adventure. The level of challenge is akin to classic roguelikes in that monsters are fierce and there is a constant tension throughout the game. However you always have the tools (or arcade strategies) to overcome every situation if you are resourceful enough. Most frustratingly, for a very skilled player all deaths can be averted. Sadly, I still die plenty of times.
The levelling up is exciting and the 'skill' tree is well-balanced. You can vary your role although the game does tend to reward certain play styles.
At a deeper level, the game really is an exploration of your personal character. You are repeatedly asked two key questions: Will you quit? If not, what will you change? Ultimately you realise you can improve and prevail in spite of tremendous frustration.
The storyline was hard to follow (however it becomes clearer as you replay it) and to truly understand the questlines I suspect spoilers are necessary. I'd recommend this for anyone who loves a 3D RPG and is prepared to develop their playstyle because walkthroughs will not solve it for you.
Completions: 4.

One of the greatest RPGs of all time.  The incredible graphics look fantastic even by today's standards, the gameplay is solid and fair, the lore is incredibly deep and is still not fully understood by its players to this day, the bosses are extremely memorable and they're a definite challenge to beat, character creation and leveling are incredibly detailed as well allowing for hundreds of different kinds of builds.  The only thing really wrong with this game is crappy stability that it has on PC.  In order to get this game to function properly on PC you need to use Durante's dsfix.  This will allow you to run the game at 60 FPS and at any resolution you want.  Enabling 60 FPS however will cause a lot of weird physics gliches in the game such as falling through the world, not being able to make certain jumps, or taking weird amounts of damage in certain instances.
Overall though, the pros definitely outweigh the cons.  If this game were to be remastered on PC then it would easily be one of the greatest games ever made.

Night In The Woods is a new take on visual novels. It's refreshing, funny, grim, satirical. Everything a good story has, along with the many themes and sub-plots that it has for you to explore and ponder about, as well as a lot of hidden gems that the explorers out there will appreciate.
The game itself is very simple, with no new groundbreaking game mechanic(s). There are a few mini-games to play, along with a few quirks here n' there. The game is purely story-driven.
The writing was amazing. I feel as if there is at least one character in the game you'd be able to relate with, whether it be a background character, or one of the main characters. The story was relatively easy to follow as well. There were some points where I was like "
", and there were a few minor plotholes I noticed (though, may have been me not looking hard enough :P).
The artstyle is simplistic and pleasing. I really enjoyed it!
The soundtrack is also superb (though some songs seem recycled/remixed, which is alright with me). Gives off a Jazzy punk vibe, overall.
The only downside is that the ending is a bit abrupt, and seems incomplete. But at the same time, is still a very nice ending, and a good way to wrap up the game. The games ending also doesn't scream "Sequel! Cliffhanger!", but leaves it open for one.
All in all, I'd recommend this game to those who look for story-rich games, and are willing to invest a 10-12 hours into a beautifully crafted, artistic, mind-boggling adventure.
Score rating? 9/10.

Capcom updates the Street Fighter IV series on a 2-4 year basis with new characters and new modes, but is it enough to keep fans entertained and bring burned players back?
Capcom first announced the original Street Fighter IV back in 2007, when the company released the first teaser trailer featuring Ken and Ryu fighting in the stylized, sketchy style.
In 2009, producer Yoshinori Ono and his development team proved that Capcom had lost the magic that kept players glued to the older arcade cabinets back in the 90's.
Capcom's new found preference for wringing every last cent out of every property they own has unfortunately made it into Street Fighter IV, so here we stand in 2015, with the release of Street Fighter V just around the corner.  There are so many different versions of Street Fighter.
For the fourth major instalment, I had hoped for new content, but it's clear that Ono and his team just rehashed the same material.  It feels the same as most other Street Fighter games.  There is not much new or different to recommend it.
Right from the beginning, the visual additions only come in the form of five new characters.
Well, "new" is a bit of a misleading way of putting it, being that the characters Elena, Poison, Rolento, and Hugo are directly copied from Street Fighter x Tekken without any tweaks at all.
The models of the original cast have seen no extra upgrades, as they still look very unfinished.
They all have sharp edges on the models and some parts of the models such as accessories are clearly low poly.
The newer models from SFXT look a lot better as they are high polygon models.
He is completely in line with his arcade Alpha incarnation, dedicated to hit-and-run tactics and misdirections.
He retains his Escape Roll and Wall Bounce which move him out of the line-of-fire, while his Forward Roll and Patriot Circle moves add to his offensive capabilities. The EX versions of those moves add distance, making Rolento a wily opponent with some meter under his belt.
She is a kick-based offensive character, just like she was in SFXT. She has a few mid-range moves with her long legs, two low-hitting specials, and a solid anti-air move to boot. Her old Healing art from Third Strike re-appears here as her second Ultra.
He is an odd character. He's cut from the same cloth as Zangief and Hakan, being a throw-based brawler, but he's easily the biggest Street Fighter character period. He's slow and provides a rather large target, but he can take the hits thanks to his high health. Hugo has a few moves to help close the distance and EX specials improve his ability to grapple with opponents. His anti-air Backbreaker and standing Splash throw mean major damage if they connect.
Like her SF x Tekken incarnation, her projectile, Aeolus Edge, has different ranges depending on the strength used and her straight vertical dragon punch-style move, Kissed by a Goddess, is there to punish jumpers. Poison also has a leap attack that can be turned into a throw and triplicate whip attack for pushing opponents back. She's probably the most standard / basic of the "new" cast.
Decapre is a Shadowloo Doll that comes from the comics.
She uses most of Cammy's animations in different configurations, outside of a few moves, and her costume is directly pulled from Cammy's Alpha outfit. Like Rolento, Decapre's a misdirection character; she has dash and teleport moves to give her the chance to attack from multiple angles and a standing uppercut for her wake-up defense. Decapre also retains a slow, rolling fireball as one of her two Ultra moves, which is fun for playing around with opponents.
Is the character "new" or just a Cammy reskin / clone? The reused animations hurt the character a lot considering she was a cool character in the comic book. I personally loved her back story and found it so interesting.
Both new and reused additions fit in rather well with the existing cast and systems from the arcade release of "Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition" which launched back in 2012.
The returning cast have also seen some extensive balance changes for competitive play.
These changes include being able to cancel Ryu's EX Shoryuken into almost anything, toning down Cammy's stun ability and the damage on her primary Ultra, increases in Yang's walk speed, and adding a bit more punish-ability to Akuma's moves. If you're interested in learning more about what changed about your favourite character, Capcom has outlined the changes in an official YouTube playlist.
Capcom has been big on supporting the competitive fighting scene and most of these tweaks are meant to flatten the tiers, which are determined by how a character matches up against the rest of the cast if two equally-skilled players were involved.
Like MMOs, Capcom is eternally trying to make every character equally good in a competitive sense, but they just end up shuffling the deck over and over. Sagat was a top tier character in vanilla Street Fighter IV, characters like Honda and Chun-Li held top spots in Super SFIV, while Cammy and Akuma are the hot business in Arcades.
Capcom seems to have realized how much people care about the tiers, because another new feature in Ultra Street Fighter IV is the Edition Select system for local battles.
Sadly, you can't take this awesome feature online, but in a local match, you can select the version of the character you'd like to play.
The available character versions you can choose from include:
Street Fighter IV,
Super Street Fighter IV
Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition
Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition: Version 2012)
Ultra Street Fighter IV.
Ever wanted the Arcade Cammy from revision II (2012) to defeat vanilla Sagat?
Well now you can find out who would win from two high tier fighters.
This is probably my favourite new feature and it's a shame it can't be taken into online matches.
Ultra Street Fighter IV also creates a few more options for the competitive scene. They expanded the Focus system with Red Focus, allowing players to drop even more Super Meter to absorb multiple hits, which you can cancel into nearly anything. There's Delayed Wake Up, allowing you to change the timing of getting up from a knockdown; you could previously get up quicker than normal, but now you have the option to slow it down as well. Finally, Ultra Combo W (Double) allows you to take both of a character's Ultra moves into battle, albeit at a weaker level than choosing a single Ultra.
Overall, Ultra Street Fighter: IV is hugely disappointing. It shamelessly reuses content from previous versions and has a "save error" bug that has still not been fixed.
The bug forced me to replay the entire game again while also not registering any previous achievements I had earned from the Arcade edition.
Keep in mind that this problem may only be for people that upgrade their original SSFIV: AE and don’t buy the standalone version.
I found the reused characters and assets disappointing, particularly Decapre the Shadowloo Doll, as her story and premise that comes from the comics is very interesting.
However, in-game, she falls prey to the "let's reuse Cammy's assets syndrome" and she is only a shadow of what she could have been.
I find the whole Shadowloo Doll story line interesting, as Tekken 6 and Tekken: Blood Vengeance did a similar story.
In future games, I hope Street fighter improves both the way it handles upgrades and gameplay as this version is too similar to the Arcade version for me to say it's "worth buying".

Ignore my hours played, I've been playing Ryzom since 2012. I can't recommend this game enough, but I wouldn't say it's for everyone. If you're looking for a straightforward carrot on a stick type game then this isn't for you. This is a sandbox game. It's for people who want a creative and challenging experience that requires you to think for yourself and encourages collaboration with other players. The community here is amazingly friendly, welcoming, and helpful.
The graphics might look a bit dated compared to some other games, but I am still in awe at the unique beauty and originality of this world. I love the interactions between carnivores and herbivores, and the animals themselves seem to have personality. Some herbivores will take an interest and follow you for a while, and some will actually pull aggro towards you to take it off themselves. Herds migrate with the seasons and there is a lot to learn about their different behaviours and traits. Some creatures resist certain attacks and some will swarm you if you attack a member of their group. You learn through experience which are dangerous and which are not, and which strategies to use for hunting different creatures. The wildlife can be ruthless and even an experienced player has to watch their step.
I see some reviews from people who have only played for a few minutes or a few hours and didn't like it. Ryzom has a bit of a learning curve and you really won't understand much if you just dip your toes in and judge it by your first impressions. There is a lot more to it than meets the eye, and I highly recommend giving it a chance. There is a complex crafting system and a huge number of skills to train. You don't have to commit to a class and can change roles in a team on a whim. Harvesting and crafting are complex activities requiring thought and planning. You can customize all your actions to make the most of your skills, rather than just pushing premade buttons.
The game is free to play for half of all levels. That's 125 out of 250 levels, for every skill in the tree. That is a LOT of gameplay with very few restrictions and is nothing to complain about. There is no "pay to win" system where you buy stuff that gives you an advantage over other players. When I first started I played for about six months for free and was quite happy, so decided to subscribe not because I felt restricted but because I was enjoying the game and wanted to support it.  The subscription costs less than going to see a movie each month and personally I get a lot more out of this.
Ryzom takes time to learn, and you shouldn't expect it to be like other games you've played. Talk to any experienced player and you will see that the game itself is like a beloved friend to them. It is well worth getting to know :)
