This is the first review I have ever written on Stream, but I decided that I needed to for Ryzom mainly because of the bad reviews that I was reading.  They all seen to fall into 2 main groups: That is it older game (with older graphics) and that is it not a true F2P game.

So the first issue, the graphics, let my just say so far what I have seen of the game I have been impressed with. The day-night changes, The season changes, the sun rising and sun setting. At one point in the game (on the starting island) I just stopped and watched the sun set because the way the red to purples mixed with the sky was so well done. It might not be that most upto date game out there, but if you really look, damn does it have some beautliful detail work to it.
And now on the F2P, most people are wining about the lvl caps at 125, etc. because they will not beable to 'max' their toon out on a F2P account.  But not a single one of them is taking in the amount of time it will take to even get to lvl 125.  By the time anyone gets any of their skills even close to lvl 125, they will have a VERY good idea if this is the game for them. To me that is a HELL of a lot better deal then any other F2P game out there that is nothing but a F2W in truth. No real content is blocked, you are free to play just about anywhere you want (The only place that is blocked F2P is the top end area which you would not want to be in anyway). The is no time limit like with 21 day trails or anything like that, and you can completely play at you own pace to lvl your skills in whatever why you want. Honestly, I wish more MMOs were like this so that I had a real chance to try them out before deciding if they deserved any of my money later on and with a sub fee of only $10 if I do make it passed lvl 125, I have a very strong feeling that Ryzom will be deserving of that money.

The NGE or New Game Experience for new players in this game is absolutely terrible and is the reason for all of the negative reviews.  The fact remains that this game isn't easy to get into and isn't easy to learn.  The developers have refused to convert this game into a cash shop based free to play model and so it's still a freemium model.  These are the two main reasons for the negative reviews, other then people complaining the graphics are out-dated. (they are 10 years old so ya...)
Freemium means there are two tiers, a free tier and a premium tier, since this game isn't pvp focused at all being restricted as a free user means absolutely nothing.  This game can be played free forever and a lot of users who play this game have never subscribed.
I honestly never expect this game to ever get a high review score purely because the majority of the users don't use steam nor will they, so the only people posting reviews here are steam users exclusively and since this game has a steep learning curve and the newbie island essentially hasn't changed in years all new players will get a stagnated experience...
After actually giving this game enough time to really see what the game is all about though I can say that the depth of it is impressive and I've been playing mmo's since they were text only (muds mushes and moo's oh my), so not that much impresses me anymore.
I'd actually go as far as to say that this game has actually done a lot to steer away what most modern mmo's try to do, which is to endlessly dumb down their gameplay (coughWOWcough) until anyone with half a brain can play their game.
If you are truly looking for something refreshing then you need to really give a good long hard look at this game, and please give it a chance, don't spend 5-10 hours on it and quit because you will still be confused after 5-10 hours.
Just wanted to add something as well since there does seem to be a LOT of misinformation about it, this game is 100% open source, google Ryzom open source and check yourself.  Now to those attempting to state that the current devs are 'riding high on their money train' you really need to do more research on this game...as stated this game is 100% open source so you can download the code and run your own server.
Seriously...the current server administrators of Ryzom don't want your money, they want you to try out this unique experience that they've saved from disappearing into obscurity and I honestly beleive they've done a damn good job at it, I doubt it was an easy task to get an open source mmo on steam...

Right, well, I have probably around 2400+ hours into this game, including the original, (don't mind what it says above, I have far more hours into Rebirth, but I'd rather not get into it). Incredibly annoying to play, while leaving the feeling that you've been treated *extremely* unfairly by the game's designers.
Imagine having to walk blind-folded through a maze littered with traps. Each time you walk into one, you have attained the dubious ability to avoid it on your next trip through the labyrinth. That, basically, is what playing "Long Live the Queen" is like. Or actually, it's even worse than that. Since knowing where a trap is and how to avoid it are two different things. But once you've figured out one of the ways of surviving a trap, you'll have to perform it (in terms of getting certain stats high enough in time) every time you replay the game. The developer actually prides him/herself that there is that there are actually two or three ways to survive a trap (scripted event) out of the circa 30 different stat bars this game sports. Injustifiably so, in my opinion, since this still leaves numerous trial & error runs until the player has found one of the solutions.
Surely the option to save your game means that you won't have to replay every single event time and again? Well, only in so far as you haven't blown any of the other choices for maxing the proper stat-bars needed for other events that will be coming soon. And you'll have to write down all the choices you've made up to the moment you saved your game. For *every* savegame, or else there is no real point in saving any of your games.
So basically, your princess character gets to die. A lot. Which is illustrated with slightly comical visuals.
Does all of that stat-maxing, route-mapping, savegame-documenting and dying over and over again sound like fun to you? Then this is just the game for you...

Initially when this came out, I felt the controversy surrounding it was justification enough to hold off until the price dropped and then decide for myself if this game was a good direction to take the series.
I gave it a chance, but the moment that an enemy locked onto me with DFM and subsequently near teleported behind me to blow me out of the sky... I just said screw it. I have no qualms with hard games and have played the previous titles all on Ace difficulty to my immense enjoyment. But the mechanics of this game are just over the top asinine.
Some people say that DFM is option, and it's not. Whenever the game wants to put a tutorial in your way to show off the new system you can't opt out of it, as planes will literally spam flares, pull off absurd manuevers, and if all else fails disappear and reappear to the side to dodge an attack until you let the game put you on rails and watch the pretty explosions. No indication that it's a tutorial or rails showcase until you waste ~10 missles
Games like this that put the spectacle above the gameplay are becomming far too common. I enjoyed with the prior games just how much control you had, and the times where you had to fly through seemingly impossible turrain and tunnels gave the best adrenalline rush. It was the perfect level of arcade action that still felt 'grounded' because in the end, you were always in control.
Also, moving away from a fictional world to 'modern' era ballocks... I'm tired of reality and the current political bull that plagues us with varying shades of gray. So I count this against the game as well.
At least I got this on sale, but as of now I think I'm done with the series. I wouldn't mind seeing an HD collection of the prior games though, 1920x1080 @144hz... that would be something I'd definately pay a good price for.

This game is frustrating with how close it is to being something truly amazing. I went in expecting a 4X strategy game and instead got what could best be described as a more in-depth RTS. If you're someone who has never played a 4X game then this would definitely be the place to start. It's a much more relaxed game, strategically speaking, than something like Civilization, but that does not mean it is not fun. Warlock gave me flashbacks to Populous and being able to cast spells to wipe out my enemies. There's a variety of spells you can get, though there's no research tree so getting them is RNG, and the spells you get can be really powerful. While I might have been frustrated with how easy the game was, I had to keep playing because I just wanted to toss one more lightning bolt at an enemy, or summon one more volcano on top of his capital. It can be brutal learning everything about the game since it lacks a database or tutorial, but that brutality is just another part of Warlock's fun. You'll get a great idea of what you can do and then travel through a portal only to find new enemies and units for you to obtain. Really fun and worth it if you get it on sale.

Shenmue, Animal Crossing and Maniac Mansion get thrown in a blender. What do you get? Something pretty damn good, it turns out. The platformer controls are solid, the core cast all have solid writing, and the visual style is charming. I'd say NITW has earned the rep it's built up since release.
However, is it for everyone? NITW is a game anyone can play and i'd reccomend giving it a shot, but this is a slower-paced, minigame-heavy character drama about how people interact and what secrets lurk in small towns. If fast paced action is what you're looking for in a game, this isn't gonna deliver on that end and it's honest about that from the get-go. Fans of Twin Peaks, Deadly Premonition, Stranger Things, Maniac Mansion or Life is Strange will be right at home, however. and pretty much any bedraggled college student or 20-something year old out there is gonna find something to relate to in this one. By all means, give the game a look!
Also, as a plus, the 20-something year old cast all actually talk more or less in a realistic way. No tasty plasmas to be found in this one.

If there's any game I'll be playing when I'm eighty, it will be Street Fighter. And that's a promise.

This is actually a fun tower defense game. One downside, or plus depending on your point of view, each campaing mission has a set wave enemy generation and direction, so you can plan ahead if you play a mission over.
The music is repetative and so are the voice overs. Each enemy unit takes more damage each wave, so what once worked gets swarmed by increasingly useless damaging turrets.
You can designate what individual turrets do, such as target nearest to turret, closest to exit/entrance, weakest, strongest, fastest or slowest. Giving you a more custom targeting setup, since default behavior targeting is a bit awful.
If you strive for platinum on each mission, it can get intense.

Starbound is a game completely worth buying if you love pixel art and the unending idea of exploration and research. Building and (after the recent update.) constructing Space stations.
Planet exploration:
The planets... lack variety to sum it short. yeah you have the basics such as ocean planets, or ones heavily radiated or just flat out barren. But really doesn't show any hazard or risk factors other than the environment and the possibility of falling. or having unkillable/respawning enemies at areas.
Weapons:
The weapons stick to the simplistics as well, One or two-handed, do toxic, or burning or slows, etc. Some guns, staffs, etc. But are always unique, never do you really find two of the same weapon unless its scripted and not a random generated one you can find.
The main quest/storyline:
The storyline truth be told, can seem semi-what geenric due to certain items and the main threat. But still keeps the player interested as you're having the main idea of exploring, finding clues on how you can find and continue your quest to save the universe from a creature bent to the destruction of life.
Mods/addons:
The addons or mods the workshop provides allows you to make your game more towards serious, or just humorous. Or can flat out make you extend your overall playtime (Frakin' universe) but still keeps the game lovable if you want characters to have traits or just have more species.
(NOTICE: Some addons can/will remove character data due to their modifications, save a copy of player data beforehand!)
All in all, the game is still very lovable and enjoyable despite some having a dislike to the lack of planet variety. But you can easily fix this if you like mods. then getting the frakin' universe will easily fix that ordeal.

As a longtime fan of the Ace Combat series, I have always enjoyed it's place in the arcade fighter simulator genre. Cool planes, crazy aerial boss battles, canyon/trench run challenges and conflicts in the fictional Ace Combat universe were hallmarks of the series. Unfortunately, Assault Horizon decided to completely throw out many of the core gameplay elements and themes that had made previous Ace Combat games so enjoyable, and decided to pursue a Call-of-Duty approach to gameplay and storyline.
One of the most egregious additions is the Dog-fighting mode, where with the press of 2 buttons, your plane magically maneuevers itself on the tail of the enemy and sticks there with minimal effort. Meant to highlight the "action" it just turns dogfighting into a glorified QTE.
One new direction that AC:AH took that had promise, but was poorly executed, was the expansion into other types of aircraft, including bombers and helicopters. Unfortunately, these levels seemed less about flying and more about aiming your recticle over targets on a screen (think AC-130). The end result was gimmicky execution of what could have been some very interesting and fun set pieces.
Overall, AC:AH has been a disappoinment. It could not deliver the experience of previous installments and failed to win me over with its new mechanics.

Incredibly annoying to play, while leaving the feeling that you've been treated *extremely* unfairly by the game's designers.
Imagine having to walk blind-folded through a maze littered with traps. Each time you walk into one, you have attained the dubious ability to avoid it on your next trip through the labyrinth. That, basically, is what playing "Long Live the Queen" is like. Or actually, it's even worse than that. Since knowing where a trap is and how to avoid it are two different things. But once you've figured out one of the ways of surviving a trap, you'll have to perform it (in terms of getting certain stats high enough in time) every time you replay the game. The developer actually prides him/herself that there is that there are actually two or three ways to survive a trap (scripted event) out of the circa 30 different stat bars this game sports. Injustifiably so, in my opinion, since this still leaves numerous trial & error runs until the player has found one of the solutions.
Surely the option to save your game means that you won't have to replay every single event time and again? Well, only in so far as you haven't blown any of the other choices for maxing the proper stat-bars needed for other events that will be coming soon. And you'll have to write down all the choices you've made up to the moment you saved your game. For *every* savegame, or else there is no real point in saving any of your games.
So basically, your princess character gets to die. A lot. Which is illustrated with slightly comical visuals.
Does all of that stat-maxing, route-mapping, savegame-documenting and dying over and over again sound like fun to you? Then this is just the game for you...

People tend to tell themselves, and other people, a story about what they do in a game. They'll say "I shot a bunch of aliens" in stead of "I moved the crossharirs around the screen and clicked the left mouse button" or, in this case, "I ate poison" or "I fought a duel" instead of describing the game itself. I bring this up because the story you're meant to tell yourself about this game, guiding a moe princess named Elodie through a brutal fantasy world, is pretty cool, but what you're actually doing is trial and error based resource management.
So I'm going to say what you actually do in Long Live The Queen, divorced of what those actions are supposed to mean. The game is broken into weeks. Each week you have Elodi study two skills from a wide-ranging list, with the progress affected by her mood. After that, you choose what she does on the weekend from a list, which will alter her mood and can occasionally unlock plot decisions. TSometimes you will also be given a test, where the game will check if some skill is at a high enough level, or make a decision on a branching decision tree. Sometimes failing the test or making the wrong decision will kill you, at which point you will have to go back and either get your skill high enough to survive or make a different decision.
It's all a bit abstract, then, but what's actually wrong with it? The skill checks , especially the ones that kill Elodie, just come out of nowhere. There is no warning that you're going to need a particular skill until something appears that kills her. There are exceptions. If a party is coming up you can assume there will be checks for social skills. If a war is about to happen you'll guess that war-related skill are going to be needed. These are exceptions though. Most of the time you are given no warning until you suddenly need medicine or something to not die.
There is no skill progression for the player. There is no possibility I am aware of that as you get better at the game you will develop the ability to plan ahead and prevent the next arbitrary death. You can only watch what happens and then redo your decisions to prevent it after the fact, or occasionally just luck out. So there are, really, only two ways to play this game. You can progress along a particular path until you reach a skill check that kills Elodie or blocks off whatever path you wanted to go down, then you go back and redo the training decisions to pass that skill check over and over and over again; or you can use a walkthrough that just tells you what skills to train and what decisions to make. To me, both of those options are intensely boring.
That being said, the basic joke of the game, the contrast between a cutesy anime style and a horrible setting, is amusing for a little while. If you can get the game cheap you might enjoy that part of it for a bit. I just don't see it as a  game I'm going to play now that I've seen one of the ending, thanks to a walkthrough, and I'm over the art style.

Now I'm a fan of the Railroad Tycoon franchise and OpenTTD and I was really looking forward to enjoying this game.
The first experience was horrible. The text was all fuzzy and barely readable on a Win10 4k resolution. That problem went away after I restarted the game, however the mouse pointer was restricted to 3/4 of the screen. Lowering the resolution at that point didn't fix it, playing in a window did.
The game lacks a tutorial. It lacks a campain. You're just thrown in the game on your own. It's unbelievable how unpolished the UI is in this game. It really feels like splatted buttons and text by a novice.
Laying rail track is a pain. Raising a road to create a bridge over rail tracks is easy, but that is a whole different ball game for rail bridges over roads. Go figure.
I kept going though, looking at guides and reading forums. But I immediately stopped playing and asked for a refund when I realized that every time the game was computing the finances and displaying the maintenance cost for 3 !!! running vehicles froze the game for a fraction of a second on a 6 core I7 and a 980TI. I'm a software developer and I immediately understood that the simulation is running on a single thread. If this was happening in the first hour of playing the game, imagine what it would be like later on in the game.
UPDATE: Digging into the forums, this is indeed one of the top complaints:

It becomes unplayable later on in the game or on a large map.
Don't believe the excuse that synchronizing resource access in a multi-threaded app is killing its performance. If the code is done right, and the synchronization primitives are being used correctly, you'll get a cool working game with nicely balanced work loads on all the available CPU cores and even on the GPU compute cores. If things get too hectic and the load reaches a high threshold value, the code can simply lower the simulation speed or coarse grain the steps in order to compensate, but still run tasks in parallel. Nowadays, there is no excuse for not fully taming the power we've got in our computers. Multi-core CPUs weren't invented yesterday!
The graphics are nice, that's the only positive about the game. The developers simply stopped short of finishing the game and moved on to DLCs and future titles. Or I could give them the benefit of the doubt and say that they lacked the skill. Simulations are not easy to get right.

A swiss company tried to do the next "Transport Tycoon", but they are not Chris Sawyer  (the creator of the Transport Tycoon games) and now we are not in the 90's.
The result? They built a slow-at-the-end tiny-map game that at maximum is a communter train simulator for a middle-sized city in a incredibly boring map. Graphics, other than trains, are simply "meh". Plus, you do by far more revenue with buses (in a game called "TRAIN fever") that with trains, even more, you go bankrupcy with trains if they are no 100% full all the time and only 5 years old.
What has gone wrong? Easy, Chris Sawyer developed the original game using a programming language called "Assembler" that allowed him to juice ALL the resources of the computer at that time so the result was amaizing. The swiss team but used a 3D engine base, that also is based in tons of another programs, so they had little control of where the resources of the computer are spent. Actually is not their fault, the 3D simulation and its level of freedom of possibilities is by far more complex than the 2D graphics of the original game plus using that kind of programs is a normal choice by small software companies.
What to do? Play OpenTTD (it's FREE), and if you love it, help it to fund a better graphics patch. That's all.
Finally, please note that is simply impossible to do a decent high-scale 3D transport game, too many resources spent for a game that will be used by not a big chunk of people (hoping that I'm wrong about that last sentence).

Absolutely NOT worth asking price!! Grab thier other game, Transport Fever, instead. Or Rise of Industry on itch.io. Or Mashinky.
Do not waste your money on this.

I love this game so much. I didn't, at first, but I do now.
I tried to play DS:PtDE on Steam back in like, 2014, at a friend's recommendation. Jaded and cynical, this, he said, was the only good game on the market anymore...the only game that didn't suck. So I fired it up, and it was a little unattractive graphically, and wildly unintuitive, and didn't do much in the way of teaching me before throwing my first boss at me. I put the game down for a few months, and when I came back, I finally made it out of the Undead Asylum, the game's opening area. But I ran the wrong way and got killed by skeletons, and threw up my hands and said "♥♥♥♥ it". It was over a year until I picked the game up on Xbox and set out to beat it. And with a little sage wisdom from my friend on how to get started, a lot of tenacity, and some helpful folks on the wikis and Reddit, I did finally plow through to the end. In the year since then I've beaten both sequels, and gotten a tattoo on my arm. I love this game.
I built a new gaming PC and re-downloaded Dark Souls with the intention of installing DSfix and giving it a shot with fancy-shmancy graphics and a knowledge of what I was actually doing, and Steam told me in those first two attempts at playing the game, I put in a grand total of 47 minutes. I felt so silly looking at that number, and thought of what a shame it is that so many people will be like I was, and give up immediately, blaming the game for being too opaque or difficult. But my friend was (sort of) right in his enthusiasm. This was a life-changing game. It changed the way I think about video games and the way they are designed. It's flawed, but it's a masterpiece. Everyone should play it, and everyone should let themselves be challenged by it. 15 years of set-your-own-difficulty 8-hour campaign games and quick-time events have likely spoiled you, and you owe it to yourself to remind yourself what games used to be like, particularly if you, like me, come from the age of Mega Man. The age of owning only the handful of games your parents bought you, and you were going to beat them come hell or high water. The age of smashing your head into video game brick walls with the intent to succeed in breaking them down.
Come sit by the bonfire a while. You won't regret it.

Night in the Woods is a great Visual Novel Platformer Guitar Hero Slice of Life (VNPGHSoL) game that blends each of it's elements into a fantastic experience. Each of the characters in Night in the Woods is memorable in some way, be it the calm Angus or the pessimistic Bea, the Night in the Woods team has made sure that every character in the world is unique in some way, making them all memorable. Night in the Woods also has a dynamic, changing world. Thoughout the Weird Autumn that the game takes place in, conflicts arise, characters develop...even without player interaction. In NITW, the Player can walk around Possum Springs everyday, seeing just how the verious stories of each of the characters develops, creating a dynamic environment.
The Story of Night in the Woods has a fantastic blend between realism, wackiness, seriousness, and fun. With it's various minigames and branching paths, Night in the Woods has a ton of replay value, allowing the player to experience the story of Mae between two major paths, depending on which of two friends - Bea and Gregg you hang out with more. With it's themes of friendship, mental illness, returning home, and personal growth, Night in the Woods is a game with a compelling story, witty dialogue, and fun characters that will leave you thinking about it for months afterward, and is worth the time of any story enthusiast. Night in the Woods is one of my favorite games of all time, and I would rate it a 10/10

Excellent sandbox game!
The graphics are generally good, however without a great PC it is hard sometimes to obtain an adequate framerate. The environment is well designed, and the sensation of... decay and fear that a zombie apocalypse should cause is always present. Gosh, how I hate to be surprised by a sneaking zombie while scavenging.
The story is ok, the voice acting could be better, but it's ok. It would be great to have a wider variety of phrases instead of... you know... stuff.
So, what is it to like? The freedom to explore and decide where you want to put your survivors, the missions are mostly interesting and the hard ones can sometimes catch you by surprise. The perma-death adds a sense of sadness in this post-apocalyptic scenario and it is really devastating when you grow attached to your characters. The day-night cycle is interesting, it's a shame that there are not ways to spend the night besides keep going outside.
My only complaint is the existence of freak zeds. It seems unnecessary, it is like the game is trying to emulate left4dead with this variety... the real threat should be the sheer numbers of brainless undead, not special zed with insta-kill-like powers. This universe could be a lot better if it were more like The Walking Dead.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is a mix of tower defense and third person action. You have to defend your base(s), called rifts in this game, against a horde of Orcs. To do that you build traps and shoot at your enemies with weapons.
The game feels very polished, the graphics have a nice cartoon look, the ragdolls and animations are nice. There is a large variety of traps, weapons and trinkets (artifacts that give special abilities) and all of them can be upgraded. You can build traps wherever you want, which allows for an endless amount of different tactics. The action part isn't about quick reflexes and aiming skills either, it's more part of the tactic you use. Will you defend only a part of the level with traps and try to hold back the hordes in the other part yourself? Or will you put less traps throughout the whole level and kill any enemies that may come through, wherever that may be? What weapon will you use? Use traps to kill the larger enemies and have a weapon that is good for crowd control? Or the other way around? Not kill enemies at all and slow them down instead so your traps can do their dirty work? Lots of possibilities there.
But not everything about the game is great unfortunately. The multiplayer can only be played with (Steam) friends, so no playing with random people like in other games.
The biggest flaw in my opinion are the difficulty levels though. There are three difficulty levels, easy (called Apprentice), normal (called War Mage) and hard (called Nightmare). Easy is not worth playing for anyone who played tower defense games before. Normal can be challenging at times (especially if you want to get the highest rating), but once you've upgraded a good amount of your equipment it's not that hard anymore. After you have completed the game in normal mode you unlock hard mode.
And that's where the problem is. Hard mode could be a real challenge and a lot of fun. More enemies, harder enemies, more madness. But unfortunately they decided to remove the planning phase between waves on that difficulty level. Sure, the game becomes even harder that way. But is that what tower defense games should be about? I want to plan where I put my traps, I want to use a nice tactic. This is not possible in hard mode. After the initial planning phase (where you naturally can only spend the money you start with, which isn't much) you run around like a mad man trying to kill enemies while placing traps and trying to stay alive. No time for thinking, no time to analyze where your defenses aren't strong enough or what you could improve. It's also (more or less, you actually have 3 seconds between waves for it) impossible to sell/replace traps. The game turns from a game that is about tactics and careful planning with a bit of action thrown into the mix into a mad hack and slash action game with a tiny amount of tactics only on that difficulty level. That's a shame and makes the hard difficulty not worth playing in my opinion.
But overall I can still recommend the game, especially since it's cheap and the Complete Edition offers a lot of content that is fun to play at least on normal difficulty.

Long Live the Queen is a fun little visual novel where the main object is to... well, live long.

The game also deserves credit for having a very nicely realized world, with lots of background detail that adds to its charm. The geography, history, and characterization all add up to complex land with all kinds of variables that will change your game.
Seriously, though, this game is addicting. All of the different paths you can take, all of the different deaths, and, true to visual novel form, all of the different possible endings (and that's aside from the death ones!).

Anyways. This game is pretty fun. You could say it's a management game in away, in the sense that you manage the protag's skills, mood, and decisions you make as Queen-to-be.
Basically you're sent back home to the castle and you have to start taking private lessons with your tutors to increase your skills in things like your knowledge of Medicine, Economy, Military, Faith, Royal Demeanor, Conversation, Expression, Animal Handling, Weapons, Athletics, History, and Intrigue. All of those are just the categories, there's like three sub-categories you can choose within each of those, so you kind of have to experiment what you think would be more useful before something happens; which is why it's nice they give you more than enough saves.

The significance of those skills is that if you have one of them high enough you can make decisions or it'll help you decide on what decision to make before something happens. It'll also make your situation better, like I maxed out my Military skills (Strategy, Naval Strategy, and Logistics) and I won a civil, pretty straightforward.
Then there's the mood system, where it adds a bonus when taking a class of a certain category, which just means you get more skill points in said class. Each mood has a set of bonus categories and a penalty to others. The penalty just does the opposite of what the bonus does, meaning you don't gain as many skill points in that category as much as you would normally if there wasn't a penalty
If you train a skill category far enough, you'll get an outfit; which boosts that category you got the outfit from. It adds some skill points when equipped, not too much but it can help.
The story, I'll leave that to the individual to decide. Eveyone has different likes and dislikes about things and I figure my opinion on such wouldn't hold much weight.
If you do buy this game, prepare to make mistakes and die a lot. You'd probably have to be pretty carefully about what skills you train to not die.

This is not your average visual novel. You are in charge and you make every decision. And there are a LOT of decisions. You will die in many more ways than you'll ever win.
In Long Live the Queen, you guide Princess Elodie on her journey to becoming the Queen of Nova, an empire that has lost a lot of its old strength. It's up to you to prepare yourself for your coronation in 40 weeks on your 15th birthday. There are many obstacles in your path such as warring neighbors, magical secrets, and flirty princes. How you establish yourself as the Queen is entirely up to you.
The game is played one week at a time allowing you to train Elodie in two skills from a list of about forty and usually followed by an event in the evening that forces you to make a game changing decision. Making these decisions is difficult due to the cost and reward trade-offs that are not always visible. Your available options during events as well as the outcome of your choices are determined by skill checks that show if you've failed, succeeded, or partially succeeded. It's impossible to play a perfect game as you cannot train your skills to pass each event. This gives the game an ample amount of replay value to go back and train different skills to pass different events.
Training skills is more complicated than simply picking a class to learn. There are bonuses and penalties applied to learning skill groups based on your current most overwhelming mood. Throughout the game you will encounter events that make you angry, afraid, cheerful, depressed, willful, yielding, pressured, and/or lonely and it's a difficult balancing act to push Elodie into the mood that fits your current strategy. At the end of each week you also get the opportunity to do a simple activity that gives you some control over which mood Elodie will be in during the following week. Mastering control of Elodie's mood is extremely important and learning the mechanics behind it is vital to your success.
The setting, story, and mood all play very well together in Long Live the Queen. The developer clearly had a strong idea of what stories were to be presented and, although it might not look like it at first, everything has an importance. The music can be a little repetitive, but it does change frequently enough between classes, events, and activities that I never grew tired of it. I was often aware of where the game was headed based on music cues and facial expressions of the characters without having to read any of the text. The dialog never drags on, but if you've viewed the scene before you have the option to skip the text which I never used until I had completed the majority of the game.

As an Ace Combat game, it's not great. Assault Horizon does away with the pretty in depth fictional universe that the Ace series was known for on PS2. Gone are Mobius Squadron, Razgriz, Thunderhead, Skye Eye, and the various fictional countries with their histories. This is basically MURIKA VERSUS THE TERRORISTS like you'd see in CoD or the like, only in planes. It's pretty silly and modern war-sy, but it's tolerable.
As an action / arcade dogfight game though, it's fun. It still maintains the "Planes carry absurd amounts of missiles" feature from the Ace series, and the graphics are pretty awesome. Not only that, but as scripted feeling and over the top action movie-ish the new Dog Fight Mode may be, it can still be fun at times. Weaving between buildings, struggling to maintain a lock, and peppering an enemy fighter with cannon fire is genuinely thrilling. I can't say I'm a big fan of the helicopter levels, nor the AC-130 one (Because what modern war game would be complete without an AC-130 level?), but in terms of overall enjoyability, I liked it. It was worth buying on sale, and while it may not be as amazing as 4/5/Zero, it's worth a look if you just want to fly around and take down entire wings of planes with your Ultimate Hero Guy abilities.

I returned my Dreamcast to buy the original Playstation 20 years ago because I spent hours in ToysRus playing the demo of Air Combat. One night I went in and some kid was hogging the Playstation station. He wouldn't get off so I bought my own console because Air Combat was just that good. It wasn't til a few weeks later that I discovered Doom and then Tomb Raider and Resident Evil. Air Combat sold me on Playstation.
Action, action, action. As soon as you shoot down one bunch, they're replaced with another bunch. That could be a good thing but in this game I just found it to be tedious. You're constantly turning, pulling G's. It seems like it never ends and then they give you an awful cut scene and then they turn you into a helicopter gunner. If fighter jets fought in stadium sized battles then this would be an accurate sim. I almost never feel like I'm flying. I'm just steering a camera around some tight turns with a picture of a jet plane in front of me. They never let you do your own thing like explore the world or the capabilities of the jet. It never feels like anything more than a game.
The game is constantly telling you to do things. Sure it is helpful to integrate the tutorial with the gameplay but it sucks when a huge flashing "Y" button starts throbbing in the middle of your intense dogfight. The game is ordering you to eject into a cutscene.
For an action game I'm surprised they weren't concerned how bad this game is at giving you the feeling of speed and acceleration. At least in the early game the feeling of S and A just isn't there for more than a second. I never feel like I am moving through air or being lifted by lift. I just turn my camera with the pasted on HUD and go to different parts of the background picture. Then they have that part where your computer or console takes you down real low through a forest of smoke stacks and girders. That might have been cool if I felt like I actually was steering or choosing to go there. I am moving sticks and such but obviously there's a lot of "assists" going on or something. Its almost a cutscene. You'd think that would be a good thing to be at the controls going through those maneuvers but the whole thing is so fudged and predetermined its just disappointing and annoying.
The sophisticated navigation consists of a little map in the corner with glowing arrows. It makes me feel so like I'm in a modern fighter plane.
You also won't be bowled over by the airplane models, the HUD models or anything like that. They all are definitely blah.
I was a fan of the original Air Combat as it came out on the PS1 and while that wasn't really a sim, it was better than this. If you like a lot of fast action and constant battle or you're just wondering how something this action packed can be so boring  then Ace Combat might be the game for you.

Some great spiritual sequels to Master of Magic have been made over the years, and Warlock - Master of the Arcane is definitely one of the best and is an absolute joy to play (as you can tell from the hours I've put into it lol). Warlock doesn't have much in the way of cutscenes, story or ultra fancy graphics as it focuses more on the strategic magical world conquest side of things so the game looks pretty good but still runs great even on older systems. The strategy and RPG elements are awesome, there is just so much depth that I had to play the game 3 times just to make sure that I'd done everything haha! Just like in master of magic you colonise cities, research spells, hire/rescue heroes, explore dark dangerous mirror/paradise/lava/ice/desert worlds (up to 8 in total you can conquer and colonise) and command great armies that all level up with skill choices.
Some of the interesting differences in Warlock to MoM are worshipping gods & performing their quests for rewards (much like in Age of Wonders), building city buildings on surrounding map squares with specific terrain bonuses (like Civ 6), and no zoomed in tactical combat with instead more of a Civilization series style combat on the world view. I highly recommend this game & I'm very much looking forward to playing the sequel soon!
I recommend you get all the dlc as they add cool things like artefact crafting & an extra playable race. Without these the game feels a little 'light'.

So, for those that have wondered whether or not to get this game, let start off with asking, do you like "realistic" zombie games? If your answer is yes, then this is the game for you.
You start off out in the wilderness, having come back from some good old fashioned fun with a buddy, and of course, come to civilization being a living hell. What happened you ask, the hell if I know, them damns government folks won't talk, and you have bigger problems then asking why it happened, because hey, an endless horde of flesh eating dead people are coming for you. Its a baptisim by fire, and you are at the center of the complete and utter decay of humanity.
The map is huge, and I really mean huge. Not as large as Red Dead Redemption, but, that is hardly relevant. Think of the Undead Nightmare expansion, but, in modern times, with cars, better guns, and having to actually survive. You build your fortress amongst the ruins of the old world, scavenging supplies and rounding up other survivors to further supplement your bastion of life in the seas of the dead. Zombies range from the normal slow shambly kind, to the specials, who are a world of hurt for the unprepared. This game brings forth the true feeling of despair, and cruise ship loads of fun.
The map is beautiful, the landscape amazing. From the untouched reaches of some little prairie house, to the blood spattered streets of the bigger towns. Gun stores, food marts, gas stations, and everything else play crucial roles in everything you will do to linger on. Building barricades, using your flash light, melee or ranged, all this comes together to  envelop the user with crucial choices. Because there is sound, and sound attracts the attention of the dead, and those dead can be in lone pairs, being flanked by a special super zombie, or if you are unlucky, in a horde.
I have had the most fun playing this game compared to all other zombie games. Trust me, if you are rearing for a true zombie survival horror game, then splurge on yourself and get this. Hell, if you are still unsure, as maybe you don't like using mouse and keyboard, you can hook up a game controller to the good ol' USB port, and play that way. Tell your friends, and all of you rush to your wallets, and buy this ASAP. You will not regret your decision. And, when you've played to the end, been there and back again, you can always up the difficulty, or even, if you are a fun loving gun fanatic, use some cheats and get infinite ammo, and go to town on these deaders.

Here's the deal with Thinking with Time Machine.
It's a free mod trying to be a sort of "fan-fictionesque" epilogue to Portal 2, which, really didn't need one.
I wouldn't find this an issue if it weren't for a couple facts.
One, the puzzles are simple to figure out, but difficult to execute. Some puzzles can even become impossible to solve because you can trap yourself. The element of using a past self to solve puzzles is neat and brings a unique element into it, but it ultimately doesn't feel challenging or mind blowing in any way. Most puzzles just feel frustrating because you have to avoid getting your cube or sphere disintegrated by all of the emancipation grills shoved in every corner instead of, y'know, strategically. Nothing feels like it was tested to make sure it was not only challenging, but fun. It just feels like "Well, here's some puzzles, I guess."
And two, while visually impressive, everything else is just lacking. There is no real story to speak of, no dialog outside of a line at the very end, and no real atmosphere. It feels like a facade of Aperture, not something I felt I would really see in the lab itself. And it ultimately kills it. There's no real drive to continue, and it's quite a short mod. I was startled when I just suddenly finished it.
It just... doesn't have any personality or challenge. I'm certainly glad it was just a free mod, and in that sense, I suppose it's worth a play if you want to have a few more Portal-style puzzles. But if you're expecting something, anything, similar to what Portal or Portal 2 was, you will be disappointed.
I know it seems silly to rate a free mod so poorly. I don't think ill of it, it just wasn't what I had hoped it would be.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is a mix of tower defense and third person action. You have to defend your base(s), called rifts in this game, against a horde of Orcs. To do that you build traps and shoot at your enemies with weapons.
The game feels very polished, the graphics have a nice cartoon look, the ragdolls and animations are nice. There is a large variety of traps, weapons and trinkets (artifacts that give special abilities) and all of them can be upgraded. You can build traps wherever you want, which allows for an endless amount of different tactics. The action part isn't about quick reflexes and aiming skills either, it's more part of the tactic you use. Will you defend only a part of the level with traps and try to hold back the hordes in the other part yourself? Or will you put less traps throughout the whole level and kill any enemies that may come through, wherever that may be? What weapon will you use? Use traps to kill the larger enemies and have a weapon that is good for crowd control? Or the other way around? Not kill enemies at all and slow them down instead so your traps can do their dirty work? Lots of possibilities there.
But not everything about the game is great unfortunately. The multiplayer can only be played with (Steam) friends, so no playing with random people like in other games.
The biggest flaw in my opinion are the difficulty levels though. There are three difficulty levels, easy (called Apprentice), normal (called War Mage) and hard (called Nightmare). Easy is not worth playing for anyone who played tower defense games before. Normal can be challenging at times (especially if you want to get the highest rating), but once you've upgraded a good amount of your equipment it's not that hard anymore. After you have completed the game in normal mode you unlock hard mode.
And that's where the problem is. Hard mode could be a real challenge and a lot of fun. More enemies, harder enemies, more madness. But unfortunately they decided to remove the planning phase between waves on that difficulty level. Sure, the game becomes even harder that way. But is that what tower defense games should be about? I want to plan where I put my traps, I want to use a nice tactic. This is not possible in hard mode. After the initial planning phase (where you naturally can only spend the money you start with, which isn't much) you run around like a mad man trying to kill enemies while placing traps and trying to stay alive. No time for thinking, no time to analyze where your defenses aren't strong enough or what you could improve. It's also (more or less, you actually have 3 seconds between waves for it) impossible to sell/replace traps. The game turns from a game that is about tactics and careful planning with a bit of action thrown into the mix into a mad hack and slash action game with a tiny amount of tactics only on that difficulty level. That's a shame and makes the hard difficulty not worth playing in my opinion.
But overall I can still recommend the game, especially since it's cheap and the Complete Edition offers a lot of content that is fun to play at least on normal difficulty.

The differences between (for example) Diablo and Diablo 2 are very stark and there's no way you could play for a few minutes without being sure which game you're playing. Not the case here. This is essentially the difference between playing Diablo 2 with or without the Lord of Destruction expansion.
Again, not saying it's not worth the money or any such thing. I'm just a little disappointed that it's so similar to the original.
So yes, it's a good game. But if you already own Orcs Must Die, wait for this to go on sale. If you don't already play OMD, skip it. This is better. You'll miss a little bit of the "plot," (such as it is), but it won't detract from your enjoyment of the game. Definitely get it. It's an excellent expansion.

Dark Souls is one of those games that can really make one reconsider their outlook on games and general game value. For me, personally, this was a game that made me rethink my outlook on games and especially singleplayer RPG experiences.
Everything, from the way the world of Dark Souls is portrayed to the player through its subtle and environment based storytelling to one of the best level designs in video game history since some of the best Zelda games, this game only gets better the more you discover it.
Dark Soul's is highly renown and marketed by many for its overall difficulty and punishing combat, but I truly feel like that image doesn't give the game enough justice. I think that Dark Souls isn't so much a game about difficulty as it is a game about LEARNING to overcome challenge and that patience and resilience no matter how skilled or unskilled you are will inevitably allow you to overcome hurdles and learn from your failures. I discovered about 30 hours into the game that Dark Souls truly isn't a game that focuses solely on difficulty even though I had just fought what seemed as one of the hardest bosses in any video game. Ironic, isn't it? Sure, one of the core aspects at the start of the game is difficulty, but the game becomes much more streamlined and intuitive as you, the player learn how to act and behave in the game.
Once you understand Dark Soul's mentality you become much more cautious and for the most part learn to one-shot a lot more corridors and maybe even bosses. This however, to me had no effect on my enjoyment of the game. I discovered by the end of the game that even with lower difficulty, the game never becomes dull or a chore. Every new environment you discover and new characters and plots you follow continue to impress you until the very end regardless of how much of its difficulty your playthrough and character build allow you to retain.
I truly hope you give Dark Souls a chance and that perhaps in the process you discover a new type of appreciation for video games that you maybe didn't have before!
Good luck and have fun!

This game is awesome. The developers are constantly adding new cool stuff, expanding the map, and fixing bugs and exploits. There are many servers to choose from, and each has different rules (PvE, PvP, no base raiding...), so that you can easily find what can give you the best experience. It's true that the population is still fluctuating, since some players come back only after major updates, but trust me, when you start playing this game there are countless hours of fun before you get bored and have seen and looted everything. The map is very large, and the very realistic graphics and weather effects make exploration very immersive. Weapons are very varied and detailed. Mutants are everywhere and are pretty scary, at least until you find some good weapons and lots of ammo. AI is still being worked on, and although the occasional mutant may glitch every now and then and freeze on the spot, in general it's pretty good. Base building is fun, although placing the parts is a bit frustrating without a snap feature (but this will be fixed in the near future).
For those who don't like the PvP aspect of the game there are now quite a few PvE servers.
Also, most of the negative reviews here are from people who lament the fact that they get killed a lot on the PvP servers, but that's because they are silly and join high population servers straight away. New players should start from low population servers (low chance of meeting hostile players) or PvE servers.
And last but not least, permadeath (another general complaint) is not really accurate. If your character dies, you have a 10 minutes time frame to find your body and loot everything back (of course if you have been killed by another player some items will be gone, most likely your ammo and food, but most of your gear would still be there). This may seem hard to do at the beginning, when you respawn in the middle of nowhere and you have no clue where you are, but once you have familiarized with the map it's very feasible (you'll soon recognize where you have spawned and know where you need to go to retrieve your body; the map is large, but there is plenty of landmarks).
If you haven't tried this game yet I definitely recommend it, you won't regret it.

The game itself hasn't changed since I last played, hopefully with a steam release they'll get the players they need to start making the game great again (see what I did?). Ryzom is an AMAZING MMORPG, and I have no issue with the ART STYLE at all. The graphics may not be the most high end, however the game looks amazing because of the art style they chose to go with it. And the non-high end graphics also mean even very old PCs/macs/linux users can almost certainly still play Ryzom on. This actually is very smart as far as gaming goes, because it allows far more players into the game.
Animals interact with you, each other and even the world. On mainland, when it rains, animals go for shelter under the trees. On silan (the starting/tutorial island), you'll first notice Yubos examining you, looking up at you with their cute faces or a herd of animals migrating depending on the day. Animals (some of them) migrate depending on the season, or even the weather. There are herbivores and carnivores, and the carnivores will attack the herbivores and the herbivores will group together to take down the carnivore (or sometimes the carnivore gets away). You never see that kind of VERY advanced AI in even singleplayer RPGs, and Ryzom came out years ago.
And crafting. If you played SWG (star wars galaxies) pre-cu...and loved the crafting there. You'll love this just as much. Different resources give different stats/bonuses to each crafted item, and there is quality to think of to. There are hundreds of thousands or even more, of items of different qualities, stats and bonuses you can craft. Its very much like SWG in that regard.
Harvesting (digging) however is pretty unique in Ryzom. But they didn't have much funding for art of each resource. So it feels pretty meh, when all I do is harvest the same thing and get different items out of it. As far as I have seen, each resource looks exactly the same. A green cluster of blobs. No blue blob, no yellow blob, not even different shapes. They just re-used the art of one harvest "node" and copy/pasted it to each and every single one. So even if you are harvesting shells or whatever, its just a boring green blob of resources. Feels like they didn't have funding for an artstyle for each type of resource. They probably put in a lore reason (I'm sure there is) for that to hide the fact they couldn't afford it, but...well... still feels like they couldn't afford more art for different resources. Or even different colors of it. Of course, that is just the "looks". But it does make it feel meh to me.
When digging, you can interact with said resource. You can "gently" harvest, where you probably won't get as much out of it, but you won't take damage if it "explodes" in gas (that happens and you CAN die when digging). And then there is "harmful" digging of said resource, where you get more quality overall, and the potential to get 2 (or more) of that resource. However, you'll have a bigger chance of a gas cloud, and a higher chance of destroying the resource.
Of course, there is a lot more to harvesting. Different types of resources appear in different seasons (some only appear in winter for example), only in day, or only in night. Its quite involved. And like I said, can even die when harvesting.
There WAS a severe lack of content update...not just for months and months...but for YEARS. I looked on the forums for any significant content update and saw none.  Last big one was being able to create your own dungeon or something with Ryzom Ring, but it was abandoned (lack of funds?) and it also didn't give out any rewards or anything at all, so pretty much most lost interest quick. So like the harvesting artwork (whether there is "lore" reason for the lack of it or not), they haven't had much funding for big updates. With that said, there have been other MMOs (free to play) on Steam that were in the same shape Ryzom is/was in, and then benefited so much that the developers were able to start putting out significant updates to them.
According to wiki's (google search "define free to play") definition of what free to play.
"Free-to-play (F2P) refers to video games which give players access to a significant portion of their content without paying. There are several kinds of free-to-play games, but the most common is based on the freemium software model."
As for the "free to play" negative reviews. That definition is exactly Ryzom's free to play model. There is no wrong advertisement or cheating of words that Ryzom is using. It is literally free to play as defined by wiki and google.
I highly recommend Ryzom, despite a lot of negative reviews, I'd say try it for yourself :) Especially if you like harder MMOs or SWG. Might end up liking it :) Or might not, its very different and very challenging, so won't be for everyone.

Ignore my played time please.  I have played this game on and off for many years.  The Saga of Ryzom....I guess they dropped the Saga part now and just call it Ryzom, is a very unique world.  It is a living world where the npc animals interact wiith each other and you.  Often while sitting digging up resources a curious animal will wander up and stare at you...and sometimes pee on you. Carnivores eat herbivores and you...herbivores won't attack you. .I'm glad it has come to Steam as it could use an infusion of players that this offers, just in the few minutes I logged in I saw loads of new players in the tutorial area.  I'll get to the point...or points.  Here goes.
Pros:
- Living world that interacts with itself and the player.
-One of the best Craft systems any MMO has to offer....on par with Star Wars Galaxies (may it rest in peace).  Each ingredient has a level, quality, and color that all affect the final product.  As well as stats  for various things like hardness and flexibility depending on what you are crafting.  You don't want a flexible sword....
- "Craft" your own skills and spells.  When you learn a skill you get a set of parts that make up the skill.  Want it to do more damage?  Ok...but you may need to make it cost more mana.  Want to find 3 harvest nodes instead of 1...sure but you will need to balance it out with something.  You can use the premade ones...or tailor them to your play style.
- A classless and leveless system.  Gain exp in what you are doing.  Make your character the way you want.  Mix and match skills at will.
- Two different..."religious" type sets that affect the players in interesting ways.
- Four races that are not elves and dwarves....each race has it's own craft style.
- Colorful and interesting world to explore with unique monsters.  No rats or bears here.
Cons
- It is an aging game so the graphics are a little out dated, but not that bad.
- Once off the tutorial island....the player density drops....I am hoping that with the Steam boost it will change.
- The UI is a little...wierd.  You can move stuff around and such to make it more on par with what you like.
- More like a free trial than free to play, although you can go fairly far without paying into it and have a good time.  If you manage to make out your skills on the free account...you probably want to buy it anyway.
- The classless/leveless skill system is great....but it has always felt a little flat to me.  There is no reason to pick one race or another, no advantage other thank looks.  I feel it would be more...individual...if you were limited to how many skills you could learn.  Then there would be some thought into the process.  But as it stands everyone can get every skill to either 125 for free or 250 for paid.  This is probably more something that bothers me and most won't care.
Overall well worth downloading and trying it out.  At least run through the tutorial Island and missions for the various skill sets and see how interesting the world is.  It has many unique features that we still don't see in other games.  If I had to pick a game that it is most similar too....I would say Star Wars Galaxies for it's crafting system, harvesting and skill system (before they ruined and killed SWG that is).

I am a fan of Railroad Tycoon Simulator and decided to try this one to see what do I get.
The pros: the bus system is a great plus to the train builder which allows you the perfect support for your trains to reach anywhere (no need to set a station next to a hub of farms just to get their cargo for example). The graphics are clearly great in details and the map builder engine allows each map to be always different.
The cons:
- The user interface is TERRIBLE, sometimes I feel I am in some sort of tool like Photoshop with lots of mini Windows instead than having a clear UI designed and themed as a game.
- The graphics are good, but on auto-generating it you can feel it's not that beautiful. I prefer to play real life maps like England or France and feel like the tycoons of its day building the railroad and connecting historical cities.
- The options to set up the trains are very limited, even the buses, you can play a few hours but there isn't much to it, not much strategy or required set up to adapt to changes as there aren't that many changes or doesn't seem to.
- The building tracks engine is terrible. It generates unnecessary climbs or tunnels and requires to invest massive fortunes just to connect to pieces that aren't that unlevelled and in other games are much easier to connect. Ok I know RailroadTyccon is quite unrealistic with certain train tracks but in the end you can connect the pieces without so much hassle and play, which is the point after all, having fun, not realism.
- Didn't play enough as to know this, but doesn't seem to allow me to build factories or any other sort of business like hotels or pubs which usually increases the game possibilities as you are running a company and not necessarily want to stick to trains only, giving you full control of goods transport and production. Though in compensation you have the buses and roads.
I still haven't played it that much as to completely value it and I'm certain there is more to it than what I've seen, will update this review if I see more pros or I change my mind on certain cons, but so far this is what I saw.
Personally, having Railroad Tycoon 2 and 3, any of those is more fun from minute 1 and makes me evade from this world consuming hours of my life without realizing, which probes how good they are as games, this game instead made me check the clock several times as I was getting bored and stressed. This game should have never been made. I'll review the game in the form of a pros and cons list, but with a brief preface. I refuse to compromise my experience in a flight sim. I don't care if a dev or community says "It's meant to be played with gamepad!" or "It's not good for a stick". I don't care. I expect my flight sims to work well with a stick, and when they don't, that's an incomplete game to me. I was not able to get very far without quitting due to frustration.
PROS
+Graphics are great. Naturally better than the consoles due to being on PC
+Actual menu options
+Similar HUD style to the console ACE games
CONS
-Atrocious controls, the game will abscond with aileron control if you so much as even think about not being 100% level with the ground
-Bad joystick optimization. It's either oversensitive or undersensitive and the default button layout is pretty bad, IMHO.
-Weird key mapping. Controls and commands are not clustered for your fingers' convenience or by similarity in function or frequency of use. If you expect to use a keyboard, get the stretchy guy from Fantastic 4 to help out.
-Storyline is thin gruel. Voicework, story, setting, and characters are all 100% generic or overdone. It is the opposite of ACE 04, which had an interesting story and method of delivering it and an effective, interesting cast of characetsr (that interestingly enough didn't really include the player)
-Dogfight sequences. It's like a bad on-rails shooter sequence that makes you control the rails as well as shoot, and you can't damage a lot of important enemies outside of this sequence.
-You are required to pay money to experience this. Goat Simulator is much cheaper (ignoring current sale price) and is far more intuitive and motivating

Long story short, tl’dr version? It’s a completely sub-average action game that has a few high moments but also has some really low ones evening it out. If you can get it on sale then it’s probably worth your time, but at full price I can’t recommend it. Also as I always like to mention when reviewing a game in this genre, Ace Combat is an ARCADE flight game, meaning it’s not a hyper-realistic flight-sim but instead an action game in the air which is something I see getting confused about a lot.
Much longer version? Assault Horizon isn’t a horrible game, and if you enjoy the arcade flight genre you’ll likely get at least one playthrough out of it. That said it’s definitely one if not the weakest entry in the Ace Combat series and some really weird design decisions keep it from being infinitely replayable like its forbearers.  Positives include some attractive if not top-of-the-line visuals, good voice work, and a really strong score.

But that’s where the praise ends really and it can’t make up for what the game’s lacking, and some really atrocious gameplay mechanics. First-and-foremost is the big elephant in the room that every review touches on, the automated dogfighting mode (DFM). Basically once you’ve gotten within shooting distance of an enemy you hit a key and the game pulls into a close-cam attack that has the computer automatically trailing the enemy, with you focusing on achieving lock-on.
I think I know what they were going for here. They wanted to create a more cinematic experience allowing you to go through all sorts of tight turns and close-ground fly-bys that just aren’t possible for most players. But in actuality what you get is a system that takes 90% of the gameplay out of your hands, and is buggy to boot. Now I can hear what you’re saying, “Don’t use it then”, which I would love to do but the game forces you to make use of it.
Enemy planes are capable of pulling impossible moves (not in a thrust vectoring way, in a literally turns 180 on the spot way that I’m pretty sure is a straight out bug) that absolutely require the use of this mode as trailing enemies, and switching between them is sluggish in manual. To make matters worse things get really…obvious as the max speed of the planes you fly increases. If your plane is faster than the enemies you enter a jumpy, stilted slide-show as your plane forcibly slows down so that you don’t go flying past the enemy making the fact that the system is totally on-rails really blatant. I’m not averse to making the experience more cinematic and entertaining, but it shouldn’t sacrifice gameplay in the process. You also have a similar process for ground assaults and bombing runs but they’re a little less on-rails making them bearable.
Additionally perhaps about 1/3 of the game isn’t even in a plane. Several large parts or entire missions are from the perspective of a helicopter pilot or the door gunner. Another misguided attempt at expanding the experience but as all these missions are little more than “Hold mouse to win” it falls short. In particular the gunner levels require no skill as you only have to hit in the general vicinity of an enemy to kill them.
Lastly there’s the story that’s gotten a lot of flak from longtime fans, personally I can see it from both ways but I do think it’s one of the weaker ones. On one hand they ditched the somewhat fantastical Ace-world where unrealistic super-weapons and corny but enjoyable characters were the norm for a more stock story set in the “real” world. At the same time there are the makings of a traditional Aces story.  Impossibly skilled protagonist, betrayal, crazy over-the-top unlikely war that only you can solve, etc. It’s all here and on occasion when the situations right and the music kicks in you get those warm waves of nostalgia. But the gameplays too broken and the whole “set in the real world” thing makes it hard to buy.
The reason AC could get away with those silly stories was because it took place in a world where technology was different than ours, and where there were about a billion countries all vying for control, regularly splintering into new countries resulting in constant battles. It wasn’t realistic per-se but it took place in its own little bubble world that made things easier to digest. When you try to tack those same rules and morals on to the world as it exists the ridiculousness of the situation starts to shine through and become harder to enjoy. It’s not without its moments but it also limits the story. Because it takes place in the real world, or some approximation of it, that means we also don’t get any super planes/vehicles/weapons or any of the other crazy stuff AC liked to throw at you. So you’re stuck somewhere between the real and the crazy but since it can’t go full bore either way it’s just left dangling in limbo.
So, yeah, if you liked previous Ace Combats or just action games in general and can pick this up on the cheap then you’ll get your 6-hours-or-so of enjoyment out of it. But too many issues plague it to make it more than a passing fling you’ll quickly abandon for something else. My time with the game wasn’t totally unenjoyable but if I hadn’t picked it up on sale I’m not sure I would feel so forgiving.

Things I would love to see implemented are bigger and better upgrades to the craftable rafts. You can make it as long and wide as you want if you have the materials. One thing i encountered that was difficult was that you cannot move barrels or tires. I had to sail my ship tot he materials location with wood and lashings in order to further expand it.
Another thing I tried was the use of more than one sail to make the relative power of the boat go up to make up for the sheer weigh and size that my raft has become. I believe it is five long and has two additionally on the side and it makes the drag IMMENSE when turning to that side.

I'll give my two cents and then i will add some suggestions and comment on what i would like to see in future updates and development.

I'm not really here for the graphics I'm here for the ideology and immersion aspect of the game, and it does it well.
The compass in my game does not read the correct direction, i have drawn out and mapped the islands on paper and when seeing the setting sun it was not in the west, it was in the north. Weird.
I have only seen one shark and it was in shallow water near a ship wreck, no problems with them thus far.
I bought this for 15$ and I would make that decision again, very worth it for that price seeing as minecraft is pretty much the same price.....and you get more out of the survival aspect here.
What I would LOVE to see is if you put three, five, and ten sails on an appropriately sized  boat that you can create a Small Ship Sail, Medium Ship Sail, and Large Ship Sail, all requiring more materials, but it gives a HUGE speed boost tot he size of your ship, and you can then add things like water filtration systems and shelters ON YOUR BOAT.
I mean cmon, Waterworld, Kevin Costner, this has so much potential to be an awesome way to customize your raft into a boat, assuming you survive that long. People could record their speed in knots and have a leader board for Largest/Fastest boat. Just you vs. the ocean.
Being able to travel between islands without having the feeling of having to return home for water and food all the time would be an advanced achievement in the game if you survive long enough, probably past the 15-20 day mark, seeing as i have survived 13 at this point, and I have 5-6 spare tarps, 3 water stills and a massive raft.
So far I give this game an 8/10 because some things are still unresponsive and not as streamlined to be user friendly while in game, like not being able to take a bucket off of your fire spit, UNLESS the fire pit has been fully restocked with wood, super annoying. I also really want more depth to the game for advanced builds, less fort like and more raft upgradable, one of the "alternative wins" tot his game could be sailing back to the mainland or a populated island center, which would make the hull upgrades and sail upgrades and water filtration, planted food and what not make a lot more sense. THEN, the ultimate question would be come, "Am I really ready to say good bye to my island home, and go all or nothing and navigate open ocean to get back home?" Epic. I can feel it in my bones.
I mean, if we are going for the Castaway thing and all, I see a glorious future for this game. Climb aboard for a wild survival experience.

In this game, you assume the role of an entire community where survivors of the apocalypse literally put their lives in your hands. This game gives you the choice between good and evil, and shows someone's true colors... when they play the game seriously.
I highly recommend this game. There's so many little details that you miss on you first dozen play through that when you see it you go "Why didn't i notice that before?". This game is aggravating. This game makes you feel like you are actually immersed into this world, and it's quite terrifying.
+Non Linear Storyline
This games storyline (For Base game and Lifeline- Breakdown does not have a storyline at all) is very unique, and you can fail missions to continue the story as well.
+Every playthough is different
I have yet to find get the same playthough in my 40+ hours on steam.
+You control a community
Unlike other zombie games, this one is more focused on the community aspect instead of a "Lone Survivor" type game.
+Perma death
If you lose a character, they are gone. (Until you start a new game)
+You don't have to do every mission
There are consequences to not doing certain missions, but the choice is entirely yours.
+Great community
I've been a member of Undead Labs' forums for a few years now, and it's one of my favorite places to be.
-Has it's slow points
If you don't know what you are doing, or have scavenged most of the map, there seems to be nothing to do.
-Minor bugs
There's a few bugs that haven't been squashed due to the game's engine, like the erect truck glitch, where it literally stands your car straight up if you put it too close to specific objects.
-Single player only
While this game doesn't have multiplayer, it's still a great game, but later State of Decay titles will hopefully have multiplayer.
