I'm an older gamer, grew up in a different time, different era. We definitely weren't the instant gratification crowd. We knew that it takes time to make something good and we knew that something good took time, to make. As with all things, the more hard work and passion that you put into something, the better it will be.
With that said, I bought this game very early on and have seen the changes take effect, in the game and I can say that these developers have an overall plan for the game and they are doing a very good job, in implementing that plan.
I own both DayZ and Miscreated and I can honestly tell you, that when I want to play a survival game, with a zombie/mutey feel to it, I go to Miscreated more often than not. The overall feel of the world, is much more fleshed out than DayZ. IMO, the developers have done a great job, at making a world that feels lived in, yet trashed and abandoned. The world is very nice looking and I can only assume that GFX will improve, overtime, as everything else has, within this game. I remember when there was next to nothing, in the game, except the world itself, a few items and not much else. It's come a long ways and come a long ways nicely. You can tell that they are trying to put out something that fans of the survival genre will enjoy.
As far as some of these other comments, on the game. There IS a map, in the game. The game has locations, where you can grab one and you can pick them up off of mutants. You will still have to have sense enough to be able to read and use it. This game, as with most other survival games, doesn't hold your hand and coddle you, through the experience.
In regards to the game having a steep learning curve, being hard to learn and crafting being difficult. Not true. IMO, the game UI, inventory and crafting are all much easier and more straight forward than DayZ. They may not have a huge selection, of craftable items, but what there is, is easy to use. You can also find "recipes" to expand on what you are able to craft initially.
As far as acquiring things, to craft with, as stated, items are far more prevelant now, than they were when I first played the game. Yes, it may take some time to acquire a lot of material, but that is life in a post apocalyptic world. Nothing would be easy and shouldn't be easy.
I do think they should fix car hoarding, but, once again, this IS an EA game and improvements are and have been coming, at a regular pace. The game is far from being abandoned, by the devs.
If I had to do it over again, I would drop $20 on this game again. I think it will end up being a very good game. When you buy EA, you take a gamble. You could get a flop, or you could get a great game, at a great price and be actively involved in changes made to improve the game. IMO, this one will be the later of the 2..
I give it a thumbs up.
One more thing, people downvoting the game, because of the "community" are just immature, IMO. The devs have NO control over online interractions, so to give your opinion, based on that, is very childish. They also leave out the fact that there are alot of servers for this game and out of the many, there are quite a few that are NO KOS servers. So, the fact that they choose to play, on KOS servers, while ignoring the NO KOS servers, makes their entire problem, their own fault, NOT the communities or Devs. The complaint is completely invalid. If you don't want people to kill you on sight, PLAY ON A NO KOS sever. It's just common sense people.

I bought this game after watching TB's first impressions video. "The dark souls of life sims" is a good way to describe it. Everbody is out to kill you (and sometimes each other) and seize control of your kingdom. The only way to survive is to pass skill checks and make tough decisions. Failure is half the fun since you can be responsible for everything from freeing a satanic murderer to sacrificing your friend to a monster.
Mechanics:
There are 39 skills divided into 13 skill groups as well as 8 moods (excluding netural and injured). Your strongest mood will influence the rate at which a skill in an affected group will grow when you study it. Each week you are given the opportunity to study 2 skills and participate in an activity that will modify your mood. Passing a skill check can open up an additional choice in an event. For example having court manners ≥ 10 in week 5 will give you the option of not accepting a gift from a pedophile. This has lasting implications thoughout the game since he will get angry if you accept the gift and don't marry him but he will also not provide military assistance if you are invaded if you don't accept it.
In addition to the basic mechanics, you also have a treasury size, military size, cruelity meter, commoner approval, noble approval, and the strength of your magic circle. Having a low noble or commoner approval can lead to a rebellion which will at best shrink your military. Having a small miltary makes the end of the game difficult.
Criticisms:
1. Some of the skills are deceptively useless. For example putting points into history will let you know the significance of your decisions but won't affect the options available to you (at least not in the playthoughs that I've done).
2. The game doesn't tell you this but you can delete saves by mousing over the save slot and hitting the delete key (OSX: fn+delete).
Overall:
Highly recommended. Best game in the genre.

Long Live the Queen is a Visual Novel game that, instead of trying to simply win the hearts of others and fall in love, you try to survive the horrors of royal life with your head intact.  Of course, it doesn't help when everyone is a bloodthirsty murderer who's only desire is to bring forth the death of a fourteen year-old girl.  Seriously, what the hell is wrong with them?
You take the role of Princess Elodie, who needs to be trained to be a proper queen because Disney dictates that no princess is allowed to have a living mother.  You end up making all the decisions because your father is a lazy bum who's shirked off all of his responsibilities, but for some reason won't let you have your mother's keepsake.  The kingdom is a mess, everyone is evil, and no matter what you do you just can't seem to save this poor little traumatized girl.
The mechanics of the game play on themselves in a bit of a cycle.  You can upgrade Elodie's stats; which can increase slowly or rapidly based on her mood; which is based on events that have happened; which are based on your choices as well as her stats; which are upgraded accordingly based on her mood; which is ba-- ah you get the idea.  This means that every decision, even the first one, can drastically affect how the story unfolds.  No two games are alike, unless you purposefully do everything in the exact same way every time.  But that's boring.
Because of the above mentioned do-it-all-the-same concept, you can technically beat the game as many times as you like after you find out how to do it once.  But beating the game is not where this game shines.  Sure, acquiring the crown and becoming Queen Elodie is a grand event in itself; only if you get there (because you will die, and die a lot).  But one of the greatest things about this game is the ability to make different choices every time and see where it leads you.  Find out what is down each path and discover what you can and can't get away with.  And more importantly, unlock all the outfits because they're cute.  Proper wardrobe is the pinnacle detail between ratty princesses and pristine queens.
All in all, it is a great game and I'd recommend it to anyone.

Warlock is more combat-focused than Civ, so dimplomacy and city management aren't quite as good. The fantasy elements, such as spell casting, damage types, planar travel and the pantheon of gods makes up for this. Resource management also has deeper strategy; for example, on a silver node, you must choose if you want to build a mine to gain more gold per turn, or build a forge to outfit your legions with silvered weapons to combat ethereal foes.
You can manipulate the terrain with magic! How cool is that!? Lower an area into the ocean to provide passage for your navy (although naval combat can be completely ignored on most maps), or raise up mountains to provide a natural defense. Curse your foes' farmlands into a desert wasteland, or bless your own to gain increased yields. That volcano's dangerous lava flow is in your army's marching path? Freeze a safe passage through! (Disclaimer: You often can't do all of these at once. Some spells are only offered by certain gods who happen to hate eachother, so you can't be good at everything).
Each faction has a primary resource focus which changes the way you play. For example, food production can be ignored by the Undead, while it is almost exclusively focused on by the Beasts. The player also controls different units based on your faction, which are further suplemented by the gods you choose to worship. Varied buffs provided by equipment, buildings and spells, and unique items coupled with the large selection of units allows a wide variety of combat strategies available. Choose from a selection of Lord units with varied upgradeable abilities to further enhance your force.
The Armageddon DLC is a fun and difficult race against the clock; the squabbles of nations are inturrupted by an invasion of hell-like creatures that permanently corrupt the land. An enemy mage defeated by the invaders becomes a shade and joins their side, making it more difficult for everyone else. I wouldn't recommend enabling this on your first game.
My favorite victory conditions are Conquest (kill everyone) and the Armageddon victory if you're playing with it. The Avatar victory (kill a god)  is pretty cool, but it can be cheesed, and Unity (science victory) is the best option if you're turtling, but feels rather lackluster. I'd recommend turning off the Holy Sites condition (control 50% of all holy sites), as it just gets in the way of the others.

(NOTE: This game was played with an XBox controller and only takes into consideration the Single Player portion of the game).
Ace Combat Assault Horizon is an interesting attempt at making a more accessible Aerial Combat game, which, not helped by a lacklustre story, fails to get the blood pumping or really manages to keep you engaged. It's a very arcadey approach to the genre that often feels like its a compilation of the variety missions that appear in modern military shooter games, rather than its own game.
The mission variety is very good, from dogfighting over cities in a selection of modern fighter jets and weaving an Apache Helicopter between buildings to providing air support from an AC-130 Spectre Gunship or a series of late night bombing runs; what's on offer is varied and has a nice pace to it, changing things up so you don't tire of the same thing again and again.
The biggest let-down for me and my main reason for purchasing the game originally is the Dogfighting. Ace Combat Assault Horizon introduces a feature known as DFM, which is clearly an attempt to keep engagements fast and thrilling. The problem is, in most cases it feels like you've been strapped into a rollercoaster and been given some bread rolls to throw at the head of the person in the seat in front of you when ever you line up. Enemy planes can absorb a large amount of bullets and apart from a few non-essential targets, will quite happily shrug off direct missile hits - it just seems to lack impact or enough fidelity to get the blood pumping and tends to feel like you're chipping away at a health bar until the target explodes. This is made slightly worse if you decide to replay a mission and notice some essential targets are heavily scripted and fly the same paths along specific set pieces.
The visuals do a good job although are nothing special, vehicles are decent, explosions look good, smoke trails don't look out of place and the quantity of modelled buildings rather than just a ground texture is nice to see.
I played with an XBox Controller and the controls never caused frustration, the game certainly lends itself more to the arcadey approach than a Simulation.
All in all, the mission variety on offer doesn't make up for the run of the mill story and disappointing combat. The games singleplayer clocks in at around seven hours with the ability to replay missions and I personally didn't experience the multiplayer, although I imagine with the removal of Games for Windows Live (Ace Combat Assault Horizon - Enhanced Edition now requires Steam only!) more people will be willing to give it a try.
It's not a bad game and is indeed, well made - they just should have waited for a clear lock before firing this one off.

As Street Fighter V inches ever so closer, I think it's time to take a look back on the lifespan of one of the more well-known entries in the series. Initally released in 2008, Street Fighter IV has seen so many subsequent updates and rereleases, some of which admittedly feel a bit unnecessary. Nonetheless, all of these versions have ensured the core game's place in the fighting game scene, It had its ups and downs, but Street Fighter IV is still a very robust and shining example of practically everything the series has to offer.
PROS
-Characters from all sorts of games (The original, II, Alpha, III, and a few new ones)
-The biggest roster of a Street Fighter game I know
-Several alternate costumes on top of that
-Easy-to-play, hard-to-master control scheme
-Version select (only available in local versus(sorry, Omega mode))
-Evil Ryu is waaaaaay better than regular Ryu
Of, course, it's not without its flaws:
CONS
-Character imbalance still sneaks through every once in a while
-Alternate costumes are paid DLC in spearate bundles organized by character archetytpes
-Arcade-Last-Boss Seth is still a cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
-Lag can pose a greater threat than your opponent, depending on the connection
-Decapre (Would this be considered petty?)
Even with these flaws, Ultra Street Fighter IV is still the definitive version of the game(even if Seth Killian said that about Arcade Edition), and PC users can mod even more costumes in the game (can you say Spider-Man Fei-Long?). So, in short, I'd still recommend it. It could certainly make the time go by a little faster while waiting for Street Fighter V.

I could give you a long complicated review of the pros and cons, wheather this is a good game etc etc, but there are already hundreds of those ( and yes it is a good game).
Here is am going to tell you wheather or not you should buy it based on your favourite genres and the amount of money you have free for games.
I have picked the 3 genres/ tags that will help you decide.
So, first pick the genre or genres of games you like the most then read on from there:
IF YOUR FAVOURITE GENRE IS ZOMBIES:
This is a great zombie game that i really enjoyed. This will be one of your favourites that will go on your list of true zombie survival games. Note: all these prices are based on the presumption you are buying the game on sale
So if you have $ free:
$20+: Definatly grab this
$10-20: Grab this
$5: As long as you are not saving up for anything grab this
$0: I would suggest getting some more steam credit and buying this
IF YOUR FAVOURITE GENRE IS SURVIVAL:
This will be a decent surival game that you will remember. It lacks the basic functions such as a hunger and a food bar. However it makes up in the fact that it requires you to gather neccasary resources, and has fatigue and sickness ( as well as a few others). Note: all these prices are based on the presumption you are buying the game on sale
So if you have $ free:
$20+: Grab this, you will enjoy it
$10-20: Nothing to run out for, only grab this if you have already played the major surivivals such as
dayz, dont starve etc.
$0- 5 If you are getting more game money soon then grab it, but dont go out of your way for just this
IF YOU ENJOY BOTH SURVIVAL AND AND ZOMBIE GAMES:
Chuck what you were playing out the window and grab this!
IF YOUR FAVOURITE GENRE IS SHOOTERS
This is not a shooting game! Dont think that for one second. It has guns however you wont be using them much and they have a very slow progression. If you want to try out the other 2 listed genres then grab this but not if your looking for a shooting game!
IF YOU PLAY NONE OF THESE GENRES:
This is a good taste test for a zombie and survival game. It includes solid but not everwhelming gameplay, and should give you a good idea of wheather or not you like the genre. However if you have no urge to start playing zombie/ survival games then move on.

A LITTLE OF WHAT RYZOM HAS TO OFFER
------------------------------
Ryzom does things differently to most mmorpgs, there is no *classes* you can learn all skills with multiple off branches, in total there is about 63 skill tree lines you can level each one to 250 if you sub, otherwise 125 without sub. that is alot of levels and months or years of gameplay even for a f2p player.
-----
COMBAT
-----
Ryzom has unique indepth style of actions / abilities you can actually edit and modify the way you want them with different effects, to combine into your own attacks or spells. its not your basic *press slash to slash a mob* you can input aimed shots to areas such as legs or head that add debuffs aswell as increase accuracy or damage of skills consuming more resources, further from this you have a few options on what your abilities cost to use them. for example, instead of stamina it could require some HP instead, or you can add special requirements like *skill is available after a parry or dodge. this all depends on how YOU build your skills.  some mobs can also disarm you in combat and cause effects, aswell as certain mobs being more resistant to different types of damage.
---------
HARVESTING / CRAFTING
------
In my opinion Ryzom has the best harvesting and crafting system from any mmorpg similar to the attack abilities you can customise what type of resource you want to look for, the quality etc, and when you actually find resources to harvest then starts somewhat a mini game, where you have different abilities that determine the quality and amount of resource you gain using *fast, or strong or healing actions* there is chance for gas explosions that will damage you while harvesting aswell as surrounding mobs so it's not an easy mode walk in the park, you may end up with Q9 q 20 q11 mats if you arn't paying much attention. certain materials have different stat factors aswell, for example materials for ammo have different damage or weight to carry more, speed, etc all at once. Mobs also drop materials for crafting
same goes with crafting, they can sometimes *fail* somewhat so you end up with a quality lower than you wanted.   you can customize your crafting to add stats like increased parry or increased HP etc and specalize in these, you need to learn each equipment seperatly you don't go *learn armorsmith... have access to all armor* you will need to learn to craft shoulder, chest, then quality, and ontop of this you can learn to craft other races armors and wear them.
--------
Other Bits
---------
Ryzom has seasons changes, weather and day / night. which can determine which mobs are available in some area's most other mmorpgs don't have this to the same extent.
Ryzom has different factions and reputation you can align to.
Despite what I keep reading, Ryzom does have missions / quests but its not linear story guided holding your hand like most mmorpgs and there is not 100,000 of them. if you don't want to do them you don't have to and they are mainly for fun / get some coin etc (beyond the starter zone which has tutorial quests to help you out)
there is death penalty for dying, which can stack up to 10x ( need to regain xp before you can xp towards skills) so dying does has its downfalls unlike most games.
As for graphics sure it is not the most up to date, but it is better then alot of eastern grind clones, and if you use gfx injectors / software like SweetFX to tweak it to hdr/enhance it yourself. personally i don't care about graphics on games, it is a silly thing to judge by, its all about game mechanics.
There is housing, guilds, achievements, occuptions seperate from crafting for moneys etc,
----------------------------------
after all this and more, if you still don't like the game then that is unfortunate, but the game won't be for everyone. however those leaving silly reviews like *this is♥♥♥♥♥♥ it sucks, not an mmo, etc blah blah clearly havnt played the game past the loading screen to actually provide any reason or proof for their troll reviews.

Ryzom is an old-style mob-grinding sandbox MMORPG. Like a survival sandbox, you start with nothing and have to make everything yourself.  The focus is on exploration and harvesting/crafting, and farming mobs. Some highlights:
- skill based, no classes
- all items are player crafted, there are no armor or weapon drops from mobs
- there are no quests, except some for cash and faction (the beginner island has tutorial quests)
- there are no instances or dungeons
- real day/night cycle, weather, seasons. These make a real difference. You might only be able to find a certain mat in the fall, at night, in the rain, for example.
- advanced mob AI, mobs migrate depending on season, and have their own routines
- consensual PvP, Outpost PvP wars, PvP zones that have the best mats
- housing, mounts, packers
Lowlights, this game is not for everybody
- no quests, no storyline. There is no hand holding, and a fairly steep learning curve.
- graphics are from 2004, scenery still looks good, character models are somewhat primitive
- tab targeting, no jumping, not action combat
- difficult to solo, except for diggers
The game is at its best when you team up and go kill mobs or bosses. Or when you saddle up for a night of exploration and digging. Or when a group escorts some diggers into the Prime Roots (PvP zone) in order to dig special mats.

The game is dated, but  it is a true open world sandbox MMORPG that is based around the making their own story not following someone elses. I highly recommend it for both casual and hard core RPG fans. Though it isn't for those that want to play through a pre scripted story.  It is also one of the few games on Steam that have an Open Source development method so that is i BIG plus to the freedom lovers out there.

At first, a few words on the game and genre. This game enables the player to create a transport network with trains, trucks, buses and trams on maps up to 256 square kilometers. You have the full control over your transport empire by building tracks and streets, buying and placing vehicles and managing the lines. Besides passengers, multiple goods can be transported. The developers deliver three mods with the game, one including a sandbox mode where you don't have to worry about money at all and can build your own "model railroad layout".
In order to get the full potential out of this game, players definitely have to make use of the great amount of mods that are out there waiting for you to explore them. Vehicles from all over the world, stations, industries, assets, texture replacement, total conversions... you name it. The game greatly benefits from this variety - without it, it would not be half as good as it is now. Therefore to all new players or interested individuals out there: Please check out the great library of mods available at the community websites.
To be honest, right after release, this games was not much more than an open beta. Over time however, the developers fixed a large amount of bugs, added features, improved gameplay and performance and also delivered new and free content in form of the USA DLC. The biggest plus of this game however is without doubt the great modding community that added a huge amount of modifications to the game.
The quality of this game might not be able to compete with AAA title. however, given the price you definitely get your moneys worth when buying this game as long as you are interested in transport simulations. Given the sandbox type of games of this genre, the amount of time spend with this game can easy break through hundreds or even thousands of hours for just a few bucks.
My rating: Vanilla game: 6/10, game with modding 8/10, time for money 10/10
My recommendation: buy it and have fun with the mods

Dark Souls is one of those games that can really make one reconsider their outlook on games and general game value. For me, personally, this was a game that made me rethink my outlook on games and especially singleplayer RPG experiences.
Everything, from the way the world of Dark Souls is portrayed to the player through its subtle and environment based storytelling to one of the best level designs in video game history since some of the best Zelda games, this game only gets better the more you discover it.
Dark Soul's is highly renown and marketed by many for its overall difficulty and punishing combat, but I truly feel like that image doesn't give the game enough justice. I think that Dark Souls isn't so much a game about difficulty as it is a game about LEARNING to overcome challenge and that patience and resilience no matter how skilled or unskilled you are will inevitably allow you to overcome hurdles and learn from your failures. I discovered about 30 hours into the game that Dark Souls truly isn't a game that focuses solely on difficulty even though I had just fought what seemed as one of the hardest bosses in any video game. Ironic, isn't it? Sure, one of the core aspects at the start of the game is difficulty, but the game becomes much more streamlined and intuitive as you, the player learn how to act and behave in the game.
Once you understand Dark Soul's mentality you become much more cautious and for the most part learn to one-shot a lot more corridors and maybe even bosses. This however, to me had no effect on my enjoyment of the game. I discovered by the end of the game that even with lower difficulty, the game never becomes dull or a chore. Every new environment you discover and new characters and plots you follow continue to impress you until the very end regardless of how much of its difficulty your playthrough and character build allow you to retain.
I truly hope you give Dark Souls a chance and that perhaps in the process you discover a new type of appreciation for video games that you maybe didn't have before!

It's weird for me to start this review this way, but I've been playing the game Endless Legend lately (11 hours so far) and it seems very good, but 11 hours in I still don't feel like I comprehend the game. The reason I mention it is that I purchased it hoping to play another game just like this one (with more content, better graphics, and no memory leak), originally thinking it was by the same developers (it's not), but it hasn't been nearly as easy to pick up and play or nearly as enjoyable as this game so far. I've played Warlock 51 hours at this point so I obviously have a very firm understanding of it, but I don't recall it taking me long at all to get into it so it's most likely pretty accessible for anyone who's basically familiar with strategy games (even rts's).
The gameplay is very fun and seems like it gets going really quickly as well as being intuitive in how you do combat as well as the economy which was all I really needed to know because I didn't bother too much with diplomacy as there don't seem to be man benefits. Really, the only downside I could give is that the game can go on for an extreme amount of time (I think I spent 30 hours on one campaign), which seems like a good thing, but what can happen is that you get to a point where you know you're going to inevitably win, but still have hours until you can even do so as you go around defeating the opponents taking endless amounts of turns. (Keep in mind, I've only played single player) Another possible downside is that it seemed like the opponents will quickly go between being at war with you and being at peace. The treaties didn't last long and I don't recall them costing anything to break. But, it didn't seem to matter as long as you never really trust any of your opponents and keep your defenses up.
The graphics are fine and it has a decent aesthetic, but the visuals weren't the best even when the game came out, but that's fine because it means the game could be run on my outdated computer so that's another point for the game's accessibilty. However, though it initially runs perfectly well (I haven't played with my new PC yet so I can't speak for it), the game apparently has a memory leak so it degrades in performance over time. You can deal with that by simply restarting the game, but it doesn't take long for it to start dipping in framerate and it can get tedious to have to save and quit every so often (30 minutes to an hour if I remember correctly, maybe shorter).
If you're like me, you like to compare every game in a series to see which is the best and though I haven't played the sequel, it apparently isn't much more than essentially an expansion to this game from what I've heard, but look at it for yourself. It's actually $5 cheaper (regular price), so it might be worth it over this game, but with the expansion (which has Mostly Negative reviews) it costs $35 in all so $10 more expensive than this if you wanted the apparently terrible expansion.
I'd also like to point out that this has a demo so you can try it before you buy it which I really appreciate from developers as it actually tends to hurt sales, but is pro-consumer.

I don't usually play visual novels, but this one is special. While it doesn't have any dark secret to be found at the end of the story, it sure can surprise you. It's quite difficult to predict what's going to happen next, even after some playthroughs.
It's -not- a date simulator, and there's little to no romance in this game - of course you'll marry someone eventually, but
that's not important.
The best part is that you can actually create your own personality for Elodie in each gameplay. There are a lot of options that cover almost every type of person you want her to be. I recommend you to have a couple of saves of the same gameplay, but some weeks apart. You never know when you're going to get busted out of nowhere.
But mostly I recommend this game. If you bought it with the Humble Bundle and still did not give it a try, you should.

This reminds me of a Stephen King horror novel, a story with a lot of exposition and dialogue dealing with the everydayness of man, usually set in a small American town...and then♥♥♥♥♥♥happens.
Although the art style is anthropomorphic (Animal people) and minimal, make no mistake.  The characters are human inspite of appearances.  There is no reference to the animal characteristics of the characters, you won't find them complaining about fleas or how their tails get caught by someone slamming the door.  They seem to be human in all respects except for what they look like in-game.
The characters are Human in the sense that the characters are very contemporary young adult and quite liberal minded Americans.  If you are not part of the latter (like I am.  My country of origin is very conservative in comparison), you may find it hard to relate and find some parts totally senseless although in my case, it was an interesting study of a different mindset from my own culture.
The strength of the narrative  I find and so do others, isn't in the "horrible" situation the whole thing will morph into but in the slice of life situations, the meaning of life questions and the natural philosophies the characters expound upon as they journey along towards the conclusion.
As for gameplay, there is one in-game videogame that you can finish if you're craving for action.  Most of the time is spent as the main character, Mae as she explores the town of Possum Springs and hanging around with her, well...there's no other word I can think of...loser friends.  Some of the tasks and conversations might seem utterly pointless and shocking unless you're steeped in American culture and thus, be able to relate to it.  There is also hardly any replayability unless you hang around with a certain friend and hang around with the other friend with a totally opposite nature in your next playthrough.
For my part, I found Night in the Woods an interesting experience, like buying a playable novel.

You play as a college-drop-out-cat-girl who has just moved back to her parent's house in a rural and run down town. Although a lot of it is fun and games, there's also the dark and harsh reality of adulthood that is periodically brought up; as well as issues of mental health and general misfortunes of life. You're 90% guaranteed to get emotionally attached to several characters! They each have their own personal life stories and individuality that make them unique. There's even some subtle and not so subtle hints to some of the character's sexuality.
The achievements add plenty of replayability for game completionists since there are certain character paths you can choose to take, which allows for multiple endings to occur; plus if you missed something the first go-around, you need to play through it again to get the achievement. Doesn't take long to finish the story and the ending was left very open ended imo, but this leaves room for theories and interpretation so I don't think that's completely a bad thing.
Overall very enjoyable, entertaining, and atmospheric game. 10/10 for the characters and dialogue, 8/10 for the plot (gets kinda weird at the end)

The game starts with quite a lot of good cutscenes.
You play as a ranger whose family got murdered by orcs.
The main objective is to have revenge on those responsible for their death.
The Combat System is quite fun. The game is really easy, you can easily fight of hordes of enemies using only left and rightclick, the amazing animations make it really fun though! You can also stealth-kill enemies, execute combo's and do lots of other stuff.
The controls are a little bit weird if you're used to Source-games.
The animations are really really good! Climbing, running, fighting, just everything looks really smooth, realistic and cool.
Also the level/mapdesign is good, the game has a dark atmosphere and feels real.
The open-world-world is split into different huge parts you can travel between using the map.
The sounds are truly amazing, the voice-acting is great! Also, the music was always fitting and making some situations really intense.
The gameplay can get quite repetitive over time though. In most combat-situations spamming buttons while doing some movement will do it.
Most quests are basically about killing orcs, sometimes in different way's like without triggering the alarm. The Story is quite okay. There is no real backstory in any of the characters except for Talion (the Ranger you're playing).
It took me about 20 hours to finish the game but there's lots of stuff to do afterwards.
Also, there are other gamemodes and a full sidestory which i did not play yet.
There are runes, abilities and attributes which can be used to make yourself even stronger. Sometimes switching runes for a specific mission can be extremely helpfull since all of the "boss"-enemies have different weaknesses which can be exploited.

The screen of the past version was neat, but I would've liked to see a button that put the screen in your face, as opposed to looking down. Simple game mechanics; place traps and fire weapons to kill things befoer they escape. But for that simplicity, there's an underlying complexity involved in picking the right traps and weapons, placing them in just the right spots and giving them the right upgrades. You're going to find yourself playing levels over and over again to try and get a perfect score of 5 Skulls, getting frustrated that *ONE* freaking enemy slipped through your traps just before the end. And the dancing... at the end of every level the War Mage dances. Take that, his one-liners and the dialog from enemies (yes, they talk) and whoever wrote the script for this game deserves an award.
Oh, and for Borderlands 2 players, you may notice that the 2 characters, the War Mage and Sorceress, are voiced by the same actors that voiced Axton and Lilith. Just a fun little bit of info.

For the pricepoint, Long Live the Queen is cheaper than a movie and thus worth it.
Starting a review talking about the price is never good, and while this game tries its best to appear to be a nonlinear fantastical rpg story following the trials of a little girl turned queen-to-be, it falls flat on several key factors.
Overall: B- "A neat game for a few hours."
- I enjoyed it because I got to do crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥and then die. That's about it.
- The story is mediocre with very few nonlinear branches. There are several true endings (assuming you make it through alive), with very little deviation, though honestly, as far as I played the game, there are really two endings, both decided on a hidden value: your reputation with the common people. This was rather disappointing to learn once I got to the "end", but there were two bigger concerns that I had.
1) While appearing to be unrestricted in deciding whether or not you wanted to play with your toys all day or finally go learn magic, the game is actually extremely restricted by the scripted series of events that occur. Technically there are several ways to advance through each scripted event and avoid failing, but I found myself forced to pick just one of two ways (such as getting agility or some other skill to avoid the scripted assassinations) which led to the same event conclusion, with little deviation. I never was truly free to just be a socialite with a little bit of combat knowledge - I was pretty much forced to level my combat knowledge just to advance in the story. While disappointing, I still initially had fun doing whatever the hell I wanted and dying before finally buckling up and trying hard.
2) Dying is a main sticking point to this game, and to truly experience all the well written scenarios, one must setup a specific strategy path to get to that point, often beginning from Day 5-10. At one point, I had 12 save files just to reach different types of death scenarios around that one war, only to be unable to advance 11 to the conclusion of the game. For example, I really wanted to sing my way out of this one part, but it turned out I needed 100 rating in voice to get there (among other things), leading to a very specialized decision tree. Of course, this led to me being deficient in other areas and unable to get much further in the game. This was the same for my other 10 paths, with only the 12th decision tree being the winner. This was rather upsetting. Why can't I sing my way to the end?? Blah. (Obviously I'm aware you can, but I didn't feel like restarting my game.)
Significant Opinions:
Music: B - It's a short story game with a few different arrangements. The main piano theme got repetitive on my 120493th attempt.
Art: A - Anime-styled, not really anything amazing. Still gets an A for effort.
Replay Value: C - The main selling point of this game is to die and live. Most of the time you die because you have no idea what ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous story event comes next. Then you either have to restart the game to get the optimal decision tree to that point, or reload far enough back (read: possibly several weeks) to be able to prepare for that event. It doesn't help that you don't know any of the values required to pass each of the choices in an event. LOTS of trial and error. Paper and pencil are necessary. This has been called a "princess simulator", but it is a bit more than that. What we have is a trial-and-error strategy game enmeshed in a setting which emphasises feudal politics, fantasy tropes, a story of betrayal alongside decision making, tailoring and improving your skills. All done in a setting that you will discover is a cruel and pitiless world. In this den of jackals you play a small, weak, and initially helpless young girl and heiress to a queendom.
Your Lumen (mage) mother, the Queen, is dead, and you are very young. Everyone is lying to you, including those closest to you that claim to be trying to protect you. Are they really making the best decisions for your future? Currently, it is a matriarchy but you are too young to inherit. What this means is that you are encircled by sharks, who will steal your rightful crown off of you if you are not careful (and ruthless). So play dirty, form a plan and study hard, give in to evil, paranoia or try to pursue a just path. Remember though, to prepare yourself for death.

What can I say about this game? At first glance, it looks very much like a clone of civilisation, but with a magic and monsters veneer. That impression is wrong. Very wrong. Sure, it's superficially civ-like, but it plays very differently. It's much, much more combat focused, and more or less forgoes city building, research etc.
So lets look at what I liked and disliked about it:
Liked:
1) Combat
Because you can build buildings and units at the same time, you'll quickly find you have a lot more bodies to throw at the enemy. Where in civ 5 each unit counts (at least into the medieval era, and often later) you'll pretty rapidly have hordes of little men, goblins and skeletons running around in Warlock. The world itself fights pretty hard against you at times, with dangerous monsters appearing from portals, mass spawns of demons and other monstrosities, and if you delve deep into the alternate dimensions flocks of dragons and greater elementals massing to deny you victory. The enemy AI is decent but not spectacular, and you'll be able to win pretty easily on the first 3/5 difficulties, but it can give you somewhat of a challenge I guess.
2) Magic
Sure, you can throw fireballs and enchant weapons and heal units and things like that, which is kinda okay, but terraforming is where the real fun and strategy of the magic system comes into play. Did your AI neighbor betray you and is now massing armies at your border while you lie defenseless? One mid-late game spell later and there's a mountain range there to protect you.
Or conversely, your enemy has naval dominance and thinks he is safe from invasion? Guess he wasn't expecting you to raise the seabed to create a giant landbridge to his continent. Turn those swamps in your way to verdant farmland, curse the pleasant bonus-causing terrain in your opponents city to barren wasteland, raise a freaking volcano and surrounding lava fields in an enemies expansion route. Most of the magic is relatively forgettable (although there are exceptions like granting trolls the gift of flight for a nasty surprise) but the terraforming magic is something I dearly wish I could do in civ or endless legend. It's probably the part of this game that will stick with me the longest
3) Portals.
You can more or less ignore portals if you feel like it, but if you invest the time to clear out the high-level monsters within and colonise these alternate dimensions you'll emerge with powerful dragon armies, late-game "temple units" (the best units your faction can create) and rare resources like Adamantium and Nevril. I haven't quite decided whether it's worth the time required to clear these portals out, but they're a fun distraction that really ups the power of the wandering enemies and gives you something to do. I feel like a lot more could have been done with portals (how about alternate dimensions that can connect to each other and not just the hub world (Ardania) you start on? Or being able to enter a portal and through a short trip through another dimension rock up on the other side of Ardania. These are major missed opportunities that may or may not have been used in Warlock 2 (which I haven't played yet). But still, the portals are fun.
4) It's just cool to have armies of trolls and dragons.
What I disliked.
1) There's no option for playing tall. You pretty much just spam cities everywhere you can find a few spare tiles
2) City building is vastly inferior to games like Endless Legend and Civ 5. Vastly, vastly inferior
3) Trade and Diplomacy is near nonexistent. This game is built for war war war. If you approach it as a wargame, it's decent fun. Don't approach it looking for a science victory type thing
4) Speaking of science, there's nearly no research in the game. Sure, you research spells, but I feel like the game is poorer for the lack of tech-driven gameplay changes
5) The game feels a little too silly for its own good, but your milage may vary. I actually quite liked it for the first 30 hours.
Overall I liked the game, but it is more shallow than Civ or Endless Legend, both of which I would recommend above this game. That said I've put 40 hours into this game and can feel myself likely to put in another 20 or so before I put the game down (I want to experience the apocalypse gamemode before I uninstall and try out Warlock 2) but yeah, it's not quite as compelling as I would have liked. It's a decent, relatively solid game, but its flaws prevent it from achieving greatness

This is a stealth game entirely. If you dont  like stealth games then you will not enjoy this title at all. I however do like stealth and found this game a breath of fresh air. It is very different than anything else I have ever played. You use cameras throughout the entire game to help direct the main character safely past guards. You are also able to hack into devices and spend points to gain abilities. The mechanics work quite well. If you get caught they lock you up in a cell, setting you back some progress but it isnt too hard to get back to where you were.
There were a few times I got stuck and couldnt figure out what the game wanted me to do, mostly at the end, and I went to youtube for some help. There is a chapter where you dont have any abilities or map, this part takes place in a graveyard area. I found that part especially challenging.
The colors in the game are beautiful and the graphics are decent, overall I was happy with this. Sounds were decent too. Overall the tech specs of the game were adequate and helped envelope me in the story. The plot was well done and not confusing to follow.
Some complain about the ending but I found it satisfying enough. It was a bit anticlimatic though. Good sold game overall! I got about 15 hours playtime out of this title.

The game starts with quite a lot of good cutscenes.
You play as a ranger whose family got murdered by orcs.
The main objective is to have revenge on those responsible for their death.
The Combat System is quite fun. The game is really easy, you can easily fight of hordes of enemies using only left and rightclick, the amazing animations make it really fun though! You can also stealth-kill enemies, execute combo's and do lots of other stuff.
The controls are a little bit weird if you're used to Source-games.
The animations are really really good! Climbing, running, fighting, just everything looks really smooth, realistic and cool.
Also the level/mapdesign is good, the game has a dark atmosphere and feels real.
The open-world-world is split into different huge parts you can travel between using the map.
The sounds are truly amazing, the voice-acting is great! Also, the music was always fitting and making some situations really intense.
The gameplay can get quite repetitive over time though. In most combat-situations spamming buttons while doing some movement will do it.
Most quests are basically about killing orcs, sometimes in different way's like without triggering the alarm. The Story is quite okay. There is no real backstory in any of the characters except for Talion (the Ranger you're playing).
It took me about 20 hours to finish the game but there's lots of stuff to do afterwards.
Also, there are other gamemodes and a full sidestory which i did not play yet.
There are runes, abilities and attributes which can be used to make yourself even stronger. Sometimes switching runes for a specific mission can be extremely helpfull since all of the "boss"-enemies have different weaknesses which can be exploited.
The game runs perfectly on linux using an AMD Radeon HD7970 and xf86-video-amdgpu open-source drivers smooth and without any problems. The game warned me that my driver was not officially supported at the start of the game, yet it worked just great.

All in all i think Shadow of Mordor is a fun and unique game. I first thought i would not be going to play this game for a long time, but it's really fun and i can't stop playing it.

Fantastic Adventure Game/Life Sim/Visual Novel.  Be prepared to die.  A lot.  This game isn't Princess Maker, it's Princess Breaker!  There are a significant number of paths to choose and endings to achieve.  The art design itself is good, though technologically the graphics are decidedly low-res.  The story makes sense, with past events greatly influencing future possibilities.  The skill checks are a bit non-sensical at times, but they mostly work from a logical standpoint.  Overall, a very good game that you'll want to play over and over.

For those unfamiliar to Visual Novels, this can be a really good starting point.
Like all Visual Novels, this game is essentially a book with images, with choices you have to make around the corners. Technically, you can fit The Walking Dead into this genre - they have some action, and a somewhat unique background story (For Visual Novels). All Visual Novels generally focus on a great story, and this is no exception.
What makes Long Live The Queen unique is the stats system. Every week there would be a different event(s) which need you to check if you can pass the requirements to make your choices work (such as Climbing a wall with enough stats into Climbing). To help players, the Mood system is added, which gives bonuses or penalties to certain stats for each mood your character is currently in.
Playing as Elodie, the would-be Queen, and customize her to focus on aspects to ensure she lives through her coronation. There is no real need to excel at everything - that is practically impossible - but at what you want. For the more casual players, Elodie can just do what she wants, and hope she lives until her coronation, or for the more intense players, Elodie can be specifically trained to prepare for certain scenarios.
This game has a good story, well planned routes, decent art and really worthwhile gameplay. Highly recommended.

If you play the game as an action RPG, persistently advertised as 'Prepare to Die' experience, it will be exactly that - a decent, albeit underdeveloped game, layered with multiple challenges, ranging from hard encounters, spotting and avoiding traps to reactive + proactive combat. Player character is thrown into a dark and forsaken world, place where information is scarce, help is rare and greately appreciated, while dangers cater not to the player but mercilessly deliver punishment to those who don't learn.
However, this isn't the whole reason the game obtained it's cult status. It's true strength and unique point is the narrative, a dark and atmospheric place with multitude of secrets and plots which, while completely ignorable, add a layer upon layer to the storytelling experience of the game.
Indeed, the story does not serve the player who, taking the mantle of a Nameless Accursed Undead is merely another pawn in a grand drama that is the duality of Light and Dark, told indirectly through environment and item descriptions, sometimes through cryptic dialogue and, on few occasions, triggered events and choices you made in the past. Any interconnecting pieces within the game are made by you, almost none of which are given to you on a platter. Your humble beginnings as one of many believng themselves to be the "Chosen Undead" gain more and more meaning, as murky past of this world unfolds, revealing just how blurry the line is between sacrifice and treachery, heroism and desperation, and perhaps most of all how perspective may change the view whether an act is of hope or betrayal.
Yet all of the above is achieved through minimal dialogue and uncertain relationships established through visuals, short descriptions and seemingly coincidental similarities. In addition, the lack of soundtrack throughout the majority of the game adds extra weight to the situations where it finally plays, creating some magical or terrifying moments.
The characters you meet in game have their own stories to follow, which you may not even be aware of; they have their own goals, end up in places you already visited, or may even meet demise due to your actions which seemed benign at first. They're their own people and, just like you, live their own life. Maybe, if you're just lucky and attentive enough, you will obtain the right to be part of their story, as much as they are part of yours.
In the end, the game left me with a sense of awe, one which isn't easily replicated; if video games are an art, then Dark Souls is a flawed masterpiece and it's unique narrative could not be replicated using most other mediums.
: The game is an awful port of the console version, so running it might prove frustrating. Some areas are clearly unfinished due to development issues. PvP aspect remains gimmicky and is frustrating for newcomers.

I have played this game over the years and have logged at least 100 hours worth of game time independently of Steam. I am excited to see this title being available on Steam, and I hope my review is helpful to those interested in playing Ryzom.
The first section of the game is the tutorial island. This is a rather guided experience which showcases the features players can engage in when they leave. You are given quests by the master of a given discipline or the leader of the outpost. Many people enjoyed the layout and flow of this experience. Once you leave, however, the game changes remarkably. This is not to say it is good or bad, although many gamers can be caught off gaurd by it. You are no longer progressing via quests from trainers. Quests are few and far between and are NOT meant to be the rail from which one develops within Ryzom. The game expects that, once you leave the island, you are ready to engage with what you enjoyed there in the larger world scene. It is now up to YOU, not the quest giver, for direction. Ultimately, it boils down to grinding -- which is not necessarily bad. If you enjoy what you are doing, even if it is grinding, then you are enjoying yourself. Some people dislike it while others love it. That choice is yours to make.
The combat system itself is rather basic although combat is not sterile. You create your own skills through a basic formula of costs and spenders. For example, a cost could be adding a DoT while the spender could be you can only use it after you successfully dodged. A lot of possibilities are here although it will still condense down to a smaller amount of optimal skills.
Crafting is a beast all of its own. Each ingredient has a unique set of properties that, when combined with others, creates an unqiue collection of secondary stats which help refine various playstyles.
I could continue on, however, I think one can tell that each section of the game is like this. It's deep, yet someone has to peer through the layers to notice. The difficulty for a new player (especially those familiar with modern MMOs) will be to plummet the depth of the game instead of thinking the surface layer is all that exists.
Try it out. You may not like it. You may love it.

This was the first MMO that I was truly passionate about playing. Due to other MMO's (like WoW, which came out after Ryzom so you can't say it is a WoW clone) taking the spotlight this one has faded into obscurity. With this on Steam now however, it may gain the fame it truly deserves.
Ryzom doesn't hold your hand as soon as you are finished the tutorial island (A place so cosy a lot of players never leave) you are thrust into the harsh reality of that if you don't be careful you will die. From the Varinxes of the desert to the Cloppers of the wetlands you must traverse the harsh world of Atys (yes the world is called Atys not Ryzom). With a branching skill tree that makes it so that their is no definite level for a character, mix and match skills to create your ultimate attacks and by the end of it you maybe just maybe will be able to invade the Kitin Lair and take down the ones who made you abandon the Old Lands.
Oh and CHAOS FOREVER! MARAUDERS RULE!

If you have enough from your standard MMORPGs with Elves and Dwarves and Dragons and whatnot then you might want to give Ryzom a chance!
Atys, the world the game is set in is quite unique - the planet is basically one huge, living plant, inhabited by a wide variety of creatures. The characters aren't bound to classes, you can learn whatever you want, as long as you spend the time to level it up. The crafting system is quite complex - the economy is 100% player based, whatever you use will be made by other players or yourself, except for some basic starter equippment.
The ability-system is also noteworthy. You get to build your own attacks and spells too in a way: They are made out of elements you can swap and adapt everything to your playing style. For example you can raise the time it takes to cast a spell and in exchange make it cause more damage.
The community is by far the best I've come across in any MMORPG. The playerbase is mostly mature, friendly and ready to help newcomers. The way the economy runs teamwork is a must if you want to get your hands on really good equippment. Some of the places you get your resources from are pretty dangerous and should not be travelled alone...
That being said - yes, there is PvP in certain areas and guilds can fight for outposts, but it's your choice to join or not.
What else... NO CASH SHOP!
The only thing you *can* buy is a monthly subscription. The game is free to play up to lvl 125 - more than enough to see whether you like it or not - and with the subscription the lvl cap is 250. Also subscribers can rent an apartment in one of the cities PLUS they can own pack-animals - the only way to get more storage ingame.
So - go ahead, give it a try!

It's hard to say why I like Night in the Woods so much.  Everything just feels so...real.
The town, suffering from a stagnant economy and people leaving for better prospects.
The atmosphere, a decaying town in the last days of fall.

When I first started playing this I was less than impressed. The graphics made the game look like the original Tomb Raider for PS1 from the 90's, the camera was twitchy and is often blocked by foliage in wilderness areas making it impossible to see, characters would get 'caught' on small logs or stones in the forest, driving was insane (cars with F1 Ferrari acceleration and super sensitive steering), base building can be tricky (you end up accidentally building things you don't want by exploring the options available) and so the list goes........
I also struggled with the intial pointlessness of it - once I left the starting area and made it to the first homesite the game seemed to lose direction and turned into a simple resource collection process but with extremely limited storage capacity that made even that a waste of time.
But after a while the game and its characters get inside your head and a story starts to unfold, some key mission requests push the game forward and give a little direction to what you are doing and you start to realize it's not about resource gathering or building an impregnable base - it's more about keeping your people alive, happy and healthy. The voice acting is ok, although the dialogues are short, simple and at times repetitive, the requests you recieve from different people are also somewhat repetitive. I found it generally hard to bond with almost all of the individuals in my group (I ended up with 22 survivors) and in fact only interacted with a couple of them regularly - character development and depth does not have a big part of play. What the game did do well here (at least for me) was give me a sense that I wanted the group to do well, even if the individuals meant very little to me.
The game does a great job of depicting a somewhat bleak and depressive world where you never really feel safe outside of home (and sometimes not even there!). There is a sort of tragic sadness to the empty homes you have to loot to survive and, at least initially, a great sense of relief when you find some key material / item you are looking for as it means you can return to the relative safety of home. The ever present moaning and shuffling of the Zeds adds to the atmosphere enormously as you can't tell if they're outside or it's a case of 'I don't think I'm alone in here'. The map is huge, especially if you're on foot, it has varied terrain, very well laid out with points of interest hidden all over for intrepid explorers to discover. On the technical side, after 60hrs of game time I never had a single freeze, CTD or anything other than smooth running for the duration.
Overall this is a flawed gem that is an addictive and imaginative romp into a zombie apocalyse. As Ray Santos will tell you mid-game when you drive a high powered sports car thru a group of zombies and watch them explode around and over the hood....."that never gets tired, does it ?"

Wow, did I ever have it wrong. Initially when I saw State of Decay, I gave it a pass. Recently, steam put it up on sale and I picked it up just because I was bored, and OH WOW do I ever wish I'd picked it up sooner. This game is wonderful, in a way I've seen very few games be wonderful in the past.
Initially I was unimpressed, as the number of zombie games out there is getting pretty saturating, and when I first started I was getting precisely what I expected. Very basic fare in a game that wasn't doing anything well... And then I finished the tutorial and made it to the church....
This game is a HUGE world where you have to fight zombies, gather supplies, go stealth, get along with neighbors, investigate things, actually use survival skills and even build up a home base. There have been few GOOD zombie games out there, and this is one of the EXCELLENT ones. Once the tutorial was done, as I mentioned above, s**t got real, as they say, and I found myself pouring through corpse infested houses for food, building materials and medical supplies.
I'll admit, the graphics aren't perfect, but there are very few graphical ERRORS in the game, and once you get used to them, they're rather immersive. There's a couple of minor issues with the game, like bridge jumps, but don't think about it in terms of success and failure. This is a role playing game in that you can fail at something, but not have a true failure state. "OH, you messed up that run? No worries, man. We're not going to tell you that you've failed and make sure that you do it over again until you get it the way we want it... Though... There is a herd coming. You -might- want to book it, bro." I haven't felt this immersed in the ROLE of a game in a LONG time.
A fantastic atmosphere, fear inducing, there's a learning curve, and once you get used it, you're solid.
I hear there's already a sequel in the works, and as far as that goes, well.. Shut up and take my money.
My only real gripe at this point is that there's no Co-op of any kind. I would TOTALLY play with friends, and chase them with a stick until they got this game if there was Co-op. Something to consider, if you weren't already.
Hats off, Undead Labs, you've made an addict out of me, and I'm not quite ten hours in.

A highly entertaining and surprisingly deep zombie-apocalypse, community based survival game set in the US Mid-West. I'm a handful of hours in, and enjoying it. Combat - as well as mission assignment - can be a little frenetic, but it has a good, solid vibe and is really quite a satisfying piece all told.
PROS
- Lots of satisfying third person zombie slaughtering - At range, in melee, and even in vehicles. (Especially in vehicles.)
- Decent combat, in all forms. With lots of possibilities and customisation possible with a little forethought, strategy, and effort.
- Interesting and thought provoking character interactions. You watch your community either thrive and grow, or wither and fail due to your decisions. Build a base. Keep it supplied. Get to know your fellow survivors' personalities.
- Mid-sized character development and RPG elements. Once you've gotten to know them a little (and kept them alive for a while) ou can play as multiple members of your ad-hoc community. This will allow you to specialise their skillsets and perk paths to get the most out of everyone. Have a doctor, a mechnic, a melee monster, a death-handed pistolier... Or all of them.
CONS
- Feels like what it is: a console port. I hate console ports. You should too. Only continuing to play because there is a very decent game underneath.
- Can be a little buggy and unstable at times. Have encounted some frustrating Crash-To-Desktops tonight. Otherwise, it's been fine.
- Non-optional Autosave 'feature'. Games developers: lLet me save my game when I damn well want to! Not at randomly decided intervals, and only at randomly decided intervals!
Overall, 7.5/10. Will play again.

Remembering back to when I first played Civilization, Masters of Magic or Masters of Orion...these are the originals in many ways. Seems like as 'improvements' are made, some of the original fun became 'work'. More stats, more management, slower gameplay, more variables, more of what sometimes seems...just more of for the sake of more. Yes...sometimes deep is okay if that is what someone is looking for, but sometimes these type of games were just a distraction and that distraction became more of a job, more of a headache when that is not what was being looked for.
Warlock took me back somehow....back to an enjoyable game without so much work. It seems like many try to remake a classic...and in doing so, try to add and improve it. But, the "improvements" many times change the character...the feel of the experience. It is hard to explain this formula....as it is different for different people. All I can say is that, for me, Warlock was this feel I have wanted to feel again for a long time.
Does it have faults? Sure. Is it the perfect feel? Hmmm....probably not. Will something else come along? Yes. But, for a time....Warlock has been that game that I can go back to after a LONG game of Endless Lengends (Great game by the way!).
And, just like past titles....they tried to 'improve' in Warlock 2....and, for me....I go back to Warlock - Master of the Arcane. If it ain't broke...don't fix it. (Well, except for bugs...some balancing...oh, and let's add...nevermind lol)

Ace Combat Assault Horizon. When I first heard someone on my friends list say it was an arcade combat flight game with Fallout's V.A.T.S. system I was slightly intrigued. I even went as far as buying it just because of that description, and believe me when I say I normally can't enjoy these type of games, because they become repetitive too soon. And yes, Ace Combat doesn't manage to spice things up all that much, but it gives you many ways to play the game, more than many other games in this genre. Missions are diverse and the gameplay is fun, with indeed some sort of V.A.T.S. system in place to kill enemies. It's a fabulous way to make games like these more exciting. The action also regularly slows down to give you some eye candy to look at.
It all looks great in motion and playing the game with a controller (or joystick, I guess) is the right way to play it. I was really, really impressed by its visuals. Everything looked clean, and sharp and the people looked like real people (in a way). The camera is always close and the parts where you're not flying your aircraft look like you're watching a movie, with the right amount of motion blur and angles.
The game doesn't do everything right, of course. There are missions that rely on depth perception. There's one mission in particular where you have to use stealth in order to avoid getting seen by the radars. The reach of these radars is shown in large, moving, green triangles, but they're so close apart that I had to repeat the mission several times because it's so hard to see. All of this would've been unnecessary with the use of more color (darker green or light green, for example) or by setting them further apart. It's one of the few times that I was really frustrated.
Concerning the length of the game; this is perfect. It's not too long and not too short, it's just right. You can finish it in 8 or 9 hours so there's plenty of gameplay in it.
Ok, time to wrap things up again: Ace Combat Assault Horizon is by far my favorite arcade combat flight game so far. Highly recommended !
[Rating: 82/100]

Not for long though; this game is such a disappointment, and so different from the original Ace Combat - in fact, this is mostly a clone of HAWX2, which is not a compliment. Bad storyline with russian rebels as villains? Check. Missions way too long, way too boring and spent mostly moving in circles to avoid enemies or missiles? Check. Multiplayer only half working? I could say something positive about the actual dogfighting, which is not too bad... if it was not that, halfway trough the 4th mission, i noticed that the "duel mode" (which is the *only* way to kill certain enemies) is often used as a gimmick to show the admitedly nice graphic in forced cut scene. Basically, once in a while the enemy in the duel mode becomes invincible, no matter how many times you hit it, because this way the enemy plane can lead you to certain point of the map to show an action scene. Once you understand how it works, you cant avoid rolling your eyes to the sky. I dont suggest this game.... unless its on a deal for 5$ or less. Otherwise, you are better served by playing HAWX1, JASF, the old but still somehow fun Rebel Raiders or the ps2x-emulated series of ace combat from 4 to 6.

No one is happier than me that Ace Combat finally made a debut on PC, but Assault Horizon was not the title to do it with. Ace Combat's strong point, since Ace Combat 2, has been its strong singleplayer with spine-chilling stories of just-unreal-enough jet capers to keep the mythos of the unique Ace Combat world alive and believable.
Ace Combat: Assault Horizon's spineless story falls on its face, and I'm not saying that just because I'm partial to the alternate world presented in Ace Combats 2-6, Zero, X, Xi and 3D. Assault Horizon's campaign simply a cookie-cutter CoD story with your average, predictable shooter drama.
That being said, multiplayer is genuinely fun and presents a new challenge than just shooting down mooks by the thousands. Dogfight Mode, although it kind of nerfs single player, I think is a necessary evil for multiplayer--it keeps players in the game and prevents campers from hiding on the edges of the mape with long-range missiles. That's when anyone is on, that is--Games for Windows Live means almost no one wants to play online. Fingers crossed that once it's completely phased out I'll be seeing more challengers on the server list!

République’s twist digs itself into a love-it-or-hate-it situation during its final episodes, however the overall premise of the game is well done and worth a look.

*Please note, that English is not my mother tongue, so I'm very sorry for each and every not-clear sentence and wrong-used vocabularies, but in case you're no grammar-nazi, it's readable.*
Overview:
Even though it's not very long (it took me only around one hour to complete the game), the playtime was filled with many cool innovations, especially the eponymous "Time Machine", which all were much fun.
Gameplay:
The game plays smoothly as always, and the new extensions fit in very well. Especially the "Time Machine": By pressing "R" you start to record what you're doing, by pressing "Q" you stop it and by pressing "F" you reproducethe action(s) which you did while recording.
This sounds extremely simple, but it's not as trivial as it might seem. There are so many interesting and challenging new levels and possibilities of gameplay, it's really amazing. Actually, it feels a tiny bit like playing the CooP-mode, but without a partner. You are both of them in one person, and you need to think ahead and plan your moves even more than in the main game.
Each test-chamber (except the first ones, which were quite easy and are done in around one to three minutes) took me around 10 to 15 minutes, but sometimes it can happen that you place something (e.g. a cube) wrong and then you need to restart the entire level, as the cube won't spawn again. This only happened once to me, though, but it took me a while to realize, therefore I needed like 25 minutes for that specific chamber.
Graphics:
According to the graphics, there's not much to say. It looks pretty much as good as Portal 2 did, there are no groundbreaking graphical innovations, but what for? The game still looks beautiful, but hyper-technological and in some special chambers rough and dirty, but no matter how it looks, I personally was fine with it, as the graphics are still beautiful to look at. Just don't expect a new Crysis or Battlefield graphic-wise, and you'll be happy.
Specials:
Also, there are a few Easter Eggs "hidden" in the game (some are quite obvious, though; but be sure to enable subtitles!)
Conclusion:
To sum up, "Thinking with Time Machine" is a great title, which looks the same as Portal 2 did, but plays like Portal-2-CooP-Mode with a few interesting innovations, which fit into the game very well. There are no graphical improvements to the main game, and sadly, the game is a bit short, but for a Free-to-Play-title, it's still recommendable.
Additional Advice: And hey, if you don't like it (but trust me: if you liked Portal 1 and 2, you WILL like this mod), you've not spent any money on it anyway, as it is Free-to-Play.

Thinking with Time Machine is a twist on the original Portal game... but with less portal puzzles. That's the most disappointing part of the game, and although you may notice that I still recommend this game, you will know why as I explain further on.
Just like the title goes, you need to manipulate time and control your duplicate-self to solve the puzzles along with you. This mechanic can be very challenging, but if you're into time-travelling, things can get rather interesting. However, the main puzzle-solving tool of the game — the iconic portals — are not frequently applied and doesn't completely integrate into the time-travelling aspect. Since the focus is on time-manipulation, the portals were forced out of the puzzle design. As a fan of the original game, I personally find this unappealling.
Since this game is just a mod, it doesn't have the resources to build a complete narrative, humour and soundtrack. So don't get too upset if you navigate through the levels without hearing any quirky remarks from GLaDOS. Despite of all that, this game along with the fresh puzzle mechanic is still definitely worth a try. Well it's free, so why not?

I never thought I'd play a "Free 2 Play" multiplayer game in my life, heck, I even made a personal rule against it. Needless to say, The Banner Saga: Factions has become an exception to that rule.
An excellent turn-based tactical battle game, with some wonderful 2D animation, Factions finds a comfortable place between being a Tactics Ogre/FFTactics/Fire Emblem style and something much closer to Chess. The primary reason the game skews closer to the timeless tactical classic is in it's turn order/initiative system, which keeps the game remarkably fair even when one player is ahead of another. However, some of the core elements you'd draw from other tactical RPGs (or just RPGs with turn based combat) such as special attacks are present, so it really is a hybrid. As someone mentioned in chat recently, this is sort of like the holotable game R2D2 plays with Chewbacca, except with Vikings.
Now, you're not going to find much depth here beyond playing matches of this "Viking Holotable Chess" against other players. That's literally all there is. On top of that, the competition is mighty fierce, and the players who have stuck around are going to destroy you ably until you learn to form a solid strategy and build a team around it. But all that said, if you like testing your tactical mind for briefer snatches of time rather than dropping several hours into a single player outing, then this should certainly have you playing.
Plus, it's "free" (all of the buyable items are either cosmetic or boosts to unlock things faster, but unlocks do not give an edge, so it's fine balance wise), so there's little reason not to try it.

Dark Souls is a game I never knew I needed. I had always heard it was really good and really difficult. Thing is, Dark Souls isn't all about difficulty. Sure, at first its overwhelming and extremely difficult. But you struggle through this amazingly crafted world and slowly figure out mechanics and how things work. And then, it all clicks. This game has depth in every direction, from enemies, to items, to bosses, to the world, to the lore... etc. There is so much to it, but every thing has its purpose and place. One of the things I love about it, is almost any weapon/armor set is valid, for both pve and pvp. You can make up your own challenge runs or themes for your run, and really make it unique. Everyone will approach the game differently, and each person makes their own story. This game will make you angry. Frusterated when you lose all of your souls (currency) to a dumb mistake or random trash mob. You will die. And it only makes it so much more satisfying when you finally beat that boss that killed you 11 times before. This game isn't perfect, it has flaws, but what it does right hasn't been replicated since. Not only that, but with the use of a fan made application (DSCM) the multiplayer is still alive and well.
If you haven't played this game, please do so. When the going gets tough (the tough get going) and you get frusterated, take a short break. But come back. There is no better feeling than coming back and conquering the thing that previously handed your♥♥♥♥♥to you.
OVERALL:
Dark Souls is the epitomy of a love-hate relationship, but in my case extremely heavy on the love :)

Dark Souls as a series is one of my favorites. Though Dark Souls 1, as much as some hang onto the nostalgia of it, is a poorly designed game, fraught with unpolished mechanics and artificial difficulty. Still, I would recommend it, if you can get past the annoying deaths, due to mechanics being clunky. Eventually you'll get used to it and the artificial difficulty they produce.
Some bads:
1.Side sweeping weapons clip the wall and prevent a swing, due to limited animations. Use a stabbing weapon.
2.Lock on can be tedious and will sometimes lock onto secondary or out of line of sight enemies.
3.The roll mechanic sometimes will roll in a direction not intended. Easier to block or just move away.
4.Some of the hit boxes for the player and enemies incorrectly match the weapon/attack they belong to. Yay parry?
5.Game feels unpolished. Compared to previous titles, such as Armored Core series by From, I expected more.
Some goods:
1.First game in series and new game type, so unpolish is understandable. Think Final Fantasy 7, in how it was innovative.
2.Good level design/layout/boss fight concepts.
3.NPC dialogue (mostly)
4.Exploration
5.Sunlight
