Alright, so, lets get one thing straight. "I Am Caligula" is not focused on the game-play aspect, as many people seem to think it is. It is a story-based RPG Maker game, with quite an interesting story.
You play as a young man, who is heir to rule in Ancient Rome, and do so with your sister, not as your sibling, but as your lover. The art style is quite appealing, and it looks very nice overall, the
over-world is nicely designed, with many small details, making it more believable of an actual location. There is a variety of sprites you may see in the over-world, all of which have quite fluid animations,
and are very colorful and well designed. The voice acting within the game is very nice quality, some of the best I've ever heard, to be honest. Though the game-play may be repetitive, the game focuses more
on story, than on game-play. The story is very in-depth, and you can get easily immersed in the story, and the world. There are quite a few areas of the over-world to explore, each being vastly different from  the last, giving the exploration aspect of the game much more depth. There is no censorship in the game, which is always a plus. Though most RPG Maker games aren't that great in my book, this one definitely changed that. If you've ever made an RPG Maker game, you'd know how much effort and time it takes to make just a fraction of a world, and takes forever to script events and write dialogue. So, really, when people are saying that there was no effort put into this game, they look past the time it must have taken to make the game, and then the time it would have taken to draw all the art, and do all the voice acting. And really, at 99 cents, you really  can't complain. Overall, this is quite a good game, and I'd recommend it to people looking for a deep story-line to immerse themselves into. And at 99 cents, you really can't go wrong!
( Also, you can take your sisters panties, so there's always that. )

(OOC Post and Review here. Let me say this right now. This game isn't for everyone. I Am Caligula, I played this game back on Itch and i was one of the Beta Testers for it to. Jesus ****ing Christ this game is good. I remember first picking it up in a steam sale after remembering that such a game existed. Difficult. That is one of the tags for this game and wow it does not do it justice... This game is a true test of your patience and stamina. So many people will give up after the first few bosses and this is perfectly understandable as it is not a game for the faint of heart or the prone to fainting (you should probably see a doctor if that is the case to be honest).
Despite the occasional annoyance and frequent "YOU DIED" message appearing no matter how good you are, this game is a masterpiece in design above all else. If you were to stop and look at your surroundings (something highly reccomended in this game), you will quickly notice how under the slightly muddy textures is a hugely innovative and well thought out style and level design. See a small ledge over there? It is very likely that if you fall onto it you have just found a secret. Find a wall that seems a bit out of place? Hit it and you may have revealed a new area or even a bonfire. Recognise this door? Well you have beaten this whole area and are now back to the safety of firelink shrine, ready to seek out the next boss.
Overall, this game is fantastic and a must buy for those that can handle it. For those that can't handle it - in true honour of the Dark Souls community - git gud!

Every review of this game mentions the Civilization series, and since I just did, this will be no different. This game is basically Civilization, with a fantasy setting. The tech trees are replaced with spell research, which is probably the weakest part of the game. Some of the spell ideas are great, like the ability to change terrain to different types to either boost your cities or mess with opponents. For the most part though, it feels like a bit of a pointless endeavour. In general though, it's a solid 4X game, which I've put a lot of time into. There's enough that's new about it to keep it interesting, and the gameplay is solid and fun enough to feel classic.

Failure diplomacy: You can't reject proposed deals of AI opponents, this automatically means war. This is annoying! Sure, I see no problem in AI opponents attacking me, if I too often reject them, but the automatism is tedious. (In Civilisation I like the fact hat all AI ​​opponents have a "mood", which can be influenced by the actions of diplomacy.)
Failure control: Units can not wait permanently / are put to sleep. At the next round you have to give new commands to each and every one. Once you have more than 5 units, it's annoying!
Failure options: You can hardly adjust something in the options for gameplay. For example: You must always watch combat animations and your units running around. If you do not want this, you have to click for every damn unit. For experienced players this should be adjustable.
Failure steam: On the steam-start-screen you can choose whether you want to play right now or only read the manual. If you choose the manual, you get the message that this was not possible, because of some kind of “application error” and that you should contact the steam support.
If you are looking on the internet, you will find no guidance. The steam support refers to the manufacturers and your are send to a forum (where you can ask questions if you log in with an account). All unsatisfactory and very awkward.

I am really displeased with WB's handling of the Asheron's Call franchise. For those who don't know, they decided to shut down the MMO videogame Asheron's Call after 17 years of service. Afterwards, they compelled the shutdown of the community's attempt to continue playing this game via alternative/private means, presumably in order to protect their IP rights. So now this historically significant videogame has apparently been permanently shuttered, with its remaining loyal playerbase turned away, even though WB has indicated no desire to leverage this property for any future business venture.
I of course understand the nature of business and their duty to their shareholders, however I think special care is required with these kinds of products. We can just as easily make an argument for the reputational risk WB has been exposed to as a result of this decision. Google "74-Year-Old Grandpa Says Goodbye To MMO He's Played Since 1999" and I'm sure you'll agree (sorry, I can't post a link).
Ultimately, their actions display a lack of respect and appreciation for their paying customers. It also calls into question our ability to trust WB when it comes to their handling of other online properties. Is it safe to become attached to a game owned by WB? So having played this game for over 100 hours I have some thoughts to help those who are on the fence about this game.  If you like survival games, then you may like this game.  This game does look pretty, graphically pretty(running on i7 with GTX 1070 and 32gb ddr4).  What you will soon come to realize is the zombies arent anything to be concerned with most of the time, it's the other players to watch out for(trust no one).  I have found that you can play this game solo, but helps to have friends especially if you want to build a base.  You can kill a zombie with your bare hands in this game, much harder to do to a human player.  It is however frustrating that if you die, either by the hands of another player, zombie, or you fall off a structure, you almost never spawn near your body, so progress lost.  Many of the players have very good aim and tend to headshot you, helmets dont seem to help with this at all(including military helmets).  The crafting system isn't bad.  Vehicles are in the game, you just normally have to have a bunch of parts on you to get them working.
Keeping in mind that this is early alpha, the game has some issues. One of the most vexing issues is missing items when you spawn into a game.  An example of this is that you spend hours gearing up your character by finding items (some of which are hard to find), you log out of the game, then you log back in, low and behold you have no shoes, or you have everything but your shirt, perhaps you had 17 rounds of 9mm in your pistol, now you somehow only have 2 rounds.  The worst missing item I experienced was my only flashlight was gone, so playing at night was nearly impossible.  Sometimes you drop items that you intend to pick back up in a minute, but apparently they fall into a hidden hole and just dissapear.  You may find a bicycle and upon getting off the bike, it glitches and you can no longer ride it.  All that being said, it is spelled out clearly at the beginning of the game that things like this will happen.
Overall I do recommend this game if you like survival games and doing a lot of grinding.  If you are easily frustrated with losing everything if you die, this may not be the game for you.  My wife has watched me play and she couldn't play this game as she would get too angry at losing all her items if she died(which is most likely for just about anyone in this game).  I did get this game during the last sale for 10 dollars and I feel that I have more than gotten my money's worth out of this game, I would still feel the same if I spent 20.

If you ever wanted a purely singleplayer zombie apocalypse survival game in an open world environment, with lots of freedom to do the things your way (and live with the consequences) instead of being shoehorned into a linear scripted shooter, and all of it in GTA IV quality graphics, then THIS IS THE GAME YOU HAVE BEEN WAITING FOR!!!
State of Decay is an underappreciated gem that went under the radar because it isnt a massively advertised, triple A mainsteam title like Left4Dead, The Last of Us or The Walking Dead. And yet, this game is just as good as those, if not better due to its cross platform availability.
In State of Decay, you start as Marcus Campbell who goes fishing with his friend Ed Jones in Trumbull county when they are suddenly attacked by zombies. Confused, the two head toward the local ranger station to ask what the hell is going on. There they meet their first fellow survivors, and from there on out it's up to you to lead your group from one safehouse to the next, always on the vigil from the zombie threat.
Whats awesome about State of Decay is that you arent limited to playing as one character. You can switch to any of those characters that have befriended you and play as them, and the game goes on even if Marcus Campbell dies - you just continue playing as someone else. Each character has their own small unique backstory and traits, and the game makes sure that once a character is dead, they're dead. So you must always be careful. In your safehouse, you manage construction of essential things like additional bedrooms to accomodate more survivors you pick up, a medical facility to treat the sick and injured, a workshop to repair vehicles and make explosives, a kitchen to cook food and lighten up the community spirit etc. But primarily you scour the nearby towns and hamlets for food, fuel, tools, ammo and other resources essential for survival and haul them back into your safehouse.
The game is roughly 15 hours long (my playthrough took 17 hours) but you can delay the final quest and play indefinitely. In fact, in these 15 hours I only managed to raid every house in the first village you come across, "Spencer's Mill". There's two more locations, both of them actually larger towns with far more houses and a different environmental feel. These towns, villages and hamlets are separated by long stretches of highway taking you out across the countryside, where isolated farms also might harbor small groups of survivors trying to make it. The game features a nicely implemented day-night cycle and you cannot play as one character for too long or s/he will tire out and be ineffective in combat. Speaking of combat, there's a lot of close combat in this game - smashing zombies' brains in is far more silent than using guns to shoot them as that will attract more zombies. The largest zombie congregations are called hordes, and its fun running them over with your vehicle, but because vehicles take damage and repairing them is very hard, you need to be careful.
Anyways, this game gets a solid 4 out of 5 stars from me - a really fun zombie game but sadly too short, given how they could have easily extended the storyline until slow players like me would be forced to move their safehouse from Spencer's Mill (after having scoured all houses there) to the town of Marshal and eventually to Trumbull County Fairgrounds. Oh well - at least it gives this game lots of replayability.

Written Review.
Gameplay.

=== 30 Min ===
Ok First impressions, with 30 minutes in. It can be fun, but it has a bit of a learning curve. It is reminiscent of old KOEI games of past for me. Reminds me a bit of Uncharted Waters and some might consider it similar to some of the original Zelda games. If you like these kind of games, you will probably enjoy this, if not then don't buy it you will likely be unimpressed.
The game puts you in the shoes of Caligua, 1st century Roman Emperor. If you like historical games, this might be for you too. So far though I've not seen too much in the way historicalness other than the Emperor's name, this isn't to say there isn't more.
The artwork is nice, especially on the overhead screen. It can sometimes be tempting for developers to cut corners here, in this game this not the case. The game add voice actors which can be nice for those that are kinda lazy, and don't want to read. A few of them are nice, a few others are midly annoying, but no fear you can skip over them if you like. The world is enormous, at least it seems to as I am constantly getting lost in a labrinth like city.
As of right now I recommend the game. The low price doesn't hurt either, definitely worth 5x or more what I paid for it. I'll continue to play it, and follow up later on with replayability and time to complete. Good enough for not only me, but good enough that I'll be sending a few copies out as gifts.
One thing to keep in mind. Combat mode you are on the right side of the screen not the left, this can be confusing at first. To get to full screen mode hit F5, hit it again to go back to windowed mode. If you dont do this the small screen will get distracting real fast. Spacebar allows you to talk to people.
=== 2 HRS ===
Ok 2hrs in... I'll try and keep this objective. The game starts off a little wierd and is hard to follow. I spent a good time running around trying to figure out what to do. This is kinda difficult to deal with. Once the story line starts it gets going and I found myself having fun fighting anything and everything in Germania once I got the hang of the strategy involved in combat. I could offer a few tips here but I won't, I don't want to play spoiler.
Once glaring issue is spelling and grammatical errors (watch I bet I spelled that wrong.) There are a few haters who have left reviews, I recognize one of them from a hate group that was started against the developer before the game even launched.
=== 2+ HRS ===
The game started off a bit confusing. As the game picked up I became more engaged. Again mad spelling issues. I do have a few things I'm not particularly fond of. Long story short, if this is on sale for about 5-10 dollars, and you're itching to get a fix of an acceptable storyline in a flight combat type of game, then I'd recommend it. However, at full price, I would not, hence my thumbs down.
Anyways, I've played Ace Combat 4, 5, and Zero, and I really love the series. Did not get the Xbox 360 so I was unable to play Ace Combat 6. That being said, the inclusion of DogFight mode (DFM) has made, in my opinion, a rather significant paradigm shift in the game. It is still possible to shoot down enemies outside of DFM, but it is magnitudes more difficult. The missiles, for all intents and purposes, have extremely narrow tracking angles, and it's fairly easy to evade them without popping flares. If you're in DFM, however, hitting enemies is much, much easier.
So while there is a war of maneuvering in the sky, it's only to get within range of DFM. Once you get locked into DFM (or someone locks onto you in DFM), it's a bit more automatic and you just adjust speed and try to counter or counter their counter.
The storyline is your standard Tom Clancy-esque plot, and while it isn't terrible, it's nothing noteworthy. Rather predictable, but it'll still take up 5-6 hours of your time. Again, this is why if it's around 5-10USD and you find what I just said acceptable, then go ahead, because...
Multiplayer is nonexistent. I suppose it's a product of the negative reviews such that very few people got the game, and the fact that there are no dedicated servers. As a result, someone checks to see if there are any lobbies (and there usually arent), and they hop off. It's very difficult to actually find another person to play with unless you just idle in your own lobby for up to half an hour. It's disheartening, and I just play it occasionally for the free missions whenever I want to fly a plane for some time.
All in all, it's rather disappointing, and while having folks to play with would make it more palatable, the fact that you can't find people to play with makes it less so.

There are some TV shows that you watch just for the characters. Well, this is a video game that you play just for the characters.
The main cast of NITW - Mae, Bea, Gregg, and Angus - are probably the most relatable characters I've ever met in a video game. Their conflict feels all too familiar and real: struggling to make a future for themselves while living in the dying town of Possum Springs. The story forces them to deal with complex issues such as depression, insecurity, relationships, friendships, faith, and the meaning of life.
At times, you get to choose which of your friends' storylines you want to follow, and you'll need to play through NITW at least twice to complete each storyline. I'm glad the developers opted for this, because not only does it give you more time to bond with each character as their conflicts and motivations are fleshed out, but it gives you an opportunity to go back and appreciate how much detail went into the foreshadowing and symbolism in this game.
But NITW wouldn't be complete without all the emotions it'll make you feel. Episodes will range from hilarious to horrifying, from heartwarming to heart-wrenching. And thanks to the superb writing, it all feels completely genuine. I've played this game twice now to experience all of the stories, and I can attest that both times, it was a journey. I laughed. I cried. I was scared out of my mind. And I wanted to give all four of these people a big hug.
Mae, Bea, Gregg, and Angus are as unforgettable as my friends in real life. I love them, and I love this game.
And I can't wait to get the Weird Autumn Update that's coming out in December.

This game is the reverse SIMS. It is regular life through the eyes of a hipster who left college and is now floating purposeless confined in her hometown and not really ~doing~ anything. This is probably the best game I've played in the past couple years solely because of the story. This game has very charming characters, amazing music, and heavy themes. The only thing this game lacks is conventional gameplay. I'm gonna be straight up and say there isn't much "gameplay" except for the guitar hero-like segments, and some other minigames. Sometimes it feels more like a visual novel rather than a game, which is okay for me because every other facet in the game makes up for it. I wish the game was much longer and allowed you to do the missions for all the characters in one playthrough, but it's not really a con in my book. The best part about this game is the interactions and relationships between the Mae, the player's character, and her friends. The dialogue is feels real and not forced, and the struggles that the characters go through are relatable and realistic. In the review from youtuber Shammy, he eloquently said that the things the characters go through receive empathy from teens and sympathy from adults. Not everyone will be able to relate to the characters or the events, but those who do will receive a much deeper experience. The way the game handled very heavy topics like depression, death, and derealization made me think the writers went through the things that the in game characters went through. As a 19 year old I instantly felt connected to each one of the characters in some way, and it made the events in the game have a much larger impact. After I finished the game I felt a big pit well up in my chest because I just wanted the story to continue, but the way the game wrapped up was satisfying. The unfortunate thing is that you only have so many days to hang out with one of your friends, Gregg or Bea(the main ones, there are more), so you end up only being able to complete one of their personal storylines. In my first [and only playthrough so far ;) ] playthrough I decided to hang out with Bea, the alligator girl. I won't spoil but her story in the game made me want to cry manly tears. I can't imagine doing Gregg's storyline right now because I will feel so guilty not being there for Bea, which is a weird feeling considering she's just a cartoon alligator. It's so crazy that the writers elicited these emotions. I believe it's because many games barely reach half these levels of character development, which makes this game stand out even more. I really don't know how to sum up my thoughts about this game, other than that you need to play it as soon as possible, because this is a very genuine game that deserves your attention.

Given the price this is often at these days, this game is a great buy for anyone who ever played and loved Master of Magic.  I adored that game and still consider it the ultimate 4x experience.  The inspirations are obvious and many features and concepts are carried over here, including:
Square/hex based fantasy 4x TBS
Multiple dimensions (Warlock has more than one)
Heroes (which again are overpowering later with enough enchantments)
Hero equipment (Artifacts, which can be crafted here also)
City management with buildings, resources, and enchantments (though not self-contained like in MoM)
Even unit orders like Sentry and the waypointing system
It should also be noted that this game is in the lore of the Majesty series of games, and you'll recognize much of the irreverent humor and religious pantheon.  The graphics and sound design are gorgeous as well, and I've not once had the game crash on me yet, even while on a 12-hour bender, saving and loading games multiple times.
I think I still would prefer a modern remake of Master of Magic with multiplayer, but I definitely recommend Warlock.

Civ 5 with wizards.
You have 3 resources, gold, food and mana. You use mana to maintain enchantments and magical units, as well as cast spells. Food goes to supporting cities and units. Gold goes to building and army upkeep, as well as buying new units.
It's simpler, but still crazy addictive. There are also 'Lords', basically hero units that require a lot of upkeep but can equip artefacts and are essentially more powerful than standard units. Seriously, if you pile the enchantments on, these guys can get ridiculously OP, it's so fun.
There's a religion system, where you do quests to earn favour with gods that govern particular spheres (such as death, strength or the sun). At first I thought, oh great, another list of made up deity names for me to learn, but there's not so many and they all make sense. It's especially easy to remember as they have polar opposite gods as well, e.g Dauros is the god of order and law, his rival is Fervus, god of chaos and nature.
I'm not a massive strategy fan and I love this game. Fans of the 4X genre might want something more complicated, but this is a worthy buy for me.

Smart (grand and tactical) strategy with hi-fantasy; together again.
Remember the classic hexagonal war series Panzer General? The series went onto make all kinds of sequels, one of which was Fantasy General.  That game scratched an itch for me in that I like Grand Strategy War games and I like Fantasy games whether strategy, tactical, role plying or other.  It was a solid effort but something was missing.  Warlock re-treads this ground in Wizard’s robes and does it quite well.  It has the tight and balanced combat of the PG series with plausible and clever (role based) fantasy units brought from several traditions.
The Bonus to me is that there is as well a generous layer of Civ-5 era Civ-type flavour heaped on.  Research tree, Religious favour, building wonders (sorta), and cultures with distinctive units all have their place in the overall game play and strategies.
This game may not have the most original ingredients but it has taken the right amount from each of it’s influences and mixed them well.
Although I like this game quite a bit, I do have some complaints:
- There does seem to be a memory leak where one needs to reload the game every few turns to prevent processing slow down.
- The underworld's populations seem to grow exponentially out of control by mid-game.
Overall I would recommend this game to gamers who are any flavour of strategy enthusiast or specialize in turn-based-strategy, hex war games, fantasy strategy or are looking for fantasy/strategy options away from the main stream.
- Overall: 8/10.
- Tighten up the scripting: 9/10.

Once upon a time, in a kingdom far, far away...
It all began in January 2017, or even December 2016, when one of my friends invited me to join the game called "The SKIES" (free to play, survival, post-apocalyptic, blah blah kinda the same as Miscreated). I have 49h on record, I was playing both alone and together with them, it was fun. But since the developers dropped the game a while ago, it still has a potential but nothing more, it was hard to play - weapon DMGand mob HP ratio was terrible. So I dropped it.
Anyway, I bought Miscreated in the middle of February, it was on sale. So it's +/- 6 months ago. I entered the game, it was fun, played a bit but the main struggle was to find the perfect server. The server list is sooo long! So at the beginning there was not as much about the gameplay as about choosing my perfect server. I switched to 3-4 different ones, different time zones, PvE, KOS etc. Ugh.
At that time I had something like 10-15h on record, when I entered a server called "Land Of Freedom". I was on it literally as long as it takes to get some gear and food when I met a random guy. Hi - hi. How are you, etc. He and he's friend just bought this game (it was still on sale), they both came on this server (pay attention - from that huge list they picked up exactly the same I was on) and they had struggle to meet each other, since it's a random place you spawn when you first enter the game. I offered some help since I had a few gameplay hours and I already knew the South part of the map pretty well. Ever since we've played together, it's sooooo much fun! The only problem - they're both from US and I'm from Latvia. 10h time zone difference lol.
Later on, when we had a decent base and a lot of fancy gear, we were all followed and KOS and our base was raided. First we thought it's a prank. We logged in just to witness another KOS. So we all rage quitted. Literally. So much effort for nothing. It broke our hearts. One of the guys even don't talked with us for a long time. That was more than sad, hard to explain.
So we dropped the game for I dunno, like 3 months or so. Yeah, since then a lot of changes, new zones, new stuff, gear, squat toilet (!!!) but we still were soo freakin' mad at this game, we just couldn't.
Until a week ago I said, hey c'mon. Let's give this game another try. But first, we have to choose the server very carefully. It took us more than 30min to choose the right one (it's called The Sanctuary - Whitelisted). Coincidence - at that time it was not whitelisted. We entered the server, after few moments one of the admins came to visit us, we talked about this and that, about our past experience and needs and demands. We found out that this is PvE server, Whitelisted, everything just as we wanted. So we said to each other "this is it, it's the destiny". And we're back on-line. :]
Long story short - if you want to take the hard lessons about the mistakes you've made (instantly loose your gear or blow up in a car or get killed by the fat♥♥♥♥♥zombie or whatever else), if you want to witness betrayal and support, if you love CryEngine, if you can run this game, if the community and devs and updates are important, if it's ok for you to play Early Access game and if you like to play with friends or if you are willing to meet new ones, maybe even on the opposite side of the Earth, then this game is for you.
As for looting, building etc., many games offer that. But the amount of stresfull moments, the anger and sorrow, the joy and many laughter I've had since the first time I entered the game .. nothing is to compare. 10/10

A charming version of "chess with vikings". The game takes place in an arctic world, filled with vikings, giants called "Varl" and other fantasy creatures. The tone of the game is very "low-key" - there's a solemn, sad and eerie feel to everything and I found myself curious and inspired by the setting.
During the game you play as the role of several key characters as they travel with their people across the land. The story begins as the sun has frozen in the sky and an army of dark figures are marching from the outer reaches of the known civilization. Yes, this is fantasy, but the game still feels strangely realistic and believable and the tone sets it apart from other classical high-fantasy.
As you travel through the land the game swithes between two distinct modes. One mode is the actual travelling, which is centered around managing your resources and interacting with characters and people by selecting different options during dialogue and encounters. Many of the choises revolve around keeping your caravan well fed, in order and away from danger - especially the large horde of dark figures that roam through the land.
The other mode is the actual combat, which takes place on a classical square-grid with the key characters, or "heroes", that your current party consists of. The gameplay is simple, straight-forward and it reminds me of classical board games. Every character only have a couple of special abilities and the game is centered a lot around placement and using the abilities at the right moment, rather than a long range of attributes and complicated spellbooks that you might expect from this genre. It's very engaging, despite it's simplicity, and I've found myself having some of my best gaming moments with this game during some of it's most challenging encounters.
As you finish the game however you'll be faced with it's one and only big shortcoming - the lack of a proper ending. There is a poetic and beautiful ending of sorts, but it left me quite unsatisified as there's still a lot going on when the game ends. Maybe this is an evil way to get people excited about a sequel, which I am, but I don't like it when developers end things while I'm in the middle of it.
The Good:
- Very artsy - a beautiful game with inspiring visualls and graphics.
- Great music, I frequently found myself humming on similar tunes after a game session...I blame my nordic roots.
- The combat is well balanced and engaging, without any over-complicated rules or functions.
The Bad:
- You get the feeling the developers didn't quite have time to deliver as much animation and content as they may have wanted to. Some of the graphics are reused a bit too much and only the first section of the game has properly animated movies.
- Many of the choises you make throughout the story can feel bit too random and unforgiving at times.
- The game ends right in the middle of the story.
All-in-all it's a beautiful and inspiring game which I'd recommend to anyone who likes strategy- or turn-based games.

I've been playing Undead Labs's State of Decay for the past several weeks after nabbing it on sale. The game is a single-player third-person zombie apocalypse sandbox of sorts: while the main game has a storyline to follow, you certainly don't need to follow it and the story won't advance until you do, giving you a lot of time to just poke around.
I have enjoyed the game very much.  It's certainly interesting enough to play and while it starts out reasonably tame, it can get quite difficult.
The main game begins with your character and a buddy returning to the more civilization-adjacent parts of a national park after a two-week fishing trip only to find that, while you were gone, civilization kind of had a major meltdown.  From there, the game focuses on steath and survival by building up friendships with others and establishing a base from which to operate and outposts to reinforce that base and provide small "safe zones".
The criticisms I have are somewhat picky.  To start, the story is very simple and somewhat shallow — it would be easy to play through it relatively quickly and then be just done with the game.  A lot more could have been done, but, as I understand it this was Undead Labs's first game, and it was made for XBox Arcade with all the limitations that requires -- so we will perhaps see more story development in their next full release.
Second, there just isn't enough information in the tutorial; you feel bombarded with information (because a lot comes in through your Journal) that you can't make much sense of — and then lost because basic information (such as the benefits of establishing an Outpost, or whether it's wise to leave resources in Outposts or loot them thoroughly before setting one up in a location) can be a little difficult to find.
Third, there are too few voice actors, meaning that you end up with the same voice actors' lines being used for several different characters who end up sounding exactly the same while they say (verbatim) the same things; get two of them with the same voice together on a mission and it can get kind of confusing.
Finally: the driving physics and UI need some work.  The game was set up for XBox, so maybe this is where PC players like me start to have problems.  But while I can play Saints Row and Grand Theft Auto and drive just fine, I find the driving in State of Decay frustrating — especially because the smallest mistake can send a car sailing through the air as though it suddenly weighs nothing.  And cars that turn over always explode, so there's that.
Meanwhile, though, State of Decay is nice to look at: the colors are just muted enough to evoke the proper autumn at the end-of-the-world feeling, and there has been a lot of attention to detail in filling out the large area (Trumbull Valley) in which your character gets to roam.  There are three small towns to explore, as well as a lot of countryside, with a lot of interesting things to look at if you appreciate the details.
The game also makes you take a step back and figure out how to survive.  Your character can go stealth or maniac, or pretty much anything in between.  But don't count on the zombies to cooperate since that's sure to get your favorite character eaten nearly every time.  And since death is final, that really makes a difference.
Strategy and sound are important, which I really enjoy, and on top of that there is also resource management to deal with: you've got a base full of survivors who need food, medicine, and ammunition to remain survivors, and construction materials to keep their base up.  Scavenging through the zombie-infested, burnt-out world is a constant necessity.
In the end, the game is definitely worth a few bucks (especially if you can catch it on sale), and I look forward to other games from Undead Labs.

Yet another zombie survival game. Oh, don't we see them so often? The answer is: Yes, HOWEVER, this game takes a new and interesting approach to the apocolypse. Nevermind finding a cure or trying to leave town to some place nice and quiet; State of Decay forces you into a world where the main focus is to fortify a home/base and to live off the surrounding, sometimes desolate buildings. Find food, feed your community members. Find materials, upgrade your base. Find oil, power your generator. Find ammo, defend yourselves from the shambling remains of what used to be your average Joe. Find and rescue other survivors, convince them to join your community. Survive as long as you could as a community. This game makes it clear you need a hand in the end of the world. Now, let's not get too off-topic - this is a review. This brings the question: So why should I get this game?
Well, although this game had a so-so port from Xbox to PC, although it has semi-frequent glitches, and although it has rather repetetive dialogue, the game makes up for this in many other aspects. I can play this for hours on end, but for the sake of my mental health, I keep each session under 4 hours. This game is great fun, and it can seriously get nerve racking at certain points, whether from the plot or from you just scavenging a town alone. There hasn't been one point in this entire game that I didn't enjoy spending time in the destroyed world that remains. After all, you don't choose the world you live in, but you choose what role you will play in said world.
All being said, I highly recommend you give this game a go, and if you like it, get the DLC (but we'll leave the DLC for another review or two).

This is definately no Railroad Tycoon program.

It is much more simplified.
In a way it isn't even a Train Simulator.  In fact you don't even have to run any trains if you don't want to.
You can run a Stage Line instead and still make millions of dollars.  Of course you can run both trains and coaches.
The trains are hard to operate unless your simply running pont to point.  The signaling system is too simple to be of much good if you try running multiple trains on one track.  There is only one size Train Station, BIG.  There is no small Train Station that you can place at a distant Industry. There are three different sizes of train stations but even the smallest takes up space equal to 3 city blocks. They look silly sitting next to a dinky logging camp.
The industries are spread haphazardly about the map.  You might find an Oil Well but the Refinery could be halfway across the map.  It isn't cost effective to service since comodities bring very little cash compared to Passengers.  You can of course but it will take years to get a return on your investment.
Cargo hauling by Horsedrawn wagons or Freight Trucks is more cost effective than trains but unlike trains they can't haul freight to an industry and then pick up the goods produced. For example a Truck delivering lumber won't automatically change and take a load of goods made from the lumber.  You have to buy a seperate truck for goods, Not very realistic.
Graphics are pretty bad,  Inside towns or cities it's not bad but out on the highways and tracks it's bad.  The land is bare and boring with an occasional tree or two.  Even shades of green would be better than dirt and sand.
If you use a Trackball or a wheel less mouse you will have problems scrolling some popup windows once you exceed 9 Lines.  Scrolling these windows requires a Mouse wheel.  Poor design.

Now you might be wondering why I recommend this game.
I'm enjoying running Stagecoaches and fine tuning the profit making.
I like being able to zoom in and see my coaches moving along and looking at all the people inside towns.
Cute things like watching a coach stop to let pedestrians cross the street.
I'm sure to discover new things as I play along.  I'll add them here if I do.
I'm having fun,  so yes I recommend it.

As a long time fan of the Ace Combat series I would like to say a few things about Ace Combat Assault Horizon a very fun game, great for anyone who is into jets and aircrafts in general, fast paced action and great soundtracks. The series has always had some of the best soundtracks around and Assault horizon delivers again. The graphics are a step ahead of any previous entry into the series, everything is nice to look at esspecialy the jets, there is an ingame viewer just for looking at jets which is great. The story is okay but nothing particularily memorable, same with the characters but the missions are extremely fun to play (multiple times). Now on to the gameplay which has always been great but there a few features added to Assault Horizon, one being DFM which is Dog Fight Mode which basically allowd you to engage your enemy in a closer proximity and puts you right in the action and allows you to pull off some pretty awesome maneuvers BUT these maneuvers are very dumbed down from previous games (before you would have to learn and execute these maneuvers on your own) now you press a couple buttons and its done for you so alot less skill is involved which is a letdown to me. Now this is a port from the console verions of the game and its pretty much a barebones port no extra graphical features just resolution, vsync and AA options which is a big minus to me, but it also includes all the DLC from the console verions which is a plus. All and all though Ace Combat Assault Horizon is a very fun game to play with a few minor flaws in the gameplay which are my own personal taste I'd have to give this a 7.8/10. If you like this game I would recommend picking up a PS2 and playing Ace Combat 4 or 5 which are probaly the best in the series.

But, the most damning and horrible shortcoming is the control interface: You're literally forced to use a gamepad lest you have to endure shoddy keyboard controls or even worse joystick control. The Joystick support is non-existent. This is unacceptable. Some say this is a game meant to be played on a gamepad and this just smacks of apologetics for laziness that has become so familiar within the industry. Even Tom Clancy's HAWX, which wasn't all that good, had a basic dead zone slider and that came out in 2009, this was early 2013. There's no excuse for this at all. Why can't someone with a joystick enjoy a game about flight? Why is the joystick suddenly a peripheral only for the hardcore flight sim? And why are people defending this lazy thinking as if spending money on a game were a privilege for them?
In the end, this is a horrible game and for those seeking a good arcade flying experience would be better served with the original HAWX or, better still, going out and buying a PS2 with its trilogy of Ace Combats. Those games are superior in everyway to this pile of dung. If you're looking for a good arcadey experience on pc? Your regular flight sims can provide; just crank down the physic settings and difficulty. Wings of Prey is also another good choice for that when compared to this.
Either way, this games is awful. Skip.

Ultra Steet Fighter IV is an update for the original Street Fighter IV which was released in 2008. Believe it or not, but this was my first experience with the Street Fighter franchise.  This game is a standalone product too, allowing you to just purchase this definitive edition.
This update brings the total number of playable characters up to forty four - each of the characters also has a different version of them selves, meaning you have in effect eighty eighty different characters to play as. Street Fighter IV has one of the best combo systems I have played with, much better than the combo system in Mortal Kombat X to say the least. You can easily view the combos for your character on the pause menu, meaning you can learn them on the fly,
The graphics are really quite nice too, it shows a cartoony style art much like the previous games, but with a more polished and finished look to it. All of the special moves and combos each have their own animation, as well as special effects, making this a really good looking game to look at whilst spectating.
Each of the characters in Ultra Street Fighter have their own story line, so with 44 different characters, that is a lot of story to include! I was quite surprised at this amount given the very linear style of fighting games I have played in the past. Obviously some of the stories are more in depth than others, but each of them give you a good amount of content to see.
I only managed to play this game on Easy mode, and even then, on some of the latter stages to the arcade mode, I was struggling. I would hate to see how devastatingly hard the normal and hard modes are, because I was having to retry plenty of times before being able to beat some stages. That being said, this is the sort of game that you will just get better at with practice, you won't be pulling off massive combos to start with (unless you are highly experienced with this genre) so it will take some time before getting right up to speed.
I have completed four characters arcade mode, meaning I have another forty left to go, this has taken me just over two hours to do, so there is a heck of a lot of content on show here, and that is just the single player. Ultra Street Fighter also has a local and online multiplayer too which will really wrack up your hours with ease.
I had one technical issue whilst playing, I for the life of me could not get the game to run in 1920 x 1080 AND full-screen. Not sure whether this is intentional of a bug with my game. It runs fine in that resolution and windows mode though. That being said, you probably won't notice it too much given the amount of time you actually get to look at anything else whilst playing.
I can easily recommend Ultra Street Fighter IV, even though this was my first experience with the Street Fighter franchise, it really does a good job of introducing you to this style of game and giving you hours and hours of content too. To buy this game from scratch, the £22,99 price tag is easily justified with the quality and quantity of gameplay on offer.

2) Only recommended when on sale

5) This is a must play

I loved the concept of Stranded Deep right away, prior to buying the game. Not that the concept is original by any means, survivial games are a dime a dozen. But what Stranded Deep seemed offer that other survival games do not is a a relaxing island setting WITHOUT the annoyance of wacky flesh eating monsters messing up the experience. (I'm looking at you, The Forest.)

Plus, of course, I, like many people, have watched shows like "I Shouldn't Be Alive" and thought; "What a bunch of dumb asses. I bet I could survive in the wilderness, no problem."
(I couldn't, of course. I'm well aware of that. But I like the idea of trying without the risk of actual dehydration and death.)
Plus, Stranded Deep also seemed to offer the joys of exploration, emmersion, and a slow paced game style, which are qualities I've started finding very appealing as I tick over into my thirties. Giving and receiving large quantaties of bullets is just not what it used to be.
So, does Stranded Deep offer all of the above, and live up to expectations? The answer is... sort of.
In explaining my thoughts on the game, I would like to do so in the form of offering suggestions to the developers. Whether they actually read these reviews or not, I have no idea. But I'd like to pretend they do, just for the sake of this review.
First, the game looks absolutely gorgeous, and has perhaps the best lighting I have ever seen in a game. At least, the game looks gorgeous if you stand still. Upon moving forward the trees, foliage, and distant ship wrecks pop into existence with such appaling blatanteness that the emmersion is slapped right out of my face at the speed of light. Developers; I understand the need to make a game able to run on all types of computers. But PLEASE, if I put the game to ultra settings, let the game take advantage of what my computer is capable of. Add a Level Of Detail graphics option. (The water looks absolutely stunning, though. Good job on that.)
Second, if I am enjoying a relaxing night beside my campfire, marveling at how stunning the moonlight looks as it paints the foliage a dramatic silver, what I do not want is a swarm of bats above my head going SHRIEK SHRIEK SHRIEK, making my ears bleed. Perhaps island bats make this noise, I don't know, but regardless, for the love of God, make them softer, and use more then one short loop that pauses before repeating. SHRIEK SHRIEK SHRIEK!!! The God forsaken things stay there the ENTIRE NIGHT, and that you didn't think the sound would get annoying is crazy. Much of the other sound design is great, so I'm not sure why the bats seems so poorly done.
Third, you had an excellent idea making sharks trigger the Jaws style music. It makes exploring sunken ships terrifying, and is perhaps one of the best aspects of the game. Snakes, however, seem like a massively missed oppertunity. May I suggest making them hiss long before the player actually sees them, drawing attention to their presence. Plus, make their bite extremely deadly, and very much worth avoiding. In this way, much as the sharks, the player will be terrified, wondering where the snake is, as appossed to going; "Woah! Did something just happen? Why did I take damage?! Oh, is that a snake? Huh. it took one bar of health. Oh well." Just a suggestion.
Fourth; pressing the escape key should always, ALWAYS back me out of the menu I am currently in. Be it the graphics menu, audio menu, crafting menu, WHATEVER menu, the escape key should take me out of it. This is the very purpose of the escape key. My fingers have literally been trained to hit the escape key over twenty years of playing games. This lack of escape key functionality made the crafting system get annoying, among other things.
There is more, which added to the annoyance of the interface. Let me explain. I want to make a few arrows. I have to press c, click into the correct menu, click on arrow, click on craft, click to make the arrow...on the floor.... click to pick the arrow up off the floor. One arrow. Press c to go back into crafting, click the correct menu, click on arrow, click craft, click to make the arrow...on the floor.... click to pick up the arrow off the floor... etc etc. Developers; are you counting the clicks? Are you counting how many clicks it takes to make five arrows...? Suggestion; press c, select the menu, double click on arrow. I have an arrow in my inventory, accompanied by a crafting sound effect. Done.
And finally. It took me roughly two hours of fussing to figure out how to cook a fish. I had a fire, I had a fish, you would have thought the result of a cooked fish would be a simple one. It wasn't. Why did I struggle? Very simply because it did not occur to me skinning a fish would be possible ONLY with a knife, and nothing else. Will a machette work? No. A stone tool? No. Only a knife. Plus, did you guys purposfully make the skinning animation look like the character is committing Japanese style sepuku? Because it REALLY looks like that. Or perhaps like the guy has got tired of having a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
As a closing thought. If you have read this review and decided I hate the game, I really don't. I rather enjoy it, and feel that with a few tweaks Stranded Deep could be absolutely amazing. Good work, developers, I look forward to seeing how you turn this game into a classic.

There are some TV shows that you watch just for the characters. Well, this is a video game that you play just for the characters.
The main cast of NITW - Mae, Bea, Gregg, and Angus - are probably the most relatable characters I've ever met in a video game. Their conflict feels all too familiar and real: struggling to make a future for themselves while living in the dying town of Possum Springs. The story forces them to deal with complex issues such as depression, insecurity, relationships, friendships, faith, and the meaning of life.
At times, you get to choose which of your friends' storylines you want to follow, and you'll need to play through NITW at least twice to complete each storyline. I'm glad the developers opted for this, because not only does it give you more time to bond with each character as their conflicts and motivations are fleshed out, but it gives you an opportunity to go back and appreciate how much detail went into the foreshadowing and symbolism in this game.
But NITW wouldn't be complete without all the emotions it'll make you feel. Episodes will range from hilarious to horrifying, from heartwarming to heart-wrenching. And thanks to the superb writing, it all feels completely genuine. I've played this game twice now to experience all of the stories, and I can attest that both times, it was a journey. I laughed. I cried. I was scared out of my mind. And I wanted to give all four of these people a big hug.
Mae, Bea, Gregg, and Angus are as unforgettable as my friends in real life. I love them, and I love this game.
And I can't wait to get the Weird Autumn Update that's coming out in December.

This game is beautiful. It evokes an emotion, it has attitude, it clearly expresses an atmosphere. The issue that I have with the game are the characters, the storyline and the rate at which the storylines progresses. The character development is also very spotty, uneven and oh. so. slow. This game is the reverse SIMS. It is regular life through the eyes of a hipster who left college and is now floating purposeless confined in her hometown and not really ~doing~ anything. The only things that led me to play 11 hours of this game were the anomalies that occur in the story line juuust before you snooze off due to the tedious trudge in molasses that is this game. The fact that the main characters are animals makes it kind of interesting, but they'd be a lot more interesting if any of them were likable...at all. A Night in the Woods had some really cool moments! The dream sequences for instance are incredible, the symbols, floating shapes, fogginess of it all and the music was sublime. But then we wake up and we're back to being useless hipsters again! Come on! More genuine conflict in this game would have saved it for me and would have added beautiful momentum. This is probably the best game I've played in the past couple years solely because of the story. This game has very charming characters, amazing music, and heavy themes. The only thing this game lacks is conventional gameplay. I'm gonna be straight up and say there isn't much "gameplay" except for the guitar hero-like segments, and some other minigames. Sometimes it feels more like a visual novel rather than a game, which is okay for me because every other facet in the game makes up for it. I wish the game was much longer and allowed you to do the missions for all the characters in one playthrough, but it's not really a con in my book. The best part about this game is the interactions and relationships between the Mae, the player's character, and her friends. The dialogue is feels real and not forced, and the struggles that the characters go through are relatable and realistic. In the review from youtuber Shammy, he eloquently said that the things the characters go through receive empathy from teens and sympathy from adults. Not everyone will be able to relate to the characters or the events, but those who do will receive a much deeper experience. The way the game handled very heavy topics like depression, death, and derealization made me think the writers went through the things that the in game characters went through. As a 19 year old I instantly felt connected to each one of the characters in some way, and it made the events in the game have a much larger impact. After I finished the game I felt a big pit well up in my chest because I just wanted the story to continue, but the way the game wrapped up was satisfying. The unfortunate thing is that you only have so many days to hang out with one of your friends, Gregg or Bea(the main ones, there are more), so you end up only being able to complete one of their personal storylines. In my first [and only playthrough so far ;) ] playthrough I decided to hang out with Bea, the alligator girl. I won't spoil but her story in the game made me want to cry manly tears. I can't imagine doing Gregg's storyline right now because I will feel so guilty not being there for Bea, which is a weird feeling considering she's just a cartoon alligator. It's so crazy that the writers elicited these emotions. I believe it's because many games barely reach half these levels of character development, which makes this game stand out even more. I really don't know how to sum up my thoughts about this game, other than that you need to play it as soon as possible, because this is a very genuine game that deserves your attention.

This is a really fun zombie game. There's so many ones out there, but instead of a FPS, this one is all about group survival. You need to stock up on resources, find a safe place, earn the trust of others before bringing them home, and sleep after hours of searching. Dont get too attached to one person because you play as many, each with their own strengths and abilities and you have to use several of them to keep progressing.
The original story mode introduces gameplay elements gradually as you progress and after about 6 hours you'll have a good grasp of the game. Where it really shines for me is in the dlc each being a different game mode. Break down is open world with unlockable players, and a escalating scale of difficulty. Lifeline is like a second story mode, where you are working towards a cure.
There are some bugs and issues but this is a one of kind zombie game that I really enjoy and would love to see where it goes in the future. Definitely worth picking up.

Well finally a zombie game that is not ... brainless? You start out clueless on what is going on (you where on an isolated fishing trip with your best (dumb) buddy for 2 weeks) only to find the zombie apocalipse. You meet people, you find a home with more people, and then you basically interact FULLY with these people (you can ask someone to follow you to help out, then switch to play with that character and let the one you were previously playing do the support, or just go alone with any character - except Lilly, the "leader/radio girl" that needs to stay home handling the radio) ... and then the more you play (And level up) a character, the more TIRED THEY GET, so yes you end up having to play with other character/survivours to let each rest a little. It adds a fine realism to the game
And sure, to survive you need food, medicine, ammo, materials, fuel, and then build facilities on your home like more beds, a infirmary, maybe a garden and library? oh yeah. You get people around asking for help and you can choose to help or not (not helping can mean some survivor, either from your group or other, dying), you can make friendship with other survivours, and you can even merge with them! some guy had over 100 people at their home at one time, should be fun.
The point is, this is a closed valley, with limited supplies. Play long enough and you will start having trouble keeping your stocks up. So you have to play smart and try not to grow too much. Also, there IS an end-game event that is like the "escape" routine when you get bored with the game ... except you don't need to get bored to run it: you can do it, and the game will allow you to return to the last checkpoint before you did said mission, so you can keep playing =D
Awesome game.
Pros:
+ you can play with any character (need a little time to befriend everyone)
+ you can loose any character (perma-death, and there is no savegames to go back to!), so there is always that feeling about not wanting to loose someone, or not wanting to go out with this or that character you like so you don't put them in danger - except they can still go out on their own!
+ you really get an apocaliptic feeling, and the more you play, the more you realize time is running out because of supplies
+ nice mechanics like homes (you can move), outposts (safe spots you can make around your home to protect it, and also give you surplus resources), lots of zombie types, lots of weapon and play styles
Cons
- car handling and ladder handling is "weird", can get in the way sometimes
- your survivours keep getting in trouble so much that sometimes you are just rescuing them instead of doing something useful
- main plot COULD use a little more detail
- "rouge" like perma-death is fun and add to the feeling of danger, but it can be terrible to loose the strongest (or the one you like the most) character near the end .. I personally restarted my game 3 times because I didn't want to keep going without one of the "main" characters (there is no mandatory or main characters, but I don't like to loose Marcus or Maya, the ones you start with AND stronger ones ... alas, my first complete playthru they died anyway near the end =p)
- sometimes it's annoying how much "alone time" you expend - specially when you ask someone to come with you (costs influence) only to get that survivour booted out and auto-sent home because you entered a mission zone (main missions you MUST do alone and/or with the designated characters)
- The "end" is not an ending at all ... well, all zombie titles have the same end (a.k.a. no cure), but I would like to see something better ... I bet they are planning a full-fledged sequel.
- I never really felt the need to "look for resources". Finished my first complete playthru with all resources in "excess" and half the map unexplored o.O;

I was on the fence for a bit as to if I should purchase this. The mixed reviews made me cautious, but experience has told me that some of the worst rated games have been the most enjoying to me personally, so I've learned to ignore them (for the most part). I bring to you now a cautionary tale of my journey.
Day 1: I took the plunge and bought the game. Being a conductor for Union Pacific, I have a good idea of how railroads work. This game caught me by surprise. Everything in the game world is modeled realistically. Everything from the trains, industries, supply/demand, and even the individual people who walk on the street have a home, a work place, and a leisurely activity location.
Day 2: I made a large map with some hills using the USA DLC. I built a passenger line from San Diego to Temecula, the year is 1850. I enjoy the little steam engines and the simpler way of life. Horses moved my little village people to and fro. And I was satisfied.
Day 3: I've been up all night trying to establish a profitable passenger connection to Modesto and refine and upgrade my rail network to incorporate and support newer rolling stock and locomotives. My wife says I've been on the computer too much.
Day 7: My wife is worried, she says I haven't spoken to her in days. In more important matters, I've recently connected the San Diego oil fields with an oil production site. I've linked it's distribution to San Diego, Temecula, and Minniapolis - effectively shutting down and putting the local lumber company out of business. I feel invincible.
Day 12: I've lost my real life job. I've found that my virtual empire needs me more. The year is now 1950 and my rail empire now spans over a dozen cities with a conglamoration of rolling stock with newer as well as vintage locomotives plying the lines. I've established a second oil field in the town of Houston, which now distributes to over 7 outlying cities.
Day 21: My wife has left me and taken my 2 year old son. Now that I have some peace and quiet, I can continue my domination of the digital world. My diet now consists of purple coolaid and stockpiled beef jerky that I kept getting for christmas.
Day 30: My body is weak, I smell, I'm hungry, and the sunlight coming through the window hurts my eyes. But in other news, the year is now 2025 and there are but 2 cities left to conquer. They have remained untouched due to their inaccessible locations at high elevations. I plan to conquer them with trucks and busses and then tie them into the rail network.
Day 42: I have achieved perfection. Every road and rail network is upgraded. Every line is profitable. Every train is properly balanced.
Day 43: I've ventured out into the real world again. My body resembles that of a holocaust victim. I decided to go to Subway for a bite to eat. Standing in line, gazing at the menu, I decided to order a foot-long steak and cheese sandwich. As I sat down, I could hardly wait to bite into the sandwich. As my teeth sank into it's toasted, warm, and soft outer buns, a tear rolled down my cheek - not because I had forgotten how good real food tasted, but because I had remembered that I had forgotten to upgrade the old railroad crossing in San Diego.
11/10 I would buy this again.

I feel I should clarify that this is not a terrible game. But it is absolutely not worth £19.99.
The game seems to have a bit of an identity crisis. It's certainly not indepth enough to be a Tycoon game but what little financial aspects there are get in the way of it being train set. It's almost pretty enough to be a nice looking simulator but it still looks too much like a basic business simulator to represent any form of reality. It's almost decent enough for railway enthusiasts but what it has is often so poorly represented that any enthusiast would find it more frustrating than entertaining.
The game just doesn't know what it is. I have a very high Spec PC, so it runs fine on high-detail for me, but loading times and end of month freezes are still just a part of the game's threshold.
There's not very many locomotives and what it does have isn't always the finest choice for operation. The game feels unbalanced and often stupidly easy - because issues aren't raised on a scale of micromanagement. Unlike older, superior games such as Transport Tycoon, you don't get told if something's not turning a profit. It can just continue for years onwards. In direct contrast, the track restrictions and what you can and can't do in the game makes for a ridiculous catalogue of somewhat bizarre discrepancies. Engines won't use a two line terminus, meaning that no matter what you might try, terminii will become clogged. At junctions, engines can't use diamond crossings - the developers have added diamond crossOVERS but nothing else - and the game's attempts at being 'realistic' end up stopping any 'proper' set ups from being built. This means that trains are pretty much stuck to their own personal road. Shockingly, this isn't how railways work. Roads, not even as bridges, cannot be built over rail, and the track can only curve so far. Fair enough, it's realistic in terms of speed and groundwork, but it can't actually FUNCTION like a real, working railway - when so little of the game's surrounding content could in any way be a decent representation of a 'Transport' game, does it have any purpose? Track building is the game's only challenge.
It's bizarre that the game tries to enforce realism while kicking it for six in so many other departments.

As I write this, I am about 4 hours into the game and just finished the second of five chapters. Doing some maths tells me there are six more hours of gameplay. Color me Impressed.
I am not sure where to start, to be honest. République Remastered is a point-n-click stealth game, played entirely by guiding around a character point-n-click style while viewing the environment and rooms through various cameras installed at every corner. Imagine Watch_Dogs camera hacking system, except in good and as a full game. Perspective can be changed at any time, as long as there is another camera close by to take control of.
The stealth system works reasonably well. Enemies have a cone of sight and can hear footsteps if you are running. You can lure them away by activating telephones and speakers or disable them by means of either pepper spray or tazers which are just rare enough that you would rather save them for important bits. Doors can be hacked in order to shut enemies in - or out.
The character you control moves slow but very smooth and tries to stay in cover as long as a command allows for it.  Minus points for the missing feedback when clicking on items that can be picked up. On the upside, picking up items always triggers a verbal response from the protagonist once the item is in the inventory.
I have only played the first two chapters, but so far I have not encountered a puzzle I wasn't able to solve within a reasonable time frame. In addition, you can't lose at this game. If you get cought, you get escorted to the next interrogation room which you need to break out of in order to proceed. Interrogation rooms serve as shops to upgrade your hacking abilities as well as recharge station for your battery which is needed for hacking. Think of interrogation rooms as your classical save room - having said that, saving itself is done automatically. As you might imagine, I don't find this game very hard. Moving around undetected and solving puzzles in the meantime is just challenging enough to keep me both focused and interested.
The game was developed using the Unity 5 engine. "Uh, Unity" I can hear some of you moan already, but hold your horses for a second. This game does not look bad at all. It is not the crisp and shiny that we are used to from triple A games, but it stands it's ground. Apart from some blurry textures on close up camera shots I haven't really found a point I would like to complain about. My conclusion: Solid work.
I don't do that very often, but here is a new category for you. I think this is important enough to talk about seperately, especially in stealth and point-n-click games and République Remastered is both. The sound design is surprisingly solid. Electronic sounds for camera and hacking and computer stuff often manages to get on my nerves, but in this game it does not. They tie in very well with the game world and your actions as a player. The same can be said for the rest of the sounds. From closing doors to the sound of a guard talking into his headset, everything feels as if it is supposed to be that way.
In addition to the sound, the lighting in this game is well done. Nothing too spectecular, no big lens flares or sun sets or optic illusions. Instead, it feels as if the lights have been placed with the idea in mind to make everything look as normal and average as you would expect it to, if you were to ever walk those rooms. Again, very solid work.
Concluding this little excursion, I would say that both sound a lighting make for a great atmosphere.
The story of this game is set in a dystopian now. The protagonist girl - called "390-H" or "Hope" depending on who you ask - is trying to escape and underground building only referred to as "the facility", which seems to be her home, school and prison at the same time. You (as Hope refers to the player) are tasked with guiding her through that facility, evading the local security and making her way up to the surface. The facility is lead by a man only referred to as "overseer" or "headmaster" who, despite stating good intentions, seems to control the facility by propaganda and teaching programs, while keeping a close eye on it's inhabitants through the surveillance systems and delegating tasks to the security.
So far, the story follows an almost straight line through what I would like to call the "dystopian vally of total control". Government is oppressing people by exerting total control via propaganda and surveillance, people found resistance, protagonist finds resistence force, joins up and destroys government. Of course I can only speak for the first two chapters but the tendencies to go there are as inconspicuous as an elephant trumpeting the national hymn.
Having said that, I like Hope as a character. The game manages to make her someone that I actually want to help, and not only by scratching the forth wall like a wild animal while never breaking it fully, but also by the fact that she is struggling with almost mundane situations that most people are familiar with. Good job, République Remastered.
Now to the question at hand: Is this game worth it's money? To that I can only say "Yes, it is". Unlike most stealth games nowadays which seem to emphasize on knocking people out or stabbing them in the chest with weapons of varying effectiveness while they are busy staring at some mental image only they can see, this game came as a welcome surprise. I can't rightfully say that the idea is completely new, but it certainly is a game that I had - dare I say it - fun playing.
This is Luparax, signing out.

Republique is an interesting take on the stealth genre. It mixes some point and click sensibilities with classic stealth and puzzle elements. All presented in a polished and expertly crafted world.
In Republique, you don't control the girl exactly, rather, you're a 3rd party entity that can control the cameras in the world, as well as any other electronic device. You'll be task to guide the girl through the game, through simple point and click commands, while having the ability to hack devices to your advantage. The fact that you see through the camera's perspective makes for some interesting gameplay. Being able to jump from camera to camera, allowing you to scout ahead of the girl for potential danger is one that's pretty fresh. Couple that with the hacking abilities and that it's a point and click, Republique has some fresh and interesting ideas for the stealth genre.
Though I did find the gameplay and stealth satisfying I think it's only fair I also mention that it's was also not the most challenging stealth game I've ever played. Because the girl is controlled mostly by an AI, with you serving only as a guide to her destination, I feel that the enemy AI has been scaled back in order to compensate. The enemy AI isn't the greatest, often missing the girl sneaking right next to them. But as mentioned before, due to the way the game was designed, this is some what understandable, but does come with a cost to the game's overall challenge level. For those who are really into stealth games, this could be perceived as a negative, but for those who are new to the genre, or like easier going games, this could be considered "accessible". How you feel about this will be very subjective.
Republique features some impressive visuals, taking full advantage of Unity 5's technology, and leaning on the team's professional background. The aesthetics are wonderfully designed, with expertly crafted models and textures, and lighting that would make Hollywood jealous. There's also some great voice over work with well known actors in the game industry. Presentation wise, I have little to no complaints about Republique. It's polished, it's professional, and it has a ton of style.
There's a lot to like about Republique but it's not perfect. The story of the game, with as little spoilers as possible, is one of a dystopian setting. It has all the classic elements, oppression, unreasonable mass surveillance, the lost of personal identity, hell it even has some book burning involved. I usually am a sucker for dystopian stories but I found Republique's to be rather cliche, offering very little new to the genre. I've played through ep 1-3 (whats currently available as of this impression) and it just repeats the same tropes that every one have seen a thousand times over in other dystopian tales. Even the characters in the game are weak with out much development. The story of the game was my biggest point of contention. Not necessarily because it was bad, but because it was incredibly average. I'm hoping that the future installments of ep. 4-5 will fix this issue, though I feel 1-3 was weak from a narrative stand point.
Republique overall is a strong and interesting entry into the stealth and point and click genre. If you're a fan of either of those types of games, I think Republique is worth checking out. It offers a lot of fresh ideas, and a polished to a shine presentation. If you're looking for an original and engrossing dystopian tale, Republique may disappoint, but because of how interesting and how high quality the other elements that make up Republique, I would still recommend checking it out if you have the chance.
Pros:
- Professional quality presentation
- Unique and interesting ideas for both the point and click and stealth genre
- Accessible
Cons:
- Cliche story
- Could be considered overly forgiving in challenge

This is a very exciting and thrilling game.  The game plays out as a series and feels cinematic in every scene. The story itself is simplistic that it doesn't need the Hollywood touch to be any better.  You're not trying to overthrow a corrupt government or assassinate some dictator.  You're trying to save a scared teenage girl from having her brain washed, and save her from this underground re-education facility.
The game play is so simplistic in design and style it's brilliant.  Even the Emoticons made by the in game help.
Republique is an episodic game.  Each episode has a strong sense of fear and dread.  As well as the feeling of satisfaction when you seemingly accomplish your goal.
I love the fact that this game has a female protagonist and you play as her mute unseen helper.  Guiding her to safety and freedom.
